[PMC Copyright notice](/about/copyright/)

PMCID: PMC5371619  PMID: [28332114](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28332114/)

## Abstract

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract plays a critical role in delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and can therefore be a major determinant of performance. The incidence of GI problems in athletes participating in endurance events is high, indicating that GI function is not always optimal in those conditions. A substantial body of evidence suggests that the GI system is highly adaptable. Gastric emptying as well as stomach comfort can be “trained” and perceptions of fullness decreased; some studies have suggested that nutrient-specific increases in gastric emptying may occur. Evidence also shows that diet has an impact on the capacity of the intestine to absorb nutrients. Again, the adaptations that occur appear to be nutrient specific. For example, a high-carbohydrate diet will increase the density of sodium-dependent glucose-1 (SGLT1) transporters in the intestine as well as the activity of the transporter, allowing greater carbohydrate absorption and oxidation during exercise. It is also likely that, when such adaptations occur, the chances of developing GI distress are smaller. Future studies should include more human studies and focus on a number of areas, including the most effective methods to induce gut adaptations and the timeline of adaptations. To develop effective strategies, a better understanding of the exact mechanisms underlying these adaptations is important. It is clear that “nutritional training” can improve gastric emptying and absorption and likely reduce the chances and/or severity of GI problems, thereby improving endurance performance as well as providing a better experience for the athlete. The gut is an important organ for endurance athletes and should be trained for the conditions in which it will be required to function.

## Training the Gut

Athletes often underestimate the importance of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. The supply of exogenous fluid and carbohydrate sources can be critical to performance, especially during prolonged exercise [[1](#CR1)]. In addition, GI symptoms such as bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting are common in many sports, especially endurance sports [[2](#CR2)]. Without a well-functioning GI system, delivery of nutrients will be impaired and a range of GI symptoms may develop. Clearly, the intestinal tract is highly adaptable, and it has been suggested that targeted training of the intestinal tract may improve the delivery of nutrients during exercise while at the same time alleviating some (or all) of the symptoms [[3](#CR3)]. This training, sometimes referred to as “training the gut,” has received relatively little attention in the literature, and to the best of my knowledge there are no dedicated review articles on this topic. I provide a more detailed overview of the evidence that the GI system can adapt through nutritional training.

## Gastric Emptying and “Stomach Training”

Gastric emptying is an important step towards delivering exogenous carbohydrate and fluids to the working muscle. Anecdotally, athletes complain about drinks accumulating in the stomach and feeling bloated, especially during high-intensity [[4](#CR4)] or very prolonged exercise in hot conditions. Dehydration can contribute to this phenomenon and worsen complaints [[4](#CR4), [5](#CR5)]. Anecdotal evidence also shows that the stomach can adapt to ingesting large volumes of fluid, solids, or combinations. For example, serious contestants in eating competitions are known to “train” their stomach to hold larger volumes of food with less discomfort and—through regular training—are able to eat volumes of food within a small time window that are unthinkable for the average and untrained person. The current all-time record is 69 hot dogs (with bun) in 10 min. To achieve this, competitive eaters train using a variety of methods: chewing large pieces of chewing gum for longer periods of time or stomach extension by drinking fluids or by eating the competition foods. Volumes are progressively increased, and it takes many weeks to reach a level where these eaters can be competitive. This demonstrates the adaptability of the stomach. Conducting this “stomach training” has two main effects: (1) the stomach can extend and contain more food and (2) a full stomach is better tolerated and is not perceived as so full. Both aspects could be relevant to an exercise situation.

Current guidelines recommend fluid intakes during exercise that prevent 2% dehydration (2% of body weight). Recommended fluid intake can be substantial, especially in trained athletes and hot conditions when sweat rates are high. Such high intakes can cause discomfort and in some cases GI problems. Therefore, athletes are generally simultaneously managing GI comfort, hydration, and carbohydrate delivery. I and others have recommended training for these higher intakes to reduce discomfort and the chance of GI distress [[3](#CR3), [6](#CR6), [7](#CR7)]. However, very few studies have directly investigated such effects of “nutritional training of the stomach.”

Lambert et al. [[8](#CR8)] showed that trained runners were able to comfortably tolerate ingestion of a carbohydrate–electrolyte solution at a rate approximately equal to their sweat rate during 90 min of running at 65% maximum oxygen uptake (*V*O2max) in a ~25 °C, 30% relative humidity (RH) environment. Interestingly, they observed that stomach comfort significantly improved over time by practicing these high intakes. It must be noted that this improved comfort occurred without measurable changes in the rate of gastric emptying [[8](#CR8)]. Perhaps the stomach adapted by extending the stomach walls to allow greater space for fluid. This would likely reduce feelings of stomach discomfort and reduce the stimulus for faster gastric emptying. Training for intake of larger volumes could be an effective strategy to avoid these problems in races, particularly for athletes who experience GI discomfort even when ingesting relatively small volumes.

Studies have also demonstrated that gastric emptying of carbohydrate can be accelerated by increasing dietary intake of that carbohydrate. Cunningham et al. [[9](#CR9)] supplemented the diet of two groups of volunteers with glucose 400 g per day for 3 days. The half emptying time (*t* ½) for the glucose test meal was significantly faster after the standard diet had been supplemented with glucose compared with the standard diet alone (median 20.7 min [range 4.6–36.8] vs. 29.1 [range 19.8–38.4]). Interestingly, the gastric emptying of a protein drink was unchanged (median 18.0 min [range 12.5–23.6] vs. 16.1 [range 9.6–22.7]). The authors concluded that rapid and specific adaptation of the small intestinal regulatory mechanisms for gastric emptying of nutrient solutions can occur in response to increases in dietary load. Another study showed that supplementing a standard diet with glucose 440 g per day for 4–7 days accelerated gastric emptying of both glucose and fructose (*t* ½ 82 ± 8 vs. 106 ± 10 min for glucose and 73 ± 9 vs. 106 ± 9 min for fructose) [[10](#CR10)]. Plasma glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) concentrations were higher during the glucose-supplemented diet; thus the authors concluded that the gastric emptying of both glucose and fructose was accelerated probably as a result of reduced feedback inhibition from intestinal luminal receptors [[10](#CR10)].

One study showed that daily ingestion of fructose 120 g for 3 days accelerated gastric emptying of fructose but not of glucose [[11](#CR11)]. It appears that the relatively short duration of the dietary manipulation (3 days) was sufficient to cause adaptations in gastric emptying.

Such observations are not specific for carbohydrate. Studies have demonstrated that a higher-fat diet stimulated gastric emptying. Cunningham et al. [[12](#CR12)] demonstrated that gastric emptying of a test meal was accelerated after 7 days of a higher-fat diet (258 g/day). Reductions in *t* ½ of a test meal in response to the intervention reached significance after 14 days. Similar trends were observed after 4 days but did not reach statistical significance, suggesting that adaptations to fat in the diet may be slower than responses to carbohydrate. Castiglione et al. [[13](#CR13)] demonstrated a similar adaptation after 14 days of a high-fat diet and reported that these effects were highly specific to fats and that a carbohydrate meal was emptied at the same rate before and after a high-fat diet.

Adaptations are likely explained by desensitization of nutrient receptors and reduced feedback inhibition of gastric emptying. However, it is also possible that increased absorption results in reduced exposure of receptors to nutrients. Sections [6](#Sec16) and [7](#Sec17) provide evidence of increased absorption of nutrients in response to changes in diet.

### Stomach Training: Summary

Some studies have clearly demonstrated that specific nutritional challenges result in specific adaptations of gastric emptying to that challenge. For example, increased dietary glucose intake increases the gastric emptying of glucose but not protein, and increased fat intake results in faster gastric emptying of fats but not carbohydrate. Very few studies have specifically trained the gut to improve tolerance and gastric emptying during exercise, but the results generally look promising. Effects have been observed after 3 days of dietary manipulation.

## Intestinal Sugar Transport

Once emptied from the stomach, most fluid and sugar absorption will take place in the duodenum and jejunum. Glucose and galactose are transported across the luminal membrane of enterocytes by the sodium-dependent glucose transporter (SGLT)-1 (Fig. [1](#Fig1)).

### Fig. 1.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig1/)

Absorption of glucose and fructose. Glucose and fructose are absorbed from the intestinal lumen (on the left) through the enterocyte (luminal and basolateral membrane) into the circulation (on the right), via different pathways involving SGLT1 and GLUT5, respectively. *SGLT1* sodium-dependent glucose transporter 1, *GLUT5* glucose transporter 5 (fructose transporter), *GLUT2* glucose transporter 2

### Sodium-Dependent Glucose Transporter (SGLT)-1

Absorption of glucose (and galactose) is coupled with sodium transport and the associated electrochemical gradient. An Na/K+ ATP-ase, located at the basolateral membrane, is responsible for maintaining the electrochemical gradient. There have been suggestions that glucose transporter (GLUT)-2, another transporter, can be recruited to the luminal membrane when high concentrations of glucose are present in the lumen [[14](#CR14), [15](#CR15)]. This theory of additional facilitated glucose transport remains controversial, and SGLT1 is generally believed to be responsible for the vast majority of absorption of dietary sugars [[16](#CR16)].

In most mammalian studies, SGLT1 has been shown to be expressed on the brush border of enterocytes [[17](#CR17)–[21](#CR21)]. Expression levels are usually highest in the jejunum, followed by the duodenum and ileum [[22](#CR22)]. SGLT1 is not expressed in the large intestine [[22](#CR22)].

### Glucose Transporter (GLUT)-5

Fructose uses a different transporter (GLUT5) to glucose that is not sodium dependent and is highly specific to fructose. The regulation of GLUT5 is more rapid than the regulation of SGLT1. Changes in fructose transport are typically paralleled by similar changes in GLUT5 messenger RNA (mRNA) and protein abundance. In rats, GLUT5 mRNA doubles within 3 h after intestinal perfusion with a fructose solution [[23](#CR23)]. It must be noted that these effects have only been demonstrated at unnaturally high fructose intakes (at least 30% of energy in the diet coming from fructose, whereas a typical intake in a Western diet is around 9%).

### GLUT2

From the enterocyte to the systemic circulation, the sugars need to pass the basolateral membrane. All three monosaccharides use the bidirectional transporter GLUT2, which is also sodium independent. The capacity of GLUT2 to transport glucose across a concentration gradient is believed to be very large [[14](#CR14), [15](#CR15)].

### Other Transporters

There is little evidence for other carbohydrate transporters in addition to SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters at the luminal membrane and GLUT2 at the basolateral membrane. There have been suggestions of other transporters, but it seems that if they exist they will be relatively unimportant for transport of carbohydrates from a quantitative point of view. Since GLUT2 does not seem to be limiting, I focus primarily on SGLT1 and GLUT5.

## Carbohydrate Transporters and Glucose Transport During Exercise

Regulation of carbohydrate transport proteins is essential for the provision of glucose to the body in resting conditions. Furthermore, during exercise, when exogenous delivery of carbohydrate may be important for performance, the transporters will be responsible for glucose delivery to the working muscle. Exercise studies have provided indirect but strong evidence that the delivery of carbohydrate is limited by the transport capacity of SGLT1 (for reviews, see Jeukendrup [[1](#CR1), [6](#CR6), [7](#CR7)] and Jeukendrup and McLaughlin [[3](#CR3)]). A recent review based primarily on more direct measurements in animals also concluded that the intestine has the capacity to absorb glucose via basal levels of SGLT1 but that this capacity becomes limiting when dietary carbohydrate exceeds a certain level [[24](#CR24)].

At ingestion rates over 60–70 g of carbohydrate per h (glucose, sucrose, maltose, maltodextrin, starch), exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks around 60 g/h (Fig. [2](#Fig2)) [[1](#CR1), [3](#CR3), [6](#CR6), [7](#CR7)]. Even ingestion at 144 g/h [[25](#CR25)] or 180 g/h [[26](#CR26)] did not increase exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates much above 60 g/h. Because this limitation was not caused by gastric emptying, muscle glucose uptake, or liver glycogen storage, it was deduced that absorption had to be limiting [[27](#CR27)]. When fructose was ingested in addition to larger amounts of glucose, carbohydrate oxidation rates were elevated above 60 g/h [[28](#CR28)]. These studies strongly suggested that glucose transport across the epithelial cell was the limiting factor and that the maximal transport capacity of SGLT1 was reached [[29](#CR29)]. Because there also appears to be a dose–response relationship between carbohydrate intake and performance [[30](#CR30)–[32](#CR32)], and it is likely that a reduced capacity of the intestine in combination with a higher carbohydrate intake may result in GI distress [[2](#CR2)], the search for ways to increase the capacity to absorb carbohydrate continues.

### Fig. 2.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig2/)

Schematic of exogenous carbohydrate oxidation from a single carbohydrate (*black*) and multiple transportable carbohydrates (*blue*), based on data presented elsewhere [[3](#CR3), [7](#CR7), [51](#CR51), [52](#CR52)]. It is clear that higher oxidation rates can be achieved with multiple transportable carbohydrates, especially at high intakes. At intakes up to 60 g/h, there is no difference between single and multiple transportable carbohydrates, but when intake increases above 60 g/h and the sodium-dependent glucose transporter 1 (SGLT1) becomes saturated, added fructose will result in higher exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates. The recommended intake for single and multiple transportable carbohydrates are indicated with a *circle*. If single carbohydrate sources are ingested at rates higher than 60 g/h, gastrointestinal problems are likely. With multiple transportable carbohydrates, fewer symptoms have been observed, but “training the gut” (and getting used to high intakes) is recommended

Training the gut has been proposed as a way to increase SGLT1 transporter number and/or activity, but evidence in humans thus far is limited [[6](#CR6)].

Using a segmental perfusion technique, Shi et al. [[33](#CR33)] reported a close relationship between water absorption and solute absorption in the duodenojejunum, especially when multiple transportable substrates are present (i.e., glucose, sucrose, glycine, Na+). We confirmed this in humans during exercise: multiple transportable carbohydrates increased carbohydrate absorption and oxidation and this was associated with increased fluid absorption [[34](#CR34)]. Therefore, one other benefit of increasing the transport capacity for carbohydrate is that fluid intake is likely to also be improved (for a given carbohydrate intake). Improved fluid absorption can help prevent dehydration (and dehydration-induced reductions in performance), but more complete absorption may also reduce the chances of GI discomfort [[2](#CR2)].

To develop practical recommendations, it is important to understand the regulation of intestinal glucose transport. I therefore discuss the regulation in more detail before providing suggestions for practical implication.

## Regulation of Intestinal Glucose Transport

Regulation of glucose absorption has been shown to be directly linked to the expression of SGLT1 protein. Bob Crane proposed the existence of an Na+/glucose co-transport in 1960 at the Symposium on Membrane Transport and Metabolism in Prague [[35](#CR35)], but the actual transporter was not identified until the 1980s [[36](#CR36)]. Studies in the 1960s also observed that dietary carbohydrate intake can influence the capacity to absorb glucose [[37](#CR37)]. In 1983, it was demonstrated that intestinal transporters were upregulated and downregulated depending on dietary composition [[38](#CR38)]. At least in rats, it appears that dietary changes do not have to be extreme to observe effects on absorption, and these effects have been seen not only for sugars but also for amino acids [[38](#CR38)]. Increases in absorption have been observed in as little as 0.5 days in rats [[38](#CR38)]. It was also observed very early on that digestive enzymes were upregulated in response to dietary composition. For example, Deren et al. [[39](#CR39)] demonstrated in 1967 that rats who were fasted for 3 days displayed fourfold increases in sucrase and maltase activity in response to a sucrose diet compared with a casein diet [[39](#CR39)]. This was correlated with increases in sucrose hydrolysis and in fructose absorption.

When sugar transporters were identified in the gut in the 1980s, studies started to measure changes in SGLT1 content and activity in response to diet. A number of rodent models [[18](#CR18), [40](#CR40)] have shown that both the activity and the abundance of SGLT1 is regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. It is clear that SGLT1 protein responds to glucose concentrations in the lumen. However, SGLT1 was stimulated to the same degree when membrane-impermeable glucose analogues were used [[41](#CR41)], suggesting that a glucose sensor detects glucose or its analogues, initiating the upregulation of the SGLT1 transporters.

### Sensing Mechanism

Specialized cells (L cells and K cells) in the intestinal luminal membrane have been shown to express taste receptor cells. In particular, it has been demonstrated that T1R2 and T1R3 receptors detect sweetness. The T1R2 and T1R3 cells are coupled through a G-protein (alpha-gustducin) to a cascade of downstream cellular events that ultimately lead to upregulation of SGLT1. A more detailed discussion of the potential pathways involved is provided in the following sections.

### Sweeteners and Other Analogues

SGLT1 is upregulated in response not only to dietary carbohydrate but also to sweeteners. Margolskee et al. [[17](#CR17)] confirmed earlier findings that SGLT1 protein expression in wild-type mice receiving a diet supplemented with carbohydrate almost doubled compared with mice receiving a low-carbohydrate diet. However, SGLT1 expression also doubled when the low-carbohydrate diet was supplemented with the sweeteners sucralose, acesulfame K, or saccharine, but not when supplemented with aspartame. The observation that aspartame had no effect is not surprising because it is known that mice do not experience aspartame as sweet.

### Other Dietary Constituents that Regulate Intestinal Glucose Transport

A number of dietary constituents have been implicated in the regulation of glucose transport. Sodium chloride consumption appears to modulate intestinal glucose transport. Studies suggest that chronically elevated luminal concentrations of glucose and sodium will lead to increased expression of the SGLT1 protein [[42](#CR42)]. There are still many questions about the mechanisms and whether the effects of sodium and glucose are additive [[43](#CR43)].

Dietary fiber is another constituent with potential effects, but studies have been inconclusive: some studies show a decrease, some show no change, and some show an increase in intestinal glucose transport with increasing dietary fiber intake [[43](#CR43)]. Fiber is a broad term used to describe vastly different characteristics, and fiber can have effects on gastric emptying, motility, and the composition and structure of the intestinal tract. Therefore, it may not be surprising that results of studies have been inconclusive.

To the best of my knowledge, no studies in humans have investigated the effects of dietary constituents on intestinal glucose absorption. Therefore, developing firm guidelines in the absence of these findings would be premature.

### Molecular Mechanisms

SGLT1 protein is upregulated in response to a number of stimuli, including but not limited to glucose and galactose: 3-*O*-methylglucose (non-metabolizable substrate of SGLT1) and fructose (not a substrate of SGLT1). Upregulation of the SGLT1 protein depends on the availability of these sugars, but metabolism of these sugars is not necessary. The fact that SGLT1 expression responds to glucose analogues and sugars not transported by SGLT1 suggests there is a separate receptor that detects these glucose analogues.

Studies have suggested that the sugar-mediated upregulation of SGLT1 is likely to involve a G-protein-coupled second messenger pathway [[41](#CR41), [44](#CR44)] (Fig. [3](#Fig3)). More recently, it was demonstrated in mice that T1R3 and gustducin are expressed in enteroendocrine cells and are required for the expression of SGLT1 in vivo in response to luminal sugars or sweeteners [[17](#CR17)]. SGLT1, on the other hand, is expressed in enterocytes (Fig. [3](#Fig3)). This means that a signaling event must take place between chemosensory enteroendocrine cells and absorptive enterocytes. It is known that enteroendocrine cells can secrete endocrine hormones such as cholecystokinin (CCK), peptide tyrosine tyrosine (PYY), neurotensin, glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1, GLP-2, and GIP. The incretins GLP-1 and GIP are secreted in response to dietary sugars and influence glucose transport, metabolism, and homeostasis. Shirazi-Beechey et al. [[24](#CR24)] described a possible pathway of regulation. Sweet receptors T1R2 + T1R3, expressed on the luminal membrane of villus endocrine cells, sense the luminal concentration of glucose. When this glucose concentration reaches a threshold, it activates a signaling cascade in endocrine cells that involves T1R2 + T1R3 receptors, gustducin and other signaling elements. This will result in the secretion of GLP-1, GLP-2, and GIP. The binding of GLP-2 to its receptor on enteric neurons elicits an action potential. This stimulus is transmitted to sub-epithelial regions by axonal projections. This will evoke the release of a neuropeptide in the absorptive enterocytes. The binding of this neuropeptide to its receptor results in increased intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) concentrations, thereby increasing the stability of mRNA of SGLT1 and increasing the SGLT1 protein concentration.

#### Fig. 3.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig3/)

A proposed mechanism for upregulation of sodium-dependent glucose transporter 1 (SGLT1) protein. GIP has been shown to directly regulate SGLT1 and enhance absorption in the mouse jejunum. In turn, increased glucose absorption also has an effect on GIP secretion [[45](#CR45)]. Recent studies have demonstrated that a GIP receptor knockout had marked effects on SGLT1 expression, suggesting that GIP plays an important role in the upregulation of SGLT1 [[46](#CR46)].

Several aspects of this mechanism remain untested, and some aspects have been disputed [[16](#CR16)], but it is clear that somehow luminal glucose is sensed and—through a signaling cascade—SGLT1 function protein levels increase.

### Time Course

In mice, intestinal SGLT1 protein in brush–border membrane vesicles in the mid small intestine increased 1.9-fold after 2 weeks of a high-carbohydrate diet [[17](#CR17)]. In a study of horses, which are believed to be slow adapters to an increase in carbohydrate, SGLT1 protein expression from intestinal biopsies was increased after just 1 week of high-carbohydrate feeding, and the abundance increased further after 1 and 2 months on the diet. Piglets who received a higher-carbohydrate diet for 3 days showed increases of SGLT1 protein as well as glucose absorption [[47](#CR47)].

Although no direct human studies exist, a large number of animal studies suggest that the time course of changes in SGLT1 expression is relatively rapid. Several studies have observed significant changes after only a few days of dietary change [[17](#CR17)]. It seems therefore reasonable to suggest that several days of a high-carbohydrate intake can increase SGLT1 content and the capacity to absorb glucose, but more prolonged exposure to the diet could result in greater adaptations.

## Regulation of Absorption in Athletes

An elegant study by Cox et al. [[48](#CR48)] gives us the most important clues today that diet manipulation can result in improved delivery of carbohydrate during exercise. In this study, 16 endurance-trained cyclists were divided into a high-carbohydrate and a control group. For 28 days, both groups trained (16 h/week) and their performance improved as a result of this training. Both groups received a diet with a moderate carbohydrate content (5 g/kg/day). The high-carbohydrate group were supplemented with an additional 1.5 g/kg per hour of exercise performed daily. The carbohydrate supplement was provided mainly in the form of a glucose drink. In addition, they received carbohydrate-rich foods to meet the hourly demands of exercise. The control group also received a nutritional supplement, but this was composed of fat- and protein-rich foods with limited carbohydrate content. Subjects in the high-carbohydrate groups consumed the supplements before, during, and immediately after exercise. The cyclists in the control group consumed their supplement after exercise. On average, the carbohydrate-supplemented group had a high daily carbohydrate intake of 8.5 g/kg, whereas the control groups consumed 5.3 g/kg/day.

Before and after the 28-day training period, all subjects performed an exercise trial in which they received a 10% carbohydrate solution. Isotopic tracers were used to measure the oxidation of the exogenous carbohydrate. It was observed that exogenous carbohydrate oxidation was improved after the carbohydrate-supplemented diet. The most likely explanation is an increase in the ability to absorb carbohydrate as a result of an upregulation of SGLT1 transporters. It was concluded that, for athletes who compete in endurance events, where exogenous carbohydrate is an important energy source and there is ample opportunity to ingest carbohydrate, this higher carbohydrate intake approach may be beneficial [[6](#CR6), [7](#CR7), [48](#CR48)].

It has become clear that an increase in dietary carbohydrate intake can increase the abundance and activity of intestinal SGLT1 transporters and that this results in an improved capacity to absorb carbohydrate. The reverse may also be true. With carbohydrate restriction through reducing carbohydrate intake, high-fat, or even ketogenic diets, or by reducing total energy intake, the daily carbohydrate intake can become very low. Studies in lambs have demonstrated that, as the diet changes from milk to grass, so the rumen, where dietary carbohydrates are fermented into volatile fatty acids, develops. Rumen formation effectively prevents the delivery of monosaccharides to the intestine. As a result, there is a marked decrease in both the SGLT1 protein content of the intestine as well as the capacity of the small intestine to absorb carbohydrate [[49](#CR49), [50](#CR50)].

## Gastrointestinal Problems

GI problems are very common amongst athletes, and 30–50% of all athletes experience such problems regularly [[2](#CR2)]. The causes are still largely unknown but appear to be partly genetically determined and highly individual [[2](#CR2)]. The mechanisms are likely to be different for upper and lower GI problems. The symptoms are more likely to occur and are exacerbated by hot weather conditions and dehydration [[2](#CR2)].

Although a link with nutrition intake is not always found, certain practices have been found to correlate with the incidence of GI problems: fiber intake, fat intake, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions seem to increase the prevalence of GI problems.

There are probably several reasons for these problems, but two important and common reasons may be a bloated feeling and reduced gastric emptying during prolonged exercise, and diarrhea as a result of osmotic shifts.

It is thought that training the gut may alleviate some of these symptoms, perhaps by improving gastric emptying and the perception of fullness (reduced bloating), improving tolerance of larger volumes, and increasing the speed of absorption, causing less residual volume and smaller osmotic shifts [[2](#CR2)].

## Practical Implications and Conclusions

A summary of practical implications is depicted in Fig. [4](#Fig4). While some extrapolations from animal studies are required, it is likely that adaptations in the human intestine are as rapid as those seen in other mammals. This means that several days and certainly 2 weeks of a high-carbohydrate diet would result in significant increases in the SGLT1 content of the intestinal lumen. Based on animal data, an increase in dietary carbohydrate from 40 to 70% could result in a doubling of SGLT1 transporters over a period of 2 weeks.

### Fig. 4.

[Open in a new tab](figure/Fig4/)

A summary of methods to “train the gut”, the adaptations that may occur in the gut, and implications for performance

In addition to an increased absorptive capacity, it is essential that higher carbohydrate intakes can be tolerated and are also emptied from the stomach. Although it is generally believed that gastric emptying is not a limiting factor, it is likely that a combination of factors (for example, heat, high carbohydrate intake, and high-intensity exercise, which are all factors known to inhibit gastric emptying) will act together, thereby compromising gastric emptying. Therefore, it is important to practice a race nutritional strategy in training and get used to higher volumes of intake or higher carbohydrate intakes.

Most athletes consume a moderate- to high-carbohydrate diet, and it could therefore be argued that the benefits of increasing carbohydrate intake even more may only be small. At present, the link between daily carbohydrate intake and the transport capacity for glucose in the human intestine is uncertain. Perhaps the fact that we have seen little variation in the maximum exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates in many years of research involving hundreds of participants is a sign that diet has relatively small effects on the maximal carbohydrate transport capacity of the gut. The fact that transport capacity has hardly ever exceeded 60 g/h, even in individuals, may be a sign that improvements may not be dramatic. On the other hand, research such as the study by Cox et al. [[48](#CR48)] suggests that these transporters can be upregulated in a relatively short period of time.

Although the exact magnitude of effects in athletes who are already consuming a high-carbohydrate diet may be uncertain, it seems fair to conclude that those athletes who are not practicing a high-carbohydrate diet can benefit substantially. When athletes are carbohydrate restricting; following a low-carbohydrate, high-fat, or ketogenic diet; or are reducing energy intake to lose weight, the reduced daily carbohydrate load will likely reduce the capacity to absorb carbohydrates during competition. This could be a reason why these athletes anecdotally seem to report more GI problems. These athletes would be advised to include some high-carbohydrate days in their training.

Current guidelines recommend a carbohydrate intake up to about 60 g for exercise lasting for up to 2 h. When the exercise lasts ≥2 h, slightly greater amounts of carbohydrate (90 g/h) would be recommended, and these carbohydrates should consist of a mix of multiple transportable carbohydrates, e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose. To obtain a carbohydrate intake of 90 g/h, athletes could “mix and match” to fulfil their personal preferences and take into account their tolerance [[6](#CR6), [7](#CR7)]. Since the gut is so adaptable, it seems wise to include training with high-carbohydrate intake into the weekly routine and regularly ingest carbohydrate during exercise. With these strategies, the gut may be trained to absorb and oxidize more carbohydrate, which in turn should result in less GI distress and better performance.

This is a scientific review article by Asker E. Jeukendrup (Loughborough University) published in Sports Medicine (2017, Vol 47, Suppl 1, pp. 101-110, DOI: 10.1007/s40279-017-0690-6, PMCID: PMC5371619, PMID: 28332114) on "Training the Gut for Athletes." The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License and was published in a supplement supported by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI).

The paper argues that the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is highly adaptable and can be "trained" through nutritional strategies to improve endurance performance. Key points include:

1. GASTRIC EMPTYING/STOMACH TRAINING: Gastric emptying and stomach comfort can be trained. Studies show nutrient-specific adaptations—increased dietary glucose accelerates gastric emptying of glucose but not protein; higher-fat diets accelerate emptying of fats but not carbohydrates. Effects can occur in as little as 3 days of dietary manipulation. Anecdotal evidence from competitive eaters (e.g., 69 hot dogs in 10 minutes record) demonstrates stomach adaptability. Lambert et al. showed trained runners could comfortably tolerate carbohydrate-electrolyte solution at sweat-rate intake during 90 min running, with improved stomach comfort over time without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate.

2. INTESTINAL SUGAR TRANSPORT: Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent glucose transporter (SGLT1), while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides cross the basolateral membrane via GLUT2. SGLT1 expression is highest in the jejunum. Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks around 60 g/h even at ingestion rates of 144-180 g/h, indicating SGLT1 transport capacity is the limiting factor. Combining glucose and fructose (multiple transportable carbohydrates) can elevate oxidation above 60 g/h.

3. REGULATION OF SGLT1: Dietary carbohydrate intake upregulates SGLT1 transporter density and activity. A high-carbohydrate diet increases SGLT1 expression. The sensing mechanism involves sweet taste receptors T1R2+T1R3 on enteroendocrine cells, coupled via alpha-gustducin, leading to secretion of GLP-1, GLP-2, and GIP, which ultimately increase SGLT1 protein via a cAMP-mediated pathway. Sweeteners (sucralose, acesulfame K, saccharine) also upregulate SGLT1, while aspartame does not (mice don't taste it as sweet). Time course is rapid: increases seen in 3 days in piglets, 1 week in horses, 1.9-fold increase after 2 weeks of high-carbohydrate diet in mice. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over 2 weeks based on animal data.

4. KEY HUMAN STUDY: Cox et al. (2015) studied 16 endurance-trained cyclists over 28 days. The high-carbohydrate group (8.5 g/kg/day) showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation during exercise trials compared to controls (5.3 g/kg/day), likely due to SGLT1 upregulation.

5. GI PROBLEMS: 30-50% of all athletes experience GI problems regularly. Fiber intake, fat intake, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions increase prevalence. Hot weather and dehydration exacerbate symptoms. Training the gut may alleviate symptoms by improving gastric emptying, reducing bloating, and increasing absorption speed.

6. PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: Current guidelines recommend carbohydrate intake up to ~60 g/h for exercise up to 2 hours, and ~90 g/h (using multiple transportable carbohydrates like glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose) for exercise ≥2 hours. Athletes should practice race nutrition strategies in training, get used to higher intake volumes, and include high-carbohydrate days in training—especially those on low-carbohydrate, high-fat, or ketogenic diets who may have reduced absorptive capacity. The exact magnitude of benefit for athletes already on high-carbohydrate diets is uncertain, but those not practicing high-carbohydrate intake can benefit substantially.

--- SOURCE 1: Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The article was authored by Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, and Carola Severi (from the Gastroenterology Department, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy) and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan, Italy). It was submitted July 26, 2023, revised August 30, 2023, accepted September 12, 2023, and published September 19, 2023. The article has been cited 26 times and has 61,433 views.

**Key Content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition caused by strenuous exercise that affects up to 70% of athletes, manifesting as upper-GI symptoms (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower-GI symptoms (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two primary pathways are identified:
1. **Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway**: Increased sympathetic activation reduces overall GI functional capacity. Physical activity alters gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and neurotransmitters (catecholamines, serotonin). Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max represents the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. **Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway**: Blood redistribution during exercise depletes splanchnic blood flow by up to 80%, causing intestinal hypoperfusion, epithelial damage, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Elevated I-FABP levels indicate intestinal epithelial damage. Heat stress and dehydration exacerbate these effects.

**GI Symptoms Prevalence:** An estimated 30-90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms during exercise. Upper-GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn prevalence is 15-20% in runners. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Lower-GI symptoms can reach 30% in recreational runs, 50% in cyclists, and 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) occurs in 18% of recreational run competitors. IBS is underdiagnosed in endurance athletes (9.8% overall prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed). Female athletes and younger athletes report more GI symptoms.

**Nutritional Management:** The review specifically explores gluten-free diet and low-FODMAP diet strategies for managing Ex-GIS, noting that symptoms resemble IBS (defined by Rome IV Criteria) and respond to similar nutritional approaches. Additional strategies include managing dehydration, environmental temperature, exercise modality, and behavioral interventions.

**Methods:** The authors searched PubMed, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases (up to March 2023), identifying 142 research articles for inclusion based on established criteria.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed case-series study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (2025, Vol. 4, pp. 337-354) by Rachel Scrivin, Gary Slater, and Ricardo J.S. Costa (DOI: 10.1123/ijsnem.2024-0133). The study evaluates a four-phase management approach for exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) in endurance athletes using a high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP therapeutic intervention.

METHODOLOGY: The case series implemented the GastroAxEx assessment protocol with 9 recreational-to-elite endurance athletes who experienced recurrent severe Ex-GIS and 2 controls without symptoms. The four-phase approach included: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic interventions including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of interventions.

KEY RESULTS:
- Most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2-4% body mass loss
- 8/9 athletes consumed <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate during GastroAxEx
- 4/9 athletes reported severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) during exercise; 8/9 reported severe Ex-GIS during recovery
- All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery
- Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes
- 8/9 athletes successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to their targeted events
- The intervention improved intake tolerance, reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS, and improved perceived work output during targeted events

CONCLUSION: A 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate Ex-GIS. The study has been cited 3 times and is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science, with 40 references in the bibliography.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Endurance Exercise and Your Gut: Strategies to Outrun the Runs ---
URL: https://blog.nasm.org/fitness/endurance-exercise-gut-strategies-outrun-runs-gi-complaints

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Endurance Exercise and Your Gut: Strategies to Outrun the Runs and other GI Complaints

This article by Dr. Geoff Lecovin, published on the NASM (National Academy of Sports Medicine) blog, addresses adverse gastrointestinal (GI) complaints—such as cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea—that affect up to 90% of endurance athletes. These symptoms can negatively impact performance and, in some cases, lead to long-term health consequences.

### Causes of Exercise-Induced GI Complaints
The article identifies several multifactorial causes:

1. **Decreased GI Perfusion (Hypoperfusion):** Strenuous exercise triggers catecholamine release from the sympathetic nervous system, causing splanchnic vasoconstriction while shunting blood to the heart, lungs, muscles, and skin. This can lead to gut mucosal ischemia, increased mucosal permeability, and symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.

2. **Changes in Motility:** Heavy exercise can decrease peristalsis, reduce lower esophageal sphincter tone, and increase transient lower sphincter relaxation, linked to gastroesophageal reflux and impaired gastric emptying.

3. **Absorption and Gut Permeability:** High-intensity exercise compromises intestinal blood flow, leading to increased intestinal permeability, gut damage, impaired gut function, decreased nutrient absorption, and potentially a dysbiotic microbacterial environment with pathogenic bacteria and endotoxins entering the bloodstream.

4. **Mechanical Causes:** Repetitive high-impact mechanics and postures (common in runners and cyclists) can damage the intestinal lining. Poor posture, increased abdominal pressure, and aerophagia (swallowing air while drinking from water bottles) contribute to GI symptoms like flatulence, diarrhea, and urgency.

5. **Nutritional Causes:** Fiber, fat, protein, and fructose can cause GI symptoms. Concentrated carbohydrate solutions (beverages with high osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying. Beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose and fructose combined) reduce the likelihood of GI symptoms.

6. **NSAIDs:** Use of anti-inflammatory medications is associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction.

7. **Hyperthermia:** Heat exposure during exercise leads to intestinal ischemia from blood shunting; heat acclimatization and optimal hydration can help mitigate these effects.

8. **Dehydration:** Blood flow to the gut and liver can be reduced by up to 80% during exercise, adversely affecting nutrient absorption, motility, and mucosal integrity. GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume.

### Training the Gut
Conditioning the gut through practice can help athletes become more accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise, improving nutrient absorption and tolerance.

### Practical Guidelines for Athletes
- Avoid high-fiber foods on competition day and for several days leading up to the event
- Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities (e.g., dairy, gluten)
- Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol)
- Avoid NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen
- Avoid high-fructose foods; a fructose-glucose combination may be better tolerated
- Avoid dehydration—prevention is key
- Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water
- Choose carbohydrate drinks with lower concentrations to prevent high osmolalities in the stomach
- Practice new nutrition strategies before race day

The article includes extensive scientific references (De Oliveira et al. 2014, van Wijck et al. 2012, Gisolfi 2000, Lambert 2004, Murray 2006, and others) and is authored by Dr. Geoff Lecovin, a chiropractor, naturopathic physician, and acupuncturist with advanced degrees in nutrition and exercise science and multiple certifications including NASM CPT, CES, PES, and Nutrition Coach.
</summary>

"Adverse gastrointestinal (GI) complaints, such as cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are common problems faced by up to 90% of endurance athletes."

--- SOURCE 4: Nutritional Recommendations To Avoid Gastrointestinal Distress During Exercise - Gatorade Sports Science Institute ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/sse-114-nutritional-recommendations-to-avoid-gastrointestinal-distress-during-exercise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #114 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published in May 2013 and authored by Erick Prado de Oliveira. The article provides nutritional recommendations to avoid gastrointestinal (GI) distress during exercise, particularly for endurance athletes.

**Key Statistics on GI Problems in Athletes:**
- 30% to 90% of distance runners experience exercise-related intestinal problems, depending on methodology and events studied
- In exhausting endurance events, 30-50% of participants suffer from one or more GI symptoms (Brouns & Beckers, 1993)
- Up to 93% of long-distance triathletes in extreme conditions reported any GI symptom; 43% reported serious GI problems and 7% abandoned the race due to GI issues (Jeukendrup et al., 2000)
- 70% of elite endurance athletes reported exercise-induced GI symptoms (Peters et al., 1999)
- In an internet-based study of 1,281 athletes, 45% reported at least one GI symptom (Ter Steege et al., 2008)
- Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon running/cycling up to 32% in Ironman races (Pfeiffer et al., 2011)
- Athletes not accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise had a two-fold risk of GI symptoms compared to accustomed athletes

**Causes of GI Problems:**
1. **Splanchnic hypoperfusion** - During maximal exercise, splanchnic blood flow may be reduced by up to 80% to supply working muscle and skin. Norepinephrine release induces splanchnic vasoconstriction, which can lead to gut mucosal ischemia and increased mucosal permeability.
2. **Changes in motility** - Decreased esophageal peristalsis and lower esophageal sphincter tone, increased transient sphincter relaxation, and altered gastric emptying (mainly at high exercise intensities).
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** - Studies show increased intestinal permeability after marathons, though effects are inconclusive at moderate intensities. Symptomatic runners showed greater permeability than asymptomatic runners.
4. **Mechanical causes** - Repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut; symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists. Posture (e.g., "aero" position on bicycles) and swallowing air can contribute.
5. **Nutritional causes** - Fiber, fat, protein, fructose, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>500 mOsm/L osmolality) are associated with increased GI symptoms. Dairy products and mild lactose intolerance can cause problems.

**Prevention Guidelines:**
- **Avoid milk products** containing lactose (use lactose-free, soy, rice, or almond milk alternatives)
- **Avoid high-fiber foods** in the day(s) before competition; choose processed white foods (regular pasta, white rice, plain bagels) instead of whole grains
- **Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen) as they increase intestinal permeability; NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI complications
- **Avoid high-fructose foods** and exclusively-fructose drinks (though fructose with glucose may be better tolerated)
- **Avoid dehydration**; start races well hydrated
- **Practice new nutrition strategies** by experimenting with pre-race and race-day plans many times before race day
- **"Train the gut"** - A study by Cox et al. (2010) showed that 28 days of high-carbohydrate training improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates, attributed to improved intestinal absorption

**Serious Symptoms:** Mucosal erosions, ischemic colitis, blood loss in feces, hemorrhagic gastritis, and small bowel infarction have been reported in endurance athletes, occasionally requiring surgery.

The article concludes that GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and that nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"More marathons are won or lost in the portable toilets than at the dinner table." - Bill Rodgers, marathon legend with four victories in both the Boston and New York City Marathons in the late 1970s.

--- SOURCE 5: Frontiers | Gastrointestinal Assessment and Therapeutic Intervention for the Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Case Series Translational and Professional Practice Approach ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2021.719142/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Physiology (Vol 12, 07 September 2021, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2021.719142) by Stephanie K. Gaskell, Christopher E. Rauch, and Ricardo J. S. Costa from the Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food at Monash University (Melbourne, Australia). The study presents a translational research case series implementing a four-phase gastrointestinal assessment protocol during exercise (GastroAxEx) to inform individualized therapeutic interventions for endurance athletes affected by exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS) and associated gastrointestinal symptoms (GIS).

**Methodology (Four-Phase Approach):**
- Phase 1: Clinical assessment exploring background history of exercise-associated GIS
- Phase 2: Individual tailored GastroAxEx laboratory simulation mirroring exercise stress
- Phase 3: Individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes
- Phase 4: Monitoring and readjustment based on field testing under training and race conditions

**Study Population:** Nine endurance athletes (recreational to elite level) with EIGS and two control athletes without EIGS completed Phase 2. Most common reported GIS was nausea and vomiting (n=8/9) that negatively influenced feeding tolerance. All cases (n=9/9) resulted in reduced event workload, with majority withdrawing from competition (n=5/9). Rapid onset of GIS commonly occurred later in exercise (≥3 h).

**Key Results:**
- Two athletes experienced significant thermoregulatory strain (peak core temperature >40°C)
- Plasma cortisol increased substantially pre- to post-exercise in n=6/7 (Δ >500 nmol/L)
- Plasma I-FABP (marker of enterocyte injury) increased substantially in n=2/8 (Δ >1,000 pg/ml)
- No substantial change in systemic endotoxin and inflammatory profiles in all athletes
- Breath H2 testing showed orocecal transit time (OCTT) was delayed in n=5/9 (90–150 min post-exercise), with n=4/9 showing no H2 turning point by 180 min (indicative of suspected exercise-associated gastroparesis and/or paralytic ileus)
- Severe GIS during exercise experienced by n=5/9, with n=2/9 having to dramatically reduce work output or cease exercise
- All athletes (n=9/9) were identified as having the neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway of EIGS as the proposed causal factor

**Interventions (Phase 3):** All 9/9 athletes implemented lead-in diet, gut training, exogenous fuel provision, hydration provision, thermoregulation/heat acclimation/cooling strategies, and pre-exercise management. Additional interventions included pharmacotherapy (ondansetron prescription, n=7/9), fat oxidation adaptation training (n=3/9), and pacing strategies (n=2/9).

**Outcomes:** After intervention, n=8/9 reported improvements in GIS during exercise. Only n=1/9 reported withdrawal from competition due to similar pre-intervention GIS (versus n=8/9 previously). N=7/9 completed training and competition with minimal GIS. N=8/9 reported improved feeding tolerance.

**Conclusions:** GIS during exercise in endurance athletes are predominantly related to gastrointestinal functional and feeding tolerance issues (neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway), not necessarily gastrointestinal integrity and/or systemic issues (circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway). GastroAxEx allows informed identification of potential causal pathways and exacerbation factors at an individual level, providing a valuable individualized therapeutic intervention approach. The study emphasizes there is no "one-size-fits-all" approach due to the multifactorial nature of EIGS and the large individual variation in responses.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion results in gut dysfunction in healthy men - Maastricht University ---
URL: https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/exercise-induced-splanchnic-hypoperfusion-results-in-gut-dysfunct

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Maastricht University research publication record (CRIS) for a peer-reviewed scientific article titled "Exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion results in gut dysfunction in healthy men," published in PLOS ONE on July 21, 2011 (Volume 6, Issue 7, Article 22366, DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0022366).

**Authors:** K. van Wijck (corresponding author), K. Lenaerts, L.J.C. van Loon, W.H. Peters, W.A. Buurman, and C.H.C. Dejong, affiliated with the Departments of Surgery and Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University.

**Study Background & Methods:** Splanchnic hypoperfusion (reduced blood flow to abdominal organs) is common in various pathophysiological conditions and is thought to lead to gut dysfunction. This study examined the effects of exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion on the gut in healthy men. Healthy male participants cycled for 60 minutes at 70% of maximum workload capacity. Splanchnic hypoperfusion was measured using gastric tonometry. Blood samples taken every 10 minutes were analyzed for enterocyte damage markers (intestinal fatty acid binding protein, I-FABP, and ileal bile acid binding protein, I-BABP). Intestinal permeability changes were assessed using sugar probes, and liver and renal parameters were also evaluated.

**Key Results:**
- Splanchnic perfusion rapidly decreased during exercise, as shown by increased gap(g-a)pCO₂ from -0.85±0.15 to 0.85±0.42 kPa (p<0.001).
- Plasma I-FABP increased from 309±46 to 615±118 pg/ml (p<0.001).
- Plasma I-BABP increased from 5.06±1.27 to 14.30±2.20 ng/ml (p<0.001).
- Hypoperfusion correlated significantly with small intestinal damage (r(S) = 0.59; p<0.001).
- Small intestinal permeability increased after exercise (p<0.001) and correlated with intestinal injury (r(S) = 0.50; p<0.001).
- Liver parameters were elevated, but renal parameters were not.

**Conclusions:** Exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion results in quantifiable small intestinal injury. The extent of intestinal injury correlates with transiently increased small intestinal permeability, indicating gut barrier dysfunction in healthy individuals. These findings enhance understanding of splanchnic hypoperfusion sequelae and may help in understanding and preventing these phenomena in patients.

**Additional details:** The article is published under a CC BY license, has 9 pages, and the publication is listed under keywords including GLUTATHIONE-S-TRANSFERASE, LONG-DISTANCE RUNNERS, CHRONIC HEART-FAILURE, BLOOD-FLOW, GASTROINTESTINAL COMPLICATIONS, ABDOMINAL-SURGERY, INTRAGASTRIC PCO2, INFLAMMATION, ISCHEMIA, and DISEASE. The page records 255 downloads from Pure.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific study by Jamie N. Pugh and colleagues from Liverpool John Moores University (UK) and Royal Cornwall Hospital (Truro, UK), published in a sports medicine journal, examining the acute effects of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) running on gastrointestinal (GI) damage and permeability markers, alongside subjective GI discomfort symptoms.

**Study Design and Methods:**
- Eleven trained male runners (VO2max 60.0 ± 3.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, mean age 33.1 years, body mass 75.1 kg) completed the study. Inclusion required a minimum 10km race time of 39 minutes and at least 5 training sessions per week. Exclusions included medication use, history of GI disease (e.g., IBS), or abdominal surgery.
- A repeated measures counter-balanced design was used: participants completed a HIIT trial and a resting control trial, separated by at least 7 days.
- The HIIT protocol consisted of 18 × 400m interval runs at 120% VO2max (divided into 3 sets of 6 runs with 3 minutes of complete rest between sets), with recovery running at 50% VO2max.
- GI permeability was assessed using sugar probes (5g lactulose, 2g rhamnose, 1g sucrose, 0.5g D-xylose), measured in both serum and urine at 120 minutes post-baseline. Intestinal damage was measured via plasma I-FABP (intestinal fatty acid binding protein) using ELISA.
- GI symptoms were assessed using a modified Likert scale and a detailed questionnaire (adapted from Pfeiffer et al.), scored during exercise and at 24 hours post-activity.

**Key Results:**
1. **Serum permeability markers increased:** Serum lactulose:rhamnose (L:R) ratio was 59% higher after HIIT vs. rest (0.051 ± 0.016 vs. 0.031 ± 0.021, p = 0.0047), and serum sucrose recovery was significantly higher (0.388 ± 0.217% vs. 0.137 ± 0.148%, p < 0.001).
2. **Urinary markers showed no difference:** Urinary L:R (0.032 vs. 0.030, p = 0.3) and urinary sucrose (0.169% vs. 0.123%, p = 0.54) did not differ between conditions—demonstrating that serum sampling detects changes in GI permeability over a 2-hour period that urinary sampling cannot.
3. **I-FABP increased:** Plasma I-FABP rose 72% during HIIT (from 481 ± 334 pg/mL at baseline to a peak of 829 ± 448 pg/mL immediately post-exercise, p < 0.001), with no change during rest.
4. **GI symptoms were mild but increased:** Global peak GI symptoms were higher during HIIT vs. rest (3.0 ± 2.5 vs. 0.3 ± 0.5, p < 0.01). Specific symptoms significantly increased during HIIT included bloating, urge to burp, and flatulence; at 24 hours, bloating, flatulence, and stomach cramps were higher. However, all symptom scores were low-to-mild (median < 4), and **none of the GI symptoms correlated with markers of GI permeability or I-FABP.**

**Conclusions:**
- This is the first study to report that acute HIIT running increases markers of GI permeability (L:R and sucrose) and small intestinal injury (I-FABP) in trained male runners.
- The increases in GI damage markers did not correlate with GI discomfort symptoms, which remained low to mild—consistent with other laboratory-based studies that show increased intestinal damage without corresponding symptom severity.
- Serum sampling proved more time-efficient (detecting changes within 2 hours) than traditional 5-hour urinary collection methods for assessing GI permeability, which may be advantageous for future research with elite athletes.

**Study Limitations (acknowledged by authors):**
- No workload-matched steady-state exercise control condition.
- No female participants (despite GI symptoms being more prevalent in female athletes).
- Splanchnic hypoperfusion (the hypothesized primary mechanism) was not directly measured due to technical difficulties during high-intensity running.
- Large day-to-day variation in I-FABP baselines was observed within participants.

The study was approved by the Liverpool John Moores University Ethics Committee and received funding in part from Aliment Nutrition™.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We report for the first time, that in a group of trained male runners, acute HIIT increased markers of gastrointestinal permeability (both L:R and sucrose) and small intestinal injury (I-FABP). Runners also reported acute symptoms of GI discomfort (bloating, urge to burp, stomach cramps and flatulence) during and in the 24 h post exercise, although these markers of discomfort did not correlate with measures of GI permeability or damage."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Exercise-Induced Splanchnic Hypoperfusion Results in Gut Dysfunction in Healthy Men ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3141050

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in PLoS One (July 21, 2011; doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0022366; PMID: 21811592) titled "Exercise-Induced Splanchnic Hypoperfusion Results in Gut Dysfunction in Healthy Men" by Kim van Wijck and colleagues from Top Institute Food and Nutrition (Wageningen), NUTRIM School (Maastricht), Maastricht University Medical Center, and Radboud University Nijmegen Medical Center, Netherlands.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Twenty healthy male volunteers (mean age 23.6±0.7 years, BMI 21.0±0.4 kg/m²) cycled for 60 minutes at 70% of maximum workload capacity. Splanchnic hypoperfusion was assessed using gastric tonometry (gap g-a pCO₂). Blood was sampled every 10 minutes and analyzed for enterocyte damage markers (intestinal fatty acid binding protein [I-FABP] and ileal bile acid binding protein [I-BABP]). Intestinal permeability was assessed using sugar probes (lactulose/L-rhamnose ratio) analyzed in both urine and plasma via a novel HPLC/MS approach. Liver parameters (L-FABP, ALT, AST, alpha-GST), renal parameters (NAG), and inflammatory markers (MPO, calprotectin) were also measured.

KEY RESULTS:
1. Splanchnic hypoperfusion occurred rapidly during exercise: gap g-a pCO₂ increased from -0.85±0.15 to 0.85±0.42 kPa (p<0.001), with the most pronounced change in the first 10 minutes. Perfusion recovered to baseline within 1 hour post-exercise.
2. Small intestinal damage was confirmed: plasma I-FABP increased from 309±46 to 615±118 pg/ml (p<0.001), and I-BABP increased from 5.06±1.27 to 14.3±2.20 ng/ml (p<0.001), indicating both jejunal and ileal enterocyte damage.
3. Hypoperfusion correlated significantly with intestinal damage (Spearman r=0.59; p<0.001, with a 20-minute time lag).
4. Small intestinal permeability increased after exercise (p<0.001, detected via plasma analysis), and correlated with intestinal injury (r=0.50; p<0.001). Large intestinal permeability remained unchanged. No significant endotoxemia or bacterial translocation was detected.
5. Liver parameters were elevated: L-FABP (4.75±0.30 to 14.2±1.38 ng/ml, p<0.001), ALT (16.5 to 20.0 U/l, p<0.01), AST (18.5 to 23.8 U/l, p<0.001), and alpha-GST (significant at 1 hour post-exercise), suggesting mild hepatocyte damage.
6. No significant renal damage was observed (urinary NAG unchanged).
7. Inflammatory response was activated: plasma MPO increased from 4.4±0.8 to 33±4.7 ng/ml (p<0.001) and calprotectin increased significantly (p<0.0001), with elevated faecal calprotectin suggesting gut-origin inflammation.
8. No reperfusion injury was detected in the 60-minute recovery period.
9. Some participants reported minor GI complaints (nausea, abdominal pain, flatulence, belching), but these were not associated with higher I-FABP levels.

CONCLUSIONS: A single 60-minute bout of moderate-to-high intensity exercise in healthy young men results in quantifiable small intestinal injury associated with transiently increased small intestinal permeability (gut barrier dysfunction), mild liver injury, and systemic inflammation, without renal damage or bacterial translocation. This demonstrates the gut's ability to withstand transient physiological hypoperfusion, but highlights potential risks for individuals with compromised vascular function, in whom such exercise-induced effects could lead to endotoxaemia and chronic inflammation. The study increases understanding of splanchnic hypoperfusion sequelae, relevant to critically ill patients and those with chronic conditions like heart failure.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion results in quantifiable small intestinal injury. Importantly, the extent of intestinal injury correlates with transiently increased small intestinal permeability, indicating gut barrier dysfunction in healthy individuals." (Abstract Conclusions), "The steepness of the gap g-a pCO₂ slope was most pronounced during the first 10 minutes of exercise, suggesting that functional splanchnic adaptations occur rapidly after altered perfusion demands in other parts of the body during physical activity." (Results), "The rapid decline in splanchnic perfusion during cycling was followed by the development of significant intestinal damage with a time lag of 20 minutes." (Discussion), "Our data imply that the healthy human small intestine can withstand transient hypoperfusion, since the observed enterocyte injury did not produce GI symptoms in our healthy individuals. However, prolonged episodes of hypoperfusion may cause more severe epithelial injury that may give rise to abdominal symptoms, as observed in endurance trained athletes." (Discussion), "In conclusion, our study demonstrates that a single, 60-minute bout of moderate-to-high intensity exercise is accompanied by splanchnic hypoperfusion and transient epithelial integrity loss in healthy young males, reflecting the ability of the gut to withstand to episodes of physiological stress with minor consequences." (Conclusion)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Gastroparesis ---
URL: https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/gastroparesis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) provides comprehensive information about gastroparesis, a gastrointestinal motility disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. CHOP uses a stricter definition than most published literature, requiring objective delay in gastric emptying while excluding mechanical obstruction, biochemical disorders (electrolyte imbalance, diabetes, hypothyroidism), gastric infections (H. pylori, CMV), medication side effects, and significant non-infectious gastroduodenal inflammation (eosinophilic gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn's disease, vasculitis).

Key content areas covered:

**Causes**: The exact cause is unknown; gastroparesis is a neuromuscular disorder involving antral hypomotility, gastric dysrhythmia, impaired fundic accommodation, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychological factors. Diabetes is the most frequently identified linked disease.

**Symptoms**: Early satiety, abdominal bloating, abdominal pain/burning, nausea, indigestion, episodic vomiting, fear of eating, feeding difficulty in infants, and weight loss. Symptoms are non-specific and don't distinguish gastroparesis from other causes. In children, gastroparesis often overlaps with GERD, functional dyspepsia, IBS, cyclical vomiting, enteric dysmotility, and pseudo-obstruction.

**Diagnosis**: The diagnostic process at CHOP's Suzi and Scott Lustgarten Center for GI Motility involves:
- Barium contrast upper GI series (rules out mechanical obstruction, malrotation, partial small bowel obstruction)
- Upper endoscopy (rules out H. pylori, peptic ulcer, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn's)
- Biochemical testing (rules out electrolyte, renal, and endocrine disorders)
- Gastric emptying study (the "gold standard" using radio-labeled solid meal; CHOP uses criteria of less than 10% emptying at 60 minutes or less than 50% at 2 hours as delayed, which is less strict than adult consensus guidelines)
- Antroduodenal manometry (measures muscle/nerve activity of stomach and small bowel over ~6 hours)

Notably, there is a lack of national standardization of pediatric test protocols, and normal pediatric values have not been established.

**Treatment**: No standardized medical therapy exists. CHOP uses a step-up symptom-based protocol with:
- Nutritional management: small frequent meals, avoiding high-fat and high-fiber foods, FODMAP diet, nutritional supplements (PediaSure, Boost), and for severe cases gastrostomy/jejunostomy tubes, venting gastrostomy, or central IV hyperalimentation
- Pharmacological therapies: Erythromycin, metoclopramide (high side effect profile including tardive dyskinesia), domperidone (FDA-regulated, requires cardiac monitoring), botulinum toxin (Botox), and cisapride (FDA-regulated, strict eligibility)
- Anti-nausea medications: ondansetron, granisetron, prochlorperazine, antihistamines, cyproheptadine, scopolamine patch
- Pain medications: tricyclic antidepressants, cyproheptadine, proton pump inhibitors
- Anti-bloating medications: simethicone, activated charcoal, rifaximin, Flagyl
- Non-pharmacological: child psychology support (stress management, CBT, relaxation therapy, biofeedback), social workers for school accommodations (504 planning)

**Outlook**: With successful diagnosis and treatment, children can lead relatively normal lives, attend school, get jobs, and have families, though they need ongoing medical follow-up into adulthood.

Contact information: Lustgarten Center at 215-590-1678.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Most published literature describes gastroparesis as delayed gastric emptying without a mechanical obstruction."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Abnormal gastric myoelectrical activity and delayed gastric emptying in patients with symptoms suggestive of gastroparesis - Johns Hopkins University ---
URL: https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/abnormal-gastric-myoelectrical-activity-and-delayed-gastric-empty-3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in 1996 in the journal Digestive Diseases and Sciences (Volume 41, Issue 8, pages 1538-1545) by J.D.Z. Chen, Zhiyue Lin, Jie Pan, and Richard W. McCallum. The study investigated the correlation between gastric myoelectrical activity and gastric emptying in 97 patients with symptoms suggestive of gastroparesis. Gastric myoelectrical activity was recorded using surface electrogastrography (EGG) for 30 minutes in the fasting state and 120 minutes after a solid test meal, with gastric emptying monitored simultaneously for 120 minutes. Key findings include: (1) patients with delayed gastric emptying showed a significantly lower percentage of normal gastric slow waves (P < 0.03) and a significantly reduced increase in dominant power in the postprandial EGG (P < 0.02); (2) postprandial gastric dysrhythmia predicted delayed gastric emptying with 78% accuracy, while abnormality in postprandial EGG power predicted it with 75% accuracy; (3) all patients with abnormalities in both rhythmicity and power had delayed gastric emptying; and (4) while postprandial EGG abnormalities can predict delayed emptying, a normal EGG does not guarantee normal gastric emptying. The article is associated with Scopus (PMID/scopus ID: 0029819577), has a DOI of 10.1007/BF02087897, and has been cited 245 times in Scopus.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Postprandial gastric dysrhythmia predicts delayed gastric emptying with an accuracy of 78%, while the abnormality in postprandial EGG power predicts delayed gastric emptying with an accuracy of 75%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Intestinal Motility Disorders: Background, Etiology, Pathophysiology ---
URL: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/179937-overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Medscape eMedicine article provides a comprehensive overview of intestinal motility disorders, which refer to abnormal intestinal contractions (spasms, paralysis) where the gut loses its ability to coordinate muscular activity due to endogenous or exogenous causes. The disorders are categorized as upper GI (gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastroparesis, achalasia, biliary dyskinesia) or lower GI (irritable bowel syndrome, colonic inertia, intestinal pseudo-obstruction/Ogilvie syndrome, pelvic floor dyssynergia, Hirschsprung disease, fecal incontinence, constipation).

**Etiology highlights:**
- Achalasia is primarily autoimmune; secondary causes include Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), iatrogenic surgical errors, and infiltrative diseases (tumors, amyloidosis)
- Gastroparesis etiologies: idiopathic (36%), diabetes mellitus (29%), postsurgical (13%)
- Colonic inertia involves dysfunction of the enteric nerve plexus with decreased/absent interstitial cells of Cajal
- Hirschsprung disease is congenital, from failure of neural crest cells to migrate during fetal development
- Fecal incontinence causes include aging, dementia, stroke, Parkinson disease, spinal cord injuries, diabetes, and surgical complications

**Pathophysiology:** GI motility requires coordinated contractions generated by nerves and muscles within GI walls. Intrinsic innervation (Auerbach/myenteric plexus) coordinates motor activity. The gastric pacemaker generates slow waves at 3 cycles per minute; migrating myoelectric complexes regulate gastric emptying every 90 minutes. Recent evidence suggests low-grade mucosal inflammation, immune activation (mast cell involvement), impaired epithelial barrier function, and aberrant neuronal sensitivity play roles in functional GI disorders. A Knowles-Martin classification categorizes disorders as well-defined entities, entities with variable dysfunction-symptom relations, questionable entities, and entities associated with behavioral disorders.

**Epidemiology:** Up to 30 million Americans have intestinal motility disorders; worldwide, 30-45% of all GI conditions are referable to these disorders. Idiopathic disorders have minimal morbidity and low mortality (1-1.5%), except intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Female-to-male ratio is 2.8:1. IBS occurs most frequently in ages 20-40; primary disorders are most common in white persons.

**Prognosis:** Generally good for primary disorders not secondary to malignancy. IBS and mild fecal incontinence have excellent prognosis. Intestinal pseudo-obstruction has high mortality (15-30%), usually due to delayed diagnosis. Constipation can lead to impaction, which may be fatal if unrecognized; impaction can cause vomiting, dehydration, hypoxia, and altered mental status.

**Patient Education:** Support groups include Association of Gastrointestinal Motility Disorders, Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome Association, Gastroparesis Patient Association for Cures and Treatment, International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders, and IBS Patient Support Group.

The article lists extensive references including guidelines from the European Society of Neurogastroenterology and Motility, European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, and American College of Radiology. Contributors include gastroenterologists and surgeons from multiple institutions including Wayne State University, Mount Sinai, and Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most common etiologies of gastroparesis noted in tertiary care centers include idiopathic (36%), diabetes mellitus (29%), and postsurgical (13%)."
</key_excerpts>
