## Discussion

PARTICIPANT: This damage is associated with running or is it associated with other types of activity as well?

DR. GISOLFI: It is primarily associated with running, but has been observed in triathletes and elite cyclists.

I think it is important that over at least a 90-minute period of intense exercise, we had one subject reach a core temperature of 40°C and observed no reduction in intestinal absorption of either active or passive solutes nor did we observe any change in fluid absorption.

If you exceed 90 minutes of strenuous exercise, especially if it is performed in a warm environment, I don't know the consequences on the GI tract. There is no data.

PARTICIPANT: Would you care to speculate on the differences between indirect and direct evidence on the deuterated water versus the sampling from the intestine?

DR. GISOLFI: This is a good point. Using the direct method of segmental perfusion you are looking at absorption from just a segment of the intestine. Using the indirect method of D2O accumulation in the blood, you are looking at absorption from the entire intestine.

Some studies have demonstrated that deuterium oxide is taken up by the stomach. How much this contributes to overall absorption is not clear.

When you look at the accumulation of a substance in the blood, you need to know the rate at which the substance is coming into the vascular compartment and the rate at which it is leaving. How is it being distributed to different organs? At what rate is it moving from the vascular compartment into the interstitial fluid compartment and at what rate is it being filtered off by the kidney? Without knowing the dynamics of that situation, it is difficult to say what the accumulation in the vascular compartment really means.

This webpage is Chapter 4 ("Effects of Exercise and Heat on Gastrointestinal Function") from the National Academies Press book "Nutritional Needs in Hot Environments: Applications for Military Personnel in Field Operations" (1993), published on the NCBI Bookshelf. The chapter is written by Carl V. Gisolfi of the Department of Exercise Science at The University of Iowa. It reviews research on how exercise-heat stress affects gastrointestinal (GI) function.

KEY CONTENT:
- GI symptoms (bleeding, vomiting black mucus, black diarrhea) are common in endurance athletes, often associated with overtraining, dehydration, aspirin use, and high ascorbic acid intake. Notable example: marathoner Derek Clayton after his 2:08:33.6 marathon. Symptoms may be reduced by cimetidine treatment or an elemental diet.
- Severe heat exposure mimics hemorrhage and intestinal ischemia: blood pools in cutaneous vessels, splanchnic blood flow declines, causing mucosal lesions, increased capillary permeability (attributed to superoxide radicals), and endotoxemia. Endotoxemia has been shown in human heat stroke victims and in ultramarathon runners collapsing in heat.
- Endoscopy studies (Gaudin et al., 1990) found pathological features (vascular lesions from congestion to hemorrhage, reduced mucosal secretion) in all runners after maximal distance runs (18-50 km). Schwartz et al. (1990) studied 41 Chicago Marathon runners; 9 experienced GI bleeding, with findings of gastric antral erosions and hyperemic eroded mucosa. Lesions heal quickly once resting state is restored. Note: 60% of the "bleeding group" used NSAIDs, which produce similar lesions.
- In the 1986 Comrades Marathon (89.4 km), 81% of 89 exhausted runners admitted to the medical tent had endotoxemia, significantly correlated with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. A primate study (Gathiram et al., 1987) showed kanamycin prevented endotoxemia during heat exposure at 44.5°C core temperature.
- GASTRIC EMPTYING: Reduced in heat. Owen et al. (1986) found subjects emptied 79% of ingested water in 25°C vs. only 59% at 35°C. Neufer et al. (1989) found significant negative correlation between GE and rectal temperature; hypohydration also reduced GE.
- INTESTINAL ABSORPTION: Williams et al. (1964) found prolonged exercise in heat reduced active but not passive carbohydrate absorption. Maughan et al. (1990) found reduced absorption with exercise. However, direct segmental perfusion studies (Fordtran and Saltin, 1967; Gisolfi et al., 1991) found NO effect of exercise intensity (30-70% VO2max) or duration (60-90 min) on fluid absorption.
- DISCUSSION: GI damage is primarily associated with running but also observed in triathletes and elite cyclists. In a 90-minute intense exercise test, one subject reached 40°C core temperature with no reduction in intestinal absorption. No data exist for exercise exceeding 90 minutes in warm environments. The chapter contrasts direct (segmental perfusion, segment-specific) vs. indirect (D2O blood accumulation, whole-intestine) measurement methods, noting complexities in interpreting blood accumulation data (distribution, kidney filtration, etc.).
- The chapter includes tables on GI disturbances in long-distance running, histological observations of runners after maximal distance runs, and gastric emptying during ingestion of different beverages, plus a flow diagram of hypothesized mechanisms of endotoxemia and thermal injury.
args.key_excerpts: "Two hours later, the elation had worn off. I was urinating quite large clots of blood, and I was vomiting black mucus and had a lot of black diarrhea. I don't think too many people can understand what I went through for the next 48 hours." — Derek Clayton

# Resistance Exercise Increases Gastrointestinal Symptoms, Markers of Gut Permeability, and Damage in Resistance-Trained Adults

![](https://acsm.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/GettyImages-616122214.jpg)

Gastrointestinal (GI) discomfort can occur as an unfortunate byproduct of physical exercise. While this phenomenon has been thoroughly outlined in endurance athletes, only [one study](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00294.2012) to date has measured and reported increased markers of GI injury following resistance exercise that coincided with decreased nutrient absorption.

Grand View Market research estimates the global digestive health market will reach $58 billion by 2025. Currently, dietary supplements and food products (e.g., probiotics, prebiotics, green powders, fermented drinks) aimed at improving GI function are heavily marketed toward active individuals with anecdotal or limited peer-reviewed evidence indicating the occurrence of GI damage in resistance-trained individuals. We sought to replicate these earlier findings while providing additional data on GI symptoms and permeability in resistance-trained individuals.

In [our study](https://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/Abstract/9900/Resistance_Exercise_Increases_Gastrointestinal.46.aspx) recently published in *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise®*, we examined the effect of acute resistance exercise on GI symptomology, damage and permeability in resistance-trained individuals.

To accomplish this, we utilized GI symptom questionnaires previously implemented with aerobic athletes and measured common blood markers of GI damage (intestinal fatty-acid binding protein) and GI permeability (lactulose/rhamnose ratio). Our trained participants (15 men and 15 women aged 23.9 [± 3.9] years with 6.3 [± 3.9] years of resistance training experience) completed a hypertrophy-style workout consisting of exercises that produce high amounts of intra-abdominal pressure (i.e., squat, deadlift, leg press) as we hypothesized that intra-abdominal pressure was likely a primary contributing mechanism for GI damage and distress during resistance exercise.

Our results suggest that resistance exercise induces significant GI distress, with 70% of participants reporting at least one GI symptom, most commonly nausea, and 60% reporting at least one moderate symptom after the exercise session, with no differences between sexes. Similar to studies examining GI distress following aerobic exercise, it appears that biomarkers of GI injury do not seem to consistently relate to subjective symptoms. Furthermore, resistance exercise induced elevation in GI permeability (measured by lactulose/rhamnose ratio) with males experiencing a greater magnitude of permeability compared to females. Additionally, males experienced a greater magnitude of GI damage following exercise (measured by intestinal fatty-acid binding protein) compared to the female conditions.

So, do males experience more GI distress from lifting weights? Interestingly, our findings indicated that the magnitude of GI damage following exercise is directly correlated with absolute strength. Thus, it is likely that our male participants experienced more GI distress because they lifted heavier absolute loads resulting in higher amounts of intra-abdominal pressure.

Our findings suggest that resistance exercise produces GI distress and that absolute load may be a primary mechanism. Our data are also in agreement with aerobic exercise studies, which demonstrate that GI symptoms do not always correlate to markers of GI damage following exercise.

With limited research in this area, our results emphasize the need for examining further implications of increased GI permeability, damage and subjective GI symptoms in resistance-trained athletes. We hope our study encourages future work to identify strategies (e.g., dietary supplements, nutritional regimens) that alleviate these side effects to optimize performance and nutrient utilization.

This article from the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) presents a study published in *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise®* examining the effects of acute resistance exercise on gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, damage, and permeability in resistance-trained individuals.

**Study Background:** While GI discomfort during endurance exercise has been well-documented, only one prior study measured increased GI injury markers following resistance exercise coinciding with decreased nutrient absorption. This study aimed to replicate those findings and add data on GI symptoms and permeability. The global digestive health market is projected to reach $58 billion by 2025, with many products marketed to active individuals despite limited evidence of GI damage in resistance-trained populations.

**Methodology:** Researchers used GI symptom questionnaires (previously used with aerobic athletes) and measured blood markers of GI damage (intestinal fatty-acid binding protein) and GI permeability (lactulose/rhamnose ratio). Participants included 30 resistance-trained individuals (15 men and 15 women, average age 23.9 ± 3.9 years, with 6.3 ± 3.9 years of training experience). They completed a hypertrophy-style workout featuring exercises generating high intra-abdominal pressure (squat, deadlift, leg press), based on the hypothesis that intra-abdominal pressure is a primary mechanism for GI distress during resistance exercise.

**Key Results:**
- 70% of participants reported at least one GI symptom (most commonly nausea), and 60% reported at least one moderate symptom after exercise, with no sex differences in symptom reports.
- Consistent with aerobic exercise studies, biomarkers of GI injury did not consistently correlate with subjective symptoms.
- Resistance exercise increased GI permeability (lactulose/rhamnose ratio), with males showing greater permeability than females.
- Males experienced greater GI damage (intestinal fatty-acid binding protein) than females.
- The magnitude of GI damage correlated directly with absolute strength, suggesting males experienced more GI distress because they lifted heavier loads, generating higher intra-abdominal pressure.

**Conclusions:** Resistance exercise produces GI distress, and absolute load appears to be a primary mechanism. The findings align with aerobic exercise research showing GI symptoms do not always correlate with markers of GI damage. The authors call for further research on the implications of increased GI permeability, damage, and symptoms in resistance-trained athletes, and for strategies (e.g., dietary supplements, nutritional regimens) to alleviate these side effects to optimize performance and nutrient utilization.

**Authors:** Tricia Hart, MS (Ph.D. student in nutritional sciences at Penn State University) and Jeremy R. Townsend, PhD (associate professor in exercise and nutrition science at Lipscomb University, Nashville, Tennessee).

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1003445/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sec. Sport and Exercise Nutrition, Volume 9, November 9, 2022) titled "An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms" by Rachel Scrivin, Ricardo J.S. Costa, Fiona Pelly, Dana Lis, and Gary Slater (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand; Monash University, Australia; and UCLA, United States).

STUDY DESIGN AND PARTICIPANTS:
The study used a validated online questionnaire to investigate self-reported exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) and management strategies among 137 adult endurance athletes (≥18 years) participating in events ≥60 minutes. Participants included runners (55%, n=75), triathletes (22%, n=30), and non-running sports (23%, n=32) at recreationally competitive (37%), recreationally non-competitive (32%), and competitive regional/national/international (31%) levels. Females comprised 63% of respondents (n=86) and males 37% (n=51) (p<0.001); mean age was 41.6 ± 11.1 years. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia (approval S201402).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Athletes were categorized into groups based on when Ex-GIS developed: around training only (AT, 21%), around competitions only (AC, 30%), or equally around both (ET/EC, 49%).
- Lower gastrointestinal symptoms were more commonly reported than upper GI symptoms across all groups.
- Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during training and competitions than before or after exercise. The only severe symptom of significance was the urge to defecate during training in the ET group (Z=-0.536, p=0.01). Most Ex-GIS severity was rated as mild (<5/10 on a 0-10 visual analog scale).
- 67% (n=92) of athletes reported using dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting 277 total strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.

MOST POPULAR DIETARY STRATEGIES:
- Dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42) - the most popular
- Dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16)
- Low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15)
- Avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose, 6.1%, n=17) were the most popular FODMAPs avoided
- Non-dietary strategies included medications (4.7%, n=13) and relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11)

MOST SUCCESSFUL STRATEGIES (Likert scale 1-5, with 5 = significant improvement):
- Dietary fiber reduction (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Low FODMAP diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Dairy-free diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Increasing carbohydrates (median = 4, IQR = 3,4)
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed at all time points.

SUPPLEMENTS: Probiotics (median=4, n=26) were the most commonly used supplement; arginine was rated highest for success (median=5, n=1, though very small sample). Other supplements trialed included prebiotics, antioxidants, L-citrulline, glutamine, curcumin, and nitrates.

INFORMATION SOURCES: Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated as the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29). No significant associations were found between information sources and sport type, participation level, event characteristics, or biological sex.

CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS: Fifteen athletes (11%) reported a diagnosed gastrointestinal disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, n=6). Thirteen athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS.

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS:
- Reducing dietary fiber, especially before exercise, aligns with current sports nutrition guidelines and works via reducing luminal contents and extending GI transit time, though a low-fiber diet may require implementation 1-3 days before exercise.
- Low FODMAP diets are effective for both IBS and Ex-GIS, but are not intended for long-term use; a rechallenge and personalization phase is recommended for extended use.
- Dairy avoidance may relate to lactose intolerance, which has overlapping symptoms with IBS.
- Increasing carbohydrate intake can help mitigate Ex-GIS through improved splanchnic blood flow and reduced intestinal epithelial damage; however, high intake rates (>60-90 g/h) may trigger symptoms unless preceded by gut training.
- Carbohydrate or whey protein hydrolysate ingestion before/during exercise ameliorates intestinal epithelial injury; carbohydrate is preferential due to fewer GI symptoms and its value as an exogenous fuel source.
- Non-dietary interventions (medications, relaxation, psychological therapies) are used less frequently but have potential; further randomized controlled trials are needed.
- Study limitations include convenience sampling and possible over-representation of APDs as information sources due to researcher backgrounds as registered dietitians.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Endurance athletes use a variety of strategies to manage their Ex-GIS, with dietary manipulation being the most common."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Nutritional strategies for minimizing gastrointestinal symptoms during endurance exercise: systematic review of the literature ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12258207

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2025 Jul 11;22(1):2529910, doi:10.1080/15502783.2025.2529910) by Janez Mlinaric and Nina Mohorko (University of Primorska, Faculty of Health Sciences, Izola, Slovenia; Ruhr University Bochum, Germany; Human Performance Centre, Ljubljana, Slovenia), examining nutritional strategies to minimize gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms during endurance exercise.

METHODS: The review used PRISMA methodology, searching PubMed from January 2023 to March 2023. It included randomized controlled trials, crossover trials, and case studies. 31 studies were selected for inclusion, with quality assessment using the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias (RoB 2) tool. The majority of studies showed low risk of bias, though some had concerns regarding blinding and randomization.

The studies were categorized into five research areas:

1. **Gut training protocols**: Two weeks of purposeful repetitive CHO intake during running lowered GI symptom severity and reduced breath H₂ response (indicating reduced CHO malabsorption). Repetitive running sessions with higher liquid intake improved fluid tolerance over time. However, minor effects were seen in race walkers and runners with high daily CHO intake. The mechanisms may involve increased expression of SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters, but gut training is likely to reduce symptoms by reducing CHO malabsorption and increasing tolerance to higher CHO intakes.

2. **Carbohydrate solutions and mixtures**: CHO bars were the worst tolerated form (causing more nausea, fullness, and fatigue). Highly concentrated CHO solutions increased symptoms. Fructose caused more GI symptoms than glucose or sucrose due to slower absorption (facilitated diffusion vs. active transport). High glucose intake (SGLT1 saturation at ~60 g/h) caused bloating. Mixed CHOs recruit GLUT5 transporter, improving absorption. A 0.8 ratio MD:FRU solution was superior to 0.5 and 1.25 ratios for performance and GI comfort, suggesting ratios close to unity may be better than the traditional 2:1 ratio.

3. **Low FODMAP diet**: Multiple studies showed significant reductions in GI symptoms (gut discomfort, flatulence, urge to defecate, loose stool, diarrhea) with low FODMAP diets compared to high FODMAP diets. 69% of participants reported positive effects on low FODMAP vs. 25% on high FODMAP. However, the restrictive nature of the diet could negatively affect athletes in other ways.

4. **Hydrogel CHO products**: Current evidence does not demonstrate benefits of hydrogel CHO products over standard CHO products. One study showed lower GI symptoms with hydrogel, but others found no differences between conditions.

5. **Probiotic supplementation**: Evidence is mixed. Some studies showed reductions in GI symptoms (e.g., 27% reduction during training, fewer episodes of nausea, belching, vomiting), while others found no substantial differences or even increases in mild GI symptoms. LGG (Limosilactobacillus rhamnosus GG) shortened GI symptom episode duration by 33-57%.

CONCLUSION: The onset of GI symptoms is very complex and influenced by a huge variety of factors. Elimination of GI symptoms in each athlete must be approached individually and thoughtfully. At least 30-50% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms regularly during exercise, with estimates of 30-90% for endurance trained runners. Four main causes of GI symptoms: physiological (splanchnic hypoperfusion), mechanical, psychological, and nutritional.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"At least 30 to 50 % of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise on a regular basis, with especially high occurrence in long duration endurance exercise. In endurance trained runners it is estimated that between 30 and 90 % may experience them."

--- SOURCE 3: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in ... ---
URL: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/9QnW5DQA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a peer-reviewed case series published in 2025 in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (Vol. 4, pp. 337-354) by Rachel Scrivin, Gary Slater, and Ricardo J.S. Costa (DOI: 10.1123/ijsnem.2024-0133). The study evaluated a four-phase management approach for exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) in endurance athletes using the GastroAxEx (gastrointestinal assessment during exercise) protocol combined with a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP therapeutic dietary intervention.

METHODOLOGY: Nine recreational-to-elite athletes with recurrent severe Ex-GIS and two controls (without Ex-GIS) participated. The four phases included: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention including a 48-hr high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet based on Phase 2 outcomes, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of interventions.

KEY RESULTS: 
- Most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2%-4% body mass loss
- 8/9 athletes consumed <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate during the GastroAxEx
- 4/9 athletes reported severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) during exercise; 8/9 reported severe Ex-GIS in the recovery period
- All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery
- Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes
- 8/9 athletes successfully implemented the 48-hr high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to targeted events

CONCLUSION: The 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to endurance exercise reduced the incidence and severity of Ex-GIS, improved intake tolerance, and resulted in improved perceived work output during targeted events. The authors conclude this dietary approach appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions for mitigating Ex-GIS.

The article has 3 citations and 40 references, and is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science. The webpage also lists citing publications, including related work on FODMAP manipulation for Ex-GIS, practitioner guides to gut issue management in athletes, and research on high-amylose maize starch and hydration.
</summary>

"A 48-hr high carbohydrate low FODMAP before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to suggested therapeutic interventions used to mitigate Ex-GIS."

--- SOURCE 4: Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The article was authored by Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Gastroenterology, Department of Translational and Precision Medicine, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy) and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (Department of Gastroenterology, IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Milan, Italy). Submission received 26 July 2023; accepted 12 September 2023; published 19 September 2023. The article has been cited 26 times and viewed 61,433 times.

**Purpose:** The review explores the pathophysiology, clinical aspects, and nutritional/behavioral management strategies for Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome (Ex-GIS), with particular focus on gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023. Searches for pathophysiology returned 290 results (PubMed), 216 (MEDLINE), and 97 trials (Cochrane); diet/nutrition searches returned 2663, 2197, and 1038 results respectively. After inclusion/exclusion criteria (English language, relevant to diet and endurance performance), 142 research articles were identified.

**Key Findings on Pathophysiology:**
- Ex-GIS involves two primary pathways: (I) the neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway (sympathetic activation reducing GI functional capacity) and (II) the circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway (blood flow redistribution away from splanchnic circulation).
- Splanchnic blood flow (SBF) can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing significant GI tract hypoperfusion and damage.
- Splanchnic hypoperfusion leads to loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia (LPS in circulation), triggering pro-inflammatory cytokines.
- A 1965-era study by Brock-Utne found 81% of 89 marathon runners were endotoxemic.
- Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max represents the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
- Endurance exercise alters gut peptide levels (increases PYY and GLP-1, affects ghrelin, CCK) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) which affect GI motility and blood flow.
- Gut microbiota differences exist between athletes and sedentary individuals; probiotics (e.g., UCC118 strain) may attenuate exercise-induced intestinal hyperpermeability.
- Carbohydrate malabsorption was found in 68% of 25 healthy endurance-trained runners during recovery.

**Epidemiology/Prevalence:**
- 30-90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms during exercise.
- Ter Steege study of 2076 long-distance runners: 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% serious complaints, 2.7% within 24 hours post-run; 3 athletes dropped out.
- Pfeiffer study: severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon/cycling to 32% in Ironman races.
- Upper-GI symptoms in up to 40% of runners, up to 70% in cyclists; reflux/heartburn prevalence 15-20% in runners.
- Lower-GI symptoms: up to 30% in recreational runs, up to 50% in cyclists, up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners.
- Exercise-induced transient abdominal pain (ETAP) reported in 18% of recreational run competitors.
- IBS underdiagnosis in endurance athletes: Killian et al. documented 9.8% IBS prevalence overall with only 2.8% diagnosed; Hungin et al. reported 14.1% overall with 10.8% undiagnosed.
- Female athletes, especially younger ones, report higher GI symptom prevalence; increased age may be protective due to reduced splanchnic vasoconstriction.

**Management Implications:** The review highlights nutritional and behavioral interventions as the principal strategies to avoid symptoms, including evaluation of exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet. It examines gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets as potential management approaches, noting that Ex-GIS symptoms resemble IBS (defined by Rome IV Criteria) and may respond to analogous nutritional strategies.
</summary>

"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."

--- SOURCE 5: Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s44410-025-00019-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access scoping review article published in the journal "Performance Nutrition" (Volume 2, article number 4, published February 4, 2026) titled "Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review." The study aimed to assess the prevalence of GI symptoms in non-endurance sport athletes, as GI symptoms are well-documented in endurance athletes but less clear across other sports.

METHODS: A scoping review was conducted following JBI guidelines with the PCC mnemonic. Searches were performed on Medline and SportDiscus databases (via EBSCO) until September 1, 2025, using keywords including "gastrointestinal," "athlete*/player*/sport*," and "prevalence/frequency/proportion." Only cross-sectional studies in highly trained (Tier 3) or higher athletes were included. Endurance sports (distance running, cycling, triathlons) and clinical settings were excluded.

RESULTS: The search yielded 482 articles; after screening, seven studies were included. Six different questionnaires were used across studies. In total, 1,087 athletes (682 male, 405 female) were analyzed. Prevalence of at least one GI symptom ranged from 11.5–80.0%. Any GI symptom prevalence in males was 13.9–61% and in females 26–80%. Three studies reported symptom timing around training/competition ranging from 24.5–52.0%, more common in females (37.5–67.0%) than males (13.9–52.0%). The most common symptoms were flatulence (2.8–48%), stomach cramps/rumbling (5.1–37%), and bloating (2.5–32%). Diarrhoea and urge to defecate were more common during exercise than at rest (19% vs. 8%, and 13% vs. 11%, respectively). Specific findings included: American footballers (61% reported ≥1 symptom, 52% during exercise), rugby players (61% male, 72% female with ≥1 symptom), powerlifters/weightlifters with anal incontinence (61.8% male vs. 80.0% female), and celiac disease symptoms higher in athletes than general population (2.9% vs. 0.4%).

CONCLUSIONS: GI symptoms are common in non-endurance athletes, with approximately 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes experiencing symptoms around competition. The wide variation in prevalence (11.5–80%) is likely due to heterogeneity in screening tools, with studies using different numbers of symptoms assessed (2–15), different Likert scales (0–4, 0–7, 0–10), and varying recall windows (past week to 12 months). Female athletes were more likely to report symptoms affecting performance. The authors call for standardized methods for assessing GI issues in athletes and note that existing questionnaires may be suitable only for research, not clinical diagnosis, suggesting future research should consider validated criteria such as ROME IV for IBS.
</summary>

"The prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes varies widely, which may be due to heterogeneity in screening tools. There is a lack of studies discerning the severity and timing of symptoms, but it appears that around 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes may experience gastrointestinal symptoms around competing."

--- SOURCE 6: Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete | Musculoskeletal Key ---
URL: https://musculoskeletalkey.com/gastrointestinal-medicine-in-the-athlete

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete

This chapter from the Musculoskeletal Key website (DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) addresses common gastrointestinal (GI) conditions in athletes and active persons, focusing on recognition and management. GI conditions are common in athletes, with exercise placing significant stress on the GI tract, resulting in characteristic disorders that can impair athletic performance.

### Key Points:

**General Pathophysiology:**
- 20–50% of high-performance athletes report undesirable GI symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea)
- Symptoms are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes
- Cyclists appear somewhat protected from GI issues due to forward positioning, while runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling
- Increased catecholamines and GI peptides (gastrin, motilin, secretin, etc.) increase gut transit time, negatively affecting GI homeostasis

**GI Tract Ischemia:**
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction
- Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation
- Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa" (per ter Steege et al.)
- Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms

**Upper GI Conditions:**
- Upper GI complaints affect 30–70% of athletes
- Three primary mechanisms: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes
- GERD is the most common cause of upper GI symptoms in athletes
- Exercise ≥90% VO2 max increases frequency/duration of esophageal reflux episodes
- Weightlifters have the highest rate of heartburn and reflux; runners have a threefold increase in GERD when running 45 minutes after a meal

**GERD Management:**
- Lifestyle modifications first-line: sleeping on two pillows, avoiding lying down within 4 hours of evening meal, avoiding postprandial exercise, limiting foods that relax the LES (high-fat foods, coffee, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods)
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training
- Pharmacologic therapy: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective
- H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers
- Upper endoscopy for diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended

**Other Conditions:**
- **Functional heartburn:** Up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset; treatment is biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, prokinetics
- **Dyspepsia:** Caused by GERD, gastritis, or peptic ulcer disease; ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms; PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence
- **Aspirin/NSAIDs:** Block cyclooxygenase and protective prostaglandins; add daily PPI for GI protection in athletes requiring NSAIDs with ulcer history
- **Pill esophagitis:** NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and mefloquine are highest risk; take with food/fluid in morning and remain upright
- **Dysphagia:** Divided into oropharyngeal and esophageal subtypes; most commonly caused by irritative effects of GERD
- **Nausea/Vomiting:** Linked to postprandial exercise; avoid solid food within 3 hours of events; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events; H2 blockers and PPIs can help

**GERD-Asthma Connection:**
- Up to 90% of persons with asthma have GERD; up to 40% have esophagitis
- Treatment only benefits asthma in patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms
- Atypical GERD presentations include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, and chest pain
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These symptoms are reported by approximately 20% to 50% of high-performance athletes and are encountered more commonly in women than in men."

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Proton pump inhibitors may enhance the risk of digestive diseases by regulating intestinal microbiota ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2023.1217306/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Proton Pump Inhibitors May Enhance the Risk of Digestive Diseases by Regulating Intestinal Microbiota

This is a peer-reviewed review article published in *Frontiers in Pharmacology* (July 17, 2023) by Liang Tian, Jinqiu Yuan, Wenbo Meng and colleagues from Lanzhou University (China) and Sun Yat-sen University (China). The article reviews the growing evidence linking proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use to digestive complications through PPI-induced alterations of the intestinal microbiota.

### Key Points:

**Background:** PPIs are the most widely used acid-suppressive agents and first-line therapy for gastric acid-related disorders (peptic ulcer disease, GERD, Barrett's esophagus). However, increasing evidence links PPIs to adverse digestive events including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Clostridium difficile-associated disease (CDAD), functional dyspepsia, lower GI bleeding, infectious diseases, cholelithiasis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

**Mechanisms of PPI effects on intestinal flora:**
- pH-dependent: PPIs reduce gastric acid, disrupting the gastric acid barrier, allowing exogenous bacteria to invade the GI tract; affects microorganisms with specific pH requirements (e.g., H. pylori)
- Non-pH-dependent: PPI-induced hypergastrinemia and hyperparathyroidism affect intestinal osmolality and calcium/phosphorus metabolism; PPIs alter digestive functions and nutrient absorption; PPIs directly bind to non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases on microbes (fungi, H. pylori, Streptococcus pneumoniae)
- PPI treatment increases Planococcaceae, Oxalobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae in the proximal small intestine; decreases Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae

**Specific disease associations with altered flora:**
1. **Functional Dyspepsia (FD):** Decreased Bifidobacterium reduces butyric acid production, increasing intestinal permeability. Reduced Streptococcus, Prevotella, Veillonella, Actinomyces, and Lactobacillus may also contribute.
2. **Lower GI Bleeding:** Decreased Lactobacillus johnsonii (lactic acid production inhibits NF-κB/TNF-α pathway) and reduced Actinomycetes/Bifidobacterium contribute to NSAID-induced intestinal injury.
3. **SIBO:** Results are inconsistent across studies; a 2018 meta-analysis showed PPI use moderately increased SIBO risk, though diagnostic method variability (aspirate culture vs. breath tests) is a major confounder.
4. **CDAD:** PPIs regulate C. difficile toxin gene expression (up to 120-fold), accelerate spore-to-trophic-form transition via elevated pH, diminish salivary nitrite antimicrobial effects, and disrupt normal flora. Risk can be up to 7.15-fold higher.
5. **Gastrointestinal Infectious Diseases:** PPIs increase risk of bacterial gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter), Candida infections (reduced Lactobacillus), and multidrug-resistant organism infections (75% increased infection rate).
6. **Cholelithiasis:** PPI use increases abundance of bile salt hydrolase (BSH)-producing bacteria (Lactobacillus, Clostridium, Eubacterium), increasing secondary bile acids (especially deoxycholic acid) that promote gallstone formation. PPIs also reduce gallbladder motility by delaying gastric emptying.
7. **Inflammatory Bowel Disease:** PPI use is linked to IBD through reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (anti-inflammatory), reduced Lactobacillus reuteri (which normally produces histamine to suppress TNF-α), increased intestinal infections, and CDAD promotion.

**Conclusions:** The evidence supports a link between PPI-induced intestinal flora disruption and digestive complications. The gut microbiota represents a promising target for prevention and treatment (e.g., fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics like Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium). However, most studies are retrospective with relatively weak evidence and confounding factors. Clinicians should carefully evaluate and individually manage patients requiring PPI therapy to avoid long-term abuse. More high-quality clinical studies and research into specific mechanisms and molecular targets are needed.
</summary>

However, recently, there has been a growing number of digestive complications linked to PPIs, and several studies have indicated that the intestinal flora play an important role in these complications."

<summary>

Both the intensity of sport and the type of sporting activity have been shown to be contributing factors in the development of GI symptoms. Three important factors have been postulated as contributing to the pathophysiology of GI complaints in athletes: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes."

--- SOURCE 9: Exercise & GI Symptoms - IFFGD ---
URL: https://iffgd.org/manage-your-health/tips-and-daily-living/exercise-gi-symptoms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders (IFFGD) addresses whether intense exercise can lead to GI symptoms such as diarrhea and heartburn. The article answers a reader's question about experiencing diarrhea and heartburn after increasing exercise intensity.

Key content covered:

**Benefits vs. risks of exercise:** While regular exercise offers documented benefits (better sleep, stronger bones, weight loss, fewer heart problems, better glucose control), it can also contribute to GI disorders causing symptoms including reflux/heartburn, belching, bloating, stomach pain/cramps, vomiting, nausea, side ache, flatulence, urgency, diarrhea, and intestinal bleeding.

**Heartburn:** Exercise can decrease lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, leading to more reflux episodes. Eating too soon before exercise and high-impact activities (like running) can worsen reflux compared to low-impact exercises like cycling. Treatment includes H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and switching to lower-impact exercises.

**Diarrhea:** Diarrhea and urgency are common in endurance athletes, especially long-distance runners. Approximately 90% of long-distance runners experience some GI symptoms during exercise but accept them as normal and don't consult a physician.

**Three main causes of GI symptoms during intense exercise:**
1. **Mechanical:** Repetitive body movement from running causes trauma that can damage the intestinal lining, contributing to diarrhea, urgency, or GI bleeding.
2. **Ischemic:** During intense exercise, blood flow shifts to working muscles and away from the GI tract (up to 80% reduction), causing ischemia, reduced gut function, increased leakiness, malabsorption, and looser stools.
3. **Nutritional:** Fiber, fat, protein, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>7% carbohydrate) are associated with greater risk of GI symptoms.

**Prevention tips:** Stay well hydrated, avoid lactose-containing products, and avoid high-fructose foods and fructose-only drinks.

**Medical treatment:** Patients should consult healthcare providers about persistent or bleeding diarrhea, which may signal a severe condition. Loperamide (over-the-counter) has been shown to decrease stool frequency when taken before intense exercise. Caution is advised with antispasmodic and antimotility drugs, as they can inhibit perspiration and impair core body temperature control.

The article was authored by Renata Korczak, RD CSSD (University of Minnesota), adapted from an article by Thomas Puetz, M.D. (Aurora Advanced Healthcare), and edited by William D. Chey, MD (University of Michigan). It is IFFGD publication #231.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"According to research, about 90% of long-distance runners experience some form of GI symptoms (including diarrhea) during exercise and accept their symptoms as a normal consequence of running and therefore do not consult a physician."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Gastrointestinal distress: Can a low-fodmap diet help? - The Centre for Integrative Sports Nutrition ---
URL: https://intsportsnutrition.com/articles/exercise-induced-gastrointestinal-distress-can-a-low-fodmap-diet-help

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Simone do Carmo (MSci SENr CISNCert), a sports nutritionist and exercise physiologist, investigates whether a low-FODMAP diet can help alleviate exercise-induced gastrointestinal (GI) distress in athletes. The article covers the causes, prevalence, and potential nutritional strategies for GI distress, with a focus on the low-FODMAP diet as an emerging therapeutic approach.

**Key points on GI distress in athletes:**
- Prevalence ranges from 30-90% depending on methodology, study populations, and environmental conditions
- Symptoms are categorized as upper GI (heartburn, bloating, nausea) or lower GI (cramps, diarrhea, intestinal bleeding)
- Causes are physiological (ischemia from blood shunting to active muscles, reduced splanchnic blood flow, compromised gut permeability, risk of endotoxemia), mechanical (posture changes in cycling, bouncing impact in running causing intestinal bleeding), and nutritional (dehydration, high-fibre/high-fat/high-protein foods, fructose, milk, concentrated carbohydrate drinks)
- A study of 55 male triathletes in a half-Ironman race found 52% reported urge to defecate and 42% reported flatulence; all who ate 30 minutes before the race vomited during the swim leg; 93% of those who vomited consumed hypertonic drinks; all with intestinal cramps had eaten high-fibre foods
- NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI symptoms and intestinal bleeding
- Sports drinks should be below 8% carbohydrate concentration (preferably glucose and fructose combination) to prevent dehydration

**Low-FODMAP diet findings:**
- FODMAPs = Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides and Polyols, which are poorly absorbed and rapidly fermented by colonic bacteria
- The diet was initially developed for IBS patients; up to 86% of IBS patients alleviate symptoms on it
- A survey of 910 athletes found 55% actively avoided at least one high-FODMAP food; 93% reported that food elicited GI symptoms, and 86.5% reported improvement through avoidance
- Lactose was the highest trigger (86.5%), followed by galacto-oligosaccharides (23.9%), fructose (23.0%), fructans (6.2%), and polyols (5.4%)
- Long-term adherence is not recommended due to risk of inadequate nutritional intake and negative effects on gut microbiota (reduced SCFA-producing bacteria, which produce butyrate, propionate, and acetate essential for colonic health)
- A case study used a six-day low-FODMAP diet in a runner, which resolved running-specific GI symptoms and improved psychological well-being (assessed via DALDA scores)
- Prudent recommendation: follow a low-FODMAP diet for 2-3 days prior to a race or important training session

**Gut trainability:**
- A 28-day study of 16 trained cyclists/triathletes found that high-carbohydrate diets led to greater maximal citrate synthase activity and higher carbohydrate exogenous oxidation rates during submaximal exercise, attributed to enhanced intestinal absorption and improved tolerance
- The gut is a highly dynamic, adaptable organ that athletes can train through nutritional experimentation during training

The article concludes that eliminating certain high-FODMAP food triggers with a prudent, individualised, and focused approach may be an effective nutritional strategy to reduce GI distress in athletes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The prevalence of gastrointestinal distress is highly variable, ranging from 30 to 90 per cent, which can partly be explained by the different methodologies, study populations and environmental conditions in research studies."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Effect of a short-term low fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide and polyol (FODMAP) diet on exercise-related gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12970-019-0268-9

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published on January 15, 2019, in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (Volume 16, article number 1) examining the effect of a short-term low FODMAP diet on exercise-related gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms in recreational runners.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Sixteen healthy, recreationally active runners (10 female, 6 male; age 44 ± 10 years) completed a randomized crossover trial. Participants followed either a LOW FODMAP (16.06 ± 1.79 g/day) or HIGH FODMAP (38.65 ± 6.66 g/day) diet for 7 days, with a one-week washout period before switching. GI symptoms were rated using the Irritable Bowel Syndrome-Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS) questionnaire, perceived ability to exercise was rated on a visual analogue scale, and resting blood samples were collected to measure plasma intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP) as a marker of acute GI injury.

KEY RESULTS:
- Overall IBS-SSS score significantly reduced on the LOW FODMAP diet from 81.1 ± 16.4 to 31.3 ± 9.2 (P = 0.004), while HIGH FODMAP showed a non-significant increase from 51.1 to 104.0 (P = 0.08)
- 69% of participants (11/16) reported positive effects of the LOW FODMAP diet versus only 25% (4/16) on HIGH FODMAP
- Perceived exercise frequency (P = 0.02) and intensity (P = 0.007) were significantly improved following LOW FODMAP
- No significant differences were found in plasma I-FABP between dietary conditions (P > 0.05)
- Individual symptoms of pain and bloating showed significant improvements on LOW FODMAP
- Total carbohydrate intake was lower during LOW FODMAP (2.79 g/kg/day) versus HIGH FODMAP (3.91 g/kg/day)

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: FODMAPs are short-chain carbohydrates (fructose, lactose, oligosaccharides, polyols) that can be malabsorbed, leading to gas production, increased intestinal water volume, and gut motility changes. Low FODMAP diets are established treatments for IBS (effective in ~75% of patients). While 30-50% of athletes cite GI issues as a common cause of underperformance, most prior research focused on trained athletes; this study specifically examined healthy recreational runners under free-living conditions.

CONCLUSION: A short-term LOW FODMAP diet under free-living conditions reduced exercise-related GI symptoms and improved perceived ability to exercise in healthy recreational runners, likely due to reduced indigestible carbohydrates available for fermentation. The authors recommend further investigation into therapeutic benefits of LOW FODMAP diets for recreational and trained athletes during sustained training periods. The study was conducted at Anglia Ruskin University (Cambridge Centre for Sport and Exercise Sciences) with ethical approval (Project Number: FST/FREP/15/567).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A short-term LOW FODMAP diet under free-living conditions reduced exercise-related GI symptoms and improved the perceived ability to exercise in otherwise healthy, recreational runners." — Study conclusion

It positions the diet as beneficial on an ad hoc basis before important events or during intensive training phases, rather than removing high-FODMAP foods entirely.

This webpage is the International Probiotics Association (IPA) website, featuring a scientific committee article titled "How Probiotics are Reshaping Sports Performance" by Brandy Webb, ND, BSc, Scientific Affairs Manager at Probi AB (part of Symrise AG), dated March 30, 2026.

**Key Content on Probiotics and Sports Performance:**
- A meta-analysis published in Nutrients by Jarrett et al. (2025) discusses how probiotic supplementation may improve exercise parameters like endurance, recovery, and nutrient absorption.
- Probiotics may improve protein absorption, increase circulating branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), and support fatty acid oxidation during exercise.

**Documented Probiotic Benefits for Athletes:**
1. **Faster recovery:** Strains like Lactobacillus paracasei lower biomarkers (creatine kinase, myoglobin, C-reactive protein) indicating reduced muscle injury and inflammation; athletes report less soreness, better sleep, and improved recovery.
2. **Better nutrient absorption:** Enhanced bioavailability of BCAAs (valine, leucine, isoleucine), improved carbohydrate metabolism, glucose oxidation, and iron status.

5. **Mental resilience:** Anxiolytic effects observed; studies in badminton and football players found reduced stress/anxiety and improved focus and attention.

- Effects on strength and power are less clear; some studies combining probiotics with protein supplements report increased muscle strength in resistance-trained athletes.

**Future Directions:** More research needed on strength/power effects; effectiveness varies by strain, dosage, duration, and individual gut microbiome differences. The author calls for standardized protocols tailored to different sports.

**About the Author:** Brandy Webb has nearly two decades of experience across clinical practice, higher education, and industry, including roles as Chief Medical Officer and Scientific Advisory Board Chair, with previous positions at Bastyr University.

--- SOURCE 8: The Influence of Dietary Supplements on Exercise-Induced Gut Damage and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/3/443

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a peer-reviewed open-access systematic review and meta-analysis published in the MDPI journal *Nutrients* (2025, Vol. 17, Issue 3, Article 443; DOI: 10.3390/nu17030443), titled "The Influence of Dietary Supplements on Exercise-Induced Gut Damage and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis." The authors are Robyn Aitkenhead, Mark Waldron, Gillian E. Conway, Katy Horner, and Shane M. Heffernan, affiliated with Swansea University (A-STEM Centre, Welsh Institute of Performance Science), University of the Sunshine Coast (Australia), and University College Dublin. The article was submitted 8 January 2025, revised 20 January 2025, accepted 23 January 2025, and published 25 January 2025. It belongs to the special issue on nutritional strategies or dietary supplementation on exercise performance in hot environments. The article has an Altmetric score of 8, 11,135 article views, and 5 citations.

**Background and Purpose:** Endurance exercise, especially under heat stress, temporarily compromises intestinal barrier integrity in healthy individuals. The study aimed to (i) systematically review and meta-analyse the effect of exercise and dietary supplements on gastrointestinal symptoms (GISs) and biomarkers of gut damage, and (ii) assess the effect of supplements targeted for GISs and gut damage on endurance exercise performance.

**Methods:** The search followed PRISMA guidelines (search performed December 2022, updated June 2023 and November 2024) across four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Science Direct, Sports Discus). The initial search retrieved 91,105 articles; after screening, 27 studies were included. Inclusion criteria were English-language studies with healthy adults ≥18 years, randomized controlled trials with at least one gut outcome measure. Exclusion criteria included animal/in vitro studies, grey literature, and participants <18 years or with disease. Three meta-analyses were performed: between-groups for GISs, between-groups for exercise performance, and within-groups for circulating i-FABP pre- to post exercise (10, 6, and 12 comparison groups, respectively). Data were analysed with random-effects models in RStudio, with heterogeneity assessed using I². Risk of bias was assessed per Cochrane guidelines, and certainty of evidence per GRADE.

**Key Results:**
- No pooled effect of supplement interventions on gastrointestinal symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.42, 95% CI −0.17: 1.02, p = 0.15), with high heterogeneity (I² = 82%).
- Probiotics showed a moderate significant effect for gastrointestinal symptoms (Hedges' g = −0.62, 95% CI −1.01 to 1.01, p = 0.05), favouring the supplement.
- Significant increase in i-FABP concentrations pre- to post exercise (106%; Hedges' g = 1.01, 95% CI 0.63; 1.38, p = 0.01), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 62%).
- No pooled or sub-group differences for exercise performance for any supplements (Hedges' g = 0.09, p = 0.67; I² = 43%).
- Subgroup analysis: glutamine (g = 1.18) and carbohydrates (g = 1.38) had large significant effects on increasing i-FABP; capsaicin (g = 1.36) and carbohydrates (g = 0.93) had large non-significant effects favouring placebo for GISs; sodium bicarbonate showed a non-significant moderate effect favouring the supplement for GISs.
- Moderate-to-large heterogeneity observed across studies (I² ≥ 58.6%); candidate moderators (exercise duration, modality, and environmental temperature) had no significant effect on any outcomes (p > 0.05).

**Participants and Study Characteristics:** 495 participants (average age 28 ± 6 y, 90% male), average O2peak of 54.7 ± 7.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Supplements studied included bovine colostrum, probiotics, curcumin (Meriva), glutamine, L-cystine, carbohydrates (including hydrogel forms), sodium nitrate, high flavonoids, collagen peptides, capsaicin, and sodium bicarbonate. Exercise modalities included running, cycling, walking, cross-country skiing, and combinations. Environments ranged from hot/humid (>23°C) to thermoneutral (19–23°C) and cold (−5°C).

**Conclusion:** A significant increase in circulating i-FABP during exercise was observed, but changes in i-FABP, gastrointestinal symptoms, and exercise performance were outside of clinical relevance. Although probiotics showed a moderate significant effect for gastrointestinal symptoms, conflicting findings across studies may be due to inadequate control of confounding variables. The authors call for further research on alternative dietary supplements' effects on gastrointestinal health and exercise performance under varied environmental conditions with more rigorous control for confounding factors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Overall, there was no pooled effect of supplement interventions on gastrointestinal symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.42, 95% CI −0.17: 1.02, p = 0.15), and probiotics had a moderate significant effect for gastrointestinal symptoms (Hedges' g = −0.62, 95% CI −1.01; 1.01, p = 0.05)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: The Role of the Gut Microbiome and Probiotics in Sports Performance: A Narrative Review Update ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/4/690

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review article published in the journal Nutrients (2025, Vol 17, Issue 4, Article 690, DOI: 10.3390/nu17040690) titled "The Role of the Gut Microbiome and Probiotics in Sports Performance: A Narrative Review Update." The article is an open-access, Editor's Choice review authored by Harry Jarrett (Head of Science and Research at Heights supplement brand, London), Sophie Medlin (City Dietitians, London), and James C. Morehen (Liverpool John Moores University). The paper was received January 31, 2025, accepted February 13, 2025, and published February 14, 2025, with 15 citations and 14,814 views.

PURPOSE: The review investigates the mechanisms underpinning the ergogenic (performance-enhancing) benefits of probiotics and defines the current evidence base for specific performance domains (endurance and power).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Exercise impacts gut microbiome diversity: moderate-intensity exercise improves diversity, while sustained high-intensity exercise (elite athletes) significantly reduces microbial diversity due to hypoperfusion and immune system disturbance. In one ultramarathon study, 96% of runners experienced GI symptoms and 36% of non-finishers cited these as cause for stopping.
- ENDURANCE PERFORMANCE: Several RCTs show probiotics improve aerobic capacity and endurance. A 6-week intervention increased aerobic capacity by 6% in healthy adults. A 5-week probiotic intervention (Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, 10 billion CFU) significantly improved Cooper test distance in marathon runners and improved post-exercise muscle microperfusion (fMRI), plus improved mood. A 4-month intervention in cyclists increased time to exercise failure and 5% increase in VO2max. An 8-week intervention in female swimmers improved VO2max and reduced respiratory tract infections. In badminton players, a 6-week intervention produced a 6% increase in aerobic capacity and 16%/20% reductions in anxiety/stress.
- POWER PERFORMANCE: Limited but promising evidence. A meta-analysis found probiotics significantly improved global muscle strength and mass (most efficacious at 12 weeks with Bifidobacterium strains). In triathletes, probiotics improved mean power output and fatigue index. A 60-day probiotic+protein intervention in resistance-trained males increased one-rep max by 17% and vertical jump power by 8%. Probiotic+protein also reduced decline in peak power and improved recovery at 24h and 72h post-exercise.
- MECHANISMS: (1) Exercise recovery - probiotics reduced biomarkers of muscle injury (creatine kinase, myoglobin) and inflammation (CRP); improved muscle soreness, leg heaviness, and sleep in elite rugby players. (2) Nutrient absorption - 8-week probiotic supplementation in triathletes increased circulating BCAAs by 24-60%; probiotic+whey protein increased plasma-free amino acids and circulating isoleucine (34%), leucine (43%), and valine (32%); improved carbohydrate oxidation and iron status. (3) GI symptoms - a 90-day multistrain probiotic in elite cyclists significantly reduced GI symptoms at rest and during exercise; marathon runners on probiotics had fewer/less severe GI symptoms and maintained running speed better at race end. (4) Immune function - probiotics reduced upper respiratory tract illness frequency and severity in athletes (28-day and 4-month interventions); in 721 healthy adults, a synbiotic reduced illness episode frequency/duration by 30-45% over three winters. (5) Performance anxiety - a 6-week Lactobacillus Casei Shirota intervention reduced anxiety by 16% and stress by 20% in badminton players; in football players it increased delta and theta brain waves (attention/relaxation indicators).

CONCLUSIONS: The most substantial evidence supports multistrain probiotic interventions for improving endurance performance. Preliminary evidence suggests potential benefits for power performance, but further research is needed. Future research should examine combined prebiotic+probiotic (synbiotic) effects, isolated probiotic effects on power performance, optimal dosages/timings/strains, and psychological benefits. The review's limitations include its narrative (non-systematic) nature and the limited number of trials available.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The current evidence indicates that gut microbiome modulation by means of probiotic supplementation can have ergogenic benefits in regard to performance endurance."

### Causes of Exercise-Induced GI Complaints
The article identifies several multifactorial causes:

1. **Decreased GI Perfusion (Hypoperfusion):** Strenuous exercise triggers catecholamine release from the sympathetic nervous system, causing splanchnic vasoconstriction while shunting blood to the heart, lungs, muscles, and skin. This can lead to gut mucosal ischemia, increased mucosal permeability, and symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.

2. **Changes in Motility:** Heavy exercise can decrease peristalsis, reduce lower esophageal sphincter tone, and increase transient lower sphincter relaxation, linked to gastroesophageal reflux and impaired gastric emptying.

3. **Absorption and Gut Permeability:** High-intensity exercise compromises intestinal blood flow, leading to increased intestinal permeability, gut damage, impaired gut function, decreased nutrient absorption, and potentially a dysbiotic microbacterial environment with pathogenic bacteria and endotoxins entering the bloodstream.

4. **Mechanical Causes:** Repetitive high-impact mechanics and postures (common in runners and cyclists) can damage the intestinal lining. Poor posture, increased abdominal pressure, and aerophagia (swallowing air while drinking from water bottles) contribute to GI symptoms like flatulence, diarrhea, and urgency.

5. **Nutritional Causes:** Fiber, fat, protein, and fructose can cause GI symptoms. Concentrated carbohydrate solutions (beverages with high osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying. Beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose and fructose combined) reduce the likelihood of GI symptoms.

6. **NSAIDs:** Use of anti-inflammatory medications is associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction.

7. **Hyperthermia:** Heat exposure during exercise leads to intestinal ischemia from blood shunting; heat acclimatization and optimal hydration can help mitigate these effects.

8. **Dehydration:** Blood flow to the gut and liver can be reduced by up to 80% during exercise, adversely affecting nutrient absorption, motility, and mucosal integrity. GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume.

### Training the Gut
Conditioning the gut through practice can help athletes become more accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise, improving nutrient absorption and tolerance.

- Avoid high-fiber foods on competition day and for several days leading up to the event
- Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities (e.g., dairy, gluten)
- Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol)
- Avoid NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen
- Avoid high-fructose foods; a fructose-glucose combination may be better tolerated
- Avoid dehydration—prevention is key
- Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water
- Choose carbohydrate drinks with lower concentrations to prevent high osmolalities in the stomach
- Practice new nutrition strategies before race day

This demonstrates the gut's ability to withstand transient physiological hypoperfusion, but highlights potential risks for individuals with compromised vascular function, in whom such exercise-induced effects could lead to endotoxaemia and chronic inflammation. The study increases understanding of splanchnic hypoperfusion sequelae, relevant to critically ill patients and those with chronic conditions like heart failure.
</summary>

"Exercise-induced splanchnic hypoperfusion results in quantifiable small intestinal injury. Importantly, the extent of intestinal injury correlates with transiently increased small intestinal permeability, indicating gut barrier dysfunction in healthy individuals." (Abstract Conclusions), "The steepness of the gap g-a pCO₂ slope was most pronounced during the first 10 minutes of exercise, suggesting that functional splanchnic adaptations occur rapidly after altered perfusion demands in other parts of the body during physical activity." (Results), "The rapid decline in splanchnic perfusion during cycling was followed by the development of significant intestinal damage with a time lag of 20 minutes." (Discussion), "Our data imply that the healthy human small intestine can withstand transient hypoperfusion, since the observed enterocyte injury did not produce GI symptoms in our healthy individuals. However, prolonged episodes of hypoperfusion may cause more severe epithelial injury that may give rise to abdominal symptoms, as observed in endurance trained athletes." (Discussion), "In conclusion, our study demonstrates that a single, 60-minute bout of moderate-to-high intensity exercise is accompanied by splanchnic hypoperfusion and transient epithelial integrity loss in healthy young males, reflecting the ability of the gut to withstand to episodes of physiological stress with minor consequences." (Conclusion)

--- SOURCE 10: Gastroparesis ---
URL: https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/gastroparesis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) provides comprehensive information about gastroparesis, a gastrointestinal motility disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. CHOP uses a stricter definition than most published literature, requiring objective delay in gastric emptying while excluding mechanical obstruction, biochemical disorders (electrolyte imbalance, diabetes, hypothyroidism), gastric infections (H. pylori, CMV), medication side effects, and significant non-infectious gastroduodenal inflammation (eosinophilic gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn's disease, vasculitis).

Key content areas covered:

**Causes**: The exact cause is unknown; gastroparesis is a neuromuscular disorder involving antral hypomotility, gastric dysrhythmia, impaired fundic accommodation, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychological factors. Diabetes is the most frequently identified linked disease.

**Symptoms**: Early satiety, abdominal bloating, abdominal pain/burning, nausea, indigestion, episodic vomiting, fear of eating, feeding difficulty in infants, and weight loss. Symptoms are non-specific and don't distinguish gastroparesis from other causes. In children, gastroparesis often overlaps with GERD, functional dyspepsia, IBS, cyclical vomiting, enteric dysmotility, and pseudo-obstruction.

**Diagnosis**: The diagnostic process at CHOP's Suzi and Scott Lustgarten Center for GI Motility involves:
- Barium contrast upper GI series (rules out mechanical obstruction, malrotation, partial small bowel obstruction)
- Upper endoscopy (rules out H. pylori, peptic ulcer, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, celiac disease, Crohn's)
- Biochemical testing (rules out electrolyte, renal, and endocrine disorders)
- Gastric emptying study (the "gold standard" using radio-labeled solid meal; CHOP uses criteria of less than 10% emptying at 60 minutes or less than 50% at 2 hours as delayed, which is less strict than adult consensus guidelines)
- Antroduodenal manometry (measures muscle/nerve activity of stomach and small bowel over ~6 hours)

Notably, there is a lack of national standardization of pediatric test protocols, and normal pediatric values have not been established.

**Treatment**: No standardized medical therapy exists. CHOP uses a step-up symptom-based protocol with:
- Nutritional management: small frequent meals, avoiding high-fat and high-fiber foods, FODMAP diet, nutritional supplements (PediaSure, Boost), and for severe cases gastrostomy/jejunostomy tubes, venting gastrostomy, or central IV hyperalimentation
- Pharmacological therapies: Erythromycin, metoclopramide (high side effect profile including tardive dyskinesia), domperidone (FDA-regulated, requires cardiac monitoring), botulinum toxin (Botox), and cisapride (FDA-regulated, strict eligibility)
- Anti-nausea medications: ondansetron, granisetron, prochlorperazine, antihistamines, cyproheptadine, scopolamine patch
- Pain medications: tricyclic antidepressants, cyproheptadine, proton pump inhibitors
- Anti-bloating medications: simethicone, activated charcoal, rifaximin, Flagyl
- Non-pharmacological: child psychology support (stress management, CBT, relaxation therapy, biofeedback), social workers for school accommodations (504 planning)

**Outlook**: With successful diagnosis and treatment, children can lead relatively normal lives, attend school, get jobs, and have families, though they need ongoing medical follow-up into adulthood.

Contact information: Lustgarten Center at 215-590-1678.
</summary>

"Most published literature describes gastroparesis as delayed gastric emptying without a mechanical obstruction."

--- SOURCE 11: Abnormal gastric myoelectrical activity and delayed gastric emptying in patients with symptoms suggestive of gastroparesis - Johns Hopkins University ---
URL: https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/abnormal-gastric-myoelectrical-activity-and-delayed-gastric-empty-3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in 1996 in the journal Digestive Diseases and Sciences (Volume 41, Issue 8, pages 1538-1545) by J.D.Z. Chen, Zhiyue Lin, Jie Pan, and Richard W. McCallum. The study investigated the correlation between gastric myoelectrical activity and gastric emptying in 97 patients with symptoms suggestive of gastroparesis. Gastric myoelectrical activity was recorded using surface electrogastrography (EGG) for 30 minutes in the fasting state and 120 minutes after a solid test meal, with gastric emptying monitored simultaneously for 120 minutes. Key findings include: (1) patients with delayed gastric emptying showed a significantly lower percentage of normal gastric slow waves (P < 0.03) and a significantly reduced increase in dominant power in the postprandial EGG (P < 0.02); (2) postprandial gastric dysrhythmia predicted delayed gastric emptying with 78% accuracy, while abnormality in postprandial EGG power predicted it with 75% accuracy; (3) all patients with abnormalities in both rhythmicity and power had delayed gastric emptying; and (4) while postprandial EGG abnormalities can predict delayed emptying, a normal EGG does not guarantee normal gastric emptying. The article is associated with Scopus (PMID/scopus ID: 0029819577), has a DOI of 10.1007/BF02087897, and has been cited 245 times in Scopus.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: Intestinal Motility Disorders: Background, Etiology, Pathophysiology ---
URL: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/179937-overview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Medscape eMedicine article provides a comprehensive overview of intestinal motility disorders, which refer to abnormal intestinal contractions (spasms, paralysis) where the gut loses its ability to coordinate muscular activity due to endogenous or exogenous causes. The disorders are categorized as upper GI (gastroesophageal reflux disease, gastroparesis, achalasia, biliary dyskinesia) or lower GI (irritable bowel syndrome, colonic inertia, intestinal pseudo-obstruction/Ogilvie syndrome, pelvic floor dyssynergia, Hirschsprung disease, fecal incontinence, constipation).

**Etiology highlights:**
- Achalasia is primarily autoimmune; secondary causes include Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), iatrogenic surgical errors, and infiltrative diseases (tumors, amyloidosis)
- Gastroparesis etiologies: idiopathic (36%), diabetes mellitus (29%), postsurgical (13%)
- Colonic inertia involves dysfunction of the enteric nerve plexus with decreased/absent interstitial cells of Cajal
- Hirschsprung disease is congenital, from failure of neural crest cells to migrate during fetal development
- Fecal incontinence causes include aging, dementia, stroke, Parkinson disease, spinal cord injuries, diabetes, and surgical complications

**Pathophysiology:** GI motility requires coordinated contractions generated by nerves and muscles within GI walls. Intrinsic innervation (Auerbach/myenteric plexus) coordinates motor activity. The gastric pacemaker generates slow waves at 3 cycles per minute; migrating myoelectric complexes regulate gastric emptying every 90 minutes. Recent evidence suggests low-grade mucosal inflammation, immune activation (mast cell involvement), impaired epithelial barrier function, and aberrant neuronal sensitivity play roles in functional GI disorders. A Knowles-Martin classification categorizes disorders as well-defined entities, entities with variable dysfunction-symptom relations, questionable entities, and entities associated with behavioral disorders.

**Epidemiology:** Up to 30 million Americans have intestinal motility disorders; worldwide, 30-45% of all GI conditions are referable to these disorders. Idiopathic disorders have minimal morbidity and low mortality (1-1.5%), except intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Female-to-male ratio is 2.8:1. IBS occurs most frequently in ages 20-40; primary disorders are most common in white persons.

**Prognosis:** Generally good for primary disorders not secondary to malignancy. IBS and mild fecal incontinence have excellent prognosis. Intestinal pseudo-obstruction has high mortality (15-30%), usually due to delayed diagnosis. Constipation can lead to impaction, which may be fatal if unrecognized; impaction can cause vomiting, dehydration, hypoxia, and altered mental status.

**Patient Education:** Support groups include Association of Gastrointestinal Motility Disorders, Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome Association, Gastroparesis Patient Association for Cures and Treatment, International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders, and IBS Patient Support Group.

The article lists extensive references including guidelines from the European Society of Neurogastroenterology and Motility, European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, and American College of Radiology. Contributors include gastroenterologists and surgeons from multiple institutions including Wayne State University, Mount Sinai, and Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most common etiologies of gastroparesis noted in tertiary care centers include idiopathic (36%), diabetes mellitus (29%), and postsurgical (13%)."
</key_excerpts>
