--- SOURCE 13: Gastroparesis: Symptoms, Causes, Diagnosis & Treatment ---
URL: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/15522-gastroparesis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cleveland Clinic health article provides a comprehensive overview of gastroparesis, a condition meaning "paralysis of the stomach" that affects the nerves and muscles of the stomach, weakening and slowing muscle contractions needed to digest food and pass it to the intestines. Food consequently sits too long in the stomach.

**Types and Causes:** Gastroparesis is classified into subtypes based on cause: diabetes-related, post-surgical, and idiopathic (no identifiable cause). Between a quarter and a half of cases are idiopathic, while diabetes is the most common single cause (around one-third of cases). Diabetes-related gastroparesis occurs when high blood sugar damages nerves (a type of diabetic neuropathy) and blood vessels. Other causes include surgery injuring the vagus nerve, gastrointestinal infections (norovirus, rotavirus, bacterial), autoimmune disease (autoantibodies damaging stomach nerves), certain medications/recreational drugs that block nerve signals, and other less common causes.

**Symptoms:** Common symptoms include feeling full quickly and for long periods after eating, stomachache, nausea, vomiting, bloating/distension, and acid reflux (heartburn). A small subset of people experience persistent stomach pain, though pain severity is not connected to gastroparesis severity. Gastroparesis can also delay bowel movements and cause constipation.

**Complications:** Weight loss, malnutrition, dehydration, electrolyte deficiencies, acid reflux complications (heartburn, esophagitis), blood sugar fluctuations (dangerous for diabetics), and bezoars (hardened masses of undigested food that can block the stomach outlet, treated with medication or surgery).

**Diagnosis:** Providers take symptom/health history, use imaging tests to rule out physical obstruction, then gastric motility tests (gastric emptying studies, gastric emptying scintigraphy). An electrogastrogram (EGG) may be used if GES results are abnormal. Blood tests may identify antibodies or autoantibodies indicating cause.

**Treatment:** Providers cannot directly fix the underlying damage but can stimulate muscle contractions. Medications (prokinetics that stimulate gastrointestinal motility) are first-line treatment, with surgery as last resort. Treatment goals include relieving symptoms, improving nutrition, and managing blood sugar. Diet changes (less fiber and fat), nutritional therapy, tube/IV feeding, and IV fluids may be needed. Surgical procedures modify the stomach to help food pass.

**Prognosis:** Gastroparesis caused by short-term drug use or short-term infection may resolve. For most, it's not curable but is manageable with treatment, often requiring trial and error. It is generally not life-threatening, though severe complications (malnutrition, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, blood sugar fluctuations with diabetes) can be life-threatening if not managed. With appropriate care, risk is very small. Cleveland Clinic notes that while there's no quick fix, many treatment options exist, and scientists continue researching new approaches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Gastroparesis means paralysis of the stomach. It's a functional disorder affecting your stomach nerves and muscles. It makes your stomach muscle contractions weaker and slower than they need to be to digest your food and pass it on to your intestines."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: What is known about the health effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use in marathon and ultraendurance running: a scoping review | BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine ---
URL: https://bmjopensem.bmj.com/content/10/1/e001846

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scoping review published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine examining the health effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use in marathon and ultraendurance running. Authored by Eve Pannone and Rebecca Abbott (University of Exeter, UK), the review searched four databases (Cochrane Library, PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus) in February 2023 and identified 30 eligible studies published between 1987 and 2022, covering running events of 26.2 miles or longer.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: The review followed PRISMA scoping review guidelines and the Arksey and O'Malley five-step framework. Included studies comprised 4 randomised controlled trials, 1 cross-sectional study, 11 retrospective reviews, 4 case reports, 1 non-randomised control trial, and 9 prospective observational studies. The initial search found 194 articles, with 30 ultimately included after screening and exclusions. Studies were predominantly from the USA (n=15) and England (n=7). Ibuprofen was the most commonly reported NSAID (in 8 studies), followed by naproxen.

KEY FINDINGS BY HEALTH CONCERN:
1. Electrolyte balance and hyponatraemia (14 studies): Mixed results, with 6 studies showing no significant correlation, 6 showing a correlation between NSAID use and disturbed electrolytes, and 2 with insufficient data. One RCT (54 participants in the 160km Western States Endurance Run) found no significant alteration in serum electrolytes. A UK study found marathon runners taking ibuprofen had average serum Na decrease of 2.1 mmol/L vs. control increase of 2.3 mmol/L (p=0.0039), indicating increased hyponatraemia risk. A 2004 New Zealand study found an 8.3% increase in mean potassium levels in NSAID users (p=0.0007). A Davis et al study found 28% of runners hospitalized with severe hyponatraemia had taken NSAIDs vs. just 4.6% of those without.

2. Acute kidney injury (AKI) (6 studies): All reported a potential link between NSAID use and AKI, but none showed statistically significant results. One double-blind RCT found participants taking 400mg ibuprofen during a multi-stage ultra-race were more likely to develop AKI (22 of 42 vs. 16 of 47 placebo, p=0.14). A retrospective case series of four runners developing AKI after the 89km Comrade's Marathon (South Africa) found three had ingested NSAIDs during the race. A 2020 case report described a runner developing AKI after a 110km ultramarathon after consuming 500mg naproxen immediately before the race.

3. GI disturbances (4 studies): None found a clear correlation between NSAID use and GI issues. One prospective observational study found significant increases in faecal blood loss during marathon running exacerbated by analgesic consumption, but not clinically important. Case reports of Boerhaave's syndrome and ischaemic colitis were documented but NSAID causation was not established.

4. Oxidative stress and muscle damage (3 studies): All three found statistically significant results, but mixed direction - two found increased oxidative stress and one found decreased. An RCT found lower creatine kinase levels in ibuprofen users suggesting lower oxidative stress. A non-randomised trial of 160km ultrarunners found significantly increased F2 iso-prostanes (oxidative stress marker) in ibuprofen users (1800mg total). An observational study of Western States 100 found 25-88% higher plasma cytokine levels in the ibuprofen group.

5. Other medical concerns: A 2012 RCT found NSAIDs blunt the exercise-induced increase in collagen synthesis in the patellar tendon. A case report of cardiac injury (viral acute pericarditis) suggested NSAIDs may have masked symptoms rather than caused them.

CONCLUSIONS: The review found very limited evidence that NSAIDs negatively impact the health of ultrarunning athletes. Potential links were shown especially for AKI and electrolyte balance, but indications from a few non-randomised studies need exploring with more high-quality research. Major limitations include small sample sizes (only 7 of 30 studies had over 100 participants), only 4 RCTs, lack of consistency in NSAID type/dose, and confounding external factors (heat, hydration, race profile). The review recommends larger randomised controlled studies, consideration of body-weight-adjusted dosing, research on different NSAID types/doses, and investigation of external contributory factors. While some biochemical markers showed significant changes, these did not affect performance or overall health, raising questions about whether practice guidelines need changing. The authors note the 'perfect storm' hypothesis where NSAID use combines with heat stress and dehydration to cause AKI.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This review suggests there is very limited evidence to show that NSAIDs have a negative impact on the health of ultrarunning athletes. Indications from a few non-randomised studies of a possible effect on kidney function need exploring with more high-quality research."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The use of pain killers (NSAIDs) in athletes: How large is the risk? - ScienceDirect ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1440244024005851

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a cornerstone review article published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (Volume 28, Issue 3, March 2025, Pages 198-205) titled "The use of pain killers (NSAIDs) in athletes: How large is the risk?" authored by Daniel Fitzpatrick, Todd Leckie, Gunnar Heine, and Luke Hodgson (DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2024.11.010). The article was published by Sports Medicine Australia via Elsevier.

KEY FINDINGS:
- NSAID use is highly prevalent in sport, particularly in professional football, where it is sometimes used routinely without medical indication or supervision. Exact prevalence estimates are difficult due to inconsistent reporting methods across sports.
- In recreational sport, a UK survey found 68% of amateur endurance athletes reported NSAID use for sport-related analgesia in the preceding year (88.4% of triathletes, 70.9% of runners, 52.5% of cyclists). A UK 'Parkrun' study found 57% of respondents had taken NSAIDs before a run and 67.7% after running.
- NSAIDs have good evidence for use following acute injury, but may prevent normal tissue healing and remodelling if used longer term for musculoskeletal injuries.
- A Cochrane review on NSAID use in acute soft tissue injury found no benefit over paracetamol for pain at 1 hour or in the first week after injury.
- Known risks include cardiac, gastrointestinal, and renal side effects, though little specific data exists for athletes.

ADVERSE EFFECTS:
- GASTROINTESTINAL: Most common adverse events; dyspepsia occurs in 10% of NSAID users; risk of significant upper GI events (ulcers, perforations, bleeding) increased 2-4 times by NSAID use; risk increases with higher dosages or multiple concurrent NSAIDs.
- CARDIOVASCULAR: Increased risk of major coronary events, stroke, heart failure, and atrial arrhythmias, primarily via COX-2 inhibition leading to vasoconstriction, increased prothrombotic molecules, reduced sodium excretion, and increased intravascular volume.
- RENAL: A systematic review (Zhang et al.) of 1,609,163 participants found pooled odds ratio of 1.7 (95% CI 1.4-2.1) for acute kidney injury with current NSAID exposure, higher in older people (OR 2.5). NSAIDs combined with dehydration and concurrent illness can produce significant renal and systemic insult. NSAIDs may also contribute to exercise-induced hyponatremia by inhibiting prostaglandins that normally suppress vasopressin activity.
- MUSCULOSKELETAL: NSAIDs may impair optimal healing following injury or surgery.
- EXERTIONAL HEAT ILLNESS (EHI): NSAIDs do not reduce hyperthermia in EHI and should not be used in acute treatment; they may actually increase EHI risk by reducing gastric mucosa integrity.

CLINICAL RECOMMENDATIONS:
- The "lowest effective dose for the shortest duration" principle should apply.
- Multiple consensus statements support NSAID use in the first 14 days after ligamentous injury.
- Clinicians should use a pragmatic prescribing framework such as the 'Keeping SCORE' approach, which incorporates safety checks, appraisal of clinical indication, open dialogue, and accurate administration.
- Health care professionals should be aware that NSAID use is likely higher than reported and should aim to prescribe in a rational, safe manner.
- Personalised risk stratification is vital to mitigating NSAID risk.

The review notes that NSAIDs are a major cause of adverse drug reactions requiring hospital admission in the USA and UK, and use is often driven by performance pressures and a 'macho culture' in sport, sometimes used prophylactically for important games.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Use is very high in sports such as professional football and is sometimes by routine without indication and without medical supervision. However there is a paucity of evidence in other sports." "There is good evidence for use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs following an acute injury but they may prevent normal tissue healing and remodelling if used longer term for musculoskeletal injuries." "Renal events are discussed in detail including the cumulative effect that nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, dehydration and concurrent illness can have to produce significant renal and systemic insult." "One survey of amateur endurance athletes in the United Kingdom (UK) found that 68 % of athletes reported NSAID use for sport related analgesia in the preceding year. This was higher in triathletes (88.4 %) than runners (70.9 %) or cyclists (52.5 %)." "From 1,609,163 participants, the pooled odds ratio (OR) for current NSAID exposure was 1.7 (95 % CI 1.4 to 2.1), with higher risk observed in older people (OR 2.5, 95 % CI 1.5 to 2.7)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: NSAIDs and Stomach Risk: Ibuprofen & Naproxen Dangers ---
URL: https://corycalendinemd.com/blog/the-hidden-dangers-of-ibuprofen-and-naproxen-protecting-your-digestive-system-from-nsaids

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a blog article from Dr. Cory Calendine, MD, a board-certified, fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon at the Bone and Joint Institute of Tennessee in Franklin, TN, specializing in hip and knee replacement. The article educates patients about the hidden digestive dangers of NSAIDs like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve).

KEY POINTS:
- NSAIDs are the second leading cause of stomach ulcers (after bacterial infection). They work by blocking COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes; blocking COX-1 strips the protective mucus barrier from the stomach lining, exposing it to stomach acid.
- Key statistics: ~1/3 of NSAID users develop digestive symptoms; 2-4% of chronic users develop serious complications like bleeding ulcers each year; up to 70% of long-term users show stomach damage on imaging even when they feel fine; only ~10% of people with that damage notice warning symptoms.
- Risk varies by NSAID: Naproxen carries ~5.6x baseline bleeding risk; Diclofenac ~4.0x; Ibuprofen ~2.7x; COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) ~1.9x. Switching from naproxen to ibuprofen may cut stomach-bleeding risk by more than half.
- Higher-risk groups include: age 65+, prior stomach ulcers, taking blood thinners/aspirin, corticosteroids/SSRIs, H. pylori infection, high doses or long-term use. Patients on blood thinners plus NSAIDs face more than double the bleeding risk.
- Warning signs: black/tarry stools, blood in stool, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, severe stomach pain, unexplained fatigue, dizziness/lightheadedness.
- Protection strategies: lowest effective dose for shortest time, alternating with acetaminophen (Tylenol), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs like omeprazole), COX-2 inhibitors, topical NSAIDs, physical therapy, and testing/treating H. pylori before long-term use.
- Small intestine damage is harder to detect and treat; combining NSAIDs with a PPI may worsen small-intestine problems while protecting the stomach. Some clinicians prefer a COX-2 inhibitor alone.
- Drug interactions: ibuprofen can blunt aspirin's heart-protective effect, so aspirin should be taken at least 2 hours before ibuprofen.
- The article is by Dr. Cory Calendine (performs 700+ hip and knee replacements annually, Stryker consultant for Mako robotic platform), who sees patients at 3000 Edward Curd Lane, Franklin, TN (Williamson Medical Center campus, I-65 Exit 65), phone (615) 791-2630, no referral required. Includes a medical disclaimer that the article is educational only and not a substitute for professional medical advice.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NSAIDs are the second leading cause of stomach ulcers, after bacterial infection. Medications like Advil, Motrin, and Aleve work by blocking pain-causing enzymes, but they also strip away the stomach's protective mucus barrier. That leaves the digestive tract exposed to its own acid and raises the risk of internal bleeding."

--- SOURCE 6: P158 A Systematic Review of the Low FODMAP Diet as a Treatment for Gastrointestinal Distress in Endurance Athletes ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1499404622003281

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an abstract of a systematic review (P158) published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior (Volume 54, Issue 7, Supplement, July 2022, Page S93), presented at the 55th Annual Conference on Re-engineering Nutrition Education and Behavior. The review examines the Low FODMAP (fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide, and polyol) diet as a treatment for gastrointestinal (GI) distress in endurance athletes. 

Background: GI distress affects 30-50% of endurance athletes and can result in underperformance. Common symptoms include gas, intestinal cramping, urge to defecate, loose stools, and diarrhea. The Low FODMAP diet has been shown to reduce GI symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome patients, and emerging research suggests benefits for exercise-related GI distress.

Methodology: A systematic search of PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar databases was conducted, along with bibliography searching. The review identified 111 records, removed 60 duplicates, screened 51 records, excluded 35 by title/abstract, assessed 16 full-text articles, and ultimately included 7 studies meeting inclusion criteria. Of these, three were randomized controlled trials, two were observational, and two were case studies.

Results: Six of the seven articles showed reduced GI symptom severity after short-term Low FODMAP implementation. However, in three studies, athletes were unable to meet estimated energy requirements and expressed difficulty following the restrictive diet while maintaining training loads.

Conclusions: The review highlights the scarcity of research on Low FODMAP for GI distress in endurance athletes. Short-term Low FODMAP use shows promising evidence as a beneficial intervention, but more research is needed on best approaches for educating athletes on adherence while maintaining appropriate fueling practices given the diet's restrictive nature. Funding: None. The study authors are Grace Thomas BS, Jackie Buell PhD, RDN, CSSD, ATC, and Julie Kennel PhD, RDN, LD.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog article from Epicured (a healthcare food company specializing in low FODMAP meals) titled "The Low FODMAP Athlete: How to Handle the Low FODMAP Diet While Training," published on July 30, 2021. The article addresses the challenges endurance athletes face with gastrointestinal (GI) issues, which affect an estimated 30-90% of athletes around athletic events.

Key content includes:
- Causes of athlete GI issues: blood flow redirected away from organs toward muscles during vigorous exercise, heightened anxiety before events, dehydration from high temperatures, and contorted postures (e.g., cyclists/triathletes) putting pressure on the intestines.
- The low FODMAP diet is challenging for athletes because many nutrient-dense whole grain carbohydrates used for "carb loading" are high in FODMAPs. Alternative low FODMAP carbs include gluten-free bread and pasta, rice, quinoa, baked potatoes, and oats.
- High-fiber foods should be avoided on event day; sugar alcohols, beans/legumes, and lactose are major FODMAP offenders.
- High-FODMAP foods to watch include apples, pears, onions, garlic, stone fruits, and cauliflower.
- Recommendations include working with a Registered Dietitian (RD) trained in sports nutrition, especially during the three phases of the elimination diet (elimination, reintroduction, personalization).
- The low FODMAP diet should generally be temporary (about 4 weeks) for athletes, followed by reintroduction of foods individually.
- Avoid major dietary changes before a big event; experiment with pre-game meals many times in advance.
- Basic non-dietary tips: get enough sleep, stay hydrated, and avoid excessive stress.

The article cites four references from scientific and nutrition sources, including research from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (Sports Med journal) and Spartan Race's nutrition blog. The page also includes Epicured branding and promotional content for their low FODMAP meal delivery service.
</summary>

This is SSE #114 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published in May 2013 and authored by Erick Prado de Oliveira. The article provides nutritional recommendations to avoid gastrointestinal (GI) distress during exercise, particularly for endurance athletes.

**Key Statistics on GI Problems in Athletes:**
- 30% to 90% of distance runners experience exercise-related intestinal problems, depending on methodology and events studied
- In exhausting endurance events, 30-50% of participants suffer from one or more GI symptoms (Brouns & Beckers, 1993)
- Up to 93% of long-distance triathletes in extreme conditions reported any GI symptom; 43% reported serious GI problems and 7% abandoned the race due to GI issues (Jeukendrup et al., 2000)
- 70% of elite endurance athletes reported exercise-induced GI symptoms (Peters et al., 1999)
- In an internet-based study of 1,281 athletes, 45% reported at least one GI symptom (Ter Steege et al., 2008)
- Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon running/cycling up to 32% in Ironman races (Pfeiffer et al., 2011)
- Athletes not accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise had a two-fold risk of GI symptoms compared to accustomed athletes

**Causes of GI Problems:**
1. **Splanchnic hypoperfusion** - During maximal exercise, splanchnic blood flow may be reduced by up to 80% to supply working muscle and skin. Norepinephrine release induces splanchnic vasoconstriction, which can lead to gut mucosal ischemia and increased mucosal permeability.
2. **Changes in motility** - Decreased esophageal peristalsis and lower esophageal sphincter tone, increased transient sphincter relaxation, and altered gastric emptying (mainly at high exercise intensities).
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** - Studies show increased intestinal permeability after marathons, though effects are inconclusive at moderate intensities. Symptomatic runners showed greater permeability than asymptomatic runners.
4. **Mechanical causes** - Repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut; symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists. Posture (e.g., "aero" position on bicycles) and swallowing air can contribute.
5. **Nutritional causes** - Fiber, fat, protein, fructose, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>500 mOsm/L osmolality) are associated with increased GI symptoms. Dairy products and mild lactose intolerance can cause problems.

**Prevention Guidelines:**
- **Avoid milk products** containing lactose (use lactose-free, soy, rice, or almond milk alternatives)
- **Avoid high-fiber foods** in the day(s) before competition; choose processed white foods (regular pasta, white rice, plain bagels) instead of whole grains
- **Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen) as they increase intestinal permeability; NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI complications
- **Avoid high-fructose foods** and exclusively-fructose drinks (though fructose with glucose may be better tolerated)
- **Avoid dehydration**; start races well hydrated
- **Practice new nutrition strategies** by experimenting with pre-race and race-day plans many times before race day
- **"Train the gut"** - A study by Cox et al. (2010) showed that 28 days of high-carbohydrate training improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates, attributed to improved intestinal absorption

**Serious Symptoms:** Mucosal erosions, ischemic colitis, blood loss in feces, hemorrhagic gastritis, and small bowel infarction have been reported in endurance athletes, occasionally requiring surgery.

The article concludes that GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and that nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion.
</summary>

**Study Background:** While GI discomfort during endurance exercise has been well-documented, only one prior study measured increased GI injury markers following resistance exercise coinciding with decreased nutrient absorption. <webpage_content>
Powered by **Outside**

# Ask Stacy: Should I take Anti-Diarrheal Meds Before a Race?

"Dear Stacy: I've heard some triathletes take anti-diarrheal medicines like Imodium before a race to prevent GI distress. Is this a good idea?"

![A row of port-a-potties, which some athletes try to avoid by taking Imodium before a race](https://cdn.triathlete.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Featured-6-2.jpg?auto=webp&width=3840&quality=75&fit=cover)

(Photo: Getty Images)

[Dr. Stacy Sims](/byline/dr-stacy-sims)

Published August 10, 2022 06:00AM

***Dear Stacy: I’ve heard some triathletes take anti-diarrheal medicines like Imodium before a race to prevent GI distress. Is this a good idea?***

The short answer is “no,” especially if you will be racing in warm to hot conditions. Imodium (Loperamide) is designed to slow gut motility in resting conditions, but it should not be used in high stress, high sweat, long duration exercise; the primary mechanism of action is to slow gut motility by altering water and electrolyte movement through the bowel. The drug binds to an opiate receptor in the gut wall, and inhibits the release of chemicals responsible for intestinal muscle contraction; thus increasing intestinal transit time.

There is also an increased risk of heart rhythm disruption (QT prolongation), due to dehydration coupled with lower blood levels of magnesium and potassium. Although loperamide alters the intestinal transport of water and electrolytes by increasing absorption, it does the opposite with glucose and other nutrients from the small intestines. From a fueling standpoint, the use of loperamide has a direct effect on glucose utilization: the activation of those opioid receptors in the gut wall  also increases glucose utilization in the peripheral tissues and  increases liver gluconeogenesis. The long and the short of it is that by using Imodium, you are reducing absorption of nutrients from the intestines, which reduces blood glucose and the ability to regenerate glucose for fueling your race. Because loperamide reduces fluid and electrolyte movement into the intestines, (to reduce loose stools), there can be a misstep in fluid and electrolyte balance thermoregulation (sweating and blood flow) during exercise.

ADVERTISEMENT

***RELATED:**[The Fine Art (and Science) of Fueling for Hot Races](https://www.triathlete.com/nutrition/the-fine-art-and-science-of-fueling-for-hot-races/)*

 ![](https://cdn.triathlete.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Featured-7-1.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

(Photo: Getty Images)

 

## What to do instead of taking Imodium before your race

If you’re concerned about GI distress during your race, you can try activated charcoal or attapulgite to help reduce gut motility and absorb toxins or irritants that are in the intestines. But the best option is to control as many factors to prevent the onset of gastrointestinal problems.

First, let’s unpack what is happening to cause GI distress. The exact cause of runner’s diarrhea is not really known, but there are several common factors that can exacerbate the risk; causing a  sprint to the nearest port-a-potty instead of the finish line.

1. The physical jostling of the organs due to the up and down motion of running.
2. Decreased blood flow to the intestines. When we run, our bodies divert the blood flow from the intestines to the working muscles and skin (to offload heat), which causes a disruption in normal digestion.
3. Increased intestinal hormone secretion. This hormonal imbalance inevitably speeds up the digestive process.
4. An increased amount of concentrated carbohydrates (e.g. gels, sports drinks) or introduction of a new food.
5. Pre-race anxiety and stress.

***RELATED:**[Ask Stacy: How Can I Deal With GI Distress in the Heat?](https://www.triathlete.com/nutrition/ask-stacy-how-can-i-avoid-gi-distress-in-the-heat/)*

## You probably don’t need Imodium before your race – try these strategies to prevent GI distress

Let’s look at dietary changes to make in the week leading up to the race.

**At least two days before your race**, limit or avoid high-fiber and gas-producing foods, such as beans, bran, fruit, and salad.

**In the three to six hours before racing,** limit or avoid high-fat foods. If you are not in need of a pre-race caffeine hit, it is best to avoid it as caffeine stimulates gut motility, which can lead to loose stools or diarrhea. Avoid/limit sugar substitutes such as sorbitol and sucralose, dairy products or any foods known to cause loose stools or flatulence for several days prior to the race. You will want to check your sports nutrition products as many companies are including sorbitol, mannitol, or xylitol to increase the sweetness with a sugar reduction; these sugar alcohols are notorious for increasing gas, bloating, and loose stools when consumed in moderate amounts.

Critical to race performance is also critical to avoiding GI distress: hydrate, both in the days before your race and on race day. Since dehydration can lead to diarrhea, check your levels of hydration by aiming to produce a very light yellow urine color before you begin your race.

ADVERTISEMENT

**On race morning,** be cautious of consuming energy gels and high carbohydrate sports drinks, especially if you have not trained with such products before. It is well known that these products can contribute to diarrhea by increasing the osmotic pressure in the intestines; drawing water *into* the intestines. Always avoid introducing a new food or supplement on race day.

Race morning nervousness and anxiety can definitely cause a neural trigger for gastrointestinal distress. By implementing mindfulness and a structured pre-race plan, the familiarity of the routine can help calm you down, reducing the risk for GI issues.

During the race, slow down if you experience GI distress. Yes, it is a race, but the goal is to get to the finish line! By slowing down, you will reduce the amount of heat your body is producing (from the working muscles) and will help redistribute some of your blood to the gut. This reperfusion will increase oxygen to the intestinal cells and help reduce the permeability of your intestinal cells. Eat something bland (crackers, pretzels) and stay away from warm fluids, gels, other concentrated liquid carbohydrate, salt tablets, and caffeine- all which have been shown to promote GI permeability and disrupt fluid balance of the gut.

ADVERTISEMENT

If you still have concerns and issues, Imodium can be a last resort, but know that you will need to adjust your fueling and hydration plan to accommodate the changes the loperamide induces in the gut.

This is an "Ask Stacy" advice column by Dr. Stacy Sims, published on Triathlete.com on August 10, 2022, addressing whether triathletes should take anti-diarrheal medications like Imodium (Loperamide) before a race to prevent GI distress.

**Core Answer:** Dr. Sims' short answer is "no," especially for racing in warm to hot conditions. Imodium is designed to slow gut motility in resting conditions but should not be used during high stress, high sweat, long-duration exercise. Key risks and drawbacks include:
- Heart rhythm disruption (QT prolongation) risk due to dehydration coupled with low blood magnesium and potassium levels.
- Reduced absorption of glucose and other nutrients from the small intestines (while increasing water/electrolyte absorption), which reduces blood glucose and the ability to regenerate glucose for race fueling.
- Potential missteps in fluid and electrolyte balance thermoregulation (sweating and blood flow) during exercise.

**Causes of GI distress during running (runner's diarrhea):**
1. Physical jostling of organs from the up-and-down motion of running.
2. Decreased blood flow to the intestines (blood is diverted to working muscles and skin).
3. Increased intestinal hormone secretion, which speeds up digestion.
4. Increased concentrated carbohydrates (gels, sports drinks) or introduction of new foods.
5. Pre-race anxiety and stress.

**Alternatives and prevention strategies instead of Imodium:**
- Try activated charcoal or attapulgite to reduce gut motility and absorb toxins/irritants.
- At least two days before the race: limit/avoid high-fiber and gas-producing foods (beans, bran, fruit, salad).
- In the 3-6 hours before racing: limit/avoid high-fat foods, caffeine (stimulates gut motility), sugar substitutes (sorbitol, sucralose, mannitol, xylitol - sugar alcohols that cause gas, bloating, and loose stools), and dairy.
- Hydrate properly (aim for very light yellow urine before racing).
- On race morning: be cautious with energy gels and high-carb sports drinks, especially untested products; never introduce new foods/supplements on race day.
- Use mindfulness and a structured pre-race routine to reduce nervousness/anxiety.
- During the race: slow down if GI distress occurs to reduce heat production and allow blood redistribution to the gut; eat bland foods (crackers, pretzels); avoid warm fluids, gels, concentrated liquid carbs, salt tablets, and caffeine.
- Imodium can be a "last resort," but athletes must adjust their fueling and hydration plans to accommodate the changes loperamide induces in the gut.

# What Causes Runner’s Diarrhea? Plus Tips to Prevent it

![](//i0.wp.com/post.healthline.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Jared-Meacham-500x500-Bio.png?w=105&h=105)

Medically reviewed by Jared Meacham, PhD., RD, CSCS — Written by Kathryn Watson — Updated on November 24, 2025

Runner’s diarrhea may occur because exercise can cause the intestines to allow more substances to pass into the bloodstream. Avoiding foods like FODMAPs, protein, and dairy may help.

Runner’s diarrhea, also called “runner’s colitis” and “runner’s trots,” refers to a condition that affects runners during and after a run.

Long-distance runners (those who run 3 miles or more at a given time) are the most likely to experience this. When you have runner’s diarrhea, you experience frequent bowel movements during and right after your run.

About [30% to 90%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4008808/) of endurance runners experience exercise-induced gastrointestinal disturbances, according to one 2014 review of earlier research.

While experts aren’t completely clear on what causes this, there are ways to identify and manage runner’s diarrhea.

Keep reading to learn what experts think may cause runner’s diarrhea, the symptoms and how long they last, and tips for preventing it, including foods and drinks to avoid before a run.

## What causes runner’s diarrhea?

While researchers do not understand exactly what causes runner’s diarrhea, it may be related to changes in intestinal permeability that happen when you’re running or doing other challenging endurance exercise, such as:

* cycling
* swimming
* skiing
* multisport training

According to a [2017 study,](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5694518) running at a challenging pace for 90 minutes can temporarily damage the small intestine, increasing the substances that pass from it into your bloodstream. However, not all participants experienced digestive symptoms, so it’s unclear if this intestinal permeability is the cause, one of mulitple contributing factors, or unrelated.

Other [research from 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10610183/) suggests that endurance exercise may:

* decrease gastric motility and emptying (the rate at which nutrients pass through your intestines)
* increase bacterial translocution (the process by which bacteria from the gastrointestinal tract pass through the intestinal wall to other parts of the body, like the lymph nodes, liver, and bloodstream)
* alter intestinal permeability (affecting the amount of substances that pass from it into your bloodstream)

Together, these factors may cause exercise-induced nutrient malabsorption and contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms.

## What are the symptoms of runner’s diarrhea?

Actual [diarrhea](https://www.healthline.com/symptom/diarrhea) is only one of the symptoms of runner’s diarrhea. Other symptoms you may experience include:

* gas
* acid reflux
* nausea
* cramping

It’s also possible to have gastrointestinal symptoms from running without having diarrhea.

## How long does it last?

The symptoms of runner’s diarrhea will typically begin during your workout and may continue in the hours after you’re done running.

Runner’s diarrhea shouldn’t last for more than 24 hours. If you get diarrhea during a run and your loose bowel movements don’t stop, it may be due to another medical condition, such as an infection, food intolerance, or health condition affecting your digestive system.

**»Learn more:**[Diarrhea: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatments](https://www.healthline.com/health/diarrhea)

## How do you treat runner’s diarrhea so you can keep running?

If you regularly get runner’s diarrhea, you may be able to prevent or manage it so it doesn’t get in the way of your runs.

### Taking over-the-counter (OTC) treatments before a run

OTC treatments, such as bismuth subsalicylate ([Pepto Bismol](https://www.healthline.com/health/diarrhea/pepto-bismol)) and loperamide ([Imodium](https://www.healthline.com/health/diarrhea/imodium)), might be an option to stall the diarrhea until after your run.

Note that taking these medications on an empty stomach may make you feel ill.

### Making changes to your diet before and after a run

There are steps that you can take to decrease your chances of experiencing runner’s diarrhea.

Most of the treatment relates to your diet, particularly what you choose to eat in the hours and days prior to a long run.

In the days before a run, endurance runners in a [2020 survey](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7288429) commonly avoided:

* meat (32%)
* milk products (31%)
* fish/seafood (28%)
* poultry (24%)
* high-fiber foods (23%)

However, it’s possible that some of these foods may not bother you and that others may. What foods you avoid before a run can also depend on any food intolerances you may have.

### Avoiding tight clothing

You may also consider what you wear while you’re running, as clothing that’s too tight around the midsection can constrict blood flow to your digestive tract and make your symptoms more uncomfortable.

### Treating underlying conditions

You might also want to try to determine if you have lactose intolerance or an underlying condition such as [irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)](https://www.healthline.com/health/irritable-bowel-syndrome).

## Tips to prevent runner’s diarrhea

You may be able to prevent runner’s diarrhea by adjusting your diet in the days leading up to a run.

### What to avoid eating

According to [2017 research](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27798441/), this can include avoiding:

* [dehydration](https://www.healthline.com/health/dehydration) by [staying hydrated](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/how-much-water-should-you-drink-per-day)
* [fiber](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/high-fiber-foods-chart)
* fat
* protein
* high concentrated carbohydrate beverages, like fruit juice, sugary soda, and sugary sports drinks
* [caffeine](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/what-is-caffeine), such as tea, coffee, and energy drinks
* [nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs)](https://www.healthline.com/health/side-effects-from-nsaids) like [ibuprofen](https://www.healthline.com/health/drugs/ibuprofen-tablet) (Advil, Motrin) and [naproxen](https://www.healthline.com/health/naproxen-oral-tablet) (Aleve)
* [FODMAPs](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/fodmaps), a group of fermentable carbohydrates that includes wheat and other grains, many fruits and vegetables, pulses and legumes, dairy products, and sugar-free sweeteners like sorbitol, mannitol, and xylitol

**»Learn more:**[What Common Foods Can Cause Diarrhea?](https://www.healthline.com/health/foods-that-cause-diarrhea)

### What to eat before a run

In the two hours before your run is set to begin, try to avoid eating anything besides a quick energy-boosting snack, like whole wheat toast or a banana.

Avoid caffeine of any kind in the time period immediately before you run, as it works as a diuretic. If you tend to have runner’s diarrhea, try cutting back on artificial sweeteners, sugars, and alcohol the evening prior to your run.

Avoid energy gel packs and supplements that are supposed to provide easy, portable “fuel” during a run. Many contain artificial sweeteners and preservatives that can trigger diarrhea.

Above all, always stay hydrated before, during, and after your run. Staying hydrated can help improve your athletic performance and prevent dehydration-related symptoms, like [muscle cramps](https://www.healthline.com/health/dehydration-cramps).

**»Learn more:**[What to Eat Before Running](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/what-to-eat-before-running)

## When to talk with a doctor

If you regularly experience diarrhea that is affecting your ability to run, it’s best to talk with a healthcare professional, such as a [primary care physician](https://www.healthline.com/health/how-to-choose-a-primary-care-physician), [dietitian](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/dietitian-vs-nutritionist), or a sports medicine specialist.

A sports medicine specialist is a doctor who specializes in health conditions affecting those who play sports who may be able to recommend changes to your running routine that can help reduce bothersome symptoms, including diarrhea.

If you experience diarrhea, you should take steps to prevent for dehydration. Diarrhea causes you to lose more water through your stool than is typical. Along with sweating from running, it may increase your risk of dehydration, which can cause symptoms like:

* fatigue
* [decreased urination](https://www.healthline.com/health/urine-output-decreased)
* increase thirst
* [dry mouth](https://www.healthline.com/health/dry-mouth), [eyes](https://www.healthline.com/health/dry-eyes), or [skin](https://www.healthline.com/health/dry-skin)
* [constipation](https://www.healthline.com/health/constipation)
* [dizziness](https://www.healthline.com/health/dizziness) or [lightheadedness](https://www.healthline.com/health/lightheadedness)
* [headache](https://www.healthline.com/health/dehydration-headache)

You can counteract mild dehydration by drinking electrolyte-containing liquids, like certain [sports drinks](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/sports-drinks) and [coconut water](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/coconut-water-diarrhea).

If you experience symptoms of severe dehydration, you may need urgent medical attention to help you rehydrate using an IV solution.

Symptoms of [severe dehydration](https://www.healthline.com/health/severe-dehydration) can include:

* severe [heart palpitations](https://www.healthline.com/health/dehydration-and-heart-palpitations)
* acute headache that comes on suddenly
* [fainting](https://www.healthline.com/health/fainting) or loss of consciousness
* bloody or [black stool](https://www.healthline.com/health/bloody-or-tarry-stools)
* diarrhea that lasts for 24 hours or more

**»FIND CARE:**[https://care.healthline.com/find-care/specialty/sports-medicine Find a sports medicine specialist in your area today.](https://care.healthline.com/find-care/specialty/sports-medicine)

## Frequently asked questions

Runner’s diarrhea is common and may affect between [30% to 90%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4008808/) of endurance runners.

You can take OTC medications like bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto Bismol) and loperamide (Imodium) to prevent runner’s diarrhea. However, taking either on an empty stomach may cause other digestive symptoms.

The dumping syndrome after running refers to runner’s diarrhea. Endurance running can affect the digestive system and cause malabsorption that results in loose, watery stools during and after running.

## The bottom line

By experimenting with what you eat and what time of day you run, you may be able to stop runner’s diarrhea from happening during your runs.

Make sure to drink enough fluids to avoid dehydration.

The sweat you lose during a long run, in addition to diarrhea, can compound your risk of losing too much fluid. If you have tried to change your diet and your running habits and you’re still experiencing runner’s diarrhea, you may need to speak with a healthcare professional, such as a primary care doctor, dietitian, or a sports medicine specialist.

**Causes:** While not fully understood, runner's diarrhea may relate to changes in intestinal permeability during endurance exercise. A 2017 study found running at a challenging pace for 90 minutes can temporarily damage the small intestine. Research from 2023 suggests endurance exercise may decrease gastric motility, increase bacterial translocation, and alter intestinal permeability, together causing nutrient malabsorption and GI symptoms. About 30-90% of endurance runners experience exercise-induced gastrointestinal disturbances (per a 2014 review).

Dietary changes are key: a 2020 survey found runners commonly avoided meat (32%), milk products (31%), fish/seafood (28%), poultry (24%), and high-fiber foods (23%). Foods/drinks to avoid before runs include fiber, fat, protein, concentrated carb beverages, caffeine, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), and FODMAPs. In the two hours before a run, only a quick snack like whole wheat toast or banana is advised. Avoiding tight clothing around the midsection, staying hydrated, and treating underlying conditions (lactose intolerance, IBS) can help.

**When to see a doctor:** If diarrhea regularly affects running ability, consult a primary care physician, dietitian, or sports medicine specialist. Diarrhea combined with sweating increases dehydration risk. Severe dehydration symptoms (heart palpitations, fainting, bloody/black stool, diarrhea lasting 24+ hours) require urgent medical attention.

# About loperamide - Brand name: Imodium

Loperamide is a medicine to treat [diarrhoea](/symptoms/diarrhoea-and-vomiting/) (runny poo). It can help with short-term diarrhoea or [irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)](/conditions/irritable-bowel-syndrome-ibs/).

Loperamide is also used for recurring or longer lasting diarrhoea from bowel conditions such as [Crohn's disease](/conditions/crohns-disease/), [ulcerative colitis](/conditions/ulcerative-colitis/) and short bowel syndrome.

Diarrhoea that starts suddenly usually gets better on its own within 5 to 7 days. If you need immediate short-term relief, taking loperamide can reduce the number of times you go to the toilet and it makes your poo less watery.

Loperamide works by slowing down food as it goes through your gut. Your body can then draw in more water from your intestines, so that your poos get firmer and you poo less often.

If you have a colostomy (where part of your bowel is brought through an opening made in your tummy, called a stoma) you may be prescribed loperamide. If you have a lot of poo and fluids coming through it, your stoma team may advise you to take high doses of loperamide to make your poo thicker and reduce the flow.

You can buy loperamide from pharmacies and shops. It's also available on prescription for treating some bowel conditions.

It comes as tablets, including tablets that dissolve on your tongue, and capsules. The tablets that dissolve are called Imodium Instants or Imodium Instant Melts.

Loperamide is also available combined with [simeticone](/medicines/simeticone/). Simeticone is used to treat farting (flatulence or wind). Taking these medicines together helps if you have diarrhoea with painful stomach cramps and bloating.

Loperamide mixed with simeticone is known by several brand names including Imodium Plus Caplets and Imodium Plus Comfort Tablets.

## Key facts

* Loperamide usually starts to make your diarrhoea better within 1 hour.
* If you buy loperamide from a pharmacy or shop, do not take it for more than 48 hours without talking to a doctor.
* Only take the recommended amount. Too much loperamide can cause serious heart problems (including a fast or irregular heartbeat).
* Do not drive, cycle or use machinery or tools if loperamide makes you feel dizzy, tired or sleepy.
* It's best not to drink alcohol while you're taking loperamide. Alcohol makes you more likely to have side effects.
* Pharmacies and shops may sell their own brands of loperamide, usually called anti-diarrhoea or diarrhoea relief capsules or tablets.
* Some products have IBS in the name. However, they're no different from others. If you have IBS you can also use brands without IBS in the name.

# Runner’s Diarrhea: Causes and Solutions

Updated  November 11, 2019

Brady Holmer

nutrition   running

The perfect race is unfolding. You’re right on pace through mile 13 and feeling strong. Suddenly, there’s a funny sensation in your stomach. The line of port-a-potties along the course is calling out your name, but is the pit stop worth losing out on valuable time?

If this situation sounds familiar, you aren’t alone. Runners of all types suffer from what is known as “runner’s diarrhea.” This unfortunate condition can rear its ugly head anytime, especially when you least expect it.

## You Know it When You See it

Some things don’t need explanation. The “runner's trots” is a great example of something most runners can sympathize with, though it has no single definition. Several things differentiate runner’s diarrhea from the regular form that make it particularly annoying.

Runner’s diarrhea has been observed in endurance athletes for decades.

> In contrast to normal diarrhea, runner’s diarrhea is exercise-induced, meaning it occurs in response to physical activity.

It’s characterized by frequent loose bowel movements that can occur during or immediately after a run–sometimes even in anticipation of a run.

Other than being uncomfortable and inconvenient, normal runner’s diarrhea isn’t pathological. Regular forms of diarrhea may indicate larger problems such as irritable bowel disease (IBD) or other GI disorders. Also unlike normal diarrhea, runner’s diarrhea doesn’t usually cause dehydration or electrolyte imbalance.DeOliveira2017 The only pathological symptom may be the appearance of blood in the feces. Progressing to this level might warrant a trip to your doctor.

Experiencing runner’s diarrhea can be unpleasant, embarrassing, and detrimental to training and competition.

## Why are Runners More Susceptible?

Runner’s diarrhea is more common in distance runners than any other athletic population. In exhaustive endurance events, it’s estimated that 30% - 50% of runners may experience one or more GI-related symptoms.DeOliveira2014

Need more proof you’re not alone? 83% of marathon runners interviewed after finishing a marathon indicated they experienced GI symptoms sometime during or after running.Riddoch1988 Most commonly, the “urge to have a bowel movement” and diarrhea were reported by 53% and 38% of the respondents. These runners also reported encountering issues more during hard runs than easy runs.

Long-haulers might be more at risk. 93% of triathletes experienced GI symptoms during a race, and 7% of them dropped out due to symptom severity.Jeukendrup2000 GI distress seems to be particularly present in ultra-endurance events, with 43% of all finishers in a 67km run reporting GI distress; 15% reported diarrhea.Rehrer1992

Runners have almost twice the risk of suffering GI problems than participants in cycling, swimming, and other athletes.DeOliveira2014 Have runners been hexed? Not really. The higher prevalence of GI issues in runners can be easily explained.

> The act of running leads to considerable mechanical trauma and jostling.

Compared to other sports, long distance runners also need to keep a steady intake of food and drink to maintain performance during competition. Both of these factors prime an upset stomach.

  

## The Intestines and Exercise

The “rest and digest” state is where we occupy the most time. It is controlled by part of our nervous system called the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS). Dialing up the rest and digest state prioritizes blood flow to our digestive system. This allows us to properly process food that we have consumed, store and conserve energy to meet future physical stressors.

But what happens during the stress of physical activity? It’s the opposite of rest and digest. While we aren’t exactly running from a pack of wolves (hopefully), exercise mimics the “fight or flight” response, increasing sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activity to prepare our body for battle. The idea is to shift resource allocation between the systems of the body to prioritize the systems that will help us to survive the threat and shut off those that won’t.

During exercise, blood flow is shuttled rapidly to areas where we need it–working muscles, heart, liver, brain. This delivers vital oxygen and nutrients to these systems, allowing them to deal with the huge increase in output that occurs during exercise. The process is controlled by the SNS, which constricts blood vessels leading to digestive organs. The consequence? Intestinal regions receive very little blood flow and oxygen.

During maximal exercise, GI blood flow can be reduced up to 80%.Costa2017 Forget digesting food, that can wait–the body screams at you, “run for your life!” Reduced blood flow to the GI tract during exercise leads to ischemia (lack of blood flow and oxygen), which can result in intestinal damage and function impairment, especially if it goes on a while. Dehydration may further reduce blood flow to your poor bowel. We lose blood volume during exercise through sweating, leading to thicker blood that’s even less likely to travel anywhere unnecessary.

This is an issue because gut function is still somewhat important to an athlete during exercise. It delivers water and nutrients to vital tissues, to help you push on while exercise saps water and fuel from your body. Actually, the intestines can accommodate mild-to-moderate intensity exercise without too much of a change in their function. Highly compromised digestion and absorption, and the ensuing runner’s diarrhea, may manifest only during severe exercise. Exercise at 70% [VO2 max](/blogs/blog/training-vo2-max-training-to-use-oxygen-efficiently) and above leads to the greatest overall disturbance in several GI functions:DeOliveira2014 the danger zone for runner’s diarrhea.

## What Causes “The Trots?”

Exercise changes the physiology of the GI tract, which can contribute to runner’s diarrhea and other symptoms. It’s necessary to know what might be causing runner’s diarrhea before looking for remedies.

### GI-Related Factors

Most gastrointestinal symptoms (GI) are intensity-dependent–the harder you run, the more severe they get. This might be why runner’s diarrhea is prevalent during hard workouts and races.

The factor usually blamed for runner’s diarrhea is reduced intestinal blood flow. As we discussed earlier, at 70% [VO2 max](/blogs/blog/training-vo2-max-training-to-use-oxygen-efficiently), delivery of blood to the GI tract is reduced up to 80%, leading to hypoxia (lack of oxygen) and ATP depletion.DeOliveira2014 The digestive tissues get starved of energy. Without adequate oxygen and blood flow, layers of the intestine begin breaking down, protein complexes known as “tight junctions” crumble, and intestinal permeability increases. Intestinal lining is a protection from various molecules and toxins.

“Leaky gut” allows bacterial endotoxin and other inflammatory factors to enter the intestinal lining. Heavy exercise exacerbates this. Runners who ran at 80% of their VO2 max displayed increased gut permeability compared to running at only 40% and 60% max capacity.Pals1997 An inflamed gut is primed for intestinal disaster. When blood flow resumes (after exercise stops), the "re-perfusion" process can even lead to further damage, like oxidative stress and inflammation, which probably contributes to the “post run runs.”

### Mechanical Factors

Running hard on the joints– and the intestines.

> The repetitive vertical oscillation and vibration during running causes your internal organs to jostle around your abdomen like kids in a bounce house.

The harder you run, the more they bounce. This trauma can contribute to flatulence, an urgent need to use the bathroom, and diarrhea. It may also be one reason bloody stool is often reported in runners experiencing diarrhea.

When the foot contacts the ground while running, this generates massive braking forces that are transmitted throughout the body. These forces, for lack of a better term, emulsify bowel contents, loosening the stool. Braking forces when landing during running are twice those experienced by cyclists, likely another reason runners are more affected.

### Nutritional Causes

What you eat has an impact on both performance and your chances of GI issues during exercise. Nutrition before and during exercise can contribute to runner’s diarrhea, and certain dietary hacks may reduce symptoms. Since the digestive process lasts 24 hours - 72 hours, pre-run and race-day nutrition are equally important.

The carbohydrate composition and concentration of pre-and-mid-race beverages is known to play a major role in GI issues. Beverages with high carbohydrate concentration (above 6% - 8%) are known to delay gastric emptying, lead to fluid shifts in the intestine, and result in runner’s diarrhea.RehrerTwo1992

Many athletes think more is better when it comes to hydration and nutrition. Our body can only absorb 1g - 1.2g per minute of carbohydrate during exercise, so anything ingested above this level will lead to residual un-absorbed carbohydrates in the intestine. Combining a hypertonic beverage with exercise in the heat can exacerbate the intestinal damage because of dehydration.

A group of poorly absorbed carbohydrates known as FODMAPs (Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides and Polyols) may lead to excess intestinal fluid and fermentation, leading to gas and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptoms. While few studies have evaluated the effect of FODMAPs on GI symptoms during exercise, restricting these foods around exercise may be precautionary to reduce diarrhea and other GI issues. In a study where athletes eliminated at least one FODMAP group from their diet (mainly lactose), 82.6% reported improvement in at least one GI symptom.Lis2016 As with all nutritional factors, tolerance may be highly individual.

Any foods that delay gastric emptying–fiber, fats, and protein–are candidates to induce GI symptoms. Other than sitting in the gut and leading to discomfort, these foods may also draw water into the intestinal lumen and lead to GI issues and diarrhea. A survey of a group of triathletes who experienced GI symptoms and cramps during a race found that all of them had consumed fat, fiber or protein in their pre-race meal.RehrerTwo1992 Best avoid the Raisin Bran, folks.

### Psychological Factors

Pre-race jitters? These may play a small but impactful role in runner’s diarrhea. In a survey of runners, GI symptoms were shown to be associated with having higher levels of stress and anxiety.Wilson2008

There may be an explanation for this. Psychological stress is known to induce small intestine permeability in humans,Vanuytsel2014 possibly related to the release of stress-response hormones. Stress may not cause ulcers, but it may make you poop.

## Prevention Strategies

Plan A. Bring toilet paper. Plan B? Luckily, there are several steps to mitigate or completely prevent runner’s diarrhea by manipulating diet and training

### Find the Right Beverage

Few athletes recognize the limit of how many carbohydrates the body can oxidize (utilize) during exercise, leading many to over-consume carbohydrate beverages and energy gels. The body’s inability to absorb all carbohydrates and fluid results in GI distress.

There are solutions to this. The right concoction of carbohydrates in your pre-or-mid-race beverage can prevent developing GI symptoms. The proper mix of multiple transportable carbohydrates reduces the presence of carbohydrates and fluid in the intestine during exercise. Glucose + fructose or maltodextrin + fructose are common blends found in hydration beverages due to their high absorptive capacity.

Ingesting a beverage of glucose + fructose or maltodextrin + fructose in a concentration of 6% - 8% allows for optimal absorption.Jeukendrup2017 Many beverages also contain sodium, since the uptake of glucose through GLUT5 carbohydrate transporters is sodium-dependent–they occur together.

  

### Just Say No

Avoiding certain foods or food groups may help alleviate symptoms of GI distress and runner’s diarrhea.

> Stay away from high-fiber foods, or those high in fat or protein, and certain artificial sweeteners for up to three hours before exercise.

In addition, a “low-residue” diet in the day(s) leading up to a big event will result in less intestinal content. Restricting consumption of FODMAP-containing foods before a race may alleviate symptoms, but this depends on tolerance and preference. In one preliminary study, runners reduced GI symptoms by following a low FODMAP diet for six days.Lis2018

### Hydrate (With Good Ol’ H20)

Maintaining adequate hydration before and during exercise is crucial to prevent runner’s diarrhea.

Dehydration exacerbates symptoms of GI distress. Losing just 2.7% of body mass due to dehydration impairs water flux, increases GI symptoms, and even promotes an intestinal inflammatory response during exercise.Ryan1998

Avoid over hydrating. Hyponatremia (low sodium concentration in the blood) also is associated with GI symptoms.

## Training the Gut

There is evidence the gut is capable of adapting to increased demands of exercise, just like muscles and the cardiovascular system. Many GI symptoms, such as runner’s diarrhea, may simply be a lack of “intestinal fortitude.” A gut not trained to handle both exercise and fluid intake won’t be happy when you ask too much of it.

### Practice Makes Perfect

Gut training can be accomplished by regularly taking in fluids and carbohydrate-based drinks during exercise.

One key benefit here is acclimating to the feeling of fullness during exercise. Improved liquid tolerance will reduce many symptoms of GI distress during exercise and help performance. It only takes about three days of gut training for the stomach to get used to larger volumes.Jeukendrup2017

Residual fluid and carbohydrate volume in the stomach are the main cause of runner’s diarrhea. With training, the stomach can improve how quickly it can empty fluid, and the intestines can improve how well they absorb carbohydrate and water. Improved absorption means less sloshy water in the gut during exercise, and less tummy trouble.Jeukendrup2017

> How do you train the gut? Practice drinking during exercise.

Runners who consumed a glucose and fructose-rich carbohydrate beverage during runs for two weeks improved GI symptoms during a three-hour run challenge.CostaTwo2017 This challenge involved stressing the gut by consuming 30g of carbohydrates every 20 minutes. The training gave the runners iron stomachs. Fewer GI issues, more glucose absorption and two weeks of training combined to improve performance by just over 5%.

Can improving fitness decrease the severity of runner’s diarrhea? Trained athletes have greater intestinal blood flow and better gut barrier function during exercise compared to untrained subjects.Bandyopadhyay2011 This suggests that as you improve your running fitness, “gut fitness” also improves. This may be why runner’s diarrhea occurs early in your training, during races, or when when you increase running volume or intensity. As the going gets tough, all of your resources (blood) must go to the muscles, sparing little for your intestines. Once you can better distribute blood flow, GI issues may ease up a bit.

One or two days per week, crush a [tempo run](/blogs/blog/training-tempo-runs-threshold-training-for-improved-endurance) or hard workout after consuming a simulated pre-race meal (with the right amount of time beforehand) and hydrate with your competition beverage.

Also learn [what is Supination for Athletes and Runners.](https://ketone.com/blogs/blog/training-supination-for-athletes)

### The Importance of Training Diet

Research shows that your regular diet will influence how you respond to nutrition before and during exercise.

Targeted carbohydrate supplementation during training for athletes following a normal mixed diet has been shown to be helpful. Carbohydrates were provided before, during, and after training and this improved glucose absorption during exercise and lowered GI symptoms.CoxGA2010

On the other hand, restricting carbohydrates ([ketogenic](/blogs/library/ketosis-keto-diet-fundamentals) or low-carb diets) results in a lower capacity to absorb and empty carbohydrates during exercise. This is most likely due to a lower number and activity of carbohydrate transporters in athletes on these diets. They’re simply not needed as much. If a keto athlete tries carb-loading on race day, this could spell disaster. Some keto athletes use fat as fuel on race day; as they burn more of their own fat, they need to eat less to sustain race pace and therefore reduce possible GI issues.

If you are following a low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diet, [periodized carbohydrate intake](https://ketone.com/blogs/blog/training-carb-cycling-guide-for-athletes) can improve your tolerance for certain carbohydrate-containing beverages and foods. This strategy will involve eating your normal diet but supplementing with carbohydrates for certain training sessions.

The alternative? Many ketogenic athletes forgo carbohydrates during competition, instead opting to fuel with fats like MCTs or exogenous ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyrate ([BHB](/blogs/blog/exogenous-ketones-beta-hydroxybutyrate-or-bhb-all-you-need-to-know)). If you’re going this route, make sure to practice with MCT or ketone ester ingestion before and during your training runs to get adapted.

  

## Practical Recommendations

When it comes to athletes and nutrition, there isn’t a one-size-fits-all approach. This is especially true when it comes to preventing issues like runner’s diarrhea. Find your tolerance. There are, however, plenty of evidence-based recommendations you can try out to prevent the dreaded runner’s diarrhea.

Prevent the mid race port-a-potty detour by keeping your stomach happy. Hydrate properly, and avoid upsetting foods close to exercise–this means those high in fiber, protein, and fat. Keep nutrition simple.

Don’t try any new food on race day. This is not a time to experiment with a new meal or beverage. Training is the time to test out different foods, gels, and drinks to find what works best for you.

For many runners, urinating and having a bowel movement prior to exercise can prevent a mid-run disaster. It may help to ingest a mild laxative the night before to move things along and ensure you're starting exercise with a clear colon.

And if nature calls? First of all, know where rest stops are located on your run or race. If you want to avoid the woods (or your neighbor’s backyard), having a backup plan is smart. Many runners opt to carry toilet paper on their runs. If you do have to duck into the bushes, TP is a better option than using leaves (or poison ivy).

Persistent, nagging, and inconvenient, runner’s diarrhea can ruin a race. Fortunately, nutritional strategies and gut training can help runners to avoid many symptoms of runner’s diarrhea and even prevent it from happening.

This article from the Ketone-IQ blog, published November 11, 2019 by Brady Holmer, examines "runner's diarrhea" (also called "runner's trots"), an exercise-induced condition characterized by frequent loose bowel movements during or immediately after running. Unlike normal diarrhea, runner's diarrhea is not typically pathological, doesn't usually cause dehydration or electrolyte imbalance, and only warrants medical attention if blood appears in the stool.

KEY STATISTICS: Runner's diarrhea affects 30-50% of runners in exhaustive endurance events; 83% of marathon runners reported GI symptoms during or after running, with 53% reporting "urge to have a bowel movement" and 38% reporting diarrhea. Triathletes reported 93% GI symptom prevalence (7% dropped out due to severity), and 43% of 67km ultra-marathon finishers reported GI distress (15% diarrhea). Runners have almost twice the risk of GI problems compared to cyclists, swimmers, and other athletes.

CAUSES (four categories):
1. GI-Related Factors: At 70% VO2 max and above, blood flow to the GI tract is reduced up to 80%, leading to hypoxia, ATP depletion, breakdown of intestinal "tight junctions," and increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"). Re-perfusion after exercise can cause further oxidative stress and inflammation ("post-run runs").
2. Mechanical Factors: Running's repetitive vertical oscillation causes organs to jostle, and braking forces during landing are twice those experienced by cyclists, which "emulsify" bowel contents.
3. Nutritional Causes: High-carb beverages (above 6-8% concentration) delay gastric emptying and cause fluid shifts; the body can only absorb 1g-1.2g of carbohydrate per minute during exercise. FODMAPs can cause excess intestinal fluid and fermentation (82.6% of athletes eliminating at least one FODMAP group reported improvement). Fiber, fats, and protein before exercise delay gastric emptying and can draw water into the intestine.
4. Psychological Factors: Higher stress and anxiety levels are associated with GI symptoms; psychological stress induces small intestine permeability.

PREVENTION STRATEGIES:
- Use beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose + fructose or maltodextrin + fructose) at 6-8% concentration for optimal absorption; sodium aids glucose uptake via GLUT5 transporters.
- Avoid high-fiber, high-fat, or high-protein foods and certain artificial sweeteners up to three hours before exercise; consider a "low-residue" diet in days before events.
- Maintain proper hydration (dehydration of just 2.7% of body mass impairs water flux and increases GI symptoms), but avoid over-hydration (hyponatremia also causes GI issues).
- "Gut training": practice drinking fluids and carb-based drinks during exercise; about three days of training helps the stomach adapt to larger volumes. Runners consuming a glucose + fructose beverage during runs for two weeks improved GI symptoms and performance by just over 5% during a three-hour run challenge.
- Improved fitness improves gut function—trained athletes have greater intestinal blood flow and better gut barrier function.
- For keto/low-carb athletes: periodized carbohydrate intake can improve tolerance; some use MCTs or exogenous ketones (BHB) instead, but should practice with these during training.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: Find personal tolerance; avoid new foods on race day; urinate and have a bowel movement before exercise (may help to use a mild laxative the night before); know rest stop locations and carry toilet paper. The article concludes that nutritional strategies and gut training can help runners avoid and prevent most symptoms of runner's diarrhea.
