## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)Abstract

Considering an increase in the life expectancy leading to a rise in the elderly population, it is important to recognize the changes that occur along the process of aging. Gastrointestinal (GI) changes in the elderly are common, and despite some GI disorders being more prevalent in the elderly, there is no GI disease that is limited to this age group. While some changes associated with aging GI system are physiologic, others are pathological and particularly more prevalent among those above age 65 years. This article reviews the most important GI disorders in the elderly that clinicians encounter on a daily basis. We highlight age-related changes of the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, small and large bowels, and the clinical implications of these changes. We review epidemiology and pathophysiology of common diseases, especially as they relate to clinical manifestation in elderly. Details regarding management of specific disease are discussed in detail if they significantly differ from the management for younger groups or if they are associated with significant challenges due to side effects or polypharmacy. Cancers of GI tract are not included in the scope of this article.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)1. Introduction

The main characteristic of aging is progressive loss of physiological integrity which, in turn, leads to impaired function and increased vulnerability to death. This deterioration is the primary risk factor for the majority of diseases that affect humans including cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B1)]. The elderly population is currently defined as people aged 65 years or above [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B2)], yet increasing life expectancy may move this cut off upwards in years to come. The percent of elderly population varies by country with 7.8% in Turkey, 21.5% in Germany, and 14.5% in the United States (up from 10% in the 1970s) [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B2)]. The predicted global population over the age of 80 years is expected to be 17% by 2050 [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B3)]. Aging affects all functions of the gastrointestinal system (GIS): motility, enzyme and hormone secretion, digestion, and absorption. The GIS also plays an essential role in medication absorption and metabolism, and it is commonly affected by side effects. While there is no GI disease that is specific and limited to advanced age, some illnesses are more prevalent in this age group and may require different management. Hence, the focus of this review is to highlight the most common diseases that affect the elderly while emphasizing details of clinical presentation and management if they significantly differ from the younger population. Age-related pathophysiology and clinical implications in elderly are the main focus.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)2. Oral Cavity

Changes in the oral cavity can be caused by local trauma (ill-fitting dental prosthesis, local radiotherapy), localized benign disease (aphthous stomatitis, oral candidiasis), benign systemic disease, potentially life-threatening conditions (vitamin deficiency, Sjogren's syndrome or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) or medication side effects (tricyclic antidepressants or antiparkinsonian drugs) [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B5)]. The most commonly reported disturbances among elderly include oral sensorial complaints (OSC), particularly dry mouth (xerostomia), taste disturbances (dysgeusia or ageusia), and burning mouth syndrome (BMS) [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B6)]. These complaints may be explained by decrease in salivary secretion and quality of saliva associated with normal aging. Nagler and Hershkovic discovered that reduction in salivary function and altered composition are age-related [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B7)]. OSC are more prevalent in elderly than in those of age less than 65, with 50% of elderly reporting at least one of OSC. Among them, those using prescription drugs had higher prevalence of OSCs [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B6), [7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B7)].

**Xerostomia** may occur as a part of systemic disease like Sjogren's syndrome or as a medication side effect, with tricyclic antidepressants (TCA), atropine, and antiparkinsonian drugs being the most commonly implicated medications [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B4)]. Additionally, damage to the salivary glands following radiation for head and neck cancers can lead to permanent xerostomia. When caused by medication, it is usually reversible upon the discontinuation of the offending drug [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B4)]. Salivary supplements can be used to treat irreversible causes.

**Dysgeusia and ageusia** are also frequent among elderly and are most commonly caused by medication side effects. Common offenders include lithium, metronidazole, levodopa, glipizide, captopril, and clarithromycin. Zinc deficiency is another important cause of dysgeusia, especially in elderly who are frequently malnourished [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B4), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B8)]. Diseases of the peripheral nervous system (Bell's palsy) are more commonly associated with taste disturbances than are central nervous system disorders [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B8)].

**Oropharyngeal dysphagia**is defined as a sensation of difficulty chewing food or initiation of swallowing [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B9)], and results from changes affecting the complex neuromuscular mechanism that coordinates the tongue, pharynx, and upper esophageal sphincter (UES). The most common causes of oropharyngeal dysphagia are neuromuscular disorders such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, dementia, Parkinson's disease, and muscular dystrophy. Pharyngeal cancers and strictures are local mechanical causes [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B10), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B11)]. Cough with swallowing, food sticking in the throat and nasal regurgitation are common signs of dysphagia and all increase risk for aspiration. Oropharyngeal dysphagia affects up to 13% of individuals above age of 65 and up to 50% of nursing home residents suffer from it [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B9), [12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B12)]. Elderly are usually not aware of their swallowing problems and might not seek help until complications such as aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, or dehydration develop. Diagnosis is based on detailed history and by video fluoroscopic examination [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B5)]. In many cases patients need artificial modes of feeding due to the irreversible nature of the underlying disease [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B10)]. [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#tab1) summarize diseases of oral cavity in elderly.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)3. Esophagus

Presbyesophagus is a term coined in 1964 [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B13)] to describe the aging esophagus and changes that occur along this process. Over the last 40 years, with the development of more sophisticated diagnostic techniques, our understanding about age-related changes in the esophagus has evolved and current opinion is that presbyesophagus, in its original meaning, does not exist [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B14)]. Esophageal problems in the elderly are more related to other co-morbidities rather than esophagus itself. The term presbyphagia is now used to describe characteristic physiologic changes in swallowing associated with the advanced age. While these changes are physiologic, they do increase the risk of dysphagia and aspiration in elderly, especially during acute illnesses and other stressors [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B14)]. Studies have yielded conflicting results regarding esophageal motility in the elderly. Ferriolli et al. [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B15)] demonstrated even healthy elderly patients exhibited significant changes in esophageal peristalsis and delayed esophageal emptying when compared to younger age groups. Two other studies [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B17)] found a significant decrease in peristaltic wave amplitudes as well as decreased LES and UES pressures. These studies demonstrated that the number of failed esophageal contractions and the duration of peristaltic contraction significantly increase in the elderly. Contrary to these studies, a retrospective study by Robson and Glick failed to demonstrate any significant difference in LES pressures and peristaltic duration and amplitude [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B18)]. Finally, the most recent study by Besanko et al. [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B19)] found only subtle changes in LES pressure and relaxation associated with aging. On the cellular level, these changes may be explained by loss of intrinsic enteric neurons which, in some studies have been shown to be more vulnerable to age-related degeneration and death than the other parts of the nervous systems. In particular cholinergic myenteric neurons seem to be more vulnerable than the other enteric neurons [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B20)].

**Esophageal dysphagia**is most commonly manifested as the feeling of food being stuck in the chest. It can be caused by mechanical obstruction inside the esophagus itself (stricture, tumor) or compression from surrounding tissues (vascular compression or mediastinal masses). Neuromuscular causes include achalasia, scleroderma, or diffuse esophageal spasm. Finally, inflammatory and infectious causes can lead to esophageal dysphagia (eosinophilic esophagitis, candidiasis). Endoscopy is an essential part of the evaluation and can diagnose the majority of these conditions [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B9)].

**Odynophagia** is painful swallowing. Infection and malignancy are the most common causes. Candida, herpes simplex virus, and cytomegalovirus are the most commonly found pathogens in infectious cases, especially in immunocompromised patients [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B21)]. Several studies indicate elderly patients require more stimuli to perceive the disturbance and have a higher threshold for the sensation of pain [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B22), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B23)]. Lasch et al. [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B23)] showed that elderly, nondiabetic patients required significantly higher mean balloon volumes to sense pain when compared to younger individuals. This may be explained by the previously mentioned age-related decrease of myenteric neurons. As a consequence, elderly patients frequently seek help late, when their disease is in advanced stage.

**Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)** is a “condition that develops when the reflux of stomach contents causes troublesome symptoms and/or complications” unlike nonproblematic gastroesophageal reflux which is a physiological event that occurs during and after meals [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B24)]. The prevalence of GERD among the elderly is about 23% and it was one of the most commonly found conditions among almost 20,000 nursing home residents in the study by Moore et al. [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B25)]. While one would expect that prevalence of GERD increases with age due to multiple reasons (decreased saliva production and increased prevalence of motility disorders and hiatal hernia), studies demonstrated similar prevalence of GERD among older and younger age groups [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B26), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B27)]. However, severity of GERD and its associated complications (such as Barrett's esophagus, severe esophagitis, ulcerations and strictures) are more prevalent in the elderly [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B28), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B29)]. The most common symptom associated with GERD is heartburn. The frequency of severe heartburn seems to decline with age and the elderly might have atypical signs of GERD such as dysphagia or odynophagia [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B28)]. This atypical presentation may relate to a decrease in esophageal pain perception and an increase in the prevalence of atrophic gastritis. Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) are the mainstay of treatment [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B29)], yet the side effects associated with PPI therapy (increased risk of osteoporosis, development of Clostridium difficile colitis (CDC), interstitial nephritis, and community acquired pneumonia) should be kept in mind. While some authors voice concern regarding antireflux surgery in this age group [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B30)], laparoscopic antireflux surgery should be considered in selected groups of patients. It appears to be a safe and effective treatment for GERD in elderly with low morbidity and mortality rates and excellent results [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B31)].

**Barrett's columnar-lined esophagus (CLE)**is defined as a replacement of the normal distal esophageal squamous epithelium by metaplastic columnar epithelium, which is thought to be caused by prolonged GERD [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B32), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B33)]. The most feared complication of Barrett's esophagus is development of high grade dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. The incidence of adenocarcinoma in Barrett's esophagus has been estimated to be around 0.5% annually and slightly lower at 0.32% in patients without dysplasia at index endoscopy [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B33), [34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B34)]. A study by Gatenby et al. [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B33)] found that risk of low grade dysplasia was independent of age at surveillance, yet they found that increasing age is an important risk factor for development of high-grade dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. The mean age at diagnosis of Barrett's esophagus was 61.6 and 67.3 years in males and females, respectively, and the mean life expectancy at diagnosis was 23.1 years in males, 20.7 years in females [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B35)]. These findings indicate Barrett's esophagus is more prevalent among elderly. As previously mentioned (see chapter about GERD) older patients may be asymptomatic or have atypical symptoms, leading them to present late when complications may have already developed. Patients who are diagnosed with CLE may be offered surveillance in an attempt to detect dysplasia and potentially curable cancer. However, co-morbidities, life expectancy at the time of CLE diagnosis, and yearly risk of development of adenocarcinoma should be considered. A cross sectional study done by Myung S. Ko et al. found that one third of older men diagnosed with CLE had limited life expectancy [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B36)]. They further argued that elderly patients are more likely to experience harms of surveillance than benefit from timely detection of dysplasia or early cancer and suggested that it should not be the routine strategy in this patient population.

**Medication induced esophagitis (pill esophagitis)**refers to the inflammation of the esophagus from harmful effects of medication due to their altered passage through esophagus and increased contact with esophageal mucosa. While it can occur at any age, it is more prevalent in elderly patients [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B37)]. Polypharmacy, decrease in esophageal motility, and taking medication with insufficient amounts of water are factors most commonly associated with pill esophagitis in elderly [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B38)]. Additionally, patients with cardiomegaly can develop esophageal compression from enlarged left atrium, placing them at increased risk for medication induced esophagitis. Abid et al. found female gender, presence of diabetes, and ischemic heart disease, in addition to advanced age, to be associated with pill esophagitis [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B38)]. The most commonly implied causative agents include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID), aspirin, doxycycline, bisphosphonates, ferrous sulfate, and captopril. The most common symptoms are chest pain (71.8%) and odynophagia (38.5%) [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B39)]. Detailed history, availability of accurate medication list, and endoscopy are invaluable in establishing the diagnosis. Endoscopic findings show ulceration in more than 80% of cases, while kissing ulcers are present in up to 42% of patients [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B39)]. The mainstay of treatment is withdrawal of the inciting medication and use of PPIs, leading to a favorable prognosis in most cases. [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#tab2) summarize diseases of esophagus in elderly.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)4. Stomach

Altered gastric microbiota, reduced mucosal protective mechanisms, decreased gastric blood flow, and consequently compromised repair mechanisms are the hallmarks of age-related gastric changes [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B40), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B41)]. These changes make older people more susceptible to the development of several diseases, such as gastric ulcer, atrophic gastritis, and peptic ulcer disease [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B41)]. Additionally, elderly are more likely to experience medication related gastrointestinal side effects which, in turn, can decrease their medication adherence and further contribute to morbidity and mortality. The effect of age on gastric motility has been a subject of debate resulting in numerous studies reporting conflicting evidence. Using gamma camera technique, Madsen et al. [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B42)] showed that gastric and small bowel motility were not reduced in healthy elderly subjects (mean age 81 year) when compared to control group (mean age 24 year). Additionally, they found that neither gender nor body mass index (BMI) influenced gastric and small bowel transit time. In contrast, a study by Shimamoto et al. [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B43)] demonstrated significant decrease in postprandial gastric contractile force. They also found that this reduction was more pronounced among elderly who led less active lifestyles. Among the co-morbidities frequently encountered among older people, Parkinson's disease and diabetes mellitus seem to have the greatest impact on gastric emptying [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B44)]. Loss of cholinergic enteral neurons seems the most plausible explanation for decreased motility in elderly. Although not yet seen in human studies, the current evidence for loss of these neurons is derived from animal models using rodents (rat, mouse and guinea pig). While there is so much more to discover about enteric neurodegeneration that occurs with aging, it seems reactive oxygen species (ROS) may play a central role and that, despite the absence of neurogenesis, the GIS has significant functional reserve as evidenced by relatively preserved function despite dramatic loss of enteric neurons [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B20)].

**Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG)**is more prevalent in the elderly and is associated with H. pylori infection [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B45)]. The hallmark of disease is the partial loss of glands in the gastric mucosa leading to hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria. The prevalence of CAG is higher in elderly and there are significant geographical variations showing elderly from China and Japan are particularly affected with a prevalence of up to 50% in those above age 60 years [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B45), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B46)]. While advanced age was thought to be independently related to chronic atrophic gastritis in the past, current data support the theory that atrophic changes of the gastric mucosa are associated with H. pylori infection rather than the age itself [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B47)]. Gastritis activity can be decreased by eradication of H. pylori [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B47), [48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B48)]. In their study, Kokkola et al. [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B49)] demonstrated that elderly patients who successfully eradicated infection had significantly lower mean histological scores of inflammation, atrophy, and intestinal metaplasia. Decrease in acid secretion as a consequence of chronic atrophic gastritis leads to two problems that are particularly prominent in the elderly population: small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and malabsorption [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B50), [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B51)]. A study by Parlesak et al. examined prevalence of SIBO using hydrogen breath test and found the prevalence in elderly was 15.6% compared to 5.9% found in younger age groups [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B51)]. Several studies examined the association between CAG and other co-morbidities in elderly. A cross sectional study by Hye Won et al. found significant association between presence of CAG and development of osteoporosis in elderly females in Korea [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B52)]. They explained their findings were a result of decreased calcium absorption secondary to hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria leading to decreased bone mineral density. Another cross sectional study [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B53)] found a positive association between autoimmune thyroid disease and CAG. The authors suggested that autoimmune thyroid disease and atrophic body gastritis occur in a closely linked fashion, particularly in females with positive parietal cell antibodies. Although data are still somewhat conflicting, recent studies suggest that eradicating H. pylori infection in elderly patients may prevent progression from CAG to intestinal metaplasia and gastric cancer (GC) [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B54)]. Emerging knowledge about the changes in human gastric microbiota associated with aging has shed new light on its association with gastric cancer. Pearson and co-authors [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B41)] showed that gastric microbiota varies for patients with autoimmune and H. Pylori associated atrophic gastritis, with former expressing higher bacterial diversity and abundance. Both conditions are associated with reduction in gastric acid secretion and development of gastric cancer (particularly neuroendocrine and gastric adenocarcinoma), while people treated with PPIs maintain normal gastric microbiota diversity in spite of hypochlorhydria [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B41)].

**H. pylori infection**prevalence in developing countries is the highest among the children, while in developed countries is higher with increasing age [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B55)]. This marked difference is most likely due to a cohort effect of the earlier generation exposed to poor sanitation [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B47)] which is a known risk factor for contracting the infection. On the global level, 50% of people are colonized by H. pylori [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B56)] and the prevalence varies from 7% to 87% [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B55)]. Apart from being associated with peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori is identified as a type I carcinogen associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric non-Hodgkin's lymphoma [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B57), [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B58)]. Severity of upper gastrointestinal symptoms secondary to H. pylori infection seems to be higher in the elderly [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B47)]. Several extra intestinal disorders have been associated with H. pylori seropositivity. The most notable of these for older adults include cardiovascular diseases, osteoporosis, and neurocognitive impairment. Several studies have established association between H. pylori infection and cardiovascular diseases [[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B59), [60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B60)], yet a few other studies failed to find any association [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B61), [62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B62)]. Chronic inflammation secondary to ongoing H. pylori infection may play a role in developing or worsening Alzheimer dementia [[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B63)–[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B65)] and vascular dementia [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B66)]. The association between compromised bone mineral density and H. pylori infection has been supported by recent investigations [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B52), [67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B67)]. Despite evidence associating H. Pylori infection with extra intestinal diseases (dermatological, neurologic, cardiovascular and hematologic), further studies are needed to confirm this relationship [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B68)]. Current evidence indicates H. Pylori's strongest associations are with iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)[[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B68)].

**Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)** encompasses both gastric and duodenal peptic injury that leads to a break in gastric or duodenal mucosa and, more rarely, in the esophagus or Meckel's diverticulum [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B69)]. The majority of ulcers in elderly is caused by H. pylori infection or is associated with the use of NSAIDs/aspirin [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B69), [70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B70)]. Unlike in general population, the incidence and mortality from PUD in elderly remains very high [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B71)]. Gastric ulcers in elderly are usually larger and tend to occur higher in the stomach on the lesser curve [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B72)]. The main factors contributing to this are a higher prevalence of H. pylori infection among elderly, increased NSAIDs/aspirin use, and polypharmacy including medications associated with increased risk of PUD (anticoagulants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and oral steroids). The physiologic changes associated with old age that contribute to this include reduced blood flow through GI system and decreased secretion of key components of gastrointestinal protective mechanisms such as bicarbonates, mucin, and prostaglandins [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B71)]. Gastric acid secretion is unaffected in healthy elderly [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B73)], but H. pylori infection associated changes in gastric microbiota and atrophic gastritis both lead to hypochlorhydria and a decline in gastric acid secretion in older adults [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B5), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B41)].

Clinical manifestation of PUD in elderly is often atypical. In their prospective study, Hilton et al. demonstrated that only 30% of elderly patients with endoscopy proven PUD had typical epigastric pain [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B74)]. Additionally, elderly patients with acute gastric or duodenal ulcer perforation might not exhibit classic signs of chemical peritonitis [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B75)], which is partially due to hypochlorhydria observed in this age group. While medical treatment of PUD in elderly is not significantly different than in younger patients, medication side effects and interactions must be kept in mind. Many elderly have a strong concomitant indication for antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, making exploring both individualized risks and benefits of continuing those along with H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) crucial. There is emerging evidence that PPIs are associated with community acquired pneumonia (CAP), Clostridium difficile colitis (CDC) and osteoporosis, all of which tend to be more severe in elderly. Significant correlation between hip fractures and the use of PPIs in elderly has also been reported, leading to concerns that duration of treatment should depend on indication and should not be universally lifelong [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B76)]. Elderly with bleeding PUD who underwent open surgical repair had significantly higher 30 day morbidity and mortality then younger counterparts [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B77)]. A retrospective study by Fezzi at all [[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B78)] analyzed outcomes for 98 patients admitted for bleeding peptic ulcer and found that 66% achieved hemostasis endoscopically. They found repeated endoscopic treatment was not associated with increased mortality and recommended repeated endoscopy in elderly with elevated surgical risk. Trans-catheter arterial embolization was another option to consider in this group based on the same study. [Table 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#tab3) summarize diseases of stomach in elderly.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172)5. Small Intestine

The hormonal secretion and absorptive function of the small intestine in older adults is not significantly different in comparison to younger counterparts [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B5)]. Minimal changes in small bowel motility as well as reduced mucosal immunity are seen, but they are clinically insignificant in the absence of co-existing illness. While some animal studies demonstrate age-related changes in small intestinal morphology such as increase in villous width and height and reduction in mucosal surface area, human studies did not find such changes [[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B79)]. There are few human studies on this topic and while some morphologic changes may occur they usually are not severe enough to be a cause of malabsorption [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B80)]. The studies done by Ciccocioppo and Corazza [[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B81), [82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B82)] showed that increase in proliferation and differentiation rates of enterocytes maintains unchanged intestinal architecture with increased expression of proliferating cell nuclear antigen in elderly compared to younger age groups.

**Celiac disease (CD)** is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease that affects genetically predisposed individuals secondary to exposure to dietary gluten protein [[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B83)]. The classic form of CD manifests as a malabsorption syndrome associated with chronic diarrhea, mineral deficiencies, failure to thrive, and weight loss. Many patients have only extra intestinal manifestations or even no symptoms at all. These forms are termed atypical and silent celiac disease, respectively [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B84)]. In patients who suffer from celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase (TTG) binds to gliadin in the gut level. Antigen presenting cells which express HLADQ2 and HLADQ8 present this gliadin-tissue transglutaminase complex to T cells which then stimulate B cells to produce antibodies against both gliadin and TTG [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B85)]. Typical symptoms of celiac disease are frequently absent in elderly which leads to diagnostic delay, increasing morbidity in this age group [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B86)]. Evidence suggests increasing incidence of celiac disease in older adults in North America as seen in Olmsted County, Minnesota, USA, with 15.1 new cases per 100.000 in 2000-2001 compared to zero in 1950-1559 [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B87)]. While some of these cases might be diagnosed in elderly for the first time due to diagnostic delay, there is evidence that celiac disease can truly occur for the first time in elderly in spite of long tolerance to gluten in the past [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B88)]. As is typical in many autoimmune diseases, it is typically more frequent in females, yet we see that after age 65 incidence in women starts decreasing while it gradually increases in men [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B87)]. It is unclear why gastrointestinal symptoms are less prominent in elderly patients with celiac disease, and the first sign of disease can be micronutrient deficiency [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B89)]. Iron-deficiency anemia is present in up to 80% of elderly patients with celiac disease [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B90)]. When abdominal symptoms are present in these patients, they are usually vague and nonspecific, manifesting as bloating, increased flatulence, and abdominal discomfort [[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B83), [89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B89)].

Calcium and vitamin D deficiency are frequently found in celiac disease, which leads to metabolic bone disease and increased risk of fractures, especially with falls occurring at an older age. Liver involvement in celiac disease, seen in up to 20% of patients, is termed celiac hepatitis and usually presents as hypoalbuminemia, ascites, and abnormal liver function tests [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B91), [92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B92)]. Interestingly, celiac hepatitis is not auto-immune mediated disease unlike cholestatic liver diseases like primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and auto-immune hepatitis, which are also more common in people who have celiac disease [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B85)]. Unlike celiac hepatitis, which usually resolves with gluten free diet, cholestatic liver disorders respond less favorably on gluten cessation.

Neurologic manifestation of celiac disease, particularly dementia, ataxia, and neuropathy, are especially difficult to diagnose in older adults due to the broad differential diagnosis and unfamiliarity amongst providers that celiac disease can present with neurological manifestations. This age group will frequently be misdiagnosed with Alzheimer or vascular dementia or gait instability due to age and deconditioning when, in fact, they may have atypical celiac disease. Apart from celiac disease, malabsorption syndrome in elderly might also be due to small bowel ischemia, bacterial overgrowth, and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency which makes diagnosis of celiac disease in these groups of patient with steatorrhea even more challenging.

While the diagnostic algorithm of celiac disease in elderly is the same as in younger groups, management can be particularly challenging since these patients can find complying with a strict gluten free diet more difficult. Some of this difficulty connects to residing in assisted living facilities, inability to precisely read ingredients while shopping, and finding lifelong habits difficult to break [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B85)].

**Mesenteric ischemia** results from occlusion of celiac axis arterial branches and can be either acute or chronic. Its pathophysiology is related to either arterial occlusion by embolus (superior mesenteric artery affected in more than 50% of cases), gradual development of thrombosis secondary to advanced atherosclerosis, or hypo-perfusion secondary to hypovolemia and hypotension. Historically, embolic pathophysiology was a more common cause of acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), yet more recent trends indicate atherosclerotic etiology is now more prevalent [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B93)]. This may be due to increased life expectancy and population of elderly who more commonly have severe atherosclerotic changes as well as increased use of anticoagulation which will decrease embolic phenomena. Elderly are disproportionally affected by nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia related to states of hypo-perfusion such as during cardiopulmonary bypass surgeries, dehydration, hypovolemia, sepsis, and states of shock. Additionally, splanchnic blood flow decreases with age, making elderly more vulnerable to this type of hemodynamic injury. Chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) in elderly classically presents as post prandial angina leading to decrease in food intake and subsequent weight loss. Abdominal pain, which is a hallmark of presentation of acute mesenteric ischemia, in elderly is frequently absent or minimal and vague [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B94)]. In contrast, CMI frequently presents with tachypnea, confusion, vomiting, and diarrhea. The onset of symptoms is usually insidious and when combined with ambiguity of symptoms makes establishing the correct diagnosis extremely difficult. A textbook definition of poorly localized abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical findings applies only to acute embolic mesenteric occlusion of a previously patent artery and is rarely seen nowadays.

Acute mesenteric ischemia is a more common abdominal emergency than ruptured abdominal aneurysm [[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B95)] and, in people older than 75, is a more common cause of acute abdomen than appendicitis. Elderly patients who have symptomatic chronic mesenteric ischemia are at very high risk of developing acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia. In fact, one study demonstrated that up to 80% of patients who developed acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia had been evaluated for similar complaints within 6 months before acute ischemia developed [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B96)]. Diagnosis of AMI should be based on a combination of clinical suspicion (look for risk factors like peripheral arterial disease, atrial fibrillation, prior myocardial infarct, or stroke), laboratory findings (leukocytosis, elevated lactic acid, and metabolic acidosis) and radiological findings (thrombus in the artery, increased bowel enhancement, pneumatosis, etc.). Sensitivity of CT is variable, especially early in the disease, and can be increased in the setting of high clinical suspicion. In study by Karkkainen only 50% of patients with documented bowel ischemia had CT findings of thrombus in the artery [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B93)]. Studies by Schermerhon and Arthus showed that endovascular therapy is associated with lower mortality when compared to open revascularization (16% vs 28%) [[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B97), [98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B98)] and is preferable in elderly who usually have a plethora of other co-morbidities making them poor candidates for open surgery.

**Small bowel bleeding** (SBB) makes up only 5% of GI bleeds, yet it is the most common cause of obscure GI bleeding. The small bowel is defined as the region between the ligament of Treitz and the ileocecal valve. It is called “the dark continent of the GI tract” due to its excess mobility, long length, and relative inaccessibility to endoscopy. Unlike for young adults in whom intestinal tumors and Crohn's disease are the most common causes of small bowel bleeding, vascular anomalies, small intestinal ulcers, and NSAID enteropathy are the most common etiologies in elderly populations [[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B99)]. A study by Zhang et al. [[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B100)] found that 54% of small bowel bleeding in elderly patients was due to angiodysplasia.

**Angiodysplasias** are acquired lesions associated with aging. They are characterized by the presence of a cluster of dilated, torturous, thin-walled vessels involving small capillaries, veins, and arteries [[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6354172#B101)]. The increase in incidence of angiodysplasia with age is thought to be due to changes in the composition and structure of extracellular matrix in the wall of the small intestine. This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the Canadian Journal of Gastroenterology & Hepatology (January 17, 2019, doi: 10.1155/2019/6757524) by Igor Dumic and colleagues from the Mayo Clinic Health System (Wisconsin and Rochester, MN), The Wright Center for Graduate Medical Education (Scranton, PA), and the Clinical Center of Serbia (Belgrade). The article reviews gastrointestinal tract disorders in older age (65+ years), covering age-related changes across the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large bowel.

KEY CONTENT BY SECTION:

1. INTRODUCTION: Elderly population is defined as 65+, with 7.8% elderly in Turkey, 21.5% in Germany, and 14.5% in the US (up from 10% in the 1970s). By 2050, 17% of the global population is expected to be over 80. There is no GI disease limited exclusively to the elderly, but many are more prevalent in this group.

2. ORAL CAVITY: Oral sensorial complaints (OSC) affect 50% of elderly, including xerostomia (dry mouth), dysgeusia/ageusia (taste disturbances), and burning mouth syndrome. Causes include medication side effects (tricyclic antidepressants, atropine, antiparkinsonian drugs), Sjogren's syndrome, radiation damage, and zinc deficiency. Oropharyngeal dysphagia affects up to 13% of those over 65 and up to 50% of nursing home residents, commonly from neuromuscular disorders (stroke, MS, myasthenia gravis, dementia, Parkinson's disease).

3. ESOPHAGUS: The concept of "presbyesophagus" (coined 1964) is now considered outdated; "presbyphagia" better describes physiologic swallowing changes. GERD prevalence in elderly is ~23%. Severity and complications (Barrett's esophagus, severe esophagitis, strictures) are more prevalent in elderly despite similar overall prevalence. PPI therapy is the mainstay, but side effects (osteoporosis, C. difficile colitis, interstitial nephritis, pneumonia) warrant caution. Barrett's esophagus adenocarcinoma incidence is ~0.5% annually (0.32% without dysplasia); mean age at diagnosis is 61.6 years in males and 67.3 in females. Pill esophagitis is more prevalent in elderly due to polypharmacy, reduced motility, and insufficient water intake, with NSAIDs, aspirin, doxycycline, bisphosphonates, ferrous sulfate, and captopril as common culprits. Chest pain (71.8%) and odynophagia (38.5%) are the most common symptoms.

4. STOMACH: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is more prevalent in elderly and associated with H. pylori, with up to 50% prevalence in those over 60 in China and Japan. CAG leads to hypochlorhydria, SIBO (prevalence 15.6% in elderly vs 5.9% in younger), and malabsorption. H. pylori colonizes 50% of the global population; it is a Type I carcinogen linked to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Extra-intestinal associations include cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, neurocognitive impairment, iron deficiency anemia (IDA), and immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Peptic ulcer disease in elderly is often atypical—only 30% present with typical epigastric pain. Elderly with bleeding PUD had significantly higher 30-day morbidity and mortality after open surgery.

5. SMALL INTESTINE: Small bowel function is largely preserved with age. Celiac disease incidence is rising in older adults (15.1 new cases per 100,000 in Olmsted County, MN, 2000-2001, vs zero in 1950-1959); iron-deficiency anemia is present in up to 80% of elderly celiac patients. Neurologic manifestations (dementia, ataxia, neuropathy) are often misdiagnosed as Alzheimer's or vascular dementia. Mesenteric ischemia: acute mesenteric ischemia is more common than ruptured abdominal aneurysm in the elderly and is a more common cause of acute abdomen than appendicitis in those over 75. Endovascular therapy is preferred over open revascularization (16% vs 28% mortality). Small bowel bleeding (5% of GI bleeds) is most commonly due to angiodysplasia (54% in elderly), associated with Heyde's syndrome (bleeding angiodysplasia with aortic stenosis).

The article explicitly excludes GI tract cancers from its scope. It emphasizes that management of GI disorders in the elderly often differs from younger patients due to polypharmacy, atypical presentations, delayed diagnosis, and increased vulnerability to medication side effects.
args.key_excerpts: "While some changes associated with aging GI system are physiologic, others are pathological and particularly more prevalent among those above age 65 years."

# Aging and the Digestive System



Full Review: Apr 2025 By[Michael Bartel](/home/authors/bartel-michael), MD, PhD, Fairfax, VA

Last updated: Jul 2025

v752121

VIEW PROFESSIONAL VERSION

* |
* |

Because the digestive system has a lot of reserve built into it, aging has less effect on its function than it does on the function of other organ systems. Nonetheless, aging is a factor in several digestive system disorders. In particular, older adults are more likely to develop [diverticulosis](/home/digestive-disorders/diverticular-disease/diverticulosis-of-the-large-intestine) and to have digestive tract disorders (for example, [constipation](/home/digestive-disorders/symptoms-of-digestive-disorders/constipation-in-adults)—see [Large intestine and rectum](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/aging-and-the-digestive-system#v752160)) as a side effect of taking certain medications. Also, changes in the gut microbiome (all the bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and fungi that live in the digestive tract) with age may be connected to overall healthy aging and may affect obesity, metabolic disorders, inflammation, cancer, depression, or other health issues.

A View of the Digestive System

(See also [Overview of the Digestive System](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/overview-of-the-digestive-system).)

## Esophagus

With age, the strength of [esophageal contractions](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/throat-and-esophagus) and the tension in the upper esophageal sphincter decrease (called presbyesophagus), but the movement of food is not impaired by these changes. However, some older adults can be affected by diseases that interfere with esophageal contractions.

## Stomach

With age, the stomach lining's capacity to resist damage decreases, which in turn may increase the risk of [peptic ulcer disease](/home/digestive-disorders/gastritis-and-peptic-ulcer-disease/peptic-ulcer-disease), especially in people who use aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Also with age, the [stomach](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/stomach) cannot accommodate as much food (because of decreased elasticity), and the rate at which the stomach empties food into the small intestine decreases. However, these changes typically do not cause any noticeable symptoms. Aging has little effect on the secretion of stomach juices such as acid and pepsin, but conditions that decrease acid secretion, such as [atrophic gastritis](/home/digestive-disorders/gastritis-and-peptic-ulcer-disease/gastritis#v753721), become more common. These conditions can result in subsequent problems such as [vitamin B12 deficiency](/home/disorders-of-nutrition/vitamins/vitamin-b12-deficiency) or [small intestinal bacterial overgrowth](/home/digestive-disorders/malabsorption/small-intestinal-bacterial-overgrowth-sibo).

## Small intestine

Aging has only minor effects on the structure of the [small intestine](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/small-intestine), so movement of contents through the small intestine and absorption of most nutrients do not change much. However, lactase (the enzyme that helps digest lactose) levels decrease, leading to intolerance of dairy products by many older adults ([lactose intolerance](/home/digestive-disorders/malabsorption/lactose-intolerance)). Excessive growth of certain bacteria ([small intestinal bacterial overgrowth](/home/digestive-disorders/malabsorption/small-intestinal-bacterial-overgrowth-sibo)) becomes more common with age and can lead to pain, bloating, and weight loss. Bacterial overgrowth may also lead to decreased absorption of certain nutrients, such as vitamin B12, iron, and calcium.

## Pancreas, liver, and gallbladder

With age, the [pancreas](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/pancreas) decreases in overall weight, and some tissue is replaced by scarring (fibrosis). However, these changes do not decrease the ability of the pancreas to produce digestive enzymes and sodium bicarbonate. As the [liver](/home/liver-and-gallbladder-disorders/biology-of-the-liver-and-gallbladder/liver) and [gallbladder](/home/liver-and-gallbladder-disorders/biology-of-the-liver-and-gallbladder/gallbladder-and-biliary-tract) age, a number of structural and microscopic changes occur (see also [Effects of Aging on the Liver](/home/liver-and-gallbladder-disorders/biology-of-the-liver-and-gallbladder/effects-of-aging-on-the-liver)).

## Large intestine and rectum

The [large intestine](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/large-intestine) does not undergo much change with age. The [rectum](/home/digestive-disorders/biology-of-the-digestive-system/rectum-and-anus) does enlarge somewhat. Constipation becomes more common (see also [Constipation: Essentials for Older Adults](/home/digestive-disorders/symptoms-of-digestive-disorders/constipation-in-adults#v5612592)), which is caused by many factors:

* A slight slowing in the movement of contents through the large intestine
* A modest decrease in the contractions of the rectum when filled with stool
* More frequent use of medications that can cause constipation
* Often less exercise or physical activity
* Pelvic floor weakness in older women

Pelvic floor weakness in older women can also contribute to [fecal incontinence](/home/digestive-disorders/anal-and-rectal-disorders/fecal-incontinence).

This Merck Manual (Consumer Version) article, authored by Michael Bartel, MD, PhD (Fairfax, VA), reviews the effects of aging on the digestive system (full review April 2025, last updated July 2025). It explains that because the digestive system has substantial reserve capacity, aging affects its function less than other organ systems, yet older adults are more prone to diverticulosis, constipation (often medication-induced), and digestive issues related to changes in the gut microbiome (which may influence healthy aging, obesity, metabolic disorders, inflammation, cancer, and depression). The article breaks down age-related changes by organ:

- Esophagus: Contraction strength and upper esophageal sphincter tension decrease (presbyesophagus), but food movement is not impaired; some older adults may develop diseases affecting contractions.
- Stomach: Reduced lining resistance increases peptic ulcer disease risk, especially with aspirin/NSAID use; decreased elasticity limits food accommodation and slows emptying, though usually without symptoms; acid/pepsin secretion largely unchanged, but atrophic gastritis becomes more common, potentially causing vitamin B12 deficiency or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
- Small intestine: Structure and nutrient absorption largely unchanged; lactase levels decrease leading to lactose intolerance in many older adults; small intestinal bacterial overgrowth becomes more common, causing pain, bloating, weight loss, and reduced absorption of vitamin B12, iron, and calcium.
- Pancreas, liver, gallbladder: Pancreas loses weight with some fibrosis but retains enzyme/bicarbonate production; liver and gallbladder undergo structural and microscopic changes with age.
- Large intestine and rectum: Large intestine changes little; rectum enlarges somewhat. Constipation becomes more common due to slower transit, reduced rectal contractions, more constipating medications, less physical activity, and pelvic floor weakness in older women (which can also contribute to fecal incontinence).

## Abstract

OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of exercise-related gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms and the use of medication for these symptoms among long-distance runners, cyclists, and triathletes, and to determine the relationship of different variables to GI symptoms.

METHODS: A mail questionnaire covering the preceding 12 months was sent to 606 well-trained endurance type athletes: 199 runners (114 men and 85 women), 197 cyclists (98 men and 99 women), and 210 triathletes (110 men and 100 women) and sent back by 93%, 88%, and 71% of these groups, respectively. Symptoms were evaluated with respect to the upper (nausea, vomiting, belching, [heartburn](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/heartburn), chest pain) or lower part of the [GI tract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/gastrointestinal-tract) (bloating, GI cramps, side ache, urge to defecate, defecation, diarrhea). For statistical analysis, Mann-Whitney _U_ test, [Fisher exact test](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/fisher-exact-test), or Student _t_ test were used.

RESULTS: Runners experienced more lower (prevalence 71%) than upper (36%) GI symptoms during exercise. Cyclists experienced both upper (67%) and lower (64%) symptoms. Triathletes experienced during cycling both upper (52%) and lower (45%) symptoms, and during running more lower (79%) than upper (54%) symptoms. Bloating, diarrhea, and [flatulence](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/flatulence) occurred more at rest than during exercise among all subjects. In general, exercise-related GI symptoms were significantly related to the occurrence of GI symptoms during nonexercise periods, age, gender, diet, and years of training. The prevalence of medication for exercise-related GI symptoms was 5%, 6%, and 3% for runners, cyclists, and triathletes, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: Long-distance running is mainly associated with lower GI symptoms, whereas cycling is associated with both upper and lower symptoms. Triathletes confirm this pattern during cycling and running. The prevalence of medication for exercise-related GI symptoms is lower in the Netherlands in comparison with other countries, in which a prevalence of 10–18% was reported. More research on the possible predisposition of athletes for GI symptoms during exercise is needed.

## Introduction

Nowadays, gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms during training and competition in endurance-type athletes have received increasing attention. In most studies, GI symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, belching, bloating, heartburn, chest pain, GI cramps, side ache, and diarrhea are experienced by 20–50% of the athletes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. These symptoms may limit exercise performance and exercise participation 3, 4, 9, and they are often interpreted as being a result of maldigestion, malabsorption, changes in small intestinal transit, and improper food and fluid intake.

The occurrence of GI symptoms is associated with, among others, mode of exercise (prevalence is higher during running than during cycling) and duration of exercise (the longer the duration, the higher the prevalence) 2, 3, 4, 8, 9. Therefore, in sports activity such as triathlons and marathons a relatively high prevalence of GI symptoms can be expected.

To examine exercise-related GI symptoms, most investigators have applied questionnaires immediately after the finish of an endurance competition 2, 6, 8, 9, 10. In these studies, however, a bias towards athletes who suffer most from GI symptoms and are more eager to participate cannot be excluded. These studies have been criticized for their absence of data on GI symptoms during nonexercising periods (11). Further, comparison of the prevalence of GI symptoms between different sports based on current literature is difficult as the questionnaires applied in these studies differ considerably. In a review of the literature, Moses (12) concluded that in most endurance events symptoms of the lower GI tract are more prevalent than those from the upper part, except in multisport events such as triathlons.

In this study, we investigated the prevalence of symptoms of the upper and lower GI tract in three endurance sports (long-distance running, cycling, and triathlon) using a questionnaire by mail covering the whole competition season, including the prevalence of symptoms at rest (see Appendix). Further, we determined the relative importance of different variables that may affect GI symptoms during exercise. The choice of factors under study was based on current literature: age, menstrual cycle, training status, sports experience, running speed, and the use of fluids and (solid) food before and during competition 4, 5, 13, 14.

Finally, because a French study (15) found that prevalence of medication among triathletes for exercise-related GI symptoms was high and this prevalence is unknown for the Netherlands, we also investigated this in the endurance sports chosen.

Generally, studies suggest that 30–50% of athletes experience such complaints. Most gastrointestinal symptoms during exercise are mild and of no risk to health, but hemorrhagic gastritis, hematochezia, and ischemic bowel can present serious medical challenges. Three main causes of gastrointestinal symptoms have been identified, and these are either physiological, mechanical, or nutritional in nature. During intense exercise, and especially when hypohydrated, mesenteric blood flow is reduced; this is believed to be one of the main contributors to the development of gastrointestinal symptoms. Reduced splanchnic perfusion could result in compromised gut permeability in athletes. However, although evidence exists that this might occur, this has not yet been definitively linked to the prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms. Nutritional training and appropriate nutrition choices can reduce the risk of gastrointestinal discomfort during exercise by ensuring rapid gastric emptying and the absorption of water and nutrients, and by maintaining adequate perfusion of the splanchnic vasculature. A number of nutritional manipulations have been proposed to minimize gastrointestinal symptoms, including the use of multiple transportable carbohydrates, and potentially the use of nutrients that stimulate the production of nitric oxide in the intestine and thereby improve splanchnic perfusion. However, at this stage, evidence for beneficial effects of such interventions is lacking, and more research needs to be conducted to obtain a better understanding of the etiology of the problems and to improve the recommendations to athletes.

--- SOURCE 1: An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by ... - Frontiers ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1003445/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sport and Exercise Nutrition section) on November 9, 2022, titled "An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms." The study was conducted by Rachel Scrivin (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand), Ricardo J. S. Costa (Monash University, Australia), Fiona Pelly (University of the Sunshine Coast), Dana Lis (University of California, Los Angeles), and Gary Slater (University of the Sunshine Coast).

METHODOLOGY: The exploratory study used a validated online questionnaire (via Qualtrics) to investigate self-reported exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) and management strategies in 137 adult endurance athletes (participating in events ≥60 min) with a history of Ex-GIS. Participants included runners (55%, n=75), triathletes (22%, n=30), and non-running sports (23%, n=32), competing at recreationally competitive (37%), recreationally non-competitive (32%), and competitive regional/national/international (31%) levels. The questionnaire included 43 items covering participant demographics, Ex-GIS incidence/severity (using a 0-10 visual analog scale), management strategies, and information sources. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni corrections, and chi-squared tests.

KEY RESULTS:
- More females (63%, n=86) than males (37%, n=51) completed the questionnaire; mean age was 41.6 ± 11.1 years.
- Athletes reported Ex-GIS most frequently around training (21%), competitions (30%), or equally around both (49%).
- Lower gastrointestinal symptoms were more common than upper GI symptoms across all groups.
- The only severe symptom of significance was the urge to defecate during training in the equally-training group (Z = –0.536, p = 0.01).
- Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during exercise than before or after exercise in all categories.
- 67% (n=92) of athletes used dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting a total of 277 strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.
- Most popular dietary strategies: dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42), dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16), low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15). Non-dietary strategies: medications (4.7%, n=13) and relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11).
- Avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose) (6.1%, n=17) was the most popular FODMAP avoidance.
- Most successful dietary strategies (Likert scale 1-5): dietary fiber reduction (median=4, IQR 4-5), low FODMAP diet (median=4, IQR 4-5), dairy-free diet (median=4, IQR 4-5), and increasing carbohydrates (median=4, IQR 3-4).
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed to reduce Ex-GIS.
- Arginine was rated most successful supplement (median=5, n=1), followed by probiotics (median=4, n=26) and prebiotics (median=4, n=7).
- Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29), though no significant associations were found between information sources and sport, participation level, or sex.
- 15 athletes (11%) had a diagnosed GI disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (n=6); 13 athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS.

CONCLUSIONS: Endurance athletes use a variety of strategies to manage Ex-GIS, with dietary manipulation being the most common. The most successful strategies were dietary fiber reduction, low FODMAP diets, dairy-free diets, and increasing carbohydrate intake. Athletes predominantly seek guidance from accredited practicing dietitians. The study recommends that dietary strategies (e.g., low FODMAP, dairy avoidance) should be trialed during training to establish individual tolerance before implementation during competition. Further research is needed to determine whether these strategies are best applied acutely before exercise or integrated into habitual diets.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Endurance Exercise and Your Gut: Strategies to Outrun the Runs ---
URL: https://blog.nasm.org/fitness/endurance-exercise-gut-strategies-outrun-runs-gi-complaints

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the NASM blog, written by Dr. Geoff Lecovin, addresses gastrointestinal (GI) complaints experienced by endurance athletes. Adverse GI symptoms such as cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea affect up to 90% of endurance athletes and can adversely affect performance and lead to long-term health consequences.

**Causes of exercise-induced GI complaints (multifactorial):**
1. **Decreased GI perfusion** – Hypoperfusion of the gut during exercise ranges from mild circulatory changes to ischemia, caused by catecholamine release and splanchnic vasoconstriction that shunts blood to heart, lungs, muscles, and skin. This can lead to gut mucosal ischemia, increased permeability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
2. **Changes in motility** – Heavy exercise causes decreased peristalsis, decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone, and increased transient sphincter relaxation, linked to gastroesophageal reflux and impaired gastric emptying.
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** – High-intensity exercise compromises intestinal blood flow, increasing permeability, gut damage, impaired function, decreased nutrient absorption, and potentially a dysbiotic microbiome with pathogenic bacteria and endotoxin invasion into circulation.
4. **Mechanical causes** – Posture-related issues in runners and cyclists from repetitive high-impact mechanics; aerophagia (swallowing air) from increased respiration while drinking from water bottles.
5. **Nutritional causes** – Fiber, fat, protein, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying. Beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose and fructose combined) reduce GI symptoms.
6. **NSAIDs** – Associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction.
7. **Hyperthermia** – Heat exposure leads to intestinal ischemia from shunting blood to skin and muscles; heat acclimatization and hydration help mitigate effects.
8. **Dehydration** – Blood flow to gut and liver is reduced up to 80% during exercise; GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume.

**Practical guidelines provided:**
- Avoid high-fiber foods on race day and several days leading up
- Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities
- Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol)
- Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen
- Avoid high-fructose foods; fructose-glucose combinations are better tolerated
- Prevent dehydration
- Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water
- Choose lower carbohydrate concentration drinks to avoid high osmolalities
- Practice new nutrition strategies before race day

The article also discusses "training the gut" as a strategy to reduce GI distress by helping athletes acclimate to fluid and food ingestion during exercise, improving nutrient absorption and tolerance. The author, Dr. Geoff Lecovin, is a chiropractor, naturopathic physician, and acupuncturist with extensive certifications in exercise and nutrition. The article includes 12 scholarly references from journals including Sports Medicine, Journal of Applied Physiology, and Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The authors are Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Sapienza University of Rome, Italy), and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan, Italy). The article was submitted 26 July 2023, revised 30 August 2023, accepted 12 September 2023, and published 19 September 2023. It has 26 citations and an Altmetric score of 31.

**Key content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a condition affecting up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports (marathon, triathlon, cycling, running, etc.) caused by strenuous exercise. Symptoms include upper GI issues (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower GI issues (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two main pathways are described:
1. Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway: Sympathetic activation alters the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic blood flow can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing gut hypoperfusion, ischemic damage, loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP. 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study.

**GI symptoms during exercise:** 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms. In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors.

**IBS overlap:** Ex-GIS shares pathogenesis with IBS (alterations in gut microbiota, permeability, immune function, motility, visceral sensation, brain-gut interactions). IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed.

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms).

**Management:** The review emphasizes nutritional and behavioral strategies, particularly examining gluten-free diets and low-FODMAP (fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols) diets as the principal interventions to avoid symptoms during exercise. Exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet should all be evaluated.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023, yielding 142 relevant research articles published between 1965 and 2023.
</summary>

The study implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). The four phases were: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes, specifically including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of therapeutic interventions.

The study concludes that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms.

--- SOURCE 8: The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status in Response to Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Literature Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10185635

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic literature review published in Sports Medicine (April 2023) examining the effects of "gut-training" and "feeding-challenge" interventions on markers of gastrointestinal status in response to endurance exercise. The review was conducted by researchers from Monash University (Isabel G. Martinez, Alice S. Mika, Jessica R. Biesiekierski, Ricardo J. S. Costa) and followed PRISMA guidelines.

METHODS: Five databases (Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL Plus, Web of Science Core Collection, SPORTDiscus) were searched from inception until May 2022. The PICOS framework was used for eligibility, targeting healthy endurance athletes aged 12-60 years. Interventions included structured and repetitive carbohydrate feeding during exercise (at least 2 consecutive days or across repeated trials) or feeding challenges within 48 hours before exercise. Quality assessment used the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias (RoB 2) tool.

RESULTS: Of 304 studies identified, 8 were included after screening. Studies involved participants aged 15-35 years (79% male), mostly cyclists, runners, or triathletes. Interventions included carbohydrates only (n=7) in various forms (gels, liquid solutions) during cycling or running, or carbohydrate with protein (n=1), over 4-28 days.

Key findings include:
- Gut discomfort decreased by an average of 47% and 26% with a 2-week repetitive carbohydrate feeding protocol (n=2) and through repeated fluid ingestion over five trials (n=1), respectively.
- Repetitive carbohydrate feeding during exercise for 2 weeks reduced carbohydrate malabsorption by 45-54% (n=2), but one study showed no significant change.
- Significant improvements in total, upper, and lower gastrointestinal symptoms were observed (n=2), with unclear results in 4 studies.
- No significant changes were found in gastric emptying rate (n=2) or markers of intestinal injury and permeability (I-FABP, claudin-3) (n=3).
- Inconclusive results in studies examining plasma inflammatory cytokine concentrations (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1ra) in response to exercise with increased carbohydrate feeding (n=2).

CONCLUSIONS: Gut-training or feeding-challenge around exercise may provide advantages in reducing gut discomfort and potentially improving carbohydrate malabsorption and exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS), which may have exercise performance implications. However, the effect on other gastrointestinal functional responses, gastrointestinal integrity, and systemic responses remains unclear. The review calls for future research using more sensitive tools (e.g., non-metabolizable sugar probes, modified visual analog scale) to elucidate underlying mechanisms and fine-tune gut-training guidelines.
</summary>
