### Transcript:
If you've ever tried to run your usual 
training pace in the height of summer, you'll know a certain feeling. Your 
fitness hasn't necessarily changed. Your preparation has been the same, but your 
heart rate is higher than you think it should be for the effort. Your perceived exertion is 
climbing ahead of your pace. And at some point, you're either slowing down or 
working much harder to hold on. Now, that's not just discomfort. There's a 
measurable, predictable cost to running in the heat. And it shows up really clearly in the race 
data. Studies using large datasets of marathon results have consistently shown that recreational 
runners slow somewhere between 3% and 13% in hot conditions relative to cool ones. Elite runners 
slow too, typically in the region of 2% to 5%. The hotter the conditions and the slower the runner, 
the greater the penalty. Nobody can avoid it. Now, the standard explanation is dehydration 
or perceived effort. Things simply feel harder in the heat. And that's true to a point. 
But what's actually going on in terms of physiology is that there's an internal 
competition for blood flow going on, one that your cardiovascular system is 
structurally unable to fully resolve. And understanding that competition, 
what it actually is, what drives it, and how you can partially prepare for it, 
changes how we think about the interventions: why acclimatization helps, why some pre-cooling 
strategies are more effective than others, and why adjusting your pace in hot conditions is more 
of a physiological decision than a mental one. During exercise, your cardiovascular system 
has two distinct jobs. The first is delivering oxygenated blood to working muscle. The second 
is transporting heat from your core to the skin, where it can be dissipated. Both require 
blood flow. And your total cardiac output, the amount of blood your heart 
can pump per minute, is finite. In cool conditions, these two demands can be 
balanced pretty well. In the heat, though, something kind of has to give. The two 
primary routes for dissipating heat during exercise are evaporative cooling, or sweating, and 
convective cooling via increased skin blood flow. In humid environments, evaporation is limited 
because sweat can't transfer heat to air that's already saturated. That's why humidity 
compounds heat stress. It removes the most effective cooling route and increases 
the demand on skin blood flow even further. When core temperature then starts to rise, the 
body responds by dilating the blood vessels near the skin surface. This increases blood 
flow there substantially, from under a liter per minute at rest to potentially 6 to 8 
L per minute under serious heat stress. And this works, but that blood flow has to come 
from somewhere. The consequence is that central venous pressure falls. Less blood returns to 
the heart. Stroke volume drops. The amount of blood ejected with each beat decreases. To 
compensate, heart rate then starts to increase. At a fixed exercise pace, you are now 
working at a higher heart rate than you were 10 minutes ago for exactly the 
same output. And if conditions are severe enough and exercise continues long enough, 
heart rate alone cannot compensate. Cardiac output falls. Oxygen delivery to working 
muscles falls. Pace can't be sustained. This is cardiovascular drift. 
And it's why well-hydrated, well-trained athletes still meaningfully slow 
in the heat. Dehydration makes this worse. It reduces plasma volume even further, 
compounding the fall in ventricular filling. So the two problems interact. 
But the cardiovascular conflict exists without dehydration. Hydration is more like a 
multiplier here. It isn't the main mechanism. Now, there's a second component operating in parallel with all of this. As core 
temperature rises toward around 40°C, the central nervous system generates what 
you might think of as inhibitory signals: increased perceived effort, reduced motor drive, 
making it progressively harder to sustain pace. The framing you'll commonly see is that exercise 
terminates at a core temperature of around 40°. And there is controlled laboratory evidence 
supporting that as a rough threshold. But we need to be careful here. Trained athletes 
have been shown to sustain effort with core temperatures above 40°, particularly in shorter 
efforts where thermal loading has been gradual. What the evidence supports 
is that 40° is a danger zone, the point at which things are getting 
physiologically serious, rather than a precise biological switch. What the central 
nervous system is doing is protective. It's working to prevent a more dangerous outcome. 
And I'll come back to what that looks like. So, what can you do about this? Well, there are 
two interventions with meaningful evidence behind them and one pacing principle that follows 
directly from those mechanisms. None of them eliminate the problem, though, but each 
one changes the size of the constraint. The first is heat acclimatization. Lots 
of randomized controlled trials have shown a medium-sized improvement in time 
trial performance following structured heat exposure protocols. The adaptations 
include lower heart rate at a given pace, earlier onset of sweating, a higher sweat rate, 
and reduced overall cardiovascular strain. The mechanism is usually described as plasma 
volume expansion. The blood effectively gets topped up, which resolves some of 
the cardiovascular conflict. But there's one snag with this evidence. 
Controlled trials have struggled to confirm statistically significant 
changes in blood plasma volume. Plasma volume expansion is one important 
adaptation, usually only a few percent on average, and it helps support stroke volume. But it 
doesn't explain all of the observed effect. Lower heart rate, earlier sweating, altered sweat 
sensitivity, lower thermal strain, and perceptual changes all also contribute. In any case, what we 
do see consistently is cardiovascular improvement. So, the mechanism is widely accepted and 
physiologically plausible. It's just been harder to isolate than popular accounts 
sometimes suggest. The more practically important point is the timeline: how and 
when these adaptations actually happen. When it comes to cardiovascular adaptations, 
lower heart rate and improved cardiac efficiency begin emerging within roughly 
a week of consistent heat exposure. But the thermoregulatory adaptations, 
the changes that affect how your core temperature actually responds to heat 
during exercise, take closer to two weeks. A three- or four-day heat camp in the lead-up to a 
race will produce some cardiovascular benefit. It won't produce full thermoregulatory adaptation, 
though. So if the goal is complete preparation, the protocol needs to be longer 
than most athletes allow for it. The second intervention is pre-cooling, lowering 
core temperature before exercise begins, which increases the buffer between 
your starting temperature and the threshold zone. The mechanism is pretty 
straightforward. If you begin the race cooler, you have more thermal headroom 
before the system starts to struggle. A 2024 meta-analysis of randomized controlled 
trials confirmed that pre-cooling significantly improves endurance performance in the heat. 
But the effect wasn't consistent across strategies. External cooling, ice vests, 
and cold packs applied to the skin showed consistent significant improvements in both 
time trial performance and time to exhaustion. Whereas internal cooling, things 
like ice slurry ingestion, showed no statistically significant improvement 
in time trial performance in this analysis. Now, that's a counterintuitive finding 
given how commonly ice slurry is discussed as a pre-race strategy, but ultimately, the 
evidence for external cooling is more robust. Neither intervention removes the constraint, though. Even well-acclimatized athletes slow 
in the heat. Pre-cooling helps at the start. It doesn't protect you once you're deep into 
the race and thermal load is accumulating, which is why pacing deserves more 
recognition than it typically gets. At any given pace in hot conditions, 
the cardiovascular cost is higher. Holding your marathon pace at 25° is 
physiologically not the same effort as holding that same pace at 12°, even if 
the numbers on your watch look identical. Racing to a target pace in the heat and 
ignoring what heart rate and perceived effort are telling you accelerates 
cardiovascular drift rather than preventing it. So adjusting pace in the 
heat is not a failure of fitness or a failure of will. It's an accurate response 
to what the physiology is doing. The body is measuring something precisely. It's worth 
paying attention to what it's telling you. So before we finish up, it's worth 
spending a moment on what happens when the constraint is pushed past its limit, because the clinical picture that follows 
tells you something important about severity. The cardiovascular and thermal 
processes we've described, when they're not managed or when conditions 
are severe enough to override management, produce heat illness. And there 
are two distinct presentations. Heat exhaustion is primarily cardiovascular 
failure in the context of thermal stress. The system can no longer maintain adequate 
blood flow to the brain. An athlete collapses, or comes close to it: weak, nauseous, dizzy, but conscious and oriented. Core temperature 
is typically below 40°. Rest, cooling, and fluid replacement are the immediate priorities. 
With prompt management, the prognosis is good. Heat stroke is different, though, and the 
distinction matters clinically. The defining feature of heat stroke is not temperature. It's 
central nervous system dysfunction: confusion, disorientation, altered consciousness, 
and inability to walk in a straight line. CNS involvement is the emergency signal. It's 
what separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion, and it demands an immediate response. Aggressive 
cooling by any means available before transport, not after. Delay in cooling worsens 
outcomes significantly. The question to ask practically is not, "What 
is their temperature?" It's, "Is their brain affected?" That's 
the signal that determines urgency. Researchers studying heat stress 
during exercise have increasingly used ingestible temperature sensors, 
small capsules that transmit core temperature in real time via radio 
frequency to an external receiver. Used in research settings and in some professional 
sport contexts, these sensors can provide a more accurate measure of core temperature during 
exercise than skin sensors or wrist-based devices, which are measuring something several steps 
removed from what's actually happening centrally. They aren't widely available to 
recreational athletes yet, but they represent a meaningful change in how heat stress can 
be studied and, in some settings, managed. So heat slows you down not because 
your fitness fails in warm conditions, but because your cardiovascular system 
has two jobs and cannot fully do both at once. That constraint is structural. 
It operates whether you're aware of it or not. And it responds at least 
partially to deliberate preparation. Acclimatize properly, ideally over two 
weeks, and you change how much capacity the system has to manage the conflict. 
Cool externally before the race and you start with more thermal headroom. Adjust 
your effort to physiological signals rather than target pace and you distribute the 
cost more intelligently across the race. The question heat asks is not whether 
you can tolerate discomfort. It's whether you've prepared for the specific 
physiological constraint it creates. And if you understand why that constraint exists, 
you'll be better positioned to answer it.

args.summary:
This video by Dr. Cailbhe Doherty (13500 subscribers) explains the physiology behind why running in heat feels harder even when fitness hasn't changed, focusing on the concept of cardiovascular drift. Posted 2 Aug 2026 with ~11,192 views, the video breaks down how heat forces the cardiovascular system to split blood flow between working muscles and skin cooling.

KEY POINTS:
- During exercise, the cardiovascular system has two jobs: delivering oxygenated blood to working muscles and transporting heat from the core to the skin for dissipation. Total cardiac output is finite, creating an internal competition for blood flow.
- When core temperature rises, blood vessels near the skin dilate, increasing skin blood flow from under 1 L/min at rest to 6-8 L/min under serious heat stress. This causes central venous pressure to fall, stroke volume to drop, and heart rate to rise to compensate—this is cardiovascular drift.
- Data from large marathon datasets show recreational runners slow 3-13% in hot conditions vs. cool ones; elite runners slow 2-5%. Hotter conditions and slower runners incur greater penalties.
- Humidity compounds heat stress because it limits evaporative cooling (sweating), increasing demand on skin blood flow.
- Dehydration is a multiplier on cardiovascular drift (reduces plasma volume), but the cardiovascular conflict exists even without dehydration.
- As core temperature approaches ~40°C, the CNS generates inhibitory signals (increased perceived effort, reduced motor drive). While 40°C is commonly cited as a termination threshold, trained athletes can sustain effort above this, especially in shorter efforts with gradual thermal loading. 40°C represents a "danger zone" rather than a precise biological switch.

INTERVENTIONS:
1. Heat acclimatization: Medium-sized improvements in time trial performance shown in RCTs. Cardiovascular adaptations (lower heart rate, improved cardiac efficiency) emerge within ~1 week; thermoregulatory adaptations take ~2 weeks. Plasma volume expansion is one adaptation but studies have struggled to confirm statistically significant changes—other factors (earlier sweating, higher sweat rate, reduced thermal strain, perceptual changes) also contribute. A 3-4 day heat camp provides some cardiovascular benefit but not full thermoregulatory adaptation.
2. Pre-cooling: A 2024 meta-analysis confirmed pre-cooling significantly improves endurance performance in heat. External cooling (ice vests, cold packs) showed consistent significant improvements in time trial performance and time to exhaustion; internal cooling (ice slurry ingestion) showed no statistically significant improvement in time trial performance in this analysis.
3. Pacing: Adjusting pace to physiological signals (heart rate, perceived effort) rather than target pace is an accurate response to physiology, not a failure of fitness or will. Holding marathon pace at 25°C is not the same physiological effort as at 12°C.

HEAT ILLNESS DISTINCTION:
- Heat exhaustion: Primarily cardiovascular failure in thermal stress context; athlete collapses or comes close—weak, nauseous, dizzy, but conscious and oriented. Core temperature typically below 40°C. Rest, cooling, and fluid replacement are immediate priorities; prognosis is good with prompt management.
- Heat stroke: Defining feature is central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, disorientation, altered consciousness, inability to walk straight)—not temperature. Demands immediate aggressive cooling before transport; delay worsens outcomes. The key question is "Is their brain affected?" not "What is their temperature?"

ADDITIONAL CONTENT: Researchers increasingly use ingestible temperature sensors (capsules transmitting core temperature in real-time via radio frequency) for more accurate core temperature measurement during exercise compared to skin or wrist devices, though not yet widely available to recreational athletes.

FINAL TAKEAWAY: Heat slows runners not because fitness fails in warm conditions, but because the cardiovascular system has two jobs and cannot fully do both at once. Proper preparation (2-week acclimatization, external pre-cooling, pacing to physiological signals) changes how much capacity the system has to manage the conflict. The video cites 28 academic sources.

## Abstract

During endurance exercise, two problems arise from disturbed fluid–electrolyte balance: dehydration and overhydration. The former involves water and sodium losses in sweat and urine that are incompletely replaced, whereas the latter involves excessive consumption and retention of dilute fluids. When experienced at low levels, both dehydration and overhydration have minor or no performance effects and symptoms of illness, but when experienced at moderate-to-severe levels they degrade exercise performance and/or may lead to hydration-related illnesses including hyponatremia (low serum sodium concentration). Therefore, the present review article presents (a) relevant research observations and consensus statements of professional organizations, (b) 5 rehydration methods in which pre-race planning ranges from no advanced action to determination of sweat rate during a field simulation, and (c) 9 rehydration recommendations that are relevant to endurance activities. With this information, each athlete can select the rehydration method that best allows her/him to achieve a hydration middle ground between dehydration and overhydration, to optimize physical performance, and reduce the risk of illness.

## 1. Introduction

The essential components of central nervous system maintenance of body water volume and concentration include perceptions, behavior, nervous system responses, and the release of hormones (vasopressin, AVP; angiotensin II; atrial natriuretic peptide; apelin) [[1](#B1-nutrients-13-00887),[2](#B2-nutrients-13-00887),[3](#B3-nutrients-13-00887),[4](#B4-nutrients-13-00887)]. Perturbations of whole-body water volume and concentration are monitored by the brain, the resulting thirst and oropharyngeal sensations modulate drinking, and neuroendocrine responses regulate water and electrolyte excretion or retention by the kidneys [[1](#B1-nutrients-13-00887)]. During typical daily activities that do not include exercise, these complex interactions act to maintain total body water volume and serum concentration within 1–3% of baseline each day [[5](#B5-nutrients-13-00887),[6](#B6-nutrients-13-00887),[7](#B7-nutrients-13-00887)]. However, the relative influence of these processes varies with different life activities [[8](#B8-nutrients-13-00887)]. [Table 1](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t001) explains that, during sedentary daily pursuits in a mild environment, renal responses and thirst are the primary homeostatic regulators. During prolonged endurance exercise at low intensities (5–24 h duration), renal responses and thirst have minor-to-large effects on water regulation. As the duration of exercise increases, sweat losses become a major factor in whole-body water balance [[9](#B9-nutrients-13-00887)], regardless of the volume of fluid consumed.

This review article considers endurance exercise from the perspectives of body water and electrolyte balance, the negative effects that substantial fluid–electrolyte disturbances (i.e., both water loss and gain) have on competitive performance and health, and ways that endurance athletes can minimize performance decrements and mitigate the risk of exercise-associated illness. This is important because an endurance athlete can lose as much as 11–12% (7.8–8.5 kg) of body weight in the form of water, during a 12.3-h Ironman triathlon in a cool environment (3.8-km swim, 180-km bike, 42.2-km run) [[10](#B10-nutrients-13-00887)]. This also is important because day-long walking or hiking in a desert environment can result in extreme body mass losses of 14–18% when fluids are unavailable or restricted ([Figure 1](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f001)). Conversely, excessive fluid intake (i.e., water retention) can result in a body mass gain of more than 10% (7.8 kg) in 12.7 h while competing in an ultraendurance triathlon (ambient temperature, Tamb, 20.5 °C) [[11](#B11-nutrients-13-00887)]. These vastly different changes of body mass represent the primary problem and focus of this review paper: how to maintain a rehydration middle ground during prolonged exercise that reliably reduces the risk of illness by avoiding overhydration, and maintains exercise performance by avoiding significant dehydration.

## 2. Problem: Water and Salt Losses during Endurance Exercise

Most ultraendurance competitors do not meet their fluid needs during competition [[13](#B13-nutrients-13-00887)], due primarily to three factors that interact to influence sweat volume and body mass during prolonged exercise [[14](#B14-nutrients-13-00887)]. The first of these factors is exercise intensity. [Table 2](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t002) presents whole-body water balance measurements of 32 cyclists who completed a 164-km event in the state of Texas, USA during the month of August [[15](#B15-nutrients-13-00887)]. Cyclists have been grouped on the basis of time to complete 164 km: 9.6, 6.3, and 4.8 h. The total volume of sweat lost by these groups were similar (range of 7000–7200 g), demonstrating that the higher exercise intensities of groups 4.8 and 6.3 stimulated a greater sweat rate per hour (p < 0.01 to 0.0001) than that of group 9.6. Exercise intensity also affected body mass proportionally. The body mass change values for cyclist groups 9.6, 6.3, and 4.8 (columns 2–4, row 11) were −1800, −2300, and −2750 g. The second factor is exercise duration. As shown in [Table 2](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t002), slower cyclists may be on the course at least twice as long as faster competitors. Not surprisingly, similar body mass losses occur commonly ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002)) during ultra-running, ultra-cycling, and ultra-triathlon events [[16](#B16-nutrients-13-00887)]. Environmental temperature represents a third factor that influences body water balance. During 42.2 km marathon running, mild ambient conditions of 7, 10–12, and 20 °C resulted in mean sweat rates of 0.81, 0.96, and 1.52 L/h, respectively [[17](#B17-nutrients-13-00887)]. In addition, researchers measured the sweat rates of athletes in a laboratory building (29 °C, 51% relative humidity; running and cycling protocols), a mobile laboratory (29 °C, 65% rh), or field environment (25 °C, 55% rh) [[18](#B18-nutrients-13-00887)]. The majority of these athletes competed in team/skill sports (n = 1022) and individual endurance sports (n = 255). The highest average sweat rates were observed in the sports of American football (1.51 L/h) and Endurance Sports (1.28 L/h), whereas the lowest occurred in baseball (0.83 L/h) and soccer (0.94 L/h).

Representing extreme points of reference, the following individual sweat rate values have been observed. First, an elite marathon runner (age, 26 y; height, 185 cm; body mass, 66.9 kg) produced 3.7 L of sweat per h during the 1984 Los Angeles Summer Olympics marathon (24–28 °C Tamb; time to complete 42.2-km race, 2 h 14.3 min; body mass change, 5.43 kg, −8.1%) [[21](#B21-nutrients-13-00887)]. Second, a runner (age, 30 y; height, 185 cm; body mass, 91.8 kg) who had experienced heatstroke twice previously was observed to have a sweat loss of 4.1 L during a 70-min laboratory race simulation (25 °C) [[22](#B22-nutrients-13-00887)]. Third, the sweat rate of a male tennis player (age, 26 y; height, 197 cm; body mass, 91.4 kg) was 4.3 L/h during a 60 min laboratory simulation (36.1 °C; brisk walking and jogging on a treadmill) [[23](#B23-nutrients-13-00887)]. The sweat sodium losses (i.e., calculated by multiplying the measured sweat volume times the sweat sodium concentration) during the two simulations were 5930 and 7610 mg Na+, respectively. Additionally, as noted above, extreme body mass losses of −11 to −12% were experienced by competitors in an Ironman triathlon that required an average of 12.3 h to complete [[10](#B10-nutrients-13-00887)].

### 2.1. Effects of Dehydration on Endurance Exercise Performance

The negative influences of dehydration on exercise performance are recognized by professional sports medicine organizations [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[25](#B25-nutrients-13-00887),[26](#B26-nutrients-13-00887),[27](#B27-nutrients-13-00887)] and sport governing bodies [[28](#B28-nutrients-13-00887)] in position statements regarding rehydration, exertional heat illness, and physical performance. Although the precise water deficit at which performance decrements occurs is difficult to determine because of inter-individual differences, there is overall consensus in the literature that dehydration of −2 to −4% represents the range in which endurance exercise performance declines [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[25](#B25-nutrients-13-00887),[26](#B26-nutrients-13-00887),[28](#B28-nutrients-13-00887),[29](#B29-nutrients-13-00887),[30](#B30-nutrients-13-00887),[31](#B31-nutrients-13-00887)]. This effect is illustrated in [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f003), which presents a performance analysis of 34 published studies involving dehydration; a body water deficit of 1–3% was less likely to impair endurance exercise performance significantly (p < 0.05) than dehydration of 4–7% [[32](#B32-nutrients-13-00887)]. These 60 statistical comparisons involved outdoor track running, trail running, outdoor road cycling, indoor treadmill running, indoor rowing ergometry, and indoor cycle ergometry.

It also is relevant that controlled field studies have reported statistically significant decrements of endurance exercise performance at lower levels of dehydration (−1.0 to −2.2%). These controlled protocols evaluated running competitions at (a) three distances on an outdoor all-weather track [[33](#B33-nutrients-13-00887)] and (b) an outdoor cycling hill-climbing performance competition [[34](#B34-nutrients-13-00887)]. Similar performance decrements were reported for two indoor cycling simulations [[35](#B35-nutrients-13-00887),[36](#B36-nutrients-13-00887)] when dehydration ranged from 1.0–1.8%.

Decrements of outdoor cycling performance which occur at ≤4% body mass loss have been disputed in one meta-analysis [[37](#B37-nutrients-13-00887)] which evaluated 5 research articles (13 effect estimates). However, virtually all researchers agree that moderate-to-severe dehydration (e.g., 4–7% versus 1–2% body mass loss; [Figure 3](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f003)) results in greater physiologic strain and decreased aerobic exercise performance [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[26](#B26-nutrients-13-00887),[29](#B29-nutrients-13-00887),[30](#B30-nutrients-13-00887),[32](#B32-nutrients-13-00887),[38](#B38-nutrients-13-00887),[39](#B39-nutrients-13-00887),[40](#B40-nutrients-13-00887),[41](#B41-nutrients-13-00887)].

Physiologists agree that dehydration-induced aerobic performance decrements are greater in hot versus cool environments [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[29](#B29-nutrients-13-00887),[41](#B41-nutrients-13-00887),[42](#B42-nutrients-13-00887)], due to greater thermal and cardiovascular strain (i.e., increased skin temperature and blood flow, greater plasma volume loss, decreased cardiac output) that becomes physiologically impactful in the dehydration range of 2–4% of body mass [[43](#B43-nutrients-13-00887),[44](#B44-nutrients-13-00887)]. In terms of associated physiological effects, a summary of 8 relevant publications [[29](#B29-nutrients-13-00887)] noted that a 4–5% dehydration level reduced maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) more in a hot environment (−9 to −27% when Tamb ≥ 30 °C) than in a cool or mild environment (−3 to −7% when Tamb was 15–26 °C). The consequences of this dehydration included a shorter exercise time to exhaustion, an obligatory reduction in exercise intensity, or both.

### 2.2. Effects of Dehydration on Symptomatology and Illness

The classic desert field observations of Adolph and colleagues [[12](#B12-nutrients-13-00887)] during the mid-1940s were among the first descriptions of exercise-induced dehydration that approached and exceeded 10% body mass loss. Although Adolph’s systematic observations of dehydrated soldiers walking in the desert (Tamb > 37 °C) were not subject to statistical analyses, they provide a thorough description of the detrimental health effects of prolonged dehydration. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f001) presents a summary of the signs and symptoms that were reported when dehydration exceeded 2%. The following [Section 2.2.1](#sec2dot2dot1-nutrients-13-00887) through [Section 2.2.3](#sec2dot2dot3-nutrients-13-00887) describe disorders that result from water and salt deficiencies.

#### 2.2.1. Exercise Associated Collapse

A patient classification and care matrix, developed after years of treating runners in the medical tent of the Twin Cities Marathon, Minnesota, USA [[45](#B45-nutrients-13-00887)] facilitates clinical decision making and expedites the transition of distressed runners through a field medical facility near the finish line. Treatment of exercise-associated collapse centers on fluid replacement and body cooling or warming if needed. For suspected dehydration after the marathon, oral fluid replacement is preferred (e.g., water, fluid-electrolyte beverage, or 200–300 mL of salty soup bouillon to aid fluid retention). Intravenous fluid is necessary when casualties are unable to tolerate oral intake, and when there are clinical indications of severe volume depletion or ongoing fluid losses from vomiting or diarrhea. During medical treatment, to avoid adding water to a runner who already is overhydrated, exertional hyponatremia (see [Section 3.2](#sec3dot2-nutrients-13-00887)) is ruled out before intravenous fluid administration by assessing the serum Na+ concentration of runners who finish after 4 h [[45](#B45-nutrients-13-00887)].

#### 2.2.2. Exertional Heat Illnesses

Water and salt losses in sweat have implications for the health of athletes who exercise in hot environments. Water and sodium deficits are recognized as predisposing factors for exertional heat stroke [[46](#B46-nutrients-13-00887),[47](#B47-nutrients-13-00887),[48](#B48-nutrients-13-00887)], exertional heat cramps [[49](#B49-nutrients-13-00887)], and exertional heat exhaustion [[43](#B43-nutrients-13-00887),[50](#B50-nutrients-13-00887)]. Regarding the latter illness, research has shown that (a) mild exercise (40–50%VO2max) in hot environments (34–39 °C) does not induce heat exhaustion unless a significant fluid-electrolyte loss and cardiovascular strain exist; (b) a moderate but cumulative dehydration across 3 days can result in exertional heat exhaustion [[51](#B51-nutrients-13-00887),[52](#B52-nutrients-13-00887)]; and (c) 85% of heat exhaustion patients who presented at a deep metalliferous mine infirmary exhibited a urine specific gravity of 1.020–1.040, indicating mild-to-severe dehydration [[53](#B53-nutrients-13-00887)].

#### 2.2.3. Kidney Dysfunction and Renal Stress

Failure of the kidneys to perform essential functions (i.e., the clinical disorder named acute renal failure) is possible but uncommon during marathon footraces of 42.2 km and dehydration less than 4% of body mass [[54](#B54-nutrients-13-00887)]. However, both immediate (during and post-race) and delayed effects (i.e., 1–5 d after the event) of dehydration have been reported as abnormal values for urine flow rate, osmolar clearance, creatinine clearance, and protein in the renal filtration apparatus [[54](#B54-nutrients-13-00887)]. When no renal dysfunction is observed, considerable renal concentrating stress is possible. For example, 11 out of 33 cyclists who finished a summer 164 km ultraendurance event exhibited marked urine concentration, verified with specific gravity > 1.030 [[55](#B55-nutrients-13-00887)].

## 3. Problem: Overhydration during Endurance Exercise

### 3.1. Hyperhydration and Exercise Performance

No evidence suggests that deliberate pre-exercise consumption of excess pure water has an ergogenic effect on exercise performance [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[56](#B56-nutrients-13-00887)]. Glycerol, however, often is ingested prior to exercise (e.g., 1.2 g/kg body mass with a volume of fluid equal to 26 mL/kg body mass) to hyperhydrate athletes by increasing water retention and plasma volume while decreasing urine volume [[57](#B57-nutrients-13-00887)]. This act delays reaching a level of dehydration that degrades exercise performance. Research results are not conclusive, in that studies have shown both an ergogenic effect and no effect on exercise performance [[58](#B58-nutrients-13-00887),[59](#B59-nutrients-13-00887)]. However, one caveat should be noted. As glycerol dilutes both intracellular and extracellular fluids prior to exercise, it may predispose athletes to low serum Na+ as described in the next paragraph, especially if aggressive drinking occurs during exercise. A similar predisposition to low serum Na+ has been reported for deliberate overhydration with water and dilute fluids [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887),[60](#B60-nutrients-13-00887),[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887)].

### 3.2. Exertional Hyponatremia (EHN): A Potential Medical Emergency

When overhydration during exercise dilutes blood, an osmotic pressure gradient causes water to move into cells. The resulting cell swelling can result in EHN, one of the few illnesses that is potentially fatal to otherwise healthy athletes during exercise. Recognizable symptoms appear in most athletes at a serum concentration of approximately 130–135 mmol Na+/L [[26](#B26-nutrients-13-00887),[62](#B62-nutrients-13-00887)] and include lightheadedness, dizziness, nausea, puffiness (e.g., hands and feet), and body weight gain from baseline [[63](#B63-nutrients-13-00887)]. The majority of athletes whose serum Na+ is below 130 mmol/L ([Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002)) experience symptoms; these may include headache, vomiting, frothy sputum, difficulty breathing, pulmonary edema (i.e., fluid accumulation with swelling), and altered mental status such as confusion or seizure that results from cerebral edema [[10](#B10-nutrients-13-00887),[64](#B64-nutrients-13-00887)].

The signs and symptoms of EHN do not necessarily correlate with the serum Na+ in the range shown in [Table 3](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t003) (≥130 mmol Na+/L). The total symptoms score (column 10), rated with a validated Environmental Symptoms Questionnaire [[65](#B65-nutrients-13-00887)], was not related to the change of serum Na+ (column 5). Indeed, the self-rated symptoms of hyponatremic cyclists LC and AM (serum Na+ of 130 mmol/L) ranked among the lowest in this subject sample [[66](#B66-nutrients-13-00887)]. Thus, the severity of symptoms and not the absolute value of serum Na+ concentration guide the course of medical treatment [[63](#B63-nutrients-13-00887)].

[Table 3](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t003) includes data regarding two recreational cyclists (LC and AM) who began a summer 164-km event (Tamb, 34 ± 5 °C) with normal serum electrolytes but finished the ride with a serum sodium concentration of 130 mmol/L, indicative of mild EHN. The data of 12 other finishers (A–L, column 1) are presented to allow comparisons. Although they did not ride together, both cyclists consumed a large and similar relative volume of fluid (191 and 189 mL/kg), experienced an identical 11 mmol/L decrease of serum sodium, and reported low thirst sensations. However, one (LC) gained 3.1 kg (+4.3% of body mass) during 8.9 h of exercise (i.e., suggesting a dilutional effect) and the other (AM) maintained body mass (+0.1 kg, +0.1%, 10.6 h), suggesting that no excess fluid was retained. Thus, [Table 3](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t003) suggests a complex, individualized EHN etiology [[66](#B66-nutrients-13-00887)].

After exercise, fluids should be consumed judiciously because symptoms of EHN may develop hours after excess fluid consumption, as described in two published case reports. The first involved a 21-year old man who had aggressively consumed water and gained 5.25 kg of body weight during 5 h of treadmill exercise in a hot environment [[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887)]. He was asymptomatic until he experienced nausea and malaise late that evening, and was transferred to a nearby hospital with a serum Na+ of 122 mmol/L. After a night of observation, fluid restriction, and large urine output, he was released at 11:00 a.m. the next morning without symptoms. A more serious EHN case with delayed symptom onset involved a 49-year old runner who finished a 42.2 km marathon in 4 h 22 min then boarded an airline flight to return home [[67](#B67-nutrients-13-00887)]. Approximately 5 h after he finished the race, he became ill and experienced a grand mal seizure in the aisle of the cabin. The pilots diverted the aircraft to a nearby city for an emergency landing. The runner was transported to a hospital, where he experienced two additional seizures while unconscious with a serum Na+ of 129 mmol/L. A chest x-ray indicated pulmonary edema and a brain scan revealed cerebral edema; he also was diagnosed with renal insufficiency and liver damage. During the ensuing 18 months, this runner learned that he was unable to mentally process information that had previously been routine, and he was unable to perform his professional duties.

#### 3.2.1. Predisposing Factors for EHN

Exercise duration greater than 4 h, high sweat rate, high sweat Na+, and small body size have been identified as predisposing factors for EHN [[63](#B63-nutrients-13-00887),[68](#B68-nutrients-13-00887),[69](#B69-nutrients-13-00887),[70](#B70-nutrients-13-00887)]. [Table 4](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t004) allows consideration of other risk factors; data are rank-ordered on the basis of final serum Na+ (column 5). As the severity of EHN increased (i.e., moving from top to bottom as serum Na+ decreased), both body mass change (column 6) and the rate of fluid intake (column 8) trended toward increasing. The individuals and groups in [Table 4](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t004) (labeled A through M in column 1) also are depicted in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002), allowing comparisons to a large data base of marathon runners and Ironman triathletes. The open symbols (○) in [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002) represent individuals who sought medical care for symptomatic EHN.

A few athletes possess a “perfect storm” of characteristics in which a high sweat rate (e.g., 2.0–3.0 L/h) coexists with a high sweat sodium concentration (e.g., 40–80 mmol Na+/L; 2.3–4.6 g NaCl/L). These athletes may be identified by white salt deposits on a shirt, jersey, or shorts. Due to their relatively large sodium loss in sweat, they are at increased risk of developing EHN. In a hypothetical calculation, Hiller [[68](#B68-nutrients-13-00887)] noted that an Ironman triathlete with a sweat rate of 1.5 L/h could lose 36 g of NaCl (14,040 mg of sodium) in 12 h. This observation is supported by the mathematical prediction model of Montain et al. [[76](#B76-nutrients-13-00887)], which demonstrates that a high sweat sodium concentration is an important etiological factor.

#### 3.2.2. EHN Etiologies

Multiple EHN origins have been described [[20](#B20-nutrients-13-00887),[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887),[66](#B66-nutrients-13-00887),[67](#B67-nutrients-13-00887),[71](#B71-nutrients-13-00887)], and consensus regarding a single etiology is difficult to reach because some cases reportedly involve hyponatremia with body mass gain (i.e., hypervolemic hyponatremia, water retention that exceeds sweat and urine losses) [[10](#B10-nutrients-13-00887),[77](#B77-nutrients-13-00887),[78](#B78-nutrients-13-00887),[79](#B79-nutrients-13-00887)], whereas other EHN cases involve hyponatremia with body mass loss due to partially replaced sweat water and sodium losses (hypovolemic hyponatremia) [[10](#B10-nutrients-13-00887),[68](#B68-nutrients-13-00887),[77](#B77-nutrients-13-00887),[80](#B80-nutrients-13-00887)]. Importantly, a 2015 consensus document noted that all known EHN fatalities to that date had involved overconsumption of dilute fluids [[63](#B63-nutrients-13-00887)].

#### 3.2.3. EHN Cases Involve Variable Vasopressin Responses

Vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) is the body’s principal water-regulating hormone. It functions to maintain body water balance, in conjunction with thirst, by regulating serum osmolality within narrow limits [[81](#B81-nutrients-13-00887)]. Although dehydration with elevated serum osmolality is the primary stimulus for the release of vasopressin from the pituitary, non-osmotic factors also are known, including plasma volume decrease, hypoglycemia, nausea, and vomiting [[82](#B82-nutrients-13-00887)].

In an unknown percentage of EHN cases, serum vasopressin increases abnormally during overhydration, facilitating water retention. This inappropriately high serum vasopressin also stimulates sodium excretion by the kidneys, reducing serum Na+. As vasopressin has a brief half-life and laboratory analysis is technically difficult, this hormone rarely is analyzed in cases of EHN. Nevertheless, this condition was verified during a marathon field study [[83](#B83-nutrients-13-00887)] in which 43% of runners with a serum Na+ < 130 mmol/L exhibited inappropriately high serum vasopressin levels (range, 3–17 pg/mL), and during a case of symptomatic EHN that developed during a laboratory investigation [[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887)]. A notable exception to these reports occurred among 7 symptomatic Ironman triathletes [[74](#B74-nutrients-13-00887)] who finished 12 h of exercise with a median body weight loss of 0.5%, post-exercise plasma Na+ of 128 mmol/L, and a post-exercise plasma vasopressin concentration of 1.6 pmol/L; these values represented symptomatic EHN with a low serum vasopressin concentration. A control group of 11 asymptomatic triathletes exhibited the following comparison values: body weight loss of 3.9%, plasma Na+ of 141 mmol/L, and a plasma vasopressin concentration of 4.6 pmol/L; these levels represented a typical hormonal response to moderate dehydration. These variable vasopressin responses illustrate why it is difficult to attain consensus regarding the role of arginine vasopressin in EHN.

A coherent explanation for variable vasopressin responses was published by Hew-Butler [[82](#B82-nutrients-13-00887)]. Her review article distinguished intense (brief, >90% of maximal oxygen consumption), steady state (sustained at 40–60% of maximal oxygen uptake), and prolonged endurance (>1 h) exercise. During the former, an obvious and statistically significant increase of plasma vasopressin occurs that exceeds the expected increase due to increased plasma osmolality. Steady state exercise also generally stimulates a statistically significant vasopressin increase. During prolonged competitive endurance exercise, a similar vasopressin increase occurs, with or without significant increases of serum Na+ or osmolality; this elevation persisted for 2 h after a 24 h competitive track race and for 31 h after a 38 km non-competitive run. In all of these exercise types, it appears that published vasopressin responses are difficult to interpret because of differences in exercise intensity [[82](#B82-nutrients-13-00887)].

#### 3.2.4. Evidence for an EHN Drinking Rate Threshold

A previous analysis of 6 groups of runners and triathletes reported that no case of symptomatic EHN occurred (serum sodium < 130 mmol/L during continuous exercise that lasted 3.2–12.3 h) among 270 athletes who consumed less than 750 mL of fluid per hour [[67](#B67-nutrients-13-00887)]. In addition, case reports of two female ultradistance triathletes [[73](#B73-nutrients-13-00887)] observed that their post-race hyponatremia (130 and 131 mmol Na+/L) was accompanied by weight gain (0.5 and 1.5 kg). They consumed fluids during competition at a rate of 730 and 760 mL/h. [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002) also supports this drinking rate threshold for the onset of EHN, in that all yellow highlighted square symbols represent individuals who consumed fluids at a rate > 700 mL/h, and gained weight during their respective exercise bouts. These individuals are clustered in the lower left quadrant of [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002), among symptomatic athletes (open symbols, ○). These observations suggest that endurance athletes who consume fluids at a rate < 700 mL/h have a decreased risk of EHN. This theoretical 700 mL/h fluid consumption rate threshold is consistent with the 400 to 800 mL/h recommendations of both the International Marathon Medical Directors Association [[84](#B84-nutrients-13-00887)], the American College of Sports Medicine [[24](#B24-nutrients-13-00887)], and a mathematical model that was designed to clarify the etiology of EHN [[76](#B76-nutrients-13-00887)].

#### 3.2.5. Does Sodium Intake Counteract a Low Serum Na+?

It is widely recognized that salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) capsules are consumed during triathlons and marathons. Exploring this trend within endurance sports, Hoffman & Stuempfle [[80](#B80-nutrients-13-00887)] reported that 90–96% of runners consumed sodium supplements during a 161-km ultramarathon footrace because they believed that it prevented muscle cramps and hyponatremia. However, there is little evidence to support this belief. For example, [Table 3](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t003) shows that cyclists J, K, L, LC and AM consumed the largest amounts of sodium but experienced the greatest decrease of serum Na+, whereas cyclists A, B, C and D consumed small amounts of sodium and experienced an increased serum Na+ [[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887)]. Therefore, sodium consumption did not prevent EHN from occurring in cyclists LC and AM, and low sodium intake by other cyclists was not associated with EHN. Similar conclusions have been published regarding ultramarathon competitors by Speedy et al. [[85](#B85-nutrients-13-00887)], Hew-Butler et al. [[86](#B86-nutrients-13-00887)], Hoffman and Stuempfle [[80](#B80-nutrients-13-00887)], and Hoffman and Myers [[87](#B87-nutrients-13-00887)].

Two controlled laboratory studies also have quantified the effects of sodium consumption on serum Na+. The first provided 3911 mg of sodium during 6 h of exercise in a 34 °C environment [[88](#B88-nutrients-13-00887)], and the second provided 1409 mg sodium during 3 h of exercise at 30 °C [[89](#B89-nutrients-13-00887)]. Post-exercise measurements detected a mean serum Na+ increase of 3 mmol/L (i.e., supplemented versus control experiments) in both studies, indicating that sodium supplementation had a minor influence on serum Na+ levels.

## 4. The Complexity of Thirst and Drinking

Thirst prompts seeking and consuming water, and is measured with a subjective rating scale. Drinking behavior is distinct from thirst, is measured as the volume of fluid consumed, and may involve fluid selection on the basis of preferred or required characteristics (i.e., temperature, palatability, ingredients, energy content) [[90](#B90-nutrients-13-00887)].

During sedentary daily activities (i.e., producing a small 24-h water turnover), the perception of thirst, the act of drinking, renal regulation of water and electrolytes, and neuroendocrine responses ([Table 1](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t001)) adequately regulate total body water volume and serum concentration within 1–3% of each individual’s baseline, from one day to the next [[5](#B5-nutrients-13-00887),[6](#B6-nutrients-13-00887),[7](#B7-nutrients-13-00887)]. During prolonged endurance exercise, however, the relationship between perception of thirst and whole-body fluid–electrolyte balance can be distorted by physiological challenges [[32](#B32-nutrients-13-00887),[91](#B91-nutrients-13-00887)] such as sizeable water and sodium losses in sweat, movement of water between the intracellular and extracellular spaces, or plasma volume depletion [[6](#B6-nutrients-13-00887)].

### 4.1. Multiple Factors Influence Drinking during Endurance Exercise

[Figure 4](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f004) presents several factors that influence thirst and drinking behavior, each of which is monitored and regulated continuously by the central nervous system. Thus, the phrase dynamic complexity applies to the vast, integrated, brain-wide network of nerve circuits and brain regions that regulate thirst, drinking, body water volume, and fluid concentration [[92](#B92-nutrients-13-00887)]. The findings of two recent human studies [[93](#B93-nutrients-13-00887),[94](#B94-nutrients-13-00887)] suggest that thirst is one of multiple conscious perceptions and subconscious autonomic responses ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f004)) that evolve simultaneously during dehydration and rehydration to influence drinking behavior. Simply stated, the internal motivation to consume water is influenced by multiple factors that reinforce the perception of thirst.

![Nutrients 13 00887 g004](/nutrients/nutrients-13-00887/article_deploy/html/images/nutrients-13-00887-g004-550.jpg "Nutrients 13 00887 g004")

**Figure 4.**
Influences on thirst and drinking behavior during endurance exercise. All factors in this diagram are perceived, monitored, and/or regulated by the brain.

As dehydration concentrates extracellular fluid, plasma osmolality (Posm) is recognized as the primary factor that stimulates thirst [[2](#B2-nutrients-13-00887),[81](#B81-nutrients-13-00887),[95](#B95-nutrients-13-00887)]. However, as shown in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f005), the Posm threshold at which thirst is perceived varies greatly across individuals (range, 274–293 mOsm/kg) and may be lower than the range of laboratory reference values for Posm (285–295 mOsm/kg) [[96](#B96-nutrients-13-00887)]. The data in [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f005) were compiled from 5 published human studies; the shape of this frequency distribution implies that the thirst threshold is a multifactorial (polygenic) characteristic [[97](#B97-nutrients-13-00887)]. Although inter-individual differences of the Posm threshold for thirst have not been studied during exercise, [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f005) suggests that the level of dehydration (i.e., increased Posm) that initiates drinking during exercise might differ considerably among athletes.

![Nutrients 13 00887 g005](/nutrients/nutrients-13-00887/article_deploy/html/images/nutrients-13-00887-g005-550.jpg "Nutrients 13 00887 g005")

**Figure 5.**
Frequency distribution of the plasma osmolality (Posm) threshold for the onset of thirst. The horizontal gray bar delineates the laboratory reference range of Posm values (285–295 mOsm/kg) for healthy adults. Reprinted under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license (<http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>) accessed on 2 March 2021. Modified from [[97](#B97-nutrients-13-00887)].

### 4.2. Inter-Individual Differences

[Figure 6](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f006) illustrates six factors that influence the change of body mass and serum Na+. Interactions of these factors with inherited characteristics and endurance training regimens produce great differences among athletes. In [Figure 2](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f002), for example, if a male athlete experienced a body mass change of only—0.5% (0.35 kg) during a 13 h Ironman triathlon, his serum Na+ could range from 119 (symptomatic EHN) to 157 mmol/L (severe hypernatremia). Conversely, if a male athlete finished with a serum Na+ of 140 mmol/L (i.e., in the center of the reference range for healthy adults), his body weight change could range from +5.5% (+3.9 kg) to −12.5% (−8.8 kg). These large serum Na+ and body mass ranges represent the effects of numerous perceptual, behavioral, hereditary and fluid-electrolyte variables ([Figure 4](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f004), [Figure 5](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f005) and [Figure 6](#fig_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-f006)), but are influenced mostly by the total volume of sweat produced (e.g., 15.6 L/13 h at a sweat rate of 1.2 L/h) and the total volume of fluid consumed (e.g., 9.1 L/13 h at a drinking rate of 700 mL/h).

![Nutrients 13 00887 g006](/nutrients/nutrients-13-00887/article_deploy/html/images/nutrients-13-00887-g006-550.jpg "Nutrients 13 00887 g006")

**Figure 6.**
Factors that influence the relationship between body weight gain/loss and serum Na+ during endurance exercise. The largest effects on whole body fluid–electrolyte balance are the volume of sweat lost and the volume of fluid consumed. Notes: a, water and low-sodium fluids promote dilution of body fluids; b, physical training and heat acclimatization increase sweat rate and decrease sweat sodium concentration; c, urine production decreases during exercise; d, increased dietary sodium encourages water retention but affects only a minor increase of serum Na+**.**

Large inter-individual differences also exist among elite runners. Fluid intake rates were determined for 10 men who placed 1st or 2nd (range of finish times, 2:03:59 to 2:10:55) during prestigious city marathons [[98](#B98-nutrients-13-00887)]. Each runner’s drinking behavior was recorded on videotape and fluid intake was estimated by multiplying drinking time by 45.2 mL/s (i.e., a value determined by laboratory drinking simulations). Half of these runners consumed fluids at rates that ranged from 30–300 mL/h (73–631 mL total), whereas the rate of fluid intake of the other 5 elite runners ranged from 420–1040 mL/h (886–2205 mL total). Clearly, these data indicate that elite marathon runners (a) ingest fluid at rates that span a wide range during competition (30–1040 mL/h), and (b) some individuals greatly exceed the proposed drinking rate threshold at which symptomatic EHN appears (700 mL/h), described above in [Section 3.2.4](#sec3dot2dot4-nutrients-13-00887).

### 4.3. Personal Beliefs and Sources of Rehydration Information

Personal beliefs about drinking may predispose an athlete to EHN, according to the findings of two case reports. The first [[66](#B66-nutrients-13-00887)] involved cyclists LC and AM in [Table 3](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t003) (who also are designated as athletes H and J in [Table 4](#table_body_display_nutrients-13-00887-t004)). Their urine specific gravity measurements on Day-1 (LC, 1.006; AM, 1.004; 31 control cyclists, 1.017) and the morning of the road ride (LC, 1.003; AM, 1.005; controls, 1.019) indicated that both had overhydrated before prolonged exercise. The authors suggested that their pre-event hydration behavior, coupled with high rates of fluid intake during the ride (LC, 1500 mL/h; AM, 1400 mL/h), resulted in both cyclists experiencing asymptomatic EHN. The second publication [[61](#B61-nutrients-13-00887)] involved a controlled case report of EHN (serum Na+, 122 mmol/L) observed during 5 h of intermittent treadmill walking in a hot environment (Tamb, 41 °C). A physically fit, 21 year-old male began exercise with blood values (serum Na+, 134 mmol/L; osmolality, 282 mOsm/kg) slightly below the laboratory reference ranges for healthy males, because he had voluntarily overhydrated throughout the previous day. Overhydration prior to exercise is known to lower serum Na+ and therefore increase the risk of dilutional hyponatremia if fluids are agg

This is a scientific review article titled "Rehydration during Endurance Exercise: Challenges, Research, Options, Methods" by Lawrence E. Armstrong (Human Performance Laboratory and Korey Stringer Institute, University of Connecticut), published in the journal *Nutrients* (2021, Vol. 13, Issue 3, article 887; DOI: 10.3390/nu13030887). The paper was submitted 11 February 2021, accepted 1 March 2021, and published 9 March 2021.

The article addresses the two primary problems arising from disturbed fluid-electrolyte balance during endurance exercise: dehydration (incomplete replacement of water and sodium losses in sweat and urine) and overhydration (excessive consumption and retention of dilute fluids). Both can degrade exercise performance and lead to hydration-related illnesses when experienced at moderate-to-severe levels.

Key content areas covered:

1. **Water and Salt Losses**: Most ultraendurance competitors do not meet fluid needs during competition. Three factors influence sweat volume and body mass: exercise intensity (higher intensity = greater sweat rate per hour), exercise duration (slower competitors can be on course twice as long), and environmental temperature (marathon sweat rates of 0.81, 0.96, and 1.52 L/h at 7°C, 10-12°C, and 20°C respectively). Extreme individual sweat rates observed: 3.7 L/h (elite marathon runner, 1984 LA Olympics), 4.1 L/h (laboratory race simulation), and 4.3 L/h (tennis player). Extreme body mass losses of 11-12% have been documented in Ironman triathlons.

2. **Dehydration Effects on Performance**: Consensus exists that dehydration of -2 to -4% body mass represents the range where endurance exercise performance declines. A meta-analysis of 34 studies found dehydration of 4-7% more likely to impair performance than 1-3%. Performance decrements are greater in hot versus cool environments (a 4-5% dehydration level reduced VO2max by -9 to -27% when ambient temp ≥30°C versus -3 to -7% at 15-26°C).

3. **Dehydration-Related Illnesses**: Includes exercise-associated collapse, exertional heat illnesses (heat stroke, cramps, exhaustion), and kidney dysfunction/renal stress (acute renal failure possible but uncommon at dehydration <4%; marked urine concentration seen in 11 of 33 cyclists).

4. **Overhydration and Exertional Hyponatremia (EHN)**: No evidence that pre-exercise hyperhydration improves performance. EHN is a potentially fatal illness caused by overhydration diluting blood, causing water to move into cells and cell swelling. Symptoms appear at serum concentration ~130-135 mmol Na+/L and include lightheadedness, dizziness, nausea, puffiness, and body weight gain. Below 130 mmol/L, symptoms may include headache, vomiting, pulmonary edema, and altered mental status from cerebral edema. Predisposing factors: exercise duration >4 hours, high sweat rate, high sweat sodium, and small body size. A theoretical drinking rate threshold of ~700 mL/h was identified—no cases of symptomatic EHN occurred among 270 athletes consuming less than 750 mL/h. Notably, sodium supplementation had only a minor influence on serum Na+ levels (mean increase of 3 mmol/L in controlled studies) and did not prevent EHN.

5. **Thirst Complexity**: The plasma osmolality threshold for thirst varies greatly across individuals (range 274-293 mOsm/kg, compared to laboratory reference range of 285-295 mOsm/kg). Elite marathon runners showed wide variation in fluid intake rates (30-1040 mL/h). Two case studies showed that overhydration prior to exercise combined with high fluid intake during exercise resulted in asymptomatic EHN.

The article presents 5 rehydration methods (ranging from no advanced action to determination of sweat rate during field simulation) and 9 rehydration recommendations relevant to endurance activities, allowing each athlete to select the method that best helps them achieve a "rehydration middle ground" between dehydration and overhydration. The article belongs to the Nutrients Special Issue "Hydration and Fluid Needs during Physical Activity."
args.key_excerpts: "During endurance exercise, two problems arise from disturbed fluid–electrolyte balance: dehydration and overhydration. The former involves water and sodium losses in sweat and urine that are incompletely replaced, whereas the latter involves excessive consumption and retention of dilute fluids."

<webpage_content>
[![](https://runnersconnect.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/foot-with-words.png)](https://runnersconnect.net)

 

# Masters Running Tips: 5 Evidence-Based Ways to Train Smarter After 40

![](https://masedge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Jeff-Gaudette-Author.webp)

Jeff Gaudette, MS   |

The Quick Summary

 

Masters runners (40+) lose aerobic capacity at roughly 1% per year when training consistently — about half the rate of sedentary peers.

Recovery extends to 48–72 hours between hard sessions due to anabolic resistance and declining NAD+ levels in aging cells.

Strength training for masters runners must include heavy compound lifts and plyometrics to maintain fast-twitch fiber function, not just body-weight stability work.

Easy runs should be genuinely easy — 90–120 seconds per mile slower than race pace — so quality sessions stay hard enough to drive adaptation.

Masters runners need 35–40g of leucine-rich protein per meal to overcome the age-related blunting of muscle protein synthesis.

You hit 40 and your easy pace slows down.

Your legs feel flat for three days after a hard workout that used to leave you recovered by morning.

You’re training just as consistently as you did in your 30s, and the times keep sliding anyway.

It’s a physiology problem, and it responds to a specific set of adjustments that runners over 40 rarely make because no one explained what’s actually changing and why.

In this guide, you’ll learn:

* How much performance actually declines with age, and what the research shows about the pace of that decline
* Why recovery takes longer after 40, and the cellular mechanism behind it
* The type of strength training that directly addresses the muscle changes masters runners face
* How to restructure your intensity distribution to protect your best training weeks
* Why your protein needs are higher than they were a decade ago

## How Much Does Performance Decline After 40?

The decline is real, but the picture is more encouraging than most runners expect.

> ![research](https://masedge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/academic-research.svg)  
>  **[Research tracking masters athletes in endurance events](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28018241/) found that aerobic capacity declines at roughly 1% per year in active runners after 40, about half the rate seen in sedentary adults the same age.**

The primary drivers of that decline are a drop in VO2 max, a reduction in maximal strength, and a gradual loss of running economy.

All three respond to training.

The steepest drop in VO2 max typically occurs after age 60.

Lactate threshold holds up better than VO2 max with age.

[A study of 168 master runners](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10862547/) found that lactate threshold remained a strong predictor of race performance even as VO2 max declined.

The runner who keeps threshold workouts on the calendar maintains their performance ceiling more effectively than one who shifts entirely to easy volume.

The decline is manageable with the right training adjustments.

Runners who accept the change and adjust the inputs often race their best age-graded times in their 40s and 50s.

 ![VO2 max decline after 40: active masters runners vs sedentary adults comparison chart](https://runnersconnect.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/masters-running-tips-vo2max-decline.webp)

Aerobic capacity declines at roughly 1% per year in active runners after 40, compared to 2% per year in sedentary adults. Source: Lepers & Stapley (2016)

## RunnersConnect Bonus

Download your FREE Age Grading Performance Calculator now.

It makes it easy to calculate your age graded performance to compare yourself against those young guns or your former self.

[Get My Calculator Now](https://app.monstercampaigns.com/c/ic2zth3znb4je1jfrqsg)

## Why Do Masters Runners Take Longer to Recover?

The most common complaint from masters runners is that they need more rest between hard sessions than they used to.

The mechanism is cellular.

Aging muscles develop what researchers call anabolic resistance: a [diminished ability to respond to anabolic stimuli](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41305554/) including exercise and protein intake.

The muscle protein synthesis signal that fires robustly after a hard workout in a 28-year-old is blunted in a 48-year-old running the same session at the same relative effort.

The inflammatory resolution process also slows.

The cellular repair cascade that clears exercise-induced damage and rebuilds tissue takes longer to complete.

That extends the adaptation window from 24-36 hours to 48-72 hours for most masters runners.

After a hard workout, most masters runners need 48-72 hours of recovery before their next quality session, compared to 24-36 hours for runners in their 20s.

Part of this slowdown traces to NAD+ levels.

NAD+ is a coenzyme that declines naturally with age and plays a central role in mitochondrial energy production and cellular repair.

Lower NAD+ means slower turnover of damaged mitochondria and a less efficient recovery signal between sessions.

Addressing that decline at the source is what NAD+ supplementation is designed to do. [MAS NAD+](https://masedge.com/nad-for-runners/) is targeted specifically at masters athletes who are still training consistently but not recovering or adapting the way they used to.

In practical terms, the adjustment looks like this: schedule hard workouts on Tuesday and Saturday rather than Tuesday and Thursday.

Treat the days between as genuinely easy.

## What Kind of Strength Training Do Masters Runners Need?

The general advice to do 2 strength sessions per week is correct for masters runners. But the type of strength work matters as much as the frequency.

> ![research](https://masedge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/academic-research.svg)  
>  **[Muscle fiber analysis across age groups](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3379447/) shows that fast-twitch fiber area and count decline progressively from age 25 onward, with the reduction concentrated in type II (fast-twitch) fibers.**

Fast-twitch fibers are responsible for power, speed, and running economy at race pace.

When they atrophy, your stride loses the elastic stiffness that makes fast running efficient. You can still train the aerobic engine, but the neuromuscular component that converts aerobic fitness into actual race speed deteriorates without deliberate maintenance.

The fix requires heavy resistance training combined with plyometric work.

[Research comparing masters runners to younger runners](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21982960/) found that muscle strength and power were significantly lower in the masters group and that these differences tracked directly with reduced [running economy](https://runnersconnect.net/running-economy/) at race pace.

Heavy compound movements and plyometrics are the specific training stimulus that maintains fast-twitch fiber function in masters runners.

Stability work helps with injury prevention but generates a weaker signal for fast-twitch fiber recruitment than loaded compound lifts.

Prioritize: heavy single-leg deadlifts (4-6 reps, 3 sets), split squats with load, calf raises to failure, and bounding drills 2 days per week.

## How Should Masters Runners Adjust Their Training Intensity?

The most common training error among masters runners is compressing the intensity distribution.

Easy runs get moderately hard.

Hard runs stay moderately hard.

The result is a week of medium-effort sessions that are too easy to produce adaptation and too hard to permit real recovery.

The research on lactate threshold in masters athletes points in one direction: protect threshold and VO2 max work by making everything else genuinely easy.

A runner whose current 5K pace is 8:00/mi (4:58/km) should be running most of their weekly mileage at 10:30-11:30/mi (6:31-7:08/km) or slower.

The reason is recovery arithmetic.

Every session at 75-80% max heart rate extends your next recovery window by hours.

[Running genuinely easy](https://runnersconnect.net/recovery-run/) on off days means your hard days stay hard.

Hard days are where adaptation happens for masters runners.

Masters runners who slow their easy days by 90-120 seconds per mile often find their race performance improves because their quality sessions finally produce real adaptation instead of accumulated fatigue.

 ![Masters runners training intensity distribution: common mistake vs what works comparison](https://runnersconnect.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/masters-running-tips-intensity-distribution.webp)

Masters runners who let easy runs drift moderate lose the training contrast needed for adaptation.

The practical weekly structure for a 40-mile (64 km) week masters runner: 2 quality sessions (threshold or VO2 max work), 1 long run at easy effort, and the remaining mileage across genuinely easy days with one full rest day built in.

## How Much Protein Do Masters Runners Actually Need?

Masters runners need more protein per meal than they did a decade ago.

The key variable is the threshold for triggering muscle protein synthesis per meal.

Younger muscles respond to roughly 20-25g of high-quality protein per meal with a robust muscle-building signal. Older muscles require more leucine (the amino acid that activates muscle protein synthesis) to generate the same response.

> ![research](https://masedge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/academic-research.svg)  
>  **[Studies combining leucine-rich protein with resistance training](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36364764/) in adults over 50 found significant improvements in body composition and physical function compared to resistance training alone.**

That same anabolic resistance means the old “20g per meal” target often falls short.

For masters runners training 5 or more days per week, current evidence supports targeting 35-40g of protein per meal, spaced across 3-4 meals. The post-workout window within 30-45 minutes of finishing a hard session is particularly important.

Masters runners should target 35-40g of protein per meal, roughly 50-60% more per meal than the threshold sufficient for runners in their 20s.

Leucine content matters more than protein source.

* Frequently Asked Questions

At what age does running performance start to decline?

VO2 max begins declining gradually from the mid-20s, but for active runners the impact on race performance is usually modest until the early 40s. The rate of decline is roughly 1% per year for runners who maintain training, compared to 1.5–2% per year for sedentary adults. Most masters runners don’t notice meaningful performance changes until they stop adjusting their training structure to match what their physiology actually needs after 40.

  How often should a masters runner do hard workouts?

Most masters runners perform best with 2 quality sessions per week — one threshold effort and one VO2 max or race-pace session — spaced 72 hours apart rather than 48. Adding a third hard day consistently produces accumulated fatigue rather than fitness gains because the recovery window has extended with age. The remaining days should be genuinely easy, with at least one full rest day built into the week.

  Does strength training slow the decline in running performance after 40?

Yes, and specifically the type of strength training matters. Heavy compound lifts (single-leg deadlifts, split squats) and plyometric work (bounding, box jumps) target the fast-twitch muscle fibers that decline earliest and most significantly with age. Body-weight stability circuits help with injury prevention but don’t generate the loading stimulus needed to maintain the neuromuscular component of running economy. Research shows masters runners with higher muscle strength have better running economy at race pace.

  Why do I need more rest between workouts as a masters runner?

Aging muscles develop anabolic resistance — a blunted response to the exercise signal that triggers muscle repair and adaptation. The inflammation from a hard workout resolves more slowly, extending the recovery window from roughly 24–36 hours in younger runners to 48–72 hours for most masters athletes. NAD+ levels also decline with age, reducing mitochondrial efficiency and the speed of cellular repair between sessions.

  How much protein should a masters runner eat per day?

Current evidence supports 35–40g of leucine-rich protein per meal for masters runners training 5+ days per week, spread across 3–4 meals. This is roughly 50–60% more per meal than the threshold sufficient for younger runners, because aging muscles require more leucine to trigger the same muscle protein synthesis signal. Total daily intake for an active masters runner in the 150–180 lb (68–82 kg) range typically falls between 140–180g per day.

  Can masters runners still set personal records?

Age-graded PRs — where your time is adjusted to account for typical performance decline at your age — are achievable and meaningful at any stage of masters running. Many runners set their best age-graded performances in their 40s and 50s because they are training more intelligently than they did as younger runners. Race times in absolute terms will eventually slow, but performance relative to peers and to physiological potential can continue to improve.

  What is the most important change a new masters runner should make?

Slowing down on easy days. Most runners entering masters territory are already doing strength work and recovering reasonably well. The adjustment that consistently unlocks better performance is making easy runs genuinely easy — at 90–120 seconds per mile slower than current race pace — so that hard days stay hard enough to drive real adaptation. Compressing the intensity distribution into a narrow moderate-effort zone is the single most common training error in runners over 40.

  What is age grading in running, and why does it matter for masters runners?

Age grading is a standardized method for comparing running performance across different ages. Your finishing time is divided by the world-record time for your age group, producing a percentage that represents your performance relative to the best possible at your age. A score of 70%+ is considered excellent for a masters runner. Age grading lets you track improvement meaningfully even as absolute times slow, and it makes competition across age groups fair and motivating.

### Jeff Gaudette, M.S. Johns Hopkins University

Jeff is the co-founder of RunnersConnect and a former Olympic Trials qualifier.

This article by Jeff Gaudette (co-founder of RunnersConnect, MS from Johns Hopkins) provides evidence-based training guidance for masters runners (40+). Key findings:

1. PERFORMANCE DECLINE: Aerobic capacity declines at roughly 1% per year for active runners after 40, about half the rate (2%) seen in sedentary adults. VO2 max drops most steeply after age 60, while lactate threshold holds up better with age—a study of 168 master runners found lactate threshold remained a strong predictor of race performance even as VO2 max declined.

2. RECOVERY: Aging muscles develop "anabolic resistance"—a diminished ability to respond to anabolic stimuli including exercise and protein intake. Inflammatory resolution slows, extending the adaptation window from 24-36 hours (younger runners) to 48-72 hours for most masters runners. Declining NAD+ levels (a coenzyme central to mitochondrial energy production and cellular repair) also slow recovery. Practical adjustment: schedule hard workouts on Tuesday and Saturday rather than Tuesday and Thursday, treating intervening days as genuinely easy.

3. STRENGTH TRAINING: Fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibers decline progressively from age 25 onward. Research comparing masters to younger runners found significantly lower muscle strength and power in the masters group, directly tracking with reduced running economy at race pace. Recommended: heavy compound lifts and plyometrics 2 days per week—specifically heavy single-leg deadlifts (4-6 reps, 3 sets), split squats with load, calf raises to failure, and bounding drills. Body-weight stability work helps injury prevention but generates weaker fast-twitch recruitment signals.

4. INTENSITY DISTRIBUTION: The most common training error is compressing intensity—easy runs become moderately hard and hard runs stay moderately hard. Easy runs should be 90-120 seconds per mile slower than race pace. For a runner with 8:00/mi 5K pace, most weekly mileage should be at 10:30-11:30/mi or slower. Recommended weekly structure for a 40-mile week: 2 quality sessions (threshold or VO2 max), 1 long easy run, remaining mileage on genuinely easy days, plus one full rest day.

5. PROTEIN: Masters runners need 35-40g of leucine-rich protein per meal (50-60% more per meal than the ~20-25g threshold for younger runners), spread across 3-4 meals. The post-workout window within 30-45 minutes after hard sessions is especially important. Leucine content matters more than protein source (whey, eggs, chicken, fish). Studies combining leucine-rich protein with resistance training in adults over 50 found significant improvements in body composition and physical function.

The article includes an FAQ covering age of performance decline onset, hard workout frequency (2 quality sessions spaced 72 hours apart), strength training's role in slowing decline, protein intake (140-180g/day for a 150-180lb runner), age-graded PRs, and age grading methodology (a score of 70%+ is considered excellent). References include studies by Lepers & Stapley (2016), Wiswell et al. (2000), Quinn et al. (2011), Lexell et al. (1988), Pérez-Castillo et al. (2025), and Taniguchi et al. (2022). The article also promotes a free Age Grading Performance Calculator and MAS NAD+ supplementation product.
