This is a review article published in Frontiers in Physiology (20 February 2014, Volume 5, Sec. Vascular Physiology) by Carlo Vigorito and Francesco Giallauria, titled "Effects of exercise on cardiovascular performance in the elderly." The article reviews the beneficial effects of exercise on the age-related decline in cardiovascular performance in both healthy elderly individuals and elderly patients with cardiovascular disease.

Key content covered:

**Aging effects on cardiovascular system:** Progressive aging causes reduced myocardial cell numbers, increased interstitial collagen fibers, impaired left ventricular diastolic function, reduced maximal heart rate response to exercise (due to beta1 receptor down-regulation), and peripheral changes including reduced skeletal muscle cells and decreased Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) I and IIa fibers. Even without cardiovascular disease, aging is strongly associated with reduced maximal aerobic capacity.

**Effects in healthy elderly:** Aerobic/endurance exercise improves peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope, ventilatory aerobic threshold, and Heart Rate Recovery (HRR). Mechanisms include improved chronotropic incompetence, increased stroke volume, enhanced vagal tone, improved endothelial function and arterial compliance, and favorable skeletal muscle biochemical changes (increased MHC I). Gender differences noted: men's increased peak VO2 primarily due to augmented stroke volume/CO, while women's increase is due entirely to increased A-VO2 difference. Resistance training increases muscle mass and strength but has fewer effects on maximal cardiovascular performance. The 6-Minute Walk Test is useful for submaximal performance assessment in frail/comorbid elderly.

**Oxidative stress:** Physical activity counterbalances ROS accumulation by activating antioxidant systems (SODs, heat shock proteins, catalase), reduces oxidant generation during ischemia-reperfusion, and contributes to decreased arterial stiffness and improved endothelial function.

**Sarcopenic and frail patients:** Resistance exercise training (RET) improves lean tissue mass, muscle strength, and physical performance measures (time up and go, gait speed, 6-min walking distance). Endurance training adds aerobic capacity benefits; combining both is recommended.

**HFREF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction):** Endurance training increases peak VO2 by 20-25%, which correlates with survival. Mechanisms include increased cardiac output, favorable LV remodeling, restored beta-adrenergic receptor signaling, increased skeletal muscle perfusion and oxygen extraction, reduced ergoreflexes, and reduced MuRF-1 (ubiquitin-proteasome system component). High-intensity interval training may be superior to moderate continuous training for improving LV ejection fraction and peripheral vascular function. Resistance training has modest effects compared to aerobic training.

**HFPEF (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction):** Predominantly affects elderly and female patients. Exercise training increases peak VO2 primarily through increased A-VO2 difference. Reduced peak exercise HR (chronotropic incompetence) is reversed by training. No evidence of benefit on LV diastolic properties. Gender differences in CO response noted.

**Exercise program recommendations:** Programs of 8-12 weeks provide benefits similar to adults; longer programs (>12 weeks) may be needed. Training should include endurance aerobic exercise on cycle or treadmill 3 times/week, sessions of 5-60 minutes (typically ~30 min), training HR of 50-60% to 75-80% of MHR, warm-up/cool-down periods, Borg scale for perceived exertion monitoring, and slow progression for frail/deconditioned elderly.

**Conclusion:** Aging does not contraindicate exercise training in healthy elderly or those with comorbidities. Future programs should incorporate cognitive therapy, occupational therapy, balance exercises, counseling, and dietary education. Larger controlled studies are needed to definitively confirm benefits on cardiovascular outcomes.

--- SOURCE 1: An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by ... - Frontiers ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1003445/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sport and Exercise Nutrition section) on November 9, 2022, titled "An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms." The study was conducted by Rachel Scrivin (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand), Ricardo J. S. Costa (Monash University, Australia), Fiona Pelly (University of the Sunshine Coast), Dana Lis (University of California, Los Angeles), and Gary Slater (University of the Sunshine Coast).

METHODOLOGY: The exploratory study used a validated online questionnaire (via Qualtrics) to investigate self-reported exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) and management strategies in 137 adult endurance athletes (participating in events ≥60 min) with a history of Ex-GIS. Participants included runners (55%, n=75), triathletes (22%, n=30), and non-running sports (23%, n=32), competing at recreationally competitive (37%), recreationally non-competitive (32%), and competitive regional/national/international (31%) levels. The questionnaire included 43 items covering participant demographics, Ex-GIS incidence/severity (using a 0-10 visual analog scale), management strategies, and information sources. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni corrections, and chi-squared tests.

KEY RESULTS:
- More females (63%, n=86) than males (37%, n=51) completed the questionnaire; mean age was 41.6 ± 11.1 years.
- Athletes reported Ex-GIS most frequently around training (21%), competitions (30%), or equally around both (49%).
- Lower gastrointestinal symptoms were more common than upper GI symptoms across all groups.
- The only severe symptom of significance was the urge to defecate during training in the equally-training group (Z = –0.536, p = 0.01).
- Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during exercise than before or after exercise in all categories.
- 67% (n=92) of athletes used dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting a total of 277 strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.
- Most popular dietary strategies: dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42), dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16), low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15). Non-dietary strategies: medications (4.7%, n=13) and relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11).
- Avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose) (6.1%, n=17) was the most popular FODMAP avoidance.
- Most successful dietary strategies (Likert scale 1-5): dietary fiber reduction (median=4, IQR 4-5), low FODMAP diet (median=4, IQR 4-5), dairy-free diet (median=4, IQR 4-5), and increasing carbohydrates (median=4, IQR 3-4).
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed to reduce Ex-GIS.
- Arginine was rated most successful supplement (median=5, n=1), followed by probiotics (median=4, n=26) and prebiotics (median=4, n=7).
- Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29), though no significant associations were found between information sources and sport, participation level, or sex.
- 15 athletes (11%) had a diagnosed GI disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (n=6); 13 athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS.

CONCLUSIONS: Endurance athletes use a variety of strategies to manage Ex-GIS, with dietary manipulation being the most common. The most successful strategies were dietary fiber reduction, low FODMAP diets, dairy-free diets, and increasing carbohydrate intake. Athletes predominantly seek guidance from accredited practicing dietitians. The study recommends that dietary strategies (e.g., low FODMAP, dairy avoidance) should be trialed during training to establish individual tolerance before implementation during competition. Further research is needed to determine whether these strategies are best applied acutely before exercise or integrated into habitual diets.
</summary>

URL: https://blog.nasm.org/fitness/endurance-exercise-gut-strategies-outrun-runs-gi-complaints

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the NASM blog, written by Dr. Geoff Lecovin, addresses gastrointestinal (GI) complaints experienced by endurance athletes. Adverse GI symptoms such as cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea affect up to 90% of endurance athletes and can adversely affect performance and lead to long-term health consequences.

**Causes of exercise-induced GI complaints (multifactorial):**
1. **Decreased GI perfusion** – Hypoperfusion of the gut during exercise ranges from mild circulatory changes to ischemia, caused by catecholamine release and splanchnic vasoconstriction that shunts blood to heart, lungs, muscles, and skin. This can lead to gut mucosal ischemia, increased permeability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
2. **Changes in motility** – Heavy exercise causes decreased peristalsis, decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone, and increased transient sphincter relaxation, linked to gastroesophageal reflux and impaired gastric emptying.
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** – High-intensity exercise compromises intestinal blood flow, increasing permeability, gut damage, impaired function, decreased nutrient absorption, and potentially a dysbiotic microbiome with pathogenic bacteria and endotoxin invasion into circulation.
4. **Mechanical causes** – Posture-related issues in runners and cyclists from repetitive high-impact mechanics; aerophagia (swallowing air) from increased respiration while drinking from water bottles.
5. **Nutritional causes** – Fiber, fat, protein, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying. Beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose and fructose combined) reduce GI symptoms.
6. **NSAIDs** – Associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction.
7. **Hyperthermia** – Heat exposure leads to intestinal ischemia from shunting blood to skin and muscles; heat acclimatization and hydration help mitigate effects.
8. **Dehydration** – Blood flow to gut and liver is reduced up to 80% during exercise; GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume.

**Practical guidelines provided:**
- Avoid high-fiber foods on race day and several days leading up
- Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities
- Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol)
- Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen
- Avoid high-fructose foods; fructose-glucose combinations are better tolerated
- Prevent dehydration
- Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water
- Choose lower carbohydrate concentration drinks to avoid high osmolalities
- Practice new nutrition strategies before race day

The article also discusses "training the gut" as a strategy to reduce GI distress by helping athletes acclimate to fluid and food ingestion during exercise, improving nutrient absorption and tolerance. The author, Dr. Geoff Lecovin, is a chiropractor, naturopathic physician, and acupuncturist with extensive certifications in exercise and nutrition. The article includes 12 scholarly references from journals including Sports Medicine, Journal of Applied Physiology, and Scandinavian Journal of Gastroenterology.
</summary>

URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The authors are Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Sapienza University of Rome, Italy), and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan, Italy). The article was submitted 26 July 2023, revised 30 August 2023, accepted 12 September 2023, and published 19 September 2023. It has 26 citations and an Altmetric score of 31.

**Key content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a condition affecting up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports (marathon, triathlon, cycling, running, etc.) caused by strenuous exercise. Symptoms include upper GI issues (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower GI issues (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two main pathways are described:
1. Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway: Sympathetic activation alters the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic blood flow can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing gut hypoperfusion, ischemic damage, loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP. 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study.

**GI symptoms during exercise:** 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms. In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors.

**IBS overlap:** Ex-GIS shares pathogenesis with IBS (alterations in gut microbiota, permeability, immune function, motility, visceral sensation, brain-gut interactions). IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed.

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms).

**Management:** The review emphasizes nutritional and behavioral strategies, particularly examining gluten-free diets and low-FODMAP (fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols) diets as the principal interventions to avoid symptoms during exercise. Exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet should all be evaluated.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023, yielding 142 relevant research articles published between 1965 and 2023.
</summary>

The study implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). The case series involved 9 athletes who experienced recurrent severe Ex-GIS and 2 controls without symptoms.

The four phases were: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes, specifically including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of therapeutic interventions.

All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery. Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet and improved intake tolerance during the targeted event, with reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS and improved perceived work output.

The study concludes that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms.

SUMMARY:

The article explains that GI distress is the leading cause of underperformance in endurance races, and while no scientifically established gut-training protocols exist, insights from experts like Asker Jeukendrup, Trent Stellingwerff, and Aitor Viribay provide practical guidance.

Key points include:
- For sessions over 2 hours, guidelines recommend 60-90g of carbs per hour using multiple transportable carbs (glucose and fructose), as the SGLT1 transporter limits glucose absorption to ~1g per minute (60g/hour), while fructose absorbed via GLUT5 enables oxidation beyond that limit.

- A 6-step progressive gut training guide is provided, starting with a baseline tolerable dose, increasing by 10-15g/hour every 7-14 days, with optional steps to push 10-20% beyond max tolerable dose (then reducing during taper), and stepping 4-6 involving 2-3x weekly sessions.

- Exceeding 90g/hour generally offers no additional benefit and increases GI distress risk.
- Signs of overdoing it include bloating, gas, cramping, diarrhea, feeling overly full, and sluggishness — these serve as indicators of current gut capacity and training overload stimulus.
- The key takeaway: more is not always better; gradual, personalized adjustment is the path to success. The article links to Race Smart's Race Day Fueling nutrition service for customized plans.
</summary>

"Gut training involves repeated exposure to progressive carb load during training and daily nutrition to boost gut tolerance, gastric emptying, the efficiency of intestinal carb transporters, and stomach comfort."

--- SOURCE 8: The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status in Response to Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Literature Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10185635

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic literature review published in Sports Medicine (April 2023) examining the effects of "gut-training" and "feeding-challenge" interventions on markers of gastrointestinal status in response to endurance exercise. The review was conducted by researchers from Monash University (Isabel G. Martinez, Alice S. Mika, Jessica R. Biesiekierski, Ricardo J. S. Costa) and followed PRISMA guidelines.

METHODS: Five databases (Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL Plus, Web of Science Core Collection, SPORTDiscus) were searched from inception until May 2022. The PICOS framework was used for eligibility, targeting healthy endurance athletes aged 12-60 years. Interventions included structured and repetitive carbohydrate feeding during exercise (at least 2 consecutive days or across repeated trials) or feeding challenges within 48 hours before exercise. Quality assessment used the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias (RoB 2) tool.

RESULTS: Of 304 studies identified, 8 were included after screening. Studies involved participants aged 15-35 years (79% male), mostly cyclists, runners, or triathletes. Interventions included carbohydrates only (n=7) in various forms (gels, liquid solutions) during cycling or running, or carbohydrate with protein (n=1), over 4-28 days.

Key findings include:
- Gut discomfort decreased by an average of 47% and 26% with a 2-week repetitive carbohydrate feeding protocol (n=2) and through repeated fluid ingestion over five trials (n=1), respectively.
- Repetitive carbohydrate feeding during exercise for 2 weeks reduced carbohydrate malabsorption by 45-54% (n=2), but one study showed no significant change.
- Significant improvements in total, upper, and lower gastrointestinal symptoms were observed (n=2), with unclear results in 4 studies.
- No significant changes were found in gastric emptying rate (n=2) or markers of intestinal injury and permeability (I-FABP, claudin-3) (n=3).
- Inconclusive results in studies examining plasma inflammatory cytokine concentrations (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1ra) in response to exercise with increased carbohydrate feeding (n=2).

CONCLUSIONS: Gut-training or feeding-challenge around exercise may provide advantages in reducing gut discomfort and potentially improving carbohydrate malabsorption and exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS), which may have exercise performance implications. However, the effect on other gastrointestinal functional responses, gastrointestinal integrity, and systemic responses remains unclear. The review calls for future research using more sensitive tools (e.g., non-metabolizable sugar probes, modified visual analog scale) to elucidate underlying mechanisms and fine-tune gut-training guidelines.
</summary>

"Gut-training or feeding-challenge before and/or during exercise reduces gut discomfort, upper Ex-GIS, and carbohydrate malabsorption, but the effect on other gastrointestinal functional responses, gastrointestinal integrity, and systemic responses remains unclear and elusive."

--- SOURCE 9: Training The Gut For Athletes ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/training-the-gut-for-athletes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #178 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published January 2018, authored by Asker Jeukendrup, PhD. The article examines "Training the Gut for Athletes" — the concept that the gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be trained and adapted to improve nutrient and fluid delivery during endurance exercise while reducing GI distress.

KEY POINTS:
- The GI tract is critical for delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and is a major determinant of endurance performance.
- GI problems affect 30-50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports.
- The GI tract is highly adaptable and responds to nutritional training in a nutrient-specific way.

GASTRIC EMPTYING: The stomach is the first barrier for delivering nutrients. Studies show that repeated practice of high fluid intakes during running improved stomach comfort over time (Lambert et al., 2008), though without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate. Dietary manipulation studies (Cunningham et al., 1991; Horowitz et al., 1996; Yau et al., 2014) demonstrated that supplementing with specific carbohydrates (glucose or fructose) accelerated gastric emptying of those same sugars specifically, with effects seen after as little as 3 days.

INTESTINAL SUGAR TRANSPORT: Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent SGLT1 transporter, while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are the most important transporters for carbohydrate absorption. At ingestion rates over 60-70 g of carbohydrate/hour, exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks at ~60 g/hour because SGLT1 becomes saturated. Combining glucose and fructose (using different transporters) can achieve higher oxidation rates.

TRANSPORTER REGULATION AND ADAPTATION: SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. A glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies show rapid adaptation: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses showed increases after just one week; piglets showed increases after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks.

HUMAN EVIDENCE: The landmark Cox et al. (2010) study divided 16 endurance-trained cyclists into high-carbohydrate and control groups. Over 28 days of training (16 h/week), the high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate versus 5.3 g/kg/day in controls. Post-training, the high-carb group showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, most likely due to upregulated SGLT1 transporters. Conversely, carbohydrate restriction, high-fat/ketogenic diets, or energy reduction may reduce absorptive capacity and potentially increase GI problems.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) Train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks. (2) Practice race nutritional strategies in training to adapt to higher volumes and carbohydrate intakes. (3) For exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate is recommended; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures). (4) Athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days to maintain gut absorptive capacity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The gastrointestinal (GI) tract plays a critical role in delivering carbohydrate and fluid to the blood during prolonged exercise, and can therefore be a major determinant of performance."
</key_excerpts>

- Gut training improves gastric emptying, intestinal absorption, stomach comfort, and reduces GI problems.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Practical Gastroenterology (September 2023 issue, authored by Monique Ryan) reviews the science and practical guidelines for fueling during endurance exercise, with a focus on balancing carbohydrate and fluid intake against gastrointestinal (GI) tolerances.

KEY PHYSIOLOGICAL FACTS:
- Gastric emptying is a critical step in delivering exogenous carbohydrates and fluid to working muscles. After emptying from the stomach, carbohydrate absorption occurs primarily in the duodenum and jejunum along with sodium and water.
- Individual carbohydrates are absorbed at ~1 g/minute (max 60 g/hour). Glucose and fructose are absorbed via separate transporters: SGLT 1 (sodium-dependent glucose/galactose transporter) and GLUT 5 (non-sodium dependent fructose transporter).
- Using both transporters simultaneously (mixed carbohydrates) increases intestinal absorptive capacity to 75–90 g/hour.
- Gastric emptying is slowed by hypohydration, mental stress, intense exercise (above 70% VO2 max), and high solute loads (hyperosmolar beverages >500 mOsm/kg H2O, such as 10–15% carbohydrate drinks). Sports drinks at 6% concentration are isotonic and empty quickly. Liquid temperature has little effect on emptying.
- Larger fluid volumes empty from the stomach faster than smaller volumes; a study (Mears et al.) found 200 mL every 20 min produced 2% higher carbohydrate oxidation than 50 mL every 5 min, with no difference in GI comfort.

NUTRITION GUIDELINES:
- Carbohydrates provide 50–60% of energy during 1–4 hours of continuous exercise at 70% max oxygen capacity, and up to 90% at 80–90% of oxygen consumption.
- Current recommendations: 60 g carbohydrate/hour for exercise up to 120 minutes; up to 90 g/hour for exercise lasting longer than 2 hours, using a blend of glucose and fructose sources.
- Carbohydrate combinations producing greater oxidation than glucose alone include: maltodextrin + fructose, glucose + fructose, and glucose + sucrose + fructose. A 2:1 glucose-to-fructose ratio is commonly used to formulate sports drinks, allowing comfortable consumption of 75–90 g carbohydrate/hour.
- A study (Currell & Jeukendrup) found ingesting glucose at 1.2 g/min + fructose at 0.6 g/min (108 g/hr total) improved endurance cycling time-trial performance by 8% vs. glucose-only.
- Solid versus liquid carbohydrate forms (gels, bars, drinks) produced similar oxidation rates when glucose and fructose were in 2:1 ratio.
- Hydration: sweat rates range 0.5L to over 3L/hour. Athletes should replace only 70–100% of sweat losses to avoid over-hydration, and should practice their hydration plan for at least 8 weeks prior to events.

NUTRITIONAL GUT TRAINING ("training the gut"):
- GI symptoms during endurance exercise are common, with prevalence in endurance athletes ranging from 37–93%. During exercise, blood flow is redirected from the GI tract to working muscles, causing bloating, cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and/or pain.
- Gut training involves practiced ingestion of predetermined amounts of carbohydrates and fluid during training to upregulate intestinal carbohydrate transporters (SGLT 1 and GLUT 5) and improve absorption capacity.
- Animal data suggests increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% of calories could double SGLT 1 transporters over a 2-week period.
- Recent research (Viribay et al., 2020) suggests intake of 120 g carbohydrate/hour is possible in elite marathon/ultra-marathon runners with personalized gut training (up to 90 g/hr at least 2 days weekly for 4 weeks prior). The 120 g/hr dose limited post-race exercise-induced muscle damage without GI distress.

CONCLUSION: The gut is adaptable; athletes should practice their event nutrition plan over several weeks to optimize carbohydrate absorption, reduce GI distress, and improve performance.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article titled "Fructose co-ingestion to increase carbohydrate availability in athletes," published in The Journal of Physiology on July 15, 2019, authored by Cas J Fuchs, Javier T Gonzalez, and Luc J C van Loon (corresponding author from Maastricht University). The paper is an open access review presented at the symposium 'Fructose in physiology: friend or foe?' held in London, UK, September 14-16, 2018.

KEY TOPIC: The review examines whether co-ingesting fructose with glucose can increase total carbohydrate availability for athletes during endurance exercise and acute post-exercise recovery.

MAIN FINDINGS:

1. Mechanism: Glucose is absorbed intestinally via SGLT1 transporters, while fructose uses GLUT5 transporters - a different transport system. Co-ingestion takes advantage of both transport mechanisms, increasing total carbohydrate absorption capacity. Peak exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates reach ~1.1 g/min with glucose alone but can increase to 1.75 g/min with glucose-fructose co-ingestion. Fructose is primarily metabolized in the splanchnic area (intestine, liver, kidneys) into glucose and lactate, which serve as additional fuel during exercise.

2. During Exercise: Co-ingesting glucose and fructose can improve endurance performance by ~8-9% compared to glucose only. Fructose co-ingestion lowers gastrointestinal distress when large amounts of carbohydrate (>1.2 g/kg/h) are ingested. Fructose co-ingestion does NOT prevent muscle or liver glycogen depletion more than glucose alone during exercise.

3. After Exercise (Muscle Glycogen): Fructose co-ingestion does NOT further increase muscle glycogen repletion rates compared to glucose alone, even at high ingestion rates (≥1.2 g/kg/h). However, it reduces gastrointestinal issues.

4. After Exercise (Liver Glycogen): Fructose co-ingestion significantly accelerates liver glycogen repletion - rates increase ~2-fold (from ~3.5 g/h with glucose alone to ~7.4 g/h with fructose co-ingestion). This occurs via fructose conversion to glucose/lactate in the liver and via fructose-1-phosphate acting as a signaling molecule to activate glucokinase and glycogen synthase. Fructose co-ingestion can increase endurance exercise capacity in a subsequent exercise bout by 3-5 minutes (cycling at 75% Wmax) or ~32.4% (treadmill running at 70% VO2max).

5. RECOMMENDATIONS: Well-trained athletes should ingest 90 g/h of glucose-fructose mixtures during prolonged (>2.5 h) moderate-to-high intensity exercise. For rapid recovery (<24 h), consume >1 g carbohydrate/kg body mass/h starting immediately after exercise at 15-30 minute intervals, with fructose co-ingestion beneficial for lowering GI distress and accelerating liver glycogen synthesis.

6. Health Considerations: High dietary fructose has been associated with metabolic disease, but exercise appears to correct early markers of metabolic disease induced by high fructose intake. Elite athletes typically display excellent metabolic health despite consuming >450 g/day of simple sugars during events like the Tour de France.

FUNDING: No funding sources used; authors disclosed research support from Pepsico, Arla Foods Ingredients, Lucozade Ribena Suntory, and Kenniscentrum Suiker en Voeding.
</summary>

Studies show nutrient-specific adaptations—increased dietary glucose accelerates gastric emptying of glucose but not protein; higher-fat diets accelerate emptying of fats but not carbohydrates. Hot weather and dehydration exacerbate symptoms. Training the gut may alleviate symptoms by improving gastric emptying, reducing bloating, and increasing absorption speed.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: Current guidelines recommend carbohydrate intake up to ~60 g/h for exercise up to 2 hours, and ~90 g/h (using multiple transportable carbohydrates like glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose) for exercise ≥2 hours. This webpage presents a joint position paper published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (Volume 116, Issue 3, March 2016, Pages 501-528) titled "Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and Athletic Performance." The paper was authored by D. Travis Thomas, PhD, RDN, CSSD (University of Kentucky); Kelly Anne Erdman, MSc, RD, CSSD (Canadian Sport Institute Calgary); and Louise M. Burke, OAM, PhD, APD, FACSM (Australian Institute of Sport). DOI: 10.1016/j.jand.2015.12.006.

The position statement asserts that well-chosen nutrition strategies enhance athletic performance and recovery from sporting activities. The organizations provide guidelines for the appropriate type, amount, and timing of intake of food, fluids, and supplements to promote optimal health and performance across different training scenarios and competitive sports. Key sections covered include:

- **Evidence-Based Analysis**: Developed using the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Evidence Analysis Library (EAL), with publication range spanning March 2006 to November 2014.
- **New Perspectives in Sports Nutrition**: Notes a decade-long increase in publications, consensus statements, and qualification opportunities in sports nutrition.
- **Energy Requirements, Energy Balance, and Energy Availability**: Appropriate energy intake is the cornerstone of an athlete's diet, supporting optimal body function and body composition manipulation. - **Pre-, During-, and Postevent Eating**: Strategies must address fatigue, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and glycogen depletion to support optimal performance.
- **Vegetarian Athletes**: A vegetarian diet can be nutritionally adequate, though athletes should be screened for disordered eating.
- **Roles and Responsibilities of Sports Dietitians**: Sports nutrition practice requires combined knowledge in clinical nutrition, nutrition science, exercise physiology, and evidence-based research application.

The summary notes that low energy availability can result in muscle mass loss, menstrual dysfunction, hormonal disturbances, suboptimal bone density, increased fatigue/injury/illness risk, and impaired adaptation. Athletes should be referred to a registered dietitian nutritionist for personalized nutrition plans. The position paper contains 157 references and has been cited 1121 times.

The position was adopted by the Academy House of Delegates Leadership Team on July 12, 2000, reaffirmed May 25, 2004, and February 15, 2011; approved by Dietitians of Canada on November 17, 2015; and approved by the ACSM Board of Trustees on November 20, 2015. The position was in effect until December 31, 2019. The article was published concurrently on the Dietitians of Canada website and in Medicine & Science in Sports and Exercise®.

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Nutrition and Athletic Performance ---
URL: https://femaleandmaleathletetriad.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Nutrition_and_Athletic_Performance.27.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a joint position statement from the American Dietetic Association (ADA), Dietitians of Canada (DC), and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) on Nutrition and Athletic Performance, published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2009). The position states that physical activity, athletic performance, and recovery from exercise are enhanced by optimal nutrition, recommending appropriate selection of foods and fluids, timing of intake, and supplement choices.

KEY POSITION POINTS:
- Athletes need adequate energy during high-intensity/long-duration training to maintain body weight, health, and maximize training effects. Low energy intake risks muscle loss, menstrual dysfunction, reduced bone density, fatigue, injury, and prolonged recovery.
- Body weight and composition should not be the sole criterion for sports participation; daily weigh-ins are discouraged.
- Carbohydrate recommendations: 6-10 g/kg body weight/day (2.7-4.5 g/lb/day).
- Protein recommendations: 1.2-1.7 g/kg body weight/day (0.5-0.8 g/lb/day) for endurance and strength-trained athletes, generally met through diet alone without supplements.
- Fat intake: 20%-35% of total energy intake; consuming <20% from fat does not benefit performance; high-fat diets not recommended.
- Dehydration (water deficit >2-3% body mass) decreases performance. After exercise, drink 16-24 oz (450-675 mL) fluid per pound (0.5 kg) body weight lost.
- Before exercise: meal/snack low in fat and fiber, high in carbohydrate, moderate in protein, composed of familiar foods.
- During exercise: replace fluids and provide ~30-60 g carbohydrate/hour, especially for endurance events >1 hour.
- After exercise: 1.0-1.5 g/kg body weight carbohydrate within first 30 min and every 2 hours for 4-6 hours; protein aids muscle repair.
- Vitamin/mineral supplements generally not needed if adequate energy is consumed from varied foods; supplements may be needed for athletes restricting energy, eliminating food groups, or with micronutrient deficiencies.
- Ergogenic aids should be used with caution after evaluation for safety, efficacy, potency, and legality.
- Vegetarian athletes may be at risk for low intakes of energy, protein, fat, iron, calcium, vitamin D, riboflavin, zinc, and vitamin B12.

METHODOLOGY: The paper used ADA's Evidence Analysis Process with five topic-specific questions. Inclusion criteria: adults aged 18-40, trained athletes or regularly exercising individuals. Publications ranged 1995-2006. Evidence was graded I (good) through V (no evidence).

ENERGY METABOLISM: Three energy systems—phosphagen (a few seconds, high intensity, uses ATP/creatine phosphate), anaerobic glycolytic (60-180 seconds, uses muscle glycogen/glucose), and oxidative/aerobic (events >2-3 minutes). At 70% maximal oxygen capacity for 1-4 hours, 50%-60% energy from carbohydrates, rest from free fatty acids. Training increases proportion of energy from fat.

ENERGY REQUIREMENTS: Energy balance = intake equals expenditure (BMR + thermic effect of food + activity). Low intake (<1800-2000 kcal/day for females) is a major concern. Energy availability threshold of 30 kcal/kg FFM/day for females. Harris-Benedict and Cunningham equations used to estimate BMR; activity factors of 1.8-2.3 applied.

BODY COMPOSITION: Minimum body fat compatible with health: 5% for males, 12% for females. Assessment methods include DXA, air displacement plethysmography (BodPod), skinfold measurements (typically seven sites), and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA). ISAK sum of seven skinfolds ranges: 30-60 mm (males), 40-90 mm (females). Evidence Grade III (Limited) conclusion: carbohydrate restriction is detrimental to performance; weight loss before competition may not significantly affect performance depending on refeeding protocol.

MACRONUTRIENTS: Athletes don't need diets substantially different from Dietary Guidelines. High-carbohydrate diets (>60% energy) previously advocated, but caution recommended. Micronutrients of concern: calcium, vitamin D, B vitamins, iron, zinc, magnesium, and antioxidants (vitamins C, E, beta-carotene, selenium). Athletes at greatest risk: those restricting energy, using severe weight-loss practices, eliminating food groups, or consuming low micronutrient-density diets.

SPECIFIC MICRONUTRIENT FINDINGS:
- Vitamin D: Athletes at northern latitudes or training indoors (gymnasts, figure skaters) at risk; DRI 5 mcg/day (200 IU for ages 19-49).
- Vitamin C: 100-1000 mg/day for those in habitual prolonged, strenuous exercise.
- Calcium: 1500 mg elemental calcium + 400-800 IU vitamin D daily for athletes with disordered eating, amenorrhea, or early osteoporosis risk.
- Iron: Endurance athletes (especially distance runners) need ~70% more iron. Supplementation with 100 mg ferrous sulfate for 4-6 weeks improved performance in iron-deficient athletes. Iron deficiency anemia reversal requires 3-6 months. Vegetarians and blood donors should aim for intake above RDA (18 mg women, 8 mg men). "Sports anemia" (hemodilution) is a beneficial training adaptation.
- Zinc: UL is 40 mg; caution against single-dose supplements exceeding this; may interfere with iron and copper absorption.
- Sodium: Endurance athletes need more than UL (2.3 g/day); sports drinks with sodium (0.5-0.7 g/L) and potassium (0.8-2.0 g/L) recommended for events >2 hours.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the European Journal of Applied Physiology (2017;117(12):2519, DOI: 10.1007/s00421-017-3739-1) examining exercise-induced gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms and intestinal permeability in runners. The study was conducted by researchers from the University of Helsinki, Helsinki University Hospital (HUSLAB), and the Clinic for Sports and Exercise Medicine in Helsinki, Finland.

STUDY DESIGN: Seventeen active runners (aged 24-44, avg 32.6±6.5 years) were recruited and divided into two groups based on their history of GI symptoms during running: asymptomatic (n=9; 5 males, 4 females) and symptomatic (n=8; 4 males, 4 females). Participants were deemed symptomatic if they experienced GI symptoms in at least 50% of their runs and asymptomatic if in less than 10%. Participants ran for 90 minutes at 80% of their best 10 km race speed. Intestinal permeability was measured via oral iohexol administration, and serum I-FABP (enterocyte damage marker), zonulin, bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and fecal calprotectin were measured at baseline and after running.

KEY RESULTS:
- Running induced a significant increase (p<0.05) in intestinal permeability in both groups (iohexol permeability increased from ~0.20% baseline to ~0.39% in asymptomatic and ~0.36% in symptomatic groups), with no difference between groups.
- Serum I-FABP increased significantly only in the asymptomatic group (314±152 to 804±599 pg/ml, p<0.05); the symptomatic group showed a non-significant trend (389±327 to 961±949 pg/ml).
- Serum zonulin increased significantly in the asymptomatic group (53.2±26.3 to 70.4±16.7 ng/ml) and was significantly higher in asymptomatic than symptomatic runners after running.
- Serum LPS activity did not change after running, but symptomatic runners had significantly higher baseline LPS activity (0.767±0.119 vs 0.567±0.124 EU/ml, p<0.01).
- No significant differences in fecal calprotectin between groups, though a trend toward higher values was noted in symptomatic runners after running.
- The symptomatic group reported significantly more GI symptoms overall (p<0.001), with flatulence (p<0.05) and diarrhea (p<0.001) being notably more frequent.

MAIN CONCLUSION: Running for 90 minutes at a challenging pace causes small intestinal damage and increases intestinal permeability, but these alterations in GI function do not appear to correlate with the development of GI symptoms during running. This is the first study to directly compare intestinal permeability alterations in asymptomatic versus symptomatic runners. The findings suggest increased intestinal permeability is a normal physiological response to running, and other factors—possibly inflammation, baseline LPS levels, or individual susceptibility—may play a role in exercise-induced GI symptoms. The study also highlights the difficulty of reliably classifying runners as asymptomatic or symptomatic based on self-reported symptoms.

**Key Statistics on GI Problems in Athletes:**
- 30% to 90% of distance runners experience exercise-related intestinal problems, depending on methodology and events studied
- In exhausting endurance events, 30-50% of participants suffer from one or more GI symptoms (Brouns & Beckers, 1993)
- Up to 93% of long-distance triathletes in extreme conditions reported any GI symptom; 43% reported serious GI problems and 7% abandoned the race due to GI issues (Jeukendrup et al., 2000)
- 70% of elite endurance athletes reported exercise-induced GI symptoms (Peters et al., 1999)
- In an internet-based study of 1,281 athletes, 45% reported at least one GI symptom (Ter Steege et al., 2008)
- Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon running/cycling up to 32% in Ironman races (Pfeiffer et al., 2011)
- Athletes not accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise had a two-fold risk of GI symptoms compared to accustomed athletes

**Causes of GI Problems:**
1. **Splanchnic hypoperfusion** - During maximal exercise, splanchnic blood flow may be reduced by up to 80% to supply working muscle and skin. Norepinephrine release induces splanchnic vasoconstriction, which can lead to gut mucosal ischemia and increased mucosal permeability.
2. **Changes in motility** - Decreased esophageal peristalsis and lower esophageal sphincter tone, increased transient sphincter relaxation, and altered gastric emptying (mainly at high exercise intensities).
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** - Studies show increased intestinal permeability after marathons, though effects are inconclusive at moderate intensities. Symptomatic runners showed greater permeability than asymptomatic runners.
4. **Mechanical causes** - Repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut; symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists. Posture (e.g., "aero" position on bicycles) and swallowing air can contribute.
5. **Nutritional causes** - Fiber, fat, protein, fructose, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>500 mOsm/L osmolality) are associated with increased GI symptoms. Dairy products and mild lactose intolerance can cause problems.

**Prevention Guidelines:**
- **Avoid milk products** containing lactose (use lactose-free, soy, rice, or almond milk alternatives)
- **Avoid high-fiber foods** in the day(s) before competition; choose processed white foods (regular pasta, white rice, plain bagels) instead of whole grains
- **Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen) as they increase intestinal permeability; NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI complications
- **Avoid high-fructose foods** and exclusively-fructose drinks (though fructose with glucose may be better tolerated)
- **Avoid dehydration**; start races well hydrated
- **Practice new nutrition strategies** by experimenting with pre-race and race-day plans many times before race day
- **"Train the gut"** - A study by Cox et al. (2010) showed that 28 days of high-carbohydrate training improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates, attributed to improved intestinal absorption

**Serious Symptoms:** Mucosal erosions, ischemic colitis, blood loss in feces, hemorrhagic gastritis, and small bowel infarction have been reported in endurance athletes, occasionally requiring surgery.

The article concludes that GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and that nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the University of Connecticut's Korey Stringer Institute covers two main topics: web cookies and heat acclimatization for athletes.

**Cookies Section:** The page explains that web cookies are small pieces of data websites store on devices through browsers. They serve three main purposes: session management (keeping users logged in, remembering shopping carts, saving preferences), personalization (tailoring content/ads), and tracking & analytics (monitoring browsing behavior). Cookie types include session cookies (temporary, deleted on browser close), persistent cookies (stored until expiration or manual deletion), first-party cookies (set by the visited site), and third-party cookies (set by other domains, typically advertisers, used for cross-site tracking). Authentication cookies verify logged-in users, contain a unique session ID (not passwords), and may persist with "Remember me" features. Analytics cookies collect data on page views, click paths, bounce rates, demographics, and referring websites. The page provides step-by-step instructions for disabling cookies in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge (desktop and mobile), noting that disabling cookies can break websites and cause frequent logouts.

**Heat Acclimatization Section:** Heat acclimation is defined as a series of adaptations occurring over 7-14 days in response to heat stress in a controlled environment; heat acclimatization is the same process in a natural environment. Positive adaptations include reductions in heart rate, internal body temperature, skin temperature responses, sweat electrolyte concentrations, and perceived exertion, along with increases in sweat rate, earlier sweat onset, blood flow, and exercise performance. Adaptations differ between hot/dry vs. hot/humid environments (greater sweat rate increase in humid conditions). The page provides detailed preseason guidelines (originally from NATA 2009, modeled after NCAA 2003 guidelines), including: no more than one practice per day in the first five days; max 3 hours of practice daily in the first five days; no full gear until day six; gradual intensity increase; proper hydration; increased sodium intake; and monitoring for exertional heat stroke, heat exhaustion, and heat syncope. A Wet Bulb Globe Temperature monitor is recommended for assessing risk in hot/humid environments. The Korey Stringer Institute advocates for mandatory state-level heat acclimatization guidelines, noting that states failing to mandate them place athletes at greater risk for exertional heat stroke and heat-related illnesses. The page cites 7 references including the 2015 NATA Position Statement on Exertional Heat Illnesses and the 2009 Casa & Csillan preseason guidelines.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: Why Running in Heat Feels So Hard: Cardiovascular Drift Explained ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3gh5J8F4NN8

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video by Dr. Cailbhe Doherty (13500 subscribers) explains the physiology behind why running in heat feels harder even when fitness hasn't changed, focusing on the concept of cardiovascular drift. Posted 2 Aug 2026 with ~11,192 views, the video breaks down how heat forces the cardiovascular system to split blood flow between working muscles and skin cooling.

KEY POINTS:
- During exercise, the cardiovascular system has two jobs: delivering oxygenated blood to working muscles and transporting heat from the core to the skin for dissipation. Total cardiac output is finite, creating an internal competition for blood flow.
- When core temperature rises, blood vessels near the skin dilate, increasing skin blood flow from under 1 L/min at rest to 6-8 L/min under serious heat stress. This causes central venous pressure to fall, stroke volume to drop, and heart rate to rise to compensate—this is cardiovascular drift.
- Data from large marathon datasets show recreational runners slow 3-13% in hot conditions vs. cool ones; elite runners slow 2-5%. Hotter conditions and slower runners incur greater penalties.
- Humidity compounds heat stress because it limits evaporative cooling (sweating), increasing demand on skin blood flow.
- Dehydration is a multiplier on cardiovascular drift (reduces plasma volume), but the cardiovascular conflict exists even without dehydration.
- As core temperature approaches ~40°C, the CNS generates inhibitory signals (increased perceived effort, reduced motor drive). While 40°C is commonly cited as a termination threshold, trained athletes can sustain effort above this, especially in shorter efforts with gradual thermal loading. 40°C represents a "danger zone" rather than a precise biological switch.

INTERVENTIONS:
1. Heat acclimatization: Medium-sized improvements in time trial performance shown in RCTs. Cardiovascular adaptations (lower heart rate, improved cardiac efficiency) emerge within ~1 week; thermoregulatory adaptations take ~2 weeks. Plasma volume expansion is one adaptation but studies have struggled to confirm statistically significant changes—other factors (earlier sweating, higher sweat rate, reduced thermal strain, perceptual changes) also contribute. A 3-4 day heat camp provides some cardiovascular benefit but not full thermoregulatory adaptation.
2. Pre-cooling: A 2024 meta-analysis confirmed pre-cooling significantly improves endurance performance in heat. External cooling (ice vests, cold packs) showed consistent significant improvements in time trial performance and time to exhaustion; internal cooling (ice slurry ingestion) showed no statistically significant improvement in time trial performance in this analysis.
3. Pacing: Adjusting pace to physiological signals (heart rate, perceived effort) rather than target pace is an accurate response to physiology, not a failure of fitness or will. Holding marathon pace at 25°C is not the same physiological effort as at 12°C.

HEAT ILLNESS DISTINCTION:
- Heat exhaustion: Primarily cardiovascular failure in thermal stress context; athlete collapses or comes close—weak, nauseous, dizzy, but conscious and oriented. Core temperature typically below 40°C. Rest, cooling, and fluid replacement are immediate priorities; prognosis is good with prompt management.
- Heat stroke: Defining feature is central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, disorientation, altered consciousness, inability to walk straight)—not temperature. Demands immediate aggressive cooling before transport; delay worsens outcomes. The key question is "Is their brain affected?" not "What is their temperature?"

ADDITIONAL CONTENT: Researchers increasingly use ingestible temperature sensors (capsules transmitting core temperature in real-time via radio frequency) for more accurate core temperature measurement during exercise compared to skin or wrist devices, though not yet widely available to recreational athletes.

FINAL TAKEAWAY: Heat slows runners not because fitness fails in warm conditions, but because the cardiovascular system has two jobs and cannot fully do both at once. Proper preparation (2-week acclimatization, external pre-cooling, pacing to physiological signals) changes how much capacity the system has to manage the conflict. The video cites 28 academic sources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Studies using large datasets of marathon results have consistently shown that recreational runners slow somewhere between 3% and 13% in hot conditions relative to cool ones. Elite runners slow too, typically in the region of 2% to 5%."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Rehydration during Endurance Exercise: Challenges, Research, Options, Methods ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/13/3/887

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article titled "Rehydration during Endurance Exercise: Challenges, Research, Options, Methods" by Lawrence E. Armstrong (Human Performance Laboratory and Korey Stringer Institute, University of Connecticut), published in the journal *Nutrients* (2021, Vol. 13, Issue 3, article 887; DOI: 10.3390/nu13030887). The paper was submitted 11 February 2021, accepted 1 March 2021, and published 9 March 2021.

The article addresses the two primary problems arising from disturbed fluid-electrolyte balance during endurance exercise: dehydration (incomplete replacement of water and sodium losses in sweat and urine) and overhydration (excessive consumption and retention of dilute fluids). Both can degrade exercise performance and lead to hydration-related illnesses when experienced at moderate-to-severe levels.

Key content areas covered:

1. **Water and Salt Losses**: Most ultraendurance competitors do not meet fluid needs during competition. Three factors influence sweat volume and body mass: exercise intensity (higher intensity = greater sweat rate per hour), exercise duration (slower competitors can be on course twice as long), and environmental temperature (marathon sweat rates of 0.81, 0.96, and 1.52 L/h at 7°C, 10-12°C, and 20°C respectively). Extreme individual sweat rates observed: 3.7 L/h (elite marathon runner, 1984 LA Olympics), 4.1 L/h (laboratory race simulation), and 4.3 L/h (tennis player). Extreme body mass losses of 11-12% have been documented in Ironman triathlons.

2. **Dehydration Effects on Performance**: Consensus exists that dehydration of -2 to -4% body mass represents the range where endurance exercise performance declines. A meta-analysis of 34 studies found dehydration of 4-7% more likely to impair performance than 1-3%. Performance decrements are greater in hot versus cool environments (a 4-5% dehydration level reduced VO2max by -9 to -27% when ambient temp ≥30°C versus -3 to -7% at 15-26°C).

3. **Dehydration-Related Illnesses**: Includes exercise-associated collapse, exertional heat illnesses (heat stroke, cramps, exhaustion), and kidney dysfunction/renal stress (acute renal failure possible but uncommon at dehydration <4%; marked urine concentration seen in 11 of 33 cyclists).

4. **Overhydration and Exertional Hyponatremia (EHN)**: No evidence that pre-exercise hyperhydration improves performance. EHN is a potentially fatal illness caused by overhydration diluting blood, causing water to move into cells and cell swelling. Symptoms appear at serum concentration ~130-135 mmol Na+/L and include lightheadedness, dizziness, nausea, puffiness, and body weight gain. Below 130 mmol/L, symptoms may include headache, vomiting, pulmonary edema, and altered mental status from cerebral edema. Predisposing factors: exercise duration >4 hours, high sweat rate, high sweat sodium, and small body size. A theoretical drinking rate threshold of ~700 mL/h was identified—no cases of symptomatic EHN occurred among 270 athletes consuming less than 750 mL/h. Notably, sodium supplementation had only a minor influence on serum Na+ levels (mean increase of 3 mmol/L in controlled studies) and did not prevent EHN.

5. **Thirst Complexity**: The plasma osmolality threshold for thirst varies greatly across individuals (range 274-293 mOsm/kg, compared to laboratory reference range of 285-295 mOsm/kg). Elite marathon runners showed wide variation in fluid intake rates (30-1040 mL/h). Two case studies showed that overhydration prior to exercise combined with high fluid intake during exercise resulted in asymptomatic EHN.

The article presents 5 rehydration methods (ranging from no advanced action to determination of sweat rate during field simulation) and 9 rehydration recommendations relevant to endurance activities, allowing each athlete to select the method that best helps them achieve a "rehydration middle ground" between dehydration and overhydration. The article belongs to the Nutrients Special Issue "Hydration and Fluid Needs during Physical Activity."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"During endurance exercise, two problems arise from disturbed fluid–electrolyte balance: dehydration and overhydration. The former involves water and sodium losses in sweat and urine that are incompletely replaced, whereas the latter involves excessive consumption and retention of dilute fluids."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Masters Running Tips: 5 Evidence-Based Ways to Train Smarter After 40 - Runners Connect ---
URL: https://runnersconnect.net/masters-running-tips

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Jeff Gaudette (co-founder of RunnersConnect, MS from Johns Hopkins) provides evidence-based training guidance for masters runners (40+). Key findings:

1. PERFORMANCE DECLINE: Aerobic capacity declines at roughly 1% per year for active runners after 40, about half the rate (2%) seen in sedentary adults. VO2 max drops most steeply after age 60, while lactate threshold holds up better with age—a study of 168 master runners found lactate threshold remained a strong predictor of race performance even as VO2 max declined.

2. RECOVERY: Aging muscles develop "anabolic resistance"—a diminished ability to respond to anabolic stimuli including exercise and protein intake. Inflammatory resolution slows, extending the adaptation window from 24-36 hours (younger runners) to 48-72 hours for most masters runners. Declining NAD+ levels (a coenzyme central to mitochondrial energy production and cellular repair) also slow recovery. Practical adjustment: schedule hard workouts on Tuesday and Saturday rather than Tuesday and Thursday, treating intervening days as genuinely easy.

3. STRENGTH TRAINING: Fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibers decline progressively from age 25 onward. Research comparing masters to younger runners found significantly lower muscle strength and power in the masters group, directly tracking with reduced running economy at race pace. Recommended: heavy compound lifts and plyometrics 2 days per week—specifically heavy single-leg deadlifts (4-6 reps, 3 sets), split squats with load, calf raises to failure, and bounding drills. Body-weight stability work helps injury prevention but generates weaker fast-twitch recruitment signals.

4. INTENSITY DISTRIBUTION: The most common training error is compressing intensity—easy runs become moderately hard and hard runs stay moderately hard. Easy runs should be 90-120 seconds per mile slower than race pace. For a runner with 8:00/mi 5K pace, most weekly mileage should be at 10:30-11:30/mi or slower. Recommended weekly structure for a 40-mile week: 2 quality sessions (threshold or VO2 max), 1 long easy run, remaining mileage on genuinely easy days, plus one full rest day.

5. PROTEIN: Masters runners need 35-40g of leucine-rich protein per meal (50-60% more per meal than the ~20-25g threshold for younger runners), spread across 3-4 meals. The post-workout window within 30-45 minutes after hard sessions is especially important. Leucine content matters more than protein source (whey, eggs, chicken, fish). Studies combining leucine-rich protein with resistance training in adults over 50 found significant improvements in body composition and physical function.

The article includes an FAQ covering age of performance decline onset, hard workout frequency (2 quality sessions spaced 72 hours apart), strength training's role in slowing decline, protein intake (140-180g/day for a 150-180lb runner), age-graded PRs, and age grading methodology (a score of 70%+ is considered excellent). References include studies by Lepers & Stapley (2016), Wiswell et al. (2000), Quinn et al. (2011), Lexell et al. (1988), Pérez-Castillo et al. (2025), and Taniguchi et al. (2022). The article also promotes a free Age Grading Performance Calculator and MAS NAD+ supplementation product.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Research tracking masters athletes in endurance events found that aerobic capacity declines at roughly 1% per year in active runners after 40, about half the rate seen in sedentary adults the same age."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Do older athletes reach limits in their performance during ... ---
URL: https://inserm.hal.science/inserm-00596872/file/inserm-00596872_edited.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific study by Romuald Lepers and Thomas Cattagni (Université de Bourgogne, INSERM U887) examines whether older athletes reach performance limits in marathon running. The study analyzed New York City Marathon data from 1980-2009, focusing on participation and performance trends of master athletes (40+ years).

**Methodology:** The researchers analyzed running times of the top 10 male and female finishers aged 20-79 years across three decades (1980-89, 1990-99, 2000-09). Gender differences were calculated as percent differences between top-10 male and female times. Data was obtained from the NYC Marathon website.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Participation increased dramatically:** Total finishers increased 65% between 1980-89 and 1990-99, and 25% between 1990-99 and 2000-09. Female participation grew more than male (145% vs 49% in the first decade gap; 68% vs 11% in the second). The male-to-female finisher ratio decreased from 5.1 to 3.1 to 2.1 across the three decades. Master athletes' share of finishers rose significantly—by 2000-09, masters represented 53% of male and 40% of female finishers.

2. **Performance improvements by age:** Male running times plateaued for ages <60-64 years but significantly decreased (P<0.01) for those ≥60-64 years. For example, males 65-69 improved ~8 min (3.7%) between 1980-89 and 1990-99, and ~7 min (3.2%) between 1990-99 and 2000-09. Female times plateaued for ages <45-49 years but significantly decreased for those ≥45-49 years. Females 55-59 improved ~33 min (14.5%) between 1980-89 and 1990-99.

3. **Gender gap narrowed:** Mean gender differences in running times were 28.4%, 25.8%, and 19.7% for the three decades respectively (P<0.001 for 2000-2009 vs earlier decades). During the last decade, gender differences ranged from ~12% (30-40 yrs) to ~26% (65-69 yrs), remaining relatively stable across ages. World record gender gap narrowed from 13.3% in 1980 to 9.2% currently.

**Conclusions:** Male runners ≥65 years and female runners ≥45 years have probably not yet reached their limits in marathon performance. Male masters in the 40-64 age range have plateaued, while female masters (except 40-44) continue improving. The relative stability of gender differences across ages in the last decade suggests age-related declines in physiological function do not differ between males and females. The authors call for further research on other endurance events (swimming, cycling, triathlon) and physiological parameters like lactate threshold and running economy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These data suggest that male (≥65 yrs) and female (≥45 yrs) master runners have probably not yet reached their limits in marathon performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: 24-Hour Ultra-Marathon Running: A Narrative Review of Performance Factors and Physiological Impacts ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-026-00997-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an open-access narrative review article published in Sports Medicine - Open (Volume 12, article number 32, 2026) titled "24-Hour Ultra-Marathon Running: A Narrative Review of Performance Factors and Physiological Impacts." Published March 17, 2026, the article was authored by Beat Knechtle, Lorin Braschler, Katja Weiss, Volker Scheer, Sasa Duric, Luciano Bernardes Leite, Pedro Forte, Pantelis T. Nikolaidis, Daniela Chlíbková, and Thomas Rosemann. It has 4738 accesses and 2 citations.

The review aimed to comprehensively synthesize scientific literature on 24-hour ultra-marathon running, as no such comprehensive review existed previously. The authors searched PubMed and Scopus databases for studies published through end of 2025, using search terms related to 24-hour running. They found 46 articles in PubMed and 59 in SCOPUS, retaining 62 references after excluding duplicates and unrelated studies (e.g., multi-stage races, ultra-cycling).

Key findings include:
- Participation in 24-hour ultra-marathons has increased over the past decades, with most participants being master/age-group runners older than 35 years. Youth runners under 19 also participate (805 finishes from 582 unique finishers between 1990-2018).
- Runners typically cover distances exceeding 100 km, with averages of ~150-160 km; top performers exceed 200 km.
- Men achieve greater distances than women, but the gap has been decreasing over time.
- Peak performance is achieved at ages 40-50 years.
- The most important predictive variables for performance are training, nutrition, previous experience, and pacing; anthropometric characteristics had no predictive value.
- Athletes mainly ingest carbohydrates and experience an energy deficit during the race, but rarely develop exercise-associated hyponatremia.
- A 24-hour run causes decreased body mass (from dehydration, loss of skeletal muscle and/or fat mass).
- Physiological effects include: cardiovascular (decreased blood pressure, changes in cardiac biomarkers, ECG and echocardiographic changes), renal (reversible impairment of kidney function), digestive (GI discomfort, reversible increase in liver enzymes), immune (increased immune markers), and hematological (decreased red blood cells, increased white blood cells) changes.
- Most adverse effects resolve within 2-3 days.
- Historically, the first 24-hour race took place in 1807 in Newmarket (UK) with two participants; in 2024, over 300 events were held worldwide.
- The race format is usually held on short loops, often 400-meter tracks.

The review identifies future research needs, including post-race nutrition to enhance recovery and the impact of training/competing on the locomotor system (skeleton, muscles, tendons, joints).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"24-hour ultra-runners typically cover distances exceeding 100 km per event, with an average distance ranging from ~ 150–160 km, while the top performers can achieve over 200 km."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Medium ---
URL: https://medium.com/runners-life/what-female-masters-runners-can-teach-us-about-aging-ce06ffc76dfb

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a member-only article published in the Medium publication "Runner's Life" on June 25, 2026, written by Brady Holmer, a science writer with an M.Sc. in Human Performance and an endurance athlete. The article, titled "What Female Masters Runners Can Teach Us About Aging," discusses a new mini-review in the Journal of Applied Physiology by Dr. Douglas Seals and colleagues from the University of Colorado Boulder. The research program, which began in the early 1990s, studied female masters endurance athletes (mostly runners) and compared them with healthy but non-exercising women of similar age, as well as younger women. The central thesis is that while some aspects of aging are biological, some decline may result from a lifetime of underestimating what the body can maintain when it keeps moving. The results argue that the aging body is far more adaptable than old assumptions suggested, and the findings have implications for all runners regardless of age or gender. The article notes that women were still wildly underrepresented in exercise physiology and cardiovascular aging research when the program began (and notes they still are).

SUMMARY:

This is a forum post from Science for ME (s4me.info) discussing a 2023 systematic review by Costa et al. titled "Exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome—implications for health and intestinal disease," published open access in Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/apt.14157).

Key findings of the review:
- "Exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome" refers to disturbances of gastrointestinal integrity and function common during strenuous exercise.

- As exercise intensity and duration increase, there is considerable evidence for increased intestinal injury, permeability, and endotoxaemia, along with impaired gastric emptying, slowed small intestinal transit, and malabsorption.
- Heat stress and running mode exacerbate these gastrointestinal disturbances.
- Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max appears to be the threshold at which significant gastrointestinal perturbations manifest, regardless of fitness status.
- Gastrointestinal symptoms (upper and lower tract) are common and can limit prolonged strenuous exercise.
- Moderate exercise appears to benefit patients with inflammatory bowel disease or functional gastrointestinal disorders, but the safety of more strenuous exercise in these populations has not been established.
- Conclusions: Strenuous exercise has a major reversible impact on GI integrity and function in healthy populations, but the safety and health implications of prolonged strenuous exercise in patients with chronic GI diseases remain unclear and require further investigation.

The post was created by forum member "Andy" (Senior Member with voting rights) in the "Other news and research" / "Other health news and research" forum categories.

--- SOURCE 7: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in ... ---
URL: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/9QnW5DQA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a case series study titled "Case Series: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Athletes Using a High-Carbohydrate Low-FODMAP Therapeutic Intervention," published in 2025 in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (Vol. 34, No. 4, pp. 337-354), by Rachel Scrivin, Gary Slater, and Ricardo J.S. Costa, published by Human Kinetics. The study has been cited 3 times and is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science.

The study implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). The case series involved 9 athletes who experienced recurrent severe Ex-GIS and 2 controls without symptoms.

The four phases were: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes, specifically including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of therapeutic interventions.

Key findings: The majority of athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2-4% body mass loss, and <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate (8/9) during the GastroAxEx. Severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) was reported by 4/9 athletes during exercise and 8/9 in the recovery period. All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery. Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet and improved intake tolerance during the targeted event, with reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS and improved perceived work output.

The study concludes that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms.

The webpage also lists 40 references and 4 citing publications, including a position statement response in Sports Medicine, a study on high-amylose maize starch and hydration, a practitioner's guide to managing gut issues in athletes, and a Current Opinion article on dietary FODMAP manipulation arguing that FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default based on symptom severity.

"This case-series describes a four-phase management approach implementing gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes affected by exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS)."
