--- SOURCE 8: Sports Dietitians Australia and Ultra Sports Science Foundation Joint Position Statement: A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12106582

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a joint position statement by Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and the Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) published in Sports Medicine (April 7, 2025; Vol 55, Issue 5, Article 1097; DOI: 10.1007/s40279-025-02186-6) providing a practitioner guide for the prevention and management of exercise-associated gastrointestinal perturbations and symptoms (Ex-GIS) and exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS).

KEY AUTHORS: Ricardo J. S. Costa, Stephanie K. Gaskell, Kayla Henningsen (Monash University, Australia); Nikki A. Jeacocke and Alice M. Wallett (Australian Institute of Sport); Volker Scheer (Ultra Sports Science Foundation, France); Rachel Scrivin (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia & Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand); Rhiannon M. J. Snipe (Deakin University, Australia); and Pascale Young (Monash University). The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (PMCID: PMC12106582; PMID: 40195264).

BACKGROUND & KEY CONCEPTS:
- Exercise can disturb gastrointestinal integrity and function, leading to EIGS and Ex-GIS, which are common in active and athlete populations and comprise a substantial case load for practitioners (sports dietitians, sport and exercise nutritionists, sports medical practitioners).
- EIGS comprises two primary pathophysiological pathways: (1) the circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway (splanchnic hypoperfusion and gastrointestinal ischemia due to blood flow redistribution to skeletal muscle, leading to intestinal epithelial injury, hyperpermeability, and inflammatory responses from translocated pathogens/endotoxins), and (2) the neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway (stress responses, sympathetic activation, impaired motility, transit, digestion, and nutrient absorption via effects on the enteric nervous system and interstitial cells of Cajal).
- Two additional pathways warrant investigation: mechanical strain on the splanchnic area (jarring/jolting/vibrations) and exaggerated metabolic responses (metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia) linked to exercise-associated nausea.
- Ex-GIS symptom incidence varies widely by exercise type: negligible in recreational endurance running, 4% after marathon competition, and ≥93% in ultra-endurance events. Longer-duration exercise, especially in hot conditions, promotes higher Ex-GIS incidence.
- Symptoms are classified per ROME IV criteria into upper-GIS (belching, heartburn, upper-abdominal bloating/pain, regurgitation), lower-GIS (flatulence, lower-abdominal bloating/pain, urge to defecate, abnormal defecation, fecal blood loss), and other symptoms (nausea, stitch). Contrary to mainstream dogma, upper-GIS symptoms are more commonly reported during/immediately after exercise than lower-GIS; nausea is frequently reported in ultra-endurance activities.

EXACERBATION FACTORS (with assigned impact magnitudes: unknown = ?, minimal = +, modest = ++, extensive = +++):
Extrinsic factors:
- Exercise duration (+++): considerable perturbations occur with ≥2h exercise; plateaus thereafter.
- Exercise intensity (++): continuous ≥70% VO2max or HIIT/resistance exercise ≤2h produces modest increases.
- Exercise modality (+): field studies suggest running prompts greater disturbance than swimming/cycling (due to mechanical strain), but controlled lab studies show no clear modality differences.
- Environmental conditions (+++): hot ambient conditions (~35°C) increase EIGS biomarkers and Ex-GIS; core body temperature ≥39.5°C or Δ≥2.5°C is clinically significant; ≥39.0°C or Δ≥2.0°C exceeds minimal detectable change.
- Topographical elevation/altitude (+): altitude >2500m ASL may increase disturbances.
- Time of day (++): nocturnal exercise prompts greater GI function disturbance and Ex-GIS than diurnal exercise, but no effect on EIGS integrity/systemic biomarkers.
- External pharmaceutical administration (+++): NSAIDs are GI irritants; administration prior to exercise markedly increases GI perturbations and Ex-GIS.

Intrinsic factors:
- Biological sex (+): low-to-modest differences observed; female athletes proposed to present greater EIGS/Ex-GIS due to menstrual cycle, but evidence is inconsistent.
- Age (+): modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults.
- Fitness status (+): higher-trained individuals at lower absolute risk but exposed to greater relative loads.
- GI/circulating microbial and SCFA composition (+): may impact magnitude of perturbations.
- Individual characteristics (+++): feeding tolerance (volume, concentration, type, texture), pre-existing GI diseases/disorders, and history of recurrent Ex-GIS increase risk.
- Psychological state (?): pre-exercise anxiety linked to Ex-GIS in field observations but lacks rigorous controlled evidence.

METHODOLOGY: A scoping review approach (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Ovid Medline) was used to screen relevant research studies. Evidence was graded (Grade I = Good, Grade II = Fair, Grade III = Limited, Grade IV = Not fully supported) based on adherence to best-practice recommendations in exercise gastroenterology research, including the Costa et al. (2022) experimental design checklist. Methodological concerns in existing research include participant selection/screening, exercise protocol justification, ambient temperature control, dietary control, hydration monitoring, biomarker selection, Ex-GIS assessment tool choice, power calculations, and population heterogeneity.

The paper covers disturbances categorized into: gastrointestinal epithelial integrity (tissue injury, tight-junction injury, permeability, endotoxemia/bacteremia), gastrointestinal function (gastric emptying, transit, absorption, myoelectrical activity, malabsorption), systemic responses (leukocyte trafficking, inflammatory cytokines, immune responses), GI signs/symptoms (gut comfort, total/upper/lower GIS, nausea, regurgitation/vomiting, abnormal defecation with/without blood loss), and feeding tolerance.

Key Points: Macronutrient intake during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulations (e.g., FODMAP), and gut training show beneficial outcomes in EIGS/Ex-GIS management. Heat-mitigating strategies and certain nutritional supplements (prebiotics, phenols) show promising outcomes, while other dietary manipulations and supplements appear less favorable. Individual athlete assessment to establish main causal factors aids tailored prevention/management strategies.
</summary>

The article was submitted 26 July 2023, revised 30 August 2023, accepted 12 September 2023, and published 19 September 2023. It has 26 citations and an Altmetric score of 31.

**Key content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a condition affecting up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports (marathon, triathlon, cycling, running, etc.) caused by strenuous exercise. Symptoms include upper GI issues (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower GI issues (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two main pathways are described:
1. Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway: Sympathetic activation alters the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic blood flow can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing gut hypoperfusion, ischemic damage, loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP. 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study.

**GI symptoms during exercise:** 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms. In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors.

**IBS overlap:** Ex-GIS shares pathogenesis with IBS (alterations in gut microbiota, permeability, immune function, motility, visceral sensation, brain-gut interactions). IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed.

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms).

**Management:** The review emphasizes nutritional and behavioral strategies, particularly examining gluten-free diets and low-FODMAP (fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols) diets as the principal interventions to avoid symptoms during exercise. Exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet should all be evaluated.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023, yielding 142 relevant research articles published between 1965 and 2023.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Nutrition during exercise is vital for prolonged activity and performance, but exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS) and exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) are common among endurance athletes. --- SOURCE 12: International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and performance - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2824625

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Caffeine and Performance (2010)

This is a position statement from the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), authored by Erica R. Goldstein and 14 colleagues, establishing the Society's official position on caffeine supplementation and sport performance. The paper was received December 22, 2009, accepted January 27, 2010, and is published under the Creative Commons Attribution License.

### The Society's Seven-Point Position Statement:
1. **Caffeine is effective for enhancing sport performance** in trained athletes when consumed in low-to-moderate dosages (~3-6 mg/kg); higher dosages (≥9 mg/kg) do not result in further enhancement.
2. **Anhydrous caffeine** exerts a greater ergogenic effect compared to coffee.
3. Caffeine can **enhance vigilance** during extended exhaustive exercise and periods of sustained sleep deprivation.
4. Caffeine is **ergogenic for sustained maximal endurance exercise** and highly effective for time-trial performance.
5. Caffeine is **beneficial for high-intensity exercise**, including team sports such as soccer and rugby characterized by intermittent activity over prolonged duration.
6. The literature is **equivocal on strength-power performance** effects; more research is warranted.
7. The literature does **not support caffeine-induced diuresis during exercise** or harmful changes in fluid balance affecting performance.

### Key Mechanisms of Action:
- Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is rapidly absorbed through the GI tract, metabolized by the liver into three metabolites (paraxanthine, theophylline, theobromine), with elevated blood levels appearing within 15-45 minutes and peak concentrations one hour post-ingestion.
- Caffeine easily crosses the blood-brain barrier due to lipid solubility; circulating concentrations decrease 50-75% within 3-6 hours.
- The primary mechanism is **adenosine receptor antagonism** at the CNS.
- Caffeine decreases reliance on glycogen utilization and increases free fatty acid mobilization during exercise.
- Caffeine increases β-endorphin secretion, potentially reducing pain perception.
- Caffeine promotes a significant thermogenic response (100 mg dose produced significant thermogenic effect persisting 3+ hours).
- A moderate dose (6 mg/kg) significantly enhanced isometric leg extension strength and time to fatigue.

### Cognitive Performance Findings:
- McLellan et al. studies of special force military units (600-800 mg caffeine via chewing gum during sleep deprivation) showed maintained or enhanced vigilance and improved physical performance (run times, obstacle courses) versus placebo.
- Lieberman et al. (U.S. Navy SEALs) found 200 mg significantly improved performance versus 100 mg, but 300 mg offered no additional benefit over 200 mg; 100 mg was no better than placebo.
- Caffeine's performance-enhancing effects may extend beyond its 2.5-10 hour half-life; effects on motor learning and short-term memory may relate to increased concentration ability rather than working memory itself.

### Caffeine and Carbohydrate:
- Ivy et al. (1979): 500 mg caffeine produced 7.4% greater work over control and 5.3% greater than glucose polymer; plasma FFA levels 30% greater than placebo after 2-hour isokinetic cycling.
- Graham and Spriet found performance enhancement only at 3 and 6 mg/kg doses (not 9 mg/kg), despite the higher dose producing the greatest metabolic effects—a paradox suggesting CNS overstimulation at high doses.
- Yeo et al.: 5.8% glucose solution plus 5 mg/kg caffeine enhanced exogenous carbohydrate oxidation ~26% higher than glucose alone.
- Hulston et al.: 6.4% glucose solution + 5.3 mg/kg caffeine improved time trial performance by 9% vs. placebo and 4.6% vs. glucose alone, without affecting exogenous carbohydrate oxidation.
- Battram et al. (2004): Caffeine did not hinder proglycogen or macroglycogen resynthesis following exhaustive exercise with carbohydrate repletion.
- **Pedersen et al.: Glycogen resynthesis increased by 66% with carbohydrate + 8 mg/kg caffeine** versus carbohydrate-only during 4-hour post-exercise recovery.

### Caffeine Form, Dose, and Endurance Exercise:
- Graham et al.: Caffeine capsules (4.45 mg/kg) significantly increased work capacity (additional 2-3 km run) compared to regular coffee, decaffeinated coffee, or decaf + caffeine capsules. Roasting byproducts (chlorogenic acid derivatives) may reduce caffeine's adenosine antagonism in coffee.
- McLellan and Bell: Capsule-form caffeine (3-7 mg/kg) provided average 24% increase in performance over placebo; consuming coffee before anhydrous supplementation did not interfere with ergogenic effects.
- Wiles et al.: Caffeinated coffee (150-200 mg caffeine) produced 4.2-second faster 1500-m run time vs. decaf; all 10 subjects achieved faster "final burst" speeds.
- Pasman et al.: Doses of 5, 9, and 13 mg/kg all significantly improved endurance (~27% average increase) with no statistical difference between doses.
- Graham and Spriet (elite runners): 9 mg/kg caffeine increased running time from ~49 min (placebo) to 71 min, and cycling from ~39 to ~59 min at 85% VO2max.
- Spriet et al. (1992): 9 mg/kg caffeine increased cycling time to exhaustion from 75 to 96 min at ~80% VO2max.
- McNaughton et al.: 6 mg/kg caffeine improved 1-hour time trial performance by 4-5% including hill simulations.

### High-Intensity and Team Sport Exercise:
- **Caffeine is NOT effective for untrained individuals** in high-intensity exercise (Collomp, Greer, Crowe, Lorino studies all showing no benefit or performance decline in non-trained subjects).
- Caffeine IS effective for trained athletes: 
  - Trained swimmers improved 100m freestyle velocity (Collomp) and 1,500m swim times (MacIntosh & Wright, 6 mg/kg).
  - Woolf et al.: 5 mg/kg increased peak power in trained anaerobic athletes.
  - Wiles et al.: 5 mg/kg improved 1-km time trial by 3.1% (71.1s vs. 73.4s).
  - Glaister et al.: 5 mg/kg improved first three of 12 × 30m sprints.
  - Bruce et al.: 6 mg/kg improved 2000m rowing time by 1.3% in trained oarsmen; 9 mg/kg provided no additional benefit.
  - Anderson et al.: 9 mg/kg improved 2000m rowing time by 1.3% in trained oarswomen, most evident in first 500m.
- Team sports: Stuart et al. found 6 mg/kg improved rugby ball-passing accuracy by 10% (90% successful passes vs. 83% placebo)—the first study showing caffeine improvement in a team-sport skill-related task. Schneiker et al. found 6 mg/kg induced more total sprint work in intermittent-sprint testing in team sport athletes.

### Overall Conclusions:
Caffeine is an effective ergogenic aid for trained athletes at low-to-moderate doses (3-6 mg/kg), best consumed in anhydrous form, with significant benefits for endurance, high-intensity, and team sports, cognitive performance under sleep deprivation, and post-exercise glycogen synthesis when combined with carbohydrate. High doses (≥9 mg/kg) offer no additional benefit and may impair performance through CNS overstimulation. The training status of the athlete, exercise mode/intensity/duration, and dose are critical factors determining efficacy.
</summary>

(Graham and Spriet on why 9 mg/kg failed to enhance performance), "Results were definitive in that glycogen resynthesis was increased by 66% for the carbohydrate-caffeine treatment, as compared to the carbohydrate-only condition." --- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1003445/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sec. Sport and Exercise Nutrition, Volume 9, November 9, 2022) titled "An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms" by Rachel Scrivin, Ricardo J.S. Costa, Fiona Pelly, Dana Lis, and Gary Slater (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand; Monash University, Australia; and UCLA, United States).

STUDY DESIGN AND PARTICIPANTS:
The study used a validated online questionnaire to investigate self-reported exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) and management strategies among 137 adult endurance athletes (≥18 years) participating in events ≥60 minutes. Participants included runners (55%, n=75), triathletes (22%, n=30), and non-running sports (23%, n=32) at recreationally competitive (37%), recreationally non-competitive (32%), and competitive regional/national/international (31%) levels. Females comprised 63% of respondents (n=86) and males 37% (n=51) (p<0.001); mean age was 41.6 ± 11.1 years. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia (approval S201402).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Athletes were categorized into groups based on when Ex-GIS developed: around training only (AT, 21%), around competitions only (AC, 30%), or equally around both (ET/EC, 49%).
- Lower gastrointestinal symptoms were more commonly reported than upper GI symptoms across all groups.
- Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during training and competitions than before or after exercise. The only severe symptom of significance was the urge to defecate during training in the ET group (Z=-0.536, p=0.01). Most Ex-GIS severity was rated as mild (<5/10 on a 0-10 visual analog scale).
- 67% (n=92) of athletes reported using dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting 277 total strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.

MOST POPULAR DIETARY STRATEGIES:
- Dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42) - the most popular
- Dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16)
- Low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15)
- Avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose, 6.1%, n=17) were the most popular FODMAPs avoided
- Non-dietary strategies included medications (4.7%, n=13) and relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11)

MOST SUCCESSFUL STRATEGIES (Likert scale 1-5, with 5 = significant improvement):
- Dietary fiber reduction (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Low FODMAP diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Dairy-free diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Increasing carbohydrates (median = 4, IQR = 3,4)
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed at all time points.

SUPPLEMENTS: Probiotics (median=4, n=26) were the most commonly used supplement; arginine was rated highest for success (median=5, n=1, though very small sample). Other supplements trialed included prebiotics, antioxidants, L-citrulline, glutamine, curcumin, and nitrates.

INFORMATION SOURCES: Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated as the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29). No significant associations were found between information sources and sport type, participation level, event characteristics, or biological sex.

CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS: Fifteen athletes (11%) reported a diagnosed gastrointestinal disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, n=6). Thirteen athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS.

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS:
- Reducing dietary fiber, especially before exercise, aligns with current sports nutrition guidelines and works via reducing luminal contents and extending GI transit time, though a low-fiber diet may require implementation 1-3 days before exercise.
- Low FODMAP diets are effective for both IBS and Ex-GIS, but are not intended for long-term use; a rechallenge and personalization phase is recommended for extended use.
- Dairy avoidance may relate to lactose intolerance, which has overlapping symptoms with IBS.
- Increasing carbohydrate intake can help mitigate Ex-GIS through improved splanchnic blood flow and reduced intestinal epithelial damage; however, high intake rates (>60-90 g/h) may trigger symptoms unless preceded by gut training.
- Carbohydrate or whey protein hydrolysate ingestion before/during exercise ameliorates intestinal epithelial injury; carbohydrate is preferential due to fewer GI symptoms and its value as an exogenous fuel source.
- Non-dietary interventions (medications, relaxation, psychological therapies) are used less frequently but have potential; further randomized controlled trials are needed.
- Study limitations include convenience sampling and possible over-representation of APDs as information sources due to researcher backgrounds as registered dietitians.
</summary>

"Endurance athletes use a variety of strategies to manage their Ex-GIS, with dietary manipulation being the most common."

--- SOURCE 2: Nutritional strategies for minimizing gastrointestinal symptoms during endurance exercise: systematic review of the literature ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12258207

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2025 Jul 11;22(1):2529910, doi:10.1080/15502783.2025.2529910) by Janez Mlinaric and Nina Mohorko (University of Primorska, Faculty of Health Sciences, Izola, Slovenia; Ruhr University Bochum, Germany; Human Performance Centre, Ljubljana, Slovenia), examining nutritional strategies to minimize gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms during endurance exercise.

METHODS: The review used PRISMA methodology, searching PubMed from January 2023 to March 2023. It included randomized controlled trials, crossover trials, and case studies. 31 studies were selected for inclusion, with quality assessment using the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias (RoB 2) tool. The majority of studies showed low risk of bias, though some had concerns regarding blinding and randomization.

The studies were categorized into five research areas:

1. **Gut training protocols**: Two weeks of purposeful repetitive CHO intake during running lowered GI symptom severity and reduced breath H₂ response (indicating reduced CHO malabsorption). Repetitive running sessions with higher liquid intake improved fluid tolerance over time. However, minor effects were seen in race walkers and runners with high daily CHO intake. The mechanisms may involve increased expression of SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters, but gut training is likely to reduce symptoms by reducing CHO malabsorption and increasing tolerance to higher CHO intakes.

2. **Carbohydrate solutions and mixtures**: CHO bars were the worst tolerated form (causing more nausea, fullness, and fatigue). Highly concentrated CHO solutions increased symptoms. Fructose caused more GI symptoms than glucose or sucrose due to slower absorption (facilitated diffusion vs. active transport). High glucose intake (SGLT1 saturation at ~60 g/h) caused bloating. Mixed CHOs recruit GLUT5 transporter, improving absorption. A 0.8 ratio MD:FRU solution was superior to 0.5 and 1.25 ratios for performance and GI comfort, suggesting ratios close to unity may be better than the traditional 2:1 ratio.

3. **Low FODMAP diet**: Multiple studies showed significant reductions in GI symptoms (gut discomfort, flatulence, urge to defecate, loose stool, diarrhea) with low FODMAP diets compared to high FODMAP diets. 69% of participants reported positive effects on low FODMAP vs. 25% on high FODMAP. However, the restrictive nature of the diet could negatively affect athletes in other ways.

4. **Hydrogel CHO products**: Current evidence does not demonstrate benefits of hydrogel CHO products over standard CHO products. One study showed lower GI symptoms with hydrogel, but others found no differences between conditions.

5. **Probiotic supplementation**: Evidence is mixed. Some studies showed reductions in GI symptoms (e.g., 27% reduction during training, fewer episodes of nausea, belching, vomiting), while others found no substantial differences or even increases in mild GI symptoms. LGG (Limosilactobacillus rhamnosus GG) shortened GI symptom episode duration by 33-57%.

CONCLUSION: The onset of GI symptoms is very complex and influenced by a huge variety of factors. Elimination of GI symptoms in each athlete must be approached individually and thoughtfully. At least 30-50% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms regularly during exercise, with estimates of 30-90% for endurance trained runners. Four main causes of GI symptoms: physiological (splanchnic hypoperfusion), mechanical, psychological, and nutritional.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"At least 30 to 50 % of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise on a regular basis, with especially high occurrence in long duration endurance exercise. In endurance trained runners it is estimated that between 30 and 90 % may experience them."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The article was authored by Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Gastroenterology, Department of Translational and Precision Medicine, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy) and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (Department of Gastroenterology, IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Milan, Italy). Submission received 26 July 2023; accepted 12 September 2023; published 19 September 2023. The article has been cited 26 times and viewed 61,433 times.

**Purpose:** The review explores the pathophysiology, clinical aspects, and nutritional/behavioral management strategies for Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome (Ex-GIS), with particular focus on gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023. Searches for pathophysiology returned 290 results (PubMed), 216 (MEDLINE), and 97 trials (Cochrane); diet/nutrition searches returned 2663, 2197, and 1038 results respectively. After inclusion/exclusion criteria (English language, relevant to diet and endurance performance), 142 research articles were identified.

**Key Findings on Pathophysiology:**
- Ex-GIS involves two primary pathways: (I) the neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway (sympathetic activation reducing GI functional capacity) and (II) the circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway (blood flow redistribution away from splanchnic circulation).
- Splanchnic blood flow (SBF) can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing significant GI tract hypoperfusion and damage.
- Splanchnic hypoperfusion leads to loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia (LPS in circulation), triggering pro-inflammatory cytokines.
- A 1965-era study by Brock-Utne found 81% of 89 marathon runners were endotoxemic.
- Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max represents the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
- Endurance exercise alters gut peptide levels (increases PYY and GLP-1, affects ghrelin, CCK) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) which affect GI motility and blood flow.
- Gut microbiota differences exist between athletes and sedentary individuals; probiotics (e.g., UCC118 strain) may attenuate exercise-induced intestinal hyperpermeability.
- Carbohydrate malabsorption was found in 68% of 25 healthy endurance-trained runners during recovery.

**Epidemiology/Prevalence:**
- 30-90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms during exercise.
- Ter Steege study of 2076 long-distance runners: 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% serious complaints, 2.7% within 24 hours post-run; 3 athletes dropped out.
- Pfeiffer study: severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon/cycling to 32% in Ironman races.
- Upper-GI symptoms in up to 40% of runners, up to 70% in cyclists; reflux/heartburn prevalence 15-20% in runners.
- Lower-GI symptoms: up to 30% in recreational runs, up to 50% in cyclists, up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners.
- Exercise-induced transient abdominal pain (ETAP) reported in 18% of recreational run competitors.
- IBS underdiagnosis in endurance athletes: Killian et al. documented 9.8% IBS prevalence overall with only 2.8% diagnosed; Hungin et al. reported 14.1% overall with 10.8% undiagnosed.
- Female athletes, especially younger ones, report higher GI symptom prevalence; increased age may be protective due to reduced splanchnic vasoconstriction.

**Management Implications:** The review highlights nutritional and behavioral interventions as the principal strategies to avoid symptoms, including evaluation of exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet. It examines gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets as potential management approaches, noting that Ex-GIS symptoms resemble IBS (defined by Rome IV Criteria) and may respond to analogous nutritional strategies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s44410-025-00019-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access scoping review article published in the journal "Performance Nutrition" (Volume 2, article number 4, published February 4, 2026) titled "Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review." The study aimed to assess the prevalence of GI symptoms in non-endurance sport athletes, as GI symptoms are well-documented in endurance athletes but less clear across other sports.

METHODS: A scoping review was conducted following JBI guidelines with the PCC mnemonic. Searches were performed on Medline and SportDiscus databases (via EBSCO) until September 1, 2025, using keywords including "gastrointestinal," "athlete*/player*/sport*," and "prevalence/frequency/proportion." Only cross-sectional studies in highly trained (Tier 3) or higher athletes were included. Endurance sports (distance running, cycling, triathlons) and clinical settings were excluded.

RESULTS: The search yielded 482 articles; after screening, seven studies were included. Six different questionnaires were used across studies. In total, 1,087 athletes (682 male, 405 female) were analyzed. Prevalence of at least one GI symptom ranged from 11.5–80.0%. Any GI symptom prevalence in males was 13.9–61% and in females 26–80%. Three studies reported symptom timing around training/competition ranging from 24.5–52.0%, more common in females (37.5–67.0%) than males (13.9–52.0%). The most common symptoms were flatulence (2.8–48%), stomach cramps/rumbling (5.1–37%), and bloating (2.5–32%). Diarrhoea and urge to defecate were more common during exercise than at rest (19% vs. 8%, and 13% vs. 11%, respectively). Specific findings included: American footballers (61% reported ≥1 symptom, 52% during exercise), rugby players (61% male, 72% female with ≥1 symptom), powerlifters/weightlifters with anal incontinence (61.8% male vs. 80.0% female), and celiac disease symptoms higher in athletes than general population (2.9% vs. 0.4%).

CONCLUSIONS: GI symptoms are common in non-endurance athletes, with approximately 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes experiencing symptoms around competition. The wide variation in prevalence (11.5–80%) is likely due to heterogeneity in screening tools, with studies using different numbers of symptoms assessed (2–15), different Likert scales (0–4, 0–7, 0–10), and varying recall windows (past week to 12 months). Female athletes were more likely to report symptoms affecting performance. The authors call for standardized methods for assessing GI issues in athletes and note that existing questionnaires may be suitable only for research, not clinical diagnosis, suggesting future research should consider validated criteria such as ROME IV for IBS.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete

This chapter from the Musculoskeletal Key website (DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) addresses common gastrointestinal (GI) conditions in athletes and active persons, focusing on recognition and management. GI conditions are common in athletes, with exercise placing significant stress on the GI tract, resulting in characteristic disorders that can impair athletic performance.

### Key Points:

**General Pathophysiology:**
- 20–50% of high-performance athletes report undesirable GI symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea)
- Symptoms are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes
- Cyclists appear somewhat protected from GI issues due to forward positioning, while runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling
- Increased catecholamines and GI peptides (gastrin, motilin, secretin, etc.) increase gut transit time, negatively affecting GI homeostasis

**GI Tract Ischemia:**
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction
- Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation
- Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa" (per ter Steege et al.)
- Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms

**Upper GI Conditions:**
- Upper GI complaints affect 30–70% of athletes
- Three primary mechanisms: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes
- GERD is the most common cause of upper GI symptoms in athletes
- Exercise ≥90% VO2 max increases frequency/duration of esophageal reflux episodes
- Weightlifters have the highest rate of heartburn and reflux; runners have a threefold increase in GERD when running 45 minutes after a meal

**GERD Management:**
- Lifestyle modifications first-line: sleeping on two pillows, avoiding lying down within 4 hours of evening meal, avoiding postprandial exercise, limiting foods that relax the LES (high-fat foods, coffee, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods)
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training
- Pharmacologic therapy: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective
- H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers
- Upper endoscopy for diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended

**Other Conditions:**
- **Functional heartburn:** Up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset; treatment is biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, prokinetics
- **Dyspepsia:** Caused by GERD, gastritis, or peptic ulcer disease; ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms; PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence
- **Aspirin/NSAIDs:** Block cyclooxygenase and protective prostaglandins; add daily PPI for GI protection in athletes requiring NSAIDs with ulcer history
- **Pill esophagitis:** NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and mefloquine are highest risk; take with food/fluid in morning and remain upright
- **Dysphagia:** Divided into oropharyngeal and esophageal subtypes; most commonly caused by irritative effects of GERD
- **Nausea/Vomiting:** Linked to postprandial exercise; avoid solid food within 3 hours of events; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events; H2 blockers and PPIs can help

**GERD-Asthma Connection:**
- Up to 90% of persons with asthma have GERD; up to 40% have esophagitis
- Treatment only benefits asthma in patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms
- Atypical GERD presentations include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, and chest pain
</summary>

"These symptoms are reported by approximately 20% to 50% of high-performance athletes and are encountered more commonly in women than in men."

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Proton pump inhibitors may enhance the risk of digestive diseases by regulating intestinal microbiota ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2023.1217306/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Proton Pump Inhibitors May Enhance the Risk of Digestive Diseases by Regulating Intestinal Microbiota

This is a peer-reviewed review article published in *Frontiers in Pharmacology* (July 17, 2023) by Liang Tian, Jinqiu Yuan, Wenbo Meng and colleagues from Lanzhou University (China) and Sun Yat-sen University (China). The article reviews the growing evidence linking proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use to digestive complications through PPI-induced alterations of the intestinal microbiota.

### Key Points:

**Background:** PPIs are the most widely used acid-suppressive agents and first-line therapy for gastric acid-related disorders (peptic ulcer disease, GERD, Barrett's esophagus). However, increasing evidence links PPIs to adverse digestive events including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Clostridium difficile-associated disease (CDAD), functional dyspepsia, lower GI bleeding, infectious diseases, cholelithiasis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

**Mechanisms of PPI effects on intestinal flora:**
- pH-dependent: PPIs reduce gastric acid, disrupting the gastric acid barrier, allowing exogenous bacteria to invade the GI tract; affects microorganisms with specific pH requirements (e.g., H. pylori)
- Non-pH-dependent: PPI-induced hypergastrinemia and hyperparathyroidism affect intestinal osmolality and calcium/phosphorus metabolism; PPIs alter digestive functions and nutrient absorption; PPIs directly bind to non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases on microbes (fungi, H. pylori, Streptococcus pneumoniae)
- PPI treatment increases Planococcaceae, Oxalobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae in the proximal small intestine; decreases Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae

**Specific disease associations with altered flora:**
1. **Functional Dyspepsia (FD):** Decreased Bifidobacterium reduces butyric acid production, increasing intestinal permeability. Reduced Streptococcus, Prevotella, Veillonella, Actinomyces, and Lactobacillus may also contribute.
2. **Lower GI Bleeding:** Decreased Lactobacillus johnsonii (lactic acid production inhibits NF-κB/TNF-α pathway) and reduced Actinomycetes/Bifidobacterium contribute to NSAID-induced intestinal injury.
3. **SIBO:** Results are inconsistent across studies; a 2018 meta-analysis showed PPI use moderately increased SIBO risk, though diagnostic method variability (aspirate culture vs. breath tests) is a major confounder.
4. **CDAD:** PPIs regulate C. difficile toxin gene expression (up to 120-fold), accelerate spore-to-trophic-form transition via elevated pH, diminish salivary nitrite antimicrobial effects, and disrupt normal flora. Risk can be up to 7.15-fold higher.
5. **Gastrointestinal Infectious Diseases:** PPIs increase risk of bacterial gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter), Candida infections (reduced Lactobacillus), and multidrug-resistant organism infections (75% increased infection rate).
6. **Cholelithiasis:** PPI use increases abundance of bile salt hydrolase (BSH)-producing bacteria (Lactobacillus, Clostridium, Eubacterium), increasing secondary bile acids (especially deoxycholic acid) that promote gallstone formation. PPIs also reduce gallbladder motility by delaying gastric emptying.
7. **Inflammatory Bowel Disease:** PPI use is linked to IBD through reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (anti-inflammatory), reduced Lactobacillus reuteri (which normally produces histamine to suppress TNF-α), increased intestinal infections, and CDAD promotion.

**Conclusions:** The evidence supports a link between PPI-induced intestinal flora disruption and digestive complications. The gut microbiota represents a promising target for prevention and treatment (e.g., fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics like Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium). However, most studies are retrospective with relatively weak evidence and confounding factors. Clinicians should carefully evaluate and individually manage patients requiring PPI therapy to avoid long-term abuse. More high-quality clinical studies and research into specific mechanisms and molecular targets are needed.
</summary>

"PPIs are the most used acid-inhibitory drugs, with a wide range of applications in the treatment of various digestive diseases. However, recently, there has been a growing number of digestive complications linked to PPIs, and several studies have indicated that the intestinal flora play an important role in these complications."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Exercise & GI Symptoms - IFFGD ---
URL: https://iffgd.org/manage-your-health/tips-and-daily-living/exercise-gi-symptoms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders (IFFGD) addresses whether intense exercise can lead to GI symptoms such as diarrhea and heartburn. The article answers a reader's question about experiencing diarrhea and heartburn after increasing exercise intensity.

Key content covered:

**Benefits vs. risks of exercise:** While regular exercise offers documented benefits (better sleep, stronger bones, weight loss, fewer heart problems, better glucose control), it can also contribute to GI disorders causing symptoms including reflux/heartburn, belching, bloating, stomach pain/cramps, vomiting, nausea, side ache, flatulence, urgency, diarrhea, and intestinal bleeding.

**Heartburn:** Exercise can decrease lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, leading to more reflux episodes. Eating too soon before exercise and high-impact activities (like running) can worsen reflux compared to low-impact exercises like cycling. Treatment includes H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and switching to lower-impact exercises.

**Diarrhea:** Diarrhea and urgency are common in endurance athletes, especially long-distance runners. Approximately 90% of long-distance runners experience some GI symptoms during exercise but accept them as normal and don't consult a physician.

**Three main causes of GI symptoms during intense exercise:**
1. **Mechanical:** Repetitive body movement from running causes trauma that can damage the intestinal lining, contributing to diarrhea, urgency, or GI bleeding.
2. **Ischemic:** During intense exercise, blood flow shifts to working muscles and away from the GI tract (up to 80% reduction), causing ischemia, reduced gut function, increased leakiness, malabsorption, and looser stools.
3. **Nutritional:** Fiber, fat, protein, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>7% carbohydrate) are associated with greater risk of GI symptoms.

**Prevention tips:** Stay well hydrated, avoid lactose-containing products, and avoid high-fructose foods and fructose-only drinks.

**Medical treatment:** Patients should consult healthcare providers about persistent or bleeding diarrhea, which may signal a severe condition. Loperamide (over-the-counter) has been shown to decrease stool frequency when taken before intense exercise. Caution is advised with antispasmodic and antimotility drugs, as they can inhibit perspiration and impair core body temperature control.

The article was authored by Renata Korczak, RD CSSD (University of Minnesota), adapted from an article by Thomas Puetz, M.D. (Aurora Advanced Healthcare), and edited by William D. Chey, MD (University of Michigan). It is IFFGD publication #231.
</summary>

"According to research, about 90% of long-distance runners experience some form of GI symptoms (including diarrhea) during exercise and accept their symptoms as a normal consequence of running and therefore do not consult a physician."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Gastrointestinal distress: Can a low-fodmap diet help? - The Centre for Integrative Sports Nutrition ---
URL: https://intsportsnutrition.com/articles/exercise-induced-gastrointestinal-distress-can-a-low-fodmap-diet-help

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Simone do Carmo (MSci SENr CISNCert), a sports nutritionist and exercise physiologist, investigates whether a low-FODMAP diet can help alleviate exercise-induced gastrointestinal (GI) distress in athletes. The article covers the causes, prevalence, and potential nutritional strategies for GI distress, with a focus on the low-FODMAP diet as an emerging therapeutic approach.

**Key points on GI distress in athletes:**
- Prevalence ranges from 30-90% depending on methodology, study populations, and environmental conditions
- Symptoms are categorized as upper GI (heartburn, bloating, nausea) or lower GI (cramps, diarrhea, intestinal bleeding)
- Causes are physiological (ischemia from blood shunting to active muscles, reduced splanchnic blood flow, compromised gut permeability, risk of endotoxemia), mechanical (posture changes in cycling, bouncing impact in running causing intestinal bleeding), and nutritional (dehydration, high-fibre/high-fat/high-protein foods, fructose, milk, concentrated carbohydrate drinks)
- A study of 55 male triathletes in a half-Ironman race found 52% reported urge to defecate and 42% reported flatulence; all who ate 30 minutes before the race vomited during the swim leg; 93% of those who vomited consumed hypertonic drinks; all with intestinal cramps had eaten high-fibre foods
- NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI symptoms and intestinal bleeding
- Sports drinks should be below 8% carbohydrate concentration (preferably glucose and fructose combination) to prevent dehydration

**Low-FODMAP diet findings:**
- FODMAPs = Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides and Polyols, which are poorly absorbed and rapidly fermented by colonic bacteria
- The diet was initially developed for IBS patients; up to 86% of IBS patients alleviate symptoms on it

--- SOURCE 1: Ask Stacy: Should I take Anti-Diarrheal Meds Before a Race? ---
URL: https://www.triathlete.com/nutrition/ask-stacy-should-i-take-anti-diarrheal-meds-before-a-race

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an "Ask Stacy" advice column by Dr. Stacy Sims, published on Triathlete.com on August 10, 2022, addressing whether triathletes should take anti-diarrheal medications like Imodium (Loperamide) before a race to prevent GI distress.

**Core Answer:** Dr. Sims' short answer is "no," especially for racing in warm to hot conditions. Imodium is designed to slow gut motility in resting conditions but should not be used during high stress, high sweat, long-duration exercise. Key risks and drawbacks include:
- Heart rhythm disruption (QT prolongation) risk due to dehydration coupled with low blood magnesium and potassium levels.
- Reduced absorption of glucose and other nutrients from the small intestines (while increasing water/electrolyte absorption), which reduces blood glucose and the ability to regenerate glucose for race fueling.
- Potential missteps in fluid and electrolyte balance thermoregulation (sweating and blood flow) during exercise.

**Causes of GI distress during running (runner's diarrhea):**
1. Physical jostling of organs from the up-and-down motion of running.
2. Decreased blood flow to the intestines (blood is diverted to working muscles and skin).
3. Increased intestinal hormone secretion, which speeds up digestion.
4. Increased concentrated carbohydrates (gels, sports drinks) or introduction of new foods.
5. Pre-race anxiety and stress.

**Alternatives and prevention strategies instead of Imodium:**
- Try activated charcoal or attapulgite to reduce gut motility and absorb toxins/irritants.
- At least two days before the race: limit/avoid high-fiber and gas-producing foods (beans, bran, fruit, salad).
- In the 3-6 hours before racing: limit/avoid high-fat foods, caffeine (stimulates gut motility), sugar substitutes (sorbitol, sucralose, mannitol, xylitol - sugar alcohols that cause gas, bloating, and loose stools), and dairy.
- Hydrate properly (aim for very light yellow urine before racing).
- On race morning: be cautious with energy gels and high-carb sports drinks, especially untested products; never introduce new foods/supplements on race day.
- Use mindfulness and a structured pre-race routine to reduce nervousness/anxiety.
- During the race: slow down if GI distress occurs to reduce heat production and allow blood redistribution to the gut; eat bland foods (crackers, pretzels); avoid warm fluids, gels, concentrated liquid carbs, salt tablets, and caffeine.
- Imodium can be a "last resort," but athletes must adjust their fueling and hydration plans to accommodate the changes loperamide induces in the gut.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The short answer is 'no,' especially if you will be racing in warm to hot conditions. Imodium (Loperamide) is designed to slow gut motility in resting conditions, but it should not be used in high stress, high sweat, long duration exercise."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Runner's Diarrhea: Causes, Treatment, and How Long It Lasts ---
URL: https://www.healthline.com/health/diarrhea/runners-diarrhea

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Healthline, medically reviewed by Jared Meacham, PhD., RD, CSCS and written by Kathryn Watson (updated November 24, 2025), explains runner's diarrhea (also called "runner's colitis" or "runner's trots") — a condition affecting runners, particularly long-distance runners (3 miles or more), characterized by frequent bowel movements during and right after a run.

**Causes:** While not fully understood, runner's diarrhea may relate to changes in intestinal permeability during endurance exercise. A 2017 study found running at a challenging pace for 90 minutes can temporarily damage the small intestine. Research from 2023 suggests endurance exercise may decrease gastric motility, increase bacterial translocation, and alter intestinal permeability, together causing nutrient malabsorption and GI symptoms. About 30-90% of endurance runners experience exercise-induced gastrointestinal disturbances (per a 2014 review).

**Symptoms:** Diarrhea, gas, acid reflux, nausea, and cramping. Symptoms typically begin during the workout and can last up to 24 hours; anything longer may indicate another condition (infection, food intolerance, or digestive disease).

**Treatment and Prevention:** OTC options include bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto Bismol) and loperamide (Imodium), though taking them on an empty stomach may cause illness. Dietary changes are key: a 2020 survey found runners commonly avoided meat (32%), milk products (31%), fish/seafood (28%), poultry (24%), and high-fiber foods (23%). Foods/drinks to avoid before runs include fiber, fat, protein, concentrated carb beverages, caffeine, NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen), and FODMAPs. In the two hours before a run, only a quick snack like whole wheat toast or banana is advised. Avoiding tight clothing around the midsection, staying hydrated, and treating underlying conditions (lactose intolerance, IBS) can help.

**When to see a doctor:** If diarrhea regularly affects running ability, consult a primary care physician, dietitian, or sports medicine specialist. Diarrhea combined with sweating increases dehydration risk. Severe dehydration symptoms (heart palpitations, fainting, bloody/black stool, diarrhea lasting 24+ hours) require urgent medical attention.
</summary>

About 30% to 90% of endurance runners experience exercise-induced gastrointestinal disturbances, according to one 2014 review of earlier research.

--- SOURCE 3: About loperamide - NHS ---
URL: https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/loperamide/about-loperamide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides information about loperamide (brand name Imodium), a medicine used to treat diarrhoea (runny poo). It is used for short-term diarrhoea, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and recurring or longer-lasting diarrhoea from bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and short bowel syndrome. Loperamide works by slowing food passage through the gut, allowing the body to absorb more water from the intestines, resulting in firmer stools and less frequent bowel movements. It may also be prescribed for colostomy patients, sometimes in high doses to thicken stool and reduce flow.

The medicine is available over-the-counter at pharmacies and shops, and on prescription for certain bowel conditions. It comes as tablets (including dissolvable forms called Imodium Instants or Imodium Instant Melts) and capsules. It is also available combined with simeticone (to treat wind/flatulence), marketed under brand names including Imodium Plus Caplets and Imodium Plus Comfort Tablets, which helps with diarrhoea accompanied by painful stomach cramps and bloating.

Key facts include: loperamide usually starts working within 1 hour; over-the-counter use should not exceed 48 hours without consulting a doctor; taking too much can cause serious heart problems (fast or irregular heartbeat); it may cause dizziness, tiredness, or sleepiness (affecting driving or machinery use); alcohol should be avoided as it increases side effect risk; pharmacy/shop own-brand versions are usually called anti-diarrhoea or diarrhoea relief capsules/tablets; and products with "IBS" in the name are no different from other brands. The page was last reviewed on 10 April 2024, with the next review due on 10 April 2027.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Runner’s Diarrhea: Causes and Solutions | H.V.M.N. Blog – Ketone-IQ® ---
URL: https://ketone.com/blogs/blog/training-runners-diarrhea-causes-and-solutions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Ketone-IQ blog, published November 11, 2019 by Brady Holmer, examines "runner's diarrhea" (also called "runner's trots"), an exercise-induced condition characterized by frequent loose bowel movements during or immediately after running. Unlike normal diarrhea, runner's diarrhea is not typically pathological, doesn't usually cause dehydration or electrolyte imbalance, and only warrants medical attention if blood appears in the stool.

KEY STATISTICS: Runner's diarrhea affects 30-50% of runners in exhaustive endurance events; 83% of marathon runners reported GI symptoms during or after running, with 53% reporting "urge to have a bowel movement" and 38% reporting diarrhea. Triathletes reported 93% GI symptom prevalence (7% dropped out due to severity), and 43% of 67km ultra-marathon finishers reported GI distress (15% diarrhea). Runners have almost twice the risk of GI problems compared to cyclists, swimmers, and other athletes.

CAUSES (four categories):
1. GI-Related Factors: At 70% VO2 max and above, blood flow to the GI tract is reduced up to 80%, leading to hypoxia, ATP depletion, breakdown of intestinal "tight junctions," and increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"). Re-perfusion after exercise can cause further oxidative stress and inflammation ("post-run runs").
2. Mechanical Factors: Running's repetitive vertical oscillation causes organs to jostle, and braking forces during landing are twice those experienced by cyclists, which "emulsify" bowel contents.
3. Nutritional Causes: High-carb beverages (above 6-8% concentration) delay gastric emptying and cause fluid shifts; the body can only absorb 1g-1.2g of carbohydrate per minute during exercise. FODMAPs can cause excess intestinal fluid and fermentation (82.6% of athletes eliminating at least one FODMAP group reported improvement). Fiber, fats, and protein before exercise delay gastric emptying and can draw water into the intestine.
4. Psychological Factors: Higher stress and anxiety levels are associated with GI symptoms; psychological stress induces small intestine permeability.

PREVENTION STRATEGIES:
- Use beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose + fructose or maltodextrin + fructose) at 6-8% concentration for optimal absorption; sodium aids glucose uptake via GLUT5 transporters.
- Avoid high-fiber, high-fat, or high-protein foods and certain artificial sweeteners up to three hours before exercise; consider a "low-residue" diet in days before events.
- Maintain proper hydration (dehydration of just 2.7% of body mass impairs water flux and increases GI symptoms), but avoid over-hydration (hyponatremia also causes GI issues).
- "Gut training": practice drinking fluids and carb-based drinks during exercise; about three days of training helps the stomach adapt to larger volumes. Runners consuming a glucose + fructose beverage during runs for two weeks improved GI symptoms and performance by just over 5% during a three-hour run challenge.
- Improved fitness improves gut function—trained athletes have greater intestinal blood flow and better gut barrier function.
- For keto/low-carb athletes: periodized carbohydrate intake can improve tolerance; some use MCTs or exogenous ketones (BHB) instead, but should practice with these during training.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: Find personal tolerance; avoid new foods on race day; urinate and have a bowel movement before exercise (may help to use a mild laxative the night before); know rest stop locations and carry toilet paper. The article concludes that nutritional strategies and gut training can help runners avoid and prevent most symptoms of runner's diarrhea.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In contrast to normal diarrhea, runner's diarrhea is exercise-induced, meaning it occurs in response to physical activity."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: How to get through a race without pooping yourself - Race Smart ---
URL: https://www.racesmart.com/article/how-to-get-through-a-race-without-pooping-yourself

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Race Smart (a sports nutrition and triathlon coaching site) provides a comprehensive guide to preventing gastrointestinal (GI) distress—commonly called "runner's trot"—during endurance races. The content addresses causes, prevention strategies, and training approaches.

**Causes of GI distress:** Symptoms originate from upper (belching, nausea, heartburn, bloating) and lower intestines (cramping, gas, diarrhea, urgency). Running causes the most issues due to jarring that moves food through the GI tract faster while blood is shunted away from intestines toward working muscles. Athletes with pre-existing conditions (reflux, lactose intolerance, IBD, IBS) are more susceptible. Swallowing air in the swim and bike posture pressure also contribute.

**Pre-race nutritional strategies (1–3 days out):** Reduce high-fiber foods (cruciferous vegetables, brown rice, high-fiber cereals); avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen; avoid dairy if lactose intolerant; avoid high-fructose foods (soda, juice, candy, dried fruit); avoid sugar alcohols/artificial sweeteners (sorbitol, aspartame) which pull water into intestines; reduce fat intake 12–24 hours before racing; gluten only matters for those with Celiac disease; monitor caffeine intake. Keep a food and bowel journal since food takes 24–72 hours to transit the gut.

**Training and race-day strategies:** Train the gut to process race fuel at race-day intensity, temperature, and humidity. Establish and test a fuel/hydration plan months in advance. Eat pre-race breakfast at least 2.5 hours before start. Create a race-morning routine to manage nerves; consider a short shakeout run hours before the race. Don't limit carbs—low-carb athletes have reduced carb absorption ability. Sports nutritionist Asker Jeukendrup recommends mixing sugar types and increasing carb volume during training, which can raise carbohydrate absorption by over 30% in less than two weeks (relevant to the 50% of triathletes who experience stomach problems). Avoid dehydration (keep weight loss under 4%). Avoid sports drinks with >8% carbohydrate concentration and gels without adequate water. "Sip early and often." Don't go too hard too early out of T1. Cooling strategies (cold drinks, ice, sprinklers, heat acclimation) may help in hot conditions.

**Last-ditch options:** Anti-diarrhea drugs like Imodium or Kaopectate are supported by medical experts for a single dose about an hour before a major race (unless bloody diarrhea), but shouldn't be a daily fix. Nutritional supplements (glutamine, arginine, L-citrulline, antioxidants, curcumin, nitrate, bovine colostrum, ginger) lack scientific justification for preventing gut issues.

**Core message:** There are no shortcuts—prepare and train the gut with a dialed-in fuel-hydration plan of easy-to-digest carbs and well-formulated sports drinks 6–8 weeks before race day, testing it repeatedly in training.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The inherent jarring nature of running jostles the stomach and colon more than in any other sport. This mechanical stress causes food and waste to move through the GI tract more rapidly, all the while blood is being shunted away from the intestines toward the working muscles, reducing functionality of the GI tract."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis (published June 14, 2024, in NEJM Evidence, DOI: 10.1056/EVIDoa2400134) examining the efficacy and safety of proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) for stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients. The review included 12 randomized trials enrolling 9,533 ICU patients, published between 1993 and 2024.

METHODS: The review compared PPIs versus placebo or no prophylaxis in critically ill adults, using random-effects meta-analyses, GRADE assessment for certainty of evidence, and ICEMAN criteria for subgroup analysis credibility. Within-trial subgroup data from the two largest trials (REVISE and SUP-ICU, together 7,802 patients) were combined to explore mortality effects based on disease severity.

KEY RESULTS:
- Clinically important upper GI bleeding: RR 0.51 (95% CI, 0.34–0.76), high certainty evidence — PPIs reduced bleeding risk (18 fewer per 1000 patients)
- Patient-important upper GI bleeding: HR 0.36 (95% CI, 0.25–0.53), high certainty (from one trial)
- Overt upper GI bleeding: RR 0.52 (95% CI, 0.38–0.70), high certainty
- Mortality: RR 0.99 (95% CI, 0.93–1.05), low certainty — PPIs may have little or no effect on overall mortality
- Subgroup analysis (intermediate credibility): PPIs may decrease 90-day mortality in less severely ill patients (RR 0.89; 95% CI, 0.80–0.98) but may increase mortality in more severely ill patients (RR 1.08; 95% CI, 0.96–1.20)
- Pneumonia: RR 1.00 (95% CI, 0.92–1.09), low certainty — no effect
- C. difficile infection: RR 1.20 (95% CI, 0.66–2.16), low certainty — little or no effect
- No significant effects on duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, hospital stay, or red blood cell transfusions

CONCLUSIONS: High certainty evidence supports PPIs reducing upper GI bleeding in critically ill patients. PPIs likely have little or no effect on overall mortality, but subgroup analysis with intermediate credibility suggests potential mortality reduction in less severely ill patients and potential mortality increase in more severely ill patients. The mechanisms behind this possible signal are unclear and likely multifactorial (including microbiome alterations, delirium, and effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase, inflammation, and thrombosis). The review incorporated the recent REVISE trial, which more than doubled the trial evidence on this topic. Limitations include diverse definitions of bleeding and pneumonia, low event rates for bleeding and C. difficile infection, patient-important GI bleeding available in only one trial, and inability to examine illness severity as a continuous variable without individual patient data. PROSPERO registration: CRD42023461695.
</summary>

"High certainty evidence supports the association of proton-pump inhibitors with decreased upper gastrointestinal bleeding. --- SOURCE 8: Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete ---
URL: https://musculoskeletalkey.com/gastrointestinal-medicine-in-the-athlete

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete

This chapter from the Musculoskeletal Key website (DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) addresses common gastrointestinal (GI) conditions in athletes and active persons, focusing on recognition and management. GI conditions are common in athletes, with exercise placing significant stress on the GI tract, resulting in characteristic disorders that can impair athletic performance.

### Key Points:

**General Pathophysiology:**
- 20–50% of high-performance athletes report undesirable GI symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea)
- Symptoms are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes
- Cyclists appear somewhat protected from GI issues due to forward positioning, while runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling
- Increased catecholamines and GI peptides (gastrin, motilin, secretin, etc.) increase gut transit time, negatively affecting GI homeostasis

**GI Tract Ischemia:**
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction
- Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation
- Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa" (per ter Steege et al.)
- Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms

**Upper GI Conditions:**
- Upper GI complaints affect 30–70% of athletes
- Three primary mechanisms: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes
- GERD is the most common cause of upper GI symptoms in athletes
- Exercise ≥90% VO2 max increases frequency/duration of esophageal reflux episodes
- Weightlifters have the highest rate of heartburn and reflux; runners have a threefold increase in GERD when running 45 minutes after a meal

**GERD Management:**
- Lifestyle modifications first-line: sleeping on two pillows, avoiding lying down within 4 hours of evening meal, avoiding postprandial exercise, limiting foods that relax the LES (high-fat foods, coffee, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods)
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training
- Pharmacologic therapy: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective
- H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers
- Upper endoscopy for diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended

**Other Conditions:**
- **Functional heartburn:** Up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset; treatment is biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, prokinetics
- **Dyspepsia:** Caused by GERD, gastritis, or peptic ulcer disease; ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms; PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence
- **Aspirin/NSAIDs:** Block cyclooxygenase and protective prostaglandins; add daily PPI for GI protection in athletes requiring NSAIDs with ulcer history
- **Pill esophagitis:** NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and mefloquine are highest risk; take with food/fluid in morning and remain upright
- **Dysphagia:** Divided into oropharyngeal and esophageal subtypes; most commonly caused by irritative effects of GERD
- **Nausea/Vomiting:** Linked to postprandial exercise; avoid solid food within 3 hours of events; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events; H2 blockers and PPIs can help

**GERD-Asthma Connection:**
- Up to 90% of persons with asthma have GERD; up to 40% have esophagitis
- Treatment only benefits asthma in patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms
- Atypical GERD presentations include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, and chest pain
</summary>

--- SOURCE 15: The Influence of NSAIDs on Physiologic Processes and Exercise ---
URL: https://www.physio-pedia.com/The_Influence_of_NSAIDs_on_Physiologic_Processes_and_Exercise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Physiopedia article examines the influence of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) on physiologic processes and exercise, written by contributors from the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center Exercise Science Project. The article emphasizes that physical therapists must understand NSAID effects because many patients use these drugs for pain relief, potentially before therapy sessions.

Key points include:

**Mechanism:** NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, reducing prostaglandin formation. While this reduces pain and inflammation, it can hamper gastrointestinal functions and post-exercise protein synthesis.

**Muscular Effects:** Effects differ by age and acute vs. chronic use. Short-term NSAID use is beneficial for recovery from muscle soreness, but long-term use can lead to GI complications, renal failure, liver failure, and heart failure. Interestingly, recent studies found older adults (ages 60-85) who consume NSAIDs experience GREATER muscle strength gains and hypertrophy from resistance training than non-users—contrary to initial researcher expectations. Mechanisms include reduced IL-6 and MuRF-1 (reducing muscle loss) and PGF2a receptor upregulation. The FDA recommends regular NSAID use exceeding ten consecutive days be accompanied by a healthcare provider consultation. Notably, there is no safe dosage/duration of NSAIDs for patients with existing cardiovascular disease.

**Timing of Use:** Pre-exercise NSAID administration may reduce creatine kinase circulating after exercise (indicating less muscle damage), but ibuprofen did not reduce the impact of muscle damage and pain on aerobic performance. Frequent preemptive use could mask underlying injury pain.

**Skeletal Effects:** A randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study of 95 healthy premenopausal women (ages 21-40) over 9 months found that taking 400 mg of ibuprofen immediately AFTER exercise augmented beneficial adaptations of bone mineral density (BMD), showing the largest BMD increase compared to other groups. This was the first human study on this topic.

**Cardiovascular Effects:** Chronic NSAID use in individuals with hypertension and coronary artery disease can cause stroke and myocardial infarction.

**Gastrointestinal Effects:** Daily long-term use, even at low doses, negatively affects the GI tract by blocking prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing gastric mucosal defense.

**Renal Effects:** Ibuprofen and acetaminophen inhibit the kidneys' ability to absorb water and salt, leading to rapid dehydration. Fluid intake and excretion should be monitored during exercise.

**Pulmonary Effects:** Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) combines asthma, nasal polyps, and sensitivity to aspirin/COX-1 inhibitor NSAIDs. Symptoms include coughing, chest tightness, difficulty breathing, and dizziness—important considerations for physical therapists monitoring exercise intensity.

**Implications for Physical Therapy:** Therapists should inquire whether patients are taking NSAIDs to provide insight on proper and safe use, and should understand effects across body systems.

The article is categorized under Pharmacology, Exercise Therapy, and Physiology.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Review of small bowel capsule endoscopy for diagnosis of gastrointestinal bleeding ---
URL: https://www.ijgii.org/journal/view.html?volume=14&number=3&spage=108

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in the International Journal of Gastrointestinal Intervention (Int J Gastrointest Interv 2025; 14(3): 108-112, published online July 31, 2025, DOI: 10.18528/ijgii250037) by Dong Jun Oh from the Department of Internal Medicine, Dongguk University Ilsan Hospital, Goyang, Korea. The article reviews the role of small bowel capsule endoscopy (CE) in the diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.

Key content:
- CE, introduced in 2001 and FDA-approved, is now the first-line test for small bowel (SB) bleeding (which accounts for 5-10% of GI bleeding), with a diagnostic yield of approximately 60%.
- CE shows superior diagnostic yield versus traditional modalities: 63% vs 28% for SB barium radiography, and 67% vs 8% for push enteroscopy.
- The capsule is approximately 26mm long, 11mm in diameter, weighs ~4g, captures 2-6 frames per second, with 8-12 hours of battery life; it requires no sedation.
- Guidelines recommend CE within 48 hours of overt SB bleeding for maximal yield; within 48 hours yield is 81-92%, within 14 days ~60-75%, occult bleeding 35-46%, previous overt bleeding ~13-25%.
- Common SB bleeding etiologies include angiodysplasias (most common, 30-50%, typically in older patients), ulcers/erosions, and tumors (adenocarcinoma, GIST); less common: SB varices, Peutz-Jeghers polyps, Dieulafoy lesions, intestinal parasites.
- For upper GI bleeding (UGIB), CE showed comparable accuracy to esophagogastroduodenoscopy, with sensitivity 88% for bleeding detection; CE-based triage in the emergency department reduced admission rates from 100% to ~19% while maintaining clinical outcomes. Magnetically controlled CE (MCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.8% for UGIB.
- For lower GI bleeding (LGIB), pan-enteric CE (PCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.7% vs 50.0% for colonoscopy in one study; another showed PCE diagnostic yield of 83.3%.
- Future directions include improved battery life and imaging (PillCam SB3 with ~30% improved resolution, adaptive frame rate up to 6 fps, 12-hour battery; MiroCam MC2000 with 340° viewing angle; MiroCam MC4000 with 320×320 resolution), AI-assisted reading (a multicenter study showed 73.7% vs 62.4% diagnostic yield and reading time reduction from 33.7 to 3.8 minutes; TOP100 tool achieved 92.8% accuracy; AI bleeding detection accuracy exceeds 90%), and active maneuverability via magnetic control (sensitivity 87% for gastric lesions; reduced gastric transit time from 84.5 to 22.2 minutes; 100% SB completion rate).
- The article concludes that a "mouth-to-anus" capsule examining the entire GI tract in a single noninvasive examination is a realistic future goal.

Funding: None. No conflicts of interest. Data available from corresponding author upon reasonable request. The article is open-access under CC BY-NC 4.0.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Capsule endoscopy (CE), introduced in 2001, is now a key tool for evaluating small-bowel bleeding, which accounts for 5% to 10% of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding."
