--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | Small Bowel Gastrointestinal Bleeding Diagnosis and Management—A Narrative Review ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/surgery/articles/10.3389/fsurg.2019.00025/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review article published in Frontiers in Surgery (Volume 6, 2019) by B. Murphy, D.C. Winter, and D.O. Kavanagh from University Hospital Tallaght and St. Vincent's University Hospital in Dublin, Ireland, examining the diagnosis and management of small bowel gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.

**Key Points:**

**Background & Epidemiology:**
- Small bowel bleeding accounts for 5-10% of all gastrointestinal bleeding
- Defined as bleeding distal to the ampulla of Vater and proximal to the ileocaecal valve
- Distinguishes between overt bleeding (malaena, hematochezia, hematemesis) and occult bleeding (iron deficiency anemia with/without positive fecal occult blood test)

**Aetiology:**
- Causes categorized as vascular, inflammatory, iatrogenic, diverticular, or tumoral
- Most common causes include angiodysplasia (~40% of bleeding cases), ulcers/erosions (up to 30%), Dieulafoy lesions and varices (up to 20%), and tumors (≤5%)
- Age matters: angiodysplasia, malignancy, and ulcers more common in older patients; IBD, Dieulafoy lesions, and Meckel's diverticulum more likely in younger patients

**Diagnostic Approaches:**
- 15-20% of patients have missed upper/lower GI sources on initial endoscopy; repeat endoscopy is recommended (diagnostic yield up to 29% for OGD, 6% for colonoscopy)
- CT angiography: detects bleeding at rates of 0.5-1.0 mL/min; pooled sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 85% in a meta-analysis of 9 studies
- CT enterography: pooled diagnostic yield of 40% (meta-analysis of 18 studies) versus 53% for capsule endoscopy
- Red cell scintigraphy: detects bleeding rates as low as 0.1 mL/min; positive yield ~50%; ASCRS advocates it as first-line diagnostic scan
- Angiography: diagnostic yield 27-77% overall, 61-72% in overt bleeding, <20% in occult; up to 99% technical success with superselective embolization
- Video capsule endoscopy: diagnostic yield of 62% vs 56% for double balloon enteroscopy; highest yield (87%) in overt bleeding within 48 hours; complication rate 1-3%
- Double balloon enteroscopy: allows therapeutic interventions for up to 27% of patients; complications include perforation (1%), pancreatitis (2-8%)

**Treatment:**
- Medical: iron supplementation, blood transfusion, somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide) reduce transfusion rates in angiodysplasia; thalidomide showed 71.4% response rate vs 3.7% for iron in refractory bleeding (RCT by Ge et al.); tranexamic acid reduces transfusion probability by up to 33%
- Interventional: embolization success rates 60-90%; argon plasma coagulation for angiodysplasia with high rebleeding rates (45% in meta-analysis of 623 patients)
- Surgical: intraoperative endoscopy has diagnostic yield of 58-99% and therapeutic yield of 48-94%; recommended when other modalities fail or for lesions requiring resection (Meckel's diverticulum, masses)
- Future: implantable wireless biosensors being explored for real-time bleeding detection

**Conclusions:**
- No single unifying diagnostic modality exists; approach should differentiate between overt and occult bleeding
- Always consider repeat upper ± lower GI endoscopy first
- Somatostatin analogs and thalidomide may reduce rebleeding risk
- Treatment algorithms for both overt and occult bleeding are proposed (Figures 1 and 2)
</summary>

As the capsule travels through the digestive tract, it captures about 10,000 pictures that healthcare providers review for bleeding, polyps, tumors, and inflammation. The capsule is naturally passed in stool, usually within 24 hours, and can be flushed down the toilet.

If there's uncertainty about whether the capsule passed, an X-ray or CT scan may be needed, as a retained capsule can cause a serious bowel obstruction. The capsule's main advantage is that it's one of the only tests that allows providers to examine the entire small intestine, since traditional tube-based endoscopy cannot reach all areas. --- SOURCE 6: Pros and Cons of Breath Testing for Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth - Gastroenterology & Hepatology ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyandhepatology.net/archives/march-2023/pros-and-cons-of-breath-testing-for-small-intestinal-bacterial-overgrowth-and-intestinal-methanogen-overgrowth

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Gastroenterology & Hepatology (March 2023, Volume 19, Issue 3), reviews the pros and cons of breath testing for diagnosing small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO). Authored by Jane Lim, MD, MS, and Ali Rezaie, MD, MSc, from the GI Motility Program at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, the article covers the following key points:

**Overview of SIBO and IMO:**
- SIBO involves excessive coliform bacteria in the small intestine, causing bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and constipation.
- IMO is a separate entity involving excessive methanogens (archaea) in the small and/or large intestine, causing bloating, gas, abdominal discomfort, and constipation.
- Breath testing is the most widely used diagnostic modality; IMO can ONLY be diagnosed via breath testing in clinical practice.

**SIBO Diagnosis Methods:**
- Small bowel aspiration via endoscopy (threshold: >10³ colony-forming units of coliforms/mL) is direct but invasive, costly, and has a 19.6% contamination rate (per Cangemi study).
- Breath testing detects hydrogen (from bacterial fermentation) and methane (from archaea). Per the North American Consensus, a positive SIBO result requires a rise of ≥20 ppm hydrogen above baseline by 90 minutes. A recent study proposed a cutoff of >12 ppm as more sensitive for glucose breath testing.
- Glucose and lactulose are the two main substrates. Lactulose samples the entire small intestine but has lower specificity (70.6% vs 83.2% for glucose); glucose is more specific but may miss distal SIBO. Meta-analysis: lactulose sensitivity 42%, specificity 70.6%; glucose sensitivity 54.5%, specificity 83.2%.

**Pros of Breath Testing:**
- Safe, simple, noninvasive, widely available, can be administered at home.
- Distinguishes hydrogen-predominant SIBO (responds to rifaximin) from IMO (responds better to combination rifaximin/neomycin).
- Hydrogen breath levels correlate with specific bacterial classes per 16S rRNA sequencing.

**Cons of Breath Testing:**
- Variability of orocecal transit time (OCTT) can cause false positives from colonic fermentation.
- A scintigraphy study found 88% of positive lactulose breath tests had substrate in the cecum before positive results, though this was disputed because 5% of the substrate (~0.5g) is insufficient to cause significant hydrogen rise quickly.
- False positives more common in patients with history of upper GI surgery (20 of 22 false-positive patients in the Lin and Massey study had prior upper GI surgery).
- False negatives can occur with achalasia, gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction, enterocutaneous fistula, delayed OCTT, or when methane-producing organisms consume hydrogen.

**IMO Diagnosis and Treatment:**
- Per North American Consensus, methane ≥10 ppm at any point during breath testing is diagnostic for IMO.
- IMO is not affected by OCTT; methane slows intestinal transit and is associated with constipation.
- Methane producers are more likely to be older and have lower rates of vitamin B12 deficiency or diarrhea than hydrogen-predominant SIBO patients (N=1461 study).
- IMO responds better to rifaximin/neomycin combination (85% clinical response, 87% methane eradication) vs rifaximin alone (56% response, 29% eradication).
- A fasting single methane measurement (SMM) of ≥10 ppm has 86.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing IMO and can monitor treatment response (significant decrease starting at 2 days post-antibiotic therapy).

**Emerging Breath Test Patterns:**
1. **Flat-line pattern**: No methane and low fixed hydrogen (≤3 ppm, no rise >1 ppm above baseline). More common in inflammatory bowel disease. 56% of patients with this pattern respond to antibiotics (58% to rifaximin, 47% to rifaximin/neomycin). May indicate excess hydrogenotrophic bacteria producing hydrogen sulfide.
2. **High baseline hydrogen pattern**: Baseline hydrogen >20 ppm without excessive methane. Found in 0.7% of 14,847 lactulose breath tests. 52% responded to any antibiotics; 73% responded to rifaximin alone, but only 25% responded to rifaximin/neomycin combination.

**Conclusion:** Breath testing offers rapid, safe, noninvasive diagnosis of SIBO and IMO, helps tailor antibiotic therapy, and can predict and monitor treatment response. Newer technologies such as intraluminal gas sampling and next-generation sequencing may provide greater diagnostic accuracy in the future.

**Disclosures:** Dr Rezaie is a consultant/speaker for Bausch Health, holds equity in Gemelli Biotech, and Cedars-Sinai has licensing agreements with Gemelli Biotech. Dr Lim has no relevant conflicts of interest.
</summary>

This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The authors are Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Sapienza University of Rome, Italy), and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan, Italy). The article was submitted 26 July 2023, revised 30 August 2023, accepted 12 September 2023, and published 19 September 2023. It has 26 citations and an Altmetric score of 31.

**Key content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a condition affecting up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports (marathon, triathlon, cycling, running, etc.) caused by strenuous exercise. Symptoms include upper GI issues (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower GI issues (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two main pathways are described:
1. Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway: Sympathetic activation alters the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic blood flow can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing gut hypoperfusion, ischemic damage, loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP. 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study.

**GI symptoms during exercise:** 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms. In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors.

**IBS overlap:** Ex-GIS shares pathogenesis with IBS (alterations in gut microbiota, permeability, immune function, motility, visceral sensation, brain-gut interactions). IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed.

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms).

**Management:** The review emphasizes nutritional and behavioral strategies, particularly examining gluten-free diets and low-FODMAP (fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols) diets as the principal interventions to avoid symptoms during exercise. Exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet should all be evaluated.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023, yielding 142 relevant research articles published between 1965 and 2023.
</summary>

"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."

--- SOURCE 14: Training The Gut For Athletes ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/training-the-gut-for-athletes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #178 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published January 2018, authored by Asker Jeukendrup, PhD. The article examines "Training the Gut for Athletes" — the concept that the gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be trained and adapted to improve nutrient and fluid delivery during endurance exercise while reducing GI distress.

KEY POINTS:
- The GI tract is critical for delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and is a major determinant of endurance performance.
- GI problems affect 30-50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports.
- The GI tract is highly adaptable and responds to nutritional training in a nutrient-specific way.

GASTRIC EMPTYING: The stomach is the first barrier for delivering nutrients. Studies show that repeated practice of high fluid intakes during running improved stomach comfort over time (Lambert et al., 2008), though without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate. Dietary manipulation studies (Cunningham et al., 1991; Horowitz et al., 1996; Yau et al., 2014) demonstrated that supplementing with specific carbohydrates (glucose or fructose) accelerated gastric emptying of those same sugars specifically, with effects seen after as little as 3 days.

INTESTINAL SUGAR TRANSPORT: Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent SGLT1 transporter, while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are the most important transporters for carbohydrate absorption. At ingestion rates over 60-70 g of carbohydrate/hour, exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks at ~60 g/hour because SGLT1 becomes saturated. Combining glucose and fructose (using different transporters) can achieve higher oxidation rates.

TRANSPORTER REGULATION AND ADAPTATION: SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. A glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies show rapid adaptation: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses showed increases after just one week; piglets showed increases after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks.

HUMAN EVIDENCE: The landmark Cox et al. (2010) study divided 16 endurance-trained cyclists into high-carbohydrate and control groups. Over 28 days of training (16 h/week), the high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate versus 5.3 g/kg/day in controls. Post-training, the high-carb group showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, most likely due to upregulated SGLT1 transporters. Conversely, carbohydrate restriction, high-fat/ketogenic diets, or energy reduction may reduce absorptive capacity and potentially increase GI problems.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) Train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks. (2) Practice race nutritional strategies in training to adapt to higher volumes and carbohydrate intakes. (3) For exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate is recommended; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures). (4) Athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days to maintain gut absorptive capacity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The gastrointestinal (GI) tract plays a critical role in delivering carbohydrate and fluid to the blood during prolonged exercise, and can therefore be a major determinant of performance."

--- SOURCE 15: Gut Training: Fix 90% of Runner GI Issues (Science Guide) ---
URL: https://runnersconnect.net/gut-training-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Jeff Gaudette (MS, Johns Hopkins University; co-founder of RunnersConnect and former Olympic Trials qualifier) is a comprehensive science-based guide on "gut training" for endurance athletes. It addresses the fact that nearly 90% of endurance athletes experience gastrointestinal distress during competition, and argues that the digestive system needs training just as much as the cardiovascular system.

**Key physiological mechanisms behind exercise-induced GI distress:**
- Blood flow diversion: Blood flow to the gut decreases 20% within 10 minutes of running and by 80% after 1 hour at 70% VO2max, impairing digestion and accelerating food movement through the intestines (leading to cramping and diarrhea).
- Heat stress: Heat diverts further blood away from digestion, compounding problems with increased duration and temperature.
- Mechanical trauma: Repetitive foot strike shock waves can damage the intestinal lining, increasing permeability ("leaky gut").
- Absorption bottleneck: The small intestine max absorption is ~60g glucose/hour, rising to 90g/hour with glucose-fructose combinations; exceeding this causes osmotic overload, bloating, cramping, and diarrhea.

**16-Week Progressive Gut Training Protocol:**
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1-4) Foundation Building: 30-40g carbs/hour during easy runs >90 min, using single-source carbs (glucose or maltodextrin) and planned race-day products.
- Phase 2 (Weeks 5-8) Volume Progression: Increase to 50-60g carbs/hour, introduce dual-source carbs (glucose + fructose) to upregulate SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters, fuel every 15-20 minutes.
- Phase 3 (Weeks 9-12) Intensity Integration: Fuel during tempo/marathon-pace runs, target 60-70g carbs/hour at higher intensity.
- Phase 4 (Weeks 13-16) Race Simulation: Full dress rehearsals, 70-90g carbs/hour for 2.5+ hour runs, practice complete race-day nutrition.

**Product Testing Framework:** Elimination protocol (start with simplest single-ingredient products), A/B testing (change one variable at a time), concentration testing (start with 6-8% carb solutions; highly concentrated solutions can impair gastric emptying), and environmental stress testing (heat can reduce gastric emptying by up to 50%).

**Evidence-based supplemental strategies:**
1. Probiotics: Two standout strains—Bifidobacteria (reduces GI symptoms in marathon runners, improves carb absorption/metabolism, potentially sparing muscle glycogen) and ProbioSEB Duo (survives heat conditions, unlike most probiotics, so it can be used during running).
2. Psyllium seed husks: Less fermentable than similar fibers, reduces flatulence/stomach pain/nausea; taking in evening helps runners evacuate before morning runs and adds stool bulk to reduce bathroom urgency from running jostling.
3. Blackcurrant extract (anthocyanins): Protects/strengthens gut lining; 7-day supplementation before racing in heat reduced heat-induced cell damage and "leaky gut" by 40%, reduced total gastric distress symptoms in runners by 73%, increased fat reliance for energy, and improved 5k performance by 38 seconds vs placebo.

The article concludes that the gut is trainable and responsive to progressive training like any other body system, noting even four weeks of consistent practice can improve digestive performance. It also promotes MAS Flush (a probiotic from MAS Edge, a partner of Runner's Connect, specifically designed for endurance athletes addressing runner's trots).
</summary>

In a separate study, blackcurrant was shown to reduce total gastric distress symptoms in runners by 73%."

--- SOURCE 1: Gastrointestinal bleeding in athletes ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10152804

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed review article titled "Gastrointestinal bleeding in athletes" published in Annals of Gastroenterology (Ann Gastroenterol) on April 4, 2023 (DOI: 10.20524/aog.2023.0788), with PMCID: PMC10152804 and PMID: 37144023. The authors are Konstantinos Papantoniou, Christos Michailides, and Maria Bali (Department of Internal Medicine, General University Hospital of Patras, Greece), Panagiotis Papantoniou (Private Gastroenterologist, Tripolis, Greece), and Konstantinos Thomopoulos (Department of Gastroenterology, General University Hospital of Patras, Greece). The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 License.

**Key Findings:**

**Incidence of GIB in Athletes:**
- Up to 70% of athletes experience GI symptoms, which are the most common cause of underperformance in endurance events.
- Runners are more frequently affected than cyclists or other athletes.
- Based on FOB (fecal occult blood) testing: 74 of 404 long-distance runners (19.6%) switched from negative to positive after a race; 4 of 60 cyclists (6.7%); 1 of 11 rugby players (9%); and 58 of 75 triathletes/ultra-marathoners (77%)—the highest incidence in ultra-endurance events.
- Endoscopy studies on runners revealed gastric erosions, esophagitis, gastritis with blood clots, and colon erosions at the splenic flexure.

**Pathophysiology (three main mechanisms):**
1. **Splanchnic hypoperfusion:** At rest, 25% of cardiac output goes to splanchnic organs. During exercise, sympathetic nervous system activation causes vasoconstriction reducing splanchnic blood flow by up to 80%. This leads to ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), mucosal damage, and increased intestinal permeability. The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) and recto-sigmoid (Sudeck's point) are most vulnerable due to inadequate vessel anastomosis. The colon has less blood supply per gram than the small bowel.
2. **Mechanical trauma:** Impact-related injury is greater in running than cycling, potentially causing hemorrhagic gastritis and "cecal slap syndrome" (slapping of the posterior cecal wall against the anterior wall).
3. **NSAID use:** NSAIDs are frequently used by athletes and are associated with a 3-fold higher risk of serious adverse GI events including GIB. They work by inhibiting COX-1 (reducing protective prostaglandins) and COX-2. Ibuprofen was shown to aggravate exercise-induced small intestinal injury.

**Prevention measures:**
- No specific guidelines currently exist for GIB prevention in athletes.
- Lowering exercise intensity when warning symptoms (cramping, diarrhea, nausea) appear; avoid high-intensity training in extreme heat.
- H2-receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) show promising results as short-course treatment before prolonged exercise, though not yet generally recommended.
- Discourage regular NSAID use, especially pre-race.
- Arginine, glutamine, citrulline, nitrite, and nitrate (nitric oxide availability enhancers) improve splanchnic perfusion but may cause nausea and diarrhea.
- Individualized fluid replacement to maintain hydration; avoid high-osmolality carbohydrate solutions.
- "Gut training" through gradual increases in exercise intensity and experimenting with pre-event nutrition strategies.

**Management:**
- GIB should NOT be immediately attributed to endurance exercise; endoscopy (upper and lower) should always be performed to rule out other causes (IBD, neoplasia, esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss tears, peptic ulcers, coagulopathies, hemorrhoids, fissures, diverticulosis, vascular ectasias, vasculitis).
- Overt bleeding: cease activity immediately, seek medical care, assess hemodynamic stability, IV crystalloids/transfusions for severe cases, PPIs for ulcers/gastritis, vasoactive drugs (somatostatin/octreotide) for suspected varices, emergency endoscopy or radiographic interventions for hemostasis, surgery in rare cases.
- Occult bleeding: endoscopy recommended in all athletes, especially those with anemia; iron supplementation for low ferritin; PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists effective for exercise-induced gastritis; stool softeners for fissures/hemorrhoids; repeat endoscopy if persistent GIB with negative initial findings.

**Concluding remarks:** GIB is a serious manifestation of GI distress in athletes. Larger-scale studies are needed to better understand frequency, pathophysiology, and prevention. Specific guidelines for treatment would improve care, especially for overt GIB.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding (GIB) in athletes has previously been reported in several studies, as an important factor of underperformance in competitive sports events. Yet it is still underreported, partly because it is usually occult and self-limited soon after the effort."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Review of small bowel capsule endoscopy for diagnosis of ... ---
URL: https://www.ijgii.org/journal/view.html?volume=14&number=3&spage=108

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in the International Journal of Gastrointestinal Intervention (Int J Gastrointest Interv 2025; 14(3): 108-112, published online July 31, 2025, DOI: 10.18528/ijgii250037) by Dong Jun Oh from the Department of Internal Medicine, Dongguk University Ilsan Hospital, Goyang, Korea. The article reviews the role of small bowel capsule endoscopy (CE) in the diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.

Key content:
- CE, introduced in 2001 and FDA-approved, is now the first-line test for small bowel (SB) bleeding (which accounts for 5-10% of GI bleeding), with a diagnostic yield of approximately 60%.
- CE shows superior diagnostic yield versus traditional modalities: 63% vs 28% for SB barium radiography, and 67% vs 8% for push enteroscopy.
- The capsule is approximately 26mm long, 11mm in diameter, weighs ~4g, captures 2-6 frames per second, with 8-12 hours of battery life; it requires no sedation.
- Guidelines recommend CE within 48 hours of overt SB bleeding for maximal yield; within 48 hours yield is 81-92%, within 14 days ~60-75%, occult bleeding 35-46%, previous overt bleeding ~13-25%.
- Common SB bleeding etiologies include angiodysplasias (most common, 30-50%, typically in older patients), ulcers/erosions, and tumors (adenocarcinoma, GIST); less common: SB varices, Peutz-Jeghers polyps, Dieulafoy lesions, intestinal parasites.
- For upper GI bleeding (UGIB), CE showed comparable accuracy to esophagogastroduodenoscopy, with sensitivity 88% for bleeding detection; CE-based triage in the emergency department reduced admission rates from 100% to ~19% while maintaining clinical outcomes. Magnetically controlled CE (MCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.8% for UGIB.
- For lower GI bleeding (LGIB), pan-enteric CE (PCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.7% vs 50.0% for colonoscopy in one study; another showed PCE diagnostic yield of 83.3%.
- Future directions include improved battery life and imaging (PillCam SB3 with ~30% improved resolution, adaptive frame rate up to 6 fps, 12-hour battery; MiroCam MC2000 with 340° viewing angle; MiroCam MC4000 with 320×320 resolution), AI-assisted reading (a multicenter study showed 73.7% vs 62.4% diagnostic yield and reading time reduction from 33.7 to 3.8 minutes; TOP100 tool achieved 92.8% accuracy; AI bleeding detection accuracy exceeds 90%), and active maneuverability via magnetic control (sensitivity 87% for gastric lesions; reduced gastric transit time from 84.5 to 22.2 minutes; 100% SB completion rate).
- The article concludes that a "mouth-to-anus" capsule examining the entire GI tract in a single noninvasive examination is a realistic future goal.

Funding: None. No conflicts of interest. Data available from corresponding author upon reasonable request. The article is open-access under CC BY-NC 4.0.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Capsule endoscopy (CE), introduced in 2001, is now a key tool for evaluating small-bowel bleeding, which accounts for 5% to 10% of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Evidence-Based Guide on Capsule Endoscopy for Small Bowel Bleeding - Gastroenterology & Hepatology ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyandhepatology.net/archives/february-2017/evidence-based-guide-on-capsule-endoscopy-for-small-bowel-bleeding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Gastroenterology & Hepatology (February 2017, Volume 13, Issue 2), is an evidence-based guide on capsule endoscopy for small bowel bleeding, authored by Dr. Shabana F. Pasha and Dr. Jonathan A. Leighton of the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona.

KEY POINTS:

**Background & Indications:**
- Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for overt and occult small bowel bleeding, accounting for ~5% of all GI bleeding and being the most common indication for capsule endoscopy worldwide.
- Three FDA-approved capsule endoscopy systems exist: PillCam SB (Medtronic), Endocapsule (Olympus), and MiroCam (IntroMedic).
- In a systematic review of 227 studies, 66% of capsules were used for small bowel bleeding with a pooled detection rate of 59.4%. Diagnostic yield was 66.6% in a review of 1960 IDA patients and 35% in a single-center cohort of 971 patients.
- Angioectasias are the most common finding (50%), followed by inflammation (26.8%) and tumors (8.8%).

**Predictors of Positive Results:**
- Overt bleeding is the strongest predictor (OR 3.8). Other predictors: male sex (OR 1), age >60 (OR 1.2), hospitalization (OR 1.4), transfusions (OR up to 2.72 with ≥10 units PRBCs), connective tissue disease (OR 2.24), anticoagulation, and liver comorbidity.
- Early deployment of capsule endoscopy (within 3 days of admission) yields higher detection (44.4% vs 27.8%), more therapeutic interventions, and reduced hospitalization (6.1 vs 10.3 days). Yield decreases from 87.5% to 11.1% when performed after 10 days.

**Comparison with Other Modalities:**
- Superior to push enteroscopy (72.5% vs 48.7% yield; incremental yield of 35%).
- Complementary with CTE, but CTE is superior for small bowel tumor detection (94.1% vs 35.3%).
- Superior to mesenteric angiography (53.3% vs 20% yield in one randomized trial).
- Comparable diagnostic yield to double-balloon enteroscopy (60%-62% vs 56%-57%).
- Sensitivity/specificity of 95%/75% vs intraoperative enteroscopy.

**Utility for Guiding Therapy:**
- Positive capsule result predicts higher DBE yield (75% vs 27.5% with negative result).
- Capsule endoscopy had 100% sensitivity/negative predictive value for lesions requiring therapy; DBE avoided in 60% of patients with negative capsule results.
- Capsule transit time helps determine deep enteroscopy insertion route (time index >0.75 predicts retrograde route with 94.7% PPV).

**Outcomes:**
- Rebleeding rates are higher after positive capsule results (28.6% over 48 months). Risk factors include age >60, positive result, hemoglobin >7 g/dL, nonspecific treatment, and anticoagulant/antiplatelet/NSAID use.
- Vascular lesions show 35% rebleeding despite endoscopic therapy at 1 year.
- Negative capsule results generally predict low rebleeding, though results vary across studies.

**Repeat & Emergent Capsule Endoscopy:**
- Repeat capsule endoscopy after negative/nondiagnostic results has diagnostic yield of 35%-75% and alters management in 39%-62.5% of patients.
- Emergent capsule endoscopy shows promise in acute GI bleeding (diagnostic yield 75%, colonoscopy avoided in 55%), though larger prospective studies are needed.

**Limitations & Adverse Events:**
- Miss rate for solitary small bowel lesions is 11%, including tumors (19%).
- Main adverse event is capsule retention, occurring in 1.2%-1.5% of OGIB patients; risk increases with NSAID use, Crohn's disease, tumors, and prior radiation/surgery.
- Patency capsule may be useful selectively in high-risk patients; no benefit shown from "nonselective" use in all Crohn's patients.

**Conclusions:**
- Capsule endoscopy is the initial diagnostic test for small bowel bleeding after negative bidirectional endoscopy, guiding management with deep enteroscopy or surgery.
- CTE and/or deep enteroscopy are preferred when small bowel tumor or stricture is suspected.
- Future technologies, including maneuverable capsules, may improve lesion localization and enable therapeutic intervention.

Disclosures: Dr. Pasha received research support from Medtronic and CapsoVision; Dr. Leighton received research support from Medtronic and has consulted for Medtronic, Olympus, CapsoVision, and Fujinon.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for the evaluation of overt and occult small bowel bleeding. Its yield is higher in patients presenting with overt bleeding. The yield is also improved if the capsule is performed soon after the presentation of bleeding."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Evaluating ‘Early’ Video Capsule Endoscopy as a First-Line Diagnostic for GI Bleeding - Gastroenterology Advisor ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyadvisor.com/features/evaluating-early-video-capsule-endoscopy-as-a-first-line-diagnostic-for-gi-bleeding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Gastroenterology Advisor evaluates "early" video capsule endoscopy (EVCE) as a first-line diagnostic approach for gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB). Each year, approximately 350,000 patients in the US are hospitalized for GIB, with annual costs exceeding $1 billion. Hospitalization rates for upper GI bleeding (UGIB) have declined from 81 to 67 cases per 100,000 population, with classic diagnoses (gastritis, peptic ulcer disease) declining while Dieulafoy lesions, neoplasms, angiodysplasia, and esophagitis have increased. Guidelines recommend EGD within 24 hours of admission for acute non-variceal upper GIB and within 12 hours for variceal GIB, but delays are common due to patient, staff, and facility factors.

Key evidence supporting EVCE includes:
1) Hakimian et al (presented at the 2020 American College of Gastroenterology Annual Meeting): Compared frontline VCE during the COVID-19 pandemic (March-May 2020) with a historical pre-COVID control group. Results showed no statistical difference in bleeding localization rates on the first diagnostic test (76% COVID era vs 63% pre-COVID; P=.2), but first-line VCE significantly decreased the number of patients requiring invasive procedures (44% vs 96%; P<0.001). No significant differences in transfusion requirements, hemoglobin drop, in-hospital mortality, re-admission, or re-bleeding rates. Three patients had capsule retention.

2) A randomized controlled trial (NCT02442830) comparing EVCE with standard of care (SOC) in 87 patients with nonhematemesis GI bleeding (42 in EVCE arm): Higher bleeding localization rates with EVCE (64.3% vs 31.1%, P<0.01); adjusted HR 2.77 (95% CI, 1.36-5.64) for endoscopic localization. Median time to first procedure was 6 hours with EVCE vs 21 hours with SOC. EVCE patients were more likely to have bleeding localized to the colon (aOR, 4.09), a diagnosis by end of admission (aOR, 2.67), and vascular lesions (aOR, 10.73). No procedural adverse events in either group. No significant differences in all-cause mortality or direct hospitalization costs.

Additional context: Kim et al reviewed COVID-19 pandemic outcomes in GIB patients at two NYC hospitals (pre-COVID n=123 vs pandemic n=88), finding longer hospital stays (5.5 vs 4 days), more transfusions (1 vs 0 units), and fewer endoscopies performed (28.4% vs 50.4%) during the pandemic.

Considerations for EVCE adoption include potential risks (missed lesions, capsule retention requiring surgery/endoscopy), contraindications (dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, decreased GI motility, stricture history, small bowel obstructions), insurance coverage challenges, and the need for trained staff. Various VCE versions exist (esophageal, small bowel, colon capsules). EVCE may be particularly advantageous for stable patients waiting for antiplatelet/antithrombotic agents to clear before endoscopic procedures, and it supports value-based care by reducing invasive procedures, staff exposure, and PPE use, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
</summary>

"Results showed that there was no statistical difference between rates of bleeding localization on the first diagnostic test between groups (76% COVID era vs 63% pre-COVID era; P=.2); however, first-line VCE significantly decreased the number of patients who required invasive procedures (44% vs 96%; P<0.001)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Capsule Endoscopy: Prep, Procedure, What It Can Diagnose ---
URL: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/16829-capsule-endoscopy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cleveland Clinic health article provides a comprehensive overview of capsule endoscopy, a diagnostic test used to examine the digestive tract, particularly the small intestine. The test involves swallowing a capsule roughly the size of a large vitamin tablet that contains a light, transmitter, and one or more tiny cameras. As the capsule travels through the digestive tract, it captures about 10,000 pictures that healthcare providers review for bleeding, polyps, tumors, and inflammation. The capsule is naturally passed in stool, usually within 24 hours, and can be flushed down the toilet.

Key details include: The test is recommended for patients (children and adults) with symptoms of gastrointestinal problems, including unexplained bleeding or other bowel issues. If a child cannot swallow a pill, the capsule can be inserted via endoscopy. During the procedure, patients swallow the capsule with water and wear a recording device around their waist (either wired with sticky pads to the chest/abdomen or fully wireless) that stores images from the capsule's transmitter. The test is painless and patients cannot feel the capsule moving through their system.

Preparation requires following provider instructions, and patients must ask when they can resume eating. Recovery time is minimal to none. The procedure is generally safe with rare complications, though the capsule can occasionally get stuck in narrower parts of the intestines—particularly in people who've had bowel surgery, inflammation, or tumors. If there's uncertainty about whether the capsule passed, an X-ray or CT scan may be needed, as a retained capsule can cause a serious bowel obstruction. The capsule's main advantage is that it's one of the only tests that allows providers to examine the entire small intestine, since traditional tube-based endoscopy cannot reach all areas. Most results are ready in about a week. Patients should contact their provider immediately if they experience signs of obstruction (such as abdominal pain, vomiting, or inability to pass stool). The article emphasizes that the test is very safe, painless, and provides critical diagnostic information, while stressing the importance of following all provider instructions before and during the procedure.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A capsule endoscopy is a diagnostic test. Healthcare providers use it to look for bleeding and tumors, mainly in your small intestine."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Understanding hydrogen and methane breath tests for SIBO and IMO: 6 Frequently Asked Questions | Commonwealth Diagnostics International ---
URL: https://commdx.com/understanding-hydrogen-and-methane-breath-tests-for-sibo-and-imo-6-frequently-asked-questions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from Commonwealth Diagnostics International (CDI), a provider of functional GI diagnostic testing, specifically focused on hydrogen and methane breath tests for Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO). The page presents six frequently asked questions (FAQs) compiled by CDI's provider support team to help healthcare providers understand and order these breath tests.

Key content covered in the FAQs:

1. **What is a hydrogen & methane breath test?** A non-invasive diagnostic tool that can be administered in-office or at home. Elevated levels of hydrogen or methane gas identified within 90 minutes of ingesting a substrate solution indicate bacteria or methanogens in the small intestine. The North American Consensus on Breath Testing recommends this test for detecting SIBO (abnormal bacterial growth in the small intestine) and IMO (excessive methane in the intestinal tract). - Baseline sample collected first, then substrate ingested, followed by breath samples every 15–20 minutes over ~180 minutes.

A recent colonoscopy requires waiting at least 3 weeks before scheduling the test. Diabetic patients taking insulin should consult their prescriber about reducing the dose on test day.

During the test, the patient drinks a small amount of a test sugar (lactose, sucrose, fructose, or glucose), then breathes into a collection bag at scheduled intervals for approximately three hours. Samples are analyzed with specialized equipment, and results are sent to the patient's provider. After the test, patients may return to normal diet and activities. --- SOURCE 10: Pros and Cons of Breath Testing for Small Intestinal Bacterial ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10496284

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed medical review article published in Gastroenterology & Hepatology (N Y), March 2023, Volume 19, Issue 3, pages 140-146, authored by Jane Lim, MD, MS and Ali Rezaie, MD, MSc from the GI Motility Program, Karsh Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, California. The article (PMCID: PMC10496284, PMID: 37706108) reviews the pros and cons of breath testing for diagnosing Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO).

Key content:

**Background**: Breath testing is the most widely used modality to diagnose SIBO and IMO. SIBO is characterized by excessive coliform bacteria in the small intestine causing bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, diarrhea, and constipation. IMO is an independent entity involving overgrowth of methanogenic archaea causing bloating, gas, abdominal discomfort, and constipation. IMO can only be diagnosed via breath testing in clinical practice. Glucose and lactulose are the two main substrates used.

**Diagnostic criteria (North American Consensus)**:
- SIBO: Early rise in hydrogen of ≥20 ppm above baseline by 90 minutes
- IMO: Methane of ≥10 ppm at any point during testing
- Small bowel aspiration requires >10³ CFU/mL of coliforms (but has 19.6% contamination rate per Cangemi study)

**Pros of breath testing**:
- Safe, simple, noninvasive, widely accessible, and can be administered at home
- Can distinguish SIBO from IMO and help tailor antibiotic therapy (rifaximin for hydrogen-predominant SIBO; combination therapy like rifaximin/neomycin for IMO)
- Lactulose can sample the entire small intestine and identify distal SIBO; meta-analysis shows lactulose breath test sensitivity 42%, specificity 70.6%
- Glucose is more specific (less false positives from colonic fermentation); sensitivity 54.5%, specificity 83.2%
- Lactulose preferred for diabetic patients (no hyperglycemia risk); useful for diarrhea-predominant IBS patients to predict rifaximin response
- IMO results not affected by orocecal transit time (OCTT); methane levels correlate with constipation severity
- Spot methane measurement (SMM) of ≥10 ppm has 86.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing IMO, providing rapid point-of-care testing

**Cons/limitations of breath testing**:
- Indirectly measures microbial overgrowth
- Accuracy depends on patient compliance (oral care, no exercise/smoking on test day, avoiding fermentable foods day prior, no antibiotics 4 weeks before, discontinue promotility agents/laxatives 1 week before, avoid colonoscopy prep 2 weeks before)
- Various commercial home tests may use different thresholds not supported by guidelines
- Low breath hydrogen can occur when methanogens consume hydrogen
- OCTT variability: rapid OCTT can cause false positives; slow OCTT can cause false negatives
- Conditions preventing substrate delivery to small intestine (gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction, achalasia, enterocutaneous fistula) cause false negatives
- Study by Yu et al: 88% of positive results had ≥5% substrate in cecum on scintigraphy before test became positive, though 5% (0.5g lactulose) is insufficient to cause significant hydrogen rise
- Lin and Massey found 22 of 46 patients with false-positive glucose breath tests had colon fermentation, 20 of whom had prior upper GI surgery

**IMO treatment data**:
- Low et al. study: 85% of patients treated with rifaximin + neomycin achieved clinical response vs. 56% with rifaximin alone
- 87% of combination therapy patients eradicated methane vs. only 29% with rifaximin alone
- A small RCT (N=31) in constipation-predominant IBS with methane >3 ppm showed neomycin+rifaximin reduced constipation, straining, and bloating more than rifaximin alone

**Emerging breath test patterns**:
1. **Flat-line pattern**: No methane, low fixed hydrogen (≤3 ppm, no rise >1 ppm above baseline); more common in inflammatory bowel disease; 56% of patients respond to antibiotics (58% to rifaximin, 47% to rifaximin+neomycin); may indicate excess hydrogenotrophic bacteria or gastroparesis
2. **High baseline hydrogen**: >20 ppm baseline with no excessive methane; found in 0.7% (107/14,847) of lactulose breath tests; 52% responded to antibiotics, 73% to rifaximin, only 25% to rifaximin+neomycin

**Conclusion**: Breath testing offers rapid, safe, noninvasive diagnosis with utility in tailoring therapy and monitoring treatment response. Newer technologies including intraluminal gas sampling and next-generation sequencing may improve diagnostic accuracy in the future.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for patients with irritable bowel syndrome: current insights ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5530860

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Psychology Research and Behavior Management (2017, PMCID: PMC5530860, PMID: 28790872) by Sarah W Kinsinger of Loyola University Medical Center (Division of Gastroenterology and Nutrition, Behavioral Medicine for Digestive Health), reviews current insights into cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

**Key Content:**

1. **IBS Overview:** IBS is a highly prevalent condition affecting nearly 35 million Americans, characterized by abdominal pain associated with altered gut motility causing diarrhea and/or constipation. It consumes over $20 billion in direct and indirect expenditures, with healthcare utilization equivalent to chronic diseases like asthma, hypertension, and congestive heart failure. The condition negatively impacts quality of life and is associated with increased psychological distress.

2. **Biopsychosocial Model:** IBS is now viewed as a "disorder of gut brain interaction" rather than a purely "functional" condition. The biopsychosocial model (first applied to IBS by Doug Drossman, MD) emphasizes interactions between biology (genetic predisposition, disordered gut motility, altered gut microbiota, low-grade inflammation), behavior, cognitive processes, and environment. The brain-gut axis—complex bidirectional communication between brain and gut—is a key component.

3. **Cognitive Affective Processes:** Key mechanisms include visceral hypersensitivity (increased pain response to normal bowel functions), central processing deficits (IBS patients show greater activation of emotional arousal networks and fail to activate pain-downregulating brain regions like the medial prefrontal cortex), visceral anxiety, and catastrophizing. Stress is a significant contributor to brain-gut dysregulation. Patients with IBS have increased rates of anxiety and somatization, and tend to over-rely on problem-focused coping while lacking emotion-focused coping skills (Cheng et al. study).

4. **Evidence Base for Psychological Treatments:** 41 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated psychological therapies for IBS. Psychological treatments are moderately effective and durable. CBT is the most rigorously tested approach with at least 20 published RCTs, consistently demonstrating significant and lasting symptom improvement maintained for at least 1 year after treatment. Effects directly improve IBS symptoms independent of psychological factors.

5. **Components of CBT Treatment:** Psychoeducation, relaxation strategies (diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery), cognitive restructuring (addressing catastrophizing and probability overestimation), problem-solving skills (emotion-focused coping), and exposure techniques (graduated exposure, interoceptive exposure, behavioral experiments) to address avoidance and safety behaviors.

6. **Evolution of CBT Protocols:** Early models used general stress management (10-session model; Vollmer & Blanchard found 64% of group vs 55% of individual CBT patients improved vs control). Later models focused on cognitive-affective processes (Lackner et al: 72% of self-administered CBT patients reported adequate relief vs 60% therapist-administered and 7.4% control). Most recent model (Craske et al) targets visceral anxiety using exposure-based techniques modeled after panic disorder treatment. Alternative delivery methods include minimal contact models (Lackner) and internet-delivered CBT (Ljotsson et al, which showed 42% of ICBT patients vs 12% of control reported symptom improvement).

7. **Future Directions:** Despite demonstrated benefits, very few patients have access to CBT. Primary barrier is limited number of therapists trained in GI psychology. The American Gastroenterological Association recommends psychological interventions for moderate-to-severe IBS or patients unresponsive to standard care. Future efforts should focus on: training opportunities for clinicians, integrated care models with gastroenterologists, telemedicine/web-based platforms, and customizing treatment (e.g., 4-5 session brief models rather than standard 10 sessions) to match individual patient needs.

**Conclusions:** IBS involves brain-gut axis dysregulation where psychological processes play a key role. CBT is well-established, rigorously tested, and demonstrates significant long-lasting symptom improvement, but dissemination is poor. Future focus needed on training providers and developing telemedicine platforms.
</summary>

**The Mind-Body Connection:** The article emphasizes that while IBS is a physical condition, the mind-body connection significantly impacts symptoms. The central nervous system (brain/spinal cord) and enteric nervous system (gut) communicate about digestion, thoughts, emotions, and appetite. Notably, 95% of the body's serotonin—a neurotransmitter affecting mood, sleep, appetite, and sex drive—is produced in the gut. Two types of relationships exist between IBS and anxiety: (1) anxiety triggers digestive problems through stress chemicals released in the gut, and (2) having IBS can trigger anxiety due to its impact on work, family, and social functioning. Mental health impacts range from mild stress to chronic health anxiety.

**Chronic IBS Symptoms and Anxiety:** People with IBS often suffer chronic symptoms for years before diagnosis, and the endless medical testing itself is anxiety-provoking. Symptom flare-ups can act as trauma experiences. Common fears include: not knowing when symptoms will arise, shame/embarrassment about symptoms, being in new/busy situations, discomfort in tight clothing, not wanting to eat socially, needing to carry a "kit" (fresh underwear, medications, wipes), worries about new relationships/dating, and anxiety about food choices. The brain's protective scanning behavior can become problematic when excessive.

**Chronic IBS Symptoms and Low Mood:** IBS is often comorbid with low mood due to: isolation, lower self-confidence, avoiding intimacy, reduced enjoyment of social activities, chronic pain/discomfort, low energy, hopelessness, discomfort with spontaneity, fatigue from reading ingredients, and sadness about missing social occasions.

**What CBT Is:** Research shows CBT is effective in improving bowel symptoms, psychological distress, and quality of life in all people with IBS regardless of subtype. CBT is a shorter-term, collaborative treatment of approximately 12-15 sessions (depending on agreed goals). CBT is based on the relationship between cognitions (thoughts), behaviours, and emotions—since emotions cannot be directly controlled, clients learn to modify unhelpful thought and behaviour patterns to positively influence their emotional state.

**How CBT Can Help:** CBT provides education about the mental state/IBS relationship, management of ineffective thought and behavioural patterns, self-regulation strategies for physical and mental relaxation, flexible problem-solving training, and a supportive processing space. Overall, CBT helps individuals feel more in control of their thoughts, behaviours, emotions, and IBS symptoms.

The page also promotes CDHF's free myIBS tracking app (available on App Store and Google Play) and lists numerous related articles on IBS topics including FODMAP diets, gut-brain connection, mindfulness, IBS subtypes, and various management strategies.
</summary>

"95% of our body's serotonin, a chemical messenger that impacts our mood, sleep, appetite and sex drive, can be found in our gut."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Masters Athletes and Gut Issues – NEVERSECOND ---
URL: https://never2.com/blogs/guides/masters-athletes-and-gut-issues

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog article from Neversecond (a sports nutrition brand) titled "Masters Athletes and Gut Issues," written by Marni Sumbal, MS, RD, CSSD, LD/N. The article addresses gastrointestinal (GI) distress in masters athletes (40+), a common performance limiter in endurance sport.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Carb Absorption and Age**: The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. Masters athletes can target 60-90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor—gut training is.

2. **Three Causes of GI Distress**:
   - Physiological: Exercise diverts blood away from the gut (at 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop nearly 80%), causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea.
   - Mechanical: Running jolts the GI tract, making runners more prone to lower GI issues than cyclists.
   - Nutritional: High-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods eaten too close to training, plus concentrated drinks, slow stomach emptying.

3. **Gut Training for Masters Athletes**: Gut training involves progressively practicing carbohydrate and fluid intake during workouts. Elite athletes now consume 120-150g of carbs/hour, but this takes time to build. Recommended protocol: Start at 30-40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10-15g every 1-2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt.

4. **Exercising in Heat**: Heat compounds gut issues—blood shifts to skin for cooling and gastric emptying slows. Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. Recommendations: drop carb intake by 10-20g/hour until heat-acclimated, choose liquid calories, eat small amounts every 10-15 minutes, start hydrated and cool, don't rely on thirst, include sodium in everything you drink, monitor urine color, and watch for hyponatremia.

5. **Bottom Line**: The gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly. "Age is context, not a ceiling."

The article includes references from PubMed, PMC (NIH), Gatorade Sports Science Institute, and TrainingPeaks on topics including GLUT4 protein concentration, gut training, aging gastrointestinal function, multiple transportable carbohydrates, ultra-endurance nutrition strategies, exercise-intensity thresholds and leaky gut, GI symptoms in runners, and thermoregulation in older individuals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Aging doesn't have to mean slowing down — but it does mean paying closer attention to your gut." "Masters athletes can and should target 60–90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours, using glucose-fructose blends. Age alone isn't the limiting factor, gut training is." "At 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop by nearly 80%, causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea." "Many elite endurance athletes now successfully consume 120–150g of carbs per hour, but that takes time and consistency to build." "Your gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly well into their later years. Age is context, not a ceiling."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: How to Address Gut Issues for Runners 40 and Over - RUN | Powered by Outside ---
URL: https://run.outsideonline.com/nutrition-and-health/training-nutrition/guide-to-gut-health-carb-fueling-for-masters-runners

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published May 15, 2026 on Outside Run by Marni Sumbal R.D., C.S.S.D. (a sports dietitian and masters athlete), addresses gut health and carbohydrate fueling specifically for masters athletes (those aged 40 and older). Despite being one of the largest and fastest-growing segments of endurance sport, masters athletes have been historically underrepresented in sports nutrition literature. The article covers three main areas:

**1. Carbohydrate Absorption and Aging:** The body uses two intestinal transporters—SGLT1 for glucose (max 60 grams/hour) and GLUT5 for fructose (additional 30-60 grams/hour). Combining glucose/maltodextrin with fructose in a 2:1 or 1:0.8 ratio increases carbohydrate oxidation to 1.7-1.8 grams/minute and prevents GI issues like bloating. While aging causes structural gut changes, small intestine absorption capacity generally stays steady in healthy older adults. The main concern for masters athletes is not reduced absorption but a decline in GLUT4 (insulin-regulated glucose transporter), which can lead to insulin resistance—though regular endurance training can maintain and even reverse this age-related decline. Masters athletes can benefit from 60-90 grams of carbs per hour in events lasting over two hours using glucose-fructose blends.

**2. Avoiding GI Distress:** GI issues affect 30-90% of athletes and stem from three factors: (a) Physiological—reduced blood flow to the gut (up to 80% reduction at 70% VO2max), though research suggests younger male athletes may actually experience more gut issues than older athletes; (b) Mechanical—the jostling of running contributes to "runner's trots"; (c) Nutritional—high-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods near training, and high-osmality drinks increase GI distress risk. Risk factors include lack of food variety, low-fiber diets, processed/fatty foods, skipping meals, and eating too close to bedtime. Recommendations include eating every few hours, prioritizing real foods, incorporating fermented foods (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, tempeh), staying hydrated, keeping pre-workout snacks low in fiber/fat, and allowing at least 90 minutes for digestion before exercise.

**3. Gut Training Protocol:** Gut training is a progressive strategy to condition the GI tract to handle large carbohydrate loads (elite athletes can ingest 120-150 grams/hour). While masters athletes can follow structured gut training, they may need more time to adapt. Recommendations: start at 30-40 grams of carbs per hour during sessions over 90 minutes using glucose/fructose products, increase by 10-15 grams every 1-2 weeks as tolerated, with a goal of at least 60 grams/hour. It can take up to 10 weeks of consistent practice to properly train the gut. Practice at least once weekly during high-volume sessions mimicking race conditions.

**4. Heat Considerations:** Hot/humid conditions stress the gut through reduced gut blood flow (redirected to skin for cooling) and slowed gastric emptying. Athletes tolerating 80 grams/hour in mild conditions may only tolerate 50-60 grams/hour in heat. Masters athletes face age-specific challenges: reduced cardiovascular cooling (declining cardiac output) and decreased sweating efficiency (altered sweat gland structure). Recommendations include: reducing hourly carb intake by 10-20 grams until heat-acclimated, prioritizing liquid calories over solid foods, consuming small amounts every 10-15 minutes, starting hydrated, not relying on thirst as a guide, including sodium in products (to prevent hyponatremia), monitoring urine color (should be pale yellow), and using pre/post-activity weigh-ins to track dehydration.

The article concludes that with sensible adjustments to gut training, fueling, and heat management, masters athletes can turn the perceived challenges of aging into a powerful athletic advantage.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Masters athletes can benefit from consuming 60-90 grams of carbohydrates per hour, as there is currently no strong evidence to suggest otherwise. The limiting factor tends to be proper gut training and sport nutrition product formulation, not your age."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2674-0311/2/3/21

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The authors are Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Sapienza University of Rome, Italy), and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Milan, Italy). The article was submitted 26 July 2023, revised 30 August 2023, accepted 12 September 2023, and published 19 September 2023. It has 26 citations and an Altmetric score of 31.

**Key content:**

The review examines "Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome" (Ex-GIS), a condition affecting up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports (marathon, triathlon, cycling, running, etc.) caused by strenuous exercise. Symptoms include upper GI issues (regurgitation, bloating, belching, epigastric pain, heartburn) and lower GI issues (flatulence, urge to defecate, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fecal blood loss).

**Pathophysiology:** Two main pathways are described:
1. Neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway: Sympathetic activation alters the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
2. Circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic blood flow can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing gut hypoperfusion, ischemic damage, loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP. 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study.

**GI symptoms during exercise:** 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms. In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run. Severe GI distress ranges from 4% in marathon running/cycling to 32% in Ironman races. Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors.

**IBS overlap:** Ex-GIS shares pathogenesis with IBS (alterations in gut microbiota, permeability, immune function, motility, visceral sensation, brain-gut interactions). IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed.

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms).

**Management:** The review emphasizes nutritional and behavioral strategies, particularly examining gluten-free diets and low-FODMAP (fermentable oligo-, di-, mono-saccharides and polyols) diets as the principal interventions to avoid symptoms during exercise. Exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet should all be evaluated.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023, yielding 142 relevant research articles published between 1965 and 2023.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Frontiers | Gastrointestinal symptoms among recreational long distance runners in China: prevalence, severity, and contributing factors ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1589344/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sport and Exercise Nutrition section) on July 23, 2025, examining gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms among recreational long distance runners in China. The study, conducted by researchers from Beijing Sport University, investigated the prevalence, severity, and contributing factors of GI symptoms in this population—the first large-scale study of its kind for Chinese runners.

METHODOLOGY: The China Marathon Nutrition Survey (CMNS) sub-study collected 805 valid questionnaires (86.7% effective rate) between January and December 2024 via online and offline channels. Participants were recruited through running clubs, community organizations, sports associations, and online platforms. The questionnaire covered six areas: demographics, exercise habits, dietary strategies, GI symptom severity/frequency, influencing factors, and knowledge/attitudes. GI symptoms were assessed using the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) with 11 symptoms rated on a 7-point Likert scale. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Sport University (Approval Number: 2024256H). Cronbach's alpha was 0.788, KMO was 0.839.

KEY FINDINGS:
- 26.1% of participants reported GI symptoms during races; most common symptoms were bloating (18.6%), urge to defecate (17.8%), and stomach pain (16.5%)
- Symptoms peaked during the middle phase of the race (30.0% frequency, highest severity 2.43 ± 0.22)
- Males had higher prevalence than females (27.9% vs. 20.8%, p=0.048); runners aged 34 or younger had higher symptom rates (p=0.014)
- A self-reported history of GI disorders was the strongest predictor (p<0.001)
- U-shaped relationship between training volume and GI symptoms: both low (20–50 km/month) and very high (>500 km/month) volumes increased risk (p=0.015)
- Eating within 30 minutes before a race increased risk of bloating (p=0.017), urge to defecate (p=0.040), and flatulence (p=0.011)
- Consumption of water (p=0.045), sports drinks (p=0.012), energy drinks (p=0.004), energy bars (p=0.042), and isotonic gels (p=0.002) were significantly associated with bloating
- 94.5% of runners restricted foods before races; most avoided seafood (47.5%), red meat (26.2%), legumes (25.3%), dairy (24.1%), and tea/coffee (19.4%)
- 76.2% of symptomatic runners reported negative performance impact; common relief strategies included slowing down (76.2%) and walking/stopping (41.0%)
- 3% used NSAIDs despite potential gut health risks
- 42.2% relied on social media for GI symptom information
- Majority of participants were male (74.9%), mean age 39.7 ± 10.0 years; most had <5 years running experience (60.7%) and monthly distance of 100–200 km (43%)
- No significant associations with running experience, training level, race history, or pre-race sleep/stress

DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION: The study highlights the importance of individualized dietary planning, particularly pre-race meal timing and food choices, to reduce GI symptoms. Recommendations align with ACSM guidance to consume meals 3–4 hours before exercise and smaller snacks 2–4 hours prior. Strategies such as "Training the Gut" and low-FODMAP diets are suggested. Despite the Chinese diet being rich in whole grains and plant-based FODMAP-rich foods, overall GI symptom prevalence was not particularly elevated. The findings may not fully generalize to runners from other regions due to unique Chinese dietary patterns. The study's limitations include its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data. Funding was provided by the Chinese Nutrition Society, the General Administration of Sport of China, and Beijing Sport University.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Training The Gut For Athletes ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/training-the-gut-for-athletes

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #178 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published January 2018, authored by Asker Jeukendrup, PhD. The article examines "Training the Gut for Athletes" — the concept that the gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be trained and adapted to improve nutrient and fluid delivery during endurance exercise while reducing GI distress.

KEY POINTS:
- The GI tract is critical for delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and is a major determinant of endurance performance.
- GI problems affect 30-50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports.
- The GI tract is highly adaptable and responds to nutritional training in a nutrient-specific way.

GASTRIC EMPTYING: The stomach is the first barrier for delivering nutrients. Studies show that repeated practice of high fluid intakes during running improved stomach comfort over time (Lambert et al., 2008), though without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate. Dietary manipulation studies (Cunningham et al., 1991; Horowitz et al., 1996; Yau et al., 2014) demonstrated that supplementing with specific carbohydrates (glucose or fructose) accelerated gastric emptying of those same sugars specifically, with effects seen after as little as 3 days.

INTESTINAL SUGAR TRANSPORT: Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent SGLT1 transporter, while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are the most important transporters for carbohydrate absorption. At ingestion rates over 60-70 g of carbohydrate/hour, exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks at ~60 g/hour because SGLT1 becomes saturated. Combining glucose and fructose (using different transporters) can achieve higher oxidation rates.

TRANSPORTER REGULATION AND ADAPTATION: SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. A glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies show rapid adaptation: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses showed increases after just one week; piglets showed increases after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks.

HUMAN EVIDENCE: The landmark Cox et al. (2010) study divided 16 endurance-trained cyclists into high-carbohydrate and control groups. Over 28 days of training (16 h/week), the high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate versus 5.3 g/kg/day in controls. Post-training, the high-carb group showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, most likely due to upregulated SGLT1 transporters. Conversely, carbohydrate restriction, high-fat/ketogenic diets, or energy reduction may reduce absorptive capacity and potentially increase GI problems.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) Train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks. (2) Practice race nutritional strategies in training to adapt to higher volumes and carbohydrate intakes. (3) For exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate is recommended; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures). (4) Athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days to maintain gut absorptive capacity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The gastrointestinal (GI) tract plays a critical role in delivering carbohydrate and fluid to the blood during prolonged exercise, and can therefore be a major determinant of performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Sports Dietitians Australia and Ultra Sports Science Foundation Joint Position Statement: A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40279-025-02186-6

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a joint position statement from Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and the Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) published in the journal *Sports Medicine* (Volume 55, pages 1097–1134) on April 7, 2025. It is an open-access review article titled "Sports Dietitians Australia and Ultra Sports Science Foundation Joint Position Statement: A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms."

The article provides a comprehensive practitioner guide for the prevention and management of exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS) and exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). Key content includes:

**Background:** Exercise can disturb gastrointestinal integrity and function, leading to EIGS, which can impact physical performance, require medical intervention, and in severe cases contribute to systemic responses leading to fatality. Gastrointestinal complaints during exercise have been documented in scientific literature for a century, with awareness developing during the 1980–90s. A growing number of athletes are seeking professional help for these issues, especially in endurance and ultra-endurance sports.

**Pathophysiology of EIGS:** EIGS comprises two primary pathophysiological pathways:
1. Circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway: Splanchnic hypoperfusion and gastrointestinal ischemia due to blood flow redistribution to skeletal muscle and peripheral circulation, resulting in intestinal epithelial injury, hyperpermeability, and local/systemic inflammatory effects from translocated luminal pathogens (bacteria and endotoxins).
2. Neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway: Stress responses causing increases in sympathetic activation and stress hormones, leading to impaired gastrointestinal motility, transit, digestive function, and nutrient absorption.

Two additional proposed pathways warranting further investigation include mechanical strain from exercise (jarring, vibrations, tissue friction) on the splanchnic area, and exaggerated metabolic responses (e.g., metabolic acidosis from high-intensity exercise and hypoglycemia from prolonged endurance exercise linked to exercise-associated nausea).

**Key findings on prevention/management strategies:**
- **Beneficial strategies (consistent outcomes):** Macronutrient intake (carbohydrate and protein) before and during exercise; euhydration; dietary manipulation of FODMAPs (fermentable oligo-, di-, and mono-saccharides and polyols); gut training/feeding tolerance adjustments.
- **Promising but warranting further exploration:** Heat mitigating strategies; certain nutritional supplementation (prebiotics and phenols).
- **Negative outcomes reported:** Low-carbohydrate high-fat diets; probiotic supplementation; pharmaceutical administration; feeding intolerances.

**Recommendations:** Due to individual variability in EIGS and Ex-GIS outcomes, athletes and support practitioners are encouraged to undergo gastrointestinal assessment during exercise to identify underlying causal and exacerbation factors, and adopt evidence-based strategies that provide individualized beneficial outcomes. Abstaining from strategies with unclear and/or adverse outcomes is recommended.

**Methodology:** A scoping review approach was used (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and Ovid Medline databases) to obtain and screen relevant research studies in healthy athlete or active populations. Only papers demonstrating research methodological competency or contributing to consensus discussions were included, with a "grade of evidence" established by standardized assessment and group consensus.

**Article metrics:** The article has 13,000+ accesses, 30 citations, and 9 Altmetric mentions. A Letter to the Editor was published on July 29, 2025. Key authors include Ricardo J. S. Costa, Stephanie K. Gaskell, Kayla Henningsen, Nikki A. Jeacocke, Isabel G. Martinez, Alice Mika, Volker Scheer, Rachel Scrivin, Rhiannon M. J. Snipe, Alice M. Wallett, and Pascale Young.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It is now well-established that exercise can disturb various aspects of gastrointestinal integrity and function. The pathophysiology of these perturbations, termed 'exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS),' can lead to exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptom (Ex-GIS) inconveniences."
</key_excerpts>
