--- SOURCE 6: From Celiac Disease, Gluten-Sensitivity Vs Gluten Sensationalism, To Fodmap Reduction As A Tool To Manage Gastrointestinal Symptoms In Athletes - Gatorade Sports Science Institute ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/en/sports-science-exchange/Article/from-celiac-disease-gluten-sensitivity-vs-gluten-sensationalism-to-fodmap-reduction-as-a-tool-to-manage-gastrointestinal-symptoms-in-athletes?EC=f5c89e83-7dcf-49a4-a2c9-7fc41e219852

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #189, a Sports Science Exchange article published in December 2018 by author Dana Lis, examining the relationship between gluten-free diets (GFD), FODMAPs (fermentable oligo-, di- and monosaccharides and polyols), and gastrointestinal symptoms (GIS) in athletes. The article is published by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI).

KEY POINTS:
- Exercise-induced gastrointestinal symptoms are commonly reported by athletes, with moderate/severe GIS occurring in 27% of marathon runners, 32% of Ironman competitors, and up to 60-96% of ultra-endurance event participants.
- A gluten-free diet for athletes not clinically requiring gluten avoidance has NOT been shown to have beneficial or negative effects on GI health, well-being, or athletic performance.
- Athletes may unknowingly eliminate FODMAP-rich foods while attempting to reduce GI symptoms, and strategic low-FODMAP diets may be an effective tool to reduce exercise-induced GI symptoms.

MAIN FINDINGS:
- Exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS) is triggered by splanchnic hypoperfusion (reduced blood flow to GI organs during strenuous exercise) causing ischemia, increased gut permeability, and epithelial dysregulation, plus elevated sympathetic nervous system activation reducing gastric emptying.
- An international study of 910 athletes found 41% adhered to a GFD to varying degrees—approximately 4-fold higher than the general population clinically requiring a GFD.
- A randomized crossover double-blind study (Lis et al., 2015a) in non-celiac cyclists found no differences in GI injury, GIS, systemic inflammation, perceptual well-being, or time trial performance between gluten-containing and gluten-free diets.
- Skodje et al. (2018) demonstrated that fructans (a FODMAP) triggered IBS-like symptoms in twice as many individuals with self-reported non-celiac gluten sensitivity than gluten itself—supporting the concept that FODMAP reduction, not gluten avoidance, is the modulating factor for symptom improvement.
- A low-FODMAP diet is effective for 70% of individuals with IBS for symptom reduction.
- Survey data showed 55% of 910 athletes eliminated at least one high-FODMAP food to reduce GIS, and 83% of those (501 athletes) reported successful symptom reduction.
- A seminal study found 82% of runners (9/11) with persistent exercise-associated GIS experienced significantly lower daily GIS during low-FODMAP versus high-FODMAP periods (Lis et al., 2017).
- Habitual FODMAP intake in runners with EIGS was 2-fold higher (43 g/day) than clinical classification for a high-FODMAP diet.

PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS:
- Properly diagnose gluten-related conditions and identify actual dietary triggers before adopting restrictive diets.
- A modified (not strictest) low-FODMAP diet may be appropriate; common triggers may be limited to lactose or excess fructose.
- An acute strict low-FODMAP diet for 1-3 days before and during intensive endurance exercise may be required for symptom reduction.
- Risks of unnecessary food restriction include altered gut microbiota, reduced short-chain fatty acid production, reduced bifidobacteria, and increased risk of eating disorders (e.g., orthorexia nervosa).
- Athletes should consult registered dietitians specializing in sports nutrition and low-FODMAP diet training before implementation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A gluten-free diet (GFD) for athletes not clinically requiring gluten avoidance has not been shown to have a beneficial or negative effect on gastrointestinal health, overall well-being or athletic performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Gluten Intolerance and Celiac Disease – TYM ATHLETIC PERFORMANCE ---
URL: https://www.tymperformance.com/blogs/nutrition-lifestyle-articles/nutrition-lifestyle-articles-gluten-intolerance-and-celiac-disease

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, published by TYM Athletic Performance in partnership with TheNutritionDr.com, provides an overview of gluten intolerance and Celiac Disease specifically in athletic populations. The content distinguishes between two main categories of gluten sensitivity: 1) gluten sensitivity/intolerance, and 2) gluten allergy/Celiac Disease. A true gluten allergy affects approximately 1% of the population and involves a dangerous autoimmune response with progressive destruction of the intestinal wall. An estimated 3 million Americans have been diagnosed with gluten allergy and Celiac Disease, consistent with global findings of 0.5-1.0% of people. Gluten intolerance may impact up to 13% of people, with similar symptoms but without destruction of the small intestine wall.

The page lists common symptoms of both conditions, including abdominal cramping, bloating, gas, diarrhea/constipation, vomiting, fatty stools, anemia, weight loss, depression, headaches, fatigue, weakness, and growth/behavioral issues in children. It also discusses dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), a skin condition involving blistering and itching, and explains that Celiac Disease diagnosis typically involves blood antibody tests, intestinal biopsies, and genetic marker testing.

The content explains that gluten is the dominant protein class in cereal grains (mostly gliadin and glutenin) and is found in wheat, rye, barley, and grains from regions with more extreme weather (e.g., Canada and northern US). Gluten is not found in oats, rice, millets, buckwheat, sorghum, quinoa, and amaranth, though cross-contamination can occur during milling or if grown near gluten-containing crops. Some people with Celiac Disease cannot tolerate oats due to avenin, which shares amino acid characteristics with gluten.

The article highlights that in 2013, the US FDA issued a final rule defining "gluten-free" for food labeling, requiring foods bearing the claim to contain less than 20 parts per million (ppm) of gluten. Animal foods (meats, eggs, dairy), fruits, and vegetables are naturally gluten-free. The Celiac Disease Foundation (www.Celiac.org) is cited as the leading support organization. The content notes the particular challenge for athletes, as wheat-based foods like breads and pastas have been mainstays of recovery and carbo-loading for endurance and high-intensity sport athletes. Three scientific references are cited supporting the prevalence and clinical data presented.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A true allergy to gluten affects about one percent of people and involves a dangerous auto-immune response and progressive destruction to the intestine tract wall."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Celiac Disease and the Athlete ---
URL: https://www.beyondceliac.org/wp-content/uploads/archive/SiteData/docs/CeliacDise/450f7f18693397fe/Celiac_Disease_and_the_Athlete.12.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Current Sports Medicine Reports (2011, Vol. 10, No. 2, pp. 105-108) by Lee A. Mancini, MD, Thomas Trojian, MD, and Angela C. Mancini, MD, reviews the diagnosis and management of celiac disease in athletes. Celiac disease is a hereditary autoimmune disorder causing malabsorption in the GI tract, triggered by gluten (found in wheat, barley, and rye), which causes immune system damage to small intestinal villi. Key facts include: approximately 30% of the population carries genetic markers (HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8, found in 99.6% of celiac patients), but only about 1% have active celiac disease; women are 2.5 times more likely to be affected. The article emphasizes that sports medicine physicians should include celiac disease in their differential for athletes with prolonged unexplained illness. Common symptoms include chronic diarrhea (50-70%), abdominal bloating (40-60%), malnutrition (30-60%), fatigue (30-60%), vomiting (10-40%), anemia (10-30%), and osteopenia/osteoporosis (10-20%). Initial serologic testing uses tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibody levels (sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.98) and IgA antiendomysial antibody (EMA) tests (sensitivity 0.90, specificity 0.99); the gold standard for diagnosis is small intestinal biopsy showing blunted villi. Management of newly diagnosed athletes requires a multidisciplinary approach including a nutritionist and sports psychologist. Strict gluten-free diet (GFD) is the only treatment, with carbohydrate intake of 6-10 g/kg body weight recommended; alternative carb sources include beans, rice, corn, nuts, potatoes, quinoa, and tapioca. Athletes should be evaluated for iron-deficiency anemia (present in 10-70% of newly diagnosed patients; may take 2-18 months to correct), and DEXA scans are recommended for adults to assess bone mineral density due to vitamin D and calcium malabsorption. For athletes with long-standing celiac disease (1+ years), strict GFD adherence remains critical—approximately 60% of patients follow a GFD—with ongoing vigilance needed for travel, team meals, dining halls, and workout nutrition. Gluten exposure can precipitate symptom flare-ups and decreased athletic performance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"To develop celiac disease, one must have a genetic predisposition and antigen exposure. It is believed that approximately 30% of the population carries the genetic markers for celiac disease. The genetic markers linked to celiac disease are human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8. These markers are found in 99.6% of people with celiac disease. However, only approximately 1% of the population has active celiac disease. Women are 2.5 times more likely to have celiac disease compared with men."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Celiac Disease Symptoms in Athletes: Prevalence Indicators of Perceived Quality of Life - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7222663

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in Sports Health (May-June 2020, SAGE Publications, available via PMC/NCBI) titled "Celiac Disease Symptoms in Athletes: Prevalence Indicators of Perceived Quality of Life." The authors are James E. Leone, PhD, MPH, MS, ATC, CSCS*D, CHES, FMHI (Bridgewater State University, lead author, jleone@bridgew.edu), Kimberly A. Wise, EdD, MS, ATC, Elizabeth M. Mullin, PhD, CMPC, CSCS, RFSA, Kimberly A. Gray, PhD, ATC, CSCS, CHES, RYT, Philip A. Szlosek, PhD, LAT, ATC, Matthew F. Griffin, BS, PA-S, and Cara A. Jordan, MS, CAGS.

STUDY OVERVIEW: This was a level 4 epidemiological, cross-sectional, correlational study examining the prevalence of celiac disease (CD) and related symptoms in NCAA collegiate athletes (N = 141; 84 male/40%, 57 female/60%; mean age 20.60 years; predominantly White/Caucasian 70%; top sports: track and field 33.3%, football 21.3%, basketball 14.2%, baseball 10.6%). The study was approved by the Bridgewater State University IRB and data were collected from December 2014 to December 2015 via an online survey (SurveyMonkey), recruited through athletic directors, strength coaches, and athletic trainers.

METHODS: Four validated instruments were used: (1) Celiac Symptom Index (CSI), a 16-item self-report measure; (2) WHO Quality of Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF), 26 items across physical, psychological, social, and environment domains; (3) Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), 21 items; and (4) Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-14), 14 items. CSI scores were categorized into low (<45) and high (≥45) CD symptoms. The a priori power analysis (G*Power) required a minimum sample of 126 for 70% power.

HYPOTHESES TESTED: (1) Athletes would have similar odds of CD as the general population (~1 in 141); (2) higher CSI scores correlate with lower QoL; (3) higher CSI scores correlate with higher depression; (4) higher CSI scores correlate with higher perceived stress.

KEY RESULTS: (1) Athletes were significantly more likely to report being diagnosed with CD (n=4) than expected population values (χ²(1)=8.17; P<0.01), being 3.85 times (95% CI, 0.42-34.89) more likely to be diagnosed with CD than the general population. (2) Athletes were significantly more likely to report high CD symptoms (n=16 vs n=122) compared with general population values (χ²(1)=234.04; P<0.001), being 18.36 times (95% CI, 2.40-140.48) more likely to report a high degree of CD symptoms. (3) CSI was significantly negatively correlated with all four WHOQOL-BREF domains: physical (r=-0.49), psychological (r=-0.53), social relations (r=-0.38), and environment (r=-0.36). (4) CSI was significantly positively correlated with BDI (r=0.62) and PSS-14 (r=0.53).

CONCLUSIONS: NCAA athletes may be a higher-risk population for CD, with nearly 4 times greater likelihood of CD diagnosis and 18 times greater likelihood of CD symptoms compared to general population estimates. Athletes with more CD symptoms reported worse QoL, higher depression, and higher perceived stress. CD poses unique barriers for athletes due to increased metabolic demand and nutritional needs.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Allied health care professionals should be aware of the diversity of CD symptoms and refer athletes when gastrointestinal symptoms persist. CD diagnosis averages 8-11 years from onset. Early identification yields financial return on investment and better outcomes. A team-based, interdisciplinary approach is advocated. CD can be successfully treated with a strict gluten-free diet (GFD).

KEY LIMITATIONS: Correlational design (no causality); convenience sample (<1% of ~380,000 NCAA athletes); use of general population rather than collegiate comparison estimates; self-reported CD diagnosis (no biopsy/serological confirmation); potential response bias and "healthy worker effect"; possible selection bias since athletes have frequent contact with health care providers. Sample largely drawn from Midwest (48%) and Northeast (24%) regions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Athletes were 3.85 times (95% CI, 0.42-34.89) more likely to report a CD diagnosis and were 18.36 times (95% CI, 2.40-140.48) more likely to report a high degree of CD symptoms than the general population."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Do you feed your players with sandwiches? May not be good for all! ---
URL: https://motorpreferencesexperts.com/blog/baseball-2/food-could-be-your-performance-enemy-28

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published October 21, 2024 by David Genest (Motor Preferences Experts), examines the rise of gluten sensitivity in the United States and its impact on athletes, particularly baseball and softball players.

Key facts:
- The average American consumes about 53 pounds of bread per year, mostly made from modern wheat.
- Wheat height has been genetically modified from ~5.5 feet to ~2.6 feet (part of the 1960s Green Revolution) to facilitate mechanical harvesting and reduce crop losses.
- Modern wheat strains contain up to TWICE the amount of gluten compared to ancestral varieties, due to genetic modification that boosted gluten for improved elasticity and texture in bread-making.
- French research institutions INRAE and CNRS have been involved in studying wheat genetic improvements and their health impacts.

Impact on athletes:
- Gluten sensitivity triggers immune responses causing inflammation throughout the body, including muscles and joints, reducing performance and hampering recovery.
- Baseball/softball players rely on agility, speed, and power; chronic inflammation reduces flexibility, increases muscle soreness, and impairs nutrient absorption.
- Gastrointestinal discomfort (bloating, cramping) distracts athletes during crucial game moments.

Key research findings:
- No specific studies have directly measured performance changes (like force generation) in athletes who eliminated gluten without having celiac disease or diagnosed sensitivity.
- A study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise concluded that gluten-free diets do NOT impact performance in athletes without gluten sensitivity—no changes in inflammatory markers or performance outcomes (endurance, strength) in non-celiac athletes.
- Elite athletes like Novak Djokovic reported enhanced endurance and performance after eliminating gluten due to his diagnosed sensitivity.
- Any performance changes from gluten elimination are likely due to alleviating digestive distress in sensitive individuals, not changes in muscle output.

Methods to determine gluten sensitivity/celiac status:
1. Blood tests for celiac disease (tTG-IgA antibodies)
2. Genetic testing (HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genes)
3. Symptom monitoring
4. Intestinal biopsy (gold standard for celiac diagnosis)

The article concludes that unless an athlete has specific gluten sensitivity, eliminating gluten does not lead to measurable improvements in performance, but for sensitive athletes, gluten-free diets can be a "game-changer" in managing inflammation and digestive distress.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Modern wheat strains have up to twice the amount of gluten compared to their ancestors, which poses a challenge to the digestive systems of many people."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Aging and Thermoregulatory Control: The Clinical Implications of Exercising under Heat Stress in Older Individuals ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6098859

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in BioMed Research International (August 2, 2018; doi: 10.1155/2018/8306154) by Bryce N. Balmain, Surendran Sabapathy, Menaka Louis, and Norman R. Morris from Griffith University (Gold Coast, Australia) and The Prince Charles Hospital (Brisbane, Australia), with academic editor Birgitta Langhammer. The article examines aging and thermoregulatory control, focusing on the clinical implications of exercising under heat stress in older individuals.

Key content:
- Climate change is increasing the frequency, duration, and intensity of heat waves. In Australia, heat waves cause more deaths than all other natural disasters combined. The 2003 Western European heat wave killed an estimated 13,700 people in France alone.
- Individuals over age 60 are the most vulnerable age cohort to heat-related adverse health outcomes due to impaired thermoregulatory control, particularly during physical activity in the heat.
- Thermoregulatory control: Humans maintain core body temperature of ~37°C (safe range 35-39°C). Muscular contraction is extremely inefficient—approximately 80% of generated energy is produced as heat. Sweating and skin blood flow (SkBF) are the primary mechanisms for heat dissipation.

Age-related changes in sweating:
- Older individuals show delayed core temperature onset threshold for sweating and reduced evaporative heat loss due to lower overall sweat rate.
- This is not due to fewer activated sweat glands, but to reduced sweat production per gland (sweat gland atrophy or decreased cholinergic sensitivity).
- Age-related effects are greater on forehead and limb sweat glands than on trunk glands, suggesting peripheral-to-central decline.
- Studies (Kenney & Anderson, Tankersley, Inbar) show lower local and whole-body sweat rates in older individuals during exercise at various intensities in hot environments, though biophysical differences (body mass, surface area, H prod) were not controlled in these studies.

Age-related changes in skin blood flow:
- Older individuals exhibit impaired heat-induced rises in SkBF compared to younger counterparts, even when matched for aerobic fitness, acclimation, and hydration status—suggesting this is a primary function of aging.
- SkBF plateaus at ~60% of maximum during exercise in the heat in healthy young individuals due to baroreceptor reflex-mediated control.
- Mechanisms include: reduced sympathetic cholinergic cotransmitter release, altered downstream signalling for vascular endothelial function, attenuated heat stress-induced sympathetic neural drive, compromised NO-dependent cutaneous vasodilation, reduced capillary density in aged skin, and lower cardiac output (due to lower stroke volume or blunted chronotropic response).
- Older individuals also show decrements in thirst sensation and renal sodium/water-conserving capabilities, limiting their ability to accommodate increases in intravascular blood volume.

Thermoregulation, fitness, and aging:
- Traditional research used %V̇O2peak protocols, but recent work (Jay et al., 2011) shows that fixed %V̇O2peak leads to different rates of metabolic heat production (H prod) between groups not matched for absolute V̇O2peak. Exercise at fixed absolute intensity yields similar core temperature responses regardless of fitness, supporting Nielsen's classic findings.
- No study to date has used the appropriate protocol (matching absolute H prod) to isolate the true independent influence of age and fitness on thermoregulation during exercise—identified as an area requiring further examination.

Clinical implications:
- There are currently NO public health recommendations for physical activity in the heat specifically for older individuals.
- Exercise training improves cardiac, autonomic, and vascular endothelial function, and can slow age-related decline in heat loss effector function. Inoue et al. showed fit older individuals have greater sweat gland output than unfit older individuals.
- Consecutive days (>6 days) of passive heat exposure (>40°C for min 60 min) produces heat acclimation in older individuals. Best et al. showed older cyclists achieve similar acclimation benefits as younger cyclists after 6 days.
- A large cohort study (n=2327) found repeated whole-body heat exposure associated with ~5-fold reduction in fatal cardiovascular and all-mortality events in men aged 42-60 years.
- Theoretical strategies (folic acid, beetroot juice/nitrate, electric fans) may help protect against heat-related strain but require future study.
- Individuals with heart failure show greater rises in core temperature compared to age-matched healthy controls during exercise at the same H prod in warm environments (30°C).
- The article emphasizes the urgent need for developing public health recommendations for physical activity in the heat for older individuals, and warns that rising energy costs could make air-conditioning inaccessible to low-income individuals, increasing vulnerability during heat waves.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review article published in Frontiers in Physiology (20 February 2014, Volume 5, Sec. Vascular Physiology) by Carlo Vigorito and Francesco Giallauria, titled "Effects of exercise on cardiovascular performance in the elderly." The article reviews the beneficial effects of exercise on the age-related decline in cardiovascular performance in both healthy elderly individuals and elderly patients with cardiovascular disease.

Key content covered:

**Aging effects on cardiovascular system:** Progressive aging causes reduced myocardial cell numbers, increased interstitial collagen fibers, impaired left ventricular diastolic function, reduced maximal heart rate response to exercise (due to beta1 receptor down-regulation), and peripheral changes including reduced skeletal muscle cells and decreased Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) I and IIa fibers. Even without cardiovascular disease, aging is strongly associated with reduced maximal aerobic capacity.

**Effects in healthy elderly:** Aerobic/endurance exercise improves peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope, ventilatory aerobic threshold, and Heart Rate Recovery (HRR). Mechanisms include improved chronotropic incompetence, increased stroke volume, enhanced vagal tone, improved endothelial function and arterial compliance, and favorable skeletal muscle biochemical changes (increased MHC I). Gender differences noted: men's increased peak VO2 primarily due to augmented stroke volume/CO, while women's increase is due entirely to increased A-VO2 difference. Resistance training increases muscle mass and strength but has fewer effects on maximal cardiovascular performance. The 6-Minute Walk Test is useful for submaximal performance assessment in frail/comorbid elderly.

**Oxidative stress:** Physical activity counterbalances ROS accumulation by activating antioxidant systems (SODs, heat shock proteins, catalase), reduces oxidant generation during ischemia-reperfusion, and contributes to decreased arterial stiffness and improved endothelial function.

**Sarcopenic and frail patients:** Resistance exercise training (RET) improves lean tissue mass, muscle strength, and physical performance measures (time up and go, gait speed, 6-min walking distance). Endurance training adds aerobic capacity benefits; combining both is recommended.

**HFREF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction):** Endurance training increases peak VO2 by 20-25%, which correlates with survival. Mechanisms include increased cardiac output, favorable LV remodeling, restored beta-adrenergic receptor signaling, increased skeletal muscle perfusion and oxygen extraction, reduced ergoreflexes, and reduced MuRF-1 (ubiquitin-proteasome system component). High-intensity interval training may be superior to moderate continuous training for improving LV ejection fraction and peripheral vascular function. Resistance training has modest effects compared to aerobic training.

**HFPEF (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction):** Predominantly affects elderly and female patients. Exercise training increases peak VO2 primarily through increased A-VO2 difference. Reduced peak exercise HR (chronotropic incompetence) is reversed by training. No evidence of benefit on LV diastolic properties. Gender differences in CO response noted.

**Exercise program recommendations:** Programs of 8-12 weeks provide benefits similar to adults; longer programs (>12 weeks) may be needed. Training should include endurance aerobic exercise on cycle or treadmill 3 times/week, sessions of 5-60 minutes (typically ~30 min), training HR of 50-60% to 75-80% of MHR, warm-up/cool-down periods, Borg scale for perceived exertion monitoring, and slow progression for frail/deconditioned elderly.

**Conclusion:** Aging does not contraindicate exercise training in healthy elderly or those with comorbidities. Future programs should incorporate cognitive therapy, occupational therapy, balance exercises, counseling, and dietary education. Larger controlled studies are needed to definitively confirm benefits on cardiovascular outcomes.
</summary>

# Carbohydrate knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices, of endurance athletes who report exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms

Rachel Scrivin 1,2\*

Ricardo J. S. Costa 3

Fiona Pelly 1

Dana Lis 4

Gary Slater 1

1. School of Health and Behavioural Sciences, University of the Sunshine Coast, Sippy Downs, QLD, Australia

2. Faculty of Health, Education and Environment, Te Pukenga, New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology, Tauranga, New Zealand

3. Department of Nutrition Dietetics and Food, Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia

4. Department of Neurobiology, Physiology and Behaviour, University of California, Davis, CA, United States

Article metrics

## Abstract

This study aimed to explore carbohydrate (CHO) knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices of endurance athletes who experience exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) compared to those without Ex-GIS. A validated online questionnaire was completed by endurance athletes (*n* = 201) participating in >60 min of exercise that present with Ex-GIS (*n* = 137) or without (*n* = 64). Descriptive statistics were used for parametric and non-parametric data with appropriate significance tests. Associations between categorical data were assessed by Chi-square analysis, and post-hoc Bonferroni tests were applied when significant. A content analysis of open-ended responses was grouped into themes, and quantitative statistics were applied. Participants included runners (*n =* 114, 57%), triathletes (*n* = 43, 21%) and non-running sports (*n* = 44, 21%) who participate in recreational competitive (*n* = 74, 37%), recreational non-competitive (*n* = 64, 32%), or competitive regional, national, or international levels (*n* = 63, 31%). Athletes correctly categorized CHO (*x̄* = 92–95%) and non-CHO (*x̄* = 88–90%) food and drink sources. On a Likert scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) athletes typically agree or strongly agree that consuming CHO around key training sessions and competitions enhances athletic performance [median = 4 (IQR, 4–5)], and they intend to consume more CHO around exercise [median = 3 (IQR, 2–3)]. No differences in beliefs and intentions were found among athletes with or without Ex-GIS. To enhance athletic performance, most endurance athletes intend to consume more CHO around exercise. Adequate knowledge of CHO-containing food sources was apparent; however, specific CHO ingestion practices remain to be verified.

## Introduction

Endurance athletes frequently report developing gastrointestinal symptoms around exercise, e.g., bloating, urge to defecate, burping, regurgitation, and diarrhea, referred to as exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) ([1](#ref1)–[3](#ref3)). Ex-GIS develop through the gastrointestinal circulatory or neuro-endocrine pathways or *via* mechanical strain on the peritoneal cavity ([2](#ref2), [4](#ref4)). A description of Ex-GIS has been defined within the exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome model, outlining the complex pathophysiology involved in the development of Ex-GIS ([5](#ref5), [6](#ref6)). Many endurance athletes who report Ex-GIS implement strategies to manage symptomology ([7](#ref7)–[9](#ref9)), including reducing CHO-rich foods such as bread, cereals, milk, and yoghurt ([7](#ref7)). Therefore, endurance athletes with Ex-GIS may be modifying their dietary intake to reduce Ex-GIS development, perhaps at the expense of their CHO intake. Given the critical role carbohydrates play as a substrate during exercise to support performance enhancement ([10](#ref10), [11](#ref11)), carbohydrate intake guidelines have been established for athletes, including total daily targets, plus specific guidance before, during, and after exercise ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)).

Endurance athletes typically train for >60 min several times a week. However, the recommended CHO intake ranges vary depending on the duration and intensity of exercise ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). An individualized approach is recommended for CHO consumption, however as a general guideline of 3 g.kg−1.d−1 CHO for low-intensity or skill-based training, up to 8–10 g.kg−1.d−1 CHO for moderate to high-intensity or sustained exercise ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). For key training sessions or competitions, 10–12 g.kg−1.d−1 CHO, 24–36 h before sustained endurance events, is associated with improved performance ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). During endurance exercise lasting 1–3 h, it is recommended that athletes consume 30–60 g.h−1 CHO ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). More extended endurance activities lasting >3 h, 90 g.h−1 CHO from multiple transportable CHO sources (i.e., glucose and fructose in a ratio of 2:1) to increase CHO availability and CHO oxidation efficiency, thereby reducing fatigue and improving athletic performance ([12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). Despite these recommendations, many endurance athletes do not meet daily CHO targets leading up to competition ([14](#ref14)) or during endurance events ([3](#ref3), [15](#ref15), [16](#ref16)), possibly due to a lack of practicing with race day nutrition or experimenting with food and fluid quantities to determine feeding tolerance and preferences ([17](#ref17)). Individuals who experience Ex-GIS may be more susceptible to not achieving CHO intake targets due to varied dietary strategies implemented to reduce symptomology ([7](#ref7)–[9](#ref9)).

Interestingly, athletes that present with Ex-GIS may benefit from the ingestion of CHO during exercise, as this strategy has been shown to reduce the development and severity of Ex-GIS and mitigate disruptions to the integrity of the intestinal epithelium ([2](#ref2), [18](#ref18)–[22](#ref22)). CHO consumed during exercise increases portal vein blood supply, enhancing blood flow to the splanchnic region ([23](#ref23)). This likely increases intestinal epithelial blood flow, thereby reducing intestinal injury and the subsequent development of gastrointestinal complications ([18](#ref18), [19](#ref19)). However, ingestion of CHO above an individual’s tolerance level may exacerbate Ex-GIS, irrespective of exercise duration or intensity ([24](#ref24)).

This exploratory study investigates the CHO knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices of endurance athletes who report Ex-GIS. Due to the complex pathophysiology of the development of Ex-GIS, it is hypothesized that endurance athletes who experience Ex-GIS may have beliefs and intentions about CHO consumption that varies from sports nutrition guidelines or recommendations ([10](#ref10), [12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)).

## Methods

### Participants

This exploratory study applied a validated online questionnaire investigating endurance athletes who report Ex-GIS and their CHO knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices ([25](#ref25)) ([Supplementary file 1](#SM1)), compared to a subgroup of athletes without Ex-GIS. Convenience sampling was used for athlete recruitment given researchers had associations with endurance athlete groups or professional contacts who support endurance athletes. Endurance athletes ≥18 years (y) of age, participating in endurance events ≥60 minutes (min), were invited to participate in the study. Only questions related to CHO knowledge, beliefs, intended practices and sports nutrition strategies were included in this study. Specific questions regarding nutritional strategies for managing Ex-GIS, including the use of nutritional supplements were excluded, as this has been previously reported ([26](#ref26)).

This study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia), ethics approval number S201402 and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki for human research. Athletes accessed the questionnaire online through Qualtrics Core XM survey platform (RRID:SCR\_016728) (Qualtrics LLC, 333 West River Park Drive, Provo, UT 84604, United States). Athletes were required to provide written informed consent and all data collected was anonymous. Demographic data collected included biological sex and age. Other information collected included main sport, participation level, and event characteristics (single-day or multi-day).

### Questionnaire

Using a dichotomous scale, 15 food and drink options were categorized as CHO or non-CHO food or drink sources to determine athletes CHO knowledge. Athletes rated their beliefs about consuming CHO for enhancing athletic performance at various time points around exercise on a Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The time points assessed were 1–2 days before events lasting ≥90 min, in the last meal or snack before endurance training or events lasting ≥90 min, during endurance exercise or an event lasting ≥60 min, and within 30 min after endurance exercise when there is <8 h between events. Athletes also rated their intention to consume CHO at various time points around exercise on a Likert scale from 1 (intend to eat less), 2 (intend to eat the same) or 3 (intend to eat more). A content analysis was conducted on open-ended responses collected on self-selected nutritional strategies implemented around exercise, which were reviewed by the research team and categorized into themes ([27](#ref27)).

### Statistical analysis

To enable comparisons between larger data sets, cycling, swimming, walking, multisport, and other sports were collapsed into a new category called non-running sports. Additional data was collapsed when categories had more than 20% of the cells with less than an expected count of five, e.g., competitive regional, national, and international participation groups were collapsed into a new category, ‘CompRNI’. The Shapiro Wilks test was used to determine normality of data and homogeneity of variances before other appropriate tests were applied. Parametric data were described as the mean ± standard deviation, and for non-parametric data, the median and interquartile range (IQR). For parametric data, continuous variables were analyzed using independent samples t-tests with Cohen’s *d* for effect sizes and the Mann–Whitney U test for non-parametric data. For categorical data, sex, main sport, participation level, and event characteristics, were assessed for associations using Chi-square analysis and Bonferroni post-hoc tests applied when significant. Open-ended responses were categorized into themes, with quantitative frequency statistics applied. Significance was accepted with α ≤0.05. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0 (RRID:SCR\_019096) (IBM Corporation New Orchard Road Armonk, NY 10504-1722, United States).

## Results

Two hundred and one endurance athletes completed the validated online questionnaire ([25](#ref25)), with 137 reporting Ex-GIS. No differences were found in responses regarding CHO knowledge, beliefs or intended practices in those athletes who also reported a diagnosed gastrointestinal disease or disorder (*n* = 15). Therefore, all responses from this subgroup were collapsed and included in data analysis for those with Ex-GIS.

As this was an exploratory study, a *post-hoc* G\*Power (version 3.1.9.7 (RRID:SCR\_013726) calculation was used to determine if the desired sample size was attained. A goodness-of-fit test was used with a medium effect size (*w* = 0.3), alpha (α) of 0.05 and total sample size of 201; this determined that adequate power of 0.92 was achieved ([28](#ref28)).

### Demographics and event characteristics

When comparing athletes reporting Ex-GIS with those without Ex-GIS, no significant group differences were found for sex and age within groups or between groups ([Table 1](#tab1)). The mean age from the Ex-GIS cohort was 42 ± 11 y compared to 40 ± 11 y in those without Ex-GIS (*t*(129) = 1.1, *p* = 0.3, *d* = 0.2). More females with Ex-GIS (*n* = 86, 63%) completed the questionnaire, however this was not significantly different to males (*df* = 1, *x*2 = 0.7, *p* = 0.7) ([Table 1](#tab1)). After Chi-square analysis, no associations were found between main sport and participation level, event characteristics for both those with Ex-GIS and those without Ex-GIS ([Table 2](#tab2)).

## Discussion

This exploratory study aimed to investigate the CHO knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices of endurance athletes who report Ex-GIS. The main results from the study indicate that endurance athletes with reported Ex-GIS have similar carbohydrate knowledge scores, beliefs, intentions and nutrition strategies as endurance athletes without Ex-GIS. In contrast to our hypothesis, the majority of endurance athletes who report Ex-GIS strongly agreed or agreed that CHO consumed around exercise enhances athletic performance, and they also intend to consume more CHO around exercise to improve their athletic performance. Through a content analysis of open-ended responses, the most common self-reported dietary strategy implemented around exercise was increasing CHO intake, particularly before endurance exercise. These findings broadly align with recommended sports nutrition CHO guidelines ([10](#ref10), [12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)); however, further research is required to determine specific CHO amounts endurance athletes with Ex-GIS plan to consume around exercise. It is acknowledged that when determining specific CHO intakes during exercise, an individualized approach is advocated to gauge the upper limits of whole-body CHO oxidation rates alongside glucose availability, Ex-GIS and feeding tolerance ([24](#ref24), [29](#ref29)).

In the current investigation, it has been established that endurance athletes with reported Ex-GIS appear to have the intent and CHO knowledge to increase their daily CHO intake in preparation for, during, and in the recovery period after exercise. However, this is not always the case. Findings from a recent investigation that used a validated questionnaire to determine endurance athletes’ knowledge of competition CHO guidelines show athletes scored less than 50% of total correct responses from five areas ([30](#ref30)). The five areas investigated were knowledge about CHO storage and metabolism, pre-competition CHO loading, and CHO consumption before, during, and after competition ([30](#ref30)). When comparing studies, confirming endurance athletes’ current sports nutrition knowledge level can be challenging due to the heterogeneity between questionnaires, e.g., questionnaire design, specific questionnaire tools used, or target population ([31](#ref31)). Athletes with Ex-GIS likely require a greater level of nutrition knowledge to increase CHO intakes while moderating factors that may exacerbate Ex-GIS, such as dietary fiber or fermentable oligo-, di-, monosaccharide and polyols. Athletes may seek the support of an accredited practicing dietitian to assist them in negotiating the complex interaction that can result when attempting to increase carbohydrates for endurance exercise while moderating factors known to exacerbate Ex-GIS. Accredited dietitians are a preferred source of nutrition information for athletes with Ex-GIS ([7](#ref7)); however, as with this study, it is likely that due to convenience sampling, athletes may have had prior exposure to dietetic expertise and therefore were more likely to understand fuel mechanics for endurance exercise, thereby resulting in high CHO knowledge scores.

Increasing CHO around endurance exercise was the most commonly self-reported dietary strategy. It is well-documented that consuming CHO around exercise improves athletic performance, reduces fatigue and facilitates muscle glycogen restoration after exercise ([10](#ref10), [12](#ref12), [13](#ref13)). Furthermore, consuming CHO before and during exercise ameliorates intestinal epithelial damage and permeability during exercise ([21](#ref21)), leading to less reported Ex-GIS ([18](#ref18)). Observational field studies on endurance athletes without Ex-GIS have also found that CHO consumed during endurance events had no or minimal relationship with the development of gastrointestinal symptoms ([1](#ref1), [14](#ref14), [16](#ref16)) or performance times ([32](#ref32)). However, most athletes were not consuming recommended CHO targets of up to 90 g.h−1 CHO for endurance exercise >3 h ([1](#ref1), [15](#ref15), [16](#ref16), [32](#ref32)).

It is likely that to improve gastrointestinal tolerance (i.e., less Ex-GIS development) when consuming CHO during exercise, athletes may require a period of gut training ([19](#ref19), [20](#ref20), [24](#ref24)). Studies implementing a gut-training protocol have shown less reported Ex-GIS and improved performance times ([19](#ref19), [20](#ref20)). Therefore, in an athlete’s nutritional plan, a period of gut training may be warranted to reduce Ex-GIS development during exercise and benefit from higher CHO oxidation rates due to greater exogenous CHO availability ([19](#ref19), [20](#ref20)).

The current study did not investigate the quantification of CHO intake among endurance athletes with Ex-GIS. Athletes have indicated they intend to increase their CHO intake around exercise to enhance performance. However, it is still unknown if they meet the recommended CHO targets for endurance training and recovery; as previous research indicates that many endurance athletes without pre-existing Ex-GIS are not meeting the recommended CHO targets ([1](#ref1), [15](#ref15), [16](#ref16), [33](#ref33)). This information would be valuable for practitioners when providing nutrition education and meal planning around CHO intakes to support athletic performance.

This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (12 April 2023) by Rachel Scrivin and colleagues from the University of the Sunshine Coast (Australia), Monash University, and UC Davis. The study explored the carbohydrate (CHO) knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices of endurance athletes who report exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) compared to those without these symptoms.

METHODOLOGY: A validated online questionnaire was completed by 201 endurance athletes (≥18 years, participating in events ≥60 min), of whom 137 reported Ex-GIS and 64 did not. Participants included runners (57%), triathletes (21%), and non-running sports (21%). Athletes categorized 15 food/drink items as CHO or non-CHO sources, rated their beliefs about CHO consumption timing around exercise (1-2 days before, before, during, after) on a 5-point Likert scale, and rated their intentions to consume CHO (eat less/same/more) on a 3-point scale. Chi-square analysis with Bonferroni post-hoc adjustments and content analysis of open-ended responses were employed. The study achieved adequate power of 0.92.

KEY RESULTS:
- Athletes with Ex-GIS correctly categorized CHO foods (95%) and non-CHO foods (88%) at rates similar to athletes without Ex-GIS (92% and 90% respectively).
- No significant differences were found in CHO beliefs or intentions between athletes with and without Ex-GIS at any time point.
- The majority of athletes agreed or strongly agreed that consuming CHO around exercise enhances athletic performance (median = 4 on a 5-point scale), and intended to consume more CHO around exercise (median = 3).
- The most commonly self-reported dietary strategy was increasing CHO intake (58% of responses), reported by both groups, particularly before exercise.
- Other reported strategies included reducing dietary fiber and increasing protein, fluid, and electrolytes.
- No significant demographic differences (sex, age, sport, competition level) were found between groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Contrary to the study hypothesis, endurance athletes with Ex-GIS demonstrate adequate CHO knowledge, positive beliefs about CHO's performance-enhancing role, and intentions to increase CHO intake around exercise, similar to athletes without Ex-GIS. Findings broadly align with sports nutrition guidelines. The authors note that gut training protocols may help athletes improve gastrointestinal tolerance when consuming CHO during exercise, and that further research is needed to verify specific CHO ingestion amounts. The study was funded by the University of the Sunshine Coast and approved by its Human Research Ethics Committee (approval S201402).

# New Guidelines for Nutrition and Athletic Performance

By [The Feed.](/insider/author/the-feed)6 min read

Last week, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (AND), Dietitians of Canada (DC), and American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) published new position statement titled "Nutrition and Athletic Performance". Whether or not you believe that these organizations will make good recommendations for you specifically, it's important to note that a large group of incredibly smart people created this report based on the *latest scientific understanding*. What's that mean for you? It means that learning from position statements like this can help guide your own personal nutrition strategy. With that said, it should be no surprise to you that we've been scouring the position statement and working on condensing it down into a short version that you can review. **Position Statement**:
> *It is the position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine that the performance of, and recovery from, sporting activities are enhanced by well-chosen nutrition strategies. These organizations provide guidelines for the appropriate type, amount and timing of intake of food, fluids and dietary supplements to promote optimal health and sport performance across different scenarios of training and competitive sport.*

The study was conducted with an evidence-based analysis from data gathered over 8 years. The study outlines 10 key points which we've paraphrased for you here:

1. It's likely that your training is periodized so that you're in top shape before a key event. Your nutrition strategy during these training periods should also be periodized based on training needs.
2. Nutrition plans should always be specific to an individual athlete, and their goals.
3. Training should focus on developing metabolic efficiency, while fueling for competition should focus on meeting the energy needs for that event.
4. Energy availability is a critical variable for sports nutrition strategies.
5. Like nutrition strategy, body composition for optimal performance needs to be periodized and executed carefully. Note that being "skinnier" or "leaner" is NOT a guarantee for higher performance.
6. Strategies should be implemented during training that will help the body adapt to competition fueling.
7. Guidelines for nutrient *timing* are just as important as guidelines for grams per KG of body weight in macro-nutrients consumed (carbs, fats, proteins).
8. Fueling during competition should be focused on a strategy that reduces fatigue, and are specific to the event and conditions surrounding the event (such as weather).
9. There is robust evidence to support the idea that rinsing your mouth with a carbohydrate solution creates an immediate impact in the brain and may allow athletes to increase work-rates during exercise. Note that a mouth rinse in this case does not mean ingesting the carbohydrate!
10. While certain supplements may aid performance, athletes should consider the cost / benefit analysis before using supplemental nutrition. Supplements are generally of greatest value when used in conjunction with a good diet.

**Carbohydrate Recommendations**: It's critical to note that carbohydrate enhances performance during "prolonged sustained or intermittent high-intensity exercise". Strategies that maintain "high carbohydrate availability" before, during and after will result in performance gains. The study also notes:
> *The amount and localization of glycogen within the muscle cell alters the physical, metabolic, and hormonal environment in which the signaling responses to exercise are exerted.*

Translation: glycogen has a huge impact on more than just going fast during a race. Athletes need to be aware of this as they plan nutrition for training days, which likely needs to be done days in advance of a training session (not just the morning before). This also doesn't mean "eat a huge amount of carbohydrate". The study notes that training with reduced glycogen stores (such as two workouts per day) results in benefits beyond the actual training input. **Summary of Guidelines For Carbohydrate Intake by Athletes**: The study breaks this down into two categories: "Daily Needs for Fuel and Recovery" and "Acute Fueling Strategies" (focused on optimal performance during an event). Daily Needs for Fuel and Recovery:

* Light Activity: lower intensity or skill based activities, 3-5 grams per kg of body weight. Note that a 70 kilogram (154 lbs) athlete in this category would shoot for between 210 grams and 350 grams per day.
* Moderate Activity: exercise at a moderate pace, roughly 1 hour per day, target 5-7 grams per kg of body weight. A 70 kilogram (154 lbs) athlete would shoot for between 350 grams and 490 grams per day.
* High Activity: this is a typical endurance program, non-elite athlete, working out 1-3 hours per day and moderate to high intensity, 6-10 grams per kg of body weight. A 70 kilogram (154 lbs) athlete would shoot for between 420 grams and 700 grams per day.
* Extreme Activity: 4 to 5 hours per day of moderate to high intensity exercise (Tour de France athlete), 8-12 grams per kg of body weight. A 70 kilogram (154 lbs) athlete would shoot for between 560 grams and 840 grams per day.

Acute Fueling Strategies:

* Prep for events less than 90 minutes long: 7-12 grams per kg of body weight in 24 hours prior as daily fuel needs.
* Prep for events lasting more than 90 minutes: 10-12 grams per kg of body weight consumed each day, 36-48 hours before the event.
* Optimal recovery between 2 demanding training sessions: 1-1.2 grams per kg of body weight PER HOUR for first 4 hours.
* Pre-event fueling, exercise lasting less than 60 minutes: 1-4 grams per kg of body weight, consumed 1-4 hours before.
* During exercise lasting 45 minutes or less, food is not needed.
* During exercise lasting 45-75 minutes, small amounts of carbohydrate will help, including a mouth rinse.
* During exercise lasting 1-2.5 hours, consume 30-60 grams of carbohydrate per hour.
* During exercise longer than 2.5-3 hours, consume up to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour.

**While we have published a portion of the study here, we highly recommend reading the entire text, which can be found here**: <http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/Fulltext/2016/03000/Nutrition_and_Athletic_Performance.25.aspx>

# Position of the Working Group Sports Nutrition of the German Nutrition Society (DGE): Carbohydrates in Sports Nutrition

## Position der Arbeitsgruppe Sporternährung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Ernährung (DGE): Kohlenhydrate in der Sporternährung

1

3

4

OLYMPIASTÜTZPUNKT RHEINLAND-PFALZ/ SAARLAND, Germany

5

6

7
