........................................................................................................................................13 2 Nutrition and Performance in Masters Athletes 1.1  INTRODUCTION Ageing is associated with major changes in almost all physiological systems. These age-related changes influence both the health and exercise capacity of the masters athlete. On one level, many of these age-related changes affect appetite, food intake and nutrient absorption and thus the potential to affect substrate availability at the exercising muscle. On another level, age-related changes to the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems affect the energy systems used during exercise in addi-tion to the force-generating capacity of the muscles. This chapter reviews a number of age-related changes that occur to several physiological systems and the affect these changes may have on the nutritional needs of masters athletes. Furthermore, the chapter will examine the extent to which regular physical activity across the lifespan is likely to impact on these changes.
1.2  CHANGES IN BODY COMPOSITION AND ENERGY NEEDS 1.2.1  Sarcopenia Sarcopenia is a syndrome which can be characterised by progressive and generalised loss of muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability poor quality of life and death. In normal ageing, the rate of muscle mass decline after 40 years of age has been shown to be approximately 0.5%–1% per year which is heightened in the sixth decade of life [1]. Both men and women between the ages of 40 and 80 years lose 30%–50% of their skeletal muscle mass [2]. For most older adults, the decrease in muscle mass is accompanied by a 1%–1.5% per year reduction in strength [3] and power [4], independent of body mass [5].
Sarcopenia occurs in response to endocrine, inflammatory and nutritional changes; genetic and reduced levels of physical activity are also strong influences [6]. A change in the mass of a given muscle is due primarily to a change in the cross sectional area of individual fibres and/or a loss in the number of fibres. Age-related changes in the nervous system contribute to sarcopenia via a reduction in the number of functioning motor units [7]. The loss of motor units is marked by a grad-ual reduction during the first seven decades of life followed by a sharp decline into very old age [8].
The loss of motor units with ageing appears to involve almost exclusively the type II muscle fibres [9] and reductions in both the size and number of type II fibres is believed to explain most of the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and power [3]. Although the loss in the number of fibres within muscles appears inevitable, the magnitude of loss may be ameliorated to some degree by ade-quate dietary protein intake and resistance training [10]. The protein needs of the masters athlete will be addressed in Chapter 6. Below we provide a brief summary of the benefits of resistance training.
1.2.2  Resistance Training Although the influence of chronic resistance exercise on muscle mass and muscle function has been extensively studied in older populations, the specific effects of ageing on muscular performance or efficiency has been difficult to assess because of the confounding effects of a reduction in physical activity levels, changes in body composition and development of clinical diseases. Elite masters weightlifters appear to lose lean lower limb volume at a slower rate than age-matched untrained control subjects; however, they lose normalised (relative to body weight) isometric (static hold) strength and power in specific muscle groups at a slightly higher rate [11]. Interestingly, women appear to experience greater age-related declines in muscular strength and power than men, particu-larly in the upper extremities [12]. However, resistance-trained masters athletes have significantly greater muscle mass, higher strength per muscle thickness ratio and muscle performance charac-teristics than their age-matched sedentary peers, supporting the suggestion that chronic resistance exercise has the potential to delay and diminish alterations in skeletal muscle mass and function with ageing [13]. In addition, older strength-trained individuals have been reported to have greater 3 Physiological Changes Affecting the Nutritional Needs of Masters Athletes muscle quality as a function of power per muscle volume [14]. This is likely due to less fat intrusion and maintenance of muscle architecture.
1.2.3  Endurance Training The influence of chronic endurance training on age-related changes in muscle mass and function has also been extensively researched. Both total body mass and fat-free mass appear to be maintained in ageing endurance-trained adults, whereas sedentary adults demonstrate a significant increase in fat and total body mass with age [15]. Skeletal muscle in endurance-trained masters athletes adapts structurally and metabolically to chronic endurance training [16] with evidence suggesting that chronic intense exercise preserves muscle mass and prevents fat infiltration of muscle in masters athletes [15].
Endurance-trained masters athletes have significantly greater values of maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) compared with age-matched sedentary individuals. However, endurance-trained men and women appear to have greater absolute rates of decline in VO2max with advancing age compared with healthy sedentary adults. Yet, when expressed as a percent reduction, the approximate 10% decline in VO2max per decade from 25 years of age is similar between endurance-trained masters athletes and sedentary adults [17]. Both Katzel and others [18] and Eskurza and others [17] suggest that high-intensity endurance training may delay age-associated decrements in VO2max; however, training load reductions which appear to be inevitable with ageing, lead to accelerated losses in VO2max. Differences in the absolute rate of decline in VO2max observed between these groups may be attributed to declines in maximal stroke volume (and therefore maximal cardiac output) and/or skeletal muscle oxidative capacity. Decreases in VO2max appear to be greater than the age-related decline in endurance performance; the lactate threshold did not appear to change with age when expressed as a percentage of VO2max [19].
Despite an age-related reduction in VO2max, masters athletes retain a high capacity to store glyco-gen in liver and muscle, to use glycogen as a source of energy-producing substrate during submaxi-mal endurance exercise and to restore muscle glycogen levels post-exercise [20]. Slight reductions in glycogen concentration have been reported in older sedentary adults, possibly due to lower resting levels of insulin-regulated glucose transporter (GLUT4) and relatively reduced muscle activity [21]. However, short-duration exercise training can increase GLUT4 levels in older previously sedentary adults similar to the response seen in younger adults [22]. As well, compared to younger athletes, masters athletes may consume less than optimal amounts of carbohydrate (i.e. 6 g/kg/d) due to changes in taste and smell. This may potentially reduce muscle glycogen concentrations and poten-tially limit performance.
In summary, masters athletes who engage in regular exercise that involves the recruitment of type II (and particularly the type IIb) fibres are likely to slow the age-related loss in muscle mass and strength. In addition, the timely intake of high-quality protein may assist not only in the short-term recovery of muscle following exercise but benefit the longer-term maintenance of muscle mass. Although endurance training results in higher VO2max values compared to inactive age-matched controls, there appears an inevitable decline in maximal aerobic capacity with age.
1.3  CHANGES IN TASTE AND SMELL 1.3.1  Taste and Smell Perception The gradual loss of taste and smell that occurs with advancing age has been extensively investigated [23]. Taste changes are broadly classified into three categories: total loss of taste (ageusia), reduced ability to taste (hypogeusia) or distortion of taste (dysgeusia). While total loss of taste is rare at any age, taste perception generally changes with age. Individuals with a reduced ability to taste have a diminished capacity to detect or recognise taste stimuli. Moreover, the intensity of taste thresholds 4 Nutrition and Performance in Masters Athletes (detection thresholds and recognition thresholds) is elevated. A taste detection threshold is the con-centration for the absolute threshold of taste sensation while a taste recognition threshold is the lowest concentration at which a taste source is correctly identified. The significance of this is that taste distortions may contribute to less than optimal food choices, which potentially may result in failure to meet the nutritional needs that accompany advancing age. This has clear implications for older masters athletes who require an adequate intake of carbohydrate and fluid (pre-, during and post-exercise) in order to delay fatigue during exercise and facilitate recovery following training and competition.
Sensations of food in the mouth are presumed to be related to taste, but are in fact partially produced by aroma or smell. When food is placed in the oral cavity, the odorous molecules move up the back of the throat, and the smell is perceived retro-nasally. Odours sensed at a meal are predominantly perceived retro-nasally. With ageing, anatomical and physiological changes result in olfactory deficits and taste and smell signals cannot serve as cues for the metabolic consequences of food ingestion. Again, an awareness of these changes by masters athletes can help individuals compensate for potential changes in food choices that could compromise an adequate intake essen-tial nutrients.
1.3.2  Taste Sensitivity The decline in taste sensitivity with age appears to be greater in men than in women. Cohen and Gitman found that men had a higher incidence of taste errors than women when they had to recognise the basic tastes of sour, sweet, salty and bitter [24]. Glanville and others showed a gradual increase in sensitivity up to the age of 16–20 years, followed by an exponential decline in both men and women [25]. Weiffenbach and others [26] found that within each age group the thresholds for citric acid of men were higher than those of women, whilst other investigators did not find gender differences [27,28]. A few researchers have reported gender differences in sensi-tivity to just one or two substances. For example, Fikentscher and others [29] found that women were more sensitive than men to salt (NaCl), cane sugar, citric acid and quinine; this difference became significant in individuals older than 50 years of age. However, others reported the per-ception of salt was more affected by age in men compared to women, and was more pronounced for sucrose, citric acid, caffeine and quinine [23]. Therefore, older endurance-trained athletes, especially males, need to be aware of this potential reduction in perception of salt intake with age, particularly when exercising in hot/humid conditions where sports drinks and salt tablets may be consumed.
Older adults often have a lower salivary response to food intake [30], and dissatisfaction with the ability to taste food is associated with dry mouth during chewing [31]. With 50% of older adults experiencing saliva deficiency and dryness of the mouth [32], this dry mouth has clear implications for the masters athlete with regard to food and fluid intake, hydration and electrolyte balance during endurance training and competition. Given that there are currently no effective treatments for per-sistent impairment of the sense of taste, older athletes need to be aware of potential taste alterations and the impact these may have on their nutritional needs during training and competition.
Schiffman and others have suggested that taste impairment with age may be partially due to an increase in medication use [33]. The degree of loss in taste sensitivity may depend on the chemical structure of the compounds tested as well as the medical condition and pharmacological regimen of the individual [34]. It is important to be aware of individual differences observed for most com-pounds because individuals age physiologically at different rates and therefore the loss of taste and smell may occur earlier for some than for others [35].
In summary, loss of appetite may be experienced by many masters athletes following demanding exercise and when age-related changes in tastes and smell are considered. The masters athlete needs to consume foods with richer tastes and relatively strong but appetising smells in order for them to meet the nutritional requirements that support high-quality training and competition.
5 Physiological Changes Affecting the Nutritional Needs of Masters Athletes 1.4  CHANGES IN THE GASTROINTESTINAL TRACT 1.4.1  Motility Many older adults experience minor yet significant deterioration in gastrointestinal motility and function [36,37]. For masters athletes this may increase the risks of malnutrition and negatively impact on their capacity to train and compete. Age-related changes in gastrointestinal motility include impaired oesophageal peristalsis, delayed gastric emptying, an increase in colon transit times and eventual weight loss and nutritional deficiencies [37]. For older athletes the challenge is to ensure that these changes do not compromise energy and fluid intake. Awareness of such changes allow for the possibility to compensate so that both training and competition performances are maintained.
1.4.2  Absorption Reduced absorption of certain nutrients is a common cause of malnutrition in older adults with the primary cause being a reduced production of gastric acid (atrophic gastritis) which leads to bacterial overgrowth and a reduction in the formation of gastric intrinsic factor [32]. Sufficient stomach acid and intrinsic factor are required for the absorption of a variety of micronutrients, including iron, folate, calcium, vitamin K and vitamin B12. In addition to a reduced uptake of a number of essen-tial nutrients, atrophic gastritis can result in anaemia, abdominal discomfort, nausea, diarrhoea and weight loss [32]. Moreover, a higher bacterial content in the intestines increases the fermentation of carbohydrate which can cause flatulence, diarrhoea, obstipation (severe or chronic constipation) and abdominal cramps. This may influence the ability or willingness of the older athlete to exercise [32].
In addition to an age-related decrease in the synthesis of vitamin D in the skin, there is decreased absorption of vitamin D in the gastrointestinal tract with age due to decline in the number of vitamin D receptors in the intestinal epithelium [37]. Irrespective of whether the older individual is physically active, there will be a reduced capacity for them to synthesise Vitamin D which in turn will reduce their capacity to absorb dietary calcium and increase their risk of bone fractures. Supplementation with vitamin D and calcium may therefore be needed for older masters athletes [38].
The heterogeneity of the older population with regard to biological age, disease and medication intake makes evaluations of normal/abnormal function of the gastrointestinal tract complex. An individualised approach is therefore required to determine specific nutritional requirements of the older masters athlete or older exerciser, particularly in those individuals who have gastrointestinal issues. These individuals should consult with a dietitian to optimise their diet.
1.5  CHANGES IN WATER BALANCE 1.5.1  Water Loss Water balance is critical for both health and maintenance of exercise capacity. Indeed, a meta-​ analyses has found body water reductions in excess of 4% of body mass impairs endurance time trial performance [39]. Ingestion of both fluids and food provides the major route of water intake, though there is additional water liberated in muscle as a result of glycogen metabolism during exer-cise [40]. Water is lost from the body through urine, faeces, sweat, evaporation from the respiratory tract and diffusion through the skin [41]. Normal ageing is associated with a tendency toward nega-tive water balance, suggesting that masters athletes may be more susceptible to dehydration.
Total body water decreases with age. While approximately 80% of a child’s body mass is water, the average total body water of adults aged 61–74 years is 43% for women and 51% for men [42]. This decrease is observed even when taking into account body mass and energy intake [43]. Thus, even small decreases in fluid intake may cause proportionately greater dehydration in a masters ath-lete than in a younger athlete. Unchecked dehydration can cause changes in body chemistry, kidney 6 Nutrition and Performance in Masters Athletes failure, kidney stones, urinary tract infections, bowel cancer and death [44]. Therefore, educating and promoting adequate fluid intake in masters athletes may be the most important modifiable health behaviour for ensuring fluid homeostasis.
Masters athletes may be at increased risk of dehydration due to age-related changes in total body water, thirst perception, fluid intake, kidney function and insensible water loss. Although thirst and volume of fluid ingested are separate entities, some researchers suggest they seem to be affected in parallel by age [45]. However, other researchers report dissociated thirst ratings from fluid intake where older adults have increased thirst but consume the same volume of water [46]. Other factors that make masters athletes at higher risk to dehydration include a greater use of medications includ-ing diuretics but also sedatives and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) [47].
1.5.2  Water Intake A key factor contributing to an increased risk of dehydration in older athletes is inadequate water intake due to decreased thirst perception. Thirst manifests as a combination of sensations that increase with dehydration and decrease with rehydration (restoration of fluid balance), including a dry, scratchy mouth and throat, chapped and dry lips, light-headedness, dizziness, tiredness, irri-tability, headache, loss of appetite and feeling of an empty stomach. Thirst results from a complex interaction of behavioural influences such as beverage availability, taste, temperature and palatabil-ity, knowledge of the importance of adequate hydration, drinking in association with meals, social and societal norms and habits and even the presence of others who are consuming a beverage [48]. However, increasing the availability or palatability of fluids does not seem to significantly increase fluid intake in older men and women [49]. Of additional concern is that many older adults deliber-ately avoid drinking beverages, especially in the evening, due to fear of incontinence [50].
1.5.3  Thirst Physiological thirst is stimulated by increases in cellular tonicity (cellular dehydration) and de­ ­ creases in extracellular fluid volume (extracellular dehydration) [48]. The former senses the level of dehydration by central, and possibly peripheral osmoreceptors which feed back to the hypo-thalamus to maintain homeostasis. The latter involves monitoring decreases in blood volume from baroreceptors in large vessels and renal mechanisms which elicit the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in response to decreased renal perfusion and other stimuli. A third mechanism which helps regulate the volume of fluid ingested, the act of swallowing, also deserves mention as it provides an integrated signal proportional to the cumulative ingested volume (termed oropharyngeal metering).
Exercise, exogenous heat stress and/or fluid deprivation will decrease blood volume and increase tonicity. Fluid deprivation and exercise both create a hypovolemic (decreased volume of blood plasma), hyperosmotic (increased concentration of penetrating and non-penetrating solute within plasma) condition, the most common environment associated with dehydration. Older individuals appear to be sensitive to increased tonicity but not to fluid volume changes. When the sole stimulus for thirst and drinking is osmotic, there appears to be little difference in thirst sensation in older adults compared to younger individuals [51].
A deficit in the sensitivity of volume receptors appears to be a more important mechanism accounting for reduced thirst with ageing. Available evidence suggests that older men and women have a higher osmotic operating point for thirst sensation under normal daily conditions [45] and diminished sensitivity to thirst and satiety reflexes arising from unloading (hypovolemia) and load-ing (hypervolemia) of baroreceptors, respectively. Fluid restoration in older adults is eventually effective, but restoration of fluid balance is slower. In the longer term (i.e. days to weeks), fluid intake in response to repeated dehydrating stimuli also appears to be reduced, which may con-tribute to a relative inability to expand plasma volume [48]. This has strong implications for fluid replacement following intense exercise in masters athletes and older exercisers. These individuals 7 Physiological Changes Affecting the Nutritional Needs of Masters Athletes need to be diligent with their recovery practices to achieve effective restoration and maintenance of euhydration.
1.5.4  Fluid Regulation Body fluid regulation is influenced by acclimation status. For example, in young adults, repeated bouts of exercise in hot environments have been shown to result in plasma volume expansion pri-marily due to increased voluntary fluid intake [52]. Following 4 days of low-intensity intermittent exercise, young men (24 years) expanded their plasma volume by 10%, whereas no change was observed in the older (67 years) active male group. During the 2-hour recovery period, participants consumed a carbohydrate-electrolyte drink. The young men replaced 80% of lost fluid on average compared to only 34% in older men. This greater involuntary dehydration was accompanied by reduced thirst ratings, plasma vasopressin, aldosterone concentrations and renin activity in the older active group [52]. Zappe and others [52] speculated that the older men may have had lower barore-flex sensitivity and the acclimation program was ineffective in attenuating this sensitivity, and thus fluid intake was not altered. The researchers concluded that the risk of dehydration is increased in elderly subjects regardless of whether they were sedentary or physically active [52].
Studies of the age-related disturbance of water balance have mostly focused on urinary concen-trating ability. As people age the concentrating ability of the kidneys decline [53]. Thus, when older adults are deprived of water, urine output is not significantly reduced, increasing the likelihood of dehydration in older populations. Research suggests that ageing is also associated with kidney atrophy, decreased cortical blood flow and glomerular filtration rate and diminished maximal uri-nary concentrating capacity [53]. These changes can lead to electrolyte imbalances and enhanced water diuresis in older individuals [54]. The age-related reduction of urine concentrating ability may be attributed to decreased sensitivity to the anti-diuretic hormone, vasopressin (AVP) observed in rats [55]. Despite numerous studies of the effect of ageing on plasma AVP in humans, it is still not clear how ageing affects the level of AVP, especially in masters athletes. While some studies report increased basal plasma AVP with ageing, others do not, and some even report a decrease [56]. However, under normal daily living conditions, increased thirst and fluid intake defend against any threats to fluid homeostasis that may result from altered free-water clearance by the kidneys. Therefore, although an inadequate renal response to mild water deprivation may play a role in fluid volume depletion in masters athletes as a result of moderate to intense exercise, reduced thirst is likely more important.
Insensible water loss is a major component of water balance, comparable to daily urine volume. The average water loss through the respiratory tract is approximately 300–400 mL/d, similar to water loss via diffusion through the skin. This combined total of 600–800 mL/d represents 30%–50% of all water loss, depending on the level of water intake [41]. The effects of ageing on insensible water loss have not been extensively studied. Normal aged lungs have dilated alveoli, enlarged airspaces, decreased exchange surface area and loss of supporting tissue in the peripheral airways [57]. Dmitrieva and Burg [40] examined mice of different ages to investigate the factors that contribute to the disturbance of water balance with ageing, and found increased insensible water loss with age. This webpage is the front matter and Chapter 1 from the book "Nutrition and Performance in Masters Athletes," edited by Peter R.J. Reaburn, PhD, published by CRC Press (Taylor & Francis Group) in 2015 (eBook ISBN 978-1-4398-7188-1). The book is dedicated to Ronald (Ronnie) Cox, an inspiring masters athlete who passed away from prostate cancer in 2011. The book contains 18 chapters covering nutritional needs (energy, carbohydrate, fat, protein, vitamins, minerals, fluids, supplements, ergogenic aids) and training/nutrition needs for various masters athlete types (endurance, ultra-endurance, sprint, strength/power, and team sport athletes), plus chapters on chronic disease, drug-nutrient interactions, and physiological changes.

Chapter 1, "Physiological Changes Affecting the Nutritional Needs of Masters Athletes" by David Jenkins, Tina Skinner and Kate Bolam, reviews age-related physiological changes and their impact on nutrition for masters athletes. Key topics covered:

- Sarcopenia: Muscle mass declines ~0.5%-1% per year after age 40, heightened in the sixth decade; men and women aged 40-80 lose 30%-50% of skeletal muscle mass, accompanied by 1%-1.5% per year reduction in strength and power. Type II muscle fibers are predominantly affected. Resistance training and adequate protein can slow this loss.
- Resistance training: Masters athletes have greater muscle mass, strength, and muscle quality than sedentary peers, suggesting chronic resistance exercise delays age-related muscle decline.
- Endurance training: Masters athletes maintain higher VO2max than sedentary counterparts but experience ~10% decline per decade from age 25 (similar to sedentary adults when expressed as percentage). High-intensity training may delay VO2max declines. Masters athletes retain capacity to store and use glycogen.
- Taste and smell changes: Age-related decline in taste (more pronounced in men) can lead to suboptimal food choices and inadequate carbohydrate/fluid intake. Dry mouth affects ~50% of older adults. Medication use can worsen taste impairment.
- Gastrointestinal changes: Reduced gastric acid (atrophic gastritis), impaired motility, delayed gastric emptying, and reduced absorption of micronutrients (iron, folate, calcium, vitamin K, vitamin B12) can compromise nutrition.
- Water balance: Total body water declines with age (43% for women, 51% for men aged 61-74). Reduced thirst perception, diminished baroreceptor sensitivity, reduced kidney concentrating ability, and increased insensible water loss put masters athletes at higher dehydration risk. One study found older men replaced only 34% of lost fluid vs. 80% in young men after exercise. Dehydration >4% of body mass impairs endurance performance.
- Vitamin D: Reduced synthesis in skin and absorption in gut with age increases fracture risk; supplementation may be needed.

Each chapter in the book includes three concluding sections: Implications for Sports Medicine Professionals and Clinicians, Implications for Masters Athletes and Coaches, and Future Research Directions.
args.key_excerpts: "Ageing is associated with major changes in almost all physiological systems. These age-related changes influence both the health and exercise capacity of the masters athlete."

# Nutrition for Aging Athletes

[Diet & Nutrition](/blog/category/Diet+%26+Nutrition)

Written By [Briana Bruinooge](/blog?author=625c04af91b9de460bea228a)

***Masters Athletes aged 30+ years old***

![athlete nutrition](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/1672767932956-6RSYYRIU5BW8G54A21OD/unsplash-image-qZ-U9z4TQ6A.jpg)

As you age, you might notice changes in your body. Rather than working against it, learn more about these changes and what you can do to maintain or improve your health, fitness, body composition and energy levels. For many of my clients, weight loss is a goal because as we age, we tend to hold onto more body fat, especially around the midsection. There are physiological reasons why this may happen and the worst thing you can do is under fuel your body.

Learn more about how to do this as we review who Masters Athletes are, other symptoms of aging, age-related physiological changes and some solutions to slow down the process of age-related physiological changes and reduce symptoms of aging.  We will go over what macronutrients and micronutrients to focus on, as we age and why.

Peak performance in sport depends on optimal nutrition and fitness training. Aging athletes over the age of 30 can experience physiological changes that require special attention to certain macronutrients, proper hydration, and adequate vitamin and mineral intake.

### **Who are Masters Athletes?**

According to The World Masters Athletics organization Masters Athletes defines the age as 35 years for both women and men. For swimming, a Masters athlete begins at age 18, and for golf it is 50 years old.

### **Age-Related Physiological Changes**

* **Maximum oxygen consumption** decreases about10% per decade after age 30

  + In older endurance athletes, this occurs at a slower rate of 5% per decade
* **Type II muscle fibers** (fast-twitch muscles) decrease in size and number

  + Switch from fast to **slow fiber type** (less explosive movement muscle fibers and more sustained aerobic muscle fibers)
* **Mitochondria** decrease in number (mitochondria is where respiration and energy production occur)

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/ac15eaa6-65b0-4b9c-a3d9-da2074f03345/Screenshot+2023-01-03+at+17.30.26.png)

[Figure adapted from here.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4913107/#:~:text=Fatty%20infiltration%20of%20skeletal%20muscle%20(myosteatosis)%20has%2C%20in%20particular,in%20the%20elderly%20(27))

* **Satellite cells** are reduced (satellite cells are involved in the ability of muscle tissue to regenerate”)
* Infiltration of **fat into muscle**
* Increase in fat deposits in skeletal and heart muscle, liver and bone marrow
* **Myosin** is reduced

  + Myosin is a protein that forms (together with actin) the contractile filaments of muscle cells
* **Elasticity of muscle** is reduced

  + Reduced flexibility also due to a loss of water in our tissues and spine and increased stiffness in the joints
* **Muscle strength** declines which can cause a slower gait speed

  + Older adults with low muscle strength can have a 4.3-fold greater risk for slow gait speed and a 2.6 fold greater risk for severe mobility problems (Sports Nutrition. Karpinski et al. 6th ed. Chpt 14: Masters Athletes pg. 299)
  + Sarcopenia is the term used for loss of muscle mass as we age
* **Creatine** and phosphocreatine levels in skeletal muscle are reduced

  + Regeneration of creatine is slower following exercise. It falls about 8% per decade after the age of 30 years. (Karpinski et al.)
* **B-12 and Vitamin D** decreased absorption and utilization
* **Body weight** increases up to age 70 years

  + **Belly fat** increases
  + **Visceral fat** increases(fat around your organs)
  + **Peripheral fat** stores decrease
* Chronic low-level **inflammation**
* **Dehydration** due to less body water, decreased thirst mechanisms, decreased ability for kidneys to concentrate urine (body fluid balance is worsened)
* **Sweating** is reduced due to sweat glands changing as skin ages with less sweat produced per gland

  *\*It is unclear whether some of these age-related physiological metabolic changes are due to age or due to lifestyle such as less exercise.*

### **Solutions To Slowing Down Age-Related Physiological Changes And Reducing Symptoms of Aging**

![athlete nutrition](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/1672767995147-M2YUTFVINHJ93C034T0D/unsplash-image-ljoCgjs63SM.jpg)

**Active Lifestyle and Regular Physical Activity**

People who maintain an **active lifestyle** reap many physiological health benefits. Weight bearing exercises load the skeleton to improve the strength and density of bones**. Regular physical activity** induces a higher cardiopulmonary fitness, reduces risk of coronary heart disease and high blood pressure, reduces the risk of colon cancer, protects against diabetes, builds bone mass, increases muscle strength and balance, manages body weight, decreases anxiety and depression, and improves overall mood.

**Strength Training** **Programs**

A 6-month training program can reverse muscle weakness and improve muscle strength in healthy older adults. Nutrition and resistant exercise are both needed to stimulate muscle protein synthesis.

### **Nutrition Needs for Aging Athletes**

**Water/Fluid** recommendations: water/fluid is probably the most important macronutrient for masters athletes due to physiological changes that make staying hydrated and bouncing back from dehydration more difficult. A programmed and personalized schedule of drinking fluids can reduce the risk for dehydration without overconsuming fluids.

**Protein** recommendations: 1.2g protein per kilogram body weight per day. Older adults need higher intakes of protein than younger adults such as 35-45g protein per meal versus 15-30g protein for younger athletes. The pre-workout meal should include 25-30g protein with a focus on high leucine foods. Leucine is an amino acid involved in muscle protein synthesis. 3g of leucine per meal is recommended.

**Leucine** amounts close to 1g or more per 100g of each food:

![athlete nutrition](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/1672768086732-RPFZGY4DBCBWCGA99QOI/unsplash-image-AnC569NdAJc.jpg)

* *Meat and eggs:* baked ham, beef, chicken breast, chicken wings, deer without visible fat, pork low-fat steak, pork’s sausage, pork’s shoulder, speck, turkey breast or thigh, chicken eggs
* *Dairy*: asiago cheese, ricotta, feta, gorgonzola, gruyere, parmesan, mozzarella, low-fat Greek yogurt
* *Fish*: anchovies, clam, cod, shrimp, mackerel, mussels, salmon sardines, smoked salmon, tuna fish
* *Nuts, seeds, other:* pine nuts, cashews, pistachios, dried sweet almonds, unsweetened cocoa powder

**Creatine** supplementation for those who strength train: 5g/day creatine monohydrate allows for greater training capacity which leads to strength gains in older adults. Creatine supplementation is recommended due to the decrease in creatine and phosphocreatine in the muscles as well as the decrease in regeneration of phosphocreatine following exercise in older adults.

**Fat** recommendations: 1 g/kg body fat/ day or about 20-35% fat of total Caloric intake. Omega 3 fatty acids are anti-inflammatory and as we age, chronic low-grade inflammation can occur. Fat recommendations for older adults are the same for younger adults.

**Carbohydrate** recommendations for older adults is the same calculation for younger adults. The lowest recommended carbohydrate intake for athletes is 3 to 5 g per kg body weight per day with 10-12g/kg body weight on the upper level for athletes training 1-3 hours per day or carbohydrate loading for an endurance event longer than 90 minutes.

### **Nutrients of Concern for Aging Athletes:**

**Vitamin D, E, B12, riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6), folate (B9), calcium, magnesium and zinc**

**Vitamin D:** Aging decreases the ability of the skin to produce vitamin D3. To raise vitamin D levels above 30 ng/mL adults need to supplement with 1,500-2,000 IUs vitamin D3 per day. Minimally, older adults need 800 IUs per day. Vitamin D is a key player in immune and neuromuscular function, cell growth, glucose metabolism, absorption of calcium to avoid brittle bones and reduce inflammation.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/1672768204798-HM01ZMOZO8ADO5E5O5Y4/unsplash-image-vHbw2pf8nbw.jpg)

**Vitamin E** is an antioxidant which stops reactive oxygen species (ROS) production which naturally occurs especially following exercise. Vitamin E is a key player in immune system functioning. Food sources of Vitamin E include plant oils, seeds, and nuts such as almonds, sunflower seeds and peanut butter.

**Vitamin B12** absorption of food sources decreases with age and therefore supplementation may be needed. B12 foods are only found in animal products such as fish, meat, poultry, eggs, and dairy products or fortified cereals and nutritional yeast. If supplementation is needed, a B12 lozenge in the form of methylcobalamin could be useful.

**B2, Riboflavin** plays key roles in energy production and metabolism of fats, drugs, and steroids. Food sources include eggs, organ meats (kidneys and liver), lean meats, milk and fortified cereals and grains.

**B6, Pyridoxine** is involved in more than 100 enzyme reactions within protein, carbohydrate, and fat metabolism with an emphasis on protein metabolism. B6 daily needs increase after age 50 to 1.7 mg for men and 1.5 mg for women from the 1.3 mg recommendation for ages 19-50 years. Food sources of B6 are fish, beef, poultry, starchy vegetables, fortified cereals, and some non-citrus fruits.

**B9, Folate** is involved in making DNA, RNA and protein metabolism. Food sources include spinach, brussels sprouts and other dark leafy greens, fruits and fruit juices, nuts, beans, peas, seafood, meat, eggs, dairy and fortified grains, and cereals.

**Calcium** requirements increase to 1200 mg for women over the age of 51 and men over 71 years old. For those 19-50 years old, calcium recommendations are 1000 mg per day for the non-pregnant or lactating person. It is best to get calcium via food sources such as milk, yogurt and cheese or non-dairy sources like canned sardines and salmon with bones, kale, broccoli and bok choy or fortified foods like orange juice, dairy free milks, cereals, tofu.

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/625c04b1f476f3155fb72bed/1672768284272-XFZTU7K701FUR7QBK0TB/unsplash-image-8B8rxK16oXo.jpg)

**Magnesium** is involved in more than 300 enzymatic reactions in the body including protein synthesis, muscle and nerve function, blood glucose control, and blood pressure regulation. Magnesium is required for energy production. It is involved in bone development and creates DNA, RNA, and the antioxidant glutathione. Magnesium transports calcium and potassium ions across cell membranes which is important for nerve impulse conduction, muscle contraction, and normal heart rhythm. The highest food source of magnesium is roasted pumpkin seeds. Other food sources include: spinach, legumes, nuts, seeds, and whole grains. Adults who are 31 + years old should consume 320 mg magnesium per day for women and 420 mg per day for men. Be careful with supplementation as some supplements can cause a laxative effect. I tend to recommend magnesium glycinate as a supplement 200-300 mg at bedtime.

**Zinc** catalyzes hundreds of enzymes. Zinc is involved in immune function, protein and DNA synthesis, wound healing and cell signaling.  The recommended dietary allowances for zinc are 11 mg for male and 8 mg for females aged 19 years or older. The richest food sources of zinc are meat, fish, and seafood such as oysters and beef. Plant based sources such as beans, nuts and whole grains contain some zinc, but are not highly bioavailable meaning the absorption of zinc in these foods is low.

### **In Summary**

Those aging past 30 years should start to pay attention to protein, fluid and nutrient intakes. Not only do aging athletes need more protein and need to pay attention to fluid intake and certain nutrients, but they need to consume enough fuel to support metabolic needs AND physical activity. Older adults, especially some older women who are frustrated with body changes tend to eat less and exercise more. This effect will have your body hold onto more fat for fear that it is in a state of starvation mode. It will have negative effects on your body’s hormones including the stress-hormone called cortisol which also increases with heavy exercise as it is a sign of stress. If you are frustrated with your body and sport performance, see a Sports Dietitian to nail down nutrition and fitness tailored to your age, gender, and lifestyle.

**References**

1. Hamrick MW, McGee-Lawrence ME, Frechette DM. Fatty Infiltration of Skeletal Muscle: Mechanisms and Comparisons with Bone Marrow Adiposity. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2016 Jun 20;7:69. doi: 10.3389/fendo.2016.00069. PMID: 27379021; PMCID: PMC4913107.
2. Karpinski, Christine and Rosenbloom, Christine A., "Sports Nutrition: A Handbook for Professionals, Sixth Edition" (2017)
3. National Institutes of Health. “Office of Dietary Supplements - Folate.” *Nih.gov*, 2017, ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Folate-HealthProfessional/.
4. “Office of Dietary Supplements - Magnesium*.” Nih.gov*, 2016, ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/.
5. “Zinc.” *Nih.gov*, 2016, ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Zinc-HealthProfessional/.

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

Present your summary in the following format:

```

   "key_excerpts": "First important quote or excerpt, Second important quote or excerpt, Third important quote or excerpt, ...Add more excerpts as needed, up to a maximum of 5"
}
```

Example 1 (for a news article):

The four-person crew, led by Commander Jane Smith, will orbit the Moon for 10 days before returning to Earth. This mission is a crucial step in NASA's plans to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon by 2030.",

The mission will test critical systems for future long-duration stays on the Moon, explained Lead Engineer Sarah Johnson. We're not just going back to the Moon, we're going forward to the Moon, Commander Jane Smith stated during the pre-launch press conference."


This acceleration is primarily attributed to melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. The study projects that if current trends continue, global sea levels could rise by up to 2 meters by 2100, posing significant risks to coastal communities worldwide.",

The rate of ice sheet melt in Greenland and Antarctica has tripled since the 1990s, the study reports. Without immediate and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, we are looking at potentially catastrophic sea-level rise by the end of this century, warned co-author Professor Michael Green."

This webpage from New England Nutrition & Exercise, written by dietitian Briana Bruinooge, provides comprehensive nutrition guidance for Masters Athletes (aged 30+ years). It covers age-related physiological changes, nutrition strategies to counteract them, and specific macronutrient and micronutrient recommendations.

**Who are Masters Athletes?** Defined as age 35 for both men and women per World Masters Athletics; age 18 for swimming, and 50 for golf.

**Age-Related Physiological Changes (after age 30):**
- Maximum oxygen consumption decreases ~10% per decade (slower at 5% for older endurance athletes)
- Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers decrease in size and number; shift toward slow fiber types
- Mitochondria decrease in number
- Satellite cells reduced; fat infiltrates muscle
- Myosin reduced; muscle elasticity reduced
- Muscle strength declines; low muscle strength linked to 4.3-fold greater risk of slow gait speed and 2.6-fold greater risk of severe mobility problems
- Sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass) occurs with aging
- Creatine and phosphocreatine levels reduced; creatine regeneration falls ~8% per decade after age 30
- Reduced B12 and Vitamin D absorption
- Body weight increases up to age 70, with increased belly/visceral fat
- Chronic low-level inflammation, dehydration, and reduced sweating

**Solutions:** Active lifestyle, weight-bearing exercise, and strength training (6-month program can reverse muscle weakness in older adults). Both nutrition and resistance exercise are needed for muscle protein synthesis.

**Nutrition Recommendations:**
- **Protein:** 1.2g/kg body weight/day; 35-45g per meal (vs. 15-30g for younger athletes); pre-workout meal should include 25-30g protein with high leucine foods; 3g leucine per meal recommended. Rich sources include meat, eggs, dairy (parmesan, Greek yogurt), fish, and nuts/seeds.
- **Creatine:** 5g/day creatine monohydrate for those who strength train
- **Fat:** 1 g/kg body weight/day or 20-35% of total caloric intake; omega-3 fatty acids recommended for anti-inflammatory effects
- **Carbohydrates:** 3-5 g/kg/day minimum; up to 10-12g/kg for athletes training 1-3 hours/day or endurance events over 90 minutes
- **Fluids:** Personalized hydration schedule is critical due to age-related dehydration challenges

**Nutrients of Concern:**
- **Vitamin D:** 1,500-2,000 IUs/day to raise levels above 30 ng/mL; minimum 800 IUs/day
- **Vitamin E:** Antioxidant; sources include plant oils, seeds, nuts
- **Vitamin B12:** Supplementation may be needed (methylcobalamin lozenge form); food sources only in animal products
- **Riboflavin (B2):** Key in energy production; sources include eggs, organ meats, lean meats, milk
- **Vitamin B6:** Needs increase after age 50 to 1.7 mg (men) and 1.5 mg (women) from 1.3 mg
- **Folate (B9):** Involved in DNA/RNA/protein metabolism; sources include leafy greens, fruits, legumes
- **Calcium:** 1200 mg/day for women over 51 and men over 71 (vs. 1000 mg for ages 19-50)
- **Magnesium:** 320 mg/day women and 420 mg/day men (31+ years); magnesium glycinate 200-300 mg at bedtime recommended for supplementation
- **Zinc:** 11 mg males and 8 mg females (19+); richest sources are meat, fish, seafood

**Key Warning:** Older adults, especially women frustrated with body changes, should NOT undereat and overexercise—this causes the body to hold onto fat (starvation mode) and negatively affects hormones including cortisol. The article recommends consulting a Sports Dietitian for personalized nutrition tailored to age, gender, and lifestyle.

## REVIEW article

# Athletes’ nutritional demands: a narrative review of nutritional requirements

Adam Amawi 1

Walaa AlKasasbeh 2

Manar Jaradat 3

Amani Almasri 3

Sondos Alobaidi 3

Aya Abu Hammad 3

Taqwa Bishtawi 3

2. Department of Physical and Health Education, Faculty of Educational Sciences, Al-Ahliyya Amman University, Amman, Jordan

3. Department of Nutrition and Food Technology, School of Agriculture, The University of Jordan, Amman, Jordan

4. Department of Family and Community Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, The University of Jordan, Amman, Jordan

5. Department of Nutrition and Health, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, United Arab Emirates University, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates

6. Oxford Brookes Center for Nutrition and Health, Faculty of Health and Life Sciences, Oxford Brookes University, Oxford, United Kingdom

Article metrics

## Abstract

Nutrition serves as the cornerstone of an athlete’s life, exerting a profound impact on their performance and overall well-being. To unlock their full potential, athletes must adhere to a well-balanced diet tailored to their specific nutritional needs. This approach not only enables them to achieve optimal performance levels but also facilitates efficient recovery and reduces the risk of injuries. In addition to maintaining a balanced diet, many athletes also embrace the use of nutritional supplements to complement their dietary intake and support their training goals. These supplements cover a wide range of options, addressing nutrient deficiencies, enhancing recovery, promoting muscle synthesis, boosting energy levels, and optimizing performance in their respective sports or activities. The primary objective of this narrative review is to comprehensively explore the diverse nutritional requirements that athletes face to optimize their performance, recovery, and overall well-being. Through a thorough literature search across databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus, we aim to provide evidence-based recommendations and shed light on the optimal daily intakes of carbohydrates, protein, fats, micronutrients, hydration strategies, ergogenic aids, nutritional supplements, and nutrient timing. Furthermore, our aim is to dispel common misconceptions regarding sports nutrition, providing athletes with accurate information and empowering them in their nutritional choices.

## 1 Introduction

Achieving peak physical condition and optimizing athletic performance significantly hinge on the role of food ([1](#ref1)). Optimal nutrition is instrumental in supporting physical activity, enhancing sports performance, and facilitating post-exercise recovery. Professional athletes are expected to comprehensively meet their nutritional requirements by consuming foods in appropriate quantity and quality ([2](#ref2)).

A properly balanced diet generally provides adequate energy to sustain individuals with heightened energy needs due to physical activity, ensuring a maintained energy balance in most cases ([3](#ref3)). However, meeting the energy needs of larger athletes with increased body weight and height, as well as athletes involved in demanding, high-volume training, can present a significant difficulty. Endurance athletes such as runners, swimmers, as well as those in sports like gymnastics, wrestling, and boxing that use dietary restriction for body composition adjustments, often face a negative energy balance ([3](#ref3), [4](#ref4)).

Sports nutrition refers to the nutrients found in sports-related foods that enhance physical capabilities. These nutrients form the foundation for meeting the metabolic requirements of athletes or bodybuilders engaged in regular physical exercise, contributing to the preservation of physical health and athletic performance ([5](#ref5)).

The nutritional needs of athletes are primarily dictated by the demands of their activities and the goals they set to attain peak sports performance and overall health ([2](#ref2), [5](#ref5)). The age of athletes is critical, especially adolescents whose nutritional needs tend to be higher not only to cover the performance demands but due to growth demands also. Adhering to appropriate nutritional practices is crucial as it impacts nearly every bodily process, spanning from energy production to post-exercise recovery ([6](#ref6)). Moreover, individual dietary choices may be influenced by factors such as knowledge, attitude, and the availability of nutrition-related information resources ([7](#ref7)).

Dietitians need to consider various sport-specific factors when evaluating an athlete’s nutrition requirements and objectives. These factors include rules, arena size, competition timing, match frequency, and season length, which comprises macrocycles such as preseason, competition season, and off-season. Moreover, the physical attributes and position-specific responsibilities within the sport significantly impact the dietary requirements of athletes. For instance, rugby union forwards may require greater weight and strength compared to leaner and faster backs ([8](#ref8)). Considering these sport-specific variables, variations in physique, and distinctions in positions, individualized dietary guidance becomes crucial for athletes participating in team sports.

Nutritional knowledge is a modifiable aspect that significantly shapes dietary behaviors ([9](#ref9)). Athletes’ comprehension of sports nutrition can directly impact their food preferences, subsequently influencing their overall athletic performance ([10](#ref10)–[12](#ref12)). Therefore, athletes should seek reliable and certified sources for nutritional information, as this contributes to their understanding of nutrition ([13](#ref13), [14](#ref14)). A strategic approach to enhancing nutritional awareness among athletes involves the implementation of nutrition education programs ([15](#ref15), [16](#ref16)), including individual nutrition counseling, group workshops, or online educational materials ([17](#ref17)–[19](#ref19)).

Guidance that assists athletes in attaining adequate energy intake, achieving the right balance of macronutrients and micronutrients, and strategically timing their nutrition to enhance performance and recovery contributes to optimizing training and overall athletic performance ([20](#ref20)). A previous review ([21](#ref21)) revealed athletes in team sports frequently fail to meet the recommended dietary intake requirements ([18](#ref18), [19](#ref19)). Athletes who do not achieve sufficient energy intake and lack a well-balanced diet of macronutrients may encounter obstacles in both training adaptations and recovery processes ([20](#ref20), [22](#ref22)).

Inadequate energy intake can have adverse effects on an athlete’s performance, resulting in a reduction of fat-free mass, compromised immune function, decreased bone mineral density, heightened susceptibility to injuries, and an elevated occurrence of symptoms related to overtraining ([20](#ref20)).

The field of sports nutrition has seen the publication of numerous new research papers, accompanied by the release of 17 fresh consensus statements and recommendation papers from authoritative organizations such as the IOC, ACSM, and ISSN ([2](#ref2), [20](#ref20), [23](#ref23)–[25](#ref25)). However, there is a recurrent observation of suboptimal adherence to sports nutrition guidelines among athletes ([26](#ref26)–[28](#ref28)).

Achieving optimal performance in sports demands meticulous attention to nutrition, where athletes must strategically examine the timing, amount, and nutritional value of their food consumption, coupled with ensuring sufficient fluid consumption. A synergistic blend of essential elements such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals plays a pivotal role, acting as the energy source, foundational components, and catalysts for success in the world of sports. This research paper endeavors to comprehensively examine existing literature on the nutritional needs of athletes, aiming to pinpoint and elucidate the specific nutritional demands essential for their peak performance.

Maintaining a healthy and well-balanced diet is of paramount importance for athletes and active individuals to optimize performance and overall well-being. The athlete nutrition guidelines under scrutiny in this manuscript play a pivotal role in guiding individuals to arrange their diet according to established recommendations. These guidelines not only serve the athletes themselves but also provide invaluable assistance to sports nutrition specialists in their work. The primary goal is to prevent disordered eating and eating disorders, which have become increasingly prevalent among the active population. As such, this manuscript seeks to comprehensively review current guidelines, offering a clear and updated overview. By doing so, it aims to empower athletes and active individuals to enhance their dietary practices, mitigating the risk of potential disordered eating.

## 2 Method

A narrative review was conducted over 6 months, spanning from November 2022 to April 2023. To ensure a comprehensive and relevant collection of studies, four prominent online databases–PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science–were meticulously explored. The search aimed to encompass a broad spectrum of articles pertaining to various facets of nutrition and its impact on athletic performance. To facilitate an exhaustive search, a combination of specific search terms and keywords was employed. These included “Intake of Carbohydrates for athletes,” “Intake of Protein for athletes,” “Intake of fat for athletes,” “Vitamins,” “Minerals,” “Hydration,” “Ergogenic Aids,” “Nutritional Supplements,” and “Nutrient Timing.” These keywords were selected to cover key areas of interest within the field of sports nutrition. The search strategy involved using different combinations of the aforementioned keywords to optimize the retrieval of pertinent literature. The review specifically included studies of an experimental nature, comprising randomized controlled trials, observational studies, case studies, and case reports conducted within groups of elite or semi-elite athletes. During the evaluation process, the authors scrutinized the articles to assess how well they addressed and aligned with the overall objectives of the literature review. Only those articles deemed highly relevant were included in the final selection.

## 3 Result

### 3.1 Energy (Kcal) and energy availability

In sports, maintaining peak performance relies heavily on precise nutritional practices and optimal energy intake. This is crucial not only for effective recovery and fatigue prevention but also to reduce the risk of injuries and illnesses ([29](#ref29)).

Energy availability (EA) is a key concept, representing the dietary energy available for physiological functions after subtracting exercise energy expenditure. When there’s an imbalance, resulting in Low Energy Availability (LEA), athletes may face negative consequences across various physiological systems, including endocrine, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, reproductive, and gastrointestinal ([30](#ref30)).

Athletes persisting in a state of low energy availability may experience a range of issues, from disruptions in menstrual function to heightened focus on food, increased illness susceptibility, diminished mood, compromised performance, decreased libido, and hormonal imbalances ([31](#ref31)).

While energy availability and energy balance seem similar, they differ fundamentally. Energy balance considers all components of energy expenditure, particularly relevant in changes induced by diet and exercise on body weight and composition. In contrast, energy availability focuses specifically on exercise energy expenditure, providing a nuanced perspective on the intricate relationship between nutrition and athletic performance ([32](#ref32)).

### 3.2 Carbohydrate

A high proportion of carbohydrates in the diet can significantly enhance performance during endurance and intense training. This is achieved by increasing exogenous carbohydrate availability and storing carbohydrates, known as glycogen, in muscles and the liver ([33](#ref33)). During training, there is a gradual depletion of endogenous carbohydrates due to energy expenditure; this dependence is contingent upon the level and length of the exercise. Rapid carbohydrate intake after exercise replenishes carbohydrate stores quickly and enhances the body’s training-induced adaptation processes. Among macronutrients, carbohydrates play a particularly crucial role in athletic performance since they can be metabolized aerobically and anaerobically ([34](#ref34), [35](#ref35)). Muscle glycogen and blood glucose are key energy sources for active muscles. Achieving optimal carbohydrate intake aids recovery and optimizes glycogen stores for subsequent training sessions. The recommended carbohydrate requirement varies with training volume and intensity. Emphasize the importance of incorporating foods exhibiting a glycemic index that extends across the spectrum from low to moderate into the meal plan, including complex carbohydrates ([3](#ref3)). Nevertheless, during challenging and intense training sessions or when meeting high carbohydrate needs becomes difficult due to the substantial bulk and fiber content of complex carbohydrates, it is permissible to incorporate concentrated, nutrient-dense sources of carbohydrates. Additionally, low-risk supplements may be considered to meet daily requirements if necessary ([3](#ref3), [22](#ref22)).

The glycemic index functions as a tool to classify carbohydrate-containing foods according to their impact on blood glucose levels relative to glucose or white bread consumption ([22](#ref22)). Its application in sports nutrition remains controversial, lacking clear recommendations for athletes. Studies indicate potential improvements in metabolism and substrate utilization during exercise when incorporating low glycemic index carbohydrate-containing foods in the pre-exercise meal ([22](#ref22)). However, these findings do not consistently translate to enhanced exercise performance. Notably, the influence of glycemic index on the pre-event meal diminishes when carbohydrates are consumed during exercise ([22](#ref22)). Therefore, choosing a low glycemic index meal before exercise might prove beneficial when restricted consuming carbohydrates during physical activity.

Endurance activities of moderate to high levels of intensity, along with resistance-based workouts, heavily depend on carbohydrates as a primary fuel source. Therefore, maintaining essential glycogen stores, around 80–100 g in the liver and 300–400 g in the muscles of the skeletal system, is crucial. Numerous studies confirm the limited nature of glycogen stores ([36](#ref36), [37](#ref37)), highlighting their pivotal role as a predominant fuel source for several hours during moderate engaging in aerobic exercise at a high level of intensity ([38](#ref38)).

There is documented evidence that as glycogen stores decrease, it becomes harder to maintain a high pace of intense exercise ([23](#ref23)). Consuming a snack or meal high in carbohydrates before exercise ensures optimal muscle glycogen reserves. On the other hand, low pre-exercise glycogen levels result in early fatigue, reduced training intensity, depleted muscle glycogen, impaired muscle contraction, glycogenolysis, and protein degradation ([34](#ref34), [39](#ref39), [40](#ref40)).

A straightforward suggestion for maximizing internal glycogen reserves in high-performance athletes is to consume adequate carbohydrates based on the intensity and duration of their training. Generally, the suggested daily carbohydrate intake falls within the range of 5–12 g/kg of body weight. This is particularly relevant for athletes engaged during training sessions of moderate to high intensity, lasting over 12 h per week; it is recommended to target the upper limit of this range, precisely 8 to 10 g/kg of body weight daily ([41](#ref41)). When substantial muscle damage is not present, this level of carbohydrate intake has demonstrated effectiveness in maximizing glycogen storage. Recommendations based on percentages (for instance, aiming for 60–70% of your total daily caloric intake to come from carbohydrates) have lost favor because they fail to accurately prescribe the required carbohydrate amounts for athletes with elevated caloric intake or those following restricted energy intake ([33](#ref33)).

It is important to highlight that athletes frequently fall short of meeting the recommended levels of energy and carbs. Consequently ([42](#ref42)), emphasizing approaches to restore glycogen reserves could be essential in preparing for optimal performance in the upcoming competition.

The synthesis of glycogen after exercise is closely tied to factors considering factors like the degree of glycogen reduction, the nature, duration, and intensity of the workout session ([43](#ref43)). During the initial 6 h following exercise, there is an increased pace of muscle glycogen replenishment, and consuming sufficient carbohydrates within 24 h after the workout can lead to full restoration of glycogen stores ([44](#ref44)).

Current studies suggest that having a recovery meal within 2 h after exercise, as opposed to not eating, proves effective in enhancing recovery ([45](#ref45)). Despite optimal conditions, complete muscle glycogen resynthesis can extend up to 24 h, prompting studies to explore techniques for accelerating the pace at which muscle glycogen is restored ([46](#ref46)). Customizing the approach based on the degree of glycogen depletion, an effective strategy for adequate glycogen resynthesis involves ingesting 1.0 to 1.5 g of carbohydrates per kg of body weight per hour right after exercise and maintaining this intake at 30-min intervals for up to 6 h following the workout ([2](#ref2), [47](#ref47)). On the contrary, in instances where carbohydrate (CHO) intake is postponed by 2 h, studies indicate a 45% reduction in glycogen resynthesis rates ([48](#ref48)). The absorption of glucose in the intestines might serve as a constraint on glycogen resynthesis, especially notable when a significant quantity of carbohydrates is ingested in a single bolus after exercise ([49](#ref49)). There is a proposition that carbohydrate (CHO) supplementation administered at a rate of about 1.0 g/kg/h, given at consistent intervals (15 to 60-min intervals) post-exercise, is more efficacious than a substantial single bolus in sustaining elevated blood glucose levels. This, consequently, facilitates increased muscle glycogen restoration ([48](#ref48)).

Studies investigating glycogen resynthesis rates after varying carbohydrate consumption post-exercise yield inconsistent results ([50](#ref50)). Van Loon et al. discovered that increasing post-exercise carbohydrate consumption–raising carbohydrate intake cyclists who consumed carbohydrates ranging from 0.8 to 1.2 g per kg per hour, in terms of body weight, at 30-min intervals exhibited increased rates of muscle glycogen synthesis (16.6 vs. 35.4 mmol/kg dry weight/h) following a glycogen depletion cycling trial ([43](#ref43)). Current studies suggest that 2-h intervals may not be the most effective for promoting muscle glycogen resynthesis, especially given the rapid restoration observed within the initial 2 h post-exercise ([43](#ref43), [51](#ref51)). Additional studies have documented higher rates of glycogen resynthesis with more frequent supplement ingestion compared to a single large bolus ([52](#ref52)).

Variations in study outcomes may arise from disparities in protocols; the effectiveness of post-exercise recovery meals is influenced by factors such as the timing and intervals of consumption, the subjects’ training status, and the type of carbohydrates used. Given these limitations and variations in research protocols, the current evidence indicates that an ingestion of carbohydrates ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 grams per kilogram per hour is recommended and is sufficient to achieve maximal glycogen resynthesis ([2](#ref2), [48](#ref48), [50](#ref50)). Further research is essential, especially studies investigating the prolonged impacts of post-exercise nourishment and simulating a typical training program.

#### 3.2.1 Recommended daily intake of carbohydrates

To estimate athletes’ carbohydrate needs, a recommended guideline involves ingesting 3-12 g of carbohydrate consumption per kilogram of body weight each day, with the precise quantity contingent on the intensity and duration of their physical activity. Individual variations and the comfort of their digestive systems should also be considered. For approximate carbohydrate needs, please refer to [Table 1](#tab1) ([35](#ref35), [53](#ref53)).

| Low | <60 | 3-5 |
| Moderate | 60 | 5-7 |
| High | 60-180 | 6-10 |
| Very high | >180 | 8-12 |
