--- SOURCE 3: Evidence-Based Guide on Capsule Endoscopy for Small Bowel Bleeding - Gastroenterology & Hepatology ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyandhepatology.net/archives/february-2017/evidence-based-guide-on-capsule-endoscopy-for-small-bowel-bleeding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Gastroenterology & Hepatology (February 2017, Volume 13, Issue 2), is an evidence-based guide on capsule endoscopy for small bowel bleeding, authored by Dr. Shabana F. Pasha and Dr. Jonathan A. Leighton of the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona.

KEY POINTS:

**Background & Indications:**
- Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for overt and occult small bowel bleeding, accounting for ~5% of all GI bleeding and being the most common indication for capsule endoscopy worldwide.
- Three FDA-approved capsule endoscopy systems exist: PillCam SB (Medtronic), Endocapsule (Olympus), and MiroCam (IntroMedic).
- In a systematic review of 227 studies, 66% of capsules were used for small bowel bleeding with a pooled detection rate of 59.4%. Diagnostic yield was 66.6% in a review of 1960 IDA patients and 35% in a single-center cohort of 971 patients.
- Angioectasias are the most common finding (50%), followed by inflammation (26.8%) and tumors (8.8%).

**Predictors of Positive Results:**
- Overt bleeding is the strongest predictor (OR 3.8). Other predictors: male sex (OR 1), age >60 (OR 1.2), hospitalization (OR 1.4), transfusions (OR up to 2.72 with ≥10 units PRBCs), connective tissue disease (OR 2.24), anticoagulation, and liver comorbidity.
- Early deployment of capsule endoscopy (within 3 days of admission) yields higher detection (44.4% vs 27.8%), more therapeutic interventions, and reduced hospitalization (6.1 vs 10.3 days). Yield decreases from 87.5% to 11.1% when performed after 10 days.

**Comparison with Other Modalities:**
- Superior to push enteroscopy (72.5% vs 48.7% yield; incremental yield of 35%).
- Complementary with CTE, but CTE is superior for small bowel tumor detection (94.1% vs 35.3%).
- Superior to mesenteric angiography (53.3% vs 20% yield in one randomized trial).
- Comparable diagnostic yield to double-balloon enteroscopy (60%-62% vs 56%-57%).
- Sensitivity/specificity of 95%/75% vs intraoperative enteroscopy.

**Utility for Guiding Therapy:**
- Positive capsule result predicts higher DBE yield (75% vs 27.5% with negative result).
- Capsule endoscopy had 100% sensitivity/negative predictive value for lesions requiring therapy; DBE avoided in 60% of patients with negative capsule results.
- Capsule transit time helps determine deep enteroscopy insertion route (time index >0.75 predicts retrograde route with 94.7% PPV).

**Outcomes:**
- Rebleeding rates are higher after positive capsule results (28.6% over 48 months). Risk factors include age >60, positive result, hemoglobin >7 g/dL, nonspecific treatment, and anticoagulant/antiplatelet/NSAID use.
- Vascular lesions show 35% rebleeding despite endoscopic therapy at 1 year.
- Negative capsule results generally predict low rebleeding, though results vary across studies.

**Repeat & Emergent Capsule Endoscopy:**
- Repeat capsule endoscopy after negative/nondiagnostic results has diagnostic yield of 35%-75% and alters management in 39%-62.5% of patients.
- Emergent capsule endoscopy shows promise in acute GI bleeding (diagnostic yield 75%, colonoscopy avoided in 55%), though larger prospective studies are needed.

**Limitations & Adverse Events:**
- Miss rate for solitary small bowel lesions is 11%, including tumors (19%).
- Main adverse event is capsule retention, occurring in 1.2%-1.5% of OGIB patients; risk increases with NSAID use, Crohn's disease, tumors, and prior radiation/surgery.
- Patency capsule may be useful selectively in high-risk patients; no benefit shown from "nonselective" use in all Crohn's patients.

**Conclusions:**
- Capsule endoscopy is the initial diagnostic test for small bowel bleeding after negative bidirectional endoscopy, guiding management with deep enteroscopy or surgery.
- CTE and/or deep enteroscopy are preferred when small bowel tumor or stricture is suspected.
- Future technologies, including maneuverable capsules, may improve lesion localization and enable therapeutic intervention.

Disclosures: Dr. Pasha received research support from Medtronic and CapsoVision; Dr. Leighton received research support from Medtronic and has consulted for Medtronic, Olympus, CapsoVision, and Fujinon.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for the evaluation of overt and occult small bowel bleeding. Its yield is higher in patients presenting with overt bleeding. The yield is also improved if the capsule is performed soon after the presentation of bleeding."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Evaluating ‘Early’ Video Capsule Endoscopy as a First-Line Diagnostic for GI Bleeding - Gastroenterology Advisor ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyadvisor.com/features/evaluating-early-video-capsule-endoscopy-as-a-first-line-diagnostic-for-gi-bleeding

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Gastroenterology Advisor evaluates "early" video capsule endoscopy (EVCE) as a first-line diagnostic approach for gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB). Each year, approximately 350,000 patients in the US are hospitalized for GIB, with annual costs exceeding $1 billion. Hospitalization rates for upper GI bleeding (UGIB) have declined from 81 to 67 cases per 100,000 population, with classic diagnoses (gastritis, peptic ulcer disease) declining while Dieulafoy lesions, neoplasms, angiodysplasia, and esophagitis have increased. Guidelines recommend EGD within 24 hours of admission for acute non-variceal upper GIB and within 12 hours for variceal GIB, but delays are common due to patient, staff, and facility factors.

Key evidence supporting EVCE includes:
1) Hakimian et al (presented at the 2020 American College of Gastroenterology Annual Meeting): Compared frontline VCE during the COVID-19 pandemic (March-May 2020) with a historical pre-COVID control group. Results showed no statistical difference in bleeding localization rates on the first diagnostic test (76% COVID era vs 63% pre-COVID; P=.2), but first-line VCE significantly decreased the number of patients requiring invasive procedures (44% vs 96%; P<0.001). No significant differences in transfusion requirements, hemoglobin drop, in-hospital mortality, re-admission, or re-bleeding rates. Three patients had capsule retention.

2) A randomized controlled trial (NCT02442830) comparing EVCE with standard of care (SOC) in 87 patients with nonhematemesis GI bleeding (42 in EVCE arm): Higher bleeding localization rates with EVCE (64.3% vs 31.1%, P<0.01); adjusted HR 2.77 (95% CI, 1.36-5.64) for endoscopic localization. Median time to first procedure was 6 hours with EVCE vs 21 hours with SOC. EVCE patients were more likely to have bleeding localized to the colon (aOR, 4.09), a diagnosis by end of admission (aOR, 2.67), and vascular lesions (aOR, 10.73). No procedural adverse events in either group. No significant differences in all-cause mortality or direct hospitalization costs.

Additional context: Kim et al reviewed COVID-19 pandemic outcomes in GIB patients at two NYC hospitals (pre-COVID n=123 vs pandemic n=88), finding longer hospital stays (5.5 vs 4 days), more transfusions (1 vs 0 units), and fewer endoscopies performed (28.4% vs 50.4%) during the pandemic.

Considerations for EVCE adoption include potential risks (missed lesions, capsule retention requiring surgery/endoscopy), contraindications (dysphagia, delayed gastric emptying, decreased GI motility, stricture history, small bowel obstructions), insurance coverage challenges, and the need for trained staff. Various VCE versions exist (esophageal, small bowel, colon capsules). EVCE may be particularly advantageous for stable patients waiting for antiplatelet/antithrombotic agents to clear before endoscopic procedures, and it supports value-based care by reducing invasive procedures, staff exposure, and PPE use, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Results showed that there was no statistical difference between rates of bleeding localization on the first diagnostic test between groups (76% COVID era vs 63% pre-COVID era; P=.2); however, first-line VCE significantly decreased the number of patients who required invasive procedures (44% vs 96%; P<0.001)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Capsule Endoscopy: Prep, Procedure, What It Can Diagnose ---
URL: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/16829-capsule-endoscopy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cleveland Clinic health article provides a comprehensive overview of capsule endoscopy, a diagnostic test used to examine the digestive tract, particularly the small intestine. The test involves swallowing a capsule roughly the size of a large vitamin tablet that contains a light, transmitter, and one or more tiny cameras. As the capsule travels through the digestive tract, it captures about 10,000 pictures that healthcare providers review for bleeding, polyps, tumors, and inflammation. The capsule is naturally passed in stool, usually within 24 hours, and can be flushed down the toilet.

Key details include: The test is recommended for patients (children and adults) with symptoms of gastrointestinal problems, including unexplained bleeding or other bowel issues. If a child cannot swallow a pill, the capsule can be inserted via endoscopy. During the procedure, patients swallow the capsule with water and wear a recording device around their waist (either wired with sticky pads to the chest/abdomen or fully wireless) that stores images from the capsule's transmitter. The test is painless and patients cannot feel the capsule moving through their system.

Preparation requires following provider instructions, and patients must ask when they can resume eating. Recovery time is minimal to none. The procedure is generally safe with rare complications, though the capsule can occasionally get stuck in narrower parts of the intestines—particularly in people who've had bowel surgery, inflammation, or tumors. If there's uncertainty about whether the capsule passed, an X-ray or CT scan may be needed, as a retained capsule can cause a serious bowel obstruction. The capsule's main advantage is that it's one of the only tests that allows providers to examine the entire small intestine, since traditional tube-based endoscopy cannot reach all areas. Most results are ready in about a week. Patients should contact their provider immediately if they experience signs of obstruction (such as abdominal pain, vomiting, or inability to pass stool). The article emphasizes that the test is very safe, painless, and provides critical diagnostic information, while stressing the importance of following all provider instructions before and during the procedure.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A capsule endoscopy is a diagnostic test. Healthcare providers use it to look for bleeding and tumors, mainly in your small intestine."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Understanding hydrogen and methane breath tests for SIBO and IMO: 6 Frequently Asked Questions | Commonwealth Diagnostics International ---
URL: https://commdx.com/understanding-hydrogen-and-methane-breath-tests-for-sibo-and-imo-6-frequently-asked-questions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from Commonwealth Diagnostics International (CDI), a provider of functional GI diagnostic testing, specifically focused on hydrogen and methane breath tests for Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO). The page presents six frequently asked questions (FAQs) compiled by CDI's provider support team to help healthcare providers understand and order these breath tests.

Key content covered in the FAQs:

1. **What is a hydrogen & methane breath test?** A non-invasive diagnostic tool that can be administered in-office or at home. Elevated levels of hydrogen or methane gas identified within 90 minutes of ingesting a substrate solution indicate bacteria or methanogens in the small intestine. The North American Consensus on Breath Testing recommends this test for detecting SIBO (abnormal bacterial growth in the small intestine) and IMO (excessive methane in the intestinal tract). Symptoms can include diarrhea, nausea, bloating, gas, and abdominal cramps.

2. **Glucose vs. lactulose substrates:** Glucose is absorbed by the digestive tract, so it won't detect SIBO further along the small intestine (proximal jejunum/ileum), but it is more sensitive with fewer false positives from colonic bacteria. Lactulose is not absorbed and travels through the entire GI tract, providing a complete depiction of all intestinal segments including the colon. Providers can choose between the two substrates. Most substrates do not come with food allergy labeling, so selection is important.

3. **Risks:** No risks are involved in performing the test. Patients may experience their usual symptoms during the test, which is normal. At-home testing mitigates COVID-19 exposure risk for patients and healthcare staff.

4. **Preparation required:** Patients must discontinue antibiotics for 4 weeks before testing, discontinue laxatives and/or promotility drugs for 1 week before, not smoke or vape for at least 24 hours before and during the test, and not sleep or exercise for at least 1 hour before or during the test. A 24-hour diet preparation period includes a 12-hour limited diet and 12-hour fasting period. Patients with diabetes should not use this test due to the absorbable sugar and fasting required.

5. **What happens during the test:** The patient mixes the substrate with water, provides a baseline breath sample, drinks the substrate, then gives breath samples every 15 minutes for 2 hours and 15 minutes. Patients cannot eat, chew gum, smoke, sleep, or exercise during the test. After the test, they can resume normal activities.

6. **Getting results:** Patients ship completed test kits to CDI's CLIA-certified laboratory using a pre-paid shipping label. Samples must be received within two weeks of collection (shipping within 24 hours is recommended). Kits are typically processed and analyzed within one business day. Results are delivered via secure fax, secure email, or CDI's HIPAA-compliant web-based reporting system. Providers review results with patients, and CDI offers complimentary test result interpretation upon request.

CDI's breath test kits are available to order by healthcare providers at no cost through their online ordering portal. Contact information: 1-888-258-5966 or customerservice@commdx.com.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The North American Consensus on Breath Testing recommends using a hydrogen and methane breath test to detect Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO), abnormal growth of bacteria in a patient's small intestine, and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO), excessive levels of methane in a patient's intestinal tract."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: SIBO Test | Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth Test ---
URL: https://www.gdx.net/products/sibo

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Genova Diagnostics describes their SIBO (Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth) breath testing product. The test is a non-invasive breath test that measures exhaled hydrogen (H2) and methane (CH4) gases after the patient ingests a 10-gram Lactulose Rx solution, used to evaluate SIBO and intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO). The specimen type is breath with a turnaround time of 7 days, and only healthcare providers licensed in their state may order laboratory testing.

Clinicians can choose between a 2-hour or 3-hour SIBO assessment. The 3-hour profile is recommended for patients with slower gastrointestinal transit or constipation, and a flatline result in the third hour may indicate the presence of hydrogen sulfide gas. Genova's profiles utilize the North American Consensus Guidelines published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology.

Common symptoms and conditions associated with SIBO include bloating/distension, gas, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, IBS, IBD, Celiac Disease, diabetes, fibromyalgia, rosacea, Parkinson's Disease, and obesity. The page provides detailed test preparation instructions, including a table of recommended discontinuation timeframes for various substances: colonoscopy/barium enema (4 weeks), antibiotics (4 weeks per North American SIBO Consensus), antifungals/herbal antimicrobials (2-4 weeks), laxatives/promotility agents (7 days), a limited diet (24 hours before, extendable to 48 hours for constipated patients), fasting from food with water only (12 hours before), GLP-1 therapies (7 days), and various restrictions on smoking, exercise, toothpaste, and non-essential medications. The page also describes the four-step testing process (Consult Doctor, Activate Test, Collect Samples, Ship to Lab), includes FAQs about insurance/CPT codes and support materials, and promotes related products including GI Effects Comprehensive Stool Profile and NutrEval FMV (which evaluates over 125 biomarkers). Support materials include SIBO collection instructions, 2-hour and 3-hour sample reports, an interpretive guide, and a patient brochure.

--- SOURCE 8: Faculty from Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and ... ---
URL: https://www.upmcphysicianresources.com/news/072123-breath-testing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from UPMC Physician Resources (published July 21, 2023) announcing that faculty from the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition at the University of Pittsburgh published research on hydrogen-methane breath testing for diagnosing Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) in the journal *Clinical and Translational Gastroenterology*.

**Key Details:**

- **Authors:** Dr. David Levinthal, MD, PhD, and Dr. Aylin Tansel, MD, MPH, both experts from UPMC Digestive Health Care and the University of Pittsburgh Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition.
- **Article title:** "Understanding Our Tests: Hydrogen-Methane Breath Testing to Diagnose Small Intestine Bacterial Overgrowth"
- **Purpose:** Breath testing is an inexpensive, noninvasive alternative to diagnose SIBO (which causes diarrhea, bloating, abdominal pain), whereas direct culture of small intestinal contents (via endoscopy) remains the gold standard but is costly, invasive, and has limitations including lack of standardized aseptic collection techniques and contamination from oral bacteria.

**Test Overview:**
- The test involves administering a carbohydrate substrate (glucose or lactulose), which gut bacteria ferment to produce hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen sulfide gases. These gases are absorbed into the blood and measured via exhalation using gas analyzers.
- The test can be performed in the office or at home.

**Pre-Test Preparation Requirements:**
- Low-residue diet the day before the test (to avoid skewing results with high baseline gas levels).
- Avoid laxatives, promotility drugs, opioids, and antibiotics for specified time periods.
- Opioids delay intestinal transit time and should be stopped at least 24 hours before the test.
- Antibiotics reduce gut bacterial loads and should be stopped about a month before the test if possible.
- Cessation of smoking the night before and throughout the testing period.
- Minimize physical exercise (both smoking and exercise alter results).
- Some studies advocate chlorhexidine mouthwash before substrate administration to eliminate oral bacteria fermentation, though more research is needed.

**Administration and Interpretation:**
- Baseline sample collected first, then substrate ingested, followed by breath samples every 15–20 minutes over ~180 minutes.
- Positive test criteria: Hydrogen gas rise of ≥20 ppm from baseline by 90 minutes, OR methane gas rise of ≥10 ppm at any time during the study period.
- Breath testing is considered a moderately good diagnostic test for SIBO.

**Special Patient Populations:**
- Patients with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) often have highly variable orocecal transit time (OCTT), making the 90-minute hydrogen cutoff unreliable. Measuring OCTT alongside the breath test could help, but since it's invasive and SIBO prevalence in RYGB patients is high, empiric antibiotic treatment may be the best approach for this population.

**Future Research Needs:**
- Define ideal treatment protocols, techniques, and result interpretation.
- Develop nuanced result categories (e.g., "strongly positive" vs. "moderately positive") rather than just positive/negative.

The article also includes a quote from Dr. Tansel noting that each medication has its own unique effect on intestinal transit time, impacting breath test interpretation.
</summary>

"Each of these medications have their own unique effect on intestinal transit time, which can then impact the interpretation of the breath test," Dr. Tansel says.

--- SOURCE 9: Hydrogen/Methane Breath Test ---
URL: https://www.nationaljewish.org/conditions/tests-procedures/gastroenterology/hydrogen-methane-breath-test

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from National Jewish Health provides detailed patient information about the Hydrogen-Methane Breath Test, a noninvasive diagnostic test used to evaluate gastrointestinal conditions related to carbohydrate digestion and bacterial overgrowth. The test measures hydrogen and/or methane in a patient's breath after ingesting a specific sugar, as these gases are produced when gut bacteria ferment carbohydrates that were not properly digested or absorbed.

The test is used for two main conditions: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO), where bacteria in the small intestine ferment the test sugar prematurely, and Carbohydrate Malabsorption (sucrose, fructose, lactose), where undigested sugar passes into the colon and ferments. Side effects are generally mild, including bloating, abdominal discomfort, gas, or diarrhea, which typically resolve shortly after the test.

The preparation instructions are extensive. For 24 hours before the test, patients may only eat baked/broiled chicken, turkey, or fish with salt and pepper; plain steamed white rice; eggs; tofu; clear chicken or beef broth; small amounts of olive oil for cooking; and water. Twelve hours before the test, patients must fast except for water. Patients must not smoke or be exposed to second-hand smoke for at least one hour before and during the test, and should not sleep or do vigorous exercise for at least one hour before. Medications that must be held include: antibiotics (stop 4 weeks before), probiotics (stop 2 weeks before), antimicrobial herbs such as garlic, ginger, oregano, or elderberry (stop 1 week before), laxatives and fiber supplements (stop 3 days before), and digestive enzymes (stop 2 days before). A recent colonoscopy requires waiting at least 3 weeks before scheduling the test. Diabetic patients taking insulin should consult their prescriber about reducing the dose on test day.

During the test, the patient drinks a small amount of a test sugar (lactose, sucrose, fructose, or glucose), then breathes into a collection bag at scheduled intervals for approximately three hours. Samples are analyzed with specialized equipment, and results are sent to the patient's provider. After the test, patients may return to normal diet and activities. At National Jewish Health, the test takes place in the Minimally Invasive Diagnostic Center (MIDC); check-in is at the Front Desk, with questions handled at 303-270-2424 and rescheduling at 303-398-1355, option #4. The information was reviewed by Madison Hucke, BSN, RN on 5/30/2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Hydrogen-methane breath testing is a noninvasive diagnostic test used to evaluate certain gastrointestinal conditions related to carbohydrate digestion and bacterial overgrowth."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Pros and Cons of Breath Testing for Small Intestinal Bacterial ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10496284

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed medical review article published in Gastroenterology & Hepatology (N Y), March 2023, Volume 19, Issue 3, pages 140-146, authored by Jane Lim, MD, MS and Ali Rezaie, MD, MSc from the GI Motility Program, Karsh Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, California. The article (PMCID: PMC10496284, PMID: 37706108) reviews the pros and cons of breath testing for diagnosing Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO).

Key content:

**Background**: Breath testing is the most widely used modality to diagnose SIBO and IMO. SIBO is characterized by excessive coliform bacteria in the small intestine causing bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, diarrhea, and constipation. IMO is an independent entity involving overgrowth of methanogenic archaea causing bloating, gas, abdominal discomfort, and constipation. IMO can only be diagnosed via breath testing in clinical practice. Glucose and lactulose are the two main substrates used.

**Diagnostic criteria (North American Consensus)**:
- SIBO: Early rise in hydrogen of ≥20 ppm above baseline by 90 minutes
- IMO: Methane of ≥10 ppm at any point during testing
- Small bowel aspiration requires >10³ CFU/mL of coliforms (but has 19.6% contamination rate per Cangemi study)

**Pros of breath testing**:
- Safe, simple, noninvasive, widely accessible, and can be administered at home
- Can distinguish SIBO from IMO and help tailor antibiotic therapy (rifaximin for hydrogen-predominant SIBO; combination therapy like rifaximin/neomycin for IMO)
- Lactulose can sample the entire small intestine and identify distal SIBO; meta-analysis shows lactulose breath test sensitivity 42%, specificity 70.6%
- Glucose is more specific (less false positives from colonic fermentation); sensitivity 54.5%, specificity 83.2%
- Lactulose preferred for diabetic patients (no hyperglycemia risk); useful for diarrhea-predominant IBS patients to predict rifaximin response
- IMO results not affected by orocecal transit time (OCTT); methane levels correlate with constipation severity
- Spot methane measurement (SMM) of ≥10 ppm has 86.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing IMO, providing rapid point-of-care testing

**Cons/limitations of breath testing**:
- Indirectly measures microbial overgrowth
- Accuracy depends on patient compliance (oral care, no exercise/smoking on test day, avoiding fermentable foods day prior, no antibiotics 4 weeks before, discontinue promotility agents/laxatives 1 week before, avoid colonoscopy prep 2 weeks before)
- Various commercial home tests may use different thresholds not supported by guidelines
- Low breath hydrogen can occur when methanogens consume hydrogen
- OCTT variability: rapid OCTT can cause false positives; slow OCTT can cause false negatives
- Conditions preventing substrate delivery to small intestine (gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction, achalasia, enterocutaneous fistula) cause false negatives
- Study by Yu et al: 88% of positive results had ≥5% substrate in cecum on scintigraphy before test became positive, though 5% (0.5g lactulose) is insufficient to cause significant hydrogen rise
- Lin and Massey found 22 of 46 patients with false-positive glucose breath tests had colon fermentation, 20 of whom had prior upper GI surgery

**IMO treatment data**:
- Low et al. study: 85% of patients treated with rifaximin + neomycin achieved clinical response vs. 56% with rifaximin alone
- 87% of combination therapy patients eradicated methane vs. only 29% with rifaximin alone
- A small RCT (N=31) in constipation-predominant IBS with methane >3 ppm showed neomycin+rifaximin reduced constipation, straining, and bloating more than rifaximin alone

**Emerging breath test patterns**:
1. **Flat-line pattern**: No methane, low fixed hydrogen (≤3 ppm, no rise >1 ppm above baseline); more common in inflammatory bowel disease; 56% of patients respond to antibiotics (58% to rifaximin, 47% to rifaximin+neomycin); may indicate excess hydrogenotrophic bacteria or gastroparesis
2. **High baseline hydrogen**: >20 ppm baseline with no excessive methane; found in 0.7% (107/14,847) of lactulose breath tests; 52% responded to antibiotics, 73% to rifaximin, only 25% to rifaximin+neomycin

**Conclusion**: Breath testing offers rapid, safe, noninvasive diagnosis with utility in tailoring therapy and monitoring treatment response. Newer technologies including intraluminal gas sampling and next-generation sequencing may improve diagnostic accuracy in the future.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Breath testing is the most widely utilized diagnostic modality for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO)." "Currently in clinical practice, IMO is only diagnosed with breath testing." "Per the North American Consensus statement, an early rise in hydrogen of 20 parts per million (ppm) or more above baseline by 90 minutes is considered a positive glucose or lactulose breath test result for SIBO." "85% of patients treated with rifaximin and neomycin attained clinical response compared with 56% of patients in the rifaximin-only group. Additionally, 87% of patients treated with rifaximin and neomycin were able to eradicate methane on breath testing compared with only 29% of patients in the rifaximin-only group." "A fasting SMM of 10 ppm or more had a sensitivity of 86.4% and specificity of 100% for diagnosing IMO on the glucose and lactulose breath test."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for patients with irritable bowel syndrome: current insights ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5530860

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Psychology Research and Behavior Management (2017, PMCID: PMC5530860, PMID: 28790872) by Sarah W Kinsinger of Loyola University Medical Center (Division of Gastroenterology and Nutrition, Behavioral Medicine for Digestive Health), reviews current insights into cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

**Key Content:**

1. **IBS Overview:** IBS is a highly prevalent condition affecting nearly 35 million Americans, characterized by abdominal pain associated with altered gut motility causing diarrhea and/or constipation. It consumes over $20 billion in direct and indirect expenditures, with healthcare utilization equivalent to chronic diseases like asthma, hypertension, and congestive heart failure. The condition negatively impacts quality of life and is associated with increased psychological distress.

2. **Biopsychosocial Model:** IBS is now viewed as a "disorder of gut brain interaction" rather than a purely "functional" condition. The biopsychosocial model (first applied to IBS by Doug Drossman, MD) emphasizes interactions between biology (genetic predisposition, disordered gut motility, altered gut microbiota, low-grade inflammation), behavior, cognitive processes, and environment. The brain-gut axis—complex bidirectional communication between brain and gut—is a key component.

3. **Cognitive Affective Processes:** Key mechanisms include visceral hypersensitivity (increased pain response to normal bowel functions), central processing deficits (IBS patients show greater activation of emotional arousal networks and fail to activate pain-downregulating brain regions like the medial prefrontal cortex), visceral anxiety, and catastrophizing. Stress is a significant contributor to brain-gut dysregulation. Patients with IBS have increased rates of anxiety and somatization, and tend to over-rely on problem-focused coping while lacking emotion-focused coping skills (Cheng et al. study).

4. **Evidence Base for Psychological Treatments:** 41 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated psychological therapies for IBS. Psychological treatments are moderately effective and durable. CBT is the most rigorously tested approach with at least 20 published RCTs, consistently demonstrating significant and lasting symptom improvement maintained for at least 1 year after treatment. Effects directly improve IBS symptoms independent of psychological factors.

5. **Components of CBT Treatment:** Psychoeducation, relaxation strategies (diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery), cognitive restructuring (addressing catastrophizing and probability overestimation), problem-solving skills (emotion-focused coping), and exposure techniques (graduated exposure, interoceptive exposure, behavioral experiments) to address avoidance and safety behaviors.

6. **Evolution of CBT Protocols:** Early models used general stress management (10-session model; Vollmer & Blanchard found 64% of group vs 55% of individual CBT patients improved vs control). Later models focused on cognitive-affective processes (Lackner et al: 72% of self-administered CBT patients reported adequate relief vs 60% therapist-administered and 7.4% control). Most recent model (Craske et al) targets visceral anxiety using exposure-based techniques modeled after panic disorder treatment. Alternative delivery methods include minimal contact models (Lackner) and internet-delivered CBT (Ljotsson et al, which showed 42% of ICBT patients vs 12% of control reported symptom improvement).

7. **Future Directions:** Despite demonstrated benefits, very few patients have access to CBT. Primary barrier is limited number of therapists trained in GI psychology. The American Gastroenterological Association recommends psychological interventions for moderate-to-severe IBS or patients unresponsive to standard care. Future efforts should focus on: training opportunities for clinicians, integrated care models with gastroenterologists, telemedicine/web-based platforms, and customizing treatment (e.g., 4-5 session brief models rather than standard 10 sessions) to match individual patient needs.

**Conclusions:** IBS involves brain-gut axis dysregulation where psychological processes play a key role. CBT is well-established, rigorously tested, and demonstrates significant long-lasting symptom improvement, but dissemination is poor. Future focus needed on training providers and developing telemedicine platforms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Psychological therapies as a whole have demonstrated good efficacy in reducing the severity of IBS symptoms. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has been tested most rigorously in multiple randomized controlled trials and consistently demonstrates significant and durable effects on IBS symptoms and quality of life."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Brain-Gut Behavioral Therapies for IBS | Docwire News ---
URL: https://www.docwirenews.com/post/brain-gut-behavioral-therapies-improve-irritable-bowel-syndrome-symptoms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A large network meta-analysis published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology found that behavioral therapies, particularly brain-gut behavior therapies, significantly improve global symptoms in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The study included 67 randomized clinical trials with 7,441 adults with IBS, with a comprehensive search of major medical and psychologic research databases through April 23, 2025. Treatment efficacy was assessed using dichotomous measures of global IBS symptom improvement, with pooled relative risks calculated and therapies ranked using P scores.

The most effective interventions compared with waiting list control included: minimal contact CBT (RR 0.55; P score 0.78; 2 trials; n=511), telephone-based disease self-management (RR 0.57; P score 0.75; 2 trials; n=746), dynamic psychotherapy (RR 0.59; P score 0.72; 3 trials; n=303), and standard CBT (RR 0.65; P score 0.64; 9 trials; n=1,150). Other effective approaches included disease self-management (RR 0.68), internet-based minimal contact CBT (RR 0.77), and gut-directed hypnotherapy (RR 0.79; 12 trials; n=1,507).

In treatment-refractory IBS patients, telephone-based disease self-management and contingency management were superior to both attention placebo control and routine care, while group CBT, internet-based disease self-management, and dynamic psychotherapy were also superior to routine care. However, evidence of publication bias was identified, no trial was rated as low risk of bias across all domains, and certainty of evidence was rated low to very low. The investigators concluded that the strongest evidence for efficacy exists for forms of CBT, disease self-management, dynamic psychotherapy, and gut-directed hypnotherapy, with little evidence for behavioral therapies not classified as brain-gut behavior therapies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Beyond first-line and second-line treatments, management guidelines for IBS recommend the use of behavioural therapies, specifically brain-gut behaviour therapies. These gastrointestinal-focused behavioural interventions target brain-gut dysregulation, and are beneficial in some patients," explained the study authors.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Psychological Treatments - About IBS ---
URL: https://aboutibs.org/treatment/psychological-treatments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from IFFGD (International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders) on aboutibs.org provides a comprehensive overview of psychological treatments for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). It explains that psychological treatments are effective because of the gut-brain axis, with the enteric nervous system (ENS or "second brain") playing a key role. Patients with IBS may experience visceral hypersensitivity, a hyper-awareness of nerve behavior in the GI tract that contributes to discomfort.

The page covers the role of stress in IBS, noting that the GI tract becomes more sensitive during stressful periods, which can alter intestinal motility and increase pain. It emphasizes that consulting a behavioral health specialist with gastroenterology expertise differs from typical anxiety/depression treatment.

Four main psychological treatments are detailed:
1. **Gut-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (GI-CBT)** - Modifies thinking, feelings, behaviors, and reactions to symptoms; teaches relaxation skills; one of the most well-studied behavioral approaches with 40+ years of research; effective via individual, group, and teletherapy delivery.
2. **Gut-Directed Hypnotherapy (GDH)** - Medical hypnosis well-researched in IBS patients with 30+ published studies since the 1980s; up to 80% of IBS patients respond positively (better than traditional medications); approximately 75% of people can be hypnotized enough for positive response; addresses brain-gut communication.
3. **Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)** - Mindfulness-based therapy helping patients live flexibly with IBS; uses six principles (acceptance, cognitive defusion, being present, observing self, values clarification, committed action); still early in IBS research but shows promise.
4. **Other Mindfulness Approaches** - Focus on stress impact on IBS; most studied is Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), typically taught over 8 weeks in group/individual settings with sessions up to 3 hours; shown to improve symptom perception, quality of life, reduce symptom severity, and decrease visceral hypersensitivity.

The content was adapted from IFFGD Publication #103 by Megan Riehl & Sarah Quinton PsyD, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"GI-CBT is one of the most well studied behavioral approaches for IBS, with more than 40 years of research revealing how effective it is for improving IBS symptoms."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: CBT for IBS: Frontline Treatment? - Gastroenterology Advisor ---
URL: https://www.gastroenterologyadvisor.com/features/cbt-for-ibs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Gastroenterology Advisor features Dr. Jeffrey Lackner, PsyD, SUNY distinguished professor and chief of the Division of Behavioral Medicine at the University at Buffalo, advocating for cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) as a proven, front-line treatment for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) rather than a mere adjunct therapy.

**Key Points:**

- IBS involves bidirectional signaling between the enteric and central nervous systems (the brain-gut axis), which amplifies pain and GI urgency even without structural disease. CBT targets this signaling pathway by teaching patients to identify and change thoughts, behaviors, and stress responses that exacerbate symptoms.

- American College of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend referring patients with IBS to CBT or other gut-brain behavioral therapy, especially for those with moderate-to-severe or refractory IBS, prominent anxiety/depression, marked job or social impairment, or high health care utilization. Gastroenterologists should consider integrating CBT with dietitian referrals.

**Evidence Base:**
- A landmark 7-site randomized controlled trial (2018) enrolling 436 adults with moderate-to-severe, treatment-refractory IBS found 61% of patients in the 4-session, home-based CBT arm reported moderate-to-substantial symptom improvement, with 58% maintaining gains at 6 months. A 4-session at-home protocol performed equivalently to a 10-session clinical protocol, reducing therapist contact time by 60%. Benefits held at 12-month follow-up, with minimal-contact CBT gains increasing over time.
- A 2006 PET study showed reduced neural activity in the parahippocampal gyrus and anterior cingulate cortex following cognitive therapy, correlating with improved GI symptoms and psychological functioning.
- A 2021 microbiome study found CBT simultaneously alters gut microbial composition and brain function, with microbiome markers predicting treatment response—the first direct biological evidence that the brain-gut axis is genuinely bidirectional.
- A 2025 meta-analysis by Thakur et al confirmed that short-term, minimal-contact nonpharmacologic brain-gut behavior therapies improve IBS symptoms, with CBT being more effective than other interventions.

**Barriers to Care:**
- Insurers have shifted from viewing CBT as adjunctive to recognizing it as early-line or front-line treatment, but there remains a shortage of therapists, particularly outside urban areas.
- A 2026 online survey by Izquierdo et al of 770 US adult patients with GI disorders found 90% of patients with IBS, functional diarrhea, and functional constipation had never been offered CBT, while patients with other GI disorders were about 4 times more likely to be offered CBT.
- Clinicians may not fully understand chronic pain like IBS that occurs without structural abnormalities.

**Future Directions:**
- Not all patients respond to CBT, especially those with high baseline anxiety who may lack the cognitive resources CBT requires; these patients may benefit from patient education, therapeutic relationships, emotional support, and support groups.
- Lackner is now researching "transdiagnostic" CBT that targets multiple concurrent disorders simultaneously, which he argues is more efficient, more powerful, and less costly than sequential treatment approaches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"IBS is a real medical problem... It's not a psychiatric problem. It is a problem in how the brain and gut communicate — and there are ways that you can learn to recalibrate how the brain and gut communicate by changing how you process information or changing the way you react to stimuli." — Jeffrey Lackner, PsyD, "We don't have enough therapists, we don't have enough clinicians to go around, and that makes it really hard for people that are outside of specific urban areas to get treatment," said Lackner, who sees it as a serious public health problem., "In the absence of a cure, we need to teach people how to self-manage between times that they see their doctor." — Jeffrey Lackner, PsyD, A 2026 online survey by Izquierdo et al including 770 US adult patients with GI disorders found that 90% of patients with IBS, functional diarrhea, and functional constipation had never been offered CBT; patients with other GI disorders were about 4 times more likely to be offered CBT., The 2018 trial found 61% of patients in the 4-session, home-based CBT arm reported moderate-to-substantial symptom improvement, and 58% maintained those gains at 6 months, with a 4-session at-home protocol performing equivalently to a 10-session clinical protocol, reducing therapist contact time by 60%.

--- SOURCE 15: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for IBS - Canadian Digestive Health Foundation ---
URL: https://cdhf.ca/en/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt-for-ibs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Canadian Digestive Health Foundation (CDHF), written by Dr. Amber Cohen (PsyD, CPsych) and updated April 1, 2024, provides a comprehensive overview of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) as a treatment for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS).

Key sections of the article include:

**The Mind-Body Connection:** The article emphasizes that while IBS is a physical condition, the mind-body connection significantly impacts symptoms. The central nervous system (brain/spinal cord) and enteric nervous system (gut) communicate about digestion, thoughts, emotions, and appetite. Notably, 95% of the body's serotonin—a neurotransmitter affecting mood, sleep, appetite, and sex drive—is produced in the gut. Two types of relationships exist between IBS and anxiety: (1) anxiety triggers digestive problems through stress chemicals released in the gut, and (2) having IBS can trigger anxiety due to its impact on work, family, and social functioning. Mental health impacts range from mild stress to chronic health anxiety.

**Chronic IBS Symptoms and Anxiety:** People with IBS often suffer chronic symptoms for years before diagnosis, and the endless medical testing itself is anxiety-provoking. Symptom flare-ups can act as trauma experiences. Common fears include: not knowing when symptoms will arise, shame/embarrassment about symptoms, being in new/busy situations, discomfort in tight clothing, not wanting to eat socially, needing to carry a "kit" (fresh underwear, medications, wipes), worries about new relationships/dating, and anxiety about food choices. The brain's protective scanning behavior can become problematic when excessive.

**Chronic IBS Symptoms and Low Mood:** IBS is often comorbid with low mood due to: isolation, lower self-confidence, avoiding intimacy, reduced enjoyment of social activities, chronic pain/discomfort, low energy, hopelessness, discomfort with spontaneity, fatigue from reading ingredients, and sadness about missing social occasions.

**What CBT Is:** Research shows CBT is effective in improving bowel symptoms, psychological distress, and quality of life in all people with IBS regardless of subtype. CBT is a shorter-term, collaborative treatment of approximately 12-15 sessions (depending on agreed goals). CBT is based on the relationship between cognitions (thoughts), behaviours, and emotions—since emotions cannot be directly controlled, clients learn to modify unhelpful thought and behaviour patterns to positively influence their emotional state.

**How CBT Can Help:** CBT provides education about the mental state/IBS relationship, management of ineffective thought and behavioural patterns, self-regulation strategies for physical and mental relaxation, flexible problem-solving training, and a supportive processing space. Overall, CBT helps individuals feel more in control of their thoughts, behaviours, emotions, and IBS symptoms.

The page also promotes CDHF's free myIBS tracking app (available on App Store and Google Play) and lists numerous related articles on IBS topics including FODMAP diets, gut-brain connection, mindfulness, IBS subtypes, and various management strategies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"95% of our body's serotonin, a chemical messenger that impacts our mood, sleep, appetite and sex drive, can be found in our gut."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Masters Athletes and Gut Issues – NEVERSECOND ---
URL: https://never2.com/blogs/guides/masters-athletes-and-gut-issues

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog article from Neversecond (a sports nutrition brand) titled "Masters Athletes and Gut Issues," written by Marni Sumbal, MS, RD, CSSD, LD/N. The article addresses gastrointestinal (GI) distress in masters athletes (40+), a common performance limiter in endurance sport.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Carb Absorption and Age**: The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. Masters athletes can target 60-90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor—gut training is.

2. **Three Causes of GI Distress**:
   - Physiological: Exercise diverts blood away from the gut (at 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop nearly 80%), causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea.
   - Mechanical: Running jolts the GI tract, making runners more prone to lower GI issues than cyclists.
   - Nutritional: High-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods eaten too close to training, plus concentrated drinks, slow stomach emptying.

3. **Gut Training for Masters Athletes**: Gut training involves progressively practicing carbohydrate and fluid intake during workouts. Elite athletes now consume 120-150g of carbs/hour, but this takes time to build. Recommended protocol: Start at 30-40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10-15g every 1-2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt.

4. **Exercising in Heat**: Heat compounds gut issues—blood shifts to skin for cooling and gastric emptying slows. Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. Recommendations: drop carb intake by 10-20g/hour until heat-acclimated, choose liquid calories, eat small amounts every 10-15 minutes, start hydrated and cool, don't rely on thirst, include sodium in everything you drink, monitor urine color, and watch for hyponatremia.

5. **Bottom Line**: The gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly. "Age is context, not a ceiling."

The article includes references from PubMed, PMC (NIH), Gatorade Sports Science Institute, and TrainingPeaks on topics including GLUT4 protein concentration, gut training, aging gastrointestinal function, multiple transportable carbohydrates, ultra-endurance nutrition strategies, exercise-intensity thresholds and leaky gut, GI symptoms in runners, and thermoregulation in older individuals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Aging doesn't have to mean slowing down — but it does mean paying closer attention to your gut." "Masters athletes can and should target 60–90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours, using glucose-fructose blends. Age alone isn't the limiting factor, gut training is." "At 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop by nearly 80%, causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea." "Many elite endurance athletes now successfully consume 120–150g of carbs per hour, but that takes time and consistency to build." "Your gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly well into their later years. Age is context, not a ceiling."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: How to Address Gut Issues for Runners 40 and Over - RUN | Powered by Outside ---
URL: https://run.outsideonline.com/nutrition-and-health/training-nutrition/guide-to-gut-health-carb-fueling-for-masters-runners

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published May 15, 2026 on Outside Run by Marni Sumbal R.D., C.S.S.D. (a sports dietitian and masters athlete), addresses gut health and carbohydrate fueling specifically for masters athletes (those aged 40 and older). Despite being one of the largest and fastest-growing segments of endurance sport, masters athletes have been historically underrepresented in sports nutrition literature. The article covers three main areas:

**1. Carbohydrate Absorption and Aging:** The body uses two intestinal transporters—SGLT1 for glucose (max 60 grams/hour) and GLUT5 for fructose (additional 30-60 grams/hour). Combining glucose/maltodextrin with fructose in a 2:1 or 1:0.8 ratio increases carbohydrate oxidation to 1.7-1.8 grams/minute and prevents GI issues like bloating. While aging causes structural gut changes, small intestine absorption capacity generally stays steady in healthy older adults. The main concern for masters athletes is not reduced absorption but a decline in GLUT4 (insulin-regulated glucose transporter), which can lead to insulin resistance—though regular endurance training can maintain and even reverse this age-related decline. Masters athletes can benefit from 60-90 grams of carbs per hour in events lasting over two hours using glucose-fructose blends.

**2. Avoiding GI Distress:** GI issues affect 30-90% of athletes and stem from three factors: (a) Physiological—reduced blood flow to the gut (up to 80% reduction at 70% VO2max), though research suggests younger male athletes may actually experience more gut issues than older athletes; (b) Mechanical—the jostling of running contributes to "runner's trots"; (c) Nutritional—high-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods near training, and high-osmality drinks increase GI distress risk. Risk factors include lack of food variety, low-fiber diets, processed/fatty foods, skipping meals, and eating too close to bedtime. Recommendations include eating every few hours, prioritizing real foods, incorporating fermented foods (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, tempeh), staying hydrated, keeping pre-workout snacks low in fiber/fat, and allowing at least 90 minutes for digestion before exercise.

**3. Gut Training Protocol:** Gut training is a progressive strategy to condition the GI tract to handle large carbohydrate loads (elite athletes can ingest 120-150 grams/hour). While masters athletes can follow structured gut training, they may need more time to adapt. <summary>
This is SSE #178 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published January 2018, authored by Asker Jeukendrup, PhD. The article examines "Training the Gut for Athletes" — the concept that the gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be trained and adapted to improve nutrient and fluid delivery during endurance exercise while reducing GI distress.

KEY POINTS:
- The GI tract is critical for delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and is a major determinant of endurance performance.
- GI problems affect 30-50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports.
- The GI tract is highly adaptable and responds to nutritional training in a nutrient-specific way.

GASTRIC EMPTYING: The stomach is the first barrier for delivering nutrients. Studies show that repeated practice of high fluid intakes during running improved stomach comfort over time (Lambert et al., 2008), though without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate. Dietary manipulation studies (Cunningham et al., 1991; Horowitz et al., 1996; Yau et al., 2014) demonstrated that supplementing with specific carbohydrates (glucose or fructose) accelerated gastric emptying of those same sugars specifically, with effects seen after as little as 3 days.

INTESTINAL SUGAR TRANSPORT: Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent SGLT1 transporter, while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are the most important transporters for carbohydrate absorption. At ingestion rates over 60-70 g of carbohydrate/hour, exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks at ~60 g/hour because SGLT1 becomes saturated. Combining glucose and fructose (using different transporters) can achieve higher oxidation rates.

TRANSPORTER REGULATION AND ADAPTATION: SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. A glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies show rapid adaptation: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses showed increases after just one week; piglets showed increases after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks.

HUMAN EVIDENCE: The landmark Cox et al. (2010) study divided 16 endurance-trained cyclists into high-carbohydrate and control groups. Over 28 days of training (16 h/week), the high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate versus 5.3 g/kg/day in controls. Post-training, the high-carb group showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, most likely due to upregulated SGLT1 transporters. Conversely, carbohydrate restriction, high-fat/ketogenic diets, or energy reduction may reduce absorptive capacity and potentially increase GI problems.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) Train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks. (2) Practice race nutritional strategies in training to adapt to higher volumes and carbohydrate intakes. (3) For exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate is recommended; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures). (4) Athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days to maintain gut absorptive capacity.

## Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete

This chapter from the Musculoskeletal Key website (DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) addresses common gastrointestinal (GI) conditions in athletes and active persons, focusing on recognition and management. GI conditions are common in athletes, with exercise placing significant stress on the GI tract, resulting in characteristic disorders that can impair athletic performance.

### Key Points:

**General Pathophysiology:**
- 20–50% of high-performance athletes report undesirable GI symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea)
- Symptoms are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes
- Cyclists appear somewhat protected from GI issues due to forward positioning, while runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling
- Increased catecholamines and GI peptides (gastrin, motilin, secretin, etc.) increase gut transit time, negatively affecting GI homeostasis

**GI Tract Ischemia:**
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction
- Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation
- Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa" (per ter Steege et al.)
- Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms

**Upper GI Conditions:**
- Upper GI complaints affect 30–70% of athletes
- Three primary mechanisms: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes
- GERD is the most common cause of upper GI symptoms in athletes
- Exercise ≥90% VO2 max increases frequency/duration of esophageal reflux episodes
- Weightlifters have the highest rate of heartburn and reflux; runners have a threefold increase in GERD when running 45 minutes after a meal

**GERD Management:**
- Lifestyle modifications first-line: sleeping on two pillows, avoiding lying down within 4 hours of evening meal, avoiding postprandial exercise, limiting foods that relax the LES (high-fat foods, coffee, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods)
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training
- Pharmacologic therapy: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective
- H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers
- Upper endoscopy for diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended

**Other Conditions:**
- **Functional heartburn:** Up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset; treatment is biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, prokinetics
- **Dyspepsia:** Caused by GERD, gastritis, or peptic ulcer disease; ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms; PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence
- **Aspirin/NSAIDs:** Block cyclooxygenase and protective prostaglandins; add daily PPI for GI protection in athletes requiring NSAIDs with ulcer history
- **Pill esophagitis:** NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and mefloquine are highest risk; take with food/fluid in morning and remain upright
- **Dysphagia:** Divided into oropharyngeal and esophageal subtypes; most commonly caused by irritative effects of GERD
- **Nausea/Vomiting:** Linked to postprandial exercise; avoid solid food within 3 hours of events; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events; H2 blockers and PPIs can help

**GERD-Asthma Connection:**
- Up to 90% of persons with asthma have GERD; up to 40% have esophagitis
- Treatment only benefits asthma in patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms
- Atypical GERD presentations include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, and chest pain

Quality assessment used the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Moderate-intensity exercise (walking, cycling, swimming, yoga) consistently improves GI function across conditions including GERD, IBS, IBD, and constipation, attributed to enhanced intestinal motility, reduced systemic inflammation, and improved gut barrier integrity.
- High-intensity or prolonged exercise (e.g., marathon running, HIIT, ultra-marathons) can cause nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, and GI bleeding, primarily due to splanchnic hypoperfusion and increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut").
- Physical activity reduced GERD risk (RR = 0.80; 150 min/week reduced risk by 72%), with obesity-specific benefits (OR = 0.41 among obese individuals). However, high-impact or bending activities exacerbated GERD symptoms.
- PA reduced digestive-system cancer risk (RR = 0.82), including colon (RR = 0.81), colorectal (RR = 0.77), and gastric cancer (RR = 0.83).
- Physical activity reduced gallstone risk and improved bile flow and gallbladder motility.
- Yoga and aerobic exercise significantly reduced IBS symptoms including abdominal pain and bloating, improving quality of life and psychological well-being via the gut-brain axis.
- Physical activity was inversely associated with Crohn's disease risk (but not ulcerative colitis), and daily activity was associated with IBD remission persistence.
- Vigorous activity reduced diverticulitis risk (RR = 0.66) and diverticular bleeding (RR = 0.61); running >8 km/day reduced diverticular disease risk by 48%.
- GI bleeding is common in endurance athletes: 85% of ultramarathon participants showed occult blood post-race; 23% of 125 marathon runners converted to positive occult blood post-race; 13% tested positive in another marathon study.
- Constipation risk was reduced with higher PA levels (RR = 0.69), with benefits pronounced in Asian and Oceanian populations and among women.

RISK FACTORS FOR EXERCISE-INDUCED GI SYMPTOMS: exercise intensity, duration, type (high-impact activities like running worse than swimming/cycling), hydration status, training status (beginners more bloating; elites risk ischemic symptoms), age and gender (females and younger individuals show higher symptom prevalence), pre-exercise meal timing, and supplement overuse.

CONCLUSION: Moderate-intensity exercise is a beneficial and well-tolerated intervention for promoting GI health, while high-intensity activities require careful monitoring, particularly in individuals with pre-existing GI disorders. Personalized exercise and dietary strategies are essential for balancing benefits with GI distress risk. The article is open-access under CC BY-NC 4.0 license.
</summary>

"Intense or prolonged exercise, particularly in endurance sports, can induce various GI symptoms, including nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, and even GI bleeding. These symptoms often arise from splanchnic hypoperfusion, where blood is diverted from the GI organs to the muscles." "Moderate-intensity exercise is a beneficial and well-tolerated intervention for promoting GI health, whereas high-intensity activities require careful monitoring, particularly in individuals with pre-existing GI disorders." "In a 100-mile ultramarathon using stool tests, 85% showed occult blood post-race."

--- SOURCE 13: Prokinetics in the Management of Functional Gastrointestinal Disorders ---
URL: https://www.jnmjournal.org/journal/view.html?doi=10.5056%2Fjnm15094

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific review article titled "Prokinetics in the Management of Functional Gastrointestinal Disorders" by Eamonn M M Quigley (Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Houston Methodist Hospital, Texas, USA), published in the Journal of Neurogastroenterology and Motility in 2015 (21(3): 330-336; DOI: 10.5056/jnm15094). The article received June 1, 2015, was accepted June 23, 2015, and published online July 3, 2015.

The review focuses on prokinetic agents—drugs that promote gastrointestinal motility and transit—used in the management of functional gastrointestinal disorders. Key content includes:

**Challenges with the Prokinetic Approach:**
1. Simple stimulation of gut motility may not be a valid target—gastroparesis showed little correlation between accelerated gastric emptying and symptom relief; constipation is more than just infrequent bowel movements.
2. Target disorders (functional dyspepsia, IBS) are poorly defined and contain heterogeneous patient populations based on symptom aggregations alone.
3. Non-selective drugs have side effects—cholinergics caused bladder spasms; cisapride was withdrawn due to cardiac toxicity (hERG channel-mediated arrhythmias like Torsades de Pointes); tegaserod was withdrawn due to rare cardiovascular events.
4. Regulatory hurdles—agencies have adopted a "virtual zero tolerance stance" toward serious adverse events for prokinetic drugs, stifling drug development.

**Available Compounds Discussed:**
- **Cholinergic Agonists**: Bethanechol (largely obsolete for reflux/gastroparesis); neostigmine and pyridostigmine still used for Ogilvie's syndrome and pseudo-obstruction.
- **Dopamine Antagonists**: Metoclopramide (widely used but with CNS side effects—up to 25% of patients may experience side effects, including extrapyramidal reactions leading to a US "black box" warning); domperidone (peripheral DA2 antagonist, not available in the US); levosulpiride (DA2 antagonist in development, shown to accelerate gastric emptying in diabetics).
- **Serotonergic Agonists (5-HT4)**: Cisapride (withdrawn for cardiac arrhythmias); tegaserod (approved for constipation-predominant IBS but withdrawn for rare cardiovascular side effects); prucalopride (highly selective 5-HT4 agonist, approved in several countries for chronic constipation in women who failed laxatives, dose 2 mg once daily, 1 mg for elderly, effective in three large trials with >500 patients each; most common adverse effects were headache 25-30%, nausea 12-24%, abdominal pain 16-23%, diarrhea 12-19%); velusetrag (phase II showed increased spontaneous bowel movements); naronapride (effective in one RCT for chronic constipation); mosapride (selective 5-HT4 agonist available in Asian countries; largest FD study of 566 patients showed no difference from placebo; limited efficacy in diabetic gastropathy; safe without significant cardiovascular effects).
- **Macrolides**: Erythromycin is a motilin agonist most useful in acute gastroparesis (IV 3 mg/kg every 8 hours then oral 250 mg three times daily for 5-7 days); efficacy blunted by hyperglycemia; azithromycin has better oral bioavailability with comparable effects; search continues for non-antibiotic prokinetic macrolides.
- **Other Agents**: Itopride (dopamine D2 antagonist, benefits in FD per meta-analysis but phase III trials were negative).

**New Therapeutic Targets** (adapted from Shin et al): Ghrelin agonists (TZP-101, TZP-102, RM-131) to accelerate gastric emptying; motilin agonists (GSK962040); 5-HT1A agonists (tandospirone) to enhance gastric accommodation; cholinesterase inhibition (acotiamide).

**Future Directions**: The author emphasizes learning from past failures, selecting patients who will truly benefit, and developing highly selective agonists. However, there may be advantages to "dirty" drugs in complex multifactorial disorders—for example, a drug with 5-HT4 agonist and 5-HT3 antagonist properties would be attractive in IBS. The unexpected anti-nociceptive effects of linaclotide and neuroprotective effects of prucalopride may have significant implications.

The article is Open Access (Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License), has been cited by 56 other articles per CrossRef, and is associated with PubMed ID 26130629 and PubMed Central ID PMC4496896.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The term prokinetic means simply to promote movement and, in the context of the gastrointestinal tract, was introduced to refer to a class of drugs that promoted gastrointestinal motility and, thereby, transit."; "Gastroparesis serves as an excellent example of the shortcomings of this approach. A primary target for many new prokinetic agents, gastroparesis proved to be a most frustrating testing ground for novel compounds as little correlation could be found between the accelerating effects of various agents on gastric emptying and symptom responses."; "Chastened by their experiences with cisapride and tegaserod (as well as with other drugs targeted at IBS such as alosetron and cilansetron), regulatory agencies have raised the bar significantly when it comes to the approval of prokinetic and related drugs."; "Up to 25% of patients may experience side effects, the most troubling of which are extrapyramidal reactions."; "In the intention-to-treat analysis of 566 patients there was no difference in dyspeptic symptoms between placebo and any of the 3 mosapride treatment groups."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Buscopan (Hyoscine Butylbromide): Side Effects and Dosage ---
URL: https://patient.info/medicine/hyoscine-butylbromide-tablets-buscopan

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Patient.info medicine information leaflet about hyoscine butylbromide tablets (brand name Buscopan, also known as scopolamine in the US). The article was last updated on 16 October 2023 by Michael Stewart, MRPharmS, and peer reviewed by Sid Dajani. Next review is due 15 October 2026.

**Key details about the medicine:**
- Type: An antimuscarinic antispasmodic medicine
- Used for: Relief of lower tummy (abdominal) pain caused by spasm in the muscles of the digestive or urinary system
- Available as tablets, on prescription, or can be purchased over-the-counter from a pharmacy for IBS symptoms if previously diagnosed by a doctor
- Helps ease bloating and spasm-type pain associated with irritable bowel syndrome and diverticular disease
- Works by relaxing muscles in the gastrointestinal and urinary systems
- Distinct from hyoscine hydrobromide, which is used for travel sickness

**Before taking:** Inform doctor/pharmacist if pregnant/breastfeeding, have prostate problems, digestive issues (reflux, diarrhoea, ulcerative colitis, bowel blockage, severe constipation), high blood pressure, recent heart attack, glaucoma, fast heart rate, Down's syndrome, under 12 or over 65 years old, autonomic neuropathy, myasthenia gravis, or taking other medicines including herbal/complementary ones.

**Dosage:** Usually one or two tablets three times daily, may be increased to two tablets four times daily if needed. Swallow with water, can be taken before or after meals. Do not double up missed doses.

**Usage guidance:** Take only when necessary (during symptom flare-ups, usually within a week or two). If symptoms don't improve within two weeks of taking it (even with a prior IBS diagnosis), see a doctor. If new symptoms develop or existing ones worsen, seek medical advice.

**Side effects** (affect fewer than 1 in 100 people): dry mouth (relieve with sugar-free gum/sweets), dry skin and sweating, and itchy skin rash (which may indicate an allergic reaction).

**Storage:** Keep out of reach of children, store in a cool dry place away from direct heat and light.

**Important warnings:** Never exceed prescribed dose; in case of overdose go to A&E with the container. Never share the medicine with others. Report side effects via the Yellow Card website (yellowcard.mhra.gov.uk).

**References:** Manufacturer's Patient Information Leaflets for Buscopan IBS Relief and Buscopan 10 mg Tablets (Sanofi, September 2022) and the BNF 89th Edition.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Hyoscine butylbromide is an antispasmodic medicine which is taken to relieve cramps in the stomach, intestines or bladder. In particular, it helps to ease bloating and the spasm-type pain that can be associated with irritable bowel syndrome and diverticular disease."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>

It also helps with bladder cramps and period pain. Buscopan works by relaxing muscles in the digestive system and bladder and contains the active ingredient hyoscine butylbromide. It is distinct from hyoscine hydrobromide (Kwells and Joy-Rides), which is used to prevent motion sickness.

Buscopan comes as tablets available on prescription, and as two over-the-counter products: Buscopan Cramps and Buscopan IBS Relief. It can also be given by injection, usually only in hospital settings.

Key facts about Buscopan include: it works quickly, with painful cramps easing within 15 minutes; side effects are unusual but may include dry mouth, constipation, or blurred vision; users experiencing blurred vision should not drive, cycle, or use machinery until the effect wears off; and over-the-counter use should not exceed 2 weeks without consulting a doctor. The page was last reviewed on 13 May 2025, with the next review due on 13 May 2028.

URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-assessment-report-of-the-reclassification-of-buscopan-ibs-relief-hyoscine-butylbromide-10mg-tablets/public-assessment-report-of-the-reclassification-of-buscopan-ibs-relief-hyoscine-butylbromide-10mg-tablets

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Public Assessment Report published by the UK Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) on 11 February 2022, documenting the reclassification of Buscopan IBS Relief (Hyoscine Butylbromide 10mg tablets) to allow a 60-tablet pack size to be sold as a General Sales List (GSL) medicine through general retail outlets.

Key details:
- Product: Buscopan IBS Relief, each tablet containing 10mg hyoscine butylbromide, an antispasmodic used to relieve gastrointestinal tract spasm associated with medically confirmed irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in adults and children aged 12 years and over.
- Licence holder: Opella Healthcare UK Limited.
- Historical context: Hyoscine butylbromide 10mg tablets have been available as GSL since 2004 with a 24-tablet pack; a 40-tablet pack was approved in 2014. This application extended GSL status to a 60-tablet pack.

Terms of reclassification:
a) Maximum pack size: 60 tablets
b) Indication: relief of GI tract spasm associated with medically confirmed IBS in adults and children aged 12+
c) Maximum dose: 20mg (2 tablets)
d) Maximum daily dose: 80mg (8 tablets)
e) Maximum strength: 10mg
f) Route: Oral use

MHRA assessment findings:
- Safety: Post-marketing data showed no change in safety since the 2014 pack size increase; larger pack size unlikely to increase side effect risk.
- Pack size: 60 tablets covers 20 days at minimum dose (1 tablet TID) and 7 days at maximum dose (2 tablets QID). The maximum recommended duration of use is 2 weeks, so there is a small risk of some patients using it longer. This risk is mitigated by a new carton warning advising medical advice if symptoms persist after 2 weeks. The risk of delayed diagnosis of underlying conditions was assessed as low because the product is only for patients with an established IBS diagnosis.
- Misuse risk: No issues identified; managed by the requirement of an established medical diagnosis and existing warnings.
- Handling: No special precautions required.
- Convenience: A larger pack allows treatment of multiple IBS episodes, which is relevant given the episodic nature of IBS, and this benefit outweighs the small risks of continuous use beyond 2 weeks.

No changes to the Risk Management Plan were proposed. The MHRA did not seek advice from the Commission on Human Medicines because no major issues were identified; the proposed terms match existing approved pack sizes, there are no new safety concerns, other GSL IBS products are available in even larger pack sizes (100 capsules), and the label now includes a warning about seeking medical advice if symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks.

Conclusion: The MHRA approved GSL legal status for the 60-tablet pack size of Buscopan IBS Relief under the conditions listed above.
</summary>
