## 7. Dehydration and Hyperthermia

### 7.1 Dehydration
- Blood flow to the gut and liver can be reduced by up to 80% during exercise; GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume. [3]
- GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume. [3]
- Heat stress and dehydration exacerbate the effects of splanchnic hypoperfusion. [1]
- Avoid dehydration; start races well hydrated. [4]
- Gastric emptying is slowed by hypohydration. [63]
- Hypohydration (e.g., 3.1% BW loss) is among the most influential factors increasing GI damage. Even mild heat (<30°C) during a full marathon causes significant GI damage. [62]
- In the Scrivin et al. 2025 case series, most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2–4% body mass loss. [2]

### 7.2 Hyperthermia and Heat Stress
- Heat exposure during exercise leads to intestinal ischemia from blood shunting to skin and muscles; heat acclimatization and hydration help mitigate effects. [3]
- Exercise hyperthermia induces greater changes in gastrointestinal permeability, although whether the latter is only via hyperthermia is unclear. [25]
- Exercise-induced hyperthermia is directly associated with increases in intestinal permeability (2016), with core temperatures exceeding 39°C always associated with augmented permeability. [7]
- Pires et al. (2017) identified core temperature thresholds of 38.5°C (increased permeability in some participants) and 39°C (augmented permeability universal). [24]
- EIGS is exacerbated by heat stress only when core body temperature reaches ≥39.0°C. [44]
- Heat stress and dehydration (hypohydration, e.g., 3.1% BW loss) are the most influential factors increasing GI damage. Even mild heat (<30°C) during a full marathon causes significant GI damage. [62]
- **Smith PhD thesis (Liverpool John Moores University, 2021):** 
  - GI permeability displays a dose-response relationship with exercise intensity, but this does NOT correlate with the expression of GI symptoms. GI symptom appearance is likely due to multiple factors including physiological strain and exercise intensity, and is highly individualistic. [24]
  - For the first time, hyperthermia implemented during resting conditions (via hot water immersion), in the absence of exercise-induced mesenteric hypoperfusion, does NOT augment GI permeability or markers of GI distress. However, passive hyperthermia results in symptoms of heat illness, and core temperature is strongly correlated with nausea. [24]
  - Acute glutamine supplementation returned no protective effects on GI damage, permeability, core temperature, or heat-illness symptoms in response to passive hyperthermia exposure, despite prior research suggesting glutamine could ameliorate intestinal permeability and core temperature. [24]
  - "Exercise causes an increase in GI permeability, a response NOT observed when similar levels of core temperature are induced by passive hyperthermia. Therefore, the increase in GI permeability during exercise is likely caused by intestinal ischemia (reduced blood flow) rather than an increase in core temperature. No association between intestinal permeability and GI symptoms appears to exist." [24]
- Gastric emptying is reduced in heat. Owen et al. (1986) found subjects emptied 79% of ingested water in 25°C vs. only 59% at 35°C. Neufer et al. (1989) found significant negative correlation between GE and rectal temperature; hypohydration also reduced GE. [26]
- Williams et al. (1964) found prolonged exercise in heat reduced active but not passive carbohydrate absorption. Maughan et al. (1990) found reduced absorption with exercise. However, direct segmental perfusion studies (Fordtran and Saltin, 1967; Gisolfi et al., 1991) found NO effect of exercise intensity (30–70% VO2max) or duration (60–90 min) on fluid absorption. [26]
- No data exist for exercise exceeding 90 minutes in warm environments. [26]
- GI damage is primarily associated with running but also observed in triathletes and elite cyclists. [26]
- Heat compounds gut issues—blood shifts to skin for cooling and gastric emptying slows. [28]

### 7.3 Thermoregulation in Older Athletes
- Older individuals show delayed core temperature onset threshold for sweating and reduced evaporative heat loss due to lower overall sweat rate. This is not due to fewer activated sweat glands, but to reduced sweat production per gland (sweat gland atrophy or decreased cholinergic sensitivity). Age-related effects are greater on forehead and limb sweat glands than on trunk glands, suggesting peripheral-to-central decline. [52]
- Older individuals exhibit impaired heat-induced rises in skin blood flow (SkBF) compared to younger counterparts, even when matched for aerobic fitness, acclimation, and hydration status—suggesting this is a primary function of aging. SkBF plateaus at ~60% of maximum during exercise in the heat in healthy young individuals due to baroreceptor reflex-mediated control. [52]
- Mechanisms of impaired SkBF in older individuals include: reduced sympathetic cholinergic cotransmitter release, altered downstream signalling for vascular endothelial function, attenuated heat stress-induced sympathetic neural drive, compromised NO-dependent cutaneous vasodilation, reduced capillary density in aged skin, and lower cardiac output (due to lower stroke volume or blunted chronotropic response). [52]
- Older individuals also show decrements in thirst sensation and renal sodium/water-conserving capabilities, limiting their ability to accommodate increases in intravascular blood volume. [52]
- Individuals over age 60 are the most vulnerable age cohort to heat-related adverse health outcomes due to impaired thermoregulatory control, particularly during physical activity in the heat. [52]
- There are currently NO public health recommendations for physical activity in the heat specifically for older individuals. [52]
- Exercise training improves cardiac, autonomic, and vascular endothelial function, and can slow age-related decline in heat loss effector function. Inoue et al. showed fit older individuals have greater sweat gland output than unfit older individuals. Consecutive days (>6 days) of passive heat exposure (>40°C for min 60 min) produces heat acclimation in older individuals. Best et al. showed older cyclists achieve similar acclimation benefits as younger cyclists after 6 days. [52]
- A large cohort study (n=2327) found repeated whole-body heat exposure associated with ~5-fold reduction in fatal cardiovascular and all-mortality events in men aged 42–60 years. [52]
- Older athletes are able to thermoregulate adequately, albeit via slightly different mechanisms, during exercise in hot environments. [53]
- V̇O2max throughout aging improves thermoregulatory function, including enhanced sweating and cardiovascular responses to exercise heat-stress. [54, 56]
- High aerobic fitness improves body temperature regulation during exercise via augmented sweating and improved cardiovascular function, including cardiac output. [56]
- Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. Recommendations: drop carb intake by 10–20g/hour until heat-acclimated, choose liquid calories, eat small amounts every 10–15 minutes, start hydrated and cool, don't rely on thirst, include sodium in everything you drink, monitor urine color, and watch for hyponatremia. [28]

## 8. Mechanical/Impact Factors Specific to Running (Additional Detail)

- Mechanical causes: Repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut; symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists. Posture (e.g., "aero" position on bicycles) and swallowing air can contribute. [4]
- Poor posture, increased abdominal pressure, and aerophagia (swallowing air while drinking from water bottles) contribute to GI symptoms like flatulence, diarrhea, and urgency. [3]
- GI distress during exercise can be caused by mechanical factors including posture changes in cycling, bouncing impact in running causing intestinal bleeding, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. [23]
- Resistance exercise produces GI distress, and absolute load appears to be a primary mechanism (via intra-abdominal pressure). The findings align with aerobic exercise research showing GI symptoms do not always correlate with markers of GI damage. [27]

## 9. Age-Related Changes in Gastrointestinal Physiology (Relevant to Athletes Over 40 / Masters Runners)

### 9.1 General Age-Related GI Changes (Important Context)
- Because the digestive system has a lot of reserve built into it, aging has less effect on its function than it does on the function of other organ systems. [35]
- Age-related changes by organ (Merck Manual):
  - **Esophagus:** Contraction strength and upper esophageal sphincter tension decrease (presbyesophagus), but food movement is not impaired; some older adults may develop diseases affecting contractions. [35]
  - **Stomach:** Reduced lining resistance increases peptic ulcer disease risk, especially with aspirin/NSAID use; decreased elasticity limits food accommodation and slows emptying, though usually without symptoms; acid/pepsin secretion largely unchanged, but atrophic gastritis becomes more common, potentially causing vitamin B12 deficiency or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. [35]
  - **Small intestine:** Structure and nutrient absorption largely unchanged; lactase levels decrease leading to lactose intolerance in many older adults; small intestinal bacterial overgrowth becomes more common, causing pain, bloating, weight loss, and reduced absorption of vitamin B12, iron, and calcium. [35]
  - **Large intestine and rectum:** Large intestine changes little; rectum enlarges somewhat. Constipation becomes more common due to slower transit, reduced rectal contractions, more constipating medications, less physical activity, and pelvic floor weakness in older women (which can also contribute to fecal incontinence). [35]
- Changes in the gut microbiome with age may be connected to overall healthy aging and may affect obesity, metabolic disorders, inflammation, cancer, depression, or other health issues. [35]
- Basic mechanisms of aging GI tract (Gallo et al. 2024): Impaired esophageal peristalsis, lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction, slowed gastric emptying, increased colonic transit time (small bowel motility generally unchanged). [33]
- "Anorexia of aging" from slowed gastric emptying leading to weight loss and sarcopenia. [33]
- Presbyphagia (age-related swallowing changes) predisposes to dysphagia. [33]
- Myenteric plexus degeneration, villi degeneration, mucosal atrophy, altered tight junctions increasing intestinal permeability. [33]
- Decreased cytoprotective mucus-bicarbonate barrier, reduced gastric blood flow, impaired repair mechanisms. [33]
- Immunosenescence in gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) with increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1b, IL-6, TNFa), contributing to frailty and increased morbidity/mortality. [33]
- GI symptoms in older people more often underlie organic pathologies, while GI functional disorders are less frequently diagnosed in this age group. Moreover, gastrointestinal disease can also present in a nuanced and atypical manner, making the diagnostic hypothesis and, consequently, the correct diagnosis and therapy more challenging. [33]
- SIBO prevalence increases with age (significantly higher in those 61+). Risk factors: reduced gastric secretion (PPI use), reduced GI motility, intestinal surgery, small bowel diverticulosis. Treatment: low carbohydrate diet, prokinetics, nonabsorbable antibiotics. [33]
- Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth prevalence is 15.6% in elderly vs 5.9% in younger. [34]
- Small bowel function is largely preserved with age. [34]
- Peptic ulcer disease in elderly is often atypical—only 30% present with typical epigastric pain. [34]
- Elderly with bleeding PUD had significantly higher 30-day morbidity and mortality after open surgery. [34]
- H. pylori colonizes 50% of the global population; it is a Type I carcinogen linked to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. [34]
- Diverticular disease prevalence increases with age, reaching 70% in those over 85 (uncommon under age 40). [33]
- Acute mesenteric ischemia is an underestimated cause of acute abdomen in the elderly, with an incidence that increases exponentially with age, particularly in patients aged over 75 years, and a mortality rate ranging from 60 to 80% of affected patients. [33]
- Acute mesenteric ischemia is more common than ruptured abdominal aneurysm in the elderly and is a more common cause of acute abdomen than appendicitis in those over 75. Endovascular therapy is preferred over open revascularization (16% vs 28% mortality). [34]
- Small bowel bleeding (5% of GI bleeds) is most commonly due to angiodysplasia (54% in elderly), associated with Heyde's syndrome (bleeding angiodysplasia with aortic stenosis). [34]
- Aging reduces each organ system's capacity to maintain homeostasis. Decreased physiologic reserve leads to higher risk of malnutrition, falls, depression, social isolation, and functional deterioration. [33]

### 9.2 Masters Athletes and Gut Issues (Neversecond Article by Marni Sumbal, RD)
- The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. [28]
- Masters athletes can target 60–90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor—gut training is. [28]
- Three causes of GI distress in masters athletes:
  - Physiological: Exercise diverts blood away from the gut (at 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop nearly 80%), causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea. [28]
  - Mechanical: Running jolts the GI tract, making runners more prone to lower GI issues than cyclists. [28]
  - Nutritional: High-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods eaten too close to training, plus concentrated drinks, slow stomach emptying. [28]
- Gut training for masters athletes: Start at 30–40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10–15g every 1–2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt. [28]
- "Aging doesn't have to mean slowing down — but it does mean paying closer attention to your gut." [28]
- "Your gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly well into their later years. Age is context, not a ceiling." [28]
- Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. [28]
- Many elite endurance athletes now successfully consume 120–150g of carbs per hour, but that takes time and consistency to build. [28]

### 9.3 Masters Athlete-Specific GI Symptom Data (VIREF Study)
- A study evaluating the relationship between food restriction and gastrointestinal symptoms in master athletes, using the Food Restriction in Running Questionnaire developed by Parnell et al., found that the most common gastrointestinal symptoms experienced during racing were gas (51%), stomach pain/cramp (43%), intestinal problems (pain) (42%), reflux/heartburn (39%) and nausea/vomiting (39%). [37]
- On GI symptoms by gender, significant differences were found in constipation, gas, fullness/heaviness and burping, which were more commonly observed in the female athletes (p<0.05). [37]
- Increasing the race distance and performance level increased the food restriction rates and incidence of gastrointestinal symptoms in master athletes. Furthermore, food restriction and the incidence of gastrointestinal symptoms were observed more in the female athletes. [37]

### 9.4 Gut Microbiome in Aging and Athletes
- **Exercise and microbiome in middle-aged amateurs:** A recent study found that young people who lack exercise have higher levels of pro-inflammatory gut bacteria and lower immune resistance than elite athletes and (middle-aged amateur athletes). [32]
- Physical activity/exercise has a positive effect on the composition of the gut microbiome of older adults (Ramos et al., 2022 systematic review). Taniguchi et al. (2018) found (positive effects). [68]
- The gut microbiome changes with age; diet and exercise influence this relationship. [69]
- Moderate exercise promotes a healthy immune system, while high-intensity exercise for a long duration can cause a leaky gut and consequent systemic inflammation, which may disrupt the microbial balance. [29]
- Exercise has a "J-curve" shaped (hormetic) effect on gut health—moderate exercise benefits gut health, while intense/sustained exercise can be deleterious. [30]
- Athletes exhibit higher alpha diversity and more health-associated bacteria (e.g., Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Prevotella, Faecalibacterium). Microbiome composition varies by sport type, and microbiome composition is predictive of exercise gains. [30]
- Athletes have increased faecal SCFAs, especially butyrate. VO2 max was strongly correlated with butyrate production and butyrate-producing bacteria (Clostridiales, Roseburia, Lachnospiraceae, Erysipelotrichaceae). [30]
- Veillonella atypica was found highly enriched in marathon runners' faecal samples; supplementing mice with V. atypica significantly improved treadmill performance, possibly due to lactate metabolism. [30]
- Scheiman et al. (2019) showed Veillonella atypica inoculation in mice prolonged treadmill running; Veillonella converts lactic acid to propionate, which improved performance. Morita et al. (2023) found Bacteroides uniformis abundance correlated with 3000-m race times; 9 weeks of α-cyclodextrin supplementation increased B. uniformis and shortened 10-km cycling times in humans; propionate/acetate stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis and beta-oxidation. [62]
- Moderate exercise (<70% VO2max) has positive health effects: reduces inflammation, decreases intestinal permeability, improves body composition, and induces positive changes in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites. Intense exercise (>70% VO2max) can increase gastrointestinal epithelial wall permeability and diminish gut mucus thickness, potentially allowing pathogens to enter the bloodstream, contributing to increased inflammation. [65]
- Elite athletes tend to have higher gut microbial diversity, shifted toward bacterial species involved in amino acid biosynthesis and carbohydrate/fiber metabolism, producing key metabolites like short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). [65]
- The human gut microbiome comprises over a thousand bacterial species, with anaerobic species producing anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) through fermentation of dietary sugars. Butyrate serves as the primary energy source for colonocytes and enhances epithelial barrier function. [29]
- Single exercise/race changes: acute high-intensity exercise increased Romboutsia, Ruminococcaceae UCG-005, E. coli TOP498, Blautia; a half-marathon increased Ruminococcus bicirculans and Collinsella aerofaciens; a full marathon increased Veillonella; an ultramarathon (~44h, 96km) decreased four butyrate-producing species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increased Collinsella aerofaciens. [62]
- Repeated training (6 weeks, 3 days/week): increased Faecalibacterium and Lachnospira, decreased Bacteroides in lean subjects, with increased SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate). [62]
- Athlete vs nonathlete comparisons: findings are discrepant across studies (e.g., Faecalibacterium less abundant in marathon runners per Kulecka 2020, but more abundant in female elite endurance runners per Morishima 2021). [62]
- Athletes' gut microbiomes undergo multiple stressors from their lifestyle, causing high variability and potentially long-lasting changes. Athlete diets and activity levels change drastically between on/off seasons; dietary changes can cause significant compositional changes within 24 hours. Travel is associated with high microbiome variability and gastrointestinal distress (O'Donovan et al., 2020). [67]
- Probiotic supplementation (meta-analysis 2022) may improve performance in aerobic-trained populations, but there is likely publication bias (no studies report negative results). [62]
- The probiotic market was estimated to reach $69 billion by 2023. [30]

### 9.5 Aging Cardiovascular Performance (Relevant to Splanchnic Perfusion in Older Athletes)
- Progressive aging induces several structural and functional alterations in the cardiovascular system, among which particularly important are a reduced number of myocardial cells and increased interstitial collagen fibers, which result in impaired left ventricular diastolic function. [55]
- Aging causes reduced maximal heart rate response to exercise (due to beta1 receptor down-regulation), and peripheral changes including reduced skeletal muscle cells and decreased Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) I and IIa fibers. Even without cardiovascular disease, aging is strongly associated with reduced maximal aerobic capacity. [55]
- Aerobic/endurance exercise improves peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope, ventilatory aerobic threshold, and Heart Rate Recovery (HRR). Mechanisms include improved chronotropic incompetence, increased stroke volume, enhanced vagal tone, improved endothelial function and arterial compliance, and favorable skeletal muscle biochemical changes (increased MHC I). [55]
- Aging does not contraindicate exercise training in healthy elderly or those with comorbidities. [55]

### 9.6 Medication Interactions in Older Athletes
- Older adults are more prone to digestive issues related to medication use; constipation is often medication-induced. [35]
- Pill esophagitis is more prevalent in elderly due to polypharmacy, reduced motility, and insufficient water intake, with NSAIDs, aspirin, doxycycline, bisphosphonates, ferrous sulfate, and captopril as common culprits. Chest pain (71.8%) and odynophagia (38.5%) are the most common symptoms. [34]
- Management of GI disorders in the elderly often differs from younger patients due to polypharmacy, atypical presentations, delayed diagnosis, and increased vulnerability to medication side effects. [34]
- NSAID risk is higher in older people (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.7) for acute kidney injury. [15]
- Reduced lining resistance of the stomach increases peptic ulcer disease risk, especially with aspirin/NSAID use. [35]

### 9.7 Explicit Note on Age-Specific Data Availability
- **Direct age-specific data for masters runners (age 40+) on exercise-associated GI distress are extremely limited.** The research base is dominated by studies of younger endurance athletes (mean ages typically in the 20s–30s). [Aggregate observation from all sources]
- The most directly relevant age-specific sources identified include: the VIREF study on master athletes' GI symptoms and food restrictions [37], the Neversecond masters athletes article (which notes the small intestine's carbohydrate absorption stays largely intact with age and that masters athletes can achieve the same fueling targets as younger athletes with gut training) [28], and studies on aging thermoregulation in older athletes (Balmain et al. 2018 [52]; Kenney GSSI SSE #44 [53]; Kenney 2020/2021 [54, 56]).
- Peters et al. (1999) found that exercise-related GI symptoms were significantly related to age among other variables, but did not provide specific age-stratified data for masters athletes. [38]
- The Gallo et al. (2024) and Dumic et al. (2019) reviews describe age-related GI changes in adults over 65 (not specifically athletes over 40), so extrapolation to masters runners (40+) must be made cautiously. [33, 34]
- Merck Manual notes aging has less effect on digestive function than on other organ systems due to reserve capacity, but documents reduced gastric lining resistance, reduced elasticity/slower emptying, decreased lactase, increased SIBO, and increased constipation risk with age. [35]
- **Where findings are extrapolated:** The mechanisms of Ex-GIS/EIGS (splanchnic hypoperfusion, motility disturbance, mechanical jostling, FODMAP sensitivity, NSAID effects, dehydration/hyperthermia) established in the general endurance-athlete population are presumed to apply to masters runners, but dedicated primary studies in masters runners are largely absent from the current literature.

## 10. Resistance Exercise GI Findings (Supplementary Evidence on Intra-Abdominal Pressure Mechanism)

- Resistance exercise induces significant GI distress, with 70% of participants reporting at least one GI symptom, most commonly nausea, and 60% reporting at least one moderate symptom after the exercise session, with no differences between sexes. [27]
- Consistent with aerobic exercise studies, biomarkers of GI injury did not consistently correlate with subjective symptoms. [27]
- The magnitude of GI damage correlated directly with absolute strength, suggesting males experienced more GI distress because they lifted heavier loads, generating higher intra-abdominal pressure. [27]
- The global digestive health market is projected to reach $58 billion by 2025, with many products marketed to active individuals despite limited evidence of GI damage in resistance-trained populations. [27]

## 11. Gut Trainability and Practical Management (Cross-Cutting)

- GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion. [4]
- "More marathons are won or lost in the portable toilets than at the dinner table." — Bill Rodgers. [4, 20]
- 30–50% of all athletes experience GI problems regularly. Fiber intake, fat intake, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions increase prevalence. Hot weather and dehydration exacerbate symptoms. Training the gut may alleviate symptoms by improving gastric emptying, reducing bloating, and increasing absorption speed. [64]
- The gut is highly adaptable; athletes should practice their event nutrition plan over several weeks to optimize carbohydrate absorption, reduce GI distress, and improve performance. [63]
- Despite extensive research, there are still no sufficiently effective methods to prevent exercise-associated GI ailments. The most effective measures according to current data include reduced fiber intake in the pre-competition period and "gut training" to prepare the digestive system for such exertion. [42]
- Strategies with consistent beneficial outcomes (SDA/USSF Joint Position Statement): macronutrient intake before/during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulation of FODMAPs, and gut training/feeding tolerance adjustments. [43]
- Practical guidelines for athletes:
  - Avoid high-fiber foods on competition day and for several days leading up to the event [3]
  - Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities (e.g., dairy, gluten) [3]
  - Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol) [3]
  - Avoid NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen [3]
  - Avoid high-fructose foods; a fructose-glucose combination may be better tolerated [3]
  - Avoid dehydration—prevention is key [3]
  - Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water [3]
  - Choose carbohydrate drinks with lower concentrations to prevent high osmolalities in the stomach [3]
  - Practice new nutrition strategies before race day [3]
- Sports drinks should be below 8% carbohydrate concentration (preferably glucose and fructose combination) to prevent dehydration. [23]
- A 28-day study of 16 trained cyclists/triathletes found that high-carbohydrate diets led to greater maximal citrate synthase activity and higher carbohydrate exogenous oxidation rates during submaximal exercise, attributed to enhanced intestinal absorption and improved tolerance. [23]
- Probiotic supplementation is associated with decreased inflammation, enhanced sports performance, and fewer gastrointestinal disturbances. [29]
- Probiotic blends significantly reduce URTI incidence and symptoms in athletes. One study (Tavares-Silva) showed a 29% reduction in URTI incidents in marathon runners; another showed a 2.2-fold decrease in URTI symptoms with a probiotic blend. [30]
- 2 weeks of bovine colostrum intake increased HSP70 and reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases (shorter periods or severe heat >40°C were not effective). Single glutamine intake and 4 weeks of probiotic intake had inconsistent results. Carbohydrate drinks (alone or with protein/pectin alginate) before/during exercise reduced GI damage, especially in heat. Cold water ingestion (0–7°C) lowered rectal temperature but did not significantly reduce GI damage in heat. Wearing compression socks (25 mm Hg) during a marathon reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases but did not affect race time. [62]

## 12. Methodological Quality Concerns in the Field

- Research in exercise gastroenterology has grown exponentially, but published literature consistently suffers from substantial experimental limitations affecting the accuracy of translating study outcomes into practice. [44]
- Studies often fail to report comprehensive inclusion/exclusion criteria, including gastrointestinal diseases, dietary practices, supplement use, and pharmaceutical prescriptions. [44]
- Most studies fail to implement or report robust dietary control. Gold standard requires providing all foods and fluids at least 24 hr before trials, with low-FODMAP diet (<5 g/day total FODMAP) standardization recommended. [44]
- Standardized experimental procedures are needed for accurate interpretation of research findings, avoiding misinterpreted pathological relevance and overstated clinical/practical relevance of intervention research outcomes, supporting more accurate translation into safe practice guidelines. [44]
- The Scrivin et al. case series is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science, with 40 references in the bibliography, and has been cited 3 times. [2]
- The Ribichini et al. review searched PubMed, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases (up to March 2023), identifying 142 research articles for inclusion based on established criteria. [1]
- The Kołodziejczyk et al. narrative review searched PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, covering publications up to October 2025. ## Abstract

The special issue “Physiological Aspects of Marathon Running” in “Frontiers in Physiology” aims to evoke attentions to this field. In this minireview, the two guest editors of the special issue introduce their interest in the gastrointestinal (GI) functions with endurance running and gut microbiota on marathon running. Following the introduction, the first part summarized research examining exercise-induced GI damage and methods to mitigate the damage. The latter part summarized the influence of exercise on gut microbiota, and the gut microbiota on endurance performance. From the brief overview above, this minireview synthesizes current knowledge and identifies critical topics for future studies for optimizing GI function and the gut microbiota in endurance athletes.

**Keywords:** small intestine, microbiota, endurance athletes, recovery, endurance performance

## 1 Introduction

There has been extensive research on exercise training, recovery, and performance in endurance athletes focusing on skeletal muscle, respiratory and circulatory function, vascular function, and energy metabolism. However, recent research has emphasized the role of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, with a particular focus on “GI damage” and “gut microbiota.” Keeffe et al. reported that marathon runners experienced bowel movements (35%) and diarrhea (19%) after running, occasionally preventing them from running ([Keeffe et al., 1984](#B28)). Runners often have more abnormalities in the lower digestive tract than in the upper digestive tract ([Peters et al., 1999](#B50)). Presently, it is believed that 30%–70% of athletes experience GI problems ([de Oliveira and Burini, 2009](#B17); [Coleman, 2019](#B12)), although one study suggests that the prevalence is not that high ([ter Steege et al., 2008](#B71)). Therefore, for endurance athletes, the digestive tract is a vital organ for good training and athletic performance.

The GI tract is responsible for the digestion and absorption of ingested nutrients and acts as a protective barrier against bacterial translocation. Nevertheless, strenuous exercise (e.g., prolonged exercise) decreases GI function ([Chantler et al., 2021](#B10)). Prolonged exercise increases both GI (small intestinal) damage and the permeability of the intestinal barrier, which allows the translocation of bacteria and its unfavorable metabolites (i.e., endotoxin) into the systemic circulation, induces systemic inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion, increases body temperature, aggravates subjective GI symptom (such as gastric distention and discomfort) ([Chantler et al., 2021](#B10)). Furthermore, increased levels of intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP) in the blood, an indirect indicator of small intestinal damage, decrease the rate of digestion and absorption of ingested nutrients ([van Wijck et al., 2013](#B73)). Considering that muscle protein synthesis and muscle glycogen resynthesis are maximized in the early phase of postexercise period ([Koopman et al., 2007](#B31); [Beelen et al., 2010](#B5); [Burke et al., 2017](#B7)), the increase in exercise-induced GI damage can delay the ingested nutrients to the muscle, which might negatively impact post-exercise recovery. Therefore, reducing GI damage following endurance exercise is important in terms of improving endurance exercise performance and promoting post-exercise recovery.

Several hundred species comprising 100 trillion bacteria are estimated to live in the human gut. Endotoxins ([Simons and Kennedy, 2004](#B59)) and an imbalance in the composition of the gut microbiota (dysbiosis) ([Bonomini-Gnutzmann et al., 2022](#B6); [Patel et al., 2024](#B49)) have been implicated in lower GI symptoms in endurance athletes. One study reported that the difference in microbiota composition between rugby players and controls led to the recognition of the impact of exercise on microbiota ([Clarke et al., 2014](#B11)). Since then, several studies have been conducted and a systematic review has been published on the effects of physical activity ([Aya et al., 2021](#B4)) and endurance exercise ([Bonomini-Gnutzmann et al., 2022](#B6)) on gut microbiota. Nonetheless, discrepancies exist in those studies. For instance, *Faecalibacterium* has been reported to be less abundant in marathon runners than in sedentary controls ([Kulecka et al., 2020](#B32)); however, it has also been reported to be more abundant in female endurance runners than in age-matched controls ([Morishima et al., 2021](#B40)). Therefore, to clarify this discrepancy, this review organizes the studies on gut microbiota in terms of changes induced by a single exercise or race and those induced by repeated training, with a comparison between endurance athletes and nonathletes, and focuses on the types of microbiota composition. Finally, directions for future studies are suggested.

The purpose of this minireview is to introduce the changes in GI function with endurance exercise and role of gut microbiota in marathon running. This is one of the topics that we, the two guest editors of the special issue “Physiological Aspects of Marathon Running” in “Frontiers in Physiology”, would like to explore in the issue. The literature reviewed in this minireview was published or searched using PubMed by the 24th of December 2024.

## 2 Gastrointestinal function with endurance exercise

### 2.1 Endurance exercise and GI damage

Endurance exercise, particularly prolonged and/or high-intensity endurance exercise, induces significant GI damage. During exercise, blood flow is preferentially distributed to the skeletal muscle, which temporarily reduces GI blood flow ([van Wijck et al., 2011](#B72)). This hypoperfusion in the GI tract increases tissue hypoxia and oxidative stress, resulting in intestinal cell damage and alterations in endothelial tight junctions. In the past few years, knowledge has accumulated on the factors that elevate GI damage associated with endurance exercise. Regarding exercise intensity, higher exercise intensity increases muscle blood flow, leading to lower GI blood flow as well as higher GI damage ([Edwards et al., 2021](#B19)). Conversely, differences in exercise duration may exert a smaller effect on GI symptoms and GI damage ([Edwards et al., 2021](#B19); [Gaskell et al., 2023](#B21)). Focusing on the differences in exercise modalities, cycling or running endurance exercise for 45 min at relatively identical intensity (70% of  ) resulted in greater increases in blood I-FABP levels for cycling exercise than for running exercise ([Edwards et al., 2021](#B19)). However, RPE and HR during exercise in that study was significantly higher in the cycling trial. In contrast, GI symptoms and GI damage after exercise in the heat were similar between cycling exercise (55% of maximal aerobic power) and running exercise (55% of  ) when the RPE, HR, and rectal temperature during exercise were matched between the two trials ([Costa et al., 2022](#B14)). Further research is necessary to explore the effects of different exercise modalities on exercise-induced GI damage.

The effect of thermoregulation during exercise, involving dehydration and heat stress, has been well documented as a factor increasing exercise-induced GI damage. [Costa et al. (2019)](#B13) demonstrated that hypohydration (3.1% of BW loss) during a 2-h run significantly increased blood I-FABP concentrations associated with exercise compared with euhydration (0.6% of BW loss). They speculated that increased dehydration significantly reduced GI blood flow followed by increased GI damage. Heat stress is also a major factor that elevates GI damage ([Snipe et al., 2018a](#B63); [2018b](#B64); [Osborne et al., 2019b](#B48); [Wallett et al., 2021](#B74); [Sumi et al., 2024](#B65)). Exercise in the heat increases skin blood flow and sweat volume to promote heat dissipation from the skin compared with exercise in a thermoneutral environment, which induces a greater reduction in GI blood flow and elevated GI damage. Therefore, elevated core temperature and dehydration (or hypohydration) are probably the most influential factors that increase GI damage. Even under mild heat stress conditions (<30°C), prolonged exercise such as a full marathon would cause significant GI damage due to dehydration and elevated core temperature. In fact, a large number of runners complain of GI symptoms during full marathon races ([Kelly et al., 2023](#B29)).

In addition to heat stress, a hypoxic environment elevates exercise-induced GI damage. Endurance running in hypobaric hypoxia or normobaric hypoxia (fraction of inspired oxygen: 13.5%–13.8%) elevates GI damage and systemic inflammatory responses compared with the same exercise (i.e., same running velocity or same pedaling work load) in normoxia ([Hill et al., 2020](#B24); [McKenna et al., 2022](#B38)). Exercise in hypoxia reduces oxygen saturation in the working muscle due to lower blood oxygen saturation, which results in higher muscle blood flow than exercise in normoxia ([Casey and Joyner, 2012](#B8); [Joyner et al., 2014](#B27)). Therefore, GI blood flow may be considerably reduced and GI damage may be elevated after exercise in hypoxia. Nevertheless, the blood I-FABP response after endurance running was similar between hypoxia and normoxia when exercise intensity was relatively matched (i.e., same % of  ) between hypoxia and normoxia ([Nomura et al., 2024](#B45)).

Various factors that elevate exercise-induced GI damage have been demonstrated. Perhaps a greater reduction in GI blood flow, especially due to increased body water loss and redistribution of blood flow to the peripheral tissues (i.e., skin and working muscle), increases exercise-induced GI damage. Conversely, considering that elevated GI damage negatively affects performance and promotes recovery after exercise, it is necessary to develop strategies for reducing exercise-induced GI damage.

### 2.2 Effective strategy reducing exercise-induced GI damage

GI damage following endurance exercise induces greater inflammatory response, GI symptoms and lower absorbed and digestive capacity of macronutrients. These responses would have a negative impact on performance and recovery. For example, lower absorbed and digestive capacity of ingested macronutrient may negatively affect for recovery of nutritional aspect, considering that muscle protein synthesis and muscle glycogen resynthesis rate are maximally stimulated during the early phase of post-exercise period ([Koopman et al., 2007](#B31); [Beelen et al., 2010](#B5); [Burke et al., 2017](#B7)).

Exercise-induced GI damage can be alleviated by using various procedures, particularly macronutrient supplementation that has been widely reported. [March et al. (2017)](#B36), [March et al. (2019)](#B35) showed that 2 weeks of bovine colostrum intake improved cellular protection function via an increase in HSP70 levels, which contributed toward reducing exercise-induced increases in blood I-FABP levels. In contrast, a shorter (7 days) supplemental period ([Morrison et al., 2014](#B42)) or severe heat stress (e.g., >40°C) during exercise ([McKenna et al., 2017](#B37)) was not likely to mitigate exercise-induced GI damage following bovine colostrum supplementation. Studies have also reported the effects of a single intake of glutamine before exercise ([Pugh et al., 2017](#B51); [Osborne et al., 2019a](#B47)) and 4 weeks of probiotic intake ([Pugh et al., 2019](#B52); [2020](#B53); [Mooren et al., 2020](#B39)), although the results were inconsistent. Regarding macronutrients, ingestion of a drink containing carbohydrates alone or a mixture of carbohydrates and other nutrients (protein and pectin alginate) before and during exercise reduced exercise-induced GI damage ([Snipe et al., 2017](#B62); [Flood et al., 2020](#B20)). It has been considered that the ingestion of nutrients containing sufficient calories alleviates GI damage by increasing GI blood flow. In particular, the two abovementioned studies investigated the response to exercise in the heat. Considering that heat stress strongly affects exercise-induced GI damage, glucose ingestion may be a valuable strategy to mitigate exercise-induced GI damage in the heat. However, glucose intake in the gel form may not exert a positive effect ([Sessions et al., 2016](#B58)).

The effects of ingesting water at different temperatures on exercise-induced GI damage in the heat have also been examined ([Snipe and Costa, 2018](#B61)). Skin blood flow during exercise increases in the heat due to heat dissipation, and subsequently GI blood flow reduces. Therefore, ingestion of lower temperature water may reduce the increase in core temperature during exercise, which may contribute to a reduction in GI damage due to the maintenance of GI blood flow (decrease in skin blood flow). [Snipe and Costa (2018)](#B61) demonstrated that COOL (7°C) and COLD (0°C) water ingestion did not significantly reduce the increase in blood I-FABP levels, whereas the increase in rectal temperature (Δ) was lower in the COOL (1.7°C ± 0.4°C) and COLD (1.6°C ± 0.4°C) conditions than in the TEMP (2.0°C ± 0.5°C) condition. They speculated that water ingestion at a temperature of 0°C–7°C was insufficient to reduce heat strain and therefore did not reduce exercise-induced GI damage in the heat. Another study also examined the effects of ice-slurry ingestion before and during exercise but found no reduction in exercise-induced increases in blood I-FABP levels in the heat ([Alhadad et al., 2023](#B1)).

Conversely, [Zadow et al. (2020)](#B75) reported the effects of wearing a compression garment (socks) during endurance exercise on exercise-induced GI damage. Wearing a compression garment on the lower legs increases venous return, which may cause maintenance of blood flow in the central region (e.g., the GI tract). They showed that wearing compression socks with 25 mm Hg during a marathon race decreased the exercise-induced increases in blood I-FABP compared with that in the non-wearing group. However, no significant difference was observed in the marathon race time between the two groups ([Zadow et al., 2020](#B75)).

Most previous studies that investigated exercise-induced GI damage (elevations in blood I-FABP levels) have focused on GI permeability, systemic inflammatory response, and GI symptoms with endurance exercise. In contrast, exercise-induced elevations of blood I-FABP levels are associated with delayed digestion and absorption rates following macronutrient ingestion ([van Wijck et al., 2013](#B73)). Nonetheless, a few studies have explored the relationship between exercise-induced GI damage and the rate of digestion and absorption of ingested nutrients, but the evidence is lacking. Therefore, further studies are required to determine the nutritional aspects of recovery (e.g., muscle glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein synthesis) following exercise with a developing strategy to mitigate exercise-induced GI damage.

## 3 Roles of gut microbiota on endurance running

### 3.1 Gut microbiota of endurance athletes

Here, we discuss the literature on the gut microbiota of endurance athletes in terms of changes induced by a single exercise or race and those induced by repeated training, with a comparison of endurance athletes and focusing on the types of microbiota composition.

Regarding the changes in gut microbiota induced by a single bout of exercise and a single-stage race, Tabone et al. investigated the effect of short duration of high-intensity exercise ([Tabone et al., 2021](#B69)). In their study, 40 male endurance cross-country athletes performed an incremental treadmill run with a slope of 1% at a speed of 10 km/h, with increments of 0.3 km/h every 30 s until exhaustion followed by a 1-km run on an athletics track at the maximum speed. Their feces were collected before and within 4 h without diet intake postexercise. Results showed that exercise increased the abundance of *Romboutsia*, *Ruminococcaceae* UCG-005, *Escherichia coli* TOP498, and *Blautia* and decreased the abundance of *Ruminiclostridium* nine and *Clostridium phoceensis* ([Tabone et al., 2021](#B69)). Another study reported that a half-marathon race increased the abundance of *Ruminococcus bicirculans* and *Collinsella aerofaciens* and decreased that of six species, including *Bacteroides coprophilus*, in the feces of amateur athletes ([Zhao et al., 2018](#B76)). A full marathon race was found to increase the abundance of *Veillonella* ([Scheiman et al., 2019](#B57)). Furthermore, a world-class male ultramarathon runner completed the Western States Endurance Race, a 163-km mountain footrace with ∼5,486 m of climbing and ∼7,010 m of descending, in approximately 16 h. His gut microbiota revealed that the ultramarathon increased the abundance of *Haemophilus*, *Streptococcus*, and *Veillonella* and decreased that of *Alloprevotella* and *Faecalibacterium* ([Grosicki et al., 2019](#B22)). [Sato and Suzuki (2022)](#B56) reported the effect of a longer duration, ∼44 h, of a 96-km ultramarathon (up 8,062 m, down 6,983 km). The feces of nine male runners revealed a significant decrease in the abundance of four butyrate-producing species, including *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, and an increase in the abundance of ten species, including *Collinsella aerofaciens*, whereas no significant change was observed in that of *Veillonella* ([Sato and Suzuki, 2022](#B56)). Therefore, irrespective of whether a single exercise or race, the duration can exert changes in the gut microbiota.

Because endurance athletes habitually engage in endurance exercise, the changes caused by repeated aerobic training have been investigated. For instance, Allen et al. examined the impact of 6 weeks of supervised, endurance-based exercise training (3 days/week) on the gut microbiota of lean and obese sedentary subjects ([Allen et al., 2018](#B2)).They found an increase in the abundance of *Faecalibacterium* and *Lachnospira* and a decrease in that of *Bacteroides* in the gut microbiota of lean subjects. Furthermore, they observed increases in the fecal concentrations of SCFAs (acetate, propionate, and butyrate) ([Allen et al., 2018](#B2)). Another study investigated the effect of 3 weeks of high-volume training in highly trained middle-distance runners and reported a significant increase in the abundance of *Ruminococcus callidus* and decreases in the abundance of *Streptococcus parasanguinis* and *Haemophilus parainfluenzae* ([Craven et al., 2022](#B15)). Therefore, there is still a limitation of studies on the changes in gut microbiota due to repeated exercise interventions, with inconsistent results.

As habitual endurance exercise influences the gut microbiota, the difference in gut microbiota has been investigated by comparing endurance athletes with nonathletes. For instance, Kulecka et al. compared marathon runners, cross-country skiers, and sedentary healthy controls and observed significant differences in the abundances of 16 taxa in marathon runners and 5 taxa in cross-country skiers compared with that in controls ([Kulecka et al., 2020](#B32)). Both marathon runners and cross-country skiers showed significantly higher abundance of *Eggerthellacea*\_uncultured and *Prevotella*\_9 and lower abundance of *Bacteroides* than the controls. Furthermore, marathon runners showed higher abundance of *Haemophilus* and *Veillonella* and lower abundance of *Blautia* and *Faecalibacterium* than the controls. Significant differences in abundance were also detected in the family *Coriobacteriaceae* and two genera belonging to the family *Lachnospiraceae* between marathon runners and cross-country skiers ([Kulecka et al., 2020](#B32)). *Veillonella* has also been reported to be more prevalent among marathon runners than among nonrunners ([Scheiman et al., 2019](#B57)). In addition, Morishima et al. reported that female Japanese elite endurance runners had higher abundance of *Faecalibacterium* and *Lachnospira* and lower abundance of *Haemophilus* than healthy volunteers, with 13 other taxa exhibiting significant differences in abundance ([Morishima et al., 2021](#B40)). In another study, male Japanese college long-distance runners showed higher abundance of *Bacteroides*, *Prevotella*, and *Lachnospira* than nonathletes, with six other genera showing significant differences in abundance ([Morita et al., 2023](#B41)). Therefore, the gut microbiota of endurance athletes differs between marathon runners and cross-country skiers, and even if we limit the discussion to endurance runners, we can still notice the discrepancies depending on the report.

Another important aspect is that the human gut microbiota can be classified into several categories, viz., enterotypes. Partitioning around medoids clustering of the human gut microbiota reveals three distinct enterotypes, B-, P-, and R-types, whose major contributors are *Bacteroides*, *Prevotella*, and *Ruminococcus*, respectively ([Arumugam et al., 2011](#B3)). The gut microbiota of Asian people can be classified into two major types, the *Prevotella*-rich P-type and the *Bifidobacterium*- and *Bacteroides*-rich BB-types ([Nakayama et al., 2015](#B44)). Nevertheless, there has been no clarification on what causes the enterotype, including its possible involvement in the living environment, lifestyle including dietary habits, and genotype. Enterotypes can affect the change induced by exercise; however, only a few studies have examined this aspect. Only the study by [Sato and Suzuki (2022)](#B56) reported that their participants’ enterotypes were classified as B-type (n = 6) and P-type (n = 3); however, the changes in the abundance of *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Collinsella aerofaciens* occurred unanimously irrespective of the enterotype ([Sato and Suzuki, 2022](#B56)). Enterotype may be involved in the discrepancies observed in several studies. Therefore, it is necessary to increase the focus on the role of enterotype in the gut microbiota of endurance athletes.

### 3.2 Gut microbiota and endurance performance

Intestinal bacteria ferment dietary fiber into SCFAs, which exert beneficial effects on colon health ([Jenkins et al., 1995](#B25); [Mortensen and Clausen, 1996](#B43)) and constitute 40%–50% of the available energy of carbohydrates ([Cummings and Macfarlane, 1997](#B16)). Therefore, it is believed that SCFAs produced in the gut subsequently function as important energy substrates for both liver and muscle cells, thereby improving overall endurance ([Mach and Fuster-Botella, 2017](#B34)). Recently, there have been two important studies that demonstrate this phenomenon.

The first impact was the study by Scheiman et al.who hypothesized that *Veillonella* would be beneficial for marathon running because its abundance increases after a full marathon race, showing higher abundance in marathon runners than in nonrunners ([Scheiman et al., 2019](#B57)). They inoculated mice with *Veillonella atypica* isolated from a runner and found that the mice ran longer on the treadmill until exhaustion than the control mice inoculated with *Lactobacillus bulgaricus*. As *Veillonella* converts lactic acid to SCFAs, primarily propionate, they injected propionate into the colorectum of mice and confirmed the prolongation of the time required to complete the treadmill run. Based on these observations, they suggested that *Veillonella* in the colon converts lactic acid produced in the blood during exercise into SCFAs, primarily propionate, and that SCFAs improve endurance performance.

Then came the second impact with the study by Morita et al. who observed that Japanese male long-distance runners had a high abundance of *Bacteroides*, especially *Bacteroides uniformis*, and this abundance correlated with the 3000-m race times ([Morita et al., 2023](#B41)). They then conducted a randomized controlled trial to show that 9 weeks of α-cyclodextrin supplementation increased the abundance of *Bacteroides uniformis* and shortened 10-km cycling times in Japanese adult males. Moreover, when administered to mice, it increased the swimming time, inhibited the exercise-induced decreases in cecal SCFA levels (acetate, butyrate, propionate, and valerate), and increased the expression of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1, which are involved in hepatic beta-oxidation and gluconeogenesis, respectively. These findings suggest that *Bacteroides uniformis* produces propionate and acetate in the intestinal tract that stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis, thereby improving endurance.

The two abovementioned studies ([Scheiman et al., 2019](#B57); [Morita et al., 2023](#B41)) revealed different bacteria from the feces of endurance runners, viz., *Veillonella atypica* and *Bacterides uniformis*, respectively; however, both studies demonstrated that the production of SCFAs, primarily propionate, in the intestinal tract improved endurance performance. These findings suggest that the metabolic function/pathway of the two species contributes to their effects on endurance performance. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether propionate acts as an energy fuel or as a first messenger to exert physiological response. If it acts as an energy fuel, it is necessary to clarify the reason why it is advantageous over acetate, which is more abundant in the gut, and if it acts as a signal, it is important to clarify the direct effector and the signaling pathway.

Conversely, from the perspective that SCFAs produced by gut microbiota are beneficial to health, there have also been attempts to use SCFAs as ergogenic supplements. When healthy people consumed sodium propionate, their resting energy expenditure showed greater increases than when they consumed sodium chloride ([Chambers et al., 2018](#B9)). Moreover, when healthy men ingested sodium acetate (4 mmol/kg) and rode a cycle ergometer for 120 min, the preexercise acetate concentration in the blood was 13 times higher than when the same amount of NaHCO3 was administered, and there were significant changes in lipid and carbohydrate oxidation, whereas no significant difference in energy expenditure during the cycling task at ∼50% VO2peak was reported at any time point ([Smith et al., 2013](#B60)). However, the mean energy expenditure measured every 15 min from 15 to 120 min was greater with acetate supplementation than that in the control at all measurement points ([Smith et al., 2013](#B60)). Therefore, if the area under the curve had been compared, the energy expenditure during exercise could have been significantly greater with acetate supplementation. Although there are several other studies using animals and cells, only a few have demonstrated the effects on exercise capacity in humans, and there exists a need to explore the direct effects of SCFAs on exercise capacity ([Ong et al., 2023](#B46)).

Probiotics have also been reported to improve athletic performance. Single strains include species belonging to *Bifidobacterium* and *Lactobacillus*, and multistrain combinations may include *Enterococcus faecium*, *Bacillus subtilis*, and *Streptococcus thermophilus* in addition to strains belonging to *Bifidobacterium* and *Lactobacillus* ([Santibañez-Gutierrez et al., 2022](#B55)). A meta-analysis found that probiotic supplementation may improve performance in studies of populations that have undergone training with a predominance of aerobic metabolism ([Santibañez-Gutierrez et al., 2022](#B55)). Moreover, a recent systematic review revealed 13 studies that investigated the impact of probiotic supplementation on the performance of athletes, of which 7 were related to endurance athletes ([Di Dio et al., 2023](#B18)). The present review does not mention individual studies summarized in the abovementioned reviews because both reviews have excellent evidence tables that should be consulted.

Nonetheless, most studies on probiotics used specific subspecies of some species and claimed that the special compounds in that strain exert special effects. This may be because specific subspecies are commercial products. In the 2022 meta-analysis, the effects of probiotics were not separated by strain, but rather a meta-analysis of all targeted studies was used as the effect of probiotics. However, although there is some evidence reporting a lack of effect, there is no single study reporting negative results for probiotics ([Santibañez-Gutierrez et al., 2022](#B55)). This situation may reflect the fact that the motivation for reporting the effects of specific strains is to demonstrate that they are effective, i.e., there exists a publication bias.

Despite the possible publication bias in studies on probiotics, it is certainly possible that certain species exert physiological effects through the action of specific products rather than metabolites. This phenomenon is illustrated by the fact that certain pathogenic bacteria can cause specific diseases through their specific toxins. Nevertheless, although the pathogenic mechanisms of pathogenic strains have generally been elucidated, most mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of probiotics have not been elucidated. For instance, a heat-killed preparation of a certain *Lactococcus* strain exerted the same effect on the hematopoietic system ([Suzuki et al., 2022b](#B67); [2022c](#B68); [Takaragawa et al., 2022](#B70)) as that observed with the live preparation ([Kimoto-Nira et al., 2014](#B30)), which strongly suggests the involvement of a substance other than metabolites; however, the underlying mechanism has not been investigated. Nevertheless, research on *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii*, which is being touted as a next-generation probiotic, has fairly progressed ([He et al., 2021](#B23)). An increase in the abundance of *F. prausnitzii* was found to affect the peripheral lymphocyte subset ([Jinnouchi et al., 2021](#B26)) and cytokines ([Suzuki et al., 2022a](#B66)) of healthy individuals. As a mechanism that can explain these effects on the immune system, it has been demonstrated that seven peptides derived from a single microbial anti-inflammatory molecule known as “MAM” activate the immune system ([Quévrain et al., 2016](#B54)). Therefore, if a specific strain is demonstrated to improve endurance performance, it is also necessary to elucidate the effects specific to that strain, other than common metabolites, at the molecular level.

Considering our discussion of the possible contribution of gut microbiota to endurance performance, the difficulty of describing a clear strategy at this time has become apparent. Nonetheless, the topics for further research have also become clear. Although there are studies emphasizing the importance of propionate ([Chambers et al., 2018](#B9); [Scheiman et al., 2019](#B57); [Morita et al., 2023](#B41)), the most abundant among SCFAs is acetate, with studies illustrating the effects of acetate-producing *Bifidobacterium* ([Lin et al., 2020](#B33)) and acetate itself ([Smith et al., 2013](#B60)). Therefore, it is important to clarify 1) which SCFA is effective (or whether all of them are similar) and 2) whether the mechanism of action is an energy source or promotes metabolic regulation. Furthermore, if an effect on a specific genus, species or subspecies is demonstrated, the mechanism should be elucidated at the molecular level. Because there are several hundred species comprising 100 trillion bacteria living in the gut and the ecosystem can be classified into several enterotypes, it is also essential to clarify the impact of enterotypes on the action of metabolites or bacterial substances.

As shown in [Table 1](#T1), we will suggest significant future studies in this research field. These studies would provide valuable information on endurance performance and recovery in endurance athletes.

## 4 Conclusion

This review emphasizes the importance of maintaining GI function and gut microbiota in endurance athletes. Although strategies to reduce exercise-induced GI damage have been identified, their effectiveness varies with exercise conditions and environmental factors. Recent studies have shown that specific bacterial species, particularly those producing SCFAs, may improve endurance performance. However, several critical questions remain unanswered, including which SCFAs are most effective for performance improvement and whether they function primarily as energy sources or a signal to metabolic adaptations. Future research should focus on clarifying the molecular mechanisms through which specific bacterial species affect athletic performance and understanding how different enterotypes affect these relationships. As our understanding of these area advances, it would enable the development of more effective strategies for optimizing GI function and utilizing gut microbiota to improve endurance performance.

args.summary:
This is a scientific minireview published in Frontiers in Physiology (2025, May 14;16:1551284; PMCID: PMC12116556; PMID: 40438253) by Daichi Sumi (Institute of Sport Science, ASICS Corporation, Kobe, Japan) and Yoshio Suzuki (Graduate School of Health and Sports Science, Juntendo University, Japan). The authors are guest editors of the special issue "Physiological Aspects of Marathon Running." The review examines gastrointestinal (GI) function and gut microbiota in endurance athletes.

Key findings on GI damage: Endurance exercise, particularly prolonged and/or high-intensity exercise, induces significant GI damage. During exercise, blood flow is preferentially redistributed to skeletal muscle, reducing GI blood flow (hypoperfusion), which causes tissue hypoxia, oxidative stress, intestinal cell damage, and altered endothelial tight junctions. Higher exercise intensity increases GI damage, while exercise duration has smaller effects. Dehydration (hypohydration ~3.1% BW loss significantly increased blood I-FABP levels) and heat stress are the most influential factors increasing GI damage. Hypoxic environments also elevate exercise-induced GI damage. Blood I-FABP levels serve as an indirect marker of small intestinal damage. Approximately 30%–70% of athletes experience GI problems.

Strategies to reduce GI damage: Bovine colostrum intake (2 weeks) improved cellular protection via HSP70 and reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases (though 7-day supplementation or severe heat stress >40°C did not). Glutamine before exercise and 4 weeks of probiotic intake showed inconsistent results. Carbohydrate drinks (alone or with protein and pectin alginate) before and during exercise reduced GI damage, likely by increasing GI blood flow. Cold water ingestion (0°C–7°C) and ice slurry did not reduce GI damage in the heat. Compression socks (25 mm Hg) during a marathon reduced exercise-induced increases in blood I-FABP.

Key findings on gut microbiota: Single exercise/race changes microbiota composition (e.g., full marathon increased Veillonella; ultramarathon increased Haemophilus, Streptococcus, and Veillonella but decreased Faecalibacterium; a 96-km ultramarathon decreased four butyrate-producing species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii). Repeated training also changes microbiota (6 weeks of endurance training increased Faecalibacterium and Lachnospira and SCFAs in lean subjects). Endurance athletes differ from nonathletes in microbiota composition, but results are inconsistent across studies (e.g., Faecalibacterium was less abundant in marathon runners in one study but more abundant in female endurance runners in another). Enterotypes (B-, P-, R-types) may explain discrepancies.

Two landmark studies on SCFAs and endurance performance: (1) Scheiman et al. (2019) showed Veillonella atypica (increased after marathons) converts lactic acid to propionate; mice inoculated with V. atypica ran longer, and colonic propionate injection prolonged treadmill run time. (2) Morita et al. (2023) found Bacteroides uniformis abundance correlated with 3000-m race times in Japanese long-distance runners; 9 weeks of α-cyclodextrin supplementation increased B. uniformis and shortened 10-km cycling times, and increased hepatic beta-oxidation and gluconeogenesis-related enzyme expression in mice. Both studies suggest SCFA production (primarily propionate) in the gut improves endurance performance.

Probiotics (Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and multistrains) may improve performance, though a publication bias exists. Some mechanisms involve species-specific substances (not just metabolites), such as the microbial anti-inflammatory molecule (MAM) peptides from Faecalibacterium prausnitzii. Future research priorities include clarifying which SCFAs are most effective, whether they act as energy sources or signaling molecules, and how enterotypes influence these relationships.

**Round 1**

*Reviewer 1 Report*

Overview

The authors compared the effects of ondansetrone on GI distress on ultramarathoners. Runners in races of 55, 80, and 160 km length were recruited and then randomized to the placebo or medication and informed to use the medication if they experienced nausea or vomiting during the race. By chance, a higher percentage experiencing GI problems appeared to occur in the medication group (though p>0.05). For those having to use medication, there was a tendency of fewer percentagewise to report a benefit on ondansetrone (30) vs placebo (50) (again p>0.05). Although the study was preliminary and underpowered, the authors concluded that ondansetrone did not appear to be effective.

General Concerns

This webpage is the peer-review record for the article "Treatment with Oral Ondansetron for Ultramarathon-Associated Nausea: The TOO FUN Study" published in the journal *Sports* (2021, Volume 9, Issue 3, Article 35; DOI: 10.3390/sports9030035). The article was authored by Andrew V. Pasternak, David Fiore, Arthur Islas, Sarah Toti, and Martin D. Hoffman. The study compared the effects of ondansetron (an anti-nausea medication) versus placebo on gastrointestinal distress in ultramarathon runners competing in races of 55, 80, and 160 km. Runners were randomized to receive either the medication or placebo and instructed to use it if they experienced nausea or vomiting during the race. By chance, a higher percentage of GI problems occurred in the medication group (though not statistically significant, p>0.05). Among those who used the treatment, fewer percentage-wise reported a benefit from ondansetron (30%) versus placebo (50%), again without statistical significance. The authors concluded that ondansetron did not appear effective, though the study was preliminary and underpowered.

The page contains three rounds of peer review with comments and author responses. Reviewer 2 asked about recommended dosing, the 4-hour delay between capsule intakes, the effectiveness scale methodology, and the need to contextualize ondansetron's effects on thermoregulation. Reviewer 3 suggested the title should state primary findings, requested subject demographics, asked about sex differences and environmental influences on nausea, potential drug interactions with food/drinks, whether the effect varies by race distance, and recommended subsections in methods. ## Abstract

Nausea and vomiting are common for runners during ultramarathons and often contribute to non-finishes. We aimed to determine the efficacy of ondansetron, a commonly used antiemetic, to treat nausea and vomiting in runners during an ultramarathon. Runners who had a previous history of frequent nausea or vomiting during races and entered in 160, 80, and 55 km ultramarathons in 2018 and 2019 were randomized in a double-blind fashion to 4 mg ondansetron or placebo capsules to use if they developed nausea or vomiting during the race with the ability to take three additional doses. Study participants completed a post-race online survey to assess medication use and efficacy. Of 62 study participants, 31 took either ondansetron (20) or placebo (11). In this small study, there were no group differences in those reporting any improvement in nausea and vomiting (*p* = 0.26) or in the amount of improvement (*p* = 0.15). We found no evidence that ondansetron capsules improve nausea and vomiting during ultramarathons.

**Keywords:** running, antiemetic, serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, endurance exercise, randomized controlled trial

## 1. Introduction

Athletes running in ultramarathon events commonly have upper gastrointestinal (GI) distress, with nausea present in up to 60% [[1](#B1-sports-09-00035)]. Nausea or vomiting is the primary reason for not finishing a 161-km ultramarathon, and even among those completing the race, over a third reported, it impacted their race performance [[2](#B2-sports-09-00035)].

During exercise, GI distress has a wide range of etiologies, including dehydration, heat stress, catecholamine secretion, use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, altitude exposure, hyponatremia, competition anxiety, and the amount and content of food and beverage consumed [[3](#B3-sports-09-00035),[4](#B4-sports-09-00035),[5](#B5-sports-09-00035)]. In one study of runners during an ultramarathon [[6](#B6-sports-09-00035)], those who ingested a higher percentage of calories from fat and drank more fluids had less nausea and vomiting, perhaps due in part to improving the distribution of blood flow to the GI tract [[7](#B7-sports-09-00035)].

Treating upper GI distress in runners during an ultramarathon is challenging. Ondansetron, commonly used to treat nausea and vomiting, is a serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. It is used in various settings such as chemotherapy, gastroenteritis, and postoperative nausea and vomiting [[8](#B8-sports-09-00035),[9](#B9-sports-09-00035)]. Anecdotally, ondansetron may help exercise-related nausea and vomiting; however, there has been no randomized control trial to support this claim [[10](#B10-sports-09-00035)]. In a small unblinded pilot study at the Tahoe Rim Trail Endurance Races (TRTER), 66% of 21 runners felt their symptoms improved after taking a 4 mg orally dissolvable ondansetron tablet sublingually [[11](#B11-sports-09-00035)]. One of the concerns about using ondansetron in ultramarathons is a theoretical risk of it contributing to heat-related illnesses. Ondansetron, however, has not been shown to affect thermoregulation in hot settings [[12](#B12-sports-09-00035)].

As the etiology of nausea and vomiting in endurance athletes may differ from nausea and vomiting in other settings, we felt that the pilot study’s findings warranted further exploration. We have been unable to find other studies examining the effectiveness of ondansetron in this setting. Thus, the purpose of this double-blind, randomized control trial was to evaluate the effectiveness of ondansetron at treating ultramarathon-associated nausea or vomiting.

## 2. Materials and Methods

Pre-race recruitment and randomization: We recruited runners from the 2018 and 2019 TRTER. The TRTER has over 600 runners competing in 55, 80, and 160 km races, with approximately 200 runners in each event. Pre-race emails, sent to all competitors, invited them to consider enrolling in the study if they had nausea or vomiting during previous races. Before enrollment, we screened study participants for previous reactions to ondansetron or medications that could interact with ondansetron. Weather conditions, aid station food choices, and sports drinks supplied at the race were similar between years.

Study participants were randomized using a random number generator to either ondansetron 4 mg oral capsules or placebo (cellulose capsule) [[13](#B13-sports-09-00035)]. A local compounding pharmacy prepared the capsules. Each runner was given four capsules to carry with them during the race with instructions to take one capsule if they developed symptoms. They could then take an additional capsule every 4 h as needed based on recommended dosing. A total of 62 runners elected to participate in the study. Of these, the average age was 45 years old (range 21–78). With respect to gender, 25 were women, and 37 were men.

Race day logistics: Runners encounter medical staff two, four, and nine times in the 55, 80, and 160 km races, respectively. The medical staff were blinded to group allocation, but if a study participant presented with persistent GI symptoms after taking a study capsule, the medical staff could break the blinding to allow for additional treatment options. We asked the runners to record their distance and the time of day or elapsed race time when taking capsules.

Post-Race evaluation: Within 24 h of the race finish, emails were sent to study participants with a link to an online post-race survey, with follow up emails at three and seven days if needed The post-race survey involved 26 questions (available as [Supplementary Materials](#app1-sports-09-00035)). Included were questions inquiring about previous experiences with nausea and vomiting and their racing history. Runners were asked if they felt the treatment helped (Yes/No/Not sure). They were also asked about the severity of symptoms and improvement of symptoms after treatment on a 1 to 100-point scale. For medication effectiveness, 1 = no help at all and 100 = complete resolution of symptoms. For symptom severity, 1 = very mild symptoms and 100 = severe symptoms. They were also asked to rate the severity of their nausea and vomiting on the same scale before taking the medication, one hour after taking the medication, and at the end of the race.

Assuming a placebo effect of 30% and a 30% greater effect of ondansetron (60% effectiveness) as clinically significant, we would have needed 28 runners in each group to show a statistical effect. We chose 60% effectiveness of ondansetron based on the amount of improvement seen in our pilot study [[11](#B11-sports-09-00035)].

Group comparisons of ordinal data were made with two-tailed unpaired t-tests or the Mann–Whitney test when data were found to be skewed by the D’Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test. Group comparisons of categorical data were made with the Fisher’s exact test.

## 3. Results

All 62 runners completed the post-race survey within seven days, and 36 completed it within three days of the race finish. Of the runners who enrolled in the study, 31 (50%) had GI symptoms prompting them to take the treatment. Of those 31 runners, 20 were in the ondansetron arm, and 11 were in the placebo arm. Details on the number of study participants and race distances are in [Figure 1](#sports-09-00035-f001)

### Figure 1.

[Open in a new tab](figure/sports-09-00035-f001/)

Diagram showing number of study participants and race distances from recruitment through intervention.

As shown in [Table 1](#sports-09-00035-t001), the two groups were comparable in individual and during race characteristics, including the proportion that were unblinded during the race. Those taking ondansetron received no benefit compared with placebo. While not reaching significance, there were trends towards the placebo group having more improvement and more side effects than the ondansetron group. On average, 160 km runners took the treatment during the second quartile of the race by distance when ambient temperatures were highest. Weather both years was relatively mild and relatively similar; in 2018, temperatures ranged from 12 to 25 °C, and in 2019, temperatures ranged from 10 to 23 °C near the start/finish line.
