This article from RunnersConnect, written by Jeff Gaudette (MS, co-founder of RunnersConnect and former Olympic Trials qualifier), provides a comprehensive, science-backed guide to "gut training" for runners to prevent mid-race gastrointestinal (GI) distress. 

**Key Statistics:**
- 30-90% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise, depending on intensity and duration
- 43% of Ironman triathletes report serious GI problems; 7% abandon their race entirely due to GI issues
- During high-intensity exercise at 70% VO2max, blood flow to the gut drops by nearly 80%
- Gut training protocols reduce GI symptoms by 60-63% in just two weeks
- Performance improved by 4.3-5.2% after gut training
- Ibuprofen use increases GI complication risk by 3-5 times
- Low-FODMAP diets reduce symptoms in up to 86% of people with IBS; ~70-75% success rate for sensitive runners
- Runners consuming 60g of carbohydrates per hour finished marathons nearly 11 minutes faster than haphazardly-fueled runners

**Why GI Distress Occurs:** During running, blood flow is diverted away from the gut (splanchnic hypo-perfusion), creating an ischemic environment. This leads to increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"), allowing bacterial endotoxins (LPS) to enter the bloodstream. Mechanical jostling from running, sympathetic nervous system activation, and pre-race anxiety compound the problem. Runners experience GI issues at double the rate of cyclists or swimmers.

**Identifying Personal Triggers:** The author advises against expensive IgG food sensitivity tests, which lack scientific validation (number needed to treat of 9 vs. 1.5-2.2 for proper elimination diets). Instead, the gold standard is a systematic elimination diet combined with food journaling for 2-3 weeks. Common culprits include dairy, wheat, eggs, soy, nuts, high-FODMAP foods, high-fiber foods, high-fat meals, sugar alcohols, artificial sweeteners, excessive caffeine, and NSAIDs like ibuprofen.

**FODMAP Strategy:** FODMAPs (Fermentable Oligo-, Di-, Monosaccharides, and Polyols) are poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates that ferment in the colon, producing gas and drawing water. Runners don't need year-round low-FODMAP diets unless diagnosed with IBS; instead, many implement a modified low-FODMAP approach for 6 days before important races. A three-phase approach (strict elimination for 2-6 weeks, systematic reintroduction, personalized plan) works best.

**Gut Training Protocol:** The landmark Costa study had 25 endurance runners complete 10 sessions over 14 days, running 2 hours at 60% VO2max while consuming 30g of carbohydrates every 20 minutes (90g/hour total). This produced 60-63% reductions in GI symptoms and 4.3-5.2% performance improvements. Mechanisms include increased SGLT1 transporter density/activity (for glucose absorption), increased gastric emptying rates, and expanded stomach capacity. Practical modifications include 1-2 gut training workouts per week, starting at 30g/hour and adding 10g/hour weekly until reaching 60-90g/hour target, and using long runs for gut training.

- 3 days before: Consume 10-12g of carbohydrates per kg of body weight daily for 36-48 hours (680-816g for a 150lb/68kg runner) while tapering
- Race morning: 1-4g of carbohydrates per kg of body weight 3-4 hours before start

- For ultras >6 hours: ~15% of calories from protein; for 12+ hour events, modest fat intake; real food (potatoes, sandwiches, soup, chips, fruit) can be incorporated

# Pre-Workout and Pre-Race Meals: What, When, and How Much to Eat

[![Jim Rutberg](https://trainright.com/nitropack_static/BIxrHgiiYpbwjrpCFShHHbrBuHIwcKHu/assets/images/optimized/rev-7162544/trainright.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Jim-Rutberg-cycling-coach-headshot.jpg)](https://trainright.com/coaches/jim-rutberg/)

Written by:

## [Jim Rutberg](https://trainright.com/coaches/jim-rutberg/)

CTS Pro Endurance Coach

Updated On

July 8, 2025

One of the most frequent questions our coaches get is, “What should I eat before my race/workout?” In reality, the answer they’re seeking has additional components. It’s not just what to eat, but how much to eat and when to eat it. All of these parameters are important. When you get it right, your pre-race meal tops up energy stores and enables a strong start without gastric distress. So, here’s how to get it right.

## **What to Eat: Lead with Carbohydrates**

The big thing to remember is that carbohydrate is the fuel for high-intensity efforts, so if you’re racing or getting ready for an interval workout, you want to start with high carbohydrate availability. You are already carrying more than enough fat to provide energy for exercise, and protein is a fuel for recovery and adaptation but does not significantly contribute energy during exercise. Your carbohydrate tank is pretty limited, though. You can store about 400-500 grams of carbohydrate in your muscles and liver, enough for 1-3 hours of exercise, depending on intensity. Topping up these stores and ensuring adequate blood glucose levels (especially in the morning after sleep) are the main goals of your pre-workout/race meal.

“Lead with carbohydrate” doesn’t mean “eat only carbohydrate”. As I’ll explain below, the composition of your pre-race meal will depend on timing and how your body normally responds to ingesting food.

## **How much to eat before racing or working out**

How much you eat will depend on the amount of time between your pre-race or pre-workout meal and the start of your effort. The earlier you eat, the bigger the meal. The 2016 “[Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and Athletic Performance](https://jandonline.org/article/S2212-2672(15)01802-X/fulltext)” recommends 1-4 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram bodyweight before exercise, which we break down to 4 g/kg four hours out, reducing to 1 g/kg an hour or less before the start. (see figure).

Example: Using the stereotypical 70-kilogram(154-lb) athlete, these recommendations come out to 280 grams of CHO four hours before racing. That’s a big meal, with 1120 calories coming from CHO alone, which is why the recommendations should only serve as a starting point. In practice, athletes tend to prefer eating their last substantial meal 2-3 hours before competition, in part because the calorie intake and volume of food are less extreme.

You are trying to find a Goldilocks solution to having enough time to digest the meal yet eating enough to avoid getting hungry again too soon. If you eat too much too late, you risk GI distress from starting with a full stomach. On the other hand, if you eat too little too early, you’ll be hungry right before the start. If you have a choice, err on the side of eating too little and have a carbohydrate-rich sports drink available if you want some additional energy in the last 45 minutes before the start.

## **Pre-Exercise Meal Composition**

The macronutrient diversity of your pre-race or pre-workout meal should be greatest when you have the most time available for digestion. If you are eating four hours before the start, you want a mixed meal containing fat, protein, and carbohydrate (including fiber and both complex and simple carbohydrates). Fat, protein, and fiber slow gastric emptying and slow digestion, which helps you feel satisfied longer. They also lessen the spike in blood glucose by slowing carbohydrate transport into the bloodstream.

As you get closer to your event, you want to start encouraging more rapid digestion, so you should start removing the impediments. First, reduce fat but keep protein in order to stave off hunger and support your body’s around the clock utilization of protein. Then reduce both fat and protein but keep a mixture of simple and complex carbohydrates. And finally, in the final hour before the start, stick with low fiber, mostly simple carbohydrates so they are out of the gut and into the bloodstream quickly.

## **Examples of Good Pre-Race Meals**

**3-4 Hours Before**

* Breakfast Burrito: tortilla, potatoes, eggs, black beans (add rice to go big)
* Scramble: Potatoes, eggs, fresh vegetables, plus toast or bagel.

**2-3 Hours Before**

---

Take our free 2-minute quiz to discover how effective your training is and get recommendations for how you can improve.

---

* Eggs and Rice: Similar to examples above, but simple and easy to digest.
* Whole grain waffles with nut butter, side of fruit.
* Yogurt mixed with granola or cereal, berries, and nuts. Add banana or toast with peanut butter to bump up the calories if necessary.

**1-2 Hours Before**

* Bagel with peanut butter or similar nut butter and a banana.
* Oatmeal with nuts and berries. Add brown sugar if you tolerate simple sugars well before hard efforts. Have 1-2 hard-boiled eggs on the side if you need some protein and fat to slow the rush of blood sugar. Here’s a [good selection of ways](https://www.outsideonline.com/2242911/oatmeal-still-worlds-best-performance-breakfast) some athletes adjust the nutrition and taste of oatmeal.
* Sports drink or smoothie and a sports bar or granola bar. If you perform better with less solid food before exercise, look for liquid carbohydrate sources and a few bites of something solid.

### **Foods to Avoid**

* **Greasy, fatty, fried foods:** A bacon cheeseburger is a lot of calories, but it’s more likely to put you to sleep than help you feel energized.
* This one is a little counterintuitive because it’s hard to ever discourage people from eating vegetables. The problem with high-volume, low caloric density foods like lettuce is that before a race or hard workout you want concentrated energy sources so you don’t have to eat as much volume. However, you can construct a salad to be more energy dense by adding seeds, avocado, hard boiled eggs, etc. It’s the giant bowl of lettuce that may be more problematic, because it makes you feel full when you have not actually consumed much energy.
* **Sugar-free or diet foods.** This should seem obvious because the point of pre-race and pre-workout meals is to provide energy. However, we find many athletes make choices from habit and convenience. The other problem is that many sugar-free foods use sugar alcohols (i.e. Xylitol, Sorbitol) as sweeteners. These can contribute to gastric distress, particularly when you add in the physical and psychological stress of competition.

## **Making Personal Adjustments**

The next step is to take the starting point recommendations and adjust them to suit your personal needs. If you have a history of GI distress when you eat close to the start of events or workouts, then focus on more substantial meals 3-4 hours out and plan for smaller snacks closer to the start.

### Reactive Hypoglycemia

Some athletes experience hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) soon after the start of exercise when they eat carbohydrates 30-45 minutes beforehand. The spike in blood sugar triggers the release of insulin, which lowers blood sugar by moving carbohydrate into tissues, like muscles. High insulin response can overlap with muscles using carbohydrate for fuel at the start of intense exercise. As a result, blood sugar levels can drop to the point of hypoglycemia, characterized by feeling dizzy, lightheaded, and nauseated. Researcher Asker Jeukendrup has a [good article explaining reactive hypoglycemia](https://www.mysportscience.com/post/2015/02/05/what-to-eat-the-hour-before-a-race). The takeaway is that if you are prone to reactive hypoglycemia, you can:

* adjust carbohydrate composition to include more low glycemic index foods (complex carbs)
* eat carbohydrates very close to the start (leaves no time for the overlap to develop)
* or eat carbohydrate further ahead of time (like 90 minutes).

### Stress and pre-race foods

Anxiety and excitement can affect how you respond to eating. Stress can alter gastric emptying and gut motility, and GI distress can result from either speeding them up or slowing them down. Caffeine may exacerbate GI distress in these scenarios. If you struggle with pre-race jitters, the eating habits that work before training (a lower stress environment) may not work as well on race day. This is part of the reason you should schedule lower-priority competitions. They are a great opportunity to test out race-day nutrition in a higher stress environment.

Above all, getting your pre-race and pre-workout meals right takes practice. Start with the basics and then experiment with a variety of foods and combinations to see what works best for you.

args.summary:
This article from CTS (Carmichael Training Systems) by Jim Rutberg, a Pro Endurance Coach, provides comprehensive guidance on pre-workout and pre-race meals, covering what to eat, how much, and when. Published/updated on July 8, 2025.

**Key Points:**

**What to Eat:** Lead with carbohydrates, as carbohydrate is the fuel for high-intensity efforts. The body stores about 400-500 grams of carbohydrate in muscles and liver, enough for 1-3 hours of exercise. Fat stores are already sufficient for energy, and protein is primarily for recovery/adaptation rather than exercise fuel.

**How Much to Eat (Timing-based):** Citing the 2016 Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine on Nutrition and Athletic Performance, the recommendation is 1-4 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of bodyweight before exercise. This breaks down to 4 g/kg four hours out, reducing to 1 g/kg an hour or less before the start. For a 70-kg (154-lb) athlete, this is 280 grams of CHO four hours out (1,120 calories from CHO alone). In practice, most athletes prefer eating their last substantial meal 2-3 hours before competition.

**Pre-Exercise Meal Composition:** The macronutrient diversity should be greatest with the most digestion time. Four hours out: mixed meal with fat, protein, and carbohydrate (including fiber, complex and simple carbs). As the event approaches, reduce fat first, then protein, and in the final hour stick with low-fiber, mostly simple carbohydrates.

**Sample Meal Examples:**
- 3-4 hours before: Breakfast burrito (tortilla, potatoes, eggs, black beans); scramble with potatoes, eggs, vegetables, plus toast or bagel
- 2-3 hours before: Eggs and rice; whole grain waffles with nut butter and fruit; yogurt with granola, berries, nuts
- 1-2 hours before: Bagel with peanut butter and banana; oatmeal with nuts and berries; sports drink/smoothie with sports bar

**Foods to Avoid:** Greasy/fatty/fried foods (like bacon cheeseburgers); high-volume, low-calorie-density foods (like giant bowls of lettuce that fill you up without providing energy); sugar-free or diet foods (which may use sugar alcohols like Xylitol and Sorbitol that can cause gastric distress).

**Personal Adjustments:**
- Reactive hypoglycemia: Some athletes experience low blood sugar 30-45 minutes after eating carbs before exercise due to insulin spikes. Solutions include using more low-glycemic-index foods, eating carbs very close to the start, or eating them 90 minutes ahead.
- Stress and pre-race jitters can alter gastric emptying and gut motility, potentially causing GI distress. Caffeine may exacerbate this. Lower-priority competitions are recommended as opportunities to test race-day nutrition under stress.

The article emphasizes that getting pre-race nutrition right takes practice, starting with the basics and experimenting with various food combinations.
args.key_excerpts: "The big thing to remember is that carbohydrate is the fuel for high-intensity efforts, so if you're racing or getting ready for an interval workout, you want to start with high carbohydrate availability." — Jim Rutberg

# What To Eat The Night Before A Long Run: The Evidence

The simple dinner formula to top off glycogen, avoid GI issues, and wake up ready to run strong.

###### Last Updated:

###### [Katelyn Tocci](https://marathonhandbook.com/author/katelyn-tocci/) a smiling marathon runner [Katelyn Tocci](https://marathonhandbook.com/author/katelyn-tocci/) Katelyn Tocci is our Head Coach and Training Editor; 100-mile ultrarunner, RRCA + UESCA Certified Running Coach [Here's My Full Profile](https://marathonhandbook.com/author/katelyn-tocci/) --- [learn about our editorial process](https://marathonhandbook.com/editorial-process/)

Training Editor

Runners, especially marathoners, put significant thought into hydration and fueling *during* long runs and races.

But what you do **before** you run matters just as much. Nailing **what to eat the night before a long run or big race** helps set you up with full energy stores, a calm stomach, and the kind of steady effort you’re actually trying to practice.

And that’s the key: long runs, particularly in peak training weeks, aren’t just mileage, but **race-day rehearsals.** They’re your chance to dial in pacing, gear, hydration… and arguably the most important piece: nutrition.

What you eat the night before can significantly affect how you feel the next morning. So why not stack the deck in your favor and eat in a way that helps you run strong, steady, and confident?

Jump to:

## The Honest Truth About Pre-Long-Run Fuelling

Advice to “just eat pasta” the night before a long run is right about the macronutrient but wrong about why, when, and how much. The evidence on glycogen loading is clearer than you’d guess, and it gives you a specific target number rather than a vague “carb-heavy meal.”

### The Physiology Of Glycogen Loading

Bergström’s classic muscle-biopsy work established that skeletal muscle glycogen is the rate-limiting fuel for exercise past about 90 minutes, and that starting glycogen stores are strongly predictive of time-to-exhaustion.[1](javascript:void(0))Bergström J, Hermansen L, Hultman E, Saltin B. Diet, muscle glycogen and physical performance. Acta Physiol Scand. 1967;71(2):140-150. Hawley’s work refined the picture: you don’t need the deprivation-then-load classical protocol for runs under ≈90 minutes, but for runs 90+ minutes, topping up [glycogen in the 24-36 hours before](https://marathonhandbook.com/carb-loading/) produces measurable performance gains.[2](javascript:void(0))Hawley JA, Burke LM, Phillips SM, Spriet LL. Nutritional modulation of training-induced skeletal muscle adaptations. J Appl Physiol. 2011;110(3):834-845. Current ISSN/ACSM guidelines put the dose at 7-12 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight in the 24 hours before long events—roughly 490-840 g for a 70 kg runner, which is realistic only if spread across breakfast, lunch, and dinner with high-GI snacks.[3](javascript:void(0))Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SH, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S17-S27.

### Meal Composition And Timing For Dinner

The ACSM/Dietitians of Canada position stand recommends 1-4 g/kg of carbohydrate in the 1-4 hours before exercise, with the meal being low in fat and fiber to speed gastric emptying and reduce GI upset.[4](javascript:void(0))Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement. Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-568. For a dinner eaten 12-14 hours before a morning long run, this translates to a plate that’s 60-70% carbohydrate by calories, 15-20% protein, the rest mostly fat—so white rice or pasta with a modest portion of lean protein beats a steak with a side of pasta. Jeukendrup’s work on runner GI issues pinpoints three culprits to limit the night before: very high fat, very high fiber, and [very high protein](https://marathonhandbook.com/fatigue-after-eating-carbs/).[5](javascript:void(0))Jeukendrup AE. Nutrition for endurance sports: marathon, triathlon, and road cycling. J Sports Sci. 2011;29 Suppl 1:S91-S99. Moseley showed onset of gastric comfort-related symptoms correlates with fiber and fat intake more than with total volume, which is why the “big bowl of pasta” works as long as it’s not buried in creamy sauce.[6](javascript:void(0))Moseley L, Lancaster GI, Jeukendrup AE. Effects of timing of pre-exercise ingestion of carbohydrate on subsequent metabolism and cycling performance. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2003;88(4-5):453-458.

### Hydration And Sodium—The Quieter Levers

Pre-race hydration advice has drifted more carefully over the last two decades. Sawka’s ACSM position stand recommends starting exercise euhydrated, roughly 5-7 mL/kg of fluid in the 4 hours prior, and adding modest sodium (3-6 g at dinner plus in drinks) to improve plasma volume expansion.[7](javascript:void(0))Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007;39(2):377-390. Crucially, Almond’s study of 488 Boston Marathon runners found exercise-associated hyponatremia was more common than dehydration and linked to over-consumption of hypotonic fluids in first-time marathoners— “drink to thirst” is the safer default than rigid pre-race hydration schedules.[8](javascript:void(0))Almond CSD, Shin AY, Fortescue EB, et al. Hyponatremia among runners in the Boston Marathon. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(15):1550-1556.

### Counter-Point: The Plan Has To Be Practiced

Individual GI tolerance varies enormously; de Oliveira’s review of nutrient absorption during exercise documents 30-80% inter-individual variance in tolerated carbohydrate load.[9](javascript:void(0))de Oliveira EP, Burini RC, Jeukendrup AE. Gastrointestinal complaints during exercise: prevalence, etiology, and nutritional recommendations. Sports Med. 2014;44 Suppl 1:S79-S85. Jeukendrup’s “train the gut” protocol shows you can expand this tolerance with progressive carbohydrate exposure during training runs over 4-8 weeks.[10](javascript:void(0))Jeukendrup AE. Training the gut for athletes. Sports Med. 2017;47 Suppl 1:S101-S110. The practical consequence: race-day dinner is not the time for a new food. Use your Saturday long-run days across the training block to test portion size, timing, and specific foods, and keep a short log of what caused GI distress so the night-before menu is a rehearsal, not an experiment.

## Why Are Carbs Important?

Carbs have somehow become the villain in a lot of modern nutrition plans. Low-carb and no-carb approaches, like keto, are everywhere.

From personal experience, they *can* work for certain goals: they often help people lose weight and reduce body fat. But for most runners, that isn’t the main objective.

As a runner, the priorities are pretty simple: **perform well and feel good doing it.** And that’s where a runner-specific approach to nutrition matters.

If you want to train hard, recover well, and show up with real energy, carbohydrates aren’t optional. They’re your **primary fuel source.**

You can’t expect to run well (or enjoy your running) if you’re constantly under-fueled, stuck in a calorie deficit, or not giving your body the kind of energy endurance training demands.

## What Are Carbohydrates, Glucose, & Glycogen?

I won’t bore you with technical details; instead, I’ll give you a quick understanding of what’s what.

**Carbohydrates, more specifically glucose, fuel our bodies with the energy we need to run hard or run long, or both.**

Glucose is stored in our muscles and liver as [glycogen](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6019055/)[11](javascript:void(0))Murray, B., & Rosenbloom, C. (2018). Fundamentals of glycogen metabolism for coaches and athletes. *Nutrition Reviews*, *76*(4), 243–259. <https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuy001> and called upon when needed. In other words, “glycogen is how the body stores carbohydrates for energy at the muscular level.”

## Why Do Runners Need Carbs to Perform Well?

**Glycogen is the primary fuel source when performing high—or moderate-intensity exercise,** and fat is the second energy source.

So, whether you are running a marathon and focusing on endurance or pushing an all-out 3K, **carbs will be key to performing at your best.**

For endurance athletes, glycogen helps **maintain consistent energy** and prevents [**hitting the wall** **(bonking)**](https://marathonhandbook.com/the-wall/). It helps higher-intensity runners tolerate faster speeds for a longer period of time.

Any effort above 60% of your VO2 [max](https://marathonhandbook.com/what-is-vo2-max/) will first draw on glycogen stores for energy. If they are adequately stocked, you’ll have a better chance of feeling great and running well.

If you *do not have* the necessary glycogen levels to fuel your running, you could experience muscle damage, fatigue, and even overtraining.

**Increasing carbohydrate intake before a marathon or long run and consuming carbohydrates during it will help prevent weakness and fatigue.** This can improve not only our performance but also our speed and recovery.

In contrast, low-carbohydrate diets show a **decrease in performance** because the body is trying to work with glycogen depletion.

A moderate– to high-carbohydrate diet is ***strongly recommended***to achieve optimal results. We need to maintain our glycogen stores to have adequate energy for each subsequent training day.

We know we need to eat [carbs,](https://marathonhandbook.com/carbs-for-runners/) but what to eat the night before a long run? Simple? Complex? Let’s take a look.

## Simple and Complex Carbohydrates

**Complex carbohydrates are great for general health and nutrition, but the night before a long run, all *the rules change*.**

**Simple carbs are easier to digest** than complex carbs, which take longer to break down. Therefore, simple carbs can provide you with the energy you need to perform more efficiently.

In addition, many complex carbs are *full of fiber,* which we want to avoid the night before a long run or race.

I have provided a list of **examples** **for each carbohydrate**type to help us select the right ones for our pre-race carb-loading meals.

While I recommend simple carbs for your pre-long-run meals, you may be able to tolerate complex carbs as well. Trial and error is the way to determine the best foods for each athlete.

### Simple Carbohydrates: (Fructose, Sucrose, Glucose, Maltose, Lactose)

* **White bread**, **bagels, English muffins**
* **White rice**
* **Pasta**
* **Couscous**
* **Fruit**
* **Table Sugar**
* **Juice**
* **Honey**
* **Maple Syrup**
* **Dairy**
* **Sports Drinks such as Gatorade and Powerade** (they also provide electrolytes)
* **Energy gels, energy chews, and other sports-focused supplements**

### Complex Carbohydrates:

* **Wheat bread**
* **Brown or wild rice**
* **Barley**
* **Legumes**
* **Beans**
* **Oats**
* **Starchy veggies** **such as sweet potatoes**

I’d like to share some examples of what has worked for me over the years, such as pre-run dinners the night before events ranging from a half-marathon to a long-distance ultra.

Because I handle a significant weekly volume, I prepare these meals consistently. Some weeks, I may need to eat carb-rich meals on 2-3 evenings to ensure optimal performance for my speedwork sessions and back-to-back long runs in my training plan.

## **How To Fuel For Peak Performance On Your Long Run**

We all have different dietary needs depending on body weight, metabolism, nutritional restrictions, and specific training.

Seeing a sports nutritionist can help you calculate how many portions of carbohydrates, protein, and fat to include in your day-to-day diet and pre-training run and race carb-loading meals.

I have not included specific portion sizes in the recipe ideas below for this exact reason. It is still important to calculate how much of each meal you will need to prepare.

### #1: [Giada’s Lemon Pasta](https://giadzy.com/recipes/lemon-spaghetti-giada-de-laurentiis/)

This is my **all-time favorite meal I always eat before a race** andoften on nights before a long run. It is **high-carb, low-protein, and low-dairy**, making it easy to digest and absolutely delicious.

Of course, you can switch out the lemony sauce for a tomato-based sauce as well. However, I would avoid cream-based sauces, as too much dairy may upset your stomach.

### #2: Pizza

*Can I eat pizza the night before a long run?*

Some of you may think this one seems unusual, but it works for me. If you are lactose-intolerant, you want to ensure you **use lactose-free cheese or avoid it altogether**. The last thing we want is a GI issue during our long run.

However, I make ***homemade pizza*** instead of ordering out. This way, I know every detail in it and can cater to my needs and preferences.

When adding toppings, use whatever your stomach is used to processing. This is where you could add a bit of protein if you’d like, but the main event is the **simple-carb crust.**

### #3: Couscous

I love mixing couscous with a whole variety of things, but for carb-loading before a long run, I keep it simple. I add shrimp, parsley, and parmesan cheese to create a delicious, carb-filled skillet**.** You could add anything you like, or leave it all pasta.

Be sure it is “couscous heavy,” though, so the carb is the star of the meal.

### #4: Sandwiches

This may seem a bit odd for dinner, but I’m talking about an absolutely delicious sandwich. Not just your run-of-the-mill PB&J.

**Pick up a fresh, warm ciabatta** from the bakery and fill it up with your favorites.

My favorite is a slice of **prosciutto and manchego cheese**, with a smidge of balsamic vinegar and olive oil.

The great part about this mix is that the flavors are so intense that you only need a tiny bit of filling, keeping the majority of your meal focused on fresh, yummy bread.

### #5: Breakfast for Dinner

I absolutely *loved it* as a kid when my parents said we were having **breakfast for dinner.** Well, guess what? This works out great for us runners the night before a long run.

**How about a nice big stack of *pancakes* and *maple syrup* to stock up on those carbs?**And if you want to add a little protein, you can throw a couple of slices of bacon on top.

French toast, a bagel with nut butter (a healthy fat but delicious), or even cereal could work.

These are just some ideas that work for me, but as each of us is different, you’ll need to try out a variety of meals to see what works best for you. Here are a few final tips for selecting recipes.

## My Final tips

### #1: Avoid High-Protein Meals

Leave your high-protein meals for recovery after your morning run (but don’t forget to add carbs to your meals with lean protein; they aren’t just for before the run, but for during and after as well).

If you plan to fuel post-run with a protein powder shake, be sure to add some carbs or a healthy fat, such as peanut butter, to make it well-rounded and support recovery.

### #2: Avoid Fiber

The last thing we want to worry about during our long run is *an uncomfortable pit stop.* There’s nothing better than going out on your run knowing your tummy will behave and your digestion is at its best.

High-fiber foods can provoke [unwanted bathroom trips](https://marathonhandbook.com/avoid-unplanned-bathroom-breaks/), bloating, and discomfort. Avoid beans, lentils, whole grains, broccoli, and other high-fiber fruits and vegetables the night before a long run.

### #3: Eat Enough, But Not Too Much

When carb-loading, it’s essential to avoid both under-eating and overeating, as each has drawbacks. Undereating may leave you fatigued and low on energy, while overeating can cause GI problems.

Consult a [sports nutritionist](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4540168/)[12](javascript:void(0))Beck, K., Thomson, J. S., Swift, R. J., & von Hurst, P. R. (2015). Role of Nutrition in Performance Enhancement and Postexercise Recovery. *Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine*, *6*(6), 259. <https://doi.org/10.2147/oajsm.s33605> to help you out or calculate your estimated carb intake with the following equation:

**8 x your weight in kilos = total grams of carbohydrates per day** **during a carb load**

At the end of the day, the best solution to eating the night before a long run for maximum results is **carbs, carbs, and more carbs**.

Build up those glycogen stores, and let’s get running. For more information on carb loading, [check out our guide](https://marathonhandbook.com/carb-loading/) [here](https://marathonhandbook.com/carb-loading/).

This article from Marathon Handbook, written by Training Editor Katelyn Tocci (a 100-mile ultrarunner and RRCA/UESCA-certified running coach), provides evidence-based guidance on what to eat the night before a long run or race. The core message is that long runs serve as "race-day rehearsals" and nutrition the night before significantly impacts performance.

Key evidence-based findings:
- Bergström's classic muscle-biopsy research established that muscle glycogen is the rate-limiting fuel for exercise past ~90 minutes, and starting glycogen stores strongly predict time-to-exhaustion.
- Current ISSN/ACSM guidelines recommend 7-12 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight in the 24 hours before long events (roughly 490-840 g for a 70 kg runner), spread across breakfast, lunch, and dinner with high-GI snacks.
- The ACSM/Dietitians of Canada position stand recommends 1-4 g/kg of carbohydrate in the 1-4 hours before exercise, with meals low in fat and fiber. For a dinner eaten 12-14 hours before a morning run, this means a plate that's 60-70% carbohydrate by calories, 15-20% protein, rest mostly fat.
- Jeukendrup's research identifies three culprits to limit the night before: very high fat, very high fiber, and very high protein.
- Hydration guidance: Sawka's ACSM position stand recommends starting exercise euhydrated (5-7 mL/kg fluid in 4 hours prior) with modest sodium (3-6 g). However, Almond's study of 488 Boston Marathon runners found hyponatremia was more common than dehydration, so "drink to thirst" is the safer default.
- Individual GI tolerance varies 30-80% between runners, and Jeukendrup's "train the gut" protocol shows tolerance can expand with progressive carbohydrate exposure over 4-8 weeks.

Practical guidance:
- Simple carbohydrates (white bread, bagels, white rice, pasta, couscous, fruit, juice, honey, maple syrup, dairy, sports drinks, energy gels) are easier to digest than complex carbs and preferred the night before a long run.
- Complex carbs (wheat bread, brown/wild rice, barley, legumes, beans, oats, sweet potatoes) should generally be avoided the night before because they're high in fiber.
- Recommended meal ideas: lemon pasta (high-carb, low-protein, low-dairy), homemade pizza with simple-carb crust, couscous-based dishes, fresh bread sandwiches (e.g., ciabatta with prosciutto and manchego), and breakfast-for-dinner options like pancakes with maple syrup.
- Final tips: avoid high-protein meals, avoid fiber (beans, lentils, whole grains, broccoli), and eat enough but not too much—using the equation: 8 x weight in kilos = total grams of carbohydrates per day during a carb load.
- The night before a race is not the time to try new foods; use Saturday long runs during training to test portion sizes, timing, and specific foods, keeping a log of what causes GI distress.
- Carbohydrates are essential for runners as the primary fuel source; glycogen helps maintain consistent energy and prevents "hitting the wall" (bonking). Any effort above 60% of VO2 max draws on glycogen stores. Low-carb diets show decreased performance.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2022.1003445/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Sec. Sport and Exercise Nutrition, Volume 9, November 9, 2022) titled "An exploratory study of the management strategies reported by endurance athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms" by Rachel Scrivin, Ricardo J.S. Costa, Fiona Pelly, Dana Lis, and Gary Slater (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia; Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand; Monash University, Australia; and UCLA, United States).

STUDY DESIGN AND PARTICIPANTS:
The study used a validated online questionnaire to investigate self-reported exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) and management strategies among 137 adult endurance athletes (≥18 years) participating in events ≥60 minutes. Participants included runners (55%, n=75), triathletes (22%, n=30), and non-running sports (23%, n=32) at recreationally competitive (37%), recreationally non-competitive (32%), and competitive regional/national/international (31%) levels. Females comprised 63% of respondents (n=86) and males 37% (n=51) (p<0.001); mean age was 41.6 ± 11.1 years. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia (approval S201402).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Athletes were categorized into groups based on when Ex-GIS developed: around training only (AT, 21%), around competitions only (AC, 30%), or equally around both (ET/EC, 49%).
- Lower gastrointestinal symptoms were more commonly reported than upper GI symptoms across all groups.
- Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during training and competitions than before or after exercise. The only severe symptom of significance was the urge to defecate during training in the ET group (Z=-0.536, p=0.01). Most Ex-GIS severity was rated as mild (<5/10 on a 0-10 visual analog scale).
- 67% (n=92) of athletes reported using dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting 277 total strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.

MOST POPULAR DIETARY STRATEGIES:
- Dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42) - the most popular
- Dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16)
- Low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15)
- Avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose, 6.1%, n=17) were the most popular FODMAPs avoided
- Non-dietary strategies included medications (4.7%, n=13) and relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11)

MOST SUCCESSFUL STRATEGIES (Likert scale 1-5, with 5 = significant improvement):
- Dietary fiber reduction (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Low FODMAP diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Dairy-free diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5)
- Increasing carbohydrates (median = 4, IQR = 3,4)
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed at all time points.

SUPPLEMENTS: Probiotics (median=4, n=26) were the most commonly used supplement; arginine was rated highest for success (median=5, n=1, though very small sample). Other supplements trialed included prebiotics, antioxidants, L-citrulline, glutamine, curcumin, and nitrates.

INFORMATION SOURCES: Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated as the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29). No significant associations were found between information sources and sport type, participation level, event characteristics, or biological sex.

CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS: Fifteen athletes (11%) reported a diagnosed gastrointestinal disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, n=6). Thirteen athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS.

DISCUSSION HIGHLIGHTS:
- Reducing dietary fiber, especially before exercise, aligns with current sports nutrition guidelines and works via reducing luminal contents and extending GI transit time, though a low-fiber diet may require implementation 1-3 days before exercise.
- Low FODMAP diets are effective for both IBS and Ex-GIS, but are not intended for long-term use; a rechallenge and personalization phase is recommended for extended use.
- Dairy avoidance may relate to lactose intolerance, which has overlapping symptoms with IBS.
- Increasing carbohydrate intake can help mitigate Ex-GIS through improved splanchnic blood flow and reduced intestinal epithelial damage; however, high intake rates (>60-90 g/h) may trigger symptoms unless preceded by gut training.
- Carbohydrate or whey protein hydrolysate ingestion before/during exercise ameliorates intestinal epithelial injury; carbohydrate is preferential due to fewer GI symptoms and its value as an exogenous fuel source.
- Non-dietary interventions (medications, relaxation, psychological therapies) are used less frequently but have potential; further randomized controlled trials are needed.
- Study limitations include convenience sampling and possible over-representation of APDs as information sources due to researcher backgrounds as registered dietitians.
</summary>

"Endurance athletes use a variety of strategies to manage their Ex-GIS, with dietary manipulation being the most common."

--- SOURCE 2: Nutritional strategies for minimizing gastrointestinal symptoms during endurance exercise: systematic review of the literature ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12258207

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2025 Jul 11;22(1):2529910, doi:10.1080/15502783.2025.2529910) by Janez Mlinaric and Nina Mohorko (University of Primorska, Faculty of Health Sciences, Izola, Slovenia; Ruhr University Bochum, Germany; Human Performance Centre, Ljubljana, Slovenia), examining nutritional strategies to minimize gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms during endurance exercise.

METHODS: The review used PRISMA methodology, searching PubMed from January 2023 to March 2023. It included randomized controlled trials, crossover trials, and case studies. 31 studies were selected for inclusion, with quality assessment using the Cochrane Collaboration's risk-of-bias (RoB 2) tool. The majority of studies showed low risk of bias, though some had concerns regarding blinding and randomization.

The studies were categorized into five research areas:

1. **Gut training protocols**: Two weeks of purposeful repetitive CHO intake during running lowered GI symptom severity and reduced breath H₂ response (indicating reduced CHO malabsorption). Repetitive running sessions with higher liquid intake improved fluid tolerance over time. However, minor effects were seen in race walkers and runners with high daily CHO intake. The mechanisms may involve increased expression of SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters, but gut training is likely to reduce symptoms by reducing CHO malabsorption and increasing tolerance to higher CHO intakes.

2. **Carbohydrate solutions and mixtures**: CHO bars were the worst tolerated form (causing more nausea, fullness, and fatigue). Highly concentrated CHO solutions increased symptoms. Fructose caused more GI symptoms than glucose or sucrose due to slower absorption (facilitated diffusion vs. active transport). High glucose intake (SGLT1 saturation at ~60 g/h) caused bloating. Mixed CHOs recruit GLUT5 transporter, improving absorption. A 0.8 ratio MD:FRU solution was superior to 0.5 and 1.25 ratios for performance and GI comfort, suggesting ratios close to unity may be better than the traditional 2:1 ratio.

3. **Low FODMAP diet**: Multiple studies showed significant reductions in GI symptoms (gut discomfort, flatulence, urge to defecate, loose stool, diarrhea) with low FODMAP diets compared to high FODMAP diets. 69% of participants reported positive effects on low FODMAP vs. 25% on high FODMAP. However, the restrictive nature of the diet could negatively affect athletes in other ways.

4. **Hydrogel CHO products**: Current evidence does not demonstrate benefits of hydrogel CHO products over standard CHO products. One study showed lower GI symptoms with hydrogel, but others found no differences between conditions.

5. **Probiotic supplementation**: Evidence is mixed. Some studies showed reductions in GI symptoms (e.g., 27% reduction during training, fewer episodes of nausea, belching, vomiting), while others found no substantial differences or even increases in mild GI symptoms. LGG (Limosilactobacillus rhamnosus GG) shortened GI symptom episode duration by 33-57%.

CONCLUSION: The onset of GI symptoms is very complex and influenced by a huge variety of factors. Elimination of GI symptoms in each athlete must be approached individually and thoughtfully. At least 30-50% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms regularly during exercise, with estimates of 30-90% for endurance trained runners. Four main causes of GI symptoms: physiological (splanchnic hypoperfusion), mechanical, psychological, and nutritional.
</summary>

"At least 30 to 50 % of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise on a regular basis, with especially high occurrence in long duration endurance exercise. In endurance trained runners it is estimated that between 30 and 90 % may experience them."

The study evaluated a four-phase management approach for exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) in endurance athletes using the GastroAxEx (gastrointestinal assessment during exercise) protocol combined with a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP therapeutic dietary intervention.

METHODOLOGY: Nine recreational-to-elite athletes with recurrent severe Ex-GIS and two controls (without Ex-GIS) participated. KEY RESULTS: 
- Most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2%-4% body mass loss

- All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery
- Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes
- 8/9 athletes successfully implemented the 48-hr high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to targeted events

CONCLUSION: The 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to endurance exercise reduced the incidence and severity of Ex-GIS, improved intake tolerance, and resulted in improved perceived work output during targeted events. The authors conclude this dietary approach appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions for mitigating Ex-GIS.

<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in the MDPI journal *Dietetics* (2023, Volume 2, Issue 3, pages 289-307; DOI: 10.3390/dietetics2030021) titled "Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Sports: A Review of Pathophysiology, Symptoms, and Nutritional Management." The article was authored by Emanuela Ribichini, Giulia Scalese, Alessandra Cesarini, Chiara Mocci, Nadia Pallotta, Carola Severi (Gastroenterology, Department of Translational and Precision Medicine, Sapienza University of Rome, Italy) and Enrico Stefano Corazziari (Department of Gastroenterology, IRCCS Humanitas Research Hospital, Rozzano, Milan, Italy). Submission received 26 July 2023; accepted 12 September 2023; published 19 September 2023. The article has been cited 26 times and viewed 61,433 times.

**Purpose:** The review explores the pathophysiology, clinical aspects, and nutritional/behavioral management strategies for Exercise-Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome (Ex-GIS), with particular focus on gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets.

**Methods:** Three databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane) were searched up to March 2023. Searches for pathophysiology returned 290 results (PubMed), 216 (MEDLINE), and 97 trials (Cochrane); diet/nutrition searches returned 2663, 2197, and 1038 results respectively. After inclusion/exclusion criteria (English language, relevant to diet and endurance performance), 142 research articles were identified.

**Key Findings on Pathophysiology:**
- Ex-GIS involves two primary pathways: (I) the neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway (sympathetic activation reducing GI functional capacity) and (II) the circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway (blood flow redistribution away from splanchnic circulation).
- Splanchnic blood flow (SBF) can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing significant GI tract hypoperfusion and damage.
- Splanchnic hypoperfusion leads to loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia (LPS in circulation), triggering pro-inflammatory cytokines.
- A 1965-era study by Brock-Utne found 81% of 89 marathon runners were endotoxemic.
- Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max represents the threshold for significant GI perturbations.
- Endurance exercise alters gut peptide levels (increases PYY and GLP-1, affects ghrelin, CCK) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) which affect GI motility and blood flow.
- Gut microbiota differences exist between athletes and sedentary individuals; probiotics (e.g., UCC118 strain) may attenuate exercise-induced intestinal hyperpermeability.
- Carbohydrate malabsorption was found in 68% of 25 healthy endurance-trained runners during recovery.

**Epidemiology/Prevalence:**
- 30-90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms during exercise.
- Ter Steege study of 2076 long-distance runners: 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% serious complaints, 2.7% within 24 hours post-run; 3 athletes dropped out.
- Pfeiffer study: severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon/cycling to 32% in Ironman races.
- Upper-GI symptoms in up to 40% of runners, up to 70% in cyclists; reflux/heartburn prevalence 15-20% in runners.
- Lower-GI symptoms: up to 30% in recreational runs, up to 50% in cyclists, up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners.
- Exercise-induced transient abdominal pain (ETAP) reported in 18% of recreational run competitors.
- IBS underdiagnosis in endurance athletes: Killian et al. documented 9.8% IBS prevalence overall with only 2.8% diagnosed; Hungin et al. reported 14.1% overall with 10.8% undiagnosed.
- Female athletes, especially younger ones, report higher GI symptom prevalence; increased age may be protective due to reduced splanchnic vasoconstriction.

**Management Implications:** The review highlights nutritional and behavioral interventions as the principal strategies to avoid symptoms, including evaluation of exercise modality, dehydration state, environmental temperature, concomitant therapies, and self-managed diet. It examines gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets as potential management approaches, noting that Ex-GIS symptoms resemble IBS (defined by Rome IV Criteria) and may respond to analogous nutritional strategies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Strenuous exercise can be associated with 'Exercise Induced Gastrointestinal Syndrome' (Ex-GIS), a clinical condition characterized by a series of gastrointestinal (GI) disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s44410-025-00019-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access scoping review article published in the journal "Performance Nutrition" (Volume 2, article number 4, published February 4, 2026) titled "Gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes beyond endurance sports: a scoping review." The study aimed to assess the prevalence of GI symptoms in non-endurance sport athletes, as GI symptoms are well-documented in endurance athletes but less clear across other sports.

METHODS: A scoping review was conducted following JBI guidelines with the PCC mnemonic. Searches were performed on Medline and SportDiscus databases (via EBSCO) until September 1, 2025, using keywords including "gastrointestinal," "athlete*/player*/sport*," and "prevalence/frequency/proportion." Only cross-sectional studies in highly trained (Tier 3) or higher athletes were included. Endurance sports (distance running, cycling, triathlons) and clinical settings were excluded.

RESULTS: The search yielded 482 articles; after screening, seven studies were included. Six different questionnaires were used across studies. In total, 1,087 athletes (682 male, 405 female) were analyzed. Prevalence of at least one GI symptom ranged from 11.5–80.0%. Any GI symptom prevalence in males was 13.9–61% and in females 26–80%. Three studies reported symptom timing around training/competition ranging from 24.5–52.0%, more common in females (37.5–67.0%) than males (13.9–52.0%). The most common symptoms were flatulence (2.8–48%), stomach cramps/rumbling (5.1–37%), and bloating (2.5–32%). Diarrhoea and urge to defecate were more common during exercise than at rest (19% vs. 8%, and 13% vs. 11%, respectively). Specific findings included: American footballers (61% reported ≥1 symptom, 52% during exercise), rugby players (61% male, 72% female with ≥1 symptom), powerlifters/weightlifters with anal incontinence (61.8% male vs. 80.0% female), and celiac disease symptoms higher in athletes than general population (2.9% vs. 0.4%).

CONCLUSIONS: GI symptoms are common in non-endurance athletes, with approximately 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes experiencing symptoms around competition. The wide variation in prevalence (11.5–80%) is likely due to heterogeneity in screening tools, with studies using different numbers of symptoms assessed (2–15), different Likert scales (0–4, 0–7, 0–10), and varying recall windows (past week to 12 months). Female athletes were more likely to report symptoms affecting performance. The authors call for standardized methods for assessing GI issues in athletes and note that existing questionnaires may be suitable only for research, not clinical diagnosis, suggesting future research should consider validated criteria such as ROME IV for IBS.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes varies widely, which may be due to heterogeneity in screening tools. There is a lack of studies discerning the severity and timing of symptoms, but it appears that around 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes may experience gastrointestinal symptoms around competing."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Gastrointestinal Medicine in the Athlete

This chapter from the Musculoskeletal Key website (DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) addresses common gastrointestinal (GI) conditions in athletes and active persons, focusing on recognition and management. GI conditions are common in athletes, with exercise placing significant stress on the GI tract, resulting in characteristic disorders that can impair athletic performance.

### Key Points:

**General Pathophysiology:**
- 20–50% of high-performance athletes report undesirable GI symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea)
- Symptoms are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes
- Cyclists appear somewhat protected from GI issues due to forward positioning, while runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling
- Increased catecholamines and GI peptides (gastrin, motilin, secretin, etc.) increase gut transit time, negatively affecting GI homeostasis

**GI Tract Ischemia:**
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction
- Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation
- Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa" (per ter Steege et al.)
- Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms

**Upper GI Conditions:**
- Upper GI complaints affect 30–70% of athletes
- Three primary mechanisms: mechanical forces, altered GI blood flow, and neuroendocrine changes
- GERD is the most common cause of upper GI symptoms in athletes
- Exercise ≥90% VO2 max increases frequency/duration of esophageal reflux episodes
- Weightlifters have the highest rate of heartburn and reflux; runners have a threefold increase in GERD when running 45 minutes after a meal

**GERD Management:**
- Lifestyle modifications first-line: sleeping on two pillows, avoiding lying down within 4 hours of evening meal, avoiding postprandial exercise, limiting foods that relax the LES (high-fat foods, coffee, chocolate, peppermint, alcohol, acidic foods)
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training
- Pharmacologic therapy: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective
- H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers
- Upper endoscopy for diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended

**Other Conditions:**
- **Functional heartburn:** Up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset; treatment is biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, prokinetics
- **Dyspepsia:** Caused by GERD, gastritis, or peptic ulcer disease; ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms; PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence
- **Aspirin/NSAIDs:** Block cyclooxygenase and protective prostaglandins; add daily PPI for GI protection in athletes requiring NSAIDs with ulcer history
- **Pill esophagitis:** NSAIDs, tetracyclines, and mefloquine are highest risk; take with food/fluid in morning and remain upright
- **Dysphagia:** Divided into oropharyngeal and esophageal subtypes; most commonly caused by irritative effects of GERD
- **Nausea/Vomiting:** Linked to postprandial exercise; avoid solid food within 3 hours of events; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events; H2 blockers and PPIs can help

**GERD-Asthma Connection:**
- Up to 90% of persons with asthma have GERD; up to 40% have esophagitis
- Treatment only benefits asthma in patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms
- Atypical GERD presentations include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, and chest pain
</summary>

"These symptoms are reported by approximately 20% to 50% of high-performance athletes and are encountered more commonly in women than in men."

--- SOURCE 7: Frontiers | Proton pump inhibitors may enhance the risk of digestive diseases by regulating intestinal microbiota ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2023.1217306/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Proton Pump Inhibitors May Enhance the Risk of Digestive Diseases by Regulating Intestinal Microbiota

This is a peer-reviewed review article published in *Frontiers in Pharmacology* (July 17, 2023) by Liang Tian, Jinqiu Yuan, Wenbo Meng and colleagues from Lanzhou University (China) and Sun Yat-sen University (China). The article reviews the growing evidence linking proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use to digestive complications through PPI-induced alterations of the intestinal microbiota.

### Key Points:

**Background:** PPIs are the most widely used acid-suppressive agents and first-line therapy for gastric acid-related disorders (peptic ulcer disease, GERD, Barrett's esophagus). However, increasing evidence links PPIs to adverse digestive events including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Clostridium difficile-associated disease (CDAD), functional dyspepsia, lower GI bleeding, infectious diseases, cholelithiasis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

**Mechanisms of PPI effects on intestinal flora:**
- pH-dependent: PPIs reduce gastric acid, disrupting the gastric acid barrier, allowing exogenous bacteria to invade the GI tract; affects microorganisms with specific pH requirements (e.g., H. pylori)
- Non-pH-dependent: PPI-induced hypergastrinemia and hyperparathyroidism affect intestinal osmolality and calcium/phosphorus metabolism; PPIs alter digestive functions and nutrient absorption; PPIs directly bind to non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases on microbes (fungi, H. pylori, Streptococcus pneumoniae)
- PPI treatment increases Planococcaceae, Oxalobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae in the proximal small intestine; decreases Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae

**Specific disease associations with altered flora:**
1. **Functional Dyspepsia (FD):** Decreased Bifidobacterium reduces butyric acid production, increasing intestinal permeability. Reduced Streptococcus, Prevotella, Veillonella, Actinomyces, and Lactobacillus may also contribute.
2. **Lower GI Bleeding:** Decreased Lactobacillus johnsonii (lactic acid production inhibits NF-κB/TNF-α pathway) and reduced Actinomycetes/Bifidobacterium contribute to NSAID-induced intestinal injury.
3. **SIBO:** Results are inconsistent across studies; a 2018 meta-analysis showed PPI use moderately increased SIBO risk, though diagnostic method variability (aspirate culture vs. breath tests) is a major confounder.
4. **CDAD:** PPIs regulate C. difficile toxin gene expression (up to 120-fold), accelerate spore-to-trophic-form transition via elevated pH, diminish salivary nitrite antimicrobial effects, and disrupt normal flora. Risk can be up to 7.15-fold higher.
5. **Gastrointestinal Infectious Diseases:** PPIs increase risk of bacterial gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter), Candida infections (reduced Lactobacillus), and multidrug-resistant organism infections (75% increased infection rate).
6. **Cholelithiasis:** PPI use increases abundance of bile salt hydrolase (BSH)-producing bacteria (Lactobacillus, Clostridium, Eubacterium), increasing secondary bile acids (especially deoxycholic acid) that promote gallstone formation. PPIs also reduce gallbladder motility by delaying gastric emptying.
7. **Inflammatory Bowel Disease:** PPI use is linked to IBD through reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (anti-inflammatory), reduced Lactobacillus reuteri (which normally produces histamine to suppress TNF-α), increased intestinal infections, and CDAD promotion.

**Conclusions:** The evidence supports a link between PPI-induced intestinal flora disruption and digestive complications. The gut microbiota represents a promising target for prevention and treatment (e.g., fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics like Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium). However, most studies are retrospective with relatively weak evidence and confounding factors. Clinicians should carefully evaluate and individually manage patients requiring PPI therapy to avoid long-term abuse. More high-quality clinical studies and research into specific mechanisms and molecular targets are needed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"PPIs are the most used acid-inhibitory drugs, with a wide range of applications in the treatment of various digestive diseases. However, recently, there has been a growing number of digestive complications linked to PPIs, and several studies have indicated that the intestinal flora play an important role in these complications."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: Exercise & GI Symptoms - IFFGD ---
URL: https://iffgd.org/manage-your-health/tips-and-daily-living/exercise-gi-symptoms

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the International Foundation for Gastrointestinal Disorders (IFFGD) addresses whether intense exercise can lead to GI symptoms such as diarrhea and heartburn. The article answers a reader's question about experiencing diarrhea and heartburn after increasing exercise intensity.

Key content covered:

**Benefits vs. risks of exercise:** While regular exercise offers documented benefits (better sleep, stronger bones, weight loss, fewer heart problems, better glucose control), it can also contribute to GI disorders causing symptoms including reflux/heartburn, belching, bloating, stomach pain/cramps, vomiting, nausea, side ache, flatulence, urgency, diarrhea, and intestinal bleeding.

**Heartburn:** Exercise can decrease lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure, leading to more reflux episodes. Eating too soon before exercise and high-impact activities (like running) can worsen reflux compared to low-impact exercises like cycling. Treatment includes H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and switching to lower-impact exercises.

**Diarrhea:** Diarrhea and urgency are common in endurance athletes, especially long-distance runners. Approximately 90% of long-distance runners experience some GI symptoms during exercise but accept them as normal and don't consult a physician.

**Three main causes of GI symptoms during intense exercise:**
1. **Mechanical:** Repetitive body movement from running causes trauma that can damage the intestinal lining, contributing to diarrhea, urgency, or GI bleeding.
2. **Ischemic:** During intense exercise, blood flow shifts to working muscles and away from the GI tract (up to 80% reduction), causing ischemia, reduced gut function, increased leakiness, malabsorption, and looser stools.
3. **Nutritional:** Fiber, fat, protein, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>7% carbohydrate) are associated with greater risk of GI symptoms.

**Prevention tips:** Stay well hydrated, avoid lactose-containing products, and avoid high-fructose foods and fructose-only drinks.

**Medical treatment:** Patients should consult healthcare providers about persistent or bleeding diarrhea, which may signal a severe condition. Loperamide (over-the-counter) has been shown to decrease stool frequency when taken before intense exercise. Caution is advised with antispasmodic and antimotility drugs, as they can inhibit perspiration and impair core body temperature control.

The article was authored by Renata Korczak, RD CSSD (University of Minnesota), adapted from an article by Thomas Puetz, M.D. (Aurora Advanced Healthcare), and edited by William D. Chey, MD (University of Michigan). It is IFFGD publication #231.
</summary>

"According to research, about 90% of long-distance runners experience some form of GI symptoms (including diarrhea) during exercise and accept their symptoms as a normal consequence of running and therefore do not consult a physician."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Gastrointestinal distress: Can a low-fodmap diet help? - The Centre for Integrative Sports Nutrition ---
URL: https://intsportsnutrition.com/articles/exercise-induced-gastrointestinal-distress-can-a-low-fodmap-diet-help

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Simone do Carmo (MSci SENr CISNCert), a sports nutritionist and exercise physiologist, investigates whether a low-FODMAP diet can help alleviate exercise-induced gastrointestinal (GI) distress in athletes. The article covers the causes, prevalence, and potential nutritional strategies for GI distress, with a focus on the low-FODMAP diet as an emerging therapeutic approach.

**Key points on GI distress in athletes:**
- Prevalence ranges from 30-90% depending on methodology, study populations, and environmental conditions
- Symptoms are categorized as upper GI (heartburn, bloating, nausea) or lower GI (cramps, diarrhea, intestinal bleeding)
- Causes are physiological (ischemia from blood shunting to active muscles, reduced splanchnic blood flow, compromised gut permeability, risk of endotoxemia), mechanical (posture changes in cycling, bouncing impact in running causing intestinal bleeding), and nutritional (dehydration, high-fibre/high-fat/high-protein foods, fructose, milk, concentrated carbohydrate drinks)
- A study of 55 male triathletes in a half-Ironman race found 52% reported urge to defecate and 42% reported flatulence; all who ate 30 minutes before the race vomited during the swim leg; 93% of those who vomited consumed hypertonic drinks; all with intestinal cramps had eaten high-fibre foods
- NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI symptoms and intestinal bleeding
- Sports drinks should be below 8% carbohydrate concentration (preferably glucose and fructose combination) to prevent dehydration

**Low-FODMAP diet findings:**
- FODMAPs = Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides and Polyols, which are poorly absorbed and rapidly fermented by colonic bacteria
- The diet was initially developed for IBS patients; up to 86% of IBS patients alleviate symptoms on it
- A survey of 910 athletes found 55% actively avoided at least one high-FODMAP food; 93% reported that food elicited GI symptoms, and 86.5% reported improvement through avoidance
- Lactose was the highest trigger (86.5%), followed by galacto-oligosaccharides (23.9%), fructose (23.0%), fructans (6.2%), and polyols (5.4%)
- Long-term adherence is not recommended due to risk of inadequate nutritional intake and negative effects on gut microbiota (reduced SCFA-producing bacteria, which produce butyrate, propionate, and acetate essential for colonic health)
- A case study used a six-day low-FODMAP diet in a runner, which resolved running-specific GI symptoms and improved psychological well-being (assessed via DALDA scores)
- Prudent recommendation: follow a low-FODMAP diet for 2-3 days prior to a race or important training session

**Gut trainability:**
- A 28-day study of 16 trained cyclists/triathletes found that high-carbohydrate diets led to greater maximal citrate synthase activity and higher carbohydrate exogenous oxidation rates during submaximal exercise, attributed to enhanced intestinal absorption and improved tolerance
- The gut is a highly dynamic, adaptable organ that athletes can train through nutritional experimentation during training

The article concludes that eliminating certain high-FODMAP food triggers with a prudent, individualised, and focused approach may be an effective nutritional strategy to reduce GI distress in athletes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The prevalence of gastrointestinal distress is highly variable, ranging from 30 to 90 per cent, which can partly be explained by the different methodologies, study populations and environmental conditions in research studies."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Effect of a short-term low fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide and polyol (FODMAP) diet on exercise-related gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12970-019-0268-9

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access research article published on January 15, 2019, in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (Volume 16, article number 1) examining the effect of a short-term low FODMAP diet on exercise-related gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms in recreational runners.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Sixteen healthy, recreationally active runners (10 female, 6 male; age 44 ± 10 years) completed a randomized crossover trial. Participants followed either a LOW FODMAP (16.06 ± 1.79 g/day) or HIGH FODMAP (38.65 ± 6.66 g/day) diet for 7 days, with a one-week washout period before switching. GI symptoms were rated using the Irritable Bowel Syndrome-Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS) questionnaire, perceived ability to exercise was rated on a visual analogue scale, and resting blood samples were collected to measure plasma intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP) as a marker of acute GI injury.

KEY RESULTS:
- Overall IBS-SSS score significantly reduced on the LOW FODMAP diet from 81.1 ± 16.4 to 31.3 ± 9.2 (P = 0.004), while HIGH FODMAP showed a non-significant increase from 51.1 to 104.0 (P = 0.08)
- 69% of participants (11/16) reported positive effects of the LOW FODMAP diet versus only 25% (4/16) on HIGH FODMAP
- Perceived exercise frequency (P = 0.02) and intensity (P = 0.007) were significantly improved following LOW FODMAP
- No significant differences were found in plasma I-FABP between dietary conditions (P > 0.05)
- Individual symptoms of pain and bloating showed significant improvements on LOW FODMAP
- Total carbohydrate intake was lower during LOW FODMAP (2.79 g/kg/day) versus HIGH FODMAP (3.91 g/kg/day)

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: FODMAPs are short-chain carbohydrates (fructose, lactose, oligosaccharides, polyols) that can be malabsorbed, leading to gas production, increased intestinal water volume, and gut motility changes. Low FODMAP diets are established treatments for IBS (effective in ~75% of patients). While 30-50% of athletes cite GI issues as a common cause of underperformance, most prior research focused on trained athletes; this study specifically examined healthy recreational runners under free-living conditions.

CONCLUSION: A short-term LOW FODMAP diet under free-living conditions reduced exercise-related GI symptoms and improved perceived ability to exercise in healthy recreational runners, likely due to reduced indigestible carbohydrates available for fermentation. The authors recommend further investigation into therapeutic benefits of LOW FODMAP diets for recreational and trained athletes during sustained training periods. The study was conducted at Anglia Ruskin University (Cambridge Centre for Sport and Exercise Sciences) with ethical approval (Project Number: FST/FREP/15/567).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A short-term LOW FODMAP diet under free-living conditions reduced exercise-related GI symptoms and improved the perceived ability to exercise in otherwise healthy, recreational runners." — Study conclusion
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Low-FODMAP diet for better management of gastrointestinal issues during exercise ---
URL: https://therunningclinic.com/runners/blog/archives-anglaises/low-fodmap-diet-for-better-management-of-gastrointestinal-issues-during-exercise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from The Running Clinic (La Clinique du Coureur) discusses the use of a low-FODMAP diet to manage gastrointestinal issues in runners and endurance athletes. Key points include:

- Gastrointestinal problems affect 30-50% of endurance athletes, rising to 96% among ultra-endurance runners.
- FODMAP stands for fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols—carbohydrates that are partially digested, ferment in the colon, and can cause bloating, abdominal pain, and gas in sensitive individuals.
- The low-FODMAP diet (originally designed for irritable bowel syndrome) reduces symptoms with a success rate of around 70% in sensitive populations.
- During exercise, intestinal ischemia (reduced blood flow to the digestive system) weakens the intestine, and undigested food particles can increase osmotic load, leading to urgent defecation, loose stools, or diarrhea.
- Research evidence includes: a case study of a female runner following a low-FODMAP diet 6 days before and during a 186.7 km multistage mountain ultramarathon that significantly reduced digestive distress; a case study of a male triathlete who saw reduced GI symptoms on a 6-day low-FODMAP diet; a first intervention study with 11 runners where 9 of 11 reported fewer daily GI symptoms on the low-FODMAP diet; and a second intervention study with 16 recreational runners where 69% (11 participants) reported positive effects.
- The article notes the small sample sizes and recommends consulting a healthcare professional before adopting a long-term low-FODMAP diet. It positions the diet as beneficial on an ad hoc basis before important events or during intensive training phases, rather than removing high-FODMAP foods entirely.
- The article is written by Isabelle Morin, a nutritionist at The Running Clinic, and includes a table of high-FODMAP foods commonly consumed by athletes with low-FODMAP alternatives (table content not fully included in the raw text).
</summary>

"Gastrointestinal problems affect as much as 30 to 50% of endurance athletes. This prevalence even increases to 96% when looking more particularly at ultra-endurance runners."
