--- SOURCE 7: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in ... ---
URL: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/9QnW5DQA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a case series study titled "Case Series: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Athletes Using a High-Carbohydrate Low-FODMAP Therapeutic Intervention," published in 2025 in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (Vol. 34, No. 4, pp. 337-354), by Rachel Scrivin, Gary Slater, and Ricardo J.S. Costa, published by Human Kinetics. The study has been cited 3 times and is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science.

The study implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). The case series involved 9 athletes who experienced recurrent severe Ex-GIS and 2 controls without symptoms.

The four phases were: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes, specifically including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of therapeutic interventions.

Key findings: The majority of athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2-4% body mass loss, and <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate (8/9) during the GastroAxEx. Severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) was reported by 4/9 athletes during exercise and 8/9 in the recovery period. All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery. Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet and improved intake tolerance during the targeted event, with reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS and improved perceived work output.

The study concludes that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms.

The webpage also lists 40 references and 4 citing publications, including a position statement response in Sports Medicine, a study on high-amylose maize starch and hydration, a practitioner's guide to managing gut issues in athletes, and a Current Opinion article on dietary FODMAP manipulation arguing that FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default based on symptom severity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This case-series describes a four-phase management approach implementing gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes affected by exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Sports Dietitians Australia and Ultra Sports Science Foundation Joint Position Statement: A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12106582

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a joint position statement by Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and the Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) published in Sports Medicine (April 7, 2025; Vol 55, Issue 5, Article 1097; DOI: 10.1007/s40279-025-02186-6) providing a practitioner guide for the prevention and management of exercise-associated gastrointestinal perturbations and symptoms (Ex-GIS) and exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS).

KEY AUTHORS: Ricardo J. S. Costa, Stephanie K. Gaskell, Kayla Henningsen (Monash University, Australia); Nikki A. Jeacocke and Alice M. Wallett (Australian Institute of Sport); Volker Scheer (Ultra Sports Science Foundation, France); Rachel Scrivin (University of the Sunshine Coast, Australia & Toi Ohomai Institute of Technology, New Zealand); Rhiannon M. J. Snipe (Deakin University, Australia); and Pascale Young (Monash University). The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (PMCID: PMC12106582; PMID: 40195264).

BACKGROUND & KEY CONCEPTS:
- Exercise can disturb gastrointestinal integrity and function, leading to EIGS and Ex-GIS, which are common in active and athlete populations and comprise a substantial case load for practitioners (sports dietitians, sport and exercise nutritionists, sports medical practitioners).
- EIGS comprises two primary pathophysiological pathways: (1) the circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway (splanchnic hypoperfusion and gastrointestinal ischemia due to blood flow redistribution to skeletal muscle, leading to intestinal epithelial injury, hyperpermeability, and inflammatory responses from translocated pathogens/endotoxins), and (2) the neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway (stress responses, sympathetic activation, impaired motility, transit, digestion, and nutrient absorption via effects on the enteric nervous system and interstitial cells of Cajal).
- Two additional pathways warrant investigation: mechanical strain on the splanchnic area (jarring/jolting/vibrations) and exaggerated metabolic responses (metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia) linked to exercise-associated nausea.
- Ex-GIS symptom incidence varies widely by exercise type: negligible in recreational endurance running, 4% after marathon competition, and ≥93% in ultra-endurance events. Longer-duration exercise, especially in hot conditions, promotes higher Ex-GIS incidence.
- Symptoms are classified per ROME IV criteria into upper-GIS (belching, heartburn, upper-abdominal bloating/pain, regurgitation), lower-GIS (flatulence, lower-abdominal bloating/pain, urge to defecate, abnormal defecation, fecal blood loss), and other symptoms (nausea, stitch). Contrary to mainstream dogma, upper-GIS symptoms are more commonly reported during/immediately after exercise than lower-GIS; nausea is frequently reported in ultra-endurance activities.

EXACERBATION FACTORS (with assigned impact magnitudes: unknown = ?, minimal = +, modest = ++, extensive = +++):
Extrinsic factors:
- Exercise duration (+++): considerable perturbations occur with ≥2h exercise; plateaus thereafter.
- Exercise intensity (++): continuous ≥70% VO2max or HIIT/resistance exercise ≤2h produces modest increases.
- Exercise modality (+): field studies suggest running prompts greater disturbance than swimming/cycling (due to mechanical strain), but controlled lab studies show no clear modality differences.
- Environmental conditions (+++): hot ambient conditions (~35°C) increase EIGS biomarkers and Ex-GIS; core body temperature ≥39.5°C or Δ≥2.5°C is clinically significant; ≥39.0°C or Δ≥2.0°C exceeds minimal detectable change.
- Topographical elevation/altitude (+): altitude >2500m ASL may increase disturbances.
- Time of day (++): nocturnal exercise prompts greater GI function disturbance and Ex-GIS than diurnal exercise, but no effect on EIGS integrity/systemic biomarkers.
- External pharmaceutical administration (+++): NSAIDs are GI irritants; administration prior to exercise markedly increases GI perturbations and Ex-GIS.

Intrinsic factors:
- Biological sex (+): low-to-modest differences observed; female athletes proposed to present greater EIGS/Ex-GIS due to menstrual cycle, but evidence is inconsistent.
- Age (+): modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults.
- Fitness status (+): higher-trained individuals at lower absolute risk but exposed to greater relative loads.
- GI/circulating microbial and SCFA composition (+): may impact magnitude of perturbations.
- Individual characteristics (+++): feeding tolerance (volume, concentration, type, texture), pre-existing GI diseases/disorders, and history of recurrent Ex-GIS increase risk.
- Psychological state (?): pre-exercise anxiety linked to Ex-GIS in field observations but lacks rigorous controlled evidence.

METHODOLOGY: A scoping review approach (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Ovid Medline) was used to screen relevant research studies. --- SOURCE 12: International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and performance - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2824625

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Caffeine and Performance (2010)

This is a position statement from the International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN), authored by Erica R. Goldstein and 14 colleagues, establishing the Society's official position on caffeine supplementation and sport performance. The paper was received December 22, 2009, accepted January 27, 2010, and is published under the Creative Commons Attribution License.

### The Society's Seven-Point Position Statement:
1. **Caffeine is effective for enhancing sport performance** in trained athletes when consumed in low-to-moderate dosages (~3-6 mg/kg); higher dosages (≥9 mg/kg) do not result in further enhancement.
2. **Anhydrous caffeine** exerts a greater ergogenic effect compared to coffee.
3. Caffeine can **enhance vigilance** during extended exhaustive exercise and periods of sustained sleep deprivation.
4. Caffeine is **ergogenic for sustained maximal endurance exercise** and highly effective for time-trial performance.
5. Caffeine is **beneficial for high-intensity exercise**, including team sports such as soccer and rugby characterized by intermittent activity over prolonged duration.
6. The literature is **equivocal on strength-power performance** effects; more research is warranted.
7. The literature does **not support caffeine-induced diuresis during exercise** or harmful changes in fluid balance affecting performance.

### Key Mechanisms of Action:
- Caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) is rapidly absorbed through the GI tract, metabolized by the liver into three metabolites (paraxanthine, theophylline, theobromine), with elevated blood levels appearing within 15-45 minutes and peak concentrations one hour post-ingestion.
- Caffeine easily crosses the blood-brain barrier due to lipid solubility; circulating concentrations decrease 50-75% within 3-6 hours.
- The primary mechanism is **adenosine receptor antagonism** at the CNS.
- Caffeine decreases reliance on glycogen utilization and increases free fatty acid mobilization during exercise.
- Caffeine increases β-endorphin secretion, potentially reducing pain perception.
- Caffeine promotes a significant thermogenic response (100 mg dose produced significant thermogenic effect persisting 3+ hours).
- A moderate dose (6 mg/kg) significantly enhanced isometric leg extension strength and time to fatigue.

### Cognitive Performance Findings:
- McLellan et al. studies of special force military units (600-800 mg caffeine via chewing gum during sleep deprivation) showed maintained or enhanced vigilance and improved physical performance (run times, obstacle courses) versus placebo.
- Lieberman et al. (U.S. Navy SEALs) found 200 mg significantly improved performance versus 100 mg, but 300 mg offered no additional benefit over 200 mg; 100 mg was no better than placebo.
- Caffeine's performance-enhancing effects may extend beyond its 2.5-10 hour half-life; effects on motor learning and short-term memory may relate to increased concentration ability rather than working memory itself.

### Caffeine and Carbohydrate:
- Ivy et al. (1979): 500 mg caffeine produced 7.4% greater work over control and 5.3% greater than glucose polymer; plasma FFA levels 30% greater than placebo after 2-hour isokinetic cycling.
- Graham and Spriet found performance enhancement only at 3 and 6 mg/kg doses (not 9 mg/kg), despite the higher dose producing the greatest metabolic effects—a paradox suggesting CNS overstimulation at high doses.
- Yeo et al.: 5.8% glucose solution plus 5 mg/kg caffeine enhanced exogenous carbohydrate oxidation ~26% higher than glucose alone.
- Hulston et al.: 6.4% glucose solution + 5.3 mg/kg caffeine improved time trial performance by 9% vs. placebo and 4.6% vs. glucose alone, without affecting exogenous carbohydrate oxidation.
- Battram et al. (2004): Caffeine did not hinder proglycogen or macroglycogen resynthesis following exhaustive exercise with carbohydrate repletion.
- **Pedersen et al.: Glycogen resynthesis increased by 66% with carbohydrate + 8 mg/kg caffeine** versus carbohydrate-only during 4-hour post-exercise recovery.

### Caffeine Form, Dose, and Endurance Exercise:
- Graham et al.: Caffeine capsules (4.45 mg/kg) significantly increased work capacity (additional 2-3 km run) compared to regular coffee, decaffeinated coffee, or decaf + caffeine capsules. Roasting byproducts (chlorogenic acid derivatives) may reduce caffeine's adenosine antagonism in coffee.
- McLellan and Bell: Capsule-form caffeine (3-7 mg/kg) provided average 24% increase in performance over placebo; consuming coffee before anhydrous supplementation did not interfere with ergogenic effects.
- Wiles et al.: Caffeinated coffee (150-200 mg caffeine) produced 4.2-second faster 1500-m run time vs. decaf; all 10 subjects achieved faster "final burst" speeds.
- Pasman et al.: Doses of 5, 9, and 13 mg/kg all significantly improved endurance (~27% average increase) with no statistical difference between doses.
- Graham and Spriet (elite runners): 9 mg/kg caffeine increased running time from ~49 min (placebo) to 71 min, and cycling from ~39 to ~59 min at 85% VO2max.
- Spriet et al. (1992): 9 mg/kg caffeine increased cycling time to exhaustion from 75 to 96 min at ~80% VO2max.
- McNaughton et al.: 6 mg/kg caffeine improved 1-hour time trial performance by 4-5% including hill simulations.

### High-Intensity and Team Sport Exercise:
- **Caffeine is NOT effective for untrained individuals** in high-intensity exercise (Collomp, Greer, Crowe, Lorino studies all showing no benefit or performance decline in non-trained subjects).
- Caffeine IS effective for trained athletes: 
  - Trained swimmers improved 100m freestyle velocity (Collomp) and 1,500m swim times (MacIntosh & Wright, 6 mg/kg).
  - Woolf et al.: 5 mg/kg increased peak power in trained anaerobic athletes.
  - Wiles et al.: 5 mg/kg improved 1-km time trial by 3.1% (71.1s vs. 73.4s).
  - Glaister et al.: 5 mg/kg improved first three of 12 × 30m sprints.
  - Bruce et al.: 6 mg/kg improved 2000m rowing time by 1.3% in trained oarsmen; 9 mg/kg provided no additional benefit.
  - Anderson et al.: 9 mg/kg improved 2000m rowing time by 1.3% in trained oarswomen, most evident in first 500m.
- Team sports: Stuart et al. found 6 mg/kg improved rugby ball-passing accuracy by 10% (90% successful passes vs. 83% placebo)—the first study showing caffeine improvement in a team-sport skill-related task. Schneiker et al. found 6 mg/kg induced more total sprint work in intermittent-sprint testing in team sport athletes.

### Overall Conclusions:
Caffeine is an effective ergogenic aid for trained athletes at low-to-moderate doses (3-6 mg/kg), best consumed in anhydrous form, with significant benefits for endurance, high-intensity, and team sports, cognitive performance under sleep deprivation, and post-exercise glycogen synthesis when combined with carbohydrate. High doses (≥9 mg/kg) offer no additional benefit and may impair performance through CNS overstimulation. The training status of the athlete, exercise mode/intensity/duration, and dose are critical factors determining efficacy.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | Carbohydrate knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices, of endurance athletes who report exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2023.1133022/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Nutrition (12 April 2023) by Rachel Scrivin and colleagues from the University of the Sunshine Coast (Australia), Monash University, and UC Davis. The study explored the carbohydrate (CHO) knowledge, beliefs, and intended practices of endurance athletes who report exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS) compared to those without these symptoms.

METHODOLOGY: A validated online questionnaire was completed by 201 endurance athletes (≥18 years, participating in events ≥60 min), of whom 137 reported Ex-GIS and 64 did not. Participants included runners (57%), triathletes (21%), and non-running sports (21%). Athletes categorized 15 food/drink items as CHO or non-CHO sources, rated their beliefs about CHO consumption timing around exercise (1-2 days before, before, during, after) on a 5-point Likert scale, and rated their intentions to consume CHO (eat less/same/more) on a 3-point scale. Chi-square analysis with Bonferroni post-hoc adjustments and content analysis of open-ended responses were employed. The study achieved adequate power of 0.92.

KEY RESULTS:
- Athletes with Ex-GIS correctly categorized CHO foods (95%) and non-CHO foods (88%) at rates similar to athletes without Ex-GIS (92% and 90% respectively).
- No significant differences were found in CHO beliefs or intentions between athletes with and without Ex-GIS at any time point.
- The majority of athletes agreed or strongly agreed that consuming CHO around exercise enhances athletic performance (median = 4 on a 5-point scale), and intended to consume more CHO around exercise (median = 3).
- The most commonly self-reported dietary strategy was increasing CHO intake (58% of responses), reported by both groups, particularly before exercise.
- Other reported strategies included reducing dietary fiber and increasing protein, fluid, and electrolytes.
- No significant demographic differences (sex, age, sport, competition level) were found between groups.

CONCLUSIONS: Contrary to the study hypothesis, endurance athletes with Ex-GIS demonstrate adequate CHO knowledge, positive beliefs about CHO's performance-enhancing role, and intentions to increase CHO intake around exercise, similar to athletes without Ex-GIS. Findings broadly align with sports nutrition guidelines. The authors note that gut training protocols may help athletes improve gastrointestinal tolerance when consuming CHO during exercise, and that further research is needed to verify specific CHO ingestion amounts. The study was funded by the University of the Sunshine Coast and approved by its Human Research Ethics Committee (approval S201402).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in ... ---
URL: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/9QnW5DQA

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage describes a case series study titled "Case Series: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Athletes Using a High-Carbohydrate Low-FODMAP Therapeutic Intervention," published in 2025 in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (Vol. 34, No. 4, pp. 337-354), by Rachel Scrivin, Gary Slater, and Ricardo J.S. Costa, published by Human Kinetics. The study has been cited 3 times and is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science.

The study implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx) to develop therapeutic interventions for athletes with exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS). The case series involved 9 athletes who experienced recurrent severe Ex-GIS and 2 controls without symptoms.

The four phases were: (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx collecting physiological strain and GIS data, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention based on Phase 2 outcomes, specifically including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment of therapeutic interventions.

Key findings: The majority of athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2-4% body mass loss, and <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate (8/9) during the GastroAxEx. Severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) was reported by 4/9 athletes during exercise and 8/9 in the recovery period. All athletes reported low food and fluid intake tolerance during exercise and recovery. Orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet and improved intake tolerance during the targeted event, with reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS and improved perceived work output.

The study concludes that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms.

The webpage also lists 40 references and 4 citing publications, including a position statement response in Sports Medicine, a study on high-amylose maize starch and hydration, a practitioner's guide to managing gut issues in athletes, and a Current Opinion article on dietary FODMAP manipulation arguing that FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default based on symptom severity.
</summary>

BACKGROUND & KEY CONCEPTS:
- Exercise can disturb gastrointestinal integrity and function, leading to EIGS and Ex-GIS, which are common in active and athlete populations and comprise a substantial case load for practitioners (sports dietitians, sport and exercise nutritionists, sports medical practitioners).
- EIGS comprises two primary pathophysiological pathways: (1) the circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway (splanchnic hypoperfusion and gastrointestinal ischemia due to blood flow redistribution to skeletal muscle, leading to intestinal epithelial injury, hyperpermeability, and inflammatory responses from translocated pathogens/endotoxins), and (2) the neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway (stress responses, sympathetic activation, impaired motility, transit, digestion, and nutrient absorption via effects on the enteric nervous system and interstitial cells of Cajal).
- Two additional pathways warrant investigation: mechanical strain on the splanchnic area (jarring/jolting/vibrations) and exaggerated metabolic responses (metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia) linked to exercise-associated nausea.
- Ex-GIS symptom incidence varies widely by exercise type: negligible in recreational endurance running, 4% after marathon competition, and ≥93% in ultra-endurance events. Longer-duration exercise, especially in hot conditions, promotes higher Ex-GIS incidence.
- Symptoms are classified per ROME IV criteria into upper-GIS (belching, heartburn, upper-abdominal bloating/pain, regurgitation), lower-GIS (flatulence, lower-abdominal bloating/pain, urge to defecate, abnormal defecation, fecal blood loss), and other symptoms (nausea, stitch). Contrary to mainstream dogma, upper-GIS symptoms are more commonly reported during/immediately after exercise than lower-GIS; nausea is frequently reported in ultra-endurance activities.

EXACERBATION FACTORS (with assigned impact magnitudes: unknown = ?, minimal = +, modest = ++, extensive = +++):
Extrinsic factors:
- Exercise duration (+++): considerable perturbations occur with ≥2h exercise; plateaus thereafter.
- Exercise intensity (++): continuous ≥70% VO2max or HIIT/resistance exercise ≤2h produces modest increases.
- Exercise modality (+): field studies suggest running prompts greater disturbance than swimming/cycling (due to mechanical strain), but controlled lab studies show no clear modality differences.
- Environmental conditions (+++): hot ambient conditions (~35°C) increase EIGS biomarkers and Ex-GIS; core body temperature ≥39.5°C or Δ≥2.5°C is clinically significant; ≥39.0°C or Δ≥2.0°C exceeds minimal detectable change.
- Topographical elevation/altitude (+): altitude >2500m ASL may increase disturbances.
- Time of day (++): nocturnal exercise prompts greater GI function disturbance and Ex-GIS than diurnal exercise, but no effect on EIGS integrity/systemic biomarkers.
- External pharmaceutical administration (+++): NSAIDs are GI irritants; administration prior to exercise markedly increases GI perturbations and Ex-GIS.

Intrinsic factors:
- Biological sex (+): low-to-modest differences observed; female athletes proposed to present greater EIGS/Ex-GIS due to menstrual cycle, but evidence is inconsistent.
- Age (+): modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults.
- Fitness status (+): higher-trained individuals at lower absolute risk but exposed to greater relative loads.
- GI/circulating microbial and SCFA composition (+): may impact magnitude of perturbations.
- Individual characteristics (+++): feeding tolerance (volume, concentration, type, texture), pre-existing GI diseases/disorders, and history of recurrent Ex-GIS increase risk.
- Psychological state (?): pre-exercise anxiety linked to Ex-GIS in field observations but lacks rigorous controlled evidence.

METHODOLOGY: A scoping review approach (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Ovid Medline) was used to screen relevant research studies. Evidence was graded (Grade I = Good, Grade II = Fair, Grade III = Limited, Grade IV = Not fully supported) based on adherence to best-practice recommendations in exercise gastroenterology research, including the Costa et al. (2022) experimental design checklist. Methodological concerns in existing research include participant selection/screening, exercise protocol justification, ambient temperature control, dietary control, hydration monitoring, biomarker selection, Ex-GIS assessment tool choice, power calculations, and population heterogeneity.

The paper covers disturbances categorized into: gastrointestinal epithelial integrity (tissue injury, tight-junction injury, permeability, endotoxemia/bacteremia), gastrointestinal function (gastric emptying, transit, absorption, myoelectrical activity, malabsorption), systemic responses (leukocyte trafficking, inflammatory cytokines, immune responses), GI signs/symptoms (gut comfort, total/upper/lower GIS, nausea, regurgitation/vomiting, abnormal defecation with/without blood loss), and feeding tolerance.

Key Points: Macronutrient intake during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulations (e.g., FODMAP), and gut training show beneficial outcomes in EIGS/Ex-GIS management. Heat-mitigating strategies and certain nutritional supplements (prebiotics, phenols) show promising outcomes, while other dietary manipulations and supplements appear less favorable. Individual athlete assessment to establish main causal factors aids tailored prevention/management strategies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the official Position Stand of the Working Group Sports Nutrition of the German Nutrition Society (DGE) on carbohydrates in sports nutrition, published in the German Journal of Sports Medicine (Deutsche Zeitschrift für Sportmedizin), Volume 71, No. 7-8-9 (2020), DOI: 10.5960/dzsm.2020.456. The paper was accepted August 2020 and published online September 2020. Authors include König D, Braun H, Carlsohn A, Großhauser M, Lampen A, Mosler S, Nieß A, Oberritter H, Schäbethal K, Schek A, Stehle P, Virmani K, Ziegenhagen R, and Heseker H, representing multiple German universities and institutions including Freiburg, Cologne, Hamburg, Tübingen, Bonn, Paderborn, the DGE, the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR), and German Olympic training centers.

KEY RECOMMENDATIONS AND FINDINGS:

1. **Energy metabolism**: Carbohydrates yield higher ATP per liter of oxygen than fatty acids and provide a higher energy flux rate (ATP resynthesis per unit of time is twice as high for aerobic glucose metabolism and four times higher for anaerobic glucose metabolism compared to fatty acids). Glycogen stores are limited: muscles (approx. 1,230-2,050 kcal), liver (approx. 410 kcal), compared to fat stores of 80,000-100,000 kcal. Full glycogen stores support approx. 75-90 minutes of intense endurance exercise at the anaerobic threshold.

2. **Daily carbohydrate intake**: 6-12 g carbohydrate/kg body weight per day (kg BW/d) is recommended for athletes performing prolonged endurance or intermittent high-intensity exercise, depending on training duration and intensity (per ACSM guidelines).

3. **Carbohydrate loading**: Recommended for competition lasting more than 90 minutes. Most common method: 10-12 g carbohydrate/kg BW/d for 36-48 hours prior to competition, increasing muscle glycogen by approx. 10-15%. Alternative methods include 9-10 g/kg BW/d in the week before competition with reduced training, or glycogen-depleting exercise 72 hours prior followed by a carbohydrate-rich diet. Athletes should not experiment with new loading methods before important competitions due to gastrointestinal intolerance risks.

4. **Pre-competition meal**: For exercise >60 minutes, consume 1-4 g carbohydrate/kg BW 2-3 hours before competition. A low glycemic index pre-exercise meal may increase fat oxidation during exercise; however, meta-analyses are contradictory (Heung-Sang et al. found a performance advantage, Burdon et al. found no significant difference).

5. **Carbohydrates during exercise**: For exercise >60 minutes, consume 150-350 ml of a ~6% carbohydrate drink every 15 minutes. Exogenous glucose oxidation rate is approx. 1-1.2 g/min (limited by small intestine absorption, not gastric emptying). Combining glucose, fructose, and sucrose (different carrier systems) increases oxidation to 1.5-1.7 g/min, useful for extremely intense endurance exercise over 2.5 hours. Fructose intolerance must be excluded in advance. Adding protein to carbohydrate during exercise provides no performance benefit when carbohydrate intake is adequate. Carbohydrate mouth rinsing (without swallowing) can positively affect performance in short exercise bouts of 30-60 minutes via CNS stimulation of oral receptors.

6. **Post-exercise**: Consume 1-1.2 g carbohydrate/kg BW/h (ideally high glycemic index) in the first 2-4 hours after exercise for rapid glycogen resynthesis. Higher amounts provide no additional benefit. This timing matters only if less than 8-10 hours until next exercise session; with longer intervals, 6-10 g carbohydrate/kg BW/d suffices. Adding protein is only useful if carbohydrate intake falls below 1.2 g/kg BW/h. Glucose-fructose combinations do not enhance glycogen resynthesis post-exercise due to fructose's low glycemic index.

7. **Training low (low glycogen availability)**: Training with low glycogen stores may improve oxidative capacity via AMPK and p38 MAPK signaling pathways affecting mitochondrial biogenesis, but medium-term or long-term effects on competition performance are not conclusively established, and it may negatively affect performance by downregulating GLUT-4 transporters.

The paper includes detailed tables of carbohydrate intake recommendations (Tables 1-3) and a comprehensive reference list of 43 sources from the sports nutrition literature. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog article from Neversecond (a sports nutrition brand) titled "Masters Athletes and Gut Issues," written by Marni Sumbal, MS, RD, CSSD, LD/N. The article addresses gastrointestinal (GI) distress in masters athletes (40+), a common performance limiter in endurance sport.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Carb Absorption and Age**: The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. Masters athletes can target 60-90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor—gut training is.

2. **Three Causes of GI Distress**:
   - Physiological: Exercise diverts blood away from the gut (at 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop nearly 80%), causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea.
   - Mechanical: Running jolts the GI tract, making runners more prone to lower GI issues than cyclists.
   - Nutritional: High-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods eaten too close to training, plus concentrated drinks, slow stomach emptying.

3. **Gut Training for Masters Athletes**: Gut training involves progressively practicing carbohydrate and fluid intake during workouts. Elite athletes now consume 120-150g of carbs/hour, but this takes time to build. Recommended protocol: Start at 30-40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10-15g every 1-2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt.

4. **Exercising in Heat**: Heat compounds gut issues—blood shifts to skin for cooling and gastric emptying slows. Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. Recommendations: drop carb intake by 10-20g/hour until heat-acclimated, choose liquid calories, eat small amounts every 10-15 minutes, start hydrated and cool, don't rely on thirst, include sodium in everything you drink, monitor urine color, and watch for hyponatremia.

5. **Bottom Line**: The gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly. "Age is context, not a ceiling."

**Who are Masters Athletes?** Defined as age 35 for both men and women per World Masters Athletics; age 18 for swimming, and 50 for golf.

**Age-Related Physiological Changes (after age 30):**
- Maximum oxygen consumption decreases ~10% per decade (slower at 5% for older endurance athletes)
- Type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers decrease in size and number; shift toward slow fiber types
- Mitochondria decrease in number
- Satellite cells reduced; fat infiltrates muscle
- Myosin reduced; muscle elasticity reduced
- Muscle strength declines; low muscle strength linked to 4.3-fold greater risk of slow gait speed and 2.6-fold greater risk of severe mobility problems
- Sarcopenia (loss of muscle mass) occurs with aging
- Creatine and phosphocreatine levels reduced; creatine regeneration falls ~8% per decade after age 30
- Reduced B12 and Vitamin D absorption
- Body weight increases up to age 70, with increased belly/visceral fat
- Chronic low-level inflammation, dehydration, and reduced sweating

**Solutions:** Active lifestyle, weight-bearing exercise, and strength training (6-month program can reverse muscle weakness in older adults). Both nutrition and resistance exercise are needed for muscle protein synthesis.

**Nutrition Recommendations:**
- **Protein:** 1.2g/kg body weight/day; 35-45g per meal (vs. 15-30g for younger athletes); pre-workout meal should include 25-30g protein with high leucine foods; 3g leucine per meal recommended. Rich sources include meat, eggs, dairy (parmesan, Greek yogurt), fish, and nuts/seeds.
- **Creatine:** 5g/day creatine monohydrate for those who strength train
- **Fat:** 1 g/kg body weight/day or 20-35% of total caloric intake; omega-3 fatty acids recommended for anti-inflammatory effects
- **Carbohydrates:** 3-5 g/kg/day minimum; up to 10-12g/kg for athletes training 1-3 hours/day or endurance events over 90 minutes
- **Fluids:** Personalized hydration schedule is critical due to age-related dehydration challenges

**Nutrients of Concern:**
- **Vitamin D:** 1,500-2,000 IUs/day to raise levels above 30 ng/mL; minimum 800 IUs/day
- **Vitamin E:** Antioxidant; sources include plant oils, seeds, nuts
- **Vitamin B12:** Supplementation may be needed (methylcobalamin lozenge form); food sources only in animal products
- **Riboflavin (B2):** Key in energy production; sources include eggs, organ meats, lean meats, milk
- **Vitamin B6:** Needs increase after age 50 to 1.7 mg (men) and 1.5 mg (women) from 1.3 mg
- **Folate (B9):** Involved in DNA/RNA/protein metabolism; sources include leafy greens, fruits, legumes
- **Calcium:** 1200 mg/day for women over 51 and men over 71 (vs. 1000 mg for ages 19-50)
- **Magnesium:** 320 mg/day women and 420 mg/day men (31+ years); magnesium glycinate 200-300 mg at bedtime recommended for supplementation
- **Zinc:** 11 mg males and 8 mg females (19+); richest sources are meat, fish, seafood

**Key Warning:** Older adults, especially women frustrated with body changes, should NOT undereat and overexercise—this causes the body to hold onto fat (starvation mode) and negatively affects hormones including cortisol. - **Fat**: 20-35% of total caloric intake recommended, with saturated fat below 10%. High-fat diets (>46% of calories from fat) are not recommended as they fail to consistently improve performance. Omega-3 recommended at 450-900 mg/day (max 3g/day), taken with high-fat meals for absorption.
- **Micronutrients**: Most athletes can meet needs through a balanced diet, though nearly half use supplements. Iron supplementation may be needed at altitude; vitamin D may be low in winter/indoor sports athletes. Micronutrients do not exert ergogenic effects.
- **Hydration**: Losing 2% of body fluids affects performance. Athletes lose 0.3-2.4 L/hour of sweat. Recommended: 500-600 mL fluid 2-3 hours pre-exercise, 200-300 mL 10-20 min before, 200-300 mL every 10-20 min during training. Hyponatremia risk from overconsumption of sodium-poor fluids. Beverage hydration index evaluates drink hydrating potential; higher sodium beverages (like Pedialyte ~45 mmol) generally outperform water.
- **Supplements**: Only creatine, sodium bicarbonate, and caffeine have proven performance-enhancing effects. Canadian studies show 87% of elite athletes and 98% of young athletes (11-25 years) use supplements regularly. Creatine (0.3 g/kg/day for 3-5 days or 20 g/day for 5-7 days) increases power, muscular strength, and fat-free mass, and accelerates recovery from injury.

The review was conducted over 6 months (November 2022-April 2023) using PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science, including experimental studies (RCTs, observational studies, case studies) with elite or semi-elite athletes. The review also aims to prevent disordered eating and eating disorders among active populations.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a narrative review published in Frontiers in Nutrition (Front Nutr, 2024 Jan 18;10:1331854, doi: 10.3389/fnut.2023.1331854) titled "Athletes' nutritional demands: a narrative review of nutritional requirements." The review was conducted over 6 months (November 2022 to April 2023) across PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science databases, examining experimental studies (RCTs, observational studies, case studies) in elite and semi-elite athletes.

The paper comprehensively reviews athletes' nutritional requirements, covering:

**Energy and Energy Availability (EA):** EA represents dietary energy available for physiological functions after subtracting exercise energy expenditure. Low Energy Availability (LEA) causes negative effects across endocrine, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, reproductive, and gastrointestinal systems, including menstrual dysfunction, increased illness susceptibility, diminished mood, hormonal imbalances, and decreased performance.

**Carbohydrates:** Recommended daily intake is 3-12 g/kg body weight depending on exercise intensity and duration (Table 1): Low intensity (<60 min/day): 3-5 g/kg; Moderate (60 min): 5-7 g/kg; High (60-180 min): 6-10 g/kg; Very high (>180 min): 8-12 g/kg. --- SOURCE 1: Multiple Transportable Carbohydrates And Their Benefits - Gatorade Sports Science Institute ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/sse-108-multiple-transportable-carbohydrates-and-their-benefits

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #108 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), authored by Asker E. Jeukendrup, PhD, and published in January 2013. The article examines the benefits of ingesting multiple transportable carbohydrates during prolonged exercise.

KEY FINDINGS:
- During prolonged exercise, performance benefits from carbohydrate ingestion are achieved by maintaining plasma glucose concentration and high rates of carbohydrate oxidation.
- The limitation to exogenous carbohydrate oxidation was identified as saturation of intestinal carbohydrate transporters (specifically SGLT1 for glucose), not gastric emptying, liver glycogen synthesis, or muscle glucose uptake.
- Glucose is absorbed via SGLT1 transporter (which saturates at ~60 g/h intake), while fructose uses a separate transporter (GLUT5), allowing combined ingestion to increase total carbohydrate delivery and oxidation.
- Studies demonstrated up to 65% higher exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates with multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose:fructose) compared with a single carbohydrate, reaching peak rates of 1.75 g/min — previously thought that 1 g/min was the absolute maximum.
- The Jentjens et al. (2004) groundbreaking study showed glucose:fructose oxidation peaked at ~1.26 g/min versus ~0.8 g/min for glucose alone.
- Maltodextrin:fructose mixes are more palatable (less sweet) and reached oxidation rates of 1.5 g/min at 1.8 g/min ingestion.
- Performance benefits include reduced ratings of perceived exertion, better cadence maintenance, and an 8% additional improvement in power output over glucose alone in time trials (Currell & Jeukendrup, 2008).
- Multiple transportable carbohydrates also improve gastric emptying and fluid delivery and reduce gastrointestinal distress.
- Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation is independent of body mass, so recommendations should be given in absolute amounts, not per kg body weight.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS:
- For prolonged endurance events (2.5 h or longer), well-trained competitive athletes should consume 90 g of multiple transportable carbohydrates per hour.
- Use a mix of glucose and fructose, or maltodextrin and fructose, in roughly a 2:1 ratio (60 g/h glucose/maltodextrin to saturate SGLT1 transporters + 30 g/h fructose).
- These benefits require sufficient carbohydrate intake (at least 1 g/min of glucose) to saturate intestinal transporters, and exercise duration of 2.5 h or more. Results are specific to well-trained athletes at high power outputs and may not apply to lower-intensity exercisers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates reach values of 1.75 g/min with multiple transportable carbohydrates whereas previously it was thought that 1 g/min was the absolute maximum."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] High rates of exogenous carbohydrate oxidation from a mixture of glucose ... ---
URL: https://www.trainerroad.com/forum/uploads/short-url/8rbhMHF4viNqg8oxwjvW37IViem.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific study published in the British Journal of Nutrition (2005, Vol. 93, pp. 485–492) by Roy L.P.G. Jentjens and Asker E. Jeukendrup from the Human Performance Laboratory, School of Sport and Exercise Sciences, University of Birmingham, UK. The study investigated whether a mixture of glucose and fructose ingested at a high rate (2.4 g/min) would lead to even higher exogenous carbohydrate (CHO) oxidation rates (>1.3 g/min) during prolonged cycling exercise.

**Study Design and Methods:**
- Eight trained male cyclists (mean VO2max: 68.1 ± 0.6 ml/kg/min; age 26.3 years; Wmax 376 W) participated in a crossover study
- Each subject completed three 150-minute cycling trials at 50% Wmax (~60% VO2max) consuming either: water (WAT), 1.2 g/min glucose (GLU), or 1.2 g/min glucose + 1.2 g/min fructose (GLU+FRUC)
- Corn-derived glucose and crystalline fructose with high natural 13C abundance were used to trace exogenous CHO oxidation via stable isotope (13CO2) measurements
- Total fluid provided was 1.95 liters (600 ml initial bolus + 150 ml every 15 min)
- Substrate oxidation calculated using indirect calorimetry and stable isotope methodology; calculations performed over last 90 min of exercise

**Key Results:**
- Peak exogenous CHO oxidation rates were significantly higher (P<0.01) in GLU+FRUC (1.75 ± 0.11 g/min) vs. GLU (1.06 ± 0.05 g/min)
- Exogenous CHO oxidation rates during last 90 min were ~50% higher (P<0.05) in GLU+FRUC (1.49 g/min) vs. GLU (0.99 g/min)
- In GLU, exogenous CHO oxidation leveled off after 105–120 min, whereas GLU+FRUC increased until end of exercise (no leveling off)
- Total CHO oxidation rates (60–150 min): 1.56 (WAT), 2.26 (GLU), 2.57 (GLU+FRUC) g/min
- Fat oxidation rates: 0.97 (WAT), 0.68 (GLU), 0.51 (GLU+FRUC) g/min
- Endogenous CHO oxidation: 1.56 (WAT), 1.26 (GLU), 1.07 (GLU+FRUC) g/min
- Plasma lactate was significantly higher (P<0.01) in GLU+FRUC vs. WAT and GLU at all time points
- No significant differences in GI discomfort or RPE between trials (one subject reported severe stomach problems in GLU+FRUC)

**Mechanistic Interpretation:**
- Glucose and fructose use different intestinal transporters (SGLT1 for glucose, GLUT-5 for fructose), allowing for increased total intestinal CHO absorption
- Glucose may enhance fructose absorption via solvent drag (glucose-induced water streaming through paracellular pathway)
- Higher plasma lactate after GLU+FRUC may indicate faster intestinal CHO absorption (fructose is rapidly phosphorylated, bypassing phosphofructokinase, and converted to lactate)
- The study suggests intestinal CHO absorption is a rate-limiting factor for exogenous CHO oxidation
- Combined ingestion of glucose (1.2 g/min) + fructose (1.2 g/min) may achieve the highest physiologically possible exogenous CHO oxidation rate (~1.75 g/min)

**Funding:** Supported by a grant from GlaxoSmithKline Consumer Healthcare, Brentford, UK. Glucose donated by Cerestar (Manchester, UK) and fructose by A.E. Staley Manufacturing Company (USA).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: What is known about the health effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use in marathon and ultraendurance running: a scoping review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10840051

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a systematic scoping review published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine (2024 Feb 2;10(1):e001846, PMID 38318269) by Eve Pannone and Rebecca Abbott of the University of Exeter, examining the health risks of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use in marathon and ultraendurance running.

**Methodology:**
- Four databases were searched (Cochrane Library, PubMed, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus) in February 2023
- Studies had to focus on running events of 26.2 miles or further and report health risks of NSAID use
- No restriction on study design or publication date
- Initial search identified 194 articles; after screening, 30 studies were included: 4 randomised controlled trials, 1 cross-sectional study, 11 retrospective reviews, 4 case reports, 1 non-randomised control trial, and 9 prospective observational studies
- Studies predominantly from the USA (N=15) and England (N=7); more men than women included
- Most common distances studied: marathon and 160 km; most common NSAID reported was ibuprofen

**Key Findings by Health Concern Category:**
1. **Electrolyte balance and hyponatraemia** (14 studies): Mixed results; 6 studies showed no significant correlation, 6 showed correlation, 2 had insufficient data. One UK study found marathon runners taking ibuprofen had serum Na decrease of 2.1 mmol/L vs increase of 2.3 mmol/L in controls (p=0.0039). A New Zealand study found 8.3% increase in mean potassium levels in NSAID users (p=0.0007).

2. **Acute kidney injury (AKI)** (6 studies): All reported potential links but insufficient evidence for statistical significance. One double-blind RCT found 22 of 42 participants taking ibuprofen developed AKI vs 16 of 47 on placebo (18% difference, p=0.14).

3. **GI disturbances** (4 studies): None found clear correlation between NSAID use and GI issues.

4. **Oxidative stress and muscle damage** (3 studies): All three found statistically significant results, but results were conflicting—two found increased oxidative stress, one found decreased.

5. **Other medical concerns**: One RCT found NSAIDs blunted exercise-induced collagen synthesis in patellar tendon; one case report suggested NSAIDs may have masked pericarditis symptoms in an ironman athlete.

**Key Conclusions:**
- This is the first review bringing together evidence on NSAID health risks in ultraendurance running
- There is very limited evidence to show NSAIDs have a negative impact on ultrarunning athletes' health
- Indications from a few non-randomised studies of a possible effect on kidney function need exploring with higher-quality research
- The Ultra Tour de Mont Blanc banned ibuprofen due to 'negative health risks' despite limited research
- Authors recommend caution when taking NSAIDs prophylactically for endurance sports, especially since NSAIDs may not enhance performance
- Future research needs larger randomised controlled trials, examination of different NSAID types/dosages, and consideration of confounding factors like heat, hydration, and body weight
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This review suggests there is very limited evidence to show that NSAIDs have a negative impact on the health of ultrarunning athletes. Indications from a few non-randomised studies of a possible effect on kidney function need exploring with more high-quality research."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Running: ibuprofen use is common – but many athletes are unaware of the risks ---
URL: https://theconversation.com/running-ibuprofen-use-is-common-but-many-athletes-are-unaware-of-the-risks-141634

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from The Conversation examines the widespread but risky use of ibuprofen and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) among runners, based on recent research conducted by the authors. The study surveyed 806 participants in Parkrun UK, representing a broad cross-section of the running community. Key findings include: nearly 90% of surveyed runners used NSAIDs (usually over-the-counter ibuprofen); about one in eight had a pre-existing reason to avoid NSAIDs (such as asthma); over half took NSAIDs before a run, one in ten during a run, and two-thirds afterwards; 33% of ultra-runners took NSAIDs during runs (compared to 17.5% of marathon runners); a third experienced suspected side effects (mainly heartburn, and in some cases gastrointestinal bleeding); and over 40% were unaware of cardiovascular, kidney, or gastrointestinal side effects. Nearly half used NSAIDs without healthcare professional advice.

The article highlights significant health risks associated with NSAID use, including gastrointestinal ulcers, acute kidney injury, cardiovascular events, and hyponatraemia (a potentially fatal sodium reduction from water overload affecting one in ten marathon runners). Under the extreme physiological strain of endurance events, these risks are heightened. NSAID-related adverse reactions are responsible for 30% of all adverse drug reaction hospital admissions. One study found 46% of London Marathon runners planned to take an NSAID during the race.

The authors note that while occasional use (e.g., one tablet before or after a weekly run) carries lower risk, chronic NSAID use to run through injury and pain is counterproductive to long-term health benefits. They emphasize the need for better messaging about NSAID safety and note that the London Marathon now advises runners to avoid NSAIDs within 48 hours of the race due to potential dangers. The article concludes that using NSAIDs to run through injury and pain to achieve training targets is counterproductive, and high usage among endurance runners during demanding training and sustained physiological stress should be avoided.
</summary>

About one in eight runners had a pre-existing reason to avoid NSAIDs, such as asthma., A third of the runners in our study had experienced suspected side effects from NSAIDs, mainly heartburn and, in a few cases, gastrointestinal bleeding. --- SOURCE 8: Nutritional Recommendations To Avoid Gastrointestinal Distress ... ---
URL: https://www.gssiweb.org/sports-science-exchange/article/sse-114-nutritional-recommendations-to-avoid-gastrointestinal-distress-during-exercise

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is SSE #114 from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI), published in May 2013 and authored by Erick Prado de Oliveira. The article provides nutritional recommendations to avoid gastrointestinal (GI) distress during exercise, particularly for endurance athletes.

**Key Statistics on GI Problems in Athletes:**
- 30% to 90% of distance runners experience exercise-related intestinal problems, depending on methodology and events studied
- In exhausting endurance events, 30-50% of participants suffer from one or more GI symptoms (Brouns & Beckers, 1993)
- Up to 93% of long-distance triathletes in extreme conditions reported any GI symptom; 43% reported serious GI problems and 7% abandoned the race due to GI issues (Jeukendrup et al., 2000)
- 70% of elite endurance athletes reported exercise-induced GI symptoms (Peters et al., 1999)
- In an internet-based study of 1,281 athletes, 45% reported at least one GI symptom (Ter Steege et al., 2008)
- Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon running/cycling up to 32% in Ironman races (Pfeiffer et al., 2011)
- Athletes not accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise had a two-fold risk of GI symptoms compared to accustomed athletes

**Causes of GI Problems:**
1. **Splanchnic hypoperfusion** - During maximal exercise, splanchnic blood flow may be reduced by up to 80% to supply working muscle and skin. Norepinephrine release induces splanchnic vasoconstriction, which can lead to gut mucosal ischemia and increased mucosal permeability.
2. **Changes in motility** - Decreased esophageal peristalsis and lower esophageal sphincter tone, increased transient sphincter relaxation, and altered gastric emptying (mainly at high exercise intensities).
3. **Absorption and gut permeability** - Studies show increased intestinal permeability after marathons, though effects are inconclusive at moderate intensities. Symptomatic runners showed greater permeability than asymptomatic runners.
4. **Mechanical causes** - Repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut; symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists. Posture (e.g., "aero" position on bicycles) and swallowing air can contribute.
5. **Nutritional causes** - Fiber, fat, protein, fructose, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>500 mOsm/L osmolality) are associated with increased GI symptoms. Dairy products and mild lactose intolerance can cause problems.

**Prevention Guidelines:**
- **Avoid milk products** containing lactose (use lactose-free, soy, rice, or almond milk alternatives)
- **Avoid high-fiber foods** in the day(s) before competition; choose processed white foods (regular pasta, white rice, plain bagels) instead of whole grains
- **Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** (e.g., ibuprofen) as they increase intestinal permeability; NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI complications
- **Avoid high-fructose foods** and exclusively-fructose drinks (though fructose with glucose may be better tolerated)
- **Avoid dehydration**; start races well hydrated
- **Practice new nutrition strategies** by experimenting with pre-race and race-day plans many times before race day
- **"Train the gut"** - A study by Cox et al. (2010) showed that 28 days of high-carbohydrate training improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates, attributed to improved intestinal absorption

**Serious Symptoms:** Mucosal erosions, ischemic colitis, blood loss in feces, hemorrhagic gastritis, and small bowel infarction have been reported in endurance athletes, occasionally requiring surgery.

The article concludes that GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and that nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"More marathons are won or lost in the portable toilets than at the dinner table." - Bill Rodgers, marathon legend with four victories in both the Boston and New York City Marathons in the late 1970s.

--- SOURCE 9: Over the counter anti-inflammatory drugs could be ... ---
URL: https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/news-archive/2020/over-the-counter-anti-inflammatory-drugs-could-be-damaging-the-health-of-runners-new-study-finds

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study led by Queen Mary's University London and the University of Birmingham investigated the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) among recreational runners in the UK, finding that over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen are widely used but carry significant health risks.

The study surveyed 806 Parkrun UK participants (mean age 48, 48% women, 52% men) using self-completed questionnaires. Key findings include:
- 88% of participants had used NSAIDs in the past 12 months, with just under 80% using ibuprofen
- 70% reported a sporting injury within the last 12 months
- NSAID use before, during, and after running: 57% before a run/race, 11% during, and 67.7% afterwards
- Women were more likely to use NSAIDs after running (73%) than men (62%)
- One-third of respondents experienced a suspected adverse reaction, including gastrointestinal discomfort, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal bleeding
- Over 40% of runners were unaware of the gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and renal side effects
- The most common weekly running distance was between 11km and 20km

NSAIDs block prostaglandin production, reducing pain and inflammation, but also block protective prostaglandins in the stomach and kidneys. Risks include acute renal impairment, gastrointestinal problems, hyponatraemia (potentially fatal sodium reduction from water overload), impaired healing, and reduced training adaptation. These risks are heightened during endurance events like marathons, which put additional stress on renal and gastrointestinal systems.

Co-author Dr Anthony Cox from the University of Birmingham's School of Pharmacy highlighted that runners use NSAIDs to facilitate event participation, push through injuries by increasing pain tolerance, and deal with post-event soreness. He expressed particular concern about routine NSAID use in marathon and ultra-marathon runners and recommended that organizers of longer endurance events provide evidence-based advice on NSAID use.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"While our research has shown that injury is, as expected, associated with NSAID use, runners also reported using NSAIDs to facilitate participation in events, to push through injuries by increasing pain tolerance and to deal with post‐event soreness. Particularly concerning is the routine use of NSAIDs in marathon and ultra-marathon runners during race events, and high mileage training schedules." - Dr Anthony Cox
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: NSAIDs and Stomach Risk: Ibuprofen & Naproxen Dangers ---
URL: https://corycalendinemd.com/blog/the-hidden-dangers-of-ibuprofen-and-naproxen-protecting-your-digestive-system-from-nsaids

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a blog article from Dr. Cory Calendine, MD, a board-certified, fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon at the Bone and Joint Institute of Tennessee in Franklin, TN, specializing in hip and knee replacement. The article educates patients about the hidden digestive dangers of NSAIDs like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve).

KEY POINTS:
- NSAIDs are the second leading cause of stomach ulcers (after bacterial infection). They work by blocking COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes; blocking COX-1 strips the protective mucus barrier from the stomach lining, exposing it to stomach acid.
- Key statistics: ~1/3 of NSAID users develop digestive symptoms; 2-4% of chronic users develop serious complications like bleeding ulcers each year; up to 70% of long-term users show stomach damage on imaging even when they feel fine; only ~10% of people with that damage notice warning symptoms.
- Risk varies by NSAID: Naproxen carries ~5.6x baseline bleeding risk; Diclofenac ~4.0x; Ibuprofen ~2.7x; COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) ~1.9x. Switching from naproxen to ibuprofen may cut stomach-bleeding risk by more than half.
- Higher-risk groups include: age 65+, prior stomach ulcers, taking blood thinners/aspirin, corticosteroids/SSRIs, H. pylori infection, high doses or long-term use. Patients on blood thinners plus NSAIDs face more than double the bleeding risk.
- Warning signs: black/tarry stools, blood in stool, vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, severe stomach pain, unexplained fatigue, dizziness/lightheadedness.
- Protection strategies: lowest effective dose for shortest time, alternating with acetaminophen (Tylenol), proton pump inhibitors (PPIs like omeprazole), COX-2 inhibitors, topical NSAIDs, physical therapy, and testing/treating H. pylori before long-term use.
- Small intestine damage is harder to detect and treat; combining NSAIDs with a PPI may worsen small-intestine problems while protecting the stomach. Some clinicians prefer a COX-2 inhibitor alone.
- Drug interactions: ibuprofen can blunt aspirin's heart-protective effect, so aspirin should be taken at least 2 hours before ibuprofen.
- The article is by Dr. Cory Calendine (performs 700+ hip and knee replacements annually, Stryker consultant for Mako robotic platform), who sees patients at 3000 Edward Curd Lane, Franklin, TN (Williamson Medical Center campus, I-65 Exit 65), phone (615) 791-2630, no referral required. Includes a medical disclaimer that the article is educational only and not a substitute for professional medical advice.
</summary>

Medications like Advil, Motrin, and Aleve work by blocking pain-causing enzymes, but they also strip away the stomach's protective mucus barrier. That leaves the digestive tract exposed to its own acid and raises the risk of internal bleeding."

--- SOURCE 11: PRE-RUN NUTRITION: TIMING, MACROS, AND MISTAKES THAT CAN RUIN YOUR RACE ---
URL: https://www.infisport.com/en/blog/pre-run-nutrition-timing-macros-and-mistakes-that-can-ruin-your-race

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a scientific blog article from Infisport (a sports nutrition supplier) titled "Pre-Run Nutrition: Timing, Macros, and Mistakes That Can Ruin Your Race," authored by Miguel Ángel Cervera (Bachelor of Pharmacy, Graduate in Human Nutrition and Dietetics, Technical Director of Infisport). Posted on 2026-07-07 in the Endurance or Long-Duration Sports category.

KEY POINTS:

1. **Why pre-exercise nutrition matters**: Muscles run primarily on glycogen stored in muscle (300-500 g) and liver (80-100 g). Depletion leads to "the wall" and central fatigue. Arriving at the starting line with full glycogen stores is a performance condition.

2. **Timing recommendations**: A main meal should be eaten 3-4 hours before exercise (endorsed by Jeukendrup 2017 and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics/Dietitians of Canada/ACSM positioning, Thomas et al. 2016). If less time is available, the meal should be lighter with less fat and fiber to facilitate gastric emptying.

3. **Glycogen loading protocol** (for events lasting >90 minutes, e.g., half marathon or marathon):
   - Days -6 to -4: Normal training with regular carbohydrate intake
   - Days -3 to -1: Tapering training + increase carbs to 8-12 g/kg body weight/day
   - Race day: Breakfast rich in slow-absorbing carbs, 3-4 hours before
   - Per Burke et al. (2011), this can increase glycogen reserves 20-40% above baseline.
   - Carbohydrate guidelines: 10K = 5-7 g/kg/day; Half marathon = 7-10 g/kg/day; Marathon = 10-12 g/kg/day. For a 70 kg runner facing a marathon, that's 700-840 g of carbs per day for 2-3 days prior.
   - Glycogen loading is NOT justified for a 10K or races shorter than 90 minutes (per Burke et al. 2019); 7-10 g/kg in the 24 hours prior is sufficient.

4. **Pre-race breakfast**: 3 hours before — 80-100 g oats or cooked white rice, 1-2 ripe bananas, 1 cup of coffee, little or no added fat/fiber. If only 60-90 minutes available, a piece of toast with jam is enough.

5. **Glycemic index timing**: 3-4 hours before = low-moderate GI (oats, brown rice, al dente pasta); 60-90 minutes = moderate-high GI (ripe plantain, white rice, sliced bread); 15-30 minutes = gels/readily available foods, avoid fructose alone (can cause GI issues and reactive hypoglycemia from insulin spike).

These errors are especially critical in trail running.

   - Ready-to-use carbs (gels, drinks): 15-30 minutes before only if breakfast was meager or very early
   - Sodium/electrolyte capsules (carb-free): 1 capsule with 250 ml water or 2 capsules with 500 ml, 60-90 minutes before.

9. **FAQ highlights**: Eat 3-4 hours before for a full meal; glycogen loading only for distances >90 minutes; fasted long runs not recommended for efforts >60-75 minutes ("train low" per Impey et al. 2018 has a place in periodization but fasting increases perceived effort and reduces training quality); best marathon breakfast = white rice/oats, ripe banana, coffee, low fat/fiber, tested in training; no need for a pre-race gel if breakfast was good 3-4 hours before — first in-race carb intake in a marathon should be around km 10-12.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from RunnersConnect, written by Jeff Gaudette (MS, co-founder of RunnersConnect and former Olympic Trials qualifier), provides a comprehensive, science-backed guide to "gut training" for runners to prevent mid-race gastrointestinal (GI) distress. 

**Key Statistics:**
- 30-90% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise, depending on intensity and duration
- 43% of Ironman triathletes report serious GI problems; 7% abandon their race entirely due to GI issues
- During high-intensity exercise at 70% VO2max, blood flow to the gut drops by nearly 80%
- Gut training protocols reduce GI symptoms by 60-63% in just two weeks
- Performance improved by 4.3-5.2% after gut training
- Ibuprofen use increases GI complication risk by 3-5 times

**Why GI Distress Occurs:** During running, blood flow is diverted away from the gut (splanchnic hypo-perfusion), creating an ischemic environment. This leads to increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"), allowing bacterial endotoxins (LPS) to enter the bloodstream. Mechanical jostling from running, sympathetic nervous system activation, and pre-race anxiety compound the problem. Runners experience GI issues at double the rate of cyclists or swimmers.

**Identifying Personal Triggers:** The author advises against expensive IgG food sensitivity tests, which lack scientific validation (number needed to treat of 9 vs. 1.5-2.2 for proper elimination diets). Instead, the gold standard is a systematic elimination diet combined with food journaling for 2-3 weeks. Common culprits include dairy, wheat, eggs, soy, nuts, high-FODMAP foods, high-fiber foods, high-fat meals, sugar alcohols, artificial sweeteners, excessive caffeine, and NSAIDs like ibuprofen.

**FODMAP Strategy:** FODMAPs (Fermentable Oligo-, Di-, Monosaccharides, and Polyols) are poorly absorbed short-chain carbohydrates that ferment in the colon, producing gas and drawing water. Runners don't need year-round low-FODMAP diets unless diagnosed with IBS; instead, many implement a modified low-FODMAP approach for 6 days before important races. A three-phase approach (strict elimination for 2-6 weeks, systematic reintroduction, personalized plan) works best.

**Gut Training Protocol:** The landmark Costa study had 25 endurance runners complete 10 sessions over 14 days, running 2 hours at 60% VO2max while consuming 30g of carbohydrates every 20 minutes (90g/hour total). This produced 60-63% reductions in GI symptoms and 4.3-5.2% performance improvements. Mechanisms include increased SGLT1 transporter density/activity (for glucose absorption), increased gastric emptying rates, and expanded stomach capacity. Practical modifications include 1-2 gut training workouts per week, starting at 30g/hour and adding 10g/hour weekly until reaching 60-90g/hour target, and using long runs for gut training.

**Race-Day Fueling:**
- 3 days before: Consume 10-12g of carbohydrates per kg of body weight daily for 36-48 hours (680-816g for a 150lb/68kg runner) while tapering
- Race morning: 1-4g of carbohydrates per kg of body weight 3-4 hours before start
- During race: 60-90g of carbohydrates per hour using multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose + fructose); start fueling within first 30 minutes; smaller amounts more frequently (half gel every 20-25 min) outperform large single doses
- For ultras >6 hours: ~15% of calories from protein; for 12+ hour events, modest fat intake; real food (potatoes, sandwiches, soup, chips, fruit) can be incorporated

**Emergency Management:** For nausea, slow pace, sip fluids, try small amounts of cola, walk, stand tall, breathe deeply. For cramping/urgency, walking reduces gut motility; strategic pit stops help. Warning signs requiring stopping: bloody stool (possible ischemic colitis), profuse bleeding, severe pain, or faintness. Avoid prophylactic Imodium — it slows the entire digestive tract and can worsen symptoms; reserve for post-race or under medical guidance.

**Action Plan:** Start with trigger identification via food journaling and elimination diets; implement strategic low-FODMAP periods if sensitive; dedicate 6-8 weeks before key races to gut training; test complete race-day nutrition strategy repeatedly in training; start fueling early on race day; stay disciplined with practiced plans.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from CTS (Carmichael Training Systems) by Jim Rutberg, a Pro Endurance Coach, provides comprehensive guidance on pre-workout and pre-race meals, covering what to eat, how much, and when. Published/updated on July 8, 2025.

**Key Points:**

**What to Eat:** Lead with carbohydrates, as carbohydrate is the fuel for high-intensity efforts. The body stores about 400-500 grams of carbohydrate in muscles and liver, enough for 1-3 hours of exercise. Fat stores are already sufficient for energy, and protein is primarily for recovery/adaptation rather than exercise fuel.

**How Much to Eat (Timing-based):** Citing the 2016 Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine on Nutrition and Athletic Performance, the recommendation is 1-4 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of bodyweight before exercise. This breaks down to 4 g/kg four hours out, reducing to 1 g/kg an hour or less before the start. For a 70-kg (154-lb) athlete, this is 280 grams of CHO four hours out (1,120 calories from CHO alone). In practice, most athletes prefer eating their last substantial meal 2-3 hours before competition.

**Pre-Exercise Meal Composition:** The macronutrient diversity should be greatest with the most digestion time. Four hours out: mixed meal with fat, protein, and carbohydrate (including fiber, complex and simple carbs). As the event approaches, reduce fat first, then protein, and in the final hour stick with low-fiber, mostly simple carbohydrates.

**Sample Meal Examples:**
- 3-4 hours before: Breakfast burrito (tortilla, potatoes, eggs, black beans); scramble with potatoes, eggs, vegetables, plus toast or bagel
- 2-3 hours before: Eggs and rice; whole grain waffles with nut butter and fruit; yogurt with granola, berries, nuts
- 1-2 hours before: Bagel with peanut butter and banana; oatmeal with nuts and berries; sports drink/smoothie with sports bar

**Foods to Avoid:** Greasy/fatty/fried foods (like bacon cheeseburgers); high-volume, low-calorie-density foods (like giant bowls of lettuce that fill you up without providing energy); sugar-free or diet foods (which may use sugar alcohols like Xylitol and Sorbitol that can cause gastric distress).

**Personal Adjustments:**
- Reactive hypoglycemia: Some athletes experience low blood sugar 30-45 minutes after eating carbs before exercise due to insulin spikes. Solutions include using more low-glycemic-index foods, eating carbs very close to the start, or eating them 90 minutes ahead.
- Stress and pre-race jitters can alter gastric emptying and gut motility, potentially causing GI distress. Caffeine may exacerbate this. Lower-priority competitions are recommended as opportunities to test race-day nutrition under stress.

The article emphasizes that getting pre-race nutrition right takes practice, starting with the basics and experimenting with various food combinations.

--- SOURCE 15: What To Eat The Night Before A Long Run (Evidence-Based) ---
URL: https://marathonhandbook.com/what-to-eat-the-night-before-a-long-run

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Marathon Handbook, written by Training Editor Katelyn Tocci (a 100-mile ultrarunner and RRCA/UESCA-certified running coach), provides evidence-based guidance on what to eat the night before a long run or race. The core message is that long runs serve as "race-day rehearsals" and nutrition the night before significantly impacts performance.

Key evidence-based findings:
- Bergström's classic muscle-biopsy research established that muscle glycogen is the rate-limiting fuel for exercise past ~90 minutes, and starting glycogen stores strongly predict time-to-exhaustion.
- Current ISSN/ACSM guidelines recommend 7-12 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight in the 24 hours before long events (roughly 490-840 g for a 70 kg runner), spread across breakfast, lunch, and dinner with high-GI snacks.
- The ACSM/Dietitians of Canada position stand recommends 1-4 g/kg of carbohydrate in the 1-4 hours before exercise, with meals low in fat and fiber. For a dinner eaten 12-14 hours before a morning run, this means a plate that's 60-70% carbohydrate by calories, 15-20% protein, rest mostly fat.
- Jeukendrup's research identifies three culprits to limit the night before: very high fat, very high fiber, and very high protein.
- Hydration guidance: Sawka's ACSM position stand recommends starting exercise euhydrated (5-7 mL/kg fluid in 4 hours prior) with modest sodium (3-6 g). However, Almond's study of 488 Boston Marathon runners found hyponatremia was more common than dehydration, so "drink to thirst" is the safer default.
- Individual GI tolerance varies 30-80% between runners, and Jeukendrup's "train the gut" protocol shows tolerance can expand with progressive carbohydrate exposure over 4-8 weeks.

Practical guidance:
- Simple carbohydrates (white bread, bagels, white rice, pasta, couscous, fruit, juice, honey, maple syrup, dairy, sports drinks, energy gels) are easier to digest than complex carbs and preferred the night before a long run.
- Complex carbs (wheat bread, brown/wild rice, barley, legumes, beans, oats, sweet potatoes) should generally be avoided the night before because they're high in fiber.
- Recommended meal ideas: lemon pasta (high-carb, low-protein, low-dairy), homemade pizza with simple-carb crust, couscous-based dishes, fresh bread sandwiches (e.g., ciabatta with prosciutto and manchego), and breakfast-for-dinner options like pancakes with maple syrup.
- Final tips: avoid high-protein meals, avoid fiber (beans, lentils, whole grains, broccoli), and eat enough but not too much—using the equation: 8 x weight in kilos = total grams of carbohydrates per day during a carb load.
- The night before a race is not the time to try new foods; use Saturday long runs during training to test portion sizes, timing, and specific foods, keeping a log of what causes GI distress.
- Carbohydrates are essential for runners as the primary fuel source; glycogen helps maintain consistent energy and prevents "hitting the wall" (bonking). Any effort above 60% of VO2 max draws on glycogen stores. Low-carb diets show decreased performance.
</summary>
