## 9. Age-Related Changes in Gastrointestinal Physiology (Relevant to Athletes Over 40 / Masters Runners)

### 9.1 General Age-Related GI Changes (Important Context)
- Because the digestive system has a lot of reserve built into it, aging has less effect on its function than it does on the function of other organ systems. [35]
- Age-related changes by organ (Merck Manual):
  - **Esophagus:** Contraction strength and upper esophageal sphincter tension decrease (presbyesophagus), but food movement is not impaired; some older adults may develop diseases affecting contractions. [35]
  - **Stomach:** Reduced lining resistance increases peptic ulcer disease risk, especially with aspirin/NSAID use; decreased elasticity limits food accommodation and slows emptying, though usually without symptoms; acid/pepsin secretion largely unchanged, but atrophic gastritis becomes more common, potentially causing vitamin B12 deficiency or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. [35]
  - **Small intestine:** Structure and nutrient absorption largely unchanged; lactase levels decrease leading to lactose intolerance in many older adults; small intestinal bacterial overgrowth becomes more common, causing pain, bloating, weight loss, and reduced absorption of vitamin B12, iron, and calcium. [35]
  - **Large intestine and rectum:** Large intestine changes little; rectum enlarges somewhat. Constipation becomes more common due to slower transit, reduced rectal contractions, more constipating medications, less physical activity, and pelvic floor weakness in older women (which can also contribute to fecal incontinence). [35]
- Changes in the gut microbiome with age may be connected to overall healthy aging and may affect obesity, metabolic disorders, inflammation, cancer, depression, or other health issues. [35]
- Basic mechanisms of aging GI tract (Gallo et al. 2024): Impaired esophageal peristalsis, lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction, slowed gastric emptying, increased colonic transit time (small bowel motility generally unchanged). [33]
- "Anorexia of aging" from slowed gastric emptying leading to weight loss and sarcopenia. [33]
- Presbyphagia (age-related swallowing changes) predisposes to dysphagia. [33]
- Myenteric plexus degeneration, villi degeneration, mucosal atrophy, altered tight junctions increasing intestinal permeability. [33]
- Decreased cytoprotective mucus-bicarbonate barrier, reduced gastric blood flow, impaired repair mechanisms. [33]
- Immunosenescence in gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) with increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1b, IL-6, TNFa), contributing to frailty and increased morbidity/mortality. [33]
- GI symptoms in older people more often underlie organic pathologies, while GI functional disorders are less frequently diagnosed in this age group. Moreover, gastrointestinal disease can also present in a nuanced and atypical manner, making the diagnostic hypothesis and, consequently, the correct diagnosis and therapy more challenging. [33]
- SIBO prevalence increases with age (significantly higher in those 61+). Risk factors: reduced gastric secretion (PPI use), reduced GI motility, intestinal surgery, small bowel diverticulosis. Treatment: low carbohydrate diet, prokinetics, nonabsorbable antibiotics. [33]
- Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth prevalence is 15.6% in elderly vs 5.9% in younger. [34]
- Small bowel function is largely preserved with age. [34]
- Peptic ulcer disease in elderly is often atypical—only 30% present with typical epigastric pain. [34]
- Elderly with bleeding PUD had significantly higher 30-day morbidity and mortality after open surgery. [34]
- H. pylori colonizes 50% of the global population; it is a Type I carcinogen linked to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. [34]
- Diverticular disease prevalence increases with age, reaching 70% in those over 85 (uncommon under age 40). [33]
- Acute mesenteric ischemia is an underestimated cause of acute abdomen in the elderly, with an incidence that increases exponentially with age, particularly in patients aged over 75 years, and a mortality rate ranging from 60 to 80% of affected patients. [33]
- Acute mesenteric ischemia is more common than ruptured abdominal aneurysm in the elderly and is a more common cause of acute abdomen than appendicitis in those over 75. Endovascular therapy is preferred over open revascularization (16% vs 28% mortality). [34]
- Small bowel bleeding (5% of GI bleeds) is most commonly due to angiodysplasia (54% in elderly), associated with Heyde's syndrome (bleeding angiodysplasia with aortic stenosis). [34]
- Aging reduces each organ system's capacity to maintain homeostasis. Decreased physiologic reserve leads to higher risk of malnutrition, falls, depression, social isolation, and functional deterioration. [33]

### 9.2 Masters Athletes and Gut Issues (Neversecond Article by Marni Sumbal, RD)
- The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. [28]
- Masters athletes can target 60–90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor—gut training is. [28]
- Three causes of GI distress in masters athletes:
  - Physiological: Exercise diverts blood away from the gut (at 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop nearly 80%), causing nausea, cramping, and diarrhea. [28]
  - Mechanical: Running jolts the GI tract, making runners more prone to lower GI issues than cyclists. [28]
  - Nutritional: High-fat, high-fiber, or high-calorie foods eaten too close to training, plus concentrated drinks, slow stomach emptying. [28]
- Gut training for masters athletes: Start at 30–40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10–15g every 1–2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt. [28]
- "Aging doesn't have to mean slowing down — but it does mean paying closer attention to your gut." [28]
- "Your gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly well into their later years. Age is context, not a ceiling." [28]
- Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. [28]
- Many elite endurance athletes now successfully consume 120–150g of carbs per hour, but that takes time and consistency to build. [28]

### 9.3 Masters Athlete-Specific GI Symptom Data (VIREF Study)
- A study evaluating the relationship between food restriction and gastrointestinal symptoms in master athletes, using the Food Restriction in Running Questionnaire developed by Parnell et al., found that the most common gastrointestinal symptoms experienced during racing were gas (51%), stomach pain/cramp (43%), intestinal problems (pain) (42%), reflux/heartburn (39%) and nausea/vomiting (39%). [37]
- On GI symptoms by gender, significant differences were found in constipation, gas, fullness/heaviness and burping, which were more commonly observed in the female athletes (p<0.05). [37]
- Increasing the race distance and performance level increased the food restriction rates and incidence of gastrointestinal symptoms in master athletes. Furthermore, food restriction and the incidence of gastrointestinal symptoms were observed more in the female athletes. [37]

### 9.4 Gut Microbiome in Aging and Athletes
- **Exercise and microbiome in middle-aged amateurs:** A recent study found that young people who lack exercise have higher levels of pro-inflammatory gut bacteria and lower immune resistance than elite athletes and (middle-aged amateur athletes). [32]
- Physical activity/exercise has a positive effect on the composition of the gut microbiome of older adults (Ramos et al., 2022 systematic review). Taniguchi et al. (2018) found (positive effects). [68]
- The gut microbiome changes with age; diet and exercise influence this relationship. [69]
- Moderate exercise promotes a healthy immune system, while high-intensity exercise for a long duration can cause a leaky gut and consequent systemic inflammation, which may disrupt the microbial balance. [29]
- Exercise has a "J-curve" shaped (hormetic) effect on gut health—moderate exercise benefits gut health, while intense/sustained exercise can be deleterious. [30]
- Athletes exhibit higher alpha diversity and more health-associated bacteria (e.g., Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Prevotella, Faecalibacterium). Microbiome composition varies by sport type, and microbiome composition is predictive of exercise gains. [30]
- Athletes have increased faecal SCFAs, especially butyrate. VO2 max was strongly correlated with butyrate production and butyrate-producing bacteria (Clostridiales, Roseburia, Lachnospiraceae, Erysipelotrichaceae). [30]
- Veillonella atypica was found highly enriched in marathon runners' faecal samples; supplementing mice with V. atypica significantly improved treadmill performance, possibly due to lactate metabolism. [30]
- Scheiman et al. (2019) showed Veillonella atypica inoculation in mice prolonged treadmill running; Veillonella converts lactic acid to propionate, which improved performance. Morita et al. (2023) found Bacteroides uniformis abundance correlated with 3000-m race times; 9 weeks of α-cyclodextrin supplementation increased B. uniformis and shortened 10-km cycling times in humans; propionate/acetate stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis and beta-oxidation. [62]
- Moderate exercise (<70% VO2max) has positive health effects: reduces inflammation, decreases intestinal permeability, improves body composition, and induces positive changes in gut microbiota composition and microbial metabolites. Intense exercise (>70% VO2max) can increase gastrointestinal epithelial wall permeability and diminish gut mucus thickness, potentially allowing pathogens to enter the bloodstream, contributing to increased inflammation. [65]
- Elite athletes tend to have higher gut microbial diversity, shifted toward bacterial species involved in amino acid biosynthesis and carbohydrate/fiber metabolism, producing key metabolites like short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). [65]
- The human gut microbiome comprises over a thousand bacterial species, with anaerobic species producing anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) through fermentation of dietary sugars. Butyrate serves as the primary energy source for colonocytes and enhances epithelial barrier function. [29]
- Single exercise/race changes: acute high-intensity exercise increased Romboutsia, Ruminococcaceae UCG-005, E. coli TOP498, Blautia; a half-marathon increased Ruminococcus bicirculans and Collinsella aerofaciens; a full marathon increased Veillonella; an ultramarathon (~44h, 96km) decreased four butyrate-producing species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and increased Collinsella aerofaciens. [62]
- Repeated training (6 weeks, 3 days/week): increased Faecalibacterium and Lachnospira, decreased Bacteroides in lean subjects, with increased SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate). [62]
- Athlete vs nonathlete comparisons: findings are discrepant across studies (e.g., Faecalibacterium less abundant in marathon runners per Kulecka 2020, but more abundant in female elite endurance runners per Morishima 2021). [62]
- Athletes' gut microbiomes undergo multiple stressors from their lifestyle, causing high variability and potentially long-lasting changes. Athlete diets and activity levels change drastically between on/off seasons; dietary changes can cause significant compositional changes within 24 hours. Travel is associated with high microbiome variability and gastrointestinal distress (O'Donovan et al., 2020). [67]
- Probiotic supplementation (meta-analysis 2022) may improve performance in aerobic-trained populations, but there is likely publication bias (no studies report negative results). [62]
- The probiotic market was estimated to reach $69 billion by 2023. [30]

### 9.5 Aging Cardiovascular Performance (Relevant to Splanchnic Perfusion in Older Athletes)
- Progressive aging induces several structural and functional alterations in the cardiovascular system, among which particularly important are a reduced number of myocardial cells and increased interstitial collagen fibers, which result in impaired left ventricular diastolic function. [55]
- Aging causes reduced maximal heart rate response to exercise (due to beta1 receptor down-regulation), and peripheral changes including reduced skeletal muscle cells and decreased Myosin Heavy Chain (MHC) I and IIa fibers. Even without cardiovascular disease, aging is strongly associated with reduced maximal aerobic capacity. [55]
- Aerobic/endurance exercise improves peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope, ventilatory aerobic threshold, and Heart Rate Recovery (HRR). Mechanisms include improved chronotropic incompetence, increased stroke volume, enhanced vagal tone, improved endothelial function and arterial compliance, and favorable skeletal muscle biochemical changes (increased MHC I). [55]
- Aging does not contraindicate exercise training in healthy elderly or those with comorbidities. [55]

### 9.6 Medication Interactions in Older Athletes
- Older adults are more prone to digestive issues related to medication use; constipation is often medication-induced. [35]
- Pill esophagitis is more prevalent in elderly due to polypharmacy, reduced motility, and insufficient water intake, with NSAIDs, aspirin, doxycycline, bisphosphonates, ferrous sulfate, and captopril as common culprits. Chest pain (71.8%) and odynophagia (38.5%) are the most common symptoms. [34]
- Management of GI disorders in the elderly often differs from younger patients due to polypharmacy, atypical presentations, delayed diagnosis, and increased vulnerability to medication side effects. [34]
- NSAID risk is higher in older people (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.7) for acute kidney injury. [15]
- Reduced lining resistance of the stomach increases peptic ulcer disease risk, especially with aspirin/NSAID use. [35]

### 9.7 Explicit Note on Age-Specific Data Availability
- **Direct age-specific data for masters runners (age 40+) on exercise-associated GI distress are extremely limited.** The research base is dominated by studies of younger endurance athletes (mean ages typically in the 20s–30s). [Aggregate observation from all sources]
- The most directly relevant age-specific sources identified include: the VIREF study on master athletes' GI symptoms and food restrictions [37], the Neversecond masters athletes article (which notes the small intestine's carbohydrate absorption stays largely intact with age and that masters athletes can achieve the same fueling targets as younger athletes with gut training) [28], and studies on aging thermoregulation in older athletes (Balmain et al. 2018 [52]; Kenney GSSI SSE #44 [53]; Kenney 2020/2021 [54, 56]).
- Peters et al. (1999) found that exercise-related GI symptoms were significantly related to age among other variables, but did not provide specific age-stratified data for masters athletes. [38]
- The Gallo et al. (2024) and Dumic et al. (2019) reviews describe age-related GI changes in adults over 65 (not specifically athletes over 40), so extrapolation to masters runners (40+) must be made cautiously. [33, 34]
- Merck Manual notes aging has less effect on digestive function than on other organ systems due to reserve capacity, but documents reduced gastric lining resistance, reduced elasticity/slower emptying, decreased lactase, increased SIBO, and increased constipation risk with age. [35]
- **Where findings are extrapolated:** The mechanisms of Ex-GIS/EIGS (splanchnic hypoperfusion, motility disturbance, mechanical jostling, FODMAP sensitivity, NSAID effects, dehydration/hyperthermia) established in the general endurance-athlete population are presumed to apply to masters runners, but dedicated primary studies in masters runners are largely absent from the current literature.

## 10. Resistance Exercise GI Findings (Supplementary Evidence on Intra-Abdominal Pressure Mechanism)

- Resistance exercise induces significant GI distress, with 70% of participants reporting at least one GI symptom, most commonly nausea, and 60% reporting at least one moderate symptom after the exercise session, with no differences between sexes. [27]
- Consistent with aerobic exercise studies, biomarkers of GI injury did not consistently correlate with subjective symptoms. [27]
- The magnitude of GI damage correlated directly with absolute strength, suggesting males experienced more GI distress because they lifted heavier loads, generating higher intra-abdominal pressure. [27]
- The global digestive health market is projected to reach $58 billion by 2025, with many products marketed to active individuals despite limited evidence of GI damage in resistance-trained populations. [27]

## 11. Gut Trainability and Practical Management (Cross-Cutting)

- GI problems are highly prevalent among endurance athletes, the gut is an important athletic organ, and nutritional training plus appropriate food choices can reduce GI discomfort by ensuring rapid gastric emptying, proper absorption, and adequate splanchnic perfusion. [4]
- "More marathons are won or lost in the portable toilets than at the dinner table." — Bill Rodgers. [4, 20]
- 30–50% of all athletes experience GI problems regularly. Fiber intake, fat intake, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions increase prevalence. Hot weather and dehydration exacerbate symptoms. Training the gut may alleviate symptoms by improving gastric emptying, reducing bloating, and increasing absorption speed. [64]
- The gut is highly adaptable; athletes should practice their event nutrition plan over several weeks to optimize carbohydrate absorption, reduce GI distress, and improve performance. [63]
- Despite extensive research, there are still no sufficiently effective methods to prevent exercise-associated GI ailments. The most effective measures according to current data include reduced fiber intake in the pre-competition period and "gut training" to prepare the digestive system for such exertion. [42]
- Strategies with consistent beneficial outcomes (SDA/USSF Joint Position Statement): macronutrient intake before/during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulation of FODMAPs, and gut training/feeding tolerance adjustments. [43]
- Practical guidelines for athletes:
  - Avoid high-fiber foods on competition day and for several days leading up to the event [3]
  - Identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities (e.g., dairy, gluten) [3]
  - Avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol) [3]
  - Avoid NSAIDs such as Ibuprofen [3]
  - Avoid high-fructose foods; a fructose-glucose combination may be better tolerated [3]
  - Avoid dehydration—prevention is key [3]
  - Ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water [3]
  - Choose carbohydrate drinks with lower concentrations to prevent high osmolalities in the stomach [3]
  - Practice new nutrition strategies before race day [3]
- Sports drinks should be below 8% carbohydrate concentration (preferably glucose and fructose combination) to prevent dehydration. [23]
- A 28-day study of 16 trained cyclists/triathletes found that high-carbohydrate diets led to greater maximal citrate synthase activity and higher carbohydrate exogenous oxidation rates during submaximal exercise, attributed to enhanced intestinal absorption and improved tolerance. [23]
- Probiotic supplementation is associated with decreased inflammation, enhanced sports performance, and fewer gastrointestinal disturbances. [29]
- Probiotic blends significantly reduce URTI incidence and symptoms in athletes. One study (Tavares-Silva) showed a 29% reduction in URTI incidents in marathon runners; another showed a 2.2-fold decrease in URTI symptoms with a probiotic blend. [30]
- 2 weeks of bovine colostrum intake increased HSP70 and reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases (shorter periods or severe heat >40°C were not effective). Single glutamine intake and 4 weeks of probiotic intake had inconsistent results. Carbohydrate drinks (alone or with protein/pectin alginate) before/during exercise reduced GI damage, especially in heat. Cold water ingestion (0–7°C) lowered rectal temperature but did not significantly reduce GI damage in heat. Wearing compression socks (25 mm Hg) during a marathon reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases but did not affect race time. [62]

## 12. Methodological Quality Concerns in the Field

- Research in exercise gastroenterology has grown exponentially, but published literature consistently suffers from substantial experimental limitations affecting the accuracy of translating study outcomes into practice. [44]
- Studies often fail to report comprehensive inclusion/exclusion criteria, including gastrointestinal diseases, dietary practices, supplement use, and pharmaceutical prescriptions. [44]
- Most studies fail to implement or report robust dietary control. Gold standard requires providing all foods and fluids at least 24 hr before trials, with low-FODMAP diet (<5 g/day total FODMAP) standardization recommended. [44]
- Standardized experimental procedures are needed for accurate interpretation of research findings, avoiding misinterpreted pathological relevance and overstated clinical/practical relevance of intervention research outcomes, supporting more accurate translation into safe practice guidelines. [44]
- The Scrivin et al. case series is indexed in both Scopus and Web of Science, with 40 references in the bibliography, and has been cited 3 times. [2]
- The Ribichini et al. review searched PubMed, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases (up to March 2023), identifying 142 research articles for inclusion based on established criteria. [1]
- The Kołodziejczyk et al. narrative review searched PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar, covering publications up to October 2025. The search initially identified 412 records; after removing duplicates (356 remained) and screening, 73 publications met all inclusion criteria for final narrative synthesis. [22]
- The Pannone & Abbott scoping review followed PRISMA scoping review guidelines and the Arksey and O'Malley five-step framework. The initial search found 194 articles, with 30 ultimately included after screening and exclusions. Studies were predominantly from the USA (n=15) and England (n=7). [14]

1. **Search 1:** "treatment gastrointestinal symptoms endurance runners systematic review exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome"; "pharmacological treatment GI distress endurance athletes loperamide proton pump inhibitors evidence"
2. **Search 2:** "low-FODMAP diet runners gastrointestinal symptoms randomized controlled trial"; "probiotics endurance athletes GI symptoms meta-analysis exercise"

4. **Search 4:** "capsule endoscopy small bowel athletes runners gastrointestinal bleeding diagnosis"; "SIBO breath test endurance athletes small intestinal bacterial overgrowth runners"; "masters runners over 40 gastrointestinal symptoms aging athletes GI evidence"
5. **Search 5:** "endoscopy capsule endoscopy runner gastrointestinal bleeding diagnosis exercise athletes guidelines"; "small intestinal bacterial overgrowth SIBO breath test athletes runners hydrogen methane testing"; "cognitive behavioral therapy gut-brain axis athletes IBS psychological intervention exercise gastrointestinal"
6. **Search 6:** "masters runners 40 plus gastrointestinal function aging exercise gut symptoms older endurance athletes"; "American College of Sports Medicine position stand exercise gastrointestinal runners guidelines"; "antiemetic antispasmodic prokinetic athletes exercise gastrointestinal treatment evidence"
7. **Search 7:** "Buscopan hyoscine antispasmodic athletes exercise gastrointestinal symptoms evidence"; "anti-nausea antiemetic medication ultramarathon vomiting management athletes evidence"; "Costa exercise gastrointestinal syndrome consensus statement International Journal of Sport Nutrition Exercise Metabolism"
8. **Search 8:** "older masters athletes gastrointestinal function aging endurance exercise gut permeability 40 plus runners evidence"; "ondansetron ultramarathon nausea TOO FUN study randomized controlled trial results Pasternak 2021"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

### BACKGROUND AND EPIDEMIOLOGY OF EXERCISE-ASSOCIATED GI SYMPTOMS (Ex-GIS)

**Prevalence of GI symptoms in endurance athletes:**
- "At least 30 to 50 % of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise on a regular basis, with especially high occurrence in long duration endurance exercise. In endurance trained runners it is estimated that between 30 and 90 % may experience them" (Systematic review, J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2025) [2].
- 30–90% of endurance athletes report GI symptoms during exercise; upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (up to 70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn prevalence is 15–20% in runners; lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. Exercise-induced transient abdominal pain (ETAP) is reported in 18% of recreational run competitors (Ribichini et al., Dietetics, 2023) [4].
- In a study of 2,076 long-distance runners, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% had serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints within 24 hours post-run; 3 athletes dropped out. Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon/cycling to 32% in Ironman races (ter Steege study and Pfeiffer study, cited in Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].
- "According to research, about 90% of long-distance runners experience some form of GI symptoms (including diarrhea) during exercise and accept their symptoms as a normal consequence of running and therefore do not consult a physician" (IFFGD) [9].
- GI symptoms are reported by approximately 20% to 50% of high-performance athletes, and are more common in women, younger athletes, and endurance athletes. Runners experience more problems from high-impact abdominal jostling than cyclists (Musculoskeletal Key, DeLee & Drez's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine) [6].
- GI symptoms are common in non-endurance athletes as well: approximately 1 in 2 female and 1 in 3 male athletes experience GI symptoms around competition. In a scoping review of 7 studies with 1,087 athletes (682 male, 405 female), prevalence of at least one GI symptom ranged from 11.5–80.0%. The most common symptoms were flatulence (2.8–48%), stomach cramps/rumbling (5.1–37%), and bloating (2.5–32%) (Performance Nutrition, 2026) [5].
- About 30–90% of endurance runners experience exercise-induced gastrointestinal disturbances, according to a 2014 review of earlier research (Healthline, citing a 2014 review) [11].
- Runner's diarrhea affects 30-50% of runners in exhaustive endurance events; 83% of marathon runners reported GI symptoms during or after running, with 53% reporting "urge to have a bowel movement" and 38% reporting diarrhea. Triathletes reported 93% GI symptom prevalence (7% dropped out due to severity), and 43% of 67km ultra-marathon finishers reported GI distress (15% diarrhea). Runners have almost twice the risk of GI problems compared to cyclists, swimmers, and other athletes (Ketone-IQ blog, 2019) [14].
- Nausea and vomiting occur in 37-75% of runners in events of 67-161km, and are cited as two of the main reasons for dropping out or impaired performance in ultramarathons (UESCA) [10].
- Up to 70% of athletes experience GI symptoms, which are the most common cause of underperformance in endurance events. Runners are more frequently affected than cyclists or other athletes (Papantoniou et al., Annals of Gastroenterology, 2023) [18].
- Approximately 30%–70% of athletes experience GI problems (Sumi & Suzuki, Frontiers in Physiology, 2025) [27].
- GI problems affect 30-50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports (Jeukendrup, GSSI SSE #178, 2018) [28].
- IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes: Killian et al. documented 9.8% IBS prevalence overall with only 2.8% diagnosed; Hungin et al. reported 14.1% overall with 10.8% undiagnosed (cited in Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].

**Pathophysiology of Ex-GIS (four main causal pathways):**
- Four main causes of GI symptoms: physiological (splanchnic hypoperfusion), mechanical, psychological, and nutritional (Mlinaric & Mohorko, 2025) [2].
- Ex-GIS involves two primary pathways: (I) the neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway (sympathetic activation reducing GI functional capacity) and (II) the circulatory–gastrointestinal pathway (blood flow redistribution away from splanchnic circulation). Splanchnic blood flow (SBF) can be depleted by up to 80% during strenuous exercise, causing significant GI tract hypoperfusion and damage. Splanchnic hypoperfusion leads to loss of epithelial integrity, increased intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, and endotoxemia (LPS in circulation), triggering pro-inflammatory cytokines. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max represents the threshold for significant GI perturbations (Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].
- Exercising at 70% VO2 max reduces GI blood flow by 60–70%; higher intensity can exceed 80% reduction. Ischemia causes mucosal injury, increased permeability, occult blood loss, bacterial translocation, and endotoxin generation. Reperfusion injury after exercise may result in "leaky mucosa." Dehydration accentuates these effects; 80% of runners who lost ≥4% body weight from fluid loss experienced lower GI symptoms (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- At 70% VO2 max and above, blood flow to the GI tract is reduced up to 80%, leading to hypoxia, ATP depletion, breakdown of intestinal "tight junctions," and increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut"). Re-perfusion after exercise can cause further oxidative stress and inflammation ("post-run runs") (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].
- A 1965-era study by Brock-Utne found 81% of 89 marathon runners were endotoxemic. Endurance exercise alters gut peptide levels (increases PYY and GLP-1, affects ghrelin, CCK) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) which affect GI motility and blood flow. Gut microbiota differences exist between athletes and sedentary individuals. Carbohydrate malabsorption was found in 68% of 25 healthy endurance-trained runners during recovery (Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].
- At rest, 25% of cardiac output goes to splanchnic organs. During exercise, sympathetic nervous system activation causes vasoconstriction reducing splanchnic blood flow by up to 80%. This leads to ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), mucosal damage, and increased intestinal permeability. The splenic flexure (Griffith's point) and recto-sigmoid (Sudeck's point) are most vulnerable due to inadequate vessel anastomosis. The colon has less blood supply per gram than the small bowel. Mechanical trauma is greater in running than cycling, potentially causing hemorrhagic gastritis and "cecal slap syndrome" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- During intense exercise, blood flow shifts to working muscles and away from the GI tract (up to 80% reduction), causing ischemia, reduced gut function, increased leakiness, malabsorption, and looser stools. Mechanical repetitive body movement from running causes trauma that can damage the intestinal lining. Nutritional factors—fiber, fat, protein, and highly concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>7% carbohydrate)—are associated with greater risk of GI symptoms (IFFGD) [9].
- Higher exercise intensity increases GI damage, while exercise duration has smaller effects. Dehydration (hypohydration ~3.1% BW loss significantly increased blood I-FABP levels) and heat stress are the most influential factors increasing GI damage. Hypoxic environments also elevate exercise-induced GI damage. Blood I-FABP levels serve as an indirect marker of small intestinal damage (Sumi & Suzuki, 2025) [27].
- During high-intensity efforts, blood flow is redirected to working muscles, limiting the blood available for digestion. This "gut steal" effect can slow or even stop digestion, creating an uncomfortable buildup in the stomach (Hellemans, Endurance Essentials) [29].

**Risk factors:** Heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms) (Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].

**Exercise-induced GI bleeding (GIB) incidence:**
- Based on fecal occult blood (FOB) testing: 74 of 404 long-distance runners (19.6%) switched from negative to positive after a race; 4 of 60 cyclists (6.7%); 1 of 11 rugby players (9%); and 58 of 75 triathletes/ultra-marathoners (77%)—the highest incidence in ultra-endurance events. Endoscopy studies on runners revealed gastric erosions, esophagitis, gastritis with blood clots, and colon erosions at the splenic flexure (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- ~90% of professional long-distance runners have at least one GI mucosal lesion even without symptoms (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].

---

### CATEGORY 1: PHARMACOLOGICAL INTERVENTIONS

#### 1a. Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)

**PPIs for prevention of GI bleeding in ultramarathon runners:**
- Thalmann et al. (2006) conducted a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study titled "Proton pump inhibition prevents gastrointestinal bleeding in ultramarathon runners," published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine (40(4):359) [16][17]. The study concluded that "A three day prophylactic regimen of oral pantoprazole may decrease the incidence of gastrointestinal bleeding in ultramarathon runners" [17]. It is described as a randomised, double blinded, placebo controlled study (BJSM) [16].
- "PPI use in ultramarathon runners decreases GI bleeding incidence" (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].

**PPIs and H2 receptor antagonists for GERD and upper GI symptoms in athletes:**
- Pharmacologic therapy for GERD in athletes: H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole); a 2-week PPI trial (daily 30 minutes before morning meal) is first-line; 8-week course if effective. An H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- Proton pump inhibitors are useful for persistent symptoms of gastritis, GI bleeding, and ulcer formation in athletes; NSAID use contributes to these conditions (Kapur, Current Sports Medicine Reports, 2012) [8].
- For heartburn, treatment includes H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and switching to lower-impact exercises (IFFGD) [9].
- H2 blockers and PPIs can help with nausea/vomiting linked to postprandial exercise (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].

**PPI risks (important caveat for chronic use):**
- A peer-reviewed review in Frontiers in Pharmacology (2023) by Tian, Yuan, Meng et al. documents that PPIs (the most widely used acid-suppressive agents and first-line therapy for gastric acid-related disorders) are increasingly linked to adverse digestive events including small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Clostridium difficile-associated disease (CDAD), functional dyspepsia, lower GI bleeding, infectious diseases, cholelithiasis, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Mechanisms include pH-dependent disruption of the gastric acid barrier and non-pH-dependent effects (hypergastrinemia, direct binding to non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases on microbes). PPI treatment increases Planococcaceae, Oxalobacteraceae, Sphingomonadaceae in the proximal small intestine; decreases Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae. A 2018 meta-analysis showed PPI use moderately increased SIBO risk, though diagnostic method variability is a major confounder. CDAD risk can be up to 7.15-fold higher. Most studies are retrospective with relatively weak evidence and confounding factors; clinicians should carefully evaluate and individually manage patients requiring PPI therapy to avoid long-term abuse [7].
- PPI use is a risk factor for SIBO due to decreased bacteriostatic digestive secretions (Genova Diagnostics SIBO test page) [21].

**PPIs in general GI bleeding (contextual evidence):**
- A systematic review and meta-analysis in NEJM Evidence (June 14, 2024, DOI: 10.1056/EVIDoa2400134) examined PPIs for stress ulcer prophylaxis in critically ill patients (12 RCTs, 9,533 ICU patients). Clinically important upper GI bleeding: RR 0.51 (95% CI, 0.34–0.76), high certainty evidence — PPIs reduced bleeding risk (18 fewer per 1000 patients). Overt upper GI bleeding: RR 0.52 (95% CI, 0.38–0.70), high certainty. Mortality: RR 0.99 (95% CI, 0.93–1.05), low certainty. Pneumonia: RR 1.00 (95% CI, 0.92–1.09), low certainty. C. difficile infection: RR 1.20 (95% CI, 0.66–2.16), low certainty [19].

**PPIs in management of exercise-associated GI bleeding:**
- PPIs for ulcers/gastritis are recommended in the management of overt GI bleeding in athletes; PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists are effective for exercise-induced gastritis in occult bleeding. "H2-receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) show promising results as short-course treatment before prolonged exercise, though not yet generally recommended" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].

#### 1b. H2 Receptor Antagonists
- H2-receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine) and PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole) are pharmacologic therapy for GERD; a 2-week PPI trial is first-line; 8-week course if effective. An H2-receptor antagonist (e.g., 300mg ranitidine) 1 hour before activity can reduce exercise-induced reflux markers (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- H2 blockers and PPIs can help with nausea/vomiting (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists are effective for exercise-induced gastritis in occult bleeding in athletes (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- For heartburn, treatment includes H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and switching to lower-impact exercises (IFFGD) [9].

#### 1c. Antidiarrheal Agents (Loperamide)

**Evidence and expert opinion:**
- Loperamide (over-the-counter) "has been shown to decrease stool frequency when taken before intense exercise." Caution is advised with antispasmodic and antimotility drugs, as they can inhibit perspiration and impair core body temperature control (IFFGD) [9].
- Dr. Stacy Sims (Triathlete.com, August 10, 2022) advises "no" to taking Imodium (loperamide) before a race, "especially if you will be racing in warm to hot conditions. Imodium (Loperamide) is designed to slow gut motility in resting conditions, but it should not be used in high stress, high sweat, long duration exercise." Risks include: heart rhythm disruption (QT prolongation) risk due to dehydration coupled with low blood magnesium and potassium levels; reduced absorption of glucose and other nutrients from the small intestines (while increasing water/electrolyte absorption), which reduces blood glucose and the ability to regenerate glucose for race fueling; and potential missteps in fluid and electrolyte balance thermoregulation (sweating and blood flow) during exercise. Imodium can be a "last resort," but athletes must adjust their fueling and hydration plans to accommodate the changes loperamide induces in the gut [12].
- OTC options for runner's diarrhea include bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto Bismol) and loperamide (Imodium), though taking them on an empty stomach may cause illness (Healthline) [11].
- Anti-diarrhea drugs like Imodium or Kaopectate are "supported by medical experts for a single dose about an hour before a major race (unless bloody diarrhea), but shouldn't be a daily fix" (Race Smart) [15].
- Race Smart recommends Imodium or Kaopectate as a last-ditch option about an hour before a major race, unless bloody diarrhea is present [15].
- Loperamide pharmacology: It works by slowing food passage through the gut, allowing the body to absorb more water from the intestines, resulting in firmer stools and less frequent bowel movements. It usually starts working within 1 hour. Over-the-counter use should not exceed 48 hours without consulting a doctor; taking too much can cause serious heart problems (fast or irregular heartbeat). Available combined with simeticone for diarrhoea with cramps and bloating (NHS) [13].

#### 1d. Antiemetics (Ondansetron)

**The TOO FUN Study (RCT):**
- Pasternak et al. (2021), "Treatment with Oral Ondansetron for Ultramarathon-Associated Nausea: The TOO FUN Study," published in Sports (9(3):35; DOI: 10.3390/sports9030035; PMCID: PMC8001581; PMID: 33802399). This was the first randomized controlled trial to evaluate ondansetron for ultramarathon-associated nausea/vomiting [31][32][33].
- Background: Nausea and vomiting affect up to 60% of ultramarathon athletes and are the primary reason for not finishing a 161-km ultramarathon. Ondansetron, a serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, had only anecdotal support and a small unblinded pilot study (66% of 21 runners reported improvement) [33].
- Methods: Runners from the 2018 and 2019 Tahoe Rim Trail Endurance Races (TRTER) — 55, 80, and 160 km distances — with prior history of nausea/vomiting during races were recruited. 62 runners participated (average age 45, range 21-78; 25 women, 37 men). Randomized double-blind to 4 mg oral ondansetron capsules or placebo (cellulose capsules), with four capsules each; one at symptom onset, then one every 4 hours as needed [33].
- Results: 31 of 62 participants (50%) developed GI symptoms prompting treatment (20 ondansetron, 11 placebo). There were NO statistically significant differences between groups in those reporting any improvement (30% ondansetron vs. 55% placebo, p=0.26) or in the amount of improvement (31±32 vs. 50±42 points, p=0.15). Notably, the placebo group tended to show MORE benefit and MORE side effects than the ondansetron group [33].
- Conclusion: "We found no evidence that ondansetron capsules improve nausea and vomiting during ultramarathons" [31][32][33]. Limitations include limited power, oral capsule form requiring gastric absorption (vs. orally dissolvable tablets used in the positive pilot study), and 4 mg dose (vs. the commonly used 8 mg clinical dose) [33].
- A Narrative Review by P.B. Wilson (2019, cited 41 times) notes: "Ondansetron, which is an antiemetic from the 5-HT3 antagonist class of medications, is often kept on hand at endurance races for treating" nausea/vomiting [30].

**Antiemetic drug classes (general reference):**
- Seven subgroups of antiemetics: serotonin antagonists (Granisetron/Kytril, Ondansetron/Zofran, Palonosetron/Aloxi), antihistamines (Dimenhydrinate/Dramamine, Diphenhydramine/Benadryl, Doxylamine with vitamin B6, Meclizine/Antivert, Promethazine/Phenergan), glucocorticoids (Dexamethasone/Baycadron, Decadron), anticholinergics (Scopolamine/Transderm Scop), neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists (Aprepitant/Emend, Fosaprepitant, Netupitant/palonosetron combination/Akynzeo, Rolapitant/Varubi), dopamine antagonists (Amisulpride/Barhemsys, Chlorpromazine/Thorazine, Droperidol/Inapsine, Haloperidol/Haldol, Metoclopramide/Reglan, Olanzapine/Zyprexa, Prochlorperazine/Compro), and cannabinoids (Dronabinol/Marinol, Nabilone/Cesamet) (Cleveland Clinic) [34].

#### 1e. Antispasmodics (Hyoscine Butylbromide / Buscopan)

**Use in athletes:**
- In the Scrivin et al. (2022) exploratory study, 13 athletes (9%) used medications to manage Ex-GIS, including "Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon" — Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide, an antispasmodic) being one of the named medications [1].
- Hyoscine butylbromide is an antimuscarinic antispasmodic used for relief of lower abdominal pain caused by spasm in the muscles of the digestive system. It helps ease bloating and spasm-type pain associated with IBS and diverticular disease. It works by relaxing muscles in the gastrointestinal system. Distinct from hyoscine hydrobromide (used for travel sickness). Dosage: one or two tablets three times daily, may be increased to two tablets four times daily. It is available over-the-counter for IBS symptoms if previously diagnosed by a doctor. Side effects (fewer than 1 in 100): dry mouth, dry skin and sweating, and itchy skin rash. If symptoms don't improve within two weeks, see a doctor (Patient.info) [35].
- Buscopan (hyoscine butylbromide) relieves painful stomach cramps, including those linked with IBS. Works quickly—painful cramps ease within 15 minutes. Side effects are unusual but may include dry mouth, constipation, or blurred vision. Over-the-counter use should not exceed 2 weeks without consulting a doctor (NHS) [36].
- In the UK MHRA Public Assessment Report (11 February 2022), Buscopan IBS Relief (Hyoscine Butylbromide 10mg tablets) was reclassified to allow a 60-tablet pack as a General Sales List (GSL) medicine. Indication: relief of GI tract spasm associated with medically confirmed IBS in adults and children aged 12+. Maximum dose: 20mg (2 tablets); maximum daily dose: 80mg (8 tablets); maximum duration of use: 2 weeks [37].

#### 1f. Prokinetic Agents
- Functional heartburn (up to 60% of PPI-nonresponsive GERD-like presentations; Rome III criteria require ≥6 months symptom onset) may be treated with biofeedback, tricyclic antidepressants, and prokinetics (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- Metoclopramide (Reglan) is a dopamine antagonist antiemetic (Cleveland Clinic) [34].
- Promotility drugs must be discontinued 1 week before SIBO breath testing (Commonwealth Diagnostics International) [20].

#### 1g. Medications Targeting Splanchnic Circulation
- "Arginine, glutamine, citrulline, nitrite, and nitrate (nitric oxide availability enhancers) improve splanchnic perfusion but may cause nausea and diarrhea" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- In the Scrivin et al. (2022) survey, arginine was rated highest for success among supplements (median=5, n=1, though very small sample). Other supplements trialed included prebiotics, antioxidants, L-citrulline, glutamine, curcumin, and nitrates [1].
- Nifedipine at a low dose (2.5-5 mg) is described as a "lesser-known but effective prescription treatment" for runner's diarrhoea (nifedipine is primarily used for high blood pressure/angina; 5 mg is a very low dose with fewer side effects) (Hellemans, Endurance Essentials) [29].
- Carbohydrate or whey protein hydrolysate ingestion before/during exercise ameliorates intestinal epithelial injury; carbohydrate is preferential due to fewer GI symptoms and its value as an exogenous fuel source. Increasing carbohydrate intake can help mitigate Ex-GIS through improved splanchnic blood flow and reduced intestinal epithelial damage (Scrivin et al., 2022) [1].

**Position Statement on pharmacological approaches:**
- The Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) Joint Position Statement (Sports Medicine, April 7, 2025; Volume 55, pages 1097–1134; DOI: 10.1007/s40279-025-02186-6), "A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms," reports under "Negative outcomes reported": "Low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, probiotic supplementation, pharmaceutical administration, and feeding intolerances." Under "Strategies with consistent beneficial outcomes": "Macronutrient (carbohydrate and protein) intake before and during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulation of FODMAPs, and gut training/feeding tolerance adjustments." "Promising but needing further exploration": "Heat mitigating strategies and certain nutritional supplementation (prebiotics and phenols)." The core recommendation is individualized gastrointestinal assessment during exercise to identify underlying causal factors, and adoption of evidence-based strategies tailored to individual needs. Abstention from strategies with unclear or adverse outcomes is advised [26].

### CATEGORY 2: DIETARY AND BEHAVIORAL THERAPIES

#### 2a. Low-FODMAP Diets

**Systematic review evidence:**
- A systematic review (Mlinaric & Mohorko, J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2025) found: "Multiple studies showed significant reductions in GI symptoms (gut discomfort, flatulence, urge to defecate, loose stool, diarrhea) with low FODMAP diets compared to high FODMAP diets. 69% of participants reported positive effects on low FODMAP vs. 25% on high FODMAP. However, the restrictive nature of the diet could negatively affect athletes in other ways" [2].

**Case series evidence (IJSNEM 2025):**
- Scrivin, Slater & Costa (2025), "Case Series: Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Endurance Athletes Using a High-Carbohydrate Low-FODMAP Therapeutic Intervention," International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism (Vol. 34/4, pp. 337-354; DOI: 10.1123/ijsnem.2024-0133). Nine recreational-to-elite athletes with recurrent severe Ex-GIS and two controls participated in a four-phase management approach using the GastroAxEx (gastrointestinal assessment during exercise) protocol combined with a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP therapeutic dietary intervention. Most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum, resulting in 2%-4% body mass loss; 8/9 consumed <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate during the GastroAxEx; 4/9 reported severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) during exercise; 8/9 reported severe Ex-GIS in the recovery period; orocecal transit time was slow or delayed for 2/9 athletes. 8/9 athletes successfully implemented the 48-hr high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet prior to targeted events. Conclusion: "A 48-hr high carbohydrate low FODMAP before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to suggested therapeutic interventions used to mitigate Ex-GIS" — reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS, improved intake tolerance, and improved perceived work output during targeted events [3].

**Survey evidence on athlete self-management:**
- In the Scrivin et al. (2022) survey of 137 endurance athletes (Frontiers in Nutrition), low FODMAP diet was used by 5.4% (n=15) of athletes; avoiding disaccharides (lactose and sucrose, 6.1%, n=17) were the most popular FODMAPs avoided. Low FODMAP diets had a median success rating of 4 (IQR 4,5) on a 1-5 Likert scale (5 = significant improvement). The authors note: "Low FODMAP diets are effective for both IBS and Ex-GIS, but are not intended for long-term use; a rechallenge and personalization phase is recommended for extended use" [1].
- 82.6% of athletes eliminating at least one FODMAP group reported improvement (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].

**Review evidence:**
- The Ribichini et al. (2023) review examined gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets as potential management approaches, noting that Ex-GIS symptoms resemble IBS (defined by Rome IV Criteria) and may respond to analogous nutritional strategies [4].
- A "Current Opinion" article on dietary FODMAP manipulation argues that FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default based on symptom severity (cited as related to the IJSNEM 2025 case series) [3].

#### 2b. Gluten Elimination
- The Ribichini et al. (2023) review specifically examined "gluten-free and low-FODMAP diets" as the principal nutritional/behavioral management strategies for Ex-GIS [4].
- Gluten only matters for those with Celiac disease (Race Smart) [15].
- Celiac disease symptoms are higher in athletes than the general population (2.9% vs. 0.4%) (Performance Nutrition, 2026 scoping review) [5].

#### 2c. Elimination Diets for Food Intolerance (General Dietary Strategies)

**Survey evidence (Scrivin et al., 2022, Frontiers in Nutrition):**
- 67% (n=92) of 137 athletes reported using dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting 277 total strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods.
- Most popular dietary strategies: Dietary fiber reduction (15.2%, n=42) — the most popular; Dairy avoidance (5.8%, n=16); Low FODMAP diet (5.4%, n=15).
- Most successful strategies (Likert scale 1-5, with 5 = significant improvement): Dietary fiber reduction (median = 4, IQR = 4,5); Low FODMAP diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5); Dairy-free diets (median = 4, IQR = 4,5); Increasing carbohydrates (median = 4, IQR = 3,4).
- Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed at all time points.
- "Reducing dietary fiber, especially before exercise, aligns with current sports nutrition guidelines and works via reducing luminal contents and extending GI transit time, though a low-fiber diet may require implementation 1-3 days before exercise."
- "Dairy avoidance may relate to lactose intolerance, which has overlapping symptoms with IBS."
- Fifteen athletes (11%) reported a diagnosed gastrointestinal disease/disorder, most commonly IBS (n=6) [1].

**Other dietary strategy evidence:**
- A 2020 survey found runners commonly avoided meat (32%), milk products (31%), fish/seafood (28%), poultry (24%), and high-fiber foods (23%) (Healthline) [11].
- Avoid high-fiber foods (cruciferous vegetables, brown rice, high-fiber cereals) 1-3 days out; avoid dairy if lactose intolerant; avoid high-fructose foods (soda, juice, candy, dried fruit); avoid sugar alcohols/artificial sweeteners (sorbitol, aspartame) which pull water into intestines; reduce fat intake 12-24 hours before racing (Race Smart) [15].
- Fiber, fats, and protein before exercise delay gastric emptying and can draw water into the intestine. High-carb beverages (above 6-8% concentration) delay gastric emptying and cause fluid shifts; the body can only absorb 1g-1.2g of carbohydrate per minute during exercise (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].
- Prevention tips: stay well hydrated, avoid lactose-containing products, and avoid high-fructose foods and fructose-only drinks (IFFGD) [9].
- FODMAPs can cause excess intestinal fluid and fermentation; 82.6% of athletes eliminating at least one FODMAP group reported improvement (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].

#### 2d. Probiotics and Prebiotics

**Systematic review evidence (probiotics):**
- Mlinaric & Mohorko (2025) systematic review: "Evidence is mixed. Some studies showed reductions in GI symptoms (e.g., 27% reduction during training, fewer episodes of nausea, belching, vomiting), while others found no substantial differences or even increases in mild GI symptoms. LGG (Limosilactobacillus rhamnosus GG) shortened GI symptom episode duration by 33-57%" [2].

**Joint Position Statement (SDA/USSF, 2025):**
- Probiotic supplementation is listed under "Negative outcomes reported" — the position statement advises abstention from strategies with unclear or adverse outcomes. Prebiotics are listed under "Promising but needing further exploration" [26].

**Gut microbiota systematic review:**
- Gaskell, Martinez & Costa (Int J Sports Med 2026; 47(04): 255-286; DOI: 10.1055/a-2705-2210), "Gut Microbiota and Exercise: A Systematic Review of Interventions and Evidence Limitations." PRISMA systematic review of 18 studies (Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL Complete, Web of Science, Scopus up to February 2025). "Changes in faecal microbiota diversity and composition were highly variable and largely minimal." Only one study reported a significant increase in faecal acetate concentration (following yoghurt supplementation containing Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BL-99). Only seven studies examined the relationship between faecal bacterial profile changes and performance outcomes, with limited or inconclusive findings. "No consistent performance benefits were observed in relation to microbiota changes." Conclusion: "The current evidence base remains too limited and heterogeneous to draw firm conclusions about the efficacy of microbiota-targeted interventions for enhancing exercise performance in healthy, active adults" [25].

**Survey evidence:**
- Probiotics (median=4, n=26) were the most commonly used supplement in the Scrivin et al. (2022) survey [1].

**Mechanistic/microbiota evidence:**
- Probiotics (e.g., UCC118 strain) may attenuate exercise-induced intestinal hyperpermeability (Ribichini et al., 2023) [4].
- Sumi & Suzuki (2025) minireview: "4 weeks of probiotic intake showed inconsistent results" for reducing GI damage. Probiotics (Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and multistrains) may improve performance, though a publication bias exists. Landmark studies: Scheiman et al. (2019) showed Veillonella atypica (increased after marathons) converts lactic acid to propionate; mice inoculated with V. atypica ran longer, and colonic propionate injection prolonged treadmill run time. Morita et al. (2023) found Bacteroides uniformis abundance correlated with 3000-m race times in Japanese long-distance runners; 9 weeks of α-cyclodextrin supplementation increased B. uniformis and shortened 10-km cycling times. Single exercise/race changes microbiota composition (e.g., full marathon increased Veillonella; ultramarathon increased Haemophilus, Streptococcus, and Veillonella but decreased Faecalibacterium; a 96-km ultramarathon decreased four butyrate-producing species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii) [27].

#### 2e. Other Nutritional Strategies (Gut Training, Carbohydrates, Hydration)

**Gut training:**
- Two weeks of purposeful repetitive CHO intake during running lowered GI symptom severity and reduced breath H₂ response (indicating reduced CHO malabsorption). Repetitive running sessions with higher liquid intake improved fluid tolerance over time. Mechanisms may involve increased expression of SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters (Mlinaric & Mohorko, 2025) [2].
- The GI tract is highly adaptable and responds to nutritional training in a nutrient-specific way. SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake; a glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses after one week; piglets after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks. Cox et al. (2010): 16 endurance-trained cyclists, 28 days of training (16 h/week); high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day vs. 5.3 g/kg/day in controls, showing improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation post-training. Practical recommendations: train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks; for exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures). Conversely, carbohydrate restriction, high-fat/ketogenic diets, or energy reduction may reduce absorptive capacity and potentially increase GI problems (Jeukendrup, GSSI SSE #178, 2018) [28].
- Runners consuming a glucose + fructose beverage during runs for two weeks improved GI symptoms and performance by just over 5% during a three-hour run challenge; about three days of training helps the stomach adapt to larger volumes (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].
- Gut training protocols: research suggests 90g/hour for 2-hour daily runs for 2 weeks improves CHO absorption; practical recommendation is consuming CHO at rates 20-40% higher than race expectations for several sessions within two weeks (UESCA) [10].
- Sports nutritionist Asker Jeukendrup recommends mixing sugar types and increasing carb volume during training, which can raise carbohydrate absorption by over 30% in less than two weeks (relevant to the 50% of triathletes who experience stomach problems) (Race Smart) [15].

**Carbohydrate solutions and mixtures:**
- CHO bars were the worst tolerated form (causing more nausea, fullness, and fatigue). Highly concentrated CHO solutions increased symptoms. Fructose caused more GI symptoms than glucose or sucrose due to slower absorption. High glucose intake (SGLT1 saturation at ~60 g/h) caused bloating. Mixed CHOs recruit GLUT5 transporter, improving absorption. A 0.8 ratio MD:FRU solution was superior to 0.5 and 1.25 ratios for performance and GI comfort, suggesting ratios close to unity may be better than the traditional 2:1 ratio (Mlinaric & Mohorko, 2025) [2].
- Hydrogel CHO products: "Current evidence does not demonstrate benefits of hydrogel CHO products over standard CHO products" (Mlinaric & Mohorko, 2025) [2].
- Sports drinks with ≤10% glucose are optimal for training; 6–8% carbohydrate sports drinks for events <1 hour; 30–60g/hour carbohydrate for longer events (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- 2016 ACSM guidelines recommend CHO intakes up to 90 g/h (from multiple-transportable CHOs like glucose/fructose mixtures) for exercise lasting >2.5-3 hours. Contemporary research suggests the upper limit of CHO intake could increase from 90 to 120 g/h (at least for trained participants) (Morton et al., The Journal of Nutrition, 2026) [38].

**Other supplements:**
- Bovine colostrum intake (2 weeks) improved cellular protection via HSP70 and reduced exercise-induced I-FABP increases (though 7-day supplementation or severe heat stress >40°C did not). Glutamine before exercise showed inconsistent results. Carbohydrate drinks (alone or with protein and pectin alginate) before and during exercise reduced GI damage, likely by increasing GI blood flow. Cold water ingestion (0°C–7°C) and ice slurry did not reduce GI damage in the heat. Compression socks (25 mm Hg) during a marathon reduced exercise-induced increases in blood I-FABP (Sumi & Suzuki, 2025) [27].
- Nutritional supplements (glutamine, arginine, L-citrulline, antioxidants, curcumin, nitrate, bovine colostrum, ginger) "lack scientific justification for preventing gut issues" (Race Smart) [15].

#### 2f. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Psychological Interventions for Gut-Brain Axis Dysfunction

**CBT for IBS (general population evidence, extrapolated to athletes):**
- Kinsinger (Psychology Research and Behavior Management, 2017; PMC5530860): 41 RCTs have evaluated psychological therapies for IBS. "Psychological therapies as a whole have demonstrated good efficacy in reducing the severity of IBS symptoms. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has been tested most rigorously in multiple randomized controlled trials and consistently demonstrates significant and durable effects on IBS symptoms and quality of life." At least 20 published RCTs support CBT, with effects maintained for at least 1 year after treatment. Components: psychoeducation, relaxation strategies (diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery), cognitive restructuring, problem-solving skills, and exposure techniques. Vollmer & Blanchard found 64% of group vs 55% of individual CBT patients improved vs control. Lackner et al: 72% of self-administered CBT patients reported adequate relief vs 60% therapist-administered and 7.4% control. Ljotsson et al: 42% of internet-delivered CBT patients vs 12% of control reported symptom improvement. The American Gastroenterological Association recommends psychological interventions for moderate-to-severe IBS or patients unresponsive to standard care [24].

**Network meta-analysis (The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology):**
- A network meta-analysis of 67 RCTs with 7,441 adults with IBS (search through April 23, 2025) found brain-gut behavior therapies significantly improve global IBS symptoms. Most effective vs. waiting list control: minimal contact CBT (RR 0.55; P score 0.78; 2 trials; n=511), telephone-based disease self-management (RR 0.57; P score 0.75; 2 trials; n=746), dynamic psychotherapy (RR 0.59; P score 0.72; 3 trials; n=303), and standard CBT (RR 0.65; P score 0.64; 9 trials; n=1,150). Other effective approaches: disease self-management (RR 0.68), internet-based minimal contact CBT (RR 0.77), gut-directed hypnotherapy (RR 0.79; 12 trials; n=1,507). Evidence of publication bias was identified; no trial was rated low risk of bias across all domains; certainty of evidence was rated low to very low [23].

**Gut-focused CBT details:**
- GI-CBT is one of the most well-studied behavioral approaches for IBS, with more than 40 years of research (IFFGD/AboutIBS) [22].
- Four main psychological treatments for IBS: Gut-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (GI-CBT), Gut-Directed Hypnotherapy (GDH; up to 80% of IBS patients respond positively, better than traditional medications; approximately 75% of people can be hypnotized enough for positive response), Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT; early in IBS research but shows promise), and Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR; typically 8 weeks; shown to improve symptom perception, quality of life, reduce symptom severity, and decrease visceral hypersensitivity) (AboutIBS/IFFGD) [22].

**CBT as frontline treatment:**
- Dr. Jeffrey Lackner (Gastroenterology Advisor feature): A landmark 7-site RCT (2018) enrolling 436 adults with moderate-to-severe, treatment-refractory IBS found 61% of patients in the 4-session, home-based CBT arm reported moderate-to-substantial symptom improvement, with 58% maintaining gains at 6 months. A 4-session at-home protocol performed equivalently to a 10-session clinical protocol, reducing therapist contact time by 60%. Benefits held at 12-month follow-up, with minimal-contact CBT gains increasing over time. American College of Gastroenterology guidelines recommend referring patients with IBS to CBT or other gut-brain behavioral therapy. A 2021 microbiome study found CBT simultaneously alters gut microbial composition and brain function, with microbiome markers predicting treatment response. A 2026 online survey by Izquierdo et al of 770 US adult patients with GI disorders found 90% of patients with IBS, functional diarrhea, and functional constipation had never been offered CBT [39].

**Application to athletes:**
- Psychological factors are one of the four main causes of GI symptoms in athletes (Mlinaric & Mohorko, 2025) [2].
- Higher stress and anxiety levels are associated with GI symptoms; psychological stress induces small intestine permeability (Ketone-IQ blog) [14].
- Non-dietary interventions (medications, relaxation, psychological therapies) are used less frequently by athletes but have potential; "further randomized controlled trials are needed" (Scrivin et al., 2022) [1].
- In the Scrivin et al. (2022) survey, relaxation/meditation was used by 4.0% (n=11) of athletes as a non-dietary strategy [1].
- Pre-race anxiety and stress are a cause of GI distress during running; mindfulness and a structured pre-race routine can reduce nervousness/anxiety (Dr. Stacy Sims, Triathlete.com) [12].
- Psychological stress (cortisol) contributes to nausea and vomiting in endurance athletes (Hellemans) [29].

#### 2g. Other Behavioral/Non-Dietary Strategies
- Relaxation/meditation (4.0%, n=11) were used as non-dietary strategies (Scrivin et al., 2022) [1].
- Cooling strategies (cold drinks, ice, sprinklers, heat acclimation) may help in hot conditions (Race Smart) [15].

### CATEGORY 3: DIAGNOSTIC-DRIVEN MANAGEMENT APPROACHES

#### 3a. Upper GI Endoscopy and Colonoscopy

**Role in athletes with GI bleeding:**
- "GIB should NOT be immediately attributed to endurance exercise; endoscopy (upper and lower) should always be performed to rule out other causes (IBD, neoplasia, esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss tears, peptic ulcers, coagulopathies, hemorrhoids, fissures, diverticulosis, vascular ectasias, vasculitis)" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- "Occult bleeding: endoscopy recommended in all athletes, especially those with anemia; iron supplementation for low ferritin; PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists effective for exercise-induced gastritis; stool softeners for fissures/hemorrhoids; repeat endoscopy if persistent GIB with negative initial findings" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- "Overt bleeding: cease activity immediately, seek medical care, assess hemodynamic stability, IV crystalloids/transfusions for severe cases, PPIs for ulcers/gastritis, vasoactive drugs (somatostatin/octreotide) for suspected varices, emergency endoscopy or radiographic interventions for hemostasis, surgery in rare cases" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- Upper endoscopy is used for GERD diagnosis confirmation and concerning presentations; H. pylori testing recommended (Musculoskeletal Key) [6].
- "No specific guidelines currently exist for GIB prevention in athletes" (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18].
- Frequent or severe cases of runner's diarrhea warrant medical evaluation to rule out IBS or IBD; doctors may order blood work or stool samples (Hellemans) [29].

#### 3b. Capsule Endoscopy

**Capsule endoscopy for small bowel bleeding (general GI evidence, applicable to athletes):**
- Capsule endoscopy (CE), introduced in 2001 and FDA-approved, is now the first-line test for small bowel (SB) bleeding (which accounts for 5-10% of GI bleeding), with a diagnostic yield of approximately 60%. CE shows superior diagnostic yield versus traditional modalities: 63% vs 28% for SB barium radiography, and 67% vs 8% for push enteroscopy. Guidelines recommend CE within 48 hours of overt SB bleeding for maximal yield; within 48 hours yield is 81-92%, within 14 days ~60-75%, occult bleeding 35-46%, previous overt bleeding ~13-25%. Common SB bleeding etiologies: angiodysplasias (most common, 30-50%, typically in older patients), ulcers/erosions, and tumors (adenocarcinoma, GIST) (Oh, Int J Gastrointest Interv, 2025) [40].
- For upper GI bleeding (UGIB), CE showed comparable accuracy to esophagogastroduodenoscopy, with sensitivity 88% for bleeding detection; CE-based triage in the emergency department reduced admission rates from 100% to ~19%. Magnetically controlled CE (MCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.8% for UGIB. For lower GI bleeding (LGIB), pan-enteric CE (PCE) achieved diagnostic yield of 95.7% vs 50.0% for colonoscopy in one study; another showed PCE diagnostic yield of 83.3% (Oh, 2025) [40].
- Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for overt and occult small bowel bleeding, accounting for ~5% of all GI bleeding (Pasha & Leighton, Gastroenterology & Hepatology, 2017) [41].
- In a systematic review of 227 studies, 66% of capsules were used for small bowel bleeding with a pooled detection rate of 59.4%. Diagnostic yield was 66.6% in a review of 1960 IDA patients and 35% in a single-center cohort of 971 patients. Angioectasias are the most common finding (50%), followed by inflammation (26.8%) and tumors (8.8%). Overt bleeding is the strongest predictor of positive results (OR 3.8). Rebleeding rates are higher after positive capsule results (28.6% over 48 months). Risk factors for rebleeding include age >60, positive result, hemoglobin >7 g/dL, nonspecific treatment, and anticoagulant/antiplatelet/NSAID use. Main adverse event is capsule retention, occurring in 1.2%-1.5% of OGIB patients; risk increases with NSAID use, Crohn's disease, tumors, and prior radiation/surgery (Pasha & Leighton, 2017) [41].
- Early video capsule endoscopy (EVCE) as first-line diagnostic: A randomized controlled trial (NCT02442830) comparing EVCE with standard of care in 87 patients with nonhematemesis GI bleeding found higher bleeding localization rates with EVCE (64.3% vs 31.1%, P<0.01); adjusted HR 2.77 (95% CI, 1.36-5.64) for endoscopic localization. Median time to first procedure was 6 hours with EVCE vs 21 hours with SOC. Hakimian et al (ACG 2020): first-line VCE significantly decreased the number of patients requiring invasive procedures (44% vs 96%; P<0.001) (Gastroenterology Advisor) [42].
- Capsule endoscopy is a diagnostic test used to look for bleeding and tumors, mainly in the small intestine. It captures about 10,000 pictures; the capsule is naturally passed in stool, usually within 24 hours. Rare complications: the capsule can get stuck in narrower parts of the intestines—particularly in people who've had bowel surgery, inflammation, or tumors (Cleveland Clinic) [43].

**Application to athlete populations:**
- In the management of exercise-associated GI bleeding, endoscopy (upper and lower) should always be performed to rule out other causes before attributing GIB to endurance exercise (Papantoniou et al., 2023) [18]. Capsule endoscopy is the diagnostic test of choice for small bowel bleeding after negative bidirectional endoscopy (Pasha & Leighton, 2017) [41].

#### 3c. Breath Testing for SIBO / IMO

**Diagnostic criteria and methodology:**
- The North American Consensus on Breath Testing recommends using a hydrogen and methane breath test to detect Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO) and Intestinal Methanogen Overgrowth (IMO) (Commonwealth Diagnostics International) [20].
- Per the North American Consensus statement: "an early rise in hydrogen of 20 parts per million (ppm) or more above baseline by 90 minutes is considered a positive glucose or lactulose breath test result for SIBO." IMO: methane of ≥10 ppm at any point during testing. Small bowel aspiration requires >10³ CFU/mL of coliforms (but has 19.6% contamination rate per Cangemi study) (Lim & Rezaie, Gastroenterology & Hepatology, 2023) [44].
- Breath testing is the most widely utilized diagnostic modality for SIBO and IMO. "Currently in clinical practice, IMO is only diagnosed with breath testing" (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].
- Meta-analysis: lactulose breath test sensitivity 42%, specificity 70.6%; glucose breath test sensitivity 54.5%, specificity 83.2% (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].
- Test methodology: baseline sample collected first, then substrate (glucose or lactulose) ingested, followed by breath samples every 15-20 minutes over ~180 minutes. Positive criteria: hydrogen rise of ≥20 ppm from baseline by 90 minutes, OR methane rise of ≥10 ppm at any time (UPMC, Clinical and Translational Gastroenterology) [45].
- Preparation: Patients must discontinue antibiotics for 4 weeks before testing, discontinue laxatives and/or promotility drugs for 1 week before, not smoke or vape for at least 24 hours before and during the test, and not sleep or exercise for at least 1 hour before or during the test. A 24-hour diet preparation period includes a 12-hour limited diet and 12-hour fasting period (Commonwealth Diagnostics International) [20].
- Opioids delay intestinal transit time and should be stopped at least 24 hours before the test; antibiotics should be stopped about a month before; cessation of smoking the night before and throughout; minimize physical exercise (both smoking and exercise alter results) (UPMC) [45].
- Glucose is absorbed by the digestive tract, so it won't detect SIBO further along the small intestine (proximal jejunum/ileum), but it is more sensitive with fewer false positives from colonic bacteria. Lactulose is not absorbed and travels through the entire GI tract, providing a complete depiction of all intestinal segments including the colon (Commonwealth Diagnostics International) [20].
- The normal transit time of lactulose (10 g) in healthy fasting patients, from mouth to ileocecal junction (oro-cecal transit time, OCTT), is approximately 90 minutes (Genova Diagnostics) [21].
- Limitations: OCTT variability—rapid OCTT can cause false positives; slow OCTT can cause false negatives. Conditions preventing substrate delivery to small intestine (gastroparesis, gastric outlet obstruction, achalasia, enterocutaneous fistula) cause false negatives. Yu et al: 88% of positive results had ≥5% substrate in cecum on scintigraphy before test became positive. Lin and Massey found 22 of 46 patients with false-positive glucose breath tests had colon fermentation, 20 of whom had prior upper GI surgery (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].
- Emerging patterns: Flat-line pattern (no methane, low fixed hydrogen ≤3 ppm, no rise >1 ppm above baseline) is more common in inflammatory bowel disease; 56% of patients respond to antibiotics (58% to rifaximin, 47% to rifaximin+neomycin). High baseline hydrogen (>20 ppm baseline with no excessive methane) found in 0.7% (107/14,847) of lactulose breath tests; 52% responded to antibiotics, 73% to rifaximin, only 25% to rifaximin+neomycin (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].

**SIBO treatment implications (diagnostic-driven management):**
- Breath testing can distinguish SIBO from IMO and help tailor antibiotic therapy: rifaximin for hydrogen-predominant SIBO; combination therapy like rifaximin/neomycin for IMO (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].
- Low et al. study: 85% of patients treated with rifaximin + neomycin achieved clinical response vs. 56% with rifaximin alone. 87% of combination therapy patients eradicated methane vs. only 29% with rifaximin alone. A small RCT (N=31) in constipation-predominant IBS with methane >3 ppm showed neomycin+rifaximin reduced constipation, straining, and bloating more than rifaximin alone (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].
- Spot methane measurement (SMM) of ≥10 ppm has 86.4% sensitivity and 100% specificity for diagnosing IMO, providing rapid point-of-care testing (Lim & Rezaie, 2023) [44].

**Relevance to athletes:**
- PPI use (common in athletes for GERD) is a recognized risk factor for SIBO: "decreased bacteriostatic digestive secretions (with PPI use)" (Genova Diagnostics) [21]. A 2018 meta-analysis showed PPI use moderately increased SIBO risk (Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2023) [7].
- SIBO symptoms overlap with Ex-GIS: bloating/distension, gas, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia (Genova Diagnostics) [21].

#### 3d. Imaging and Other Diagnostics
- CTE (CT enterography) is superior to capsule endoscopy for small bowel tumor detection (94.1% vs 35.3%); CE is complementary with CTE (Pasha & Leighton, 2017) [41].
- If there's uncertainty about whether a capsule passed, an X-ray or CT scan may be needed (Cleveland Clinic) [43].
- The GastroAxEx (gastrointestinal assessment during exercise) protocol is a standardized laboratory assessment used to collect physiological strain and GIS data to guide individualized therapeutic interventions (Scrivin et al., IJSNEM 2025) [3].
