**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

The following searches were conducted via web search tools (Tavily):

1. "exercise-associated gastrointestinal distress prevention endurance runners evidence-based strategies" / "gut training adaptation carbohydrate absorption runners protocol repeated exposure" / "carbohydrate intake during running glucose fructose blend gastric emptying intestinal absorption"
2. "ACSM position stand nutrition athletic performance 2023 carbohydrate intake hydration guidelines endurance" / "NSAIDs exercise gastrointestinal distress running kidney intestinal permeability evidence" / "heat acclimatization gastrointestinal integrity endurance running splanchnic blood flow"
3. "masters runners over 40 hydration thirst perception renal function aging exercise" / "exercise induced gastrointestinal syndrome consensus statement Costa 2023" / "International Society Sports Nutrition position stand caffeine carbohydrate exercise gut"
4. "Costa exercise associated gastrointestinal syndrome consensus statement 2023 Sports Medicine International Journal Sport Nutrition" / "2023 2024 ACSM position stand nutrition performance carbohydrate exercise updated" / "aging masters athletes gastrointestinal function nutrient absorption thirst renal function review"
5. "multiple transportable carbohydrates maximal exogenous oxidation rate 1.7 g/min glucose fructose ratio Jeukendrup 90 g hour" / "NSAID ibuprofen marathon running gastrointestinal symptoms intestinal permeability randomized trial" / "pre race meal timing 3-4 hours before running gastrointestinal emptying evidence review"
6. "Costa 2022 gut training randomized controlled trial endurance athletes carbohydrate 90 g hour protocol" / "older adults 65 plus exercise induced gastrointestinal syndrome intestinal permeability heat dehydration study" / "hydration recommendations masters athletes sodium fluid balance aging kidney thirst ACSM"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Overview and Epidemiology of Exercise-Associated GI Symptoms (Ex-GIS)

Exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome (EIGS) and its clinical manifestation, exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms (Ex-GIS), are common in endurance athletes. The 2025 Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) joint position statement defines EIGS as comprising two primary pathophysiological pathways: (1) the circulatory-gastrointestinal pathway (splanchnic hypoperfusion and gastrointestinal ischemia due to blood flow redistribution to skeletal muscle, leading to intestinal epithelial injury, hyperpermeability, and inflammatory responses from translocated pathogens/endotoxins), and (2) the neuroendocrine-gastrointestinal pathway (stress responses, sympathetic activation, impaired motility, transit, digestion, and nutrient absorption via effects on the enteric nervous system and interstitial cells of Cajal). Two additional pathways warrant investigation: mechanical strain on the splanchnic area (jarring/jolting/vibrations) and exaggerated metabolic responses (metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia) linked to exercise-associated nausea [30].

- Adverse GI complaints such as cramps, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are common problems faced by up to 90% of endurance athletes [2].
- Strenuous exercise can be associated with Ex-GIS, a clinical condition characterized by a series of GI disturbances that may impact the physical and psychological performance of athletes; it affects up to 70% of athletes in endurance sports [3].
- Studies report that 30% to 90% of endurance athletes experience GI symptoms during exercise (bloating, cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); GI symptoms are one of the most common reasons athletes drop out of races [5].
- GI problems affect 30–50% of all athletes regularly, with bloating, cramping, diarrhea, and vomiting common in endurance sports [9][13].
- Up to 93% of long-distance triathletes in extreme conditions reported any GI symptom; 43% reported serious GI problems and 7% abandoned the race due to GI issues (Jeukendrup et al., 2000) [21].
- 70% of elite endurance athletes reported exercise-induced GI symptoms (Peters et al., 1999) [21].
- In an internet-based study of 1,281 athletes, 45% reported at least one GI symptom (Ter Steege et al., 2008) [21].
- Severe GI distress ranged from 4% in marathon running/cycling up to 32% in Ironman races (Pfeiffer et al., 2011) [21][3].
- In a study of 2076 athletes, 45% had at least one GI complaint, 11% reported serious complaints, and 2.7% had complaints in the first 24 hours post-run [3].
- Upper GI symptoms occur in up to 40% of runners (70% in cyclists); reflux/heartburn affects 15–20% of runners. Lower GI symptoms occur in up to 30% of recreational runners, up to 50% in cyclists, and up to 70% in competitive long-distance runners. ETAP (exercise-induced transient abdominal pain) affects 18% of recreational run competitors [3].
- Depending on the type, duration and environmental conditions, up to 85% of endurance athletes, such as marathon runners, report experiencing these gut symptoms [60].
- Ex-GIS symptom incidence varies widely by exercise type: negligible in recreational endurance running, 4% after marathon competition, and ≥93% in ultra-endurance events. Longer-duration exercise, especially in hot conditions, promotes higher Ex-GIS incidence [30].
- GI symptoms during endurance exercise are common, with prevalence in endurance athletes ranging from 37–93% [11].
- An exploratory study of 137 adult endurance athletes (mean age 41.6 ± 11.1 years; 63% female) with a history of Ex-GIS found: athletes reported Ex-GIS most frequently around training (21%), competitions (30%), or equally around both (49%); lower GI symptoms were more common than upper GI symptoms across all groups; Ex-GIS incidence was significantly higher during exercise than before or after exercise in all categories [1].
- IBS may be underdiagnosed in endurance athletes — one study documented 9.8% overall IBS prevalence with only 2.8% diagnosed [3]. In the Scrivin exploratory study, 15 athletes (11%) had a diagnosed GI disease/disorder, most commonly irritable bowel syndrome (n=6) [1].
- Risk factors for Ex-GIS include heat stress, dehydration, younger age, female sex, high exercise intensity/duration, and lack of training for fluid/food ingestion during exercise (twofold risk of GI symptoms) [3]. Athletes not accustomed to fluid and food ingestion during exercise had a two-fold risk of GI symptoms compared to accustomed athletes [21].

## 2. Pathophysiology of Exercise-Induced GI Distress

The causes of exercise-induced GI complaints are multifactorial [2][3][21]:
1. **Decreased GI perfusion (splanchnic hypoperfusion):** During maximal exercise, splanchnic blood flow may be reduced by up to 80% to supply working muscle and skin. Norepinephrine release induces splanchnic vasoconstriction, which can lead to gut mucosal ischemia, increased mucosal permeability, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea [2][21]. At 70% VO2max, gut blood flow can drop by nearly 80% [37][52]. Blood flow to gut and liver is reduced up to 80% during exercise; GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments due to systemic dehydration and lower plasma volume [2].
2. **Changes in motility:** Heavy exercise causes decreased peristalsis, decreased lower esophageal sphincter tone, and increased transient sphincter relaxation, linked to gastroesophageal reflux and impaired gastric emptying [2]. Decreased esophageal peristalsis and lower esophageal sphincter tone, increased transient sphincter relaxation, and altered gastric emptying (mainly at high exercise intensities) [21].
3. **Absorption and gut permeability:** High-intensity exercise compromises intestinal blood flow, increasing permeability, gut damage, impaired function, decreased nutrient absorption, and potentially a dysbiotic microbiome with pathogenic bacteria and endotoxin invasion into circulation [2]. Studies show increased intestinal permeability after marathons, though effects are inconclusive at moderate intensities [21].
4. **Mechanical causes:** Posture-related issues in runners and cyclists from repetitive high-impact mechanics; repetitive impact of running causes trauma to the gut (symptoms are more common in runners than cyclists); aerophagia (swallowing air) from increased respiration while drinking from water bottles [2][21].
5. **Nutritional causes:** Fiber, fat, protein, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying [2]. Fiber, fat, protein, fructose, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (>500 mOsm/L osmolality) are associated with increased GI symptoms; dairy products and mild lactose intolerance can cause problems [21].
6. **NSAIDs:** Associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction [2].
7. **Hyperthermia:** Heat exposure leads to intestinal ischemia from shunting blood to skin and muscles; heat acclimatization and hydration help mitigate effects [2].
8. **Dehydration:** Reduces gut perfusion; GI symptoms occur more often in warm environments [2].

The neuroendocrine–gastrointestinal pathway involves sympathetic activation altering the enteric nervous system, affecting gut peptides (CCK, GLP-1, PYY, ghrelin) and catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) and serotonin, leading to slowed gastric emptying and altered motility. Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations [3]. Biomarkers include increased I-FABP (intestinal fatty acid-binding protein); 81% of 89 marathon runners (89.4 km) were found to be endotoxemic in an initial study [3].

**Key mechanistic research findings:**
- Running for 90 minutes at a challenging pace causes small intestinal damage and increases intestinal permeability, but these alterations in GI function do not appear to correlate with the development of GI symptoms during running. This was the first study to directly compare intestinal permeability alterations in asymptomatic versus symptomatic runners. In 17 runners (aged 24–44), intestinal permeability (iohexol) increased significantly in both groups; serum I-FABP increased significantly only in the asymptomatic group (314±152 to 804±599 pg/ml); symptomatic runners had significantly higher baseline LPS activity (0.767±0.119 vs 0.567±0.124 EU/ml) [19].
- Acute high-intensity interval running (HIIT) increases markers of gastrointestinal permeability (both L:R and sucrose) and small intestinal injury (I-FABP) in trained male runners. In 11 trained male runners (VO2max 60.0 ± 3.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, mean age 33.1), serum L:R ratio was 59% higher after HIIT vs. rest; plasma I-FABP rose 72% during HIIT (481 ± 334 to 829 ± 448 pg/mL). Runners reported acute symptoms of GI discomfort (bloating, urge to burp, stomach cramps and flatulence) during and in the 24 h post exercise, although these markers of discomfort did not correlate with measures of GI permeability or damage [22].
- A Monash University-led study (published in *Temperature*, July 2023) identified body temperature as a major risk factor for EIGS during exercise in hot weather. A rise in core body temperature to 39°C and above, from two hours of exercise in hot conditions, can predict the onset of gut damage and the movement of pathogens from the gut into the bloodstream [60].
- A review for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics (Costa et al., 2019, *Temperature*) found: intestinal injury (I-FABP) increased proportionally with heat: >1000 pg/ml at Tamb ≥35°C, ≤600 pg/ml at ~30°C, and ≤400 pg/ml at 22–25°C after 2h running at 60–70% VO2max. A threshold core temperature of ~39.0°C appears necessary for clinically significant intestinal injury to occur. Total-GIS incidence rose from ≤70% in temperate conditions to 80% in warm conditions and ≥88% in hot conditions (≥35°C). Lower-GIS incidence was ≤30% in temperate conditions but ≥58% in warm/hot conditions. Systemic endotoxemia (≥5 pg/ml LPS above baseline) can result from exercise ≥2h or shorter high-intensity exercise in hot conditions [61].
- A PhD thesis by Stephen John Smith (Liverpool John Moores University, 2021) found: GI permeability displays a dose-response relationship with exercise intensity, but this does NOT correlate with the expression of GI symptoms. For the first time, hyperthermia implemented during resting conditions (via hot water immersion), in the absence of exercise-induced mesenteric hypoperfusion, does NOT augment GI permeability or markers of GI distress. Passive hyperthermia results in symptoms of heat illness, and core temperature is strongly correlated with nausea. Pires et al. (2017) identified core temperature thresholds of 38.5°C (increased permeability in some participants) and 39°C (augmented permeability universal). Acute glutamine supplementation returned no protective effects on GI damage, permeability, core temperature, or heat-illness symptoms in response to passive hyperthermia. Conclusion: the increase in GI permeability during exercise is likely caused by intestinal ischemia (reduced blood flow) rather than an increase in core temperature [59].
- In marathon runners at the 2019 Brighton Marathon, I-FABP increased significantly from baseline (1129 ± 493 ng·l⁻¹) to immediately upon completing the marathon (T0; 2593 ± 1373 ng·l⁻¹), returning to baseline by 4 hours. Exercise-associated collapse (EAC) cases had significantly higher I-FABP (15389 ± 8547 ng·l⁻¹) compared with controls at T0. EAC cases had a mean core (rectal) temperature of 39.7 ± 1.2°C at collapse. Ambient conditions on race day were cool (8–10°C), suggesting intestinal damage can occur without sustained heat exposure in marathon runners [24].
- Resistance exercise also induces significant GI distress: 70% of 30 resistance-trained individuals reported at least one GI symptom (most commonly nausea), and 60% reported at least one moderate symptom after exercise. Resistance exercise increased GI permeability (lactulose/rhamnose ratio), with males showing greater permeability and GI damage than females. The magnitude of GI damage correlated directly with absolute strength, suggesting higher intra-abdominal pressure is a primary mechanism [62].

## 3. Nutrition Timing Around Runs (Pre-Run Meal Timing and Composition)

**Pre-exercise meal timing (strong consensus):**
- The general recommendation, endorsed by Jeukendrup (2017) and the joint positioning of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the ACSM (Thomas et al., 2016), points to a main meal between 3 and 4 hours before exercise. If less time is available, the meal should be lighter with less fat and fiber to facilitate gastric emptying [50][53].
- The Academy/DC/ACSM position recommends 1–4 g/kg of carbohydrate in the 1–4 hours before exercise, with meals low in fat and fiber [53][54][51][14].
- For pre-exercise exercise >60 minutes, consume 1–4 g carbohydrate/kg BW 2–3 hours before competition (DGE position) [34].
- Carbohydrate guidelines: 10K = 5–7 g/kg/day; Half marathon = 7–10 g/kg/day; Marathon = 10–12 g/kg/day. For a 70 kg runner facing a marathon, that's 700–840 g of carbs per day for 2–3 days prior [50].
- Glycogen loading (carbohydrate loading) is recommended for competition lasting more than 90 minutes. Most common method: 10–12 g carbohydrate/kg BW/d for 36–48 hours prior to competition, increasing muscle glycogen by approx. 10–15% [34]. Per Burke et al. (2011), this can increase glycogen reserves 20–40% above baseline [50].
- Glycogen loading is NOT justified for a 10K or races shorter than 90 minutes (per Burke et al. 2019); 7–10 g/kg in the 24 hours prior is sufficient [50].
- Race-day targets: <45 min water only; 45–75 min ~30 g/h; 75 min–2h 30–60 g/h; 2–4h 60–90 g/h (sweet spot for most age-groupers); 4h+ 80–120 g/h; ultras 60–90 g/h plus real food [55].
- Pre-race breakfast (3 hours before): 80–100 g oats or cooked white rice, 1–2 ripe bananas, 1 cup of coffee, little or no added fat/fiber. If only 60–90 minutes available, a piece of toast with jam is enough [50].
- Glycemic index timing: 3–4 hours before = low-moderate GI (oats, brown rice, al dente pasta); 60–90 minutes = moderate-high GI (ripe plantain, white rice, sliced bread); 15–30 minutes = gels/readily available foods; avoid fructose alone (can cause GI issues and reactive hypoglycemia from insulin spike) [50].
- Race morning general recommendation: consume 1–4 grams of carbohydrate per kg of body mass in the 1–4 hours before exercise. If breakfast can be 3–4 hours before the start of a long race, ingest 3–4g/kg; if only 1–2 hours before, choose 1–2g/kg [51].
- Pre-exercise meal composition (CTS/Rutberg): The macronutrient diversity should be greatest with the most digestion time. Four hours out: mixed meal with fat, protein, and carbohydrate (including fiber, complex and simple carbs). As the event approaches, reduce fat first, then protein, and in the final hour stick with low-fiber, mostly simple carbohydrates. Foods to avoid: greasy/fatty/fried foods; high-volume, low-calorie-density foods; sugar-free or diet foods (which may use sugar alcohols like Xylitol and Sorbitol that can cause gastric distress) [53].
- The night before a long run: current ISSN/ACSM guidelines recommend 7–12 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight in the 24 hours before long events (roughly 490–840 g for a 70 kg runner). For a dinner eaten 12–14 hours before a morning run, the plate should be 60–70% carbohydrate by calories, 15–20% protein, rest mostly fat. Jeukendrup's research identifies three culprits to limit the night before: very high fat, very high fiber, and very high protein. Simple carbohydrates (white bread, bagels, white rice, pasta, couscous, fruit, juice, honey, maple syrup, dairy, sports drinks, energy gels) are easier to digest than complex carbs and preferred the night before a long run [54].
- Avoid high-fiber foods on race day and several days leading up; identify and avoid food intolerances/sensitivities; avoid sugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol, xylitol); practice new nutrition strategies before race day [2].
- Common mistakes: (a) Eating too much or too late (gastric emptying takes 3–5 hours for a standard meal); (b) Trying new foods or supplements on race day — always train your nutrition; (c) Ignoring hydration and electrolytes pre-race (sodium is critical; excess water without sodium can cause hyponatremia) [50].
- Reactive hypoglycemia: Some athletes experience low blood sugar 30–45 minutes after eating carbs before exercise due to insulin spikes. Solutions include using more low-glycemic-index foods, eating carbs very close to the start, or eating them 90 minutes ahead. Stress and pre-race jitters can alter gastric emptying and gut motility, potentially causing GI distress; caffeine may exacerbate this [53].
- Pre-event fueling for under 60 min exercise: 1–4 g/kg 1–4 hours before; no food needed for exercise under 45 min; small carb amounts or mouth rinse for 45–75 min sessions [32].
- Dietary fiber reduction (15.2% of strategies), dairy avoidance (5.8%), and low FODMAP diet (5.4%) were the most popular dietary strategies reported by endurance athletes with Ex-GIS. The most successful dietary strategies (Likert scale 1-5) were: dietary fiber reduction (median=4), low FODMAP diet (median=4), dairy-free diet (median=4), and increasing carbohydrates (median=4). Significantly less dietary fiber (p=0.05) and fat (p=0.04) were consumed before/during/after exercise, and significantly more water (p=0.01) was consumed to reduce Ex-GIS [1].
- The 2025 case series (Scrivin, Slater, Costa) found that a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet before endurance exercise appears to be a valuable addition to therapeutic interventions used to mitigate exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet and improved intake tolerance during the targeted event, with reduced incidence and severity of Ex-GIS and improved perceived work output [4].
- A Current Opinion article on dietary FODMAP manipulation argues that FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default based on symptom severity [4].
- Runners don't need year-round low-FODMAP diets unless diagnosed with IBS; many implement a modified low-FODMAP approach for 6 days before important races. A three-phase approach (strict elimination for 2-6 weeks, systematic reintroduction, personalized plan) works best [52].

## 4. Carbohydrate Type and Concentration During Runs (Glucose vs Fructose, Osmolality, Maximal Absorption Rates)

**Absorption physiology:**
- Individual carbohydrates are absorbed at a rate of 1 g per minute, or a maximum of 60 g per hour, with glucose and fructose absorbed via separate transporter mechanisms. Simultaneous use of separate carbohydrate transporters can increase the intestine's absorptive capacity to 75–90 g per hour [11].
- Glucose and galactose are absorbed via the sodium-dependent SGLT1 transporter, while fructose uses GLUT5. All three monosaccharides exit via GLUT2. SGLT1 and GLUT5 are the most important transporters for carbohydrate absorption. At ingestion rates over 60–70 g of carbohydrate/hour, exogenous carbohydrate oxidation peaks at ~60 g/hour because SGLT1 becomes saturated [9][13].
- The limitation to exogenous carbohydrate oxidation was identified as saturation of intestinal carbohydrate transporters (specifically SGLT1 for glucose), not gastric emptying, liver glycogen synthesis, or muscle glucose uptake [41].
- Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates reach values of 1.75 g/min with multiple transportable carbohydrates whereas previously it was thought that 1 g/min was the absolute maximum [41].
- The Jentjens et al. (2004) groundbreaking study showed glucose:fructose oxidation peaked at ~1.26 g/min versus ~0.8 g/min for glucose alone. Maltodextrin:fructose mixes are more palatable (less sweet) and reached oxidation rates of 1.5 g/min at 1.8 g/min ingestion [41].
- A 2005 study by Jentjens and Jeukendrup (British Journal of Nutrition) in 8 trained male cyclists (mean VO2max 68.1 ± 0.6 ml/kg/min) found peak exogenous CHO oxidation rates were significantly higher (P<0.01) in glucose+fructose (1.75 ± 0.11 g/min) vs glucose alone (1.06 ± 0.05 g/min) when ingested at 2.4 g/min during 150 min cycling. Exogenous CHO oxidation rates during the last 90 min were ~50% higher (1.49 vs 0.99 g/min). In glucose-only, exogenous CHO oxidation leveled off after 105–120 min, whereas glucose+fructose increased until end of exercise [42][43].
- Glucose and fructose use different intestinal transporters (SGLT1 for glucose, GLUT-5 for fructose), allowing for increased total intestinal CHO absorption. Glucose may enhance fructose absorption via solvent drag (glucose-induced water streaming through paracellular pathway) [42].
- Combined ingestion of glucose (1.2 g/min) + fructose (1.2 g/min) may achieve the highest physiologically possible exogenous CHO oxidation rate (~1.75 g/min) [42].
- Peak exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates typically reach 1 g·min⁻¹ during exercise when ample glucose or glucose polymers are ingested [45].
- Co-ingestion of glucose and fructose can improve endurance performance by ~8–9% compared to glucose only. Fructose co-ingestion lowers gastrointestinal distress when large amounts of carbohydrate (>1.2 g/kg/h) are ingested. Fructose co-ingestion does NOT prevent muscle or liver glycogen depletion more than glucose alone during exercise; does NOT further increase muscle glycogen repletion rates compared to glucose alone; but significantly accelerates liver glycogen repletion — rates increase ~2-fold (from ~3.5 g/h with glucose alone to ~7.4 g/h with fructose co-ingestion). Fructose co-ingestion can increase endurance exercise capacity in a subsequent exercise bout by 3–5 minutes (cycling at 75% Wmax) or ~32.4% (treadmill running at 70% VO2max) [12].
- A study (Currell & Jeukendrup) found ingesting glucose at 1.2 g/min + fructose at 0.6 g/min (108 g/hr total) improved endurance cycling time-trial performance by 8% vs. glucose-only [11][41].
- Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation is independent of body mass, so recommendations should be given in absolute amounts, not per kg body weight [41].

**Recommended intakes and ratios:**
- For prolonged endurance events (2.5 h or longer), well-trained competitive athletes should consume 90 g of multiple transportable carbohydrates per hour. Use a mix of glucose and fructose, or maltodextrin and fructose, in roughly a 2:1 ratio (60 g/h glucose/maltodextrin to saturate SGLT1 transporters + 30 g/h fructose) [41][9][13].
- Current recommendations: 60 g carbohydrate/hour for exercise up to 120 minutes; up to 90 g/hour for exercise lasting longer than 2 hours, using a blend of glucose and fructose sources [11].
- A 2:1 glucose-to-fructose ratio is commonly used to formulate sports drinks, allowing comfortable consumption of 75–90 g carbohydrate/hour. Carbohydrate combinations producing greater oxidation than glucose alone include: maltodextrin + fructose, glucose + fructose, and glucose + sucrose + fructose [11].
- Well-trained athletes should ingest 90 g/h of glucose-fructose mixtures during prolonged (>2.5 h) moderate-to-high intensity exercise [12].
- Carb ratio guidelines from Race Smart: 70g/hr (1:0.16 glucose:fructose), 80g/hr (1:0.3), 90g/hr (2:1), 100g/hr (1:0.6), 110g/hr (1:0.8), all maintaining 60g glucose base. Exceeding 90g/hour generally offers no additional benefit and increases GI distress risk [7].
- Glucose:fructose ratios are dose-dependent: 1:0 for ≤60 g/h, 2:1 for 60–90 g/h, 1:0.8–1:1 for 90–120 g/h, and 1:1 for elite >120 g/h intakes [55].
- Combining glucose, fructose, and sucrose (different carrier systems) increases oxidation to 1.5–1.7 g/min, useful for extremely intense endurance exercise over 2.5 hours. Fructose intolerance must be excluded in advance [34].
- For exercise up to 2 hours, ~60 g/h of carbohydrate is recommended; for 2+ hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose:fructose or maltodextrin:fructose mixtures) [9][13].
- Dual-carb sources (glucose + fructose) allow greater absorption than glucose alone. A 2:1 glucose-to-fructose ratio was traditionally accepted, but newer research supports a 1:0.8 maltodextrin-to-fructose ratio for even greater absorption. Fructose co-ingestion also accelerates post-exercise liver glycogen repletion [10].
- During exercise, consume 150–350 ml of a ~6% carbohydrate drink every 15 minutes (DGE) [34]. For extended (>60 min) high-intensity (>70% VO2 max) bouts, consume ~30–60 g of carbohydrate/hour in a 6–8% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution every 10–15 min (ISSN) [16].
- The most recent comprehensive review (Wilson 2025 in Sports Medicine) states: "Existing research does not directly support performance-enhancing effects of ingesting carbohydrate at ≥ 100 g/h versus 60–90 g/h" [55].
- A 2020 trail running trial found 120 g/h reduced muscle damage markers and improved 24-hour neuromuscular recovery vs 60/90 g/h, but 2 of 9 runners abandoned due to GI problems [55]. The 120 g/h dose limited post-race exercise-induced muscle damage without GI distress in elite marathon/ultra-marathon runners with personalized gut training (up to 90 g/hr at least 2 days weekly for 4 weeks prior; Viribay et al., 2020) [11].
- Contemporary research (Podlogar, University of Exeter, 2026, Journal of Nutrition) suggests that the upper limit of CHO intake could increase from 90 to 120 g/h (at least for trained participants), considering that both exogenous and whole-body rates of CHO oxidation can be increased with these higher ingestion rates [56].
- A 2022 study (PMC9560939) found exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates were higher in the 120 g h⁻¹ condition (120–180 min: 1.51 g/min) as compared to the 90 g h⁻¹ condition [44].
- Adding protein to carbohydrate during exercise provides no performance benefit when carbohydrate intake is adequate [34].

**Osmolality and gastric emptying:**
- Beverages with multiple transportable carbohydrates (e.g., glucose and fructose combined) reduce GI symptoms [2].
- Choose lower carbohydrate concentration drinks to avoid high osmolalities [2].
- Gastric emptying is slowed by hypohydration, mental stress, intense exercise (above 70% VO2 max), and high solute loads (hyperosmolar beverages >500 mOsm/kg H2O, such as 10–15% carbohydrate drinks). Sports drinks at 6% concentration are isotonic and empty quickly. Liquid temperature has little effect on emptying [11].
- Fiber, fat, protein, and concentrated carbohydrate solutions (osmolalities >500 mOsm/L) delay gastric emptying [2][21].
- Larger fluid volumes empty from the stomach faster than smaller volumes; a study (Mears et al.) found 200 mL every 20 min produced 2% higher carbohydrate oxidation than 50 mL every 5 min, with no difference in GI comfort [11].
- Product format (drink, gel, chew, combination) does not change absorption at a given dose [55]. Solid versus liquid carbohydrate forms (gels, bars, drinks) produced similar oxidation rates when glucose and fructose were in 2:1 ratio [11].
- Avoid high-fructose foods and exclusively-fructose drinks (though fructose with glucose may be better tolerated) [21]. Avoid high-fructose foods; fructose-glucose combinations are better tolerated [2].
- Hydrogels (Maurten): independent evidence mostly null; benefit may surface only under severe GI stress at high concentrations [55].
- Runners consuming 60g of carbohydrates per hour finished marathons nearly 11 minutes faster than haphazardly-fueled runners [52].

## 5. Hydration Protocols and Electrolyte Replacement

**Hydration and GI distress:**
- Avoid dehydration; start races well hydrated. Prevent dehydration; ingest carbohydrates with sufficient water [21][2]. Dehydration impairs gut emptying and carb absorption [7].
- Hydration is critical; dehydration impairs gut emptying and carb absorption [7].
- Fluid restriction exacerbates permeability; cool/cold water is better than room temperature [23].

**ACSM fluid replacement guidance:**
- Athletes typically lose 500–2,000 ml (17–67 fl oz) of sweat per hour (roughly 1–4 pounds), and should avoid losing more than 2% of body weight during exercise [64].
- Sweat rates vary tremendously from one athlete to the next, and from one activity to the next (e.g., NFL football players typically lose over twice as much sweat as cross-country runners), so hydration plans must be individualized based on personal sweat rate [64].
- Athletes don't need to exactly match sweat rate but must stay within their 2% hydration zone — a 150-pound athlete losing 2 pounds/hour can stay in zone for 3 hours by consuming just half their sweat rate (~16 fl oz/hour) [64].
- Water is fine for activities under an hour at low-to-moderate intensity in mild conditions; for endurance events of one hour or longer or hot weather, a sport drink with carbs and electrolytes (sodium and chloride, the two electrolytes lost in greatest amounts through sweat) is generally better [64].
- For post-exercise rehydration, if more than 2% of body weight was lost and recovery is needed in under 12 hours, drink about 23 fl oz of fluid per pound of weight lost, consuming it gradually, and include sodium to help retain fluids and stimulate thirst [64].
- To assess hydration status, combine morning body weight measurements with first-morning urine color (light yellow, lemonade-colored urine; dark urine indicates incomplete rehydration). For pre-exercise hydration, consume fluids at least 4 hours before exercise [64].
- Dehydration (water deficit >2–3% body mass) decreases performance. After exercise, drink 16–24 oz (450–675 mL) fluid per pound (0.5 kg) body weight lost (2009 ADA/DC/ACSM position) [15].
- Sodium should be ingested during exercise when large sweat sodium losses occur. Sports drinks with sodium (0.5–0.7 g/L) and potassium (0.8–2.0 g/L) recommended for events >2 hours (2009 position) [15].
- The fluid plan that suits most athletes and athletic events will typically achieve an intake of 0.4 to 0.8 Liters per hour, although this needs to be customized to the athlete's tolerance and experience [66].
- ISSN 2019 position stand recommends that day-to-day hydration can, in most instances, be achieved by following a drink-to-thirst (ad libitum) strategy, but to inform post-training rehydration strategies, athletes should measure pre- to post-exercise body mass losses, and monitor their hydration status [66].
- The average "drink to thirst" (or ad libitum) fluid intake during a race is ~500 mL/h, in the ballpark of the most recent ACSM guideline of 0.4 to 0.8 L/hour [66].
- Athletes lose 0.3–2.4 L/hour of sweat. Recommended: 500–600 mL fluid 2–3 hours pre-exercise, 200–300 mL 10–20 min before, 200–300 mL every 10–20 min during training. Hyponatremia risk from overconsumption of sodium-poor fluids [39][40].
- Dehydration of just 2% of body weight significantly reduces aerobic capacity. Drink 5–7 ml water/hypotonic drink per kg in the 4 hours prior; urine should be pale yellow [50].
- Hydration guidance (Marathon Handbook): start exercise euhydrated (5–7 mL/kg fluid in 4 hours prior) with modest sodium (3–6 g). However, Almond's study of 488 Boston Marathon runners found hyponatremia was more common than dehydration, so "drink to thirst" is the safer default [54].
- Mid-race mechanics: 6–8% carbohydrate concentration, 500–1000 mL/h fluid, 300–800 mg/h sodium (up to 1500 for heavy sweaters), caffeine 3–6 mg/kg pre-race with maintenance doses [55].

**Programmed vs thirst-driven hydration (ultra-endurance):**
- A 2025 narrative review (Wierick et al., Nutrients) comparing programmed fluid intake (PFI) vs thirst-driven fluid intake (TDFI) in ultra-endurance running concluded that neither strategy is universally superior; a hybrid model integrating individual sweat testing, environmental context, and responsiveness to internal cues may offer the most practical and effective hydration approach [65][67].
- Sweat rates vary widely (0.4 to over 2.5 L per hour); body mass loss is not a reliable proxy for dehydration in UER, as it includes fuel oxidation, glycogen-associated water release (glycogen stores ~3–4g water per gram carbohydrate), and respiratory loss. Athletes can lose >2% body mass yet remain clinically euhydrated [65][67].
- Laboratory studies support PFI for preserving plasma volume, reducing cardiovascular strain, and improving performance (e.g., Jeker et al. showed PFI produced better power output, lower core temperature, and greater plasma volume preservation during 5 hours of cycling in heat) [65].
- Field studies demonstrate TDFI is safe and effective for many experienced athletes. In a study of 383 participants in a 161 km trail ultramarathon (Hoffman & Stuempfle), 67% relied on thirst, with no difference in finishing time or incidence of exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH) compared to those using structured plans. Top performers with body mass losses exceeding 4% reported no adverse outcomes [65].
- A blinded IV rehydration study (Wall et al.) showed up to 3% body mass loss had no effect on performance when participants were unaware of hydration status [65]. Goulet's meta-analysis found self-paced endurance performance is typically not impaired until dehydration exceeds 3–4% and only in rare cases [65].
- EAH is a documented risk when fluid intake exceeds sweat loss, particularly with programmed strategies or sodium supplementation with high fluid volumes [65].
- TDFI limitations include suppressed thirst perception under cold exposure, hypoxia, or aging; and may underperform in individuals with high sweat rates or impaired thirst perception [65].
- Sodium losses during exercise can cause hyponatremia independent of plasma sodium being "diluted" by drinking too much fluid. If adding sodium to during-race nutrition gives peace of mind, do it, but it is probably unnecessary unless sweating a huge volume of very salty sweat, in which case "high" sodium drinks, energy gels, and real foods can be useful [66].
- A 2024 meta-analysis confirmed pre-cooling significantly improves endurance performance in heat. External cooling (ice vests, cold packs) showed consistent significant improvements in time trial performance and time to exhaustion; internal cooling (ice slurry ingestion) showed no statistically significant improvement in time trial performance [28].

## 6. Gut-Training Adaptations (Repeated Carbohydrate Exposure Protocols)

**Concept and mechanisms:**
- "Training the gut" is a nutritional strategy to improve digestive tolerance during exercise, reducing risk of GI issues during prolonged physical activity [6]. The GI tract is critical for delivering carbohydrate and fluid during prolonged exercise and can be a major determinant of endurance performance [9][13].
- Gut training involves repeated exposure to progressive carb load during training and daily nutrition to boost gut tolerance, gastric emptying, the efficiency of intestinal carb transporters, and stomach comfort [7].
- Mechanisms of adaptation: increased intestinal transporters (especially SGLT1 for glucose absorption); improved gastric tolerance (reduced nausea, heaviness, discomfort); improved gastric emptying; better utilization of exogenous carbohydrates [6].
- The concept of "training the gut" was first proposed by Rehrer et al. in the 1990s; mechanisms involve SGLT1 transporter upregulation, gastric emptying improvements [57].
- A critical distinction: tolerance does not equal absorption. You may tolerate 90g/hour but only absorb 70g. There is NO evidence that gut training improves carbohydrate absorption — it only improves tolerance [5].
- Low-carbohydrate/keto diets may cause athletes to lose carbohydrate transporters, making absorption harder and leading to GI issues during exercise. Endurance athletes should avoid low-carb diets [5].

**Transporter regulation:**
- SGLT1 protein abundance and activity are regulated by dietary carbohydrate intake. A glucose sensor in the gut lumen detects glucose and initiates SGLT1 upregulation. Animal studies show rapid adaptation: mice showed 1.9-fold increases in SGLT1 after two weeks of high-carb diet; horses showed increases after just one week; piglets showed increases after three days. Increasing dietary carbohydrate from 40% to 70% could double SGLT1 transporters over two weeks [9][13][11].
- The sensing mechanism involves sweet taste receptors T1R2+T1R3 on enteroendocrine cells, coupled via alpha-gustducin, leading to secretion of GLP-1, GLP-2, and GIP, which ultimately increase SGLT1 protein via a cAMP-mediated pathway. Sweeteners (sucralose, acesulfame K, saccharine) also upregulate SGLT1, while aspartame does not [13].
- Gastric emptying and stomach comfort can be trained. Studies show nutrient-specific adaptations — increased dietary glucose accelerates gastric emptying of glucose but not protein; higher-fat diets accelerate emptying of fats but not carbohydrates. Effects can occur in as little as 3 days of dietary manipulation [13].
- Lambert et al. showed trained runners could comfortably tolerate carbohydrate-electrolyte solution at sweat-rate intake during 90 min running, with improved stomach comfort over time without measurable changes in gastric emptying rate [13][9].

**Key human studies:**
- The landmark Cox et al. (2010) study divided 16 endurance-trained cyclists into high-carbohydrate and control groups. Over 28 days of training (16 h/week), the high-carb group consumed 8.5 g/kg/day carbohydrate versus 5.3 g/kg/day in controls. Post-training, the high-carb group showed improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, most likely due to upregulated SGLT1 transporters [9][13][21].
- A study by Cox et al. (2010) showed that 28 days of high-carbohydrate training improved exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates, attributed to improved intestinal absorption [21].
- The Costa landmark gut-training study had 25 endurance runners complete 10 sessions over 14 days, running 2 hours at 60% VO2max while consuming 30g of carbohydrates every 20 minutes (90g/hour total). This produced 60–63% reductions in GI symptoms and 4.3–5.2% performance improvements [52].
- The 2023 systematic review by Martinez et al. (Sports Medicine) found: gut discomfort decreased by an average of 47% with a 2-week repetitive carbohydrate feeding protocol (n=2) and 26% through repeated fluid ingestion over five trials (n=1). Repetitive carbohydrate feeding during exercise for 2 weeks reduced carbohydrate malabsorption by 45–54% (n=2), but one study showed no significant change. Significant improvements in total, upper, and lower gastrointestinal symptoms were observed (n=2), with unclear results in 4 studies. No significant changes were found in gastric emptying rate (n=2) or markers of intestinal injury and permeability (I-FABP, claudin-3) (n=3). Inconclusive results in studies examining plasma inflammatory cytokine concentrations (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-1ra) (n=2). The review calls for future research using more sensitive tools (e.g., non-metabolizable sugar probes, modified visual analog scale) [8][57].
- Gut-training or feeding-challenge before and/or during exercise reduces gut discomfort, upper Ex-GIS, and carbohydrate malabsorption, but the effect on other gastrointestinal functional responses, gastrointestinal integrity, and systemic responses remains unclear and elusive [8].
- Interventions in the 8 included studies involved participants aged 15–35 years (79% male), mostly cyclists, runners, or triathletes; carbohydrates only (n=7) in various forms (gels, liquid solutions) during cycling or running, or carbohydrate with protein (n=1), over 4–28 days [8].

**Practical gut-training protocols:**
- Train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6–10 weeks [9][13].
- Gut training protocol: 6–10 weeks, start at 30 g/h, add ~10 g/h weekly during 1–2 long sessions per week, reaching 80–90 g/h by weeks 6–7 [55].
- Begin gut training 8–12+ weeks before a key race during base or build phase, with gradual progression of 10–15g/hour every 1–2 weeks. Practice at least 3 sessions per week, fueling within the first 15–20 minutes, mimicking race conditions [7].
- Gradually increase fuel amounts during exercise — start with 45g of carbs near end of session, build up to 90g/hour, then exceed this target for tolerance building. Consume large volumes of fluid during exercise (can speed gastric emptying). Exercise immediately after a meal (per Asker Jeukendrup) to increase tolerance [5].
- Example 6-week progression (Hydratis): Week 1–2: 30–40 g/h; Week 3–4: 45–60 g/h; Week 5: 60–75 g/h; Week 6: 75–90 g/h+ [6].
- Gut training for masters athletes: Start at 30-40g carbs/hour during sessions over 90 minutes using a glucose/fructose product; increase by 10-15g every 1-2 weeks as tolerated, aiming for at least 60g/hour; practice at least once a week during high-volume workouts; allow up to 10 weeks to fully adapt [37].
- Recommended protocol: consume 1.2g/kg bodyweight carbs per hour for the first 4 hours post-exercise (90g/hr for a 75kg athlete). Co-ingesting 0.2-0.4g/kg/hr protein with 0.8g/kg/hr carbs is an alternative. For recovery time ≥24 hours, ingesting 6-12g/kg carbohydrates is sufficient to restore glycogen reserves [10].
- Daily nutrition for gut training: 3-5g/kg body weight on low-volume days, >6g/kg on heavier days; choose low-fiber, low-fat foods around key sessions (rice, pasta, sourdough bread, oatmeal, potatoes, crackers, applesauce, bananas) [7].
- Daily diet: 5–7 g/kg/day of carbohydrates during moderate training, 7–10 g/kg/day during intensive periods. Prioritize fiber-rich and fermented foods for gut microbiota health [6].
- Results may appear in a few days but lasting adaptations take ~4–6 weeks; fruit purees, dates, bananas, potatoes, rice, or honey work without specific products; gut training cannot be done without carbohydrates [6].
- Signs of overdoing it include bloating, gas, cramping, diarrhea, feeling overly full, and sluggishness — these serve as indicators of current gut capacity and training overload stimulus [7].
- A 6-step progressive gut training guide is provided by Race Smart: starting with a baseline tolerable dose, increasing by 10-15g/hour every 7-14 days, with optional steps to push 10-20% beyond max tolerable dose (then reducing during taper), and steps 4-6 involving 2-3x weekly sessions [7].
- Athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days to maintain gut absorptive capacity [9][13].
- Studies show that regular intake of 60-90 g/hr of carbohydrate during training can increase tolerance to aggressive feedings (Patrick Wilson, author of The Athlete's Gut). Some of the adaptations probably relate to stomach emptying, while others involve upregulating the expression of transporters that shuttle sugar molecules into intestinal cells [10].

## 7. Training Intensity and Volume Modifications, Pacing, Running Economy, and Heat Acclimatization

**Intensity and duration effects:**
- Exercise stress of ≥2 hours at 60% VO2max is the threshold for significant GI perturbations [3].
- Gastric emptying is slowed by intense exercise (above 70% VO2 max) [11]. Exercise intensity and duration are risk factors for Ex-GIS [3].
- Small intestinal damage is not evident until 40 minutes of continuous exercise. High-intensity exercise (80% VO2max) significantly increased permeability, but light or moderate intensity (40-60% VO2max) did not. One hour after exercise, permeability was significantly elevated [23].
- Exercise intensity (+): continuous ≥70% VO2max or HIIT/resistance exercise ≤2h produces modest increases in EIGS biomarkers [30].
- Exercise modality (+): field studies suggest running prompts greater disturbance than swimming/cycling (due to mechanical strain), but controlled lab studies show no clear modality differences [30]. Runners experience GI issues at double the rate of cyclists or swimmers [52].
- Topographical elevation/altitude (+): altitude >2500m ASL may increase disturbances [30].
- Time of day (++): nocturnal exercise prompts greater GI function disturbance and Ex-GIS than diurnal exercise, but no effect on EIGS integrity/systemic biomarkers [30].
- Fitness status (+): higher-trained individuals at lower absolute risk but exposed to greater relative loads [30].

**Heat and environmental conditions:**
- Environmental conditions (+++): hot ambient conditions (~35°C) increase EIGS biomarkers and Ex-GIS; core body temperature ≥39.5°C or Δ≥2.5°C is clinically significant; ≥39.0°C or Δ≥2.0°C exceeds minimal detectable change [30].
- Heat stress, dehydration, and high exercise intensity/duration are risk factors for Ex-GIS [3].
- A systematic review (Wallett et al., IJSNEM 2021) found prolonged submaximal and strenuous exercise in hot environments can acutely increase epithelial disturbance compared with cooler conditions, though disturbances were not clinically relevant. Trained and well-trained populations appear to tolerate exercise-induced GI disturbance in the heat. Whether this tolerance is an acquired adaptation related to regular training remains to be investigated [25].
- The 2025 SDA/USSF position statement lists heat-mitigating strategies and certain nutritional supplements (prebiotics, phenols) as showing promising outcomes for EIGS/Ex-GIS management [30].

**Heat acclimatization:**
- Heat acclimation is the process by which the body adapts to the stress of a hot environment, producing several benefits including increased sweat rate, lower core temperature, reduced heart rate, improved blood flow, and better electrolyte balance. Heat acclimation typically takes 10-14 days. Recommended strategies include gradual exposure to heat starting with shorter, less intense workouts during cooler parts of the day; consistent training in the heat; proper hydration with water and electrolyte beverages; wearing light, breathable, moisture-wicking clothing; listening to body signals (dizziness, fatigue, nausea as warning signs); proper cool-down techniques; and using training aids like saunas or hot baths to simulate heat when outdoor temperatures are cool [26].
- Heat acclimation is a broad term defined as a complex series of changes or adaptations that occur in response to heat stress in a controlled environment over the course of 7 to 14 days; heat acclimatization is the same process in a natural environment. Positive adaptations include reductions in heart rate, internal body temperature, skin temperature responses, sweat electrolyte concentrations, and perceived exertion, along with increases in sweat rate, earlier sweat onset, blood flow, and exercise performance. Adaptations differ between hot/dry vs. hot/humid environments (greater sweat rate increase in humid conditions) [27].
- Heat acclimatization: Medium-sized improvements in time trial performance shown in RCTs. Cardiovascular adaptations (lower heart rate, improved cardiac efficiency) emerge within ~1 week; thermoregulatory adaptations take ~2 weeks. Plasma volume expansion is one adaptation. A 3-4 day heat camp provides some cardiovascular benefit but not full thermoregulatory adaptation [28].
- Heat slows runners: recreational runners slow 3-13% in hot conditions vs. cool ones; elite runners slow 2-5%. Hotter conditions and slower runners incur greater penalties. Humidity compounds heat stress because it limits evaporative cooling (sweating). Dehydration is a multiplier on cardiovascular drift (reduces plasma volume), but the cardiovascular conflict exists even without dehydration [28].
- Pacing: Adjusting pace to physiological signals (heart rate, perceived effort) rather than target pace is an accurate response to physiology, not a failure of fitness or will. Holding marathon pace at 25°C is not the same physiological effort as at 12°C [28].
- For masters athletes exercising in heat: blood shifts to skin for cooling and gastric emptying slows. Masters athletes face reduced cardiovascular cooling and decreased sweating efficiency. Recommendations: drop carb intake by 10-20g/hour until heat-acclimated, choose liquid calories, eat small amounts every 10-15 minutes, start hydrated and cool, don't rely on thirst, include sodium in everything you drink, monitor urine color, and watch for hyponatremia [37].
- Heat-mitigating strategies show promising outcomes for EIGS/Ex-GIS management [30].

**Running economy and training status:**
- The 2025 SDA/USSF position statement notes that individual characteristics (+++) — feeding tolerance (volume, concentration, type, texture), pre-existing GI diseases/disorders, and history of recurrent Ex-GIS — increase risk [30].
- The study's exacerbation factors with assigned impact magnitudes: Exercise duration (+++): considerable perturbations occur with ≥2h exercise; plateaus thereafter. Exercise intensity (++); Exercise modality (+); Environmental conditions (+++); Topographical elevation/altitude (+); Time of day (++); External pharmaceutical administration (+++): NSAIDs are GI irritants; administration prior to exercise markedly increases GI perturbations and Ex-GIS. Biological sex (+): low-to-modest differences; female athletes proposed to present greater EIGS/Ex-GIS due to menstrual cycle, but evidence is inconsistent. Age (+): modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults. Fitness status (+); GI/circulating microbial and SCFA composition (+); Psychological state (?): pre-exercise anxiety linked to Ex-GIS in field observations but lacks rigorous controlled evidence [30].

## 8. Avoidance of NSAIDs and Other Medications

- NSAIDs are associated with mucosal bleeding, perforation, increased GI permeability, and gut barrier dysfunction [2]. Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen [2].
- Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) as they increase intestinal permeability; NSAID use is associated with a 3-5 fold increased risk of upper GI complications [21][52].
- NSAIDs work by blocking the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme, which reduces inflammation but also suppresses cytoprotective prostaglandins that maintain the intestinal barrier. Because NSAIDs block COX enzymes, they reduce not only inflammatory prostaglandins, but also these protective gut prostaglandins. A weakened gut barrier may allow bacterial compounds called endotoxins to pass from the intestines into the bloodstream — a process known as endotoxemia. Heavy exercise already stresses the gut barrier through reduced blood flow to the digestive tract, increased body temperature, and physical stress, so combining it with regular NSAID use may further increase permeability and GI symptoms such as cramping, bloating, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort. Occasional NSAID use for acute injuries or illness may absolutely be appropriate and beneficial; routinely using NSAIDs like a 'preventative supplement' for training soreness may not be ideal for long-term gut health [20].
- NSAIDs like ibuprofen dramatically exacerbate exercise-induced gut permeability and do not improve muscle recovery [23].
- Ibuprofen use increases GI complication risk by 3-5 times [52].
- External pharmaceutical administration (+++): NSAIDs are GI irritants; administration prior to exercise markedly increases GI perturbations and Ex-GIS [30].
- Historical example: Paula Radcliffe's failure to finish the 2004 Athens marathon (Tamb 35°C) due to abdominal cramping and bloating with prior NSAID use [61].

**Prevalence of NSAID use in runners:**
- A study surveying 806 Parkrun UK participants found: nearly 90% of surveyed runners used NSAIDs (usually over-the-counter ibuprofen); about one in eight had a pre-existing reason to avoid NSAIDs (such as asthma); over half took NSAIDs before a run, one in ten during a run, and two-thirds afterwards; 33% of ultra-runners took NSAIDs during runs (compared to 17.5% of marathon runners); a third experienced suspected side effects (mainly heartburn, and in some cases gastrointestinal bleeding); over 40% were unaware of cardiovascular, kidney, or gastrointestinal side effects. Nearly half used NSAIDs without healthcare professional advice. NSAID-related adverse reactions are responsible for 30% of all adverse drug reaction hospital admissions. The London Marathon now advises runners to avoid NSAIDs within 48 hours of the race because of the potential dangers [47].
- The Birmingham/Queen Mary study (2020) of 806 Parkrun UK participants (mean age 48, 48% women) found 88% had used NSAIDs in the past 12 months, with just under 80% using ibuprofen; 70% reported a sporting injury within the last 12 months; NSAID use before, during, and after running: 57% before a run/race, 11% during, and 67.7% afterwards; one-third experienced a suspected adverse reaction, including gastrointestinal discomfort, heartburn, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal bleeding [48].
- A 2024 scoping review (Pannone & Abbott, BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine) on NSAID health risks in marathon and ultraendurance running (30 studies: 4 RCTs, 1 cross-sectional, 11 retrospective reviews, 4 case reports, 1 non-randomised control trial, 9 prospective observational studies) found: (1) Electrolyte balance/hyponatraemia (14 studies): mixed results; one UK study found marathon runners taking ibuprofen had serum Na decrease of 2.1 mmol/L vs increase of 2.3 mmol/L in controls (p=0.0039); (2) Acute kidney injury (6 studies): all reported potential links but insufficient evidence for statistical significance; one double-blind RCT found 22 of 42 participants taking ibuprofen developed AKI vs 16 of 47 on placebo (18% difference, p=0.14); (3) GI disturbances (4 studies): none found clear correlation between NSAID use and GI issues; (4) Oxidative stress and muscle damage (3 studies): conflicting results. The review concluded there is very limited evidence to show NSAIDs have a negative impact on the health of ultrarunning athletes; indications from a few non-randomised studies of a possible effect on kidney function need exploring with higher-quality research. The Ultra Tour de Mont Blanc banned ibuprofen due to 'negative health risks' despite limited research [46].
- NSAIDs are the second leading cause of stomach ulcers (after bacterial infection). Risk varies by NSAID: Naproxen carries ~5.6x baseline bleeding risk; Diclofenac ~4.0x; Ibuprofen ~2.7x; COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) ~1.9x. Higher-risk groups include age 65+, prior stomach ulcers, blood thinners/aspirin, corticosteroids/SSRIs, H. pylori infection, high doses or long-term use [49].
- Other medications used by athletes to manage Ex-GIS: In the Scrivin 2022 study, 13 athletes (9%) used medications (e.g., Omeprazole, Buscopan, Gaviscon) to manage Ex-GIS [1]. Arginine was rated most successful supplement (median=5, n=1), followed by probiotics (median=4, n=26) and prebiotics (median=4, n=7) [1].

## 9. Masters-Specific Considerations for Runners Over Age 40

**Age-related physiological changes relevant to GI distress and hydration:**
- From the CRC Press book "Nutrition and Performance in Masters Athletes" (Reaburn, 2015, Chapter 1 by Jenkins, Skinner and Bolam):
  - Sarcopenia: Muscle mass declines ~0.5%-1% per year after age 40, heightened in the sixth decade; men and women aged 40-80 lose 30%-50% of skeletal muscle mass, accompanied by 1%-1.5% per year reduction in strength and power. Type II muscle fibers are predominantly affected [36].
  - Endurance training: Masters athletes maintain higher VO2max than sedentary peers but experience ~10% decline per decade from age 25. High-intensity training may delay VO2max declines. Masters athletes retain capacity to store and use glycogen [36].
  - Taste and smell changes: Age-related decline in taste (more pronounced in men) can lead to suboptimal food choices and inadequate carbohydrate/fluid intake. Dry mouth affects ~50% of older adults. Medication use can worsen taste impairment [36].
  - Gastrointestinal changes: Reduced gastric acid (atrophic gastritis), impaired motility, delayed gastric emptying, and reduced absorption of micronutrients (iron, folate, calcium, vitamin K, vitamin B12) can compromise nutrition [36].
  - Water balance: Total body water declines with age (43% for women, 51% for men aged 61-74). Reduced thirst perception, diminished baroreceptor sensitivity, reduced kidney concentrating ability, and increased insensible water loss put masters athletes at higher dehydration risk. One study found older men replaced only 34% of lost fluid vs. 80% in young men after exercise. Dehydration >4% of body mass impairs endurance performance [36].
- Maximum oxygen consumption decreases ~10% per decade after age 30 (slower at 5% for older endurance athletes) [38].
- The 2025 SDA/USSF position statement notes Age (+) is an intrinsic factor with "modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults" [30].
- The Ribichini 2023 review lists "younger age" as a risk factor for Ex-GIS (i.e., younger athletes may be at higher risk, but age-related differences are modest) [3].
- Both aging-associated chronic conditions and the natural aging process can result in reduced kidney function, which can affect fluid balance and electrolyte needs and increase recovery time. Certain blood pressure medications and diets lower in sodium and potassium may require adjustments to recommended fluid and electrolyte intake under different environmental and training conditions (U.S. Masters Swimming) [63].
- A 2025 hydration review notes TDFI (thirst-driven fluid intake) limitations include suppressed thirst perception under cold exposure, hypoxia, or aging [65].

**Carbohydrate absorption in masters athletes:**
- The small intestine's ability to absorb carbohydrates stays largely intact with age. The SGLT1 transporter (glucose) and GLUT5 transporter (fructose) remain functional in healthy older adults. The main concern is decline in GLUT4 (which moves glucose from blood into muscle cells), potentially leading to insulin resistance. Regular endurance exercise helps maintain/restore GLUT4 levels. Masters athletes can target 60-90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours using glucose-fructose blends; age isn't the limiting factor — gut training is [37].
- "Aging doesn't have to mean slowing down — but it does mean paying closer attention to your gut." "Masters athletes can and should target 60–90g of carbohydrates per hour in events over 2 hours, using glucose-fructose blends. Age alone isn't the limiting factor, gut training is." "Your gut is trainable at any age. With smart, progressive fueling, consistent practice, and heat-specific adjustments, masters athletes can perform strongly well into their later years. Age is context, not a ceiling" [37].
- Masters athletes are defined as age 35 for both men and women per World Masters Athletics; age 18 for swimming, and 50 for golf [38].

**Nutrition recommendations for masters athletes:**
- Protein: 1.2g/kg body weight/day; 35-45g per meal (vs. 15-30g for younger athletes); pre-workout meal should include 25-30g protein with high leucine foods; 3g leucine per meal recommended [38].
- Creatine: 5g/day creatine monohydrate for those who strength train [38].
- Carbohydrates: 3-5 g/kg/day minimum; up to 10-12g/kg for athletes training 1-3 hours/day or endurance events over 90 minutes [38].
- Fluids: Personalized hydration schedule is critical due to age-related dehydration challenges [38].
- Vitamin D: 1,500-2,000 IUs/day to raise levels above 30 ng/mL; minimum 800 IUs/day. Calcium: 1200 mg/day for women over 51 and men over 71 (vs. 1000 mg for ages 19-50). Magnesium: 320 mg/day women and 420 mg/day men (31+ years). Zinc: 11 mg males and 8 mg females (19+) [38].
- Older adults, especially women frustrated with body changes, should NOT undereat and overexercise — this causes the body to hold onto fat (starvation mode) and negatively affects hormones including cortisol [38].
- Reduced B12 and Vitamin D absorption occur with aging; chronic low-level inflammation, dehydration, and reduced sweating are age-related changes [38].

**Masters-specific gaps in the literature:**
- The Martinez et al. 2023 systematic review included studies of participants aged 12-60 years, with included studies involving participants aged 15-35 years (79% male) — indicating a lack of masters-specific (40+) data in gut-training trials [8][57].
- The NSAID scoping review noted studies "predominantly from the USA (N=15) and England (N=7); more men than women included" [46].
- Most carbohydrate recommendations are based on male endurance athletes; sex differences exist in carbohydrate metabolism (ISSN nutrient timing position) [16].
- The 2025 hydration review calls for research on "sex-based, age, and experience differences" in hydration strategies [65][67].
- The SDA/USSF position statement's scoping review noted methodological concerns in existing research including participant selection/screening, exercise protocol justification, ambient temperature control, dietary control, hydration monitoring, biomarker selection, Ex-GIS assessment tool choice, power calculations, and population heterogeneity [30].
- The SDA/USSF position notes "Age (+): modest differences between youth athletes, older adults, and younger adults" — but the evidence base is limited, and specific Ex-GIS prevention trials in masters runners over 40 are lacking [30].

## 10. Landscape of Official Clinical Practice Guidelines and Consensus Statements

**Recent authoritative consensus/position statements:**
1. **Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) and Ultra Sports Science Foundation (USSF) Joint Position Statement (2025)** — "A Practitioner Guide to the Prevention and Management of Exercise-Associated Gastrointestinal Perturbations and Symptoms," published in Sports Medicine (April 7, 2025; Vol 55, Issue 5, Article 1097; DOI: 10.1007/s40279-025-02186-6). Authors: Costa, Gaskell, Henningsen (Monash); Jeacocke and Wallett (Australian Institute of Sport); Scheer (USSF); Scrivin; Snipe (Deakin); Young (Monash). Key points: individual athlete assessment to establish main causal factors aids tailored prevention/management; macronutrient intake during exercise, maintenance of euhydration, dietary manipulations (e.g., FODMAP), and gut training show beneficial outcomes; heat-mitigating strategies and certain nutritional supplements (prebiotics, phenols) show promising outcomes; NSAIDs markedly increase GI perturbations. Evidence graded (Grade I = Good through Grade IV = Not fully supported) [30][31].
2. **Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM Position: "Nutrition and Athletic Performance" (2016)** — Thomas, Erdman, Burke; J Acad Nutr Diet 116(3):501-528. Position: well-chosen nutrition strategies enhance athletic performance and recovery. Provides guidelines for type, amount, and timing of food, fluids, and supplements. Developed using the Academy's Evidence Analysis Library; in effect until December 31, 2019 [14][32].
3. **2009 ADA/DC/ACSM position stand** — "Nutrition and Athletic Performance" (Rodriguez et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc). Recommends 6-10 g/kg body weight/day carbohydrate; 1.2-1.7 g/kg protein; 20-35% fat; dehydration >2-3% body mass decreases performance; 30-60 g carbohydrate/hour during endurance events >1 hour; post-exercise 1.0-1.5 g/kg carbohydrate within first 30 min and every 2 hours for 4-6 hours [15][33].
4. **ISSN Position Stand: Nutrient Timing (2017)** — Kerksick et al., JISSN 14:33. Key points: 8-12 g/kg/day maximizes endogenous glycogen stores; for extended (>60 min) high-intensity (>70% VO2max) bouts, consume ~30-60 g of carbohydrate/hour in a 6-8% carbohydrate-electrolyte solution every 10-15 min; rapid glycogen restoration (<4h recovery) requires 1.2 g/kg/h with high GI (>70) sources, caffeine (3-8 mg/kg), and/or combining carbohydrates (0.8 g/kg/h) with protein (0.2-0.4 g/kg/h). Notes most carbohydrate recommendations are based on male endurance athletes [16].
5. **German Nutrition Society (DGE) Position on Carbohydrates in Sports Nutrition (2020)** — König et al., German Journal of Sports Medicine. Recommends 6-12 g carbohydrate/kg BW/d for prolonged endurance exercise; carbohydrate loading 10-12 g/kg BW/d for 36-48 hours prior; pre-competition 1-4 g/kg BW 2-3 hours before; during exercise 150-350 ml of ~6% carbohydrate drink every 15 minutes; combining glucose, fructose, and sucrose increases oxidation to 1.5-1.7 g/min; post-exercise 1-1.2 g carbohydrate/kg BW/h in first 2-4 hours [34].
6. **ACSM Position Stands process** — Developed using ACSM's approved Evidence-based Protocol (PICOT questions, systematic literature reviews, risk-of-bias evaluation, grading of evidence strength). Published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. Serve four purposes: answer specific scientific/clinical questions; provide overall summary of literature and evidence strength; provide evidence-based recommendations; identify knowledge gaps [17].
7. **ACSM "Ten Things You Need to Know About Sports Nutrition"** — by Dr. Dan Benardot: includes poor hydration → poor performance; recovery from exercise is just as important as the exercise; RED-S can be a problem; fresh foods help the microbiome [35].
8. **GSSI Pre-Conference Session "The Physiology of Hydration: More Than Water Alone"** — covers how carbohydrate, sodium, flavor, and fluid interact to influence intake, absorption, retention, and performance, including individualized hydration strategies, sweat profiling, and mitigating performance decrements associated with >2% body-mass loss [17][35].

**GSSI Sports Science Exchange articles (industry-supported but peer-reviewed):**
- SSE #178 "Training the Gut for Athletes" (Jeukendrup, 2018): practical recommendations — train with high carbohydrate intake at least once a week, expecting improved tolerance within 6-10 weeks; practice race nutritional strategies in training; ~60 g/h for exercise up to 2 hours, up to 90 g/h using multiple transportable carbohydrates for 2+ hours; athletes on low-carb/ketogenic diets should include high-carbohydrate training days [9].
- SSE #114 "Nutritional Recommendations To Avoid Gastrointestinal Distress During Exercise" (de Oliveira, 2013): avoid milk products containing lactose; avoid high-fiber foods in the day(s) before competition (choose processed white foods); avoid aspirin and NSAIDs; avoid high-fructose foods; avoid dehydration; practice new nutrition strategies; "train the gut" [21].
- SSE #108 "Multiple Transportable Carbohydrates And Their Benefits" (Jeukendrup, 2013): 90 g/h for prolonged events (2.5h+); 2:1 glucose/maltodextrin to fructose ratio; peak oxidation 1.75 g/min; multiple transportable carbohydrates improve gastric emptying and fluid delivery and reduce GI distress [41].

**ACSM 2026 resistance training position stand (context):** The ACSM published a landmark new Position Stand on resistance training (first major update since 2009), synthesizing findings from 137 systematic reviews representing more than 30,000 participants. The message: consistency beats complexity; training all major muscle groups at least twice a week matters most [18].

## 11. Carbohydrate Knowledge and Practices Among Athletes

- A 2023 study (Scrivin et al., Frontiers in Nutrition) of 201 endurance athletes (137 with Ex-GIS, 64 without) found athletes with Ex-GIS correctly categorized CHO foods (95%) and non-CHO foods (88%) at rates similar to athletes without Ex-GIS (92% and 90% respectively). No significant differences were found in CHO beliefs or intentions between groups. The most commonly self-reported dietary strategy was increasing CHO intake (58% of responses). The authors note that gut training protocols may help athletes improve gastrointestinal tolerance when consuming CHO during exercise [29].
- A 2022 survey (Reinhard & Galloway, Frontiers in Nutrition) of 1,081 endurance athletes (58.0% male, 68.6% aged 18-39; triathletes 50.6%, cyclists 25.1%, runners 24.1%) found: 67.4% used a combination of commercial sport nutrition products and everyday foods; 67.6% of participants guided CHO intake rates by gut feeling; only 21.6% used grams of CHO/hour calculations. Sports drinks were the most frequently consumed CHO source at all exercise intensities; 95.1% consumed CHO during training at all exercise intensities [58].

## 12. Additional Evidence on Management Strategies

- 67% (n=92) of athletes in the Scrivin 2022 exploratory study used dietary or non-dietary strategies to manage Ex-GIS, reporting 277 strategies (average 3.0 ± 1.6 per athlete). Of these, 77% used only dietary strategies, 17% used both dietary and non-dietary, and 5% used only non-dietary methods. Accredited practicing dietitians (APDs) were rated the most important source of information for Ex-GIS management (n=29) [1].
- The study recommends that dietary strategies (e.g., low FODMAP, dairy avoidance) should be trialed during training to establish individual tolerance before implementation during competition [1].
- The 2025 case series (Scrivin, Slater, Costa, IJSNEM 34(4):337-354) implemented a four-phase management approach using gastrointestinal assessment during exercise (GastroAxEx): (1) clinical assessment, (2) standardized laboratory GastroAxEx, (3) individualized therapeutic intervention including a 48-hour high-carbohydrate low-FODMAP diet, and (4) monitoring and adjustment. Most athletes (6/9) consumed <400 ml/hr of fluid ad libitum (resulting in 2-4% body mass loss) and <40 g/hr of exogenous carbohydrate (8/9) during the GastroAxEx. Severe Ex-GIS (predominantly loose stools) was reported by 4/9 athletes during exercise and 8/9 in the recovery period. Most athletes (8/9) successfully implemented the diet and improved intake tolerance with reduced Ex-GIS [4].
- Emergency management for nausea: slow pace, sip fluids, try small amounts of cola, walk, stand tall, breathe deeply. For cramping/urgency, walking reduces gut motility. Warning signs requiring stopping: bloody stool (possible ischemic colitis), profuse bleeding, severe pain, or faintness. Avoid prophylactic Imodium — it slows the entire digestive tract and can worsen symptoms; reserve for post-race or under medical guidance [52].
- The feed article summarizes the 2016 AND/DC/ACSM position's carbohydrate intake guidelines: Daily needs — light activity 3-5 g/kg/day, moderate 5-7 g/kg/day, high activity/endurance 6-10 g/kg/day, extreme (Tour de France) 8-12 g/kg/day. Acute fueling — events under 90 min (7-12 g/kg in 24 hours prior); events over 90 min (10-12 g/kg daily for 36-48 hours prior); recovery between demanding sessions (1-1.2 g/kg per hour for first 4 hours); 30-60 g carbs per hour for 1-2.5 hour sessions; up to 90 g carbs per hour for sessions exceeding 2.5-3 hours [32].
- The narrative review by Amawi et al. (2024) provides comprehensive ranges: carbohydrates 3-12 g/kg daily depending on intensity (low <60 min: 3-5 g/kg; moderate 60 min: 5-7 g/kg; high 60-180 min: 6-10 g/kg; very high >180 min: 8-12 g/kg); post-exercise 1.0-1.5 g/kg/hour at 30-minute intervals for up to 6 hours (delaying by 2 hours reduces glycogen resynthesis by 45%); protein 1.4-2.0 g/kg for muscle preservation, 1.2-2.0 g/kg for endurance, 1.6-2.8 g/kg for strength; fat 20-35% of calories with saturated fat <10%; hydration: losing 2% of body fluids affects performance; 500-600 mL fluid 2-3 hours pre-exercise, 200-300 mL 10-20 min before, 200-300 mL every 10-20 min during training. Only creatine, sodium bicarbonate, and caffeine have proven performance-enhancing effects [39][40].
- Caffeine: 3-6 mg/kg 30-60 minutes before is the most scientifically backed ergogenic aid [50].
- The Modern Carbohydrate Playbook (IAMCOACH 2026) notes: the pro-level 120 g/h fueling revolution is real (Casper Stornes' 2:29:25 marathon at the 2025 IRONMAN World Championship, fueling at ~180 g/h on bike and 130 g/h on run), but for most age-group athletes, the performance edge over a well-executed 60–90 g/h plan is small, inconsistent, and requires months of gut training. "The pros are not wrong about 120 g/h — they are just answering a different question than most readers of this post are asking." Burke's "Supernova" trials: high-carb group improved 10,000 m time by 4.8% (134 s), while LCHF/ketogenic group got 2.3% slower (−86 s). Ketogenic diets impair competitive endurance performance [55].
- A practitioner's guide to managing gut issues in athletes is among the citing publications of the 2025 case series [4].

## 13. Gaps in the Current Literature Warranting Further Research

1. **Gut-training mechanisms and guidelines:** No clear guidelines yet exist on how to implement gut-training strategies. Future research requires more sensitive tools (non-metabolizable sugar probes, modified visual analog scale) to elucidate underlying mechanisms [8][57]. The effect of gut-training on gastrointestinal functional responses, integrity, and systemic responses remains unclear [8].
2. **Masters-specific data:** The systematic review on gut-training included studies of participants aged 15–35 years (79% male), with eligibility up to age 60 — but included studies did not provide masters-specific (40+) subgroup analyses. Specific Ex-GIS prevention trials in masters runners are lacking [8][57][30].
3. **Age-related hydration research:** The 2025 ultra-endurance hydration review explicitly calls for investigation of "sex-based, age, and experience differences" in hydration strategies [65][67]. TDFI limitations under aging-related thirst suppression warrant research [65].
4. **NSAID research quality:** The scoping review on NSAIDs in marathon/ultraendurance running concluded there is "very limited evidence" showing negative impact, and called for larger randomized controlled trials, examination of different NSAID types/dosages, and consideration of confounding factors like heat, hydration, and body weight [46].
5. **FODMAP approaches:** Further research is needed to determine whether low-FODMAP strategies are best applied acutely before exercise or integrated into habitual diets [1]. A Current Opinion article argues FODMAP manipulation should be used strategically rather than as a routine dietary default [4].
6. **Higher carbohydrate intakes (>90 g/h):** Whether 120 g/h improves performance over 90 g/h requires more research; existing research "does not directly support performance-enhancing effects of ingesting carbohydrate at ≥ 100 g/h versus 60–90 g/h" [55].
7. **Heat tolerance adaptation:** Whether trained athletes' tolerance to exercise-induced GI disturbance in the heat is an acquired adaptation related to regular training "remains to be investigated" [25].
8. **The SDA/USSF position statement** noted methodological concerns in existing research including participant selection/screening, exercise protocol justification, ambient temperature control, dietary control, hydration monitoring, biomarker selection, Ex-GIS assessment tool choice, power calculations, and population heterogeneity [30].
9. **Female athletes:** The HIIT GI study had no female participants (despite GI symptoms being more prevalent in female athletes); biological sex evidence on EIGS/Ex-GIS is inconsistent [22][30].

<Task>

When you are completely satisfied with the research findings returned from the tool calls, then you should call the "ResearchComplete" tool to indicate that you are done with your research.
</Task>

<Available Tools>
You have access to three main tools:

2. **ResearchComplete**: Indicate that research is complete

**CRITICAL: Use think_tool before calling ConductResearch to plan your approach, and after each ConductResearch to assess progress. Do not call think_tool with any other tools in parallel.**
</Available Tools>

</Instructions>

- **Stop when you can answer confidently** - Don't keep delegating research for perfection
- **Limit tool calls** - Always stop after 3 tool calls to ConductResearch and think_tool if you cannot find the right sources

**Maximum 3 parallel agents per iteration**
</Hard Limits>

<Show Your Thinking>

</Show Your Thinking>

<Scaling Rules>
